sections.title: Where you are

say.text: Round one. Does the consonant wake up, and where does it land.

questions.q: When does a silent final consonant come back?
questions.why: The condition is next door, not inside the word. les is /le/ before a consonant and /le.z‿/ before a vowel.
opts: when the next word starts with a vowel sound

questions.q: In « les amis », the Z sound belongs to:
questions.why: The consonant moves forward into the next word. Saying LAYZ amee keeps an English join and is what makes French sound like one long word to you.

questions.q: Which of these takes a liaison?
questions.why: Only amis begins with a vowel. The other three start with consonants, so the S of les stays asleep.

questions.q: Tap the letter that wakes up.
questions.why: The S of les, silent on its own, comes back as a /z/ on the front of amis.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: ils‿ont has a /z/ join and means they have. ils sont has no liaison and means they are. The link is the only difference.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: vous‿avez links a /z/ onto avez. vous savez has its own S at the start of savez. Same sound, different word boundary.

questions.q: Type how « nous avons » sounds.
questions.why: A subject pronoun always links to its verb. The S of nous returns as a /z/ on the front of avons.

questions.q: Say it: « Nous avons deux enfants. »
questions.why: Two liaisons, both /z/. The X of deux behaves exactly like an S.

say.text: Round two. You have decided to link. Now get the sound right.

rounds.label: The sound it comes back as

questions.q: A final S or X wakes up as:
questions.why: Both soften to /z/. This is why the corpus is full of Z liaisons and why less amis is the most audible learner error here.

questions.q: A final D wakes up as:
questions.why: grand‿arbre is grahⁿ-T-arbr. No French liaison brings a D back as a D.

questions.q: Which of these letters comes back as ITSELF?
questions.why: T, N and L return unchanged. S, X, D and F all change on the way up, so spelling tells you that a sound appears, not which.

questions.q: In « neuf heures », the F is said as:
questions.why: The one common F liaison in the language, and it goes to /v/. neu-v‿EUR.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Written with a D, said with a T. If these sound identical to you, play it at 0.65 and listen to the release.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: The /z/ is voiced and soft. An /s/ here is the single most common mistake an English reader makes in this lesson.

questions.q: A learner says [grahⁿ-D-ARBR] for « grand arbre ». Fix it.
questions.why: They linked correctly and used the written letter. A final D always surfaces as a T.

questions.q: Say it: « Elle a un petit ami. »
questions.why: petit ends on a vowel alone. Before a vowel its T wakes and lands on the front of ami.

say.text: Round three. The half that trips everyone, because by now linking is your reflex.

questions.q: How often does « et » take a liaison?
questions.why: Never, in any register, in any sentence. It is the one absolute rule in this lesson and the most tempting gap in the language.

questions.q: Why does « les héros » not link?
questions.why: H aspiré makes no sound but blocks both liaison and elision. Compare les‿hommes, where the h muet lets the link straight through.
opts: the H is aspiré and blocks it

questions.q: In « un enfant intelligent », how many liaisons do you make?
questions.why: un‿enfant links because a determiner links to its noun. enfant intelligent does not, because a singular noun never links to the adjective after it.

questions.q: Can you tell from the spelling whether an H blocks the link?
questions.why: Nothing on the page distinguishes them, and no rule derives it. You learn h aspiré words the way you learn a noun with its gender.
opts: yes, aspiré words are written with a different H
yes, if the word is short
no, you learn it word by word

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: The blocked version is the correct one. If your device links this, the recording has not been delivered yet and the fallback voice is teaching you the error.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: et keeps its gap. Compare quand‿il, which is spelled with a D and links with a /t/.

questions.q: A learner says [ay-T-EEL] for « et il ». Fix it.
questions.why: The T of et is there on the page and it never wakes. Leave the gap open.

questions.q: A learner links « un restaurant italien ». Fix it.
questions.why: A singular noun does not link to the adjective following it, however inviting that final T looks.

say.text: Round four. Real sentences, where the three states sit two words apart.

questions.q: In « Les enfants et les adultes attendent », how many liaisons are made?
questions.why: les‿enfants and les‿adultes both link. The et between them does not, and adultes attendent does not either: a plural noun does not link to its verb.

questions.q: In « Paris est une belle ville », where is the liaison?
questions.why: A proper noun does not link to what follows, so Paris est stays open. est‿une links normally.

questions.q: Which pair links?
questions.why: Short prepositions like chez, en and dans always link. selon does not, et never does, and onze behaves like an h aspiré word.

questions.q: An adjective links to its noun when it sits:
questions.why: petit‿ami links. enfant | intelligent does not. Word order decides it, not the letters involved.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Same article, same silent N, opposite results. homme has h muet and links; hasard has h aspiré and blocks.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Both end in a silent consonant before the same word. Only quand wakes it, and it wakes as a T.

questions.q: Tap the word that blocks the liaison.
questions.why: héros carries an h aspiré, so les stays unlinked. héros arrivent does not link either, because a plural noun does not link to its verb.

questions.q: Say it: « Un enfant intelligent. »
questions.why: The scored segment is the gap. Link the first join and leave the second one open.

say.text: Last round. Whole sentences, and the optional state you only need to recognise.

questions.q: An optional liaison is one where:
questions.why: Both are correct French. The linked version is more formal. This is the third state, and it is register rather than right and wrong.
opts: either version is correct, and it signals formality
young speakers link and older ones do not

questions.q: When you are not sure whether a liaison is optional, you should:
questions.why: Skipping an optional liaison sounds relaxed and native. Adding a forbidden one sounds like an error, so the risk is not symmetric.
opts: link it, to sound more French

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Je suis‿allé with the link is what a broadcaster says. Both are correct, and you are only being asked to hear the difference.

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: Both link with a /z/. Only the vowel after the join tells them apart, which is what listening at speed actually demands.

questions.q: Type the two words that made the sound « lay-z‿a-MEE ».
questions.why: Working backwards from the join is the listening skill. The Z belongs to les even though you hear it on amis.

questions.q: A learner says « les héros » with a /z/. Fix it.
questions.why: The h aspiré blocks it. This is the pair to bank against les‿amis, which looks identical and behaves the opposite way.

questions.q: Say it: « Mes amis arrivent et ils restent. »
questions.why: One liaison at the start, then two gaps that stay open: a plural noun does not link to its verb, and et never links.
questions.target: Mes amis arrivent et ils restent.

questions.q: Say it: « Vous avez un petit ami ? »
questions.why: Three joins in six words. This is the sentence from the platform, and you can say it now.

say.text: That is the lesson. Six things worth keeping, and the last one is where you go next.

sections.body: An hour ago a woman on a platform asked you a four-word question and you heard one long noise. The words were not unfamiliar and she was not speaking unusually fast. What defeated you was that French does not leave its words where the spaces are: it takes the last consonant of one and puts it on the front of the next. You now know which consonants do that, what they turn into on the way across, and which joins French keeps sealed. That is why this is the lesson that changes listening rather than just pronunciation.
sections.title: What you take with you
points: The letter was never gone. It was waiting for a vowel. A vowel next door is what wakes it, and the consonant lands on the front of that next word.
S and X wake as /z/, D wakes as /t/, F wakes as /v/. Only T, N and L come back as themselves.
Obligatoire: article and noun, pronoun and verb, possessive and noun, adjective before its noun, and the fixed blocks like c'est‿un and tout‿à fait.
Interdite: et, always. An h aspiré word. A singular noun before its adjective. A personal name before its verb. onze.
Facultative exists and is about formality. Your safe default is to leave it, because over-linking sounds like an error and under-linking does not.
Next: l'élision, where the vowel moves instead of the consonant. le + arbre becomes l'arbre, and the same small set of h aspiré words that blocked you here will block you there too.

errorTriggers.description: Leaves an obligatoire liaison out: says les | amis or vous | avez with a gap, treating every final consonant as silent the way the previous lesson taught.
Links, but with the written letter rather than the spoken one: less amis for les‿amis, grahⁿ-D-arbr for grand‿arbre.
Links across a gap French seals: et, an h aspiré word, or a singular noun and the adjective after it.
Applies the right rule to the wrong pair: links a proper noun to its verb, or a plural noun to its verb, or misses that word order decides the adjective case.
Cannot locate the word boundary at speed because the consonant has moved forward: hears vous‿avez as one word, or cannot separate ils‿ont from ils sont.

lessons.intro: You order « un café » with confidence, but the barista pauses for half a second. Most French consonants are exactly like English. This lesson isolates the handful that are not: the throaty R, the soft J, the two-sound C and G, and the CH, GN, QU, PH, TH spellings, so you can read any word and already know which sound to make.
lessons.title: Les consonnes françaises

overview.subFr: Les consonnes : ce qui change vraiment
overview.introFr: La plupart des consonnes françaises ressemblent à l’anglais. Ce cours isole celles qui diffèrent vraiment : le R du fond de la gorge, le J adouci, la règle à deux sons du C et du G, et les groupes CH, GN, QU, PH, TH.
overview.titleEn: French Consonants: The Sounds That Actually Differ

sections.say: Picture this. You order a coffee with total confidence, but the barista pauses for half a second before understanding you. Here is the reassuring part: most French consonants are nearly identical to English. B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z, say them the way you already do. This lesson is a short, closed list of exceptions, not a whole new system.
sections.body:
You say « un café, s’il vous plaît » with confidence, but the barista hesitates before understanding you. Your C slipped toward an S, and your R never left the tip of your tongue.

The good news: most French consonants are nearly identical to English. B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z sound the way you already say them. This lesson is not a new consonant system, it is a short, closed list of exceptions to the one you already have.
sections.title: Why this matters

sections.say: By the end of this lesson you can produce the throat R and soft J, apply the C and G rule from spelling alone, read every forced-spelling override, and handle CH, GN, QU, PH, TH and silent H on sight.
sections.title: What you’ll master
points: Produce the throat R instead of an English or Spanish-style R.
Produce soft French J, and hear why soft G makes the identical sound.
Apply the C rule (hard before a, o, u, soft before e, i, y) on sight.
Apply the matching G rule, plus the three forced-spelling overrides: ç, gu, ge.
Read CH, GN, QU, PH, TH and silent H correctly, every time.
Tell which ten consonants need zero new muscle memory.

sections.say: Three buckets. Bucket one is unchanged from English, nothing to learn. Bucket two is a new but fixed sound: R, J, CH, GN, QU, PH, TH, H. Bucket three is a letter that switches sound depending on what follows it: C and G. Today lives almost entirely in buckets two and three.
sections.body:
Every French consonant sorts into one of three buckets. Bucket one: unchanged from English, no new skill, that’s B D F L M N P T V Z. Bucket two: a genuinely different but fixed sound, no ambiguity once learned, that’s R, J, CH, GN, QU, PH, TH, H. Bucket three: a letter that switches between two sounds depending on the next letter, that’s C and G.

This lesson spends almost all its time in buckets two and three, because that’s where every real mistake lives.
sections.title: The three buckets

sections.say: Five letters, one grid. Tap any letter to open its card: its French name, the sound it makes inside words, and an example. C and G each carry two sounds, that’s worth extra attention, and it’s exactly what the next few cards go deep on.
sections.title: R, J, H, C, G: the five letters that ambush you

letters.memo: Not the American tongue-curl, not the Spanish trill. Build it from a relaxed hard G.
letters.name: [air]
letters.sound: a soft, throaty scrape from the very back of the mouth

letters.memo: A pure hiss, voiced. No hidden d at the front.
letters.name: [zhee]
letters.sound: the buzzy zh of measure, never the English hard j

letters.memo: A name, but never a sound. No puff of air, ever.
letters.name: [ahsh]

letters.memo: Ç forces the soft s even in front of a, o, u: garçon.
letters.name: [say]
letters.sound: k before a, o, u; s before e, i, y

letters.memo: GU forces a hard g even in front of e, i: guerre, guitare.
letters.name: [zhay]
letters.sound: hard g before a, o, u; soft zh before e, i, y

sections.say: Building the throat R, one step at a time. Start from a relaxed hard G, drop the scrape in front of a vowel, then try it in a cluster and at the end of a word. The last card stacks five R’s into one sentence.
sections.hint: One step per card

cards.body: Say an English hard g, back of the mouth. Now let a little air rasp through instead of closing fully. That controlled scrape is R.
cards.head: Start from a hard G
cards.label: STEP 1

cards.body: Same scrape, now leading into a vowel. Hold it, don’t rush past it.
cards.head: Drop it in front of a vowel
cards.label: STEP 2

cards.body: The throat R shows up in clusters too: tr, pr, gr. Same sound, no different.
cards.head: Try it after a consonant
cards.label: STEP 3

cards.body: French never drops a final R the way some English accents do. Say it fully, twice, in this one word.
cards.head: End a word on it
cards.label: STEP 4

cards.fr: Le professeur regarde trois roses rouges.
cards.sub: The teacher looks at three red roses.
cards.body: Five throat R’s, four different positions. If this feels smooth, the sound is yours.
cards.head: Say the sentence
cards.label: CHECK

sections.title: Build the throat R

sections.say: J is always soft in French, and soft G is the exact same sound wearing a different spelling. Swipe through and say each one, feeling for that buzzy measure sound with no hard stop at the front.
sections.hint: Swipe through

cards.body: Isolate the buzzy sound in the middle of the English word measure. That, at the start of a word, is French J.
cards.head: Say measure, slowly
cards.label: THE SOUND

cards.body: No hard d at the front, just the buzz.
cards.head: je

cards.body: Same buzz, straight into the throat R.
cards.head: le jour

cards.body: G before e, i, y makes the identical sound to J. One sound, two spellings.
cards.head: Soft G matches it exactly

cards.body: G before i, the same soft buzz again.
cards.head: la girafe

sections.frSub: J et G doux : un seul son
sections.title: J and soft G: one sound, two spellings

sections.say: The single most useful rule in this lesson. C and G both flip sound depending on the very next letter. A, o, u keeps them hard. E, i, y makes them soft. Tap any row for the detail, and watch the third and sixth rows: ç and gu are how French forces the “wrong” sound on purpose.

detail.body: A hard k. Café, comme, cuir.
detail.title: C before a, o, u

detail.body: A soft s. Ce, ici, cycle.
detail.title: C before e, i, y

detail.body: The cedilla forces a soft s even in front of a, o, u: garçon, français.
detail.title: Ç overrides the rule

detail.body: A hard g. Gare, gomme, aigu.
detail.title: G before a, o, u

detail.body: A soft zh, identical to J. Gel, gilet, gym.
detail.title: G before e, i, y

detail.body: A silent u forces a hard g even before e or i: guerre, guitare.
detail.title: GU overrides the rule

sections.frSub: C et G : la double porte
sections.title: C and G: the two-sound gate

sections.say: Three override spellings do all the work: ç forces a soft sound before a, o, u. Gu forces a hard sound before e, i. Ge forces a soft sound before a, o. Once you see them as a permission slip rather than an exception, they stop needing memorization word by word.
sections.hint: Same rule, deliberately broken

cards.body: Both hard g. The silent u in guerre exists for one reason: to keep the g hard in front of e.
cards.head: gare vs guerre

cards.body: Gel is the regular soft g before e. Guitare is the forced hard g, thanks to that same silent u.
cards.head: gel vs guitare

cards.body: Café is the regular hard c before a. Garçon needs the cedilla to force the c soft in front of o.
cards.head: café vs garçon

cards.body: GE keeps a G soft in front of a or o, by inserting a silent e. Same idea as gu, opposite direction.
cards.head: The mirror trick

sections.title: The forced-spelling trap

sections.say: CH and GN behave as single, indivisible units. CH is always the plain sh sound. GN is always one merged nasal sound, never a hard g followed by a separate n.
sections.hint: One sound each, no exceptions today

cards.body: Never the English hard ch of chair. Always the plain sh of shoe.
cards.head: CH is just sh

cards.body: Same sh, three syllables in.
cards.head: le chocolat

cards.body: Not g, then n. One merged sound, tongue on the roof of the mouth, like the ny in canyon.
cards.head: GN is one sound, not two

cards.body: Hard g at the start, GN at the end. Two rules in one small word.
cards.head: gagner

sections.frSub: CH et GN : deux sons fixes
sections.title: CH and GN: two fixed digraphs

sections.say: The vocabulary bank, sorted by sound rather than by topic: throat R words, soft J and soft G words, hard C and hard G words, then CH and GN. Tap a theme to open its own mini deck.
sections.title: Vocabulary bank

sections.say: A simple scanning habit turns this rule from a guess into a reflex. Spot every C and G, check the next letter, watch for the three override spellings, then speak. A few days of doing this on short phrases and it becomes automatic.
sections.frSub: Lire un C ou un G avant de le dire
steps: Spot every C and G in the phrase before you speak it.
Check the very next letter. A, O, U or a consonant means hard. E, I, Y means soft.
Watch for the three overrides: ç forces soft, gu forces hard, ge forces soft.
Say the phrase once in your head, then say it out loud.
sections.title: Read any C or G before you say it

sections.say: Four borrowed spellings, each simplified to one clean sound. QU is k, never a kw glide. PH is f. TH is t. And H, no matter where it sits, makes no sound at all.

detail.body: Never the English “kw”. Quatre is [KATR], not koo-AT-ruh.
detail.title: QU is just k

detail.body: No exceptions worth learning yet. Pharmacie, photo.
detail.title: PH is always f

detail.body: French has no equivalent of the English th in think. Thé, théâtre.
detail.title: TH is always t

detail.body: Whether at the start or mid-word, H is silent. The word opens on the next letter.
detail.title: H makes no sound

sections.frSub: QU, PH, TH et le H muet
sections.title: QU, PH, TH, and silent H

sections.say: A short phrase ladder. Tap each line, listen, then say it yourself before moving to the next. Watch the last line: it runs the C and G rule twice in one breath.
lines: un café
un grand café
un grand café, merci
Ce garçon regarde la guitare rouge.
sections.title: Say it back

sections.say: Six mistakes almost every English speaker makes with these consonants, one per card. Each one gets the fix and the reason your mouth wants to make it.
sections.hint: One trap per card

cards.body: Curling the tongue back or rolling it is the fastest signal of a foreign accent. R lives at the back of the throat.
cards.head: Using an English or Spanish R
cards.label: MISTAKE 1

cards.body: French J never starts with a hard d stop. It’s a pure buzz, like the middle of measure.
cards.head: Saying J like English jump
cards.label: MISTAKE 2

cards.body: Café is hard, ce is soft. The rule is fully predictable, there’s never a real reason to guess.
cards.head: Guessing the C sound
cards.label: MISTAKE 3

cards.body: Gare is hard, gel is soft. G follows the identical rule as C, one letter later in the alphabet.
cards.head: Guessing the G sound
cards.label: MISTAKE 4

cards.body: French almost never uses the hard English ch sound. It’s the plain sh of shoe.
cards.head: Saying CH like English chair
cards.label: MISTAKE 5

cards.body: It looks like g then n, but it functions as a single consonant, like the ny in canyon.
cards.head: Splitting GN into two sounds
cards.label: MISTAKE 6

sections.say: Speaking drills. Tap each word to hear it, say it out loud, then grade yourself: got it, or missed it. Your answers feed your review deck, so accurate grading means better practice later.
sections.title: Speaking drills

sections.say: Four minimal pairs, the exact contrasts that trip up an English-trained ear. Say each pair out loud and feel your mouth change between the two.
sections.hint: Feel your mouth change between the two

cards.body: Same letter, two sounds. Only the next vowel decides.
cards.head: Hard G, then soft G
cards.label: PAIR 1

cards.body: A opens the gate hard, e closes it soft.
cards.head: Hard C, then soft C
cards.label: PAIR 2

cards.head: Regular soft G, then forced hard G
cards.label: PAIR 3

cards.body: Both followed by a wide vowel, but the cedilla in garçon flips it back to soft.
cards.head: Regular hard C, then forced soft C
cards.label: PAIR 4

lines: Le professeur regarde trois roses rouges.

sections.say: Now ears only. Play each word without looking if you can, decide what you heard, then check. These are the digraphs and borrowed spellings that fool an English-trained ear the longest.

cards.back: At the back of the throat, a soft scrape. Never the tongue tip.

cards.back: The buzzy zh of measure, never a hard English j.
cards.front: What sound does French J make?
C before a, o, u sounds like…?
C before e, i, y sounds like…?

cards.front: G before a, o, u sounds like…?
G before e, i, y sounds like…?

sections.say: Bravo. Before the quiz, your key takeaways. Ten letters need nothing new. R is a throat scrape. J and soft G are the same buzzy sound. C and G both flip on the next letter, and ç, gu, ge are the built-in overrides. Ready? The quiz is one tap away.
sections.body: Bravo. You just isolated the handful of French consonants that genuinely differ from English, and left the other ten alone. R lives in the throat, J and soft G buzz like measure, and C and G both flip on the very next letter. One short quiz stands between you and the finish line.
sections.title: Round-up
points: Ten letters transfer free: B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z.
R is a throat scrape, never the tongue tip.
J and soft G are the exact same buzzy sound, two spellings.
C and G both flip on the next letter: a, o, u is hard, e, i, y is soft.
Ç forces soft, GU forces hard, GE forces soft. The rule’s built-in overrides.
CH is sh, GN is one merged sound, QU is k, PH is f, TH is t, H is silent.

questions.q: Where is the French R produced?
questions.why: The throat R is made near the back of the mouth, tongue tip uninvolved.
opts: With the tongue tip curled back
At the back of the throat

questions.q: French J sounds like…
questions.why: French J is a pure buzz, with no hard stop at the front.
opts: The English hard j in jump

questions.q: What does C sound like before a, o, u?
questions.why: Café, comme, cuir: the wide vowels keep C hard.

questions.q: What does C sound like before e, i, y?
questions.why: Ce, ici, cycle: the narrow vowels make C soft.

questions.q: What does the cedilla (ç) do?
questions.why: Garçon needs the cedilla to stay soft in front of o.

questions.q: How does French force a hard [g] before e or i, as in guerre?
questions.why: The silent u in gu is a permission slip, not a sound.
opts: By adding a silent u: gu
It is impossible, G is always soft there

questions.q: What does CH normally sound like?
questions.why: French almost never uses the hard English ch sound.

questions.q: How is GN pronounced, as in montagne?
questions.why: GN functions as a single consonant, not two letters in sequence.
opts: A hard g followed by n
One merged sound, like the ny in canyon

questions.q: How is quatre pronounced?
questions.why: French QU is just k. English “kw” never appears.

questions.q: Is H ever pronounced in French?
questions.why: H is always silent, whether it opens a word or sits mid-word.
opts: Only at the start of a word

questions.q: In « Ce garçon regarde la guitare », why does the C in garçon stay soft?
questions.why: The cedilla overrides the normal hard-before-o rule.

questions.q: Which sentence uses both the C/G rule and a forced-spelling override?
questions.why: Ce is soft C by the regular rule; guerre is a forced hard G via gu.

segments.text: Bonjour !
Welcome back to Sons. Today, French consonants, the ones that actually differ from English.

You already know ten of them by heart: B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z. This lesson isolates the handful that don’t transfer: the throaty R, the soft J, the two-sound C and G, and four borrowed spellings.
One useful reframe before we start. You are not learning a new consonant system. You are learning a short, closed list of exceptions to the one you already have.
Today’s focus: R, J, the C and G rule, and CH, GN, QU, PH, TH, H.
Start with R. Say an English hard g, back of the mouth. Now let a little air rasp through instead of closing fully. That controlled scrape is the French R.
la rue
The street. All throat, no tongue tip. Now the soft J: isolate the buzzy middle sound of the English word measure.
je
I. No hard d at the front, just the buzz. And that same buzz is exactly what soft G sounds like too.
le gel
The gel. Now the rule that runs all of this: C and G each carry two sounds, and the very next letter decides which. A, o, u keeps them hard. E, i, y makes them soft.
le café, ce
Coffee, this. Hard, then soft. Same letter, two jobs.
Your turn. Repeat after me, slowly. The street:
la rue
Now the boy, where the cedilla forces the c soft even before o:
le garçon
And the cat, a plain sh, never the English ch:
le chat
Now say this sentence on your own, slowly. Watch the G twice, hard, then soft.
Un grand garçon regarde la guitare.

segments.expected: Un grand garçon regarde la guitare.

segments.text: Now the mountain, one merged sound for GN, not two:
Quick check. Before a, o or u, is C hard or soft?
And what does the cedilla, ç, force?

Your cheat sheet. Ten letters transfer free: B, D, F, L, M, N, P, T, V, Z. R lives in the throat. J and soft G buzz like measure. C and G both flip on the very next letter: a, o, u keeps them hard, e, i, y makes them soft, and ç, gu, ge are the overrides. CH is sh. GN is one sound. QU is k. PH is f. TH is t. H is always silent.
Bravo, à bientôt !

lessons.intro: Every letter's real sound. Learn the French name and the in-word sound of all 26 letters, master the ones that trip up English speakers, and spell your own name and email aloud with total confidence.
lessons.title: L'alphabet français

overview.subFr: L'alphabet : le vrai son de chaque lettre
overview.introFr: Apprenez le nom et le vrai son des 26 lettres, maîtrisez celles qui piègent les anglophones, et épelez votre nom et votre email à voix haute avec une confiance totale.
overview.titleEn: The French Alphabet: Every Letter's Real Sound

sections.say: Here is a moment that catches almost every learner off guard. You are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, and the receptionist asks for your email. You start spelling: P, A, U, L. And there is a long pause. She wrote down something completely different, because the letter you call AY is actually the French E, and the letter you call EE is the French I. The good news? This is a small, closed skill. Twenty six letters, they never change, and after this lesson you will own every one of them.
sections.body:
You are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, and the receptionist asks for your email. You start reading it out: P, A, U, L. There is a long pause. She heard pay, ah, oo, ell, and wrote down something completely different, because in French the letter you call AY is actually E, and the letter you call EE is I. Two minutes later you still do not have your confirmation.

That exact moment happens to travellers every day: dictating an email, spelling a last name at a pharmacy, giving a booking reference. The good news: this is a small, closed skill. There are only 26 letters, they never change, and once you own them you can spell anything in French.
sections.title: Why this matters

sections.say: By the end of this lesson you will be able to name all twenty six letters the French way, keep a letter's name and its sound in separate boxes, survive the ambush letters, and spell your own name and email out loud, slowly and clearly, like a local.
sections.title: What you'll master
points: Say the French name of all 26 letters, the way a French person spells out loud.
Tell a letter's NAME (for spelling) from its SOUND (inside words), the mix-up beginners make most.
Handle the ambush letters: E, G, H, I, J, R, U, W, Y and the vowels.
Say double vé for W and i grec for Y like a local, instead of guessing.
Spell your own name out loud in French, slowly and clearly.
Dictate an email address in French, including the @, the dot, and the tricky letters.
Recognise the French alphabet song and why its ending sounds different.

sections.say: Here is the one idea that fixes half your mistakes. A letter has two separate jobs. Its name is what you say when you spell out loud. Its sound is the noise it makes inside a word. When you dictate your email, you use names. When you read a word aloud, you use sounds. Keep those two jobs in separate boxes in your head, and most of the confusion disappears.
sections.body:
A letter has two completely separate jobs, and beginners jam them together.

The NAME of a letter is what you say when you spell a word out loud, letter by letter. The SOUND is the noise it makes inside a word: the B in boat does not go bee, it goes a short buh.

French works the same way. When you dictate your email, you use names. When you read a French word aloud, you use sounds.

KEY RULE: Spelling out loud = letter NAMES. Reading a word = letter SOUNDS. Different tools for different jobs.
sections.title: The core concept: name versus sound

sections.say: A quick note on how sounds are written in this lesson. Every sound appears three ways: the precise phonetic symbol in slashes, a plain sounds-like hint, and a respelling in brackets with the stressed syllable in capitals. One special code to remember: z h means the soft buzzy sound in the middle of measure. Hold onto that, it is the key to the letters G and J.

rows.v: The precise symbols in slashes, like /a/. An anchor, not homework.

detail.body: The International Phonetic Alphabet gives every sound in every language its own exact symbol, so /a/ always means the same thing no matter what language you're reading it in. You never need to memorize the IPA to use this course: it's here as a precise anchor you can check against, not something to study on its own. Whenever the plain-English hint feels ambiguous, the IPA symbol next to it is the exact answer.
detail.title: IPA

rows.v: A plain English hint: ah as in father.

detail.body: The fastest way in: a short comparison to a sound you already make in English, like ah as in father. It gets you close enough to be understood on the first try. It is deliberately approximate, because French vowels and English vowels are never perfectly identical, which is exactly why every sound also gets the more precise IPA symbol and the respelling alongside it.
detail.title: Sounds like

rows.v: A respelling with the stressed syllable in CAPS: bonjour is [bon-ZHOOR].

detail.body: A respelling breaks a French word into rough English-readable chunks, with the syllable you stress hardest written in CAPS: bonjour becomes [bon-ZHOOR]. French stress is much flatter than English stress overall, but the last syllable of a phrase still lands a little heavier, and the capitalized chunk is your cue for where that is.
detail.title: [brackets]

rows.v: The soft buzz in the middle of measure or vision. The key to G and J.

detail.body: One special code worth memorizing on its own: zh is the soft, buzzy sound in the middle of the English words measure or vision: not a hard j, and not an h. It shows up constantly in French, and it is the exact sound both G (before E, I, Y) and J make. Say "mesure" slowly and feel where your tongue sits for that middle sound. That's zh.
detail.title: zh

sections.say: These are the traps, the letters that ambush English speakers. Spend most of your time here. Swipe through each card, listen, and say each French word out loud. The two biggest offenders: E, which is uh and never ee. And the great G J swap: G goes AY, J goes EE.
sections.hint: Swipe through each trap

cards.body: Its name is a soft uh: relaxed, half-open mouth. The English instinct is to call E ee, but that is the French letter I. Inside words French E is often so light it nearly vanishes. Burn it in: E is uh, I is ee.
cards.head: E is [uh], never ee
cards.label: THE TRAP · E

cards.body: In English, G is jee and J is jay. French flips it: G is [zhay], J is [zhee]. Both start with the soft zh of measure, with no hidden d at the front. Remember: G goes AY, J goes EE.
cards.head: The great swap
cards.label: THE TRAP · G and J

cards.body: The letter is named [ahsh], but inside words it makes no sound at all. Hôtel opens on the O. Heure, the hour, is [ur]. Never puff air for a French H.
cards.head: Always silent, every time
cards.label: THE TRAP · H

cards.body: Its name is [air], but the sound lives at the back of the throat, near where you gargle: a soft scrape, not the American tongue-curl. Try a gentle kh, as if lightly clearing your throat, then soften it. Feeling strange at first is completely normal.
cards.head: The throaty one
cards.label: THE TRAP · R

cards.body: English does not have it. The trick that works: say ee as in see, freeze your tongue exactly where it is, then push your lips into a tight kiss shape. Tongue says ee, lips say oo. That collision is U. It is never oo: tu is [tew], not too.
cards.head: The tight whistle vowel
cards.label: THE TRAP · U

cards.body: Worth stating because of the E and I swap: the letter I is named [ee] and usually sounds ee in words. Clean and flat, no glide.
cards.head: Just ee
cards.label: EASY WIN · I

cards.body: French borrowed W, so they literally call it double V: [DOO-bluh-vay]. Not double-you. In older borrowings it sounds like v, in newer English ones like w: le week-end.
cards.head: Double vé
cards.label: THE BORROWED ONE · W

cards.body: The name means Greek I, because the letter arrived from Greek. Say [ee-GREK]. In words it acts like a French I or a y glide.
cards.head: I grec
cards.label: THE GREEK ONE · Y

cards.body: The name is [zed], like British English, never American zee.
cards.head: Zède
cards.label: THE LAST ONE · Z

sections.title: The letters that ambush you

sections.say: English vowel letters are lazy and change constantly. French vowels are stable and clean. Tap any row to open that vowel's card and hear it. Your English autopilot will read A as ay, I as eye and E as ee. All three are wrong in French. Retrain them: A is ah, E is uh, I is ee.

detail.body: French A is an open, pure ah, as in father. Never the English ay. Ami, the friend, is [ah-MEE].
detail.title: A is [ah]

detail.body: A soft uh with a relaxed mouth, often nearly silent inside words. The English ee belongs to the letter I. Le is [luh].
detail.title: E is [uh]

detail.body: A clean, flat ee with no glide. English I is a diphthong, eye. French I never glides. Ici, here, is [ee-SEE].
detail.title: I is [ee]

detail.body: Similar to English, but tighter, with no glide at the end. Hôtel is [oh-TELL].
detail.title: O is [oh]

detail.body: No English twin. Say ee, freeze your tongue, round your lips as if to whistle. Tu is [tew], never too.
detail.title: U is [ew]

detail.body: Named Greek I after its origin. Nothing to do with why. In words it sounds ee or glides like y: yoga, [yo-GAH].
detail.title: Y is i grec

sections.say: This is the part that pays for the whole lesson. When French speakers spell something important on the phone, they do three things you should copy. One: they use the letter names, slowly. Two: they confirm blurry letters with a helper word, B comme Bernard, B as in Bernard. Three: for an email they name the symbols too. Let us build each piece.
steps: Use the letter NAMES, slowly. Paul becomes: [pay], [ah], [ew], [ell]. Names, not sounds.
Confirm blurry letters with a helper word, because B, C, D, G, P, T, V all rhyme on the phone. The formula is B comme Bernard: B as in Bernard. Any well-known first name works.
For an email, name the symbols too: arobase for @, point for the dot. The full list is two cards away.

sections.say: Good news: you already know the tune of the French alphabet song. It is Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, same as the English ABC song. Only the words change. Slow down at the unfamiliar ending: double vé, iks, i grec, zède. Singing it a few times is a genuinely good way to lock the order in.
sections.body:
Yes, there is a French alphabet song, and it uses the same tune as the English ABC song, which is the same tune as Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star. French children learn it exactly the way you did.

The difference is the names: a, bé, cé, dé, e, effe, gé, and so on. The ending feels different because W is double vé, Y is i grec and Z is zède, so the final stretch runs: double vé, iks, i grec, zède. It does not rhyme the way the English ending does.

Hum it a few times. The tune is muscle memory you already own; you are just swapping the words.

sections.say: Eight mistakes almost every English speaker makes, one per card. For each one you get the fix and the reason your mouth wants to make it. The reason matters: once you know why a mistake happens, you can catch yourself before it does.
sections.hint: One trap per card

cards.body: Why it happens: in English the letter E literally says ee, so your mouth defaults to it. Retrain: E is uh, I is ee.
cards.head: Calling E ee
cards.label: MISTAKE 1

cards.body: Why it happens: English I is a diphthong, eye. French vowels do not glide; I is a clean ee.
cards.head: Calling I eye
cards.label: MISTAKE 2

cards.body: Why it happens: English swaps them, G is jee and J is jay. French flips it back and softens both to the measure sound. Say: G goes AY, J goes EE.
cards.head: Saying G and J the English way
cards.label: MISTAKE 3

cards.body: Why it happens: English H is breathy and strong. French H makes no sound at all, so the word opens on the next letter.
cards.head: Puffing an h in hôtel
cards.label: MISTAKE 4

cards.body: Why it happens: oo is the closest English sound, so learners grab it. Say ee, then round your lips without moving your tongue.
cards.head: Saying French U like oo
cards.label: MISTAKE 5

cards.body: Why it happens: you are translating the English name. French names it after V, not U, because that is what it looks like.
cards.head: Calling W double-you
cards.label: MISTAKE 6

cards.body: Why it happens: the English name leaks through. French names it Greek I after its origin. Nothing to do with why.
cards.head: Calling Y why
cards.label: MISTAKE 7

cards.body: Why it happens: nobody teaches it, yet you need it for every email. Memorise it as its own vocabulary word.
cards.head: Forgetting the word for @
cards.label: MISTAKE 8

sections.say: Bravo! You have taken the whole French alphabet apart and put it back together. Before the quiz, here are your key takeaways. Names for spelling, sounds for reading. E is uh, I is ee. G goes AY, J goes EE. H is silent. And when it is time to give your email: arobase. Ready? The quiz is one tap away. Bonne chance!
sections.body: Bravo! You just took the French alphabet apart and put it back together. You know every letter's name, the sounds behind them, and how to spell your own name and email out loud like a local. One short quiz stands between you and the finish line.
sections.title: Round-up
points: A letter has a NAME for spelling aloud and a SOUND inside words. Keep them separate.
The big swap: E is [uh], I is [ee]. Fixing this alone prevents most spelling errors.
G is [zhay], J is [zhee], both buzzing like measure.
H is always silent. U is a rounded ee, not oo. R lives in the back of the throat.
W is double vé, Y is i grec, Z is zède.
To dictate an email: letter names, helper words like B comme Bernard, arobase and point.
Rehearse your own name and email out loud. Ninety seconds now saves a frustrating phone call later.

questions.q: Which letter is named i grec?

questions.q: The French name for W is:
questions.why: French names it after V, double V, not after U.

questions.q: In hôtel, the H is:
questions.why: French H is always silent inside words; the word opens on O.

questions.q: Which word contains the tight, rounded French U?

segments.text: Bonjour !
Welcome to your very first Sons lesson. Today we take apart the French alphabet: all twenty six letters, their real names, and the sounds they make inside words.

Picture this: you are on the phone with a hotel in Lyon, spelling your email. You say the letters the English way, and the receptionist writes down something completely different. By the end of this lesson, that can never happen to you again.
One idea fixes half your mistakes: a letter has a NAME, for spelling out loud, and a SOUND, the noise it makes inside a word. They are different tools for different jobs.
Our focus today: the letter names, the traps, and spelling your own name and email aloud.
The biggest trap first. In French, the letter E is a soft uh, never ee. The letter that says ee is I. Listen: the word for I, the pronoun, is:
je
That soft ending is the French E. Now the great swap: G is zhay, J is zhee, both buzzing like the s in measure. Listen to the hard and soft G, cake then giraffe:
le gâteau, la girafe
And the silent ghost: H has a name, ahsh, but inside a word it makes no sound at all. The hotel:
l'hôtel
No puff of air. The word opens straight on the O.
Your turn. Repeat after me, slowly. First, the pronoun I:
je
Now thank you, with the French R colouring the first syllable:
merci
And the scariest-looking word that is secretly all your friends: today.
aujourd'hui
Now the payoff. Spell your own first name out loud, letter by letter, using the French names. Slowly. Remember: E is uh, I is ee.
Beautiful. Now say the French word for the at sign, the one you need for every email address:
Quick check. Which letter says ee when you spell out loud: E, or I?
And the French name for W?

Your cheat sheet: names for spelling, sounds for reading. E is uh, I is ee. G goes AY, J goes EE. H is silent. U is a rounded ee. W is double vé, Y is i grec, and the at sign is arobase. Spell your name and email out loud once before you travel, and you are ready.
Bravo, à bientôt !

goals.s: Produce [ɑ̃] without ever sounding the N.

cards.body: A nasal vowel is one pure sound, not a vowel plus a consonant. The rule: a vowel followed by N or M at the end of a syllable nasalizes, and that N or M stays silent. bon becomes bɔ̃, temps becomes tɑ̃.
cards.head: The basic idea and the golden rule

cards.body: Nasalization is blocked in two cases: a doubled N or M, or an N or M followed by a vowel. bonne stays bɔn, ami stays ami. In both, the consonant is fully pronounced.
cards.head: The anti-rule

cards.body: The open nasal. Spelled an, am, en, or em.
cards.head: [ɑ̃] as in temps

cards.body: The rounded nasal. Spelled on or om.
cards.head: [ɔ̃] as in bon

cards.body: The front nasal. Spelled in, im, ain, aim, ein, eim, yn, or ym.
cards.head: [ɛ̃] as in pain

cards.body: The rarest nasal. Spelled un or um. Often merges with pain's sound in casual speech.
cards.head: [œ̃] as in un

sounds.sub: Lower your soft palate while keeping your mouth in the vowel position, no consonant at all
sounds.label: How to nasalize: the soft palate technique
steps: Say 'ah' [a] normally, and notice your soft palate is raised, sealing off your nose.
Now hum 'mmm' and notice the opposite: your palate is fully lowered, all air through the nose, mouth closed.
Say 'ah' again, and this time, lower your soft palate exactly as you did for 'mmm', but keep your mouth open in the 'ah' position instead of closing it.
Air should now be escaping through both your nose and your open mouth at once. That is a nasal vowel.

sounds.sub: Check what follows: a vowel or a doubled N or M blocks the nasal
sounds.label: The anti-rule in motion
steps: As you approach a nasal word, glance ahead at the very next sound.
Consonant or silence follows: keep the nasal, say the word as spelled and nasalized.
A vowel follows, and the word is an article or number (un, mon, ton, son, bien, combien...): keep the nasal AND link the consonant forward.
A vowel follows, and the word is a fronted adjective like bon: switch to the oral, N-pronounced form, exactly as the feminine would sound.

errors.why: English always sounds its written consonants, but French nasal spelling is a signal, not a sound to produce.
errors.right: The vowel alone carries the nasality, the consonant is silent.
errors.wrong: Pronouncing the N or M inside a nasal vowel, so temps comes out sounding like tahnps.

errors.why: Learners over-apply the golden rule once they've learned it, forgetting the exceptions exist for a reason.
errors.right: N or M plus a vowel, or a doubled N or M, means oral: pronounce the consonant fully.
errors.wrong: Nasalizing words where the anti-rule blocks it, so ami sounds like ahn-mee, or bonne sounds like bohn.

errors.why: Both get flattened into one vague awn sound by an untrained English ear.
errors.right: [ɑ̃] is neutral-lipped, [ɔ̃] is rounded: genuinely different vowels, different words.
errors.wrong: Confusing [ɑ̃] and [ɔ̃], so that sans and son sound the same.

errors.why: English readers default to sounding out each letter individually.
errors.right: Both are single, fixed spellings for one nasal sound, [ɛ̃].
errors.wrong: Reading ain or ein as two separate vowel sounds.

errors.why: This exception applies to some of the most frequent words in the language, bien, rien, combien.
errors.right: en after i or y is pulled to [ɛ̃]: bien is [bjɛ̃], not [bjɑ̃].
errors.wrong: Assuming en is always [ɑ̃], even after i or y, so bien comes out sounding like byahn.

errors.why: This is genuine grammar hiding inside pronunciation, not a random performance detail.
errors.right: Articles and numbers usually keep the nasal and link, as in un homme, while a small set of pre-posed adjectives denasalize, as in bon ami.
errors.wrong: Treating every nasal-plus-vowel-initial-word boundary the same way.

errors.why: Treating a live sound change as either wrong or the only correct form both cause confusion. It's genuinely a spectrum across speakers and regions.
errors.right: Learn the distinct [œ̃] first, and recognize that many speakers merge it into [ɛ̃] in casual speech. Both are fine to understand and produce.
errors.wrong: Assuming [œ̃] must always sound identical to [ɛ̃], or always keeping them artificially separate even in casual contexts.

errors.why: Written French marks gender with extra letters, spoken French frequently marks it with nasality alone.
errors.right: Give the nasal or oral contrast the same care you'd give any other grammar rule, it changes meaning, not just accent.
errors.wrong: Forgetting that nasal versus oral is often the only spoken signal of grammatical gender, as in américain versus américaine.

sections.body: You just mastered the one feature of French that English has no equivalent for at all: four pure vowel sounds carried entirely through the nose. That skill alone unlocks an entire hidden layer of French grammar you could not hear before.
sections.title: The nasals are yours
points: You can produce all four nasal vowel qualities: [ɑ̃] in temps, [ɔ̃] in bon, [ɛ̃] in pain, and [œ̃] in un.
You apply the golden rule automatically: a vowel plus N or M at the end of a syllable nasalizes, and the N or M disappears.
You catch the anti-rule every time: a doubled N or M, or an N or M followed by a vowel, keeps both sounds oral.
You hear grammatical gender that used to be invisible, in pairs like bon and bonne, un and une, américain and américaine.
You predict liaison correctly, keeping the nasal in un homme and denasalizing bon ami.
This closes out the Sons unit. Your next stop is A1.

cards.body: French vowels are pure and unmoving. Each one keeps a single mouth position from start to finish, with no glide, unlike English, where many vowels drift toward a second sound.
cards.head: Pure, held vowels

cards.body: Front versus back: where the tongue sits in the mouth. Spread versus rounded: whether the lips stretch wide or close into a small circle. These two axes map out the entire French vowel system.
cards.head: Two axes that organize everything

cards.body: A [a] and I [i] already exist, almost identically, in English. A great place to start, as long as you keep them pure and don't let them glide.
cards.head: A and I: the two easy vowels

cards.body: O changes sound depending on what follows it. Closed at the end of a word or before a silent letter (mot, beau), open before a pronounced consonant (porte, bonne).
cards.head: O: closed or open

cards.body: An unaccented E is a quiet schwa (le), an é is closed (été), an è or ê is open (mère). Three sounds, three possible meanings.
cards.head: E: three sounds in one letter

cards.body: U [y] and EU [ø] / [œ] have no equivalent in English. Once you've mastered them, they're what really makes a French accent land.
cards.head: U and EU: the two 100% French sounds

sounds.sub: The sound with no English equivalent, and trap number one
sounds.label: U [y]
steps: Say 'ee' [i], feel your tongue high and forward, lips spread.
Hold the 'ee', don't let your tongue move.
Slowly round your lips into an 'oo' shape, as if about to whistle.
The sound that comes out is [y], French U. Repeat: tu, la rue, la lune, le mur.

sounds.sub: The second 100% French sound, in two versions
sounds.label: EU fermé et EU ouvert
steps: Say the English word 'her', but drop the R entirely, you're left with a neutral central vowel.
Without moving your tongue, purse your lips forward into a small circle, like you're about to blow out a candle.
For the closed version [ø] (word-final): keep the circle tight, sound short and bright.
For the open version [œ] (before a consonant): relax the circle slightly, let your jaw drop a touch more.

errors.why: English vowels default to diphthongs, so the mouth glides automatically if you're not paying attention.
errors.right: Hold each French vowel flat and still, one mouth position from start to finish
errors.wrong: Gliding pure vowels like English does (é becomes 'ay-ee', o becomes 'oh-oo')

errors.why: English has no rounded front vowel, so the brain substitutes the closest sound it already knows: [u].
errors.right: [y] = tongue forward like for 'ee', lips rounded like for 'oo', both at the same time
errors.wrong: Pronouncing U [y] like the English 'oo' (tu becomes 'too')

errors.why: This is the most common vowel mistake among English speakers, because both sounds sound like a generic 'oo' to an untrained ear.
errors.right: Feel your tongue's position: forward for U, back for OU
errors.wrong: Confusing U [y] and OU [u] in real words (vu and vous, su and sous)

errors.why: English O varies with accent and rhythm, but it never carries meaning the way [o] and [ɔ] do in French.
errors.right: Closed at the end of a word or before a silent letter, open before a pronounced consonant
errors.wrong: Treating closed O and open O as one single sound (beau and bonne)

errors.why: Both sounds get reflexively pulled toward the English 'ay', which doesn't really match either one.
errors.right: é = a light smile, flat, no glide; è = the jaw drops, more open
errors.wrong: Treating closed é and open è as one single sound

errors.why: Tongue position is already close to the English 'er', only the lips still need to round.
errors.right: Add lip rounding, that's exactly what's missing
errors.wrong: Replacing EU [ø] / [œ] with the English 'er' in 'her', without rounding the lips

errors.why: French doesn't have a strong word-stress system like English, each syllable stays nearly equal.
errors.right: Keep the schwa weak, short, almost silent
errors.wrong: Stressing or lengthening the schwa the way English stresses syllables (petit becomes 'peh-TEE')

errors.why: An English-speaking reader reflexively breaks apart each letter, but these French letter groups are indivisible units.
errors.right: Both are a single fixed spelling for [o], to memorize as one unit
errors.wrong: Reading eau or au letter by letter, as three separate sounds

lessons.title: Rythme & intonation
lessons.reframe: Even syllables, then one push at the end.
lessons.intro: You have spent this track getting individual sounds right. This lesson is about the shape they make together. French gives every syllable the same length and saves its one push for the end of the group, which is the opposite of what English does. Get this and sentences you already know start sounding French.
grammarAssumed: present tense
question forms

syllable.title: Syllable
syllable.body: One beat of a word. French gives every one the same length, which is why nothing gets swallowed.

group.title: Rhythm group
group.body: A run of words said in one breath. The push lands at the end of each one, not once at the end of the sentence.

push.title: The push
push.body: The slight lengthening on the last syllable of a group. Nothing gets louder: it is held, not stressed.

contour.title: Contour
contour.body: Whether the voice rises or falls on that final syllable. Up is a question, down is a statement.

rows.v: Even syllables. Nothing is swallowed and nothing is stretched.
Bigger and outlined: this is the one that gets the push.
A new rhythm group. The phrase breathes here.
The pushed syllable, in the respelling.

recorded.desc: Two readings of "Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît." First with ENGLISH rhythm: stress on VOU and CA, unstressed syllables reduced to schwa, uneven lengths. Second with French rhythm: every syllable equal length, one lengthening on PLAIT only. Same voice, same speed, back to back with a 600ms gap. The contrast IS the scene, so the two must be recorded in one take.

Six short statements, 3 to 5 syllables, read with strictly even syllable lengths and a single final lengthening: Il fait froid. / Le chat dort. / Tu lis trop. / C'est trop chaud. / Il neige beaucoup. / Je pars bientôt.. 900ms between items. Metronome-flat is the target, do not perform them.

Eight medium statements read TWICE each: first with the push on the correct group-final syllable, then with the push wrongly placed on the first content word (the English instinct). 400ms between the two readings, 900ms between pairs. Both readings must be the same speed and the same voice or the contrast is unreadable.

Eight questions and eight statements, alternating, so the rise and the fall sit next to each other: Tu viens demain ? / Vous partez déjà ? / Il pleut encore ? / C'est trop tard ?. The rise is on the final syllable only; the rest of the phrase stays flat and even.

THE MOST IMPORTANT BRIEF IN THIS LESSON. Eight pairs of sentences with identical words and different grouping. Each pair MUST be recorded in one take, back to back, 500ms apart, so the two readings are directly comparable. Pair 1 for example: "On mange, les enfants." said as TWO groups (break after mange, push on MANGE and on FANTS) then "On mange les enfants." said as ONE group (no break, single push on FANTS). If these are recorded separately or on different days the lesson loses its central argument.

The eight three-group phrases, each read with two clear breaks and three pushes, at conversational speed: Le matin, je me lève, et je pars. / Ce soir, on mange tôt, puis on sort. / En été, il fait chaud, même la nuit.. The breaks are short (roughly 200ms), not dramatic pauses.

Ten phrases for the dictée, read once at natural speed with correct even rhythm. The learner writes the phrase AND marks where the break falls, so the break must be audible: a real 200ms group boundary, not a swallowed one.

A 45-second monologue at natural conversational speed, using the long phrases (11 to 15 syllables). Rhythm fully natural, not slowed for teaching. This is the only place in the lesson where the learner hears French rhythm at real speed without a beat row on screen.

Six long phrases that stack the whole track: a silent letter, an elision, a liaison AND even rhythm in the same sentence. Read at natural speed. These are the "this is what French actually sounds like" clips and they close the lesson.

say.text: Six things, and every one of them is something you do out loud, not something you know about.

goals.s: Say a five-syllable phrase with all five syllables the same length, with nothing swallowed and nothing stretched.
Put the one lengthening on the last syllable of the group, not on the word you think matters most.
Tell a two-group phrase from a one-group phrase by ear, with no comma on the page to help you.
End a question upward and a statement downward without changing a single word.
Carry a twelve-syllable sentence without speeding up in the middle or trailing off at the end.

sections.title: Five things to hold on to
sections.hint: Swipe through. Five cards.

say.text: Five cards. The whole lesson is in these, and the rest is practice.

cards.label: THE RULE
cards.head: Even syllables, then one push at the end.
cards.body: That is the entire system. Everything else in this lesson is a consequence of it.

cards.label: EVEN
cards.head: No syllable is more important
cards.body: English has strong and weak syllables: PHO-to-graph, pho-TO-gra-pher. The weak ones collapse to uh. French does not do this. Every syllable keeps its full value, which is why French can sound fast: nothing is being skipped.

cards.label: THE PUSH
cards.head: One lengthening, at the end of the group
cards.body: It is not a stress in the English sense. Nothing gets louder. The final syllable of the group is simply held a little longer, and that is what marks the end.

cards.label: THE GROUP
cards.head: A group is a breath, not a word
cards.body: The push lands at the end of the GROUP, not at the end of the sentence. A long sentence has several groups, and several pushes. This is the part learners get wrong.

cards.label: READING IT
cards.head: Chips, rows, and CAPS
cards.body: Through this lesson: even chips are even syllables, the bigger outlined chip is the push, and a new row is a new group. In the respelling, the CAPS syllable is the pushed one and the | mark is the break.

say.text: Six short ones, starting at three syllables where there is nowhere to hide. Say each one with every syllable the same length, then hold the last one slightly longer. Flat and even will feel robotic at first. That is correct.

items.note: 3 syllables, one group.

say.text: One question before you move on.

check.q: In "Il fait froid", which syllable is longest?
check.why: The last one, and only slightly. The first two are exactly equal; froid is held a little longer because it ends the group. That single lengthening is the push, and it is the only thing marking the end of the phrase.

sections.title: Training the flat line

say.text: This one is different. You are not learning to add something. You are learning to stop doing something you cannot hear yourself doing.

sections.intro: English stress is automatic and it runs before you have decided anything. You do not choose to stretch the important word, you simply do, and you cannot hear it because it is what normal sounds like. So this cannot be fixed by knowing the rule. It has to become a reflex, and reflexes are built by doing.

closing.text: Do this on one French phrase a day, out loud, anywhere. Even syllables, then one push at the end. Thirty seconds a day beats an hour once.

targets.label: The flat hand
targets.sub: For any phrase you are about to say too English
steps: Hold your hand flat, palm down, in front of you.
Say the phrase while moving your hand straight sideways, at a constant speed.
If your hand wants to bounce on a syllable, that is the English stress trying to get in.
Say it again and keep the hand moving evenly all the way to the last syllable.
On the last syllable only, let the hand slow down and stop. That is the push.

targets.label: The syllable count
targets.sub: For when a phrase keeps collapsing in the middle
steps: Count the syllables on your fingers before you speak.
Say the phrase and put down one finger per syllable.
If you run out of phrase before you run out of fingers, you swallowed one.
Say it again slower, and make the swallowed syllable as long as the others.

say.text: Tap once per syllable as you say it. Keep the taps evenly spaced, and land the last one a little later than the rest.

sections.title: The push lands at the end

say.text: Longer phrases now, six to eight syllables, and each one is still a single group. So there is still exactly one push, on the final syllable. Notice it does not move to the word carrying the meaning: it does not care what the sentence is about.

check.why: French places the push by POSITION, not by meaning. It goes at the end of the group no matter which word carries the sense. Pushing the important word is the single most recognisable English accent in French.

sections.title: Up for a question, down for a statement
sections.hint: Six cards. Same words, different endings.

say.text: The push tells you where the group ends. The direction tells you what kind of sentence it was.

cards.label: THE SECOND JOB
cards.head: The last syllable does two things
cards.body: It carries the push, and it carries the direction. Up means a question. Down means a statement. Everything before it stays flat and even either way.

cards.label: RISING
cards.head: Tu viens demain ?
cards.body: Are you coming tomorrow? The voice goes up on the final syllable only. The rest of the phrase is as flat as a statement.

cards.label: RISING
cards.head: Vous partez déjà ?
cards.body: Are you leaving already? The voice goes up on the final syllable only. The rest of the phrase is as flat as a statement.

cards.label: RISING
cards.head: Il pleut encore ?
cards.body: Is it still raining? The voice goes up on the final syllable only. The rest of the phrase is as flat as a statement.

cards.label: RISING
cards.head: C'est trop tard ?
cards.body: Is it too late? The voice goes up on the final syllable only. The rest of the phrase is as flat as a statement.

cards.label: NO WORD CHANGES
cards.head: This is the whole question form
cards.body: French can turn a statement into a question with nothing but the direction of the last syllable. No inversion, no est-ce que, no extra word. If you keep the contour flat, a question lands as a statement and gets answered as one.

rule.title: What English does to a French sentence
rule.body: English marks the important word by stretching it and shortening everything around it. In French that stretches one syllable in the middle and collapses the rest, which is the one shape French never makes.

sections.title: A comma is a breath
sections.hint: Swipe. This is where the push stops being simple.

say.text: Everything so far has been one group and one push. Real sentences are longer than that.

cards.label: THE CORRECTION
cards.head: The push is per GROUP, not per sentence
cards.body: A long sentence does not get one push at the very end. It breaks into groups, and each group gets its own. This is the part that separates a learner who knows the rule from one who can use it.

cards.label: 2 GROUPS
cards.head: J'ai trop froid ce matin, je reste sous les draps.
cards.sub: [zhay troh frwa suh ma-TAⁿ | zhuh rehst soo lay DRA]
cards.body: I'm too cold this morning, I'm staying under the covers. Two pushes, one at the end of each group. The break is where the phrase breathes.

cards.label: 2 GROUPS
cards.head: Il est tard, le petit village dort sous la neige.
cards.sub: [eel eh TAR | luh puh-tee vee-lazh dohr soo la NEHZH]
cards.body: It's late, the little village sleeps under the snow. Two pushes, one at the end of each group. The break is where the phrase breathes.

cards.label: 2 GROUPS
cards.head: Le soir, je lis un peu.
cards.body: In the evening, I read a little. Two pushes, one at the end of each group. The break is where the phrase breathes.

cards.label: 2 GROUPS
cards.head: Le matin, je bois mon café tranquillement.
cards.sub: [luh ma-TAⁿ | zhuh bwa mohⁿ ka-fay trahⁿ-keel-MAHⁿ]
cards.body: In the morning, I drink my coffee calmly. Two pushes, one at the end of each group. The break is where the phrase breathes.

cards.label: 2 GROUPS
cards.head: Après le repas, on marche dans le parc.
cards.sub: [a-preh luh ruh-PA | ohⁿ marsh dahⁿ luh PARK]
cards.body: After the meal, we walk in the park. Two pushes, one at the end of each group. The break is where the phrase breathes.

cards.label: ON THE PAGE
cards.head: The comma is a clue, not the rule
cards.body: A written comma usually marks a group boundary, which is why these are easy to see. But French breaks phrases where the sense breaks, and plenty of boundaries have no comma at all. The ear is the real guide.

sections.title: Same words, different meaning
sections.hint: Eight pairs. Listen to both before you swipe on.

say.text: This is the argument for the whole lesson. Identical words. The only difference is where the phrase breaks, and it changes what the sentence means.

cards.label: WHY THIS MATTERS
cards.head: Grouping is not decoration
cards.body: If rhythm were only an accent thing, getting it wrong would make you sound foreign and nothing worse. It is not. Where you break a phrase can change what you said.

cards.label: TWO GROUPS
cards.head: Il est là, mon frère.
cards.body: He is here, my brother. Two groups: someone is here, and I am telling my brother.

cards.label: ONE GROUP
cards.head: Il est là mon frère.
cards.body: There is my brother. One group, no comma: my brother is the one who is here.

cards.label: TWO GROUPS
cards.head: On mange, les enfants.
cards.body: We are eating, children. Two groups: I am calling the children to the table.

cards.label: ONE GROUP
cards.head: On mange les enfants.
cards.body: We are eating the children. One group: the children are the meal. The comma is the difference.

cards.label: TWO GROUPS
cards.head: Elle attend, son mari.
cards.body: She is waiting, her husband. Two groups: she waits, and I am addressing her husband.

cards.label: ONE GROUP
cards.head: Elle attend son mari.
cards.body: She is waiting for her husband. One group: the husband is what she waits for.

cards.label: TWO GROUPS
cards.head: Je bois, du lait.
cards.body: I drink, some milk. Two groups: an afterthought, tacked on.

cards.label: ONE GROUP
cards.head: Je bois du lait.
cards.body: I drink milk. One group: the ordinary sentence. One push, at the end.

cards.label: TWO GROUPS
cards.head: Tu viens, avec nous ?
cards.body: Are you coming, with us? Two groups: the question is whether you come. With us is added.

cards.label: ONE GROUP
cards.head: Tu viens avec nous ?
cards.body: Are you coming with us? One group: the whole thing is one question.

cards.label: TWO GROUPS
cards.head: Il parle, mon voisin.
cards.body: He talks, my neighbour. Two groups: he talks, and my neighbour is who I mean.

cards.label: ONE GROUP
cards.head: Il parle à mon voisin.
cards.body: He is talking to my neighbour. One group: the neighbour is who he talks to.

cards.label: TWO GROUPS
cards.head: On part, demain matin.
cards.body: We are leaving, tomorrow morning. Two groups: we are leaving. When, is a second thought.

cards.label: ONE GROUP
cards.head: On part demain matin.
cards.body: We leave tomorrow morning. One group: a single plan, said in one breath.

cards.label: TWO GROUPS
cards.head: Elle chante, très bien.
cards.body: She sings, very well. Two groups: she sings. And then: very well.

cards.label: ONE GROUP
cards.head: Elle chante très bien.
cards.body: She sings very well. One group: one statement about how she sings.

say.text: One question about the pairs.

check.q: You say "On mange les enfants" as one group, with one push at the end. What have you just said?
opts: Both readings mean the same thing
check.why: One group makes les enfants the object of mange: they are the meal. Breaking after mange makes it a separate group and turns les enfants into who you are talking TO. Same five syllables, and the break is the only thing carrying the difference.

say.text: Three groups each. Say them with a short break between the groups, and a push at the end of every one. Not three separate sentences: one sentence that breathes twice.
Twelve you can use as they are. Each one is marked with where it breaks and where the push lands.

examples.en: The wolf runs in the woods.
examples.note: [luh loo koor dahⁿ lay BWA] · 6 syllables, one group.

examples.en: It's been hot for three days.
examples.note: [eel feh shoh duh-pwee trwa ZHOOR] · 7 syllables, one group.

examples.en: The train leaves in a moment.
examples.note: [luh traⁿ par dahⁿ-z‿uhⁿ-n‿aⁿs-TAHⁿ] · 7 syllables, one group.

say.text: Ten phrases. Write the words, and put the comma where you hear the phrase breathe. The break is audible even when you cannot see it.
Natural speed, no beat row, nothing on screen to help. This is the first time you hear the rhythm without a picture of it.

lines.fr: Le petit garçon joue devant la grande maison.
lines.en: The little boy plays in front of the big house.

lines.fr: Mon grand frère travaille beaucoup depuis le printemps.
lines.en: My big brother has been working a lot since spring.

lines.fr: Elle boit un chocolat chaud au coin du feu.
lines.en: She drinks a hot chocolate by the fire.

lines.fr: Mon ami part demain matin pour un long voyage.
lines.en: My friend leaves tomorrow morning for a long trip.

lines.fr: Nous restons au chaud quand le vent devient fort.
lines.en: We stay warm when the wind gets strong.

questions.q: How many groups does the third sentence break into?
questions.why: You can hear it without counting words: the voice holds a syllable, breathes, then starts flat again. Each of those holds is the end of a group.

questions.q: Where did the speaker put the push in the last sentence?
opts: On the last syllable of each group
questions.why: Position, not meaning. However long the sentence is and whatever it is about, the push lands at the end of each group.

say.text: Ten of them, and they are long. Tap, speak, and a model plays straight after. If the middle sped up, say it again with the model.

sections.title: Everything at once

say.text: These stack the whole track. A silent letter, an elision, a liaison and even rhythm, in the same sentence. This is what French actually sounds like.

sections.text:

Le dîner est servi depuis un long moment déjà.
