Thank you.
Thank you very much.
Thank you enormously. Rare and warm.
You’re welcome. The everyday one.
You’re welcome, formal.
With pleasure.
Please, to vous.
Please, to tu.
Sorry, or excuse me getting past.
Excuse me, to vous.
Sorry. Désolée if you are a woman.
How’s it going?
I’m good.
So-so. The permitted answer.
Pleased to meet you. Enchantée if you are a woman.
My name is…
Goes after bonjour, more often than English does.

register.title: The choice you make before you speak
register.body: Register is how close you are to the person you are talking to, expressed in the words you pick. English carries it in tone: you say the same words to a friend and to a stranger and let your voice do the work. French carries it in the words themselves, so the choice is made before you open your mouth and it is visible in every sentence. This lesson teaches both settings of the switch.

vous.title: The form for distance
vous.body: Use vous for anyone you do not know, anyone older, anyone serving you, anyone at work, and any group of people. It is not stiff and it is not cold. It is the setting French leaves on by default, and using it with someone who expected tu reads as polite. Using tu with someone who expected vous does not.

examples.note: The vous form of "how are you".
Please, in the vous form. The one to reach for in a shop.

tu.title: The form for closeness
tu.body: Use tu with friends, family, children, animals, and people your own age once you have been invited to. That invitation is a real moment and it has a verb: on se tutoie, we use tu with each other. Until somebody offers it, you are not being distant by staying on vous, you are being correct.

examples.note: The tu form of the same question.
Please, in the tu form. One word swapped.

titles.title: The word that goes after bonjour
titles.body: French adds the title far more often than English adds "sir" or "madam", and it is warm rather than formal. Bonjour madame in a bakery is ordinary; bonjour on its own is slightly bare. There is no surname attached and none is expected. Mademoiselle has fallen out of use for adults, so madame covers every woman you are addressing.

examples.note: Any woman you are addressing.
Any man you are addressing.

salut.title: The greeting with a guest list
salut.body: Salut is the one greeting here that runs both ways, hello and goodbye, and the only one restricted by who rather than by the clock. It belongs to people you tutoie. Said to a shopkeeper or anyone older it does not read as friendly, it reads as over-familiar, and that lands harder than being too formal ever does. If you are unsure whether you may say salut, you may not yet.

examples.note: Hello and goodbye, but only with people you tutoie.

bonsoir.title: Same part of the day, opposite doors
bonsoir.body: Bonsoir is hello after dark. Bonne soirée is goodbye after dark. They sound close and they are not interchangeable: walking into a restaurant on bonne soirée wishes the room a good evening on your way in, which is the wrong door. Bonne nuit is a third thing again and means sleep well, so it belongs only where sleep is next.

examples.note: Arriving, once the light has gone.
Leaving, once the light has gone.

caVa.title: Two words doing three jobs
caVa.body: Rising tone and it asks. Flat tone and it answers. It is also the everyday alternative to the fuller comment allez-vous, which is why you will hear it more than any other question in this lesson. The part learners drop is the hand-back: answer and stop, and you have closed the exchange down. Add et vous or et toi and it stays a conversation.

examples.note: Asking.
Answering.
Answering when the answer is not "fine".

deRien.title: The half of politeness that gets left out
deRien.body: Courses teach merci and stop there, which leaves you silent at the exact moment someone thanks you. De rien is the everyday answer, literally "of nothing". Je vous en prie is the same move one register up and is what you will hear from anyone serving you. Answering merci with merci leaves the thanks hanging in the air.

examples.note: The everyday reply.
The same reply, one register up.

enchante.title: The one word an introduction needs
enchante.body: Said on being introduced, and it is enough on its own. A man writes enchanté and a woman writes enchantée; the extra e agrees with the speaker and changes nothing about how the word sounds, so the two are identical out loud and only ever differ on paper.

examples.note: Pleased to meet you.

lessons.title: Les nombres 1-20
lessons.intro: Twenty words you could learn from a list in an afternoon, and one thing the list cannot tell you: a French number does not have a fixed ending. It has the ending the next word gives it.

sections.title: The Train in Ten Minutes
sections.frSub: Le train part dans dix minutes

say.text: Watch this happen. You know the number, you have practised the number, and you still do not hear it.

setting.place: The ticket window at the station

beats.speaker: The clerk
beats.fr: Le train part dans dix minutes.

beats.text: You have said that number out loud a hundred times this week. You did not catch it once.

ask her to say it again

followUp.works: Good. Asked again, she will give you the number on its own, and on its own it is a word you know.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: The next word decides how a number ends. By the end of this you will expect that, instead of being caught by it.

goals.s: Say every number from un to vingt without stopping to work one out.

goals.t: Hear a number inside a sentence
goals.s: Catch dix in dix minutes and in dix ans, where it sounds like neither.
Ask for two of something, and know when un has to become une.

goals.t: Take a time off a board
goals.s: Read a departure, a price or an opening hour without freezing at the counter.

sections.title: One Number, Three Sounds
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: The next word decides how a number ends. Here is what that does to one word.

cards.label: On its own
cards.head: Ten, and nothing after it
cards.body: Alone, at the end of a phrase, or before a pause, the X is said and it sounds like an S. This is the version every list gives you, and it is the only one they give you.

cards.label: Before a consonant
cards.head: Ten minutes
cards.body: A consonant follows and the S disappears completely. Nothing on the page marks it. The number becomes one short syllable and the next word starts straight away.

cards.label: Before a vowel
cards.head: Ten years
cards.body: A vowel follows and the S comes back as a Z, said with the next word rather than with the number. Ten years is one sound, not two.

sections.title: One to Ten
sections.say: Ten words. Four of them change shape later in the lesson, and the detail card says which.

detail.title: un
detail.body: One, and the only number here with a second form. Un before a masculine noun, une before a feminine one. No number above it changes for gender.

detail.title: deux
detail.body: The X is silent on its own. Before a vowel it comes back as a Z and joins on, so deux heures is said as one piece.

detail.title: trois
detail.body: The S is silent on its own and returns as a Z before a vowel, exactly like deux. Trois heures runs the two words together.

detail.title: quatre
detail.body: Four consonants around one vowel, and the final R is fully said. English speakers reach for a vowel at the end. Let the T and the R run together instead.

detail.title: cinq
detail.body: The K is said everywhere, including in front of another consonant. Five is one of the two numbers in this lesson that never changes.

detail.title: six
detail.body: On its own the X sounds like an S. Before a consonant it vanishes. Before a vowel it becomes a Z. Three sounds, one spelling.

detail.title: sept
detail.body: The P is silent and the T is always said, wherever the number stands. Seven is the fixed point you can measure the others against.

detail.title: huit
detail.body: Starts on a W sound, not an H. The T is said on its own and before a vowel, and drops before a consonant: huit jours is WEE zhoor.

detail.title: neuf
detail.body: The F is said. In front of heures it softens to a V and joins on, giving NEU-veur. No other number in the language does that.

detail.title: dix
detail.body: The same three shapes as six: an S alone, nothing before a consonant, a Z before a vowel. This is the number the whole lesson turns on.

sections.title: The One That Has a Gender
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: French makes you decide something English never asks about, and it happens on the very first number.

cards.label: The fork
cards.head: One, twice
cards.body: One is the only number in French with two forms. The noun you are counting decides which, and it decides before you have finished saying it. Everything from two upward is one word for everyone.

cards.label: Masculine
cards.head: un
cards.body: Un for a masculine noun. It is also the word for a, which is why one coffee and a coffee are the same two words. The N is not pronounced: the vowel is made through the nose instead.

cards.label: Feminine
cards.head: une
cards.body: Une for a feminine noun, and here the N really is said. That is the difference a French ear catches first, and it is one letter on the page.

sections.title: Asking for an Amount
sections.say: The number, then the thing, and nothing in between. This is the whole shape of ordering in French.

examples.note: The number and the article are one word. Nobody says one twice.
The S on cafés is silent, so deux is the only part carrying the amount out loud.
Baguette is feminine, so un becomes une.
A measured amount takes de, and de stays bare: never de la, never des.
Point and give the number alone. Nothing follows it, so the ending is fully said.

sections.title: Listen for the Ending
sections.say: No table this time. Listen for what happens at the end of each number.

lines.fr: Le concert commence dans dix minutes.
lines.en: The concert starts in ten minutes.

lines.fr: Nous avons visité quinze pays en dix ans.
lines.en: We visited fifteen countries in ten years.

lines.fr: Le magasin ouvre à neuf heures.
lines.en: The shop opens at nine.

lines.fr: Il reste huit jours avant les vacances.
lines.en: There are eight days left before the holidays.

questions.q: In the first line, what happens to the S at the end of dix?
opts: It is said, like an S
questions.why: Minutes starts on a consonant, so the S of dix has nowhere to go and is dropped entirely.

questions.q: In the second line, dix ans. What do you hear between the two words?
questions.why: Ans starts on a vowel, so the S wakes up as a Z and joins the two words into one sound.

questions.q: Neuf heures. Which letter changes?
questions.why: The F softens to a V in front of heures. It is the only number in French that does this.

sections.title: Eleven to Twenty
sections.say: Six words with no pattern, then three that say their own arithmetic. Knowing where that break falls saves you looking for a rule that is not there.

detail.title: onze
detail.body: Eleven to sixteen are six separate words with nothing in them to work out. Learn them the way you learned the English ones, a few at a time.

detail.title: douze
detail.body: The Z is written into the word, so it is always said and never depends on what follows. That is what separates douze from deux at speed.

detail.title: treize
detail.body: Trois and treize share a beginning and nothing else. The Z ending is what tells you which of the two you just heard.

detail.title: quatorze
detail.body: Two syllables, stressed on the second, and the same built-in Z as twelve, thirteen and sixteen. Quatre is one syllable and ends on a consonant cluster.

detail.title: quinze
detail.body: The vowel is nasal, so no N is pronounced: one sound made through the nose, then a Z. Cinq has the same vowel and a K instead.

detail.title: seize
detail.body: Nothing of six survives in seize. Six ends on an S sound and seize ends on a Z, and that ending is the whole clue.

detail.title: dix-sept
detail.body: Ten seven, written out, and from here the language stops inventing words. The S of dix says nothing at all in this one.

detail.title: dix-huit
detail.body: Ten eight. The same S as in dix-sept, and here it is said, as a Z. One letter doing two different jobs three words apart.

detail.title: dix-neuf
detail.body: Ten nine, and the S is a Z again. This time it closes the first syllable instead of opening the second, so the word starts DEEZ.

detail.title: vingt
detail.body: The G and the T are both written and both silent on their own. Before a vowel the T wakes up and joins on: vingt heures is VAⁿ-teur.

sections.title: The Same S, Three Times
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: The next word decides how a number ends. These three put all of it on one screen.

cards.label: Silent
cards.head: Seventeen
cards.body: The S of dix says nothing. Read the word and you would never guess that, because the letter is right there on the page.

cards.label: A Z
cards.head: Eighteen
cards.body: The same S, one number later, and now it is a Z. Nothing about the spelling of dix has changed. What follows it has.

cards.label: A Z again
cards.head: Nineteen
cards.body: The Z again, and here it closes the first syllable rather than opening the second. Three numbers in a row, three different jobs for one letter.

sections.title: Two or Twelve?
sections.say: Six pairs that sound alike and are ten apart. The ending is the only thing separating them.

sections.title: Six Numbers, Three Ways
sections.say: The next word decides how a number ends. Every row here is one number written three times. Tap a row and only your ear can tell them apart.

detail.title: six
detail.body: SEES alone. SEE zhoor before a consonant, with nothing left of the X. SEE-zeu-roh before a vowel, where it is a Z joined to the next word.

detail.title: huit
detail.body: WEET alone. WEE zhoor before a consonant, where the T drops. WEE-teur before a vowel, where it comes back and joins on.

detail.title: dix
detail.body: DEES alone. DEE mee-nüt before a consonant. dee-ZAHⁿ before a vowel. This is the row the opening scene was built on.

detail.title: vingt
detail.body: VAⁿ alone and VAⁿ before a consonant, so twenty is the one number here that does nothing until a vowel arrives. Then the silent T wakes: VAⁿ-teur.

detail.title: neuf
detail.body: NEUF alone and NEUF before a consonant. Before heures the F softens to a V: NEU-veur. Nine is the only number that swaps a letter rather than dropping or adding one.

detail.title: sept
detail.body: SET in all three. Seven does not move, and neither does cinq. Two fixed points are worth knowing, because they tell you the movement is real and not your ear.

sections.title: Six Lines, Same Numbers
sections.say: Each number here turns up twice across the six lines, and each time it sounds different.

lines.fr: Il reste huit jours avant les vacances.
lines.en: There are eight days left before the holidays.

lines.fr: À huit heures et demie précises, le cours commence.
lines.en: The class starts at exactly half past eight.

lines.fr: Le concert commence dans dix minutes.
lines.en: The concert starts in ten minutes.

lines.fr: Nous célébrons nos dix ans de mariage.
lines.en: We are celebrating our tenth anniversary.

lines.fr: Le film commence à vingt heures trente.
lines.en: The film starts at half past eight in the evening.

lines.fr: Le magasin ouvre à neuf heures.
lines.en: The shop opens at nine.

questions.q: Two lines say huit. In which one is the T silent?
questions.why: Jours starts on a consonant, so the T drops and huit ends on its vowel. Before heures the T is said and joins on.

questions.q: Vingt heures. What can you hear that vingt on its own does not have?
questions.why: The T of vingt is silent alone and wakes up before a vowel. The G beside it stays silent either way.

questions.q: Which of these sounds the same in both halves?
questions.why: Sept keeps its T wherever it stands, which is why it is worth using as the thing you measure the moving numbers against.

sections.title: Three Traps
sections.say: Three mistakes an English speaker makes in their first week, in roughly this order.

errors.wrong: Saying « dix minutes » with the S sounded, as DEES mee-nüt.
errors.right: Saying it as DEE mee-nüt, with no S at all.
errors.why: The next word decides how a number ends. Minutes begins on a consonant, so the S has nowhere to go and French drops it rather than squeezing it in.

errors.wrong: Asking for « un baguette » at the counter.
errors.right: Asking for « une baguette » at the counter.
errors.why: Baguette is feminine, so one is une. It is one letter, and it is the fastest thing a French ear uses to place you as a beginner.

errors.wrong: Hearing « seize » and writing six.
errors.right: Hearing the Z on the end and writing sixteen.
errors.why: Six ends on an S sound and seize ends on a Z. Nothing else of six survives in seize, so the ending carries the entire difference.

sections.title: Count to Twenty
sections.say: Twenty numbers, said one at a time with a pause after each. Nothing follows them here, so every ending is fully said.

sections.title: The Words Themselves
sections.say: Four decks, split where the language splits. Open whichever you want first.

themes.title: Eleven to sixteen, one at a time
Seventeen to twenty, where the sum shows

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French out loud before you flip it.

sections.title: Write What You Hear
sections.say: Four sentences, one for each thing this lesson claims. Build each from the word tiles, and some of the tiles do not belong.

sections.title: Your Turn at the Stall
sections.say: A market stall, and you hold up the whole exchange. Every line you say has a number in it.
sections.setting: A market stall in Annecy, Saturday, just after nine.

turns.ai: Bonjour ! Vous désirez ?
turns.en: Hello! What would you like?
turns.user: Bonjour. Deux kilos de pommes, s’il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: Hello. Two kilos of apples, please.

alts.fr: Je voudrais deux kilos de pommes.
alts.en: I'd like two kilos of apples.

turns.ai: Deux kilos. Et avec ça ?
turns.en: Two kilos. Anything else?
turns.user: Une baguette, s’il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: A baguette, please.

turns.ai: Voilà. Ça fait huit euros.
turns.en: There you go. That comes to eight euros.
turns.user: Huit euros. Voilà.
turns.userEn: Eight euros. Here you go.

turns.ai: Merci. On ferme à treize heures aujourd’hui.
turns.en: Thank you. We close at one o’clock today.
turns.user: À treize heures, d’accord.
turns.userEn: At one o’clock, all right.

turns.ai: Bonne journée !
turns.en: Have a good day!
turns.user: Merci, au revoir.
turns.userEn: Thank you, goodbye.

alts.en: Thank you very much, see you soon.

sections.title: Six Moments This Week
sections.say: Every one of these is a real moment, and in every one the number is doing something to the word after it.

cases.situation: Ordering at a counter
Asking when a shop opens
Reading the answer off the door
cases.fr: Ouvert de neuf heures à dix-neuf heures.

cases.situation: Buying a single ticket
Being told how long to wait
Saying how many are eating
cases.fr: Une table pour quatre, s’il vous plaît.

sections.title: Two Tickets to Nantes
sections.say: Read it once for the shape. Tap any word you do not know.
sections.text: It is quarter past eight and Marc is at the ticket window in Tours. He needs to be in Nantes by lunchtime. « Bonjour. Deux billets pour Nantes, s’il vous plaît. » The clerk checks her screen before she answers. « Deux billets. Le train part à neuf heures. » Marc wants to know when it gets in. « À neuf heures ? Il arrive quand ? » She gives him the time, and then the price. « À onze heures dix. Ça fait trente-six euros. » He pays and looks up at the board. The platform is still not there. « Quel quai ? » She points over his shoulder. « Quai six. Vous avez quinze minutes. » « Merci beaucoup. »

glossary.note: The plural S is silent. Deux in front of it is the only thing telling you there is more than one.
From partir. Le train part is how every French departure is announced.
The F of neuf is said as a V here and runs straight into heures.
The word on every station board in France. Quai six is platform six.
The Z of quinze is part of the word, so it is said whatever follows.

questions.q: What time does the train leave, and what time does it arrive?
questions.a: It leaves at nine and arrives at ten past eleven.

questions.q: How many tickets does Marc buy, and what does he pay?
questions.a: Two tickets, for thirty-six euros.

questions.q: In « neuf heures », what does the F sound like?
questions.a: A V. The two words run together as NEU-veur.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.back: DEES. The X is said, and it sounds like an S.
DEE. The S is gone completely.
dee-Z, joined to the next word.
cinq and sept. Both keep their ending everywhere.
neuf heures. The F becomes a V.

cards.front: The T in vingt wakes up when…
cards.back: …a vowel follows. vingt heures, not vingt.
At dix-sept. Onze to seize have none.
Deux cafés. The S on cafés is silent.
seize ends on a Z, six ends on an S.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have counted to twenty out loud, heard the same number in three shapes, ordered at a stall and read a departure off a board. What is left is the part that tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Four rounds. Miss too many in one and you get its drill before the next round starts.

rounds.label: One to twenty
rounds.say: The twenty words, and the six that sound like each other.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Quinze ends on a Z and cinq ends on a K. They share a vowel, so the ending is the only thing separating five from fifteen.

questions.q: Sixteen is:
questions.why: Sixteen has its own word and nothing of six survives in it. The ten-plus pattern only begins at dix-sept.

questions.q: Write the number that comes between seize and dix-huit.
questions.why: Seventeen is where French stops inventing new words and starts saying ten seven out loud.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Deux ends on a vowel and douze ends on a Z. That Z is the whole difference between two and twelve.

questions.q: Onze to seize are six words with:
opts: a pattern you can work out
no pattern, learned one at a time
the same endings as one to six
a silent ten at the front
questions.why: There is nothing to derive in eleven to sixteen. Looking for a rule there wastes the effort those six words actually need.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Quatorze is two syllables stressed on the second. Quatre is one syllable that ends on a consonant cluster.

rounds.label: One has a gender
rounds.say: The only number that asks you a question before you say it.

questions.q: You want one baguette. Which?
questions.why: Baguette is feminine, so one is une. The noun decides, and it decides before you have finished the first word.

questions.q: Write "one coffee". Café is masculine.
questions.why: Un is both the number one and the word a, so French says it once and means both.

questions.q: How many numbers in this lesson change for gender?
questions.why: Only un has a feminine form. Everything from deux upward is the same word whatever it is counting.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: Table is feminine, so it takes une, and the N of une is fully said where the N of un is not.

questions.q: Write "two coffees". Café is masculine.
questions.why: The S on cafés is silent, so deux is the only part of the phrase a listener hears carrying the amount.

questions.q: A trader says « Deux kilos ? ». What is the S on kilos doing?
opts: it depends on the next word
questions.why: A plural S is silent in French. The number in front is what makes a quantity audible at all.

rounds.label: What the next word did
rounds.say: The next word decides how a number ends. Six questions on exactly that.

questions.q: Listen. Which is it?
questions.why: Minutes begins on a consonant, so the S of dix is gone entirely and the number is one short syllable.

questions.q: Listen. Which is it?
questions.why: Ans begins on a vowel, so the S wakes as a Z and joins the two words into a single sound.

questions.q: Which number keeps the same ending wherever it stands?
questions.why: Sept keeps its T alone, before a consonant and before a vowel. The other three all move.

questions.q: Someone has written twenty as « vin ». Write it properly.
questions.why: The G and the T are both written and both silent on their own. They are still there, and the T is what wakes up before a vowel.

questions.q: Vingt heures. What has changed?
opts: the vowel is no longer nasal
questions.why: The T of vingt is silent alone and sounds before a vowel. The G stays silent in both.

questions.q: Listen. Which is it?
questions.why: Jours begins on a consonant, so the T of huit drops and the word ends on its vowel.

rounds.label: Out loud, at the counter
rounds.say: Where all of this actually happens.

questions.q: Say it out loud: ten minutes.
questions.why: One short syllable, then the next word. If you can hear an S, that is still the English reading of the page.

questions.q: Count out loud, one to five.
questions.why: Every ending is fully said here, because each number is followed by a pause rather than by a word.

questions.q: The shop opens at nine. Write the two French words.
questions.why: Written it is neuf. Said it is NEU-veur, and that V is the only reason it is hard to catch on a doorway sign read aloud.

questions.q: Listen. What time is it?
questions.why: The Z of treize is part of the word, so it sounds the same before a vowel as it does alone. Trois only gets a Z from the vowel that follows it.

questions.q: A trader says « Ça fait huit euros ». What have you paid?
questions.why: Huit euros joins the T on, which makes eight sound longer than you expect. Dix-huit euros would have started on a D.

questions.q: The one thing that decides how a French number ends:
opts: whether it is written in figures
the word that comes after it
questions.why: The next word decides how a number ends. That is the whole lesson, and it is why no written list can teach it.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Six things you did not have this morning, and one that arrives free in a later lesson.
sections.body: You can count to twenty, and more usefully you can catch a number inside a sentence where it does not sound the way you learned it. That second thing is what a written list can never give you, and it is most of what stands between reading French numbers and hearing them.
points: The next word decides how a number ends. Learn the number and the word after it as one piece.
dix and six have three sounds each: an S alone, nothing before a consonant, a Z before a vowel.
huit and vingt hide a T that drops before a consonant and wakes before a vowel.
neuf becomes a V in front of heures, and nowhere else worth learning yet.
cinq and sept never move, which is what lets you trust that the others do.
One is the only number with a gender: un café, une baguette.
The S you have just learned at dix-sept and dix-huit behaves identically inside 77 and 78, so the seventies arrive already half done.

grammarIntroduced: Gender agreement on the number one: un / une
A consonant at the end of a number sounding, dropping or changing according to the word that follows it
Quantity with de: deux kilos de pommes

overview.introFr: Vingt mots, et le mot qui suit décide comment chaque nombre se termine.

acts.title: The number you already knew
acts.milestone: You have heard one number turn into three.

acts.title: One to ten
acts.milestone: Ten numbers, and you know which of them has a gender.

acts.title: Eleven to twenty
acts.milestone: All twenty, and you can hear two apart from twelve.

acts.title: What the next word does
acts.milestone: You can hear the ending move, and you can make it move.

acts.title: Banked, and used
acts.milestone: You have spelled them, ordered with them and read them off a board.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete.

lessons.reframe: The next word decides how a number ends.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong number, usually a teen and the unit it echoes: six for seize, cinq for quinze, deux for douze.
Uses un where the noun is feminine, or does not notice that one is the only number that asks.
Says every number with the ending it has on its own, so dix minutes keeps an S that French drops.
Does not recognise a number inside a sentence, because in a sentence it does not sound the way it was learned.

drills.title: Ten apart, one sound apart
drills.coach: Listen for the ending. A Z on the end means the bigger one, almost every time.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You hear a word ending in a Z sound, and it is either six or sixteen. Which?
drills.why: Six ends on an S sound. A Z on the end means seize, and that is the only difference between them.

drills.title: Which one is one?
drills.coach: The noun decides, not the number. Masculine takes un, feminine takes une, and nothing above one asks.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Table is feminine. You want one table.
drills.why: Une for a feminine noun, and the N is fully said. Un would be heard immediately.

drills.title: Alone, consonant, vowel
drills.coach: Read the left, say the right out loud. Listen to what happens at the end of the number each time.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Six euros. What is the X doing?
opts: sounding as a Z, joined to euros
drills.why: Euros begins on a vowel, so the X wakes up as a Z and is said with the next word rather than with the number.

drills.title: Same number, twice
drills.coach: Say the left out loud, then the right. They are the same number and they are not the same sound.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You hear DEE mee-nüt at a station. What was said?
drills.why: Dix loses its S before a consonant, so ten minutes is DEE and not DEES. Deux would end on the vowel of DEU.

sheets.title: One to twenty, on one screen

rows.v: one. The only number with a gender.
two. A Z appears before a vowel.
three. A Z appears before a vowel.
four. The final R is said.
five. Never moves.
six. S alone, nothing, then Z.
seven. Never moves. The P is silent.
eight. T alone, drops, comes back.
nine. A V before heures.
ten. S alone, nothing, then Z.
eleven.
twelve. The Z is built in.
thirteen.
fourteen.
fifteen.
sixteen. Nothing of six in it.
seventeen. The S is silent.
eighteen. The S is a Z.
nineteen. The S is a Z.
twenty. A T appears before a vowel.

sheets.title: What each number does before the next word

sections.title: Alone, before a consonant, before a vowel
What to do with this
sections.body: Do not memorise the table. Learn the four moving numbers as PHRASES instead, because that is how you will meet them: dix minutes, dix ans, huit heures, vingt heures, neuf heures. The pattern falls out of the phrases on its own, and a phrase is something you can say at a counter, which a table is not. The two fixed numbers, cinq and sept, are worth knowing precisely because they prove the movement is in the language rather than in your ear. If you cannot hear the difference between sept heures and sept jours, that is correct: there is not one.

shift.title: Why the number you learned sounds wrong in a sentence
shift.body: Six, huit, dix and vingt each have three sounds and one spelling. Said alone, the final consonant is there. Said before a word starting with a consonant, it vanishes with nothing to mark it. Said before a word starting with a vowel, it comes back and joins onto that word. This is invisible on a written list, which is exactly why a learner who studied the list still cannot hear the number in a sentence.

examples.note: Ten, in the three states the whole lesson is built on.
Ten before a consonant: the S is gone.
Ten before a vowel: the S is back, as a Z.

linkZ.title: The sound that comes from nowhere
linkZ.body: When a number ending in a written S or X meets a word starting with a vowel, that letter is pronounced as a Z and is said with the next word rather than with the number. Deux heures, trois ans, six euros, dix ans. Nothing on the page tells you this is coming, and the two words end up sounding like one, which is why a learner counting syllables loses the number entirely.

examples.note: Dix ans, said as one piece.
The same Z, inside a single number.

teens.title: Where the pattern starts, and where there is none
teens.body: Onze to seize are six separate words with nothing to work out. Trying to derive them wastes the effort they need, so learn them the way you learned English numbers, one at a time. From dix-sept the language starts saying its own arithmetic out loud: ten seven, ten eight, ten nine. Knowing where the break falls is worth more than any mnemonic, because it tells you when to stop looking for a rule.

examples.note: Eleven. No pattern in it.
Seventeen. Ten and seven, written out.

unUne.title: The only number with a gender
unUne.body: One is the single number in French that changes for what it counts: un before a masculine noun, une before a feminine one. Every other number from two upward is the same word whatever follows. It is also the same word as the article a, so un café is both one coffee and a coffee. Saying un where the noun wanted une is the most audible beginner error in this lesson, and it is one letter.

examples.note: One, before a masculine noun.
One, before a feminine noun. The N is fully said here.

quantity.title: Asking for two of something
quantity.body: A quantity in French is the number, then the thing, and nothing in between. Deux cafés. Une baguette. Where an amount has a measure it takes de: deux kilos de pommes, never de la or des. The plural S on the noun is silent, so the number in front is the only part of the phrase a listener actually hears carrying the amount. Get the number wrong and nothing else in the sentence corrects it.

examples.note: One of something, ordered.
A measured amount, with de.

hours.title: Where you will hear this every single day
hours.body: Heures starts on a vowel sound, so every number in front of it changes: neuf heures, vingt heures, huit heures, dix heures. That makes the clock the place a learner meets the shifting ending most often and recognises it least, because a time is exactly when you are least able to ask for a repeat. France uses the twenty-four hour clock for anything scheduled, so opening hours, trains and cinema times all run past twelve.

examples.note: Nine, where the F is said as a V.
Twenty, whose silent T wakes up before heures.

recorded.desc: One to twenty, each number said alone with a clear pause after it, ONE take straight through so the pace is even. Do not splice. Also supplies the tapTable rows and the flashcard deck.

dix, then dix minutes, then dix ans, IN THAT ORDER, one voice, one speed, ONE TAKE. This is the lesson's central contrast and across two takes the three are not comparable: the learner hears the difference between the recordings instead of the difference in the number. No pause longer than a beat between the three.

Six numbers in three states each, ONE TAKE PER NUMBER covering all three: six / six jours / six euros, then huit / huit jours / huit heures, dix / dix minutes / dix ans, vingt / vingt minutes / vingt heures, neuf / neuf jours / neuf heures, sept / sept jours / sept heures. Same voice and same speed throughout. The sept row must sound identical in all three, because that is what it is there to prove.

The listening lines, each read straight through as a whole sentence at natural pace and again at 0.65 from the same take. Never assembled from separately recorded words: the joins are exactly where the teaching lives.

Le magasin ouvre à neuf heures.
J'ai deux frères et une sœur.

segments.text: I am Camille. Today is one to twenty, and the thing about them nobody puts on the list.
You can learn twenty words in an afternoon. Catching one of them inside a sentence is a different skill, and it is the one we are building.
Dix.
That is ten, said on its own. Hold on to it, because it is about to change.
Dix minutes.
Same word. No S at all. Minutes starts with a consonant and the S simply goes.
Dix ans.
And now it is back, as a Z, said with the next word. The next word decides how a number ends. That is the whole lesson.
One to ten first. Say each one after me.
Un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq.
Six, sept, huit, neuf, dix.
Eleven to sixteen have no pattern in them. Do not look for one.
Onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize.
From seventeen the language says its own arithmetic out loud: ten seven, ten eight, ten nine.
Dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf, vingt.
Two numbers that are ten apart and one sound apart. Listen for the ending.
Deux. Douze.
Deux ends on a vowel. Douze ends on a Z, and that Z is built into the word, so it never leaves.
Six. Seize.
Now one is the only number that asks about gender. Un café. Une baguette.
Your turn, with nothing in front of you. Order two coffees.
And ask for two kilos of apples.
Now the hard one. Ten minutes, and remember what happens to the S.
One question. I will say a time and you tell me the hour.
Le magasin ouvre à neuf heures.
Nine. The F of neuf softened to a V and ran straight into heures, which is why it did not sound like the neuf you learned.
Three things to keep. The next word decides how a number ends.
Six, huit, dix and vingt move. Cinq and sept never do, and that is how you know the movement is real.
One is the only number with a gender. Un café, une baguette.
À bientôt.

lessons.title: Les nombres 21-100
lessons.intro: Eighty numbers, and above sixty-nine French stops naming them and starts calculating them out loud. Ninety-seven is four words and three operations. The skill this lesson builds is not doing the sum faster, it is not doing it at all.

sections.title: The Number You Could Not Write Down

say.text: Watch this happen. Every number she says is made of words you already know, and you will not catch one of them.

setting.place: The landing outside a flat, after the viewing

beats.text: A flat viewing in Lyon, six in the evening. She likes you, the flat is yours, and she is giving you her number for the keys.

beats.speaker: The landlord
beats.fr: C’est le zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze, quatre-vingt-un, trente-trois.
beats.en: It is zero six, ninety-two, seventy-five, eighty-one, thirty-three.

beats.text: You have zéro six. You were still working out the second one while she said the other three.

beats.prompt: She already has her coat on. What do you do?

options.en: say you have it, and find the number on the listing later
ask her to say it again

followUp.works: Good. Said again, each chunk is a number you can hold. Said once, only the ones you know as shapes survive.
followUp.breaks: The listing carries the agency number, not hers. Watch what she actually said.

beats.speaker: The landlord
beats.stage: She breaks it apart, and every piece is a word you already have.

beats.heading: Four, twenty, twelve. Ninety-two.
beats.body: Every piece is a number you already know. The sum is not the difficulty. Doing it while she keeps talking is, and nobody is quick enough.

wrong.en: three numbers, added at speed

beats.coach: One shape, not three. That is the difference between hearing it and computing it.

beats.speaker: The landlord
beats.stage: She has the keys in her hand.

beats.text: Two numbers, two shapes, and not one of them worth calculating.

closing.text: Learn the shape, not the sum. That is the whole of this lesson, and it starts at twenty-one.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Learn the shape, not the sum. Four things, and the arithmetic is only in the third one.

goals.s: Every number from vingt et un to cent, including the three tens that are sums.
Hear quatre-vingt-douze as ninety-two without stopping to add it up.
Hold five two-digit chunks in a row, which is how every French number is given.

goals.t: Write the two that get written wrong
goals.s: Where et appears and where it does not, and the S that comes and goes on eighty.

sections.title: Two Numbers, One Job
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: One of these is transparent and one is a sum. Your job is identical for both.

cards.label: The easy one
cards.head: Forty-five
cards.body: Forty, then five, joined with a hyphen and in that order. It maps onto English one piece at a time and there is nothing to work out. Most of this range behaves exactly like this.

cards.label: The hard one
cards.head: Ninety-two
cards.body: Four twenties and twelve. Three numbers and two operations for one two-digit figure, and French expects you to have the total while the speaker carries on.

cards.label: The same job
cards.head: One shape each
cards.body: Learn the shape, not the sum. You do not derive forty-five and you should not derive ninety-two. Both are one word meaning one number, and the work is recognition rather than arithmetic.

sections.title: The Tens
sections.say: Five tens, and only four of them are new. Everything from twenty-one to sixty-nine is one of these plus a number you already have.

detail.title: vingt
detail.body: The one you arrive with. Twenty-one to twenty-nine are built on it, and it is the only ten in this lesson you were already taught.

detail.title: trente
detail.body: Thirty. The vowel is nasal, so no N is pronounced: one sound made through the nose, then a T. Thirty-one to thirty-nine follow the same pattern as the twenties.

detail.title: quarante
detail.body: Forty. Two syllables, stressed on the second, with the same nasal vowel and final T as thirty. Nothing about it echoes quatre, which is the trap an eye makes and an ear does not.

detail.title: cinquante
detail.body: Fifty. Two nasal vowels in one word, and a K between them. Cinq is inside it and so is the sound of quinze, which is why fifty and fifteen get mixed up in prices.

detail.title: soixante
detail.body: Sixty, and the last ten in French with a word of its own. Everything above it is built out of this one, which is why it is worth more attention than the four before it.

sections.title: The One Place French Writes And
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: One rule, six numbers, and the single most common written mistake in the whole range.

cards.label: The rule
cards.head: Numbers ending in one
cards.body: Twenty-one is three separate words with et in the middle and no hyphens anywhere. Thirty-one, forty-one, fifty-one and sixty-one all do the same thing.

cards.label: Everything else
cards.head: Two to nine
cards.body: Every other unit joins straight on with a hyphen and no et. That covers forty-three of the forty-nine numbers between twenty-one and sixty-nine, so the rule is the exception.

cards.label: Where it stops
cards.head: Eighty-one and ninety-one
cards.body: Seventy-one keeps the et, as soixante et onze. Eighty-one and ninety-one drop it. There is no reason underneath that you can use, and it is the error people make most.

sections.title: Four Sentences, Four Numbers
sections.say: No table this time. The numbers arrive inside sentences, which is where you will meet them.

lines.fr: J’ai payé vingt-deux euros cinquante pour ce pull.
lines.en: I paid twenty-two euros fifty for this jumper.

lines.fr: Il habite au numéro quarante-sept de la rue.
lines.en: He lives at number forty-seven on the street.

lines.fr: Le premier ministre a quarante-neuf ans cette année.
lines.en: The prime minister is forty-nine this year.

lines.fr: Pendant notre voyage, nous avons visité vingt et une villes.
lines.en: On our trip we visited twenty-one cities.

questions.q: The jumper cost twenty-two euros and how many cents?
questions.why: Cinquante is fifty and quinze is fifteen. They share a vowel and a K, and a price tag is where the difference costs you money.

questions.q: What is his house number?
questions.why: Quarante-sept is forty then seven, hyphenated with no et. Every number below seventy that does not end in one is built exactly that way.

questions.q: The last line says vingt et une, not vingt et un. Why?
questions.why: One is the only number with a gender, so twenty-one changes to match a feminine noun. Nothing above it ever does.

sections.title: Sixty, Then Ten
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: This is where French runs out of words for tens and starts adding them up out loud.

cards.label: Seventy
cards.head: There is no word for it
cards.body: Sixty and ten, written and said exactly that way. From here every number is a small sum, and the speaker assumes you have already done it.

cards.label: Seventy-one
cards.head: And it takes et
cards.body: Sixty and eleven, with the same et that twenty-one takes, because onze is standing exactly where un would. Seventy-one is the last number in the language to get it.

cards.label: The rest
cards.head: Seventy-two to seventy-nine
cards.body: Learn the shape, not the sum. Sixty plus douze through dix-neuf, hyphenated, no et. Nine numbers, and you learned every one of the second halves in the last lesson.

sections.title: Seventy to Seventy-Nine
sections.say: Learn the shape, not the sum. The middle column is here once, so that you can stop needing it.

detail.title: soixante-dix
detail.body: Seventy. Two words you have had since the last lesson, in the order you would guess, meaning something neither of them means alone.

detail.title: soixante et onze
detail.body: Seventy-one. The et is here because onze stands where un would stand. It is the only number above sixty-nine that takes one.

detail.title: soixante-douze
detail.body: Seventy-two. Douze is built with a Z that never leaves, so this one is easier to catch than most of its neighbours.

detail.title: soixante-quinze
detail.body: Seventy-five. Also the postal code that opens every Paris address, which makes it the one number in this table you will read before you hear it.

detail.title: soixante-seize
detail.body: Seventy-six. Seize ends on a Z and six ends on an S, so seventy-six and sixty-six are told apart by the last sound and nothing else.

detail.title: soixante-dix-sept
detail.body: Seventy-seven. Three words and two operations. The S of dix says nothing here, exactly as it says nothing in dix-sept.

detail.title: soixante-dix-neuf
detail.body: Seventy-nine. The S of dix sounds as a Z here, closing the syllable, which is what it did inside dix-neuf. Nothing new was added for the seventies.

sections.title: The Seventies, In Sentences
sections.say: Four lines at normal speed. The number is never the last word, so there is no pause to work it out in.

lines.fr: Au mariage, nous avons invité soixante-dix personnes.
lines.en: At the wedding we invited seventy people.
The flat is seventy-two square metres.

lines.fr: Il reste soixante-quinze pages à lire.
lines.en: There are seventy-five pages left to read.

lines.fr: Mon voisin a soixante-dix-sept ans mais il court encore.
lines.en: My neighbour is seventy-seven and he still runs.

questions.q: How many people were invited to the wedding?
questions.why: Soixante-dix is sixty and ten, which is seventy. There is no separate word for it, and the dix on the end carries the whole difference from sixty.

questions.q: How big is the flat?
questions.why: Soixante-douze is sixty and twelve, so seventy-two. Soixante-deux ends on deux and is sixty-two, one syllable away.

questions.q: How old is the neighbour?
questions.why: Soixante-dix-sept is sixty, ten, seven. The dix in the middle is the only thing separating it from soixante-sept.

sections.title: Four Twenties
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: Eighty does not continue the seventies. It starts again, and it multiplies.

cards.label: Eighty
cards.head: Four twenties
cards.body: Not sixty-twenty, which is what the seventies would have predicted. Eighty is four times twenty, written as two words with a hyphen and said as three syllables.

cards.label: The S
cards.head: It has one, then it does not
cards.body: Eighty takes an S when it stands as exactly four twenties. Put any number after it and the S goes. You will never hear the difference; you will be marked on it in writing.

cards.label: No et
cards.head: Eighty-one
cards.body: Learn the shape, not the sum. Eighty-one refuses the et that twenty-one and seventy-one both take. Eighty-two to eighty-nine hyphenate straight on, using units you already own.

sections.title: Eighty to Eighty-Nine
sections.say: The only row that behaves differently is the first one, and the difference is a letter nobody says.

detail.title: quatre-vingts
detail.body: Eighty, with the S, because nothing follows it. This is the only spelling in the eighties that carries one.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-un
detail.body: Eighty-one. The S has gone because a number follows, and there is no et where twenty-one would have had one.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-deux
detail.body: Eighty-two. Deux ends on a vowel and douze ends on a Z, which is the whole of what separates this from ninety-two.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-cinq
detail.body: Eighty-five. Cinq ends on a K and quinze ends on a Z, so eighty-five and ninety-five are told apart by one sound at the end.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-sept
detail.body: Eighty-seven. Sept keeps its T wherever it stands, which makes this one of the steadier numbers up here.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-huit
detail.body: Eighty-eight. Huit starts on a W sound rather than an H, so the join sounds like one long word.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-neuf
detail.body: Eighty-nine. The last number before the pattern changes again, and the F on the end is fully said.

sections.title: Four Twenties and Ten
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: Ninety is eighty with ten added to it, which means it is a sum inside a sum.

cards.label: Ninety
cards.head: Where the S is already gone
cards.body: Four twenties and ten. Dix is a number, so it takes the S off quatre-vingt exactly the way un did. Ninety has no S and nobody has to remember why.

cards.label: No et again
cards.head: Ninety-one
cards.body: Four twenties and eleven, hyphenated, no et, where seventy-one took one. If you write down a single rule from this lesson, write down that eighty-one and ninety-one refuse it.

cards.label: The long one
cards.head: Ninety-seven
cards.body: Learn the shape, not the sum. Four words and three operations for one two-digit number. Anybody can build it given ten seconds, and ten seconds is not what you get.

sections.title: Ninety to Ninety-Nine
sections.say: Every second half in this table is a word from eleven to nineteen, doing exactly what it always did.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-dix
detail.body: Ninety. Never spelled with an S, because dix is a number and a number after quatre-vingt always removes it.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-onze
detail.body: Ninety-one. No et, where seventy-one took one. This and eighty-one are the two exceptions worth writing down.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-douze
detail.body: Ninety-two. The chunk most people lose in a phone number, because it is one syllable away from eighty-two and both are plausible.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-quinze
detail.body: Ninety-five. Quinze ends on a Z and cinq ends on a K, so this and eighty-five are separated by the last sound alone.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-seize
detail.body: Ninety-six. Seize ends on a Z where six ends on an S, which is the same pair you already told apart at sixteen.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-dix-sept
detail.body: Ninety-seven. Four words, three operations, one two-digit number, and the clearest argument in the language for learning shapes.

detail.title: quatre-vingt-dix-neuf
detail.body: Ninety-nine. The largest number below a hundred, and the one every price ending in ninety-nine cents will hand you without warning.

sections.title: You Already Own Two Thirds of This
sections.say: Twenty of the thirty numbers above sixty-nine end in a word you learned in the last lesson. Nothing new was invented for any of them.

examples.note: Sixty, then onze. The same eleven, and the only one of these that takes et.
Sixty, then quinze. Fifteen, doing what it has always done.
Four twenties, then treize. Thirteen again, inside a number seven times its size.
Four twenties, then seize. Sixteen, which you can already tell apart from six.
Four twenties, then dix-neuf. Nineteen, and the last number before a hundred.

sections.title: Three Traps
sections.say: Two of these are written mistakes and one is a listening one. All three are made in the first week.

errors.wrong: Writing eighty-one as « quatre-vingts-un », with the S left on.
errors.right: Writing it as « quatre-vingt-un », with no S at all.
errors.why: Eighty keeps its S only when it stands as exactly four twenties. Any number after it takes the S away, and this is the version that turns up on forms.

errors.wrong: Writing ninety-one as « quatre-vingt-et-onze ».
errors.right: Writing it as « quatre-vingt-onze », with no et.
errors.why: Twenty-one, thirty-one and seventy-one take et. Eighty-one and ninety-one do not, and there is no rule underneath it to work out.

errors.wrong: Hearing « quatre-vingt-douze » and starting to add up.
errors.right: Hearing it as ninety-two and staying with the speaker.
errors.why: Learn the shape, not the sum. By the time four, twenty and twelve are added together, the next number has already been said.

sections.title: Seventy-Two or Seventy-Six?
sections.say: Six pairs that differ by one syllable in the middle or at the end. Nothing else separates them.

sections.title: Faster Than You Can Add
sections.say: Learn the shape, not the sum. These four arrive at the speed a French speaker actually uses, and the question opens over the line rather than beside it.

lines.en: My grandmother is ninety.

lines.fr: Nous avons parcouru quatre-vingt-douze kilomètres aujourd’hui.
lines.en: We covered ninety-two kilometres today.

lines.fr: Pour ce stylo, j’ai payé quatre-vingt-dix-neuf centimes.
lines.en: For this pen I paid ninety-nine cents.

lines.fr: Pour le dîner, nous avons dépensé quatre-vingt-quinze euros.
lines.en: We spent ninety-five euros on dinner.

questions.q: How old is the grandmother?
questions.why: Quatre-vingt-dix is four twenties and ten. Quatre-vingts alone would have stopped at eighty, and the dix on the end is the entire difference.

questions.q: How far did they travel?
questions.why: Quatre-vingt-douze ends on douze, so ninety-two. Quatre-vingt-deux ends on deux and is eighty-two. One syllable, ten apart.

questions.q: Which cost more, the pen in cents or the dinner in euros?
questions.why: Ninety-nine is quatre-vingt-dix-neuf and ninety-five is quatre-vingt-quinze. Both open identically, and the last syllable is where the two separate.

sections.title: Count Out Loud To a Hundred
sections.say: The four tens, then every number from seventy to ninety-nine, then the ceiling. One at a time, with a pause after each.

sections.title: The Words Themselves
sections.say: Five decks, split where the language splits. Open whichever you want first.

cards.en: sixty, the last with its own word
eighty, and the only one with an S

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French out loud before you flip it.

sections.title: Write What You Hear
sections.say: Four sentences, one for each rule this lesson claims. Build each from the word tiles, and some of the tiles do not belong.

sections.title: Six You Will Hear This Week
sections.say: Every one of these is said once, at normal speed, by somebody who is not going to repeat it.

cases.situation: Being told a price
Giving your age
Reading a house number
Taking a phone number
cases.fr: Zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze, quatre-vingt-un, trente-trois.
cases.en: Zero six, ninety-two, seventy-five, eighty-one, thirty-three.

cases.situation: Asking how far it is
Hearing a room number
cases.fr: Chambre quarante et un, au premier étage.
cases.en: Room forty-one, on the first floor.

sections.title: Taking Her Number
sections.say: The exchange the opening scene went wrong in, and this time you hold it up.
sections.setting: The landing outside the flat in Lyon, with the keys still in her hand.

turns.ai: Alors, vous prenez l’appartement ?
turns.en: So, are you taking the flat?
turns.user: Oui. Vous avez un numéro ?
turns.userEn: Yes. Do you have a number?

alts.fr: Oui, je le prends. Votre numéro ?
alts.en: Yes, I'll take it. Your number?

alts.fr: Oui. Quel est votre numéro de téléphone ?
alts.en: Yes. What is your phone number?

turns.ai: C’est le zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze.
turns.en: It is zero six, ninety-two, seventy-five.
turns.user: Zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze.
turns.userEn: Zero six, ninety-two, seventy-five.

alts.en: Sorry, could you repeat that? Ninety-two?

turns.ai: Et la fin, quatre-vingt-un, trente-trois.
turns.en: And the end, eighty-one, thirty-three.
turns.user: Quatre-vingt-un, trente-trois. C’est noté.
turns.userEn: Eighty-one, thirty-three. Got it.

turns.ai: Le loyer, plus quatre-vingt-quinze euros de charges.
turns.en: The rent, plus ninety-five euros of charges.
turns.user: Quatre-vingt-quinze euros de charges. D’accord.
turns.userEn: Ninety-five euros of charges. All right.

alts.en: All right, ninety-five euros on top.

turns.ai: Parfait. Appelez-moi demain.
turns.en: Perfect. Call me tomorrow.
turns.user: Merci, à demain.
turns.userEn: Thank you, see you tomorrow.

alts.fr: Très bien, je vous appelle demain.
alts.en: Very good, I'll call you tomorrow.
Thank you very much, have a good day.

sections.title: Room Ninety-Two
sections.say: Read it once for the shape. Tap any word you do not know.
sections.text:
It is half past eight and Claire is checking into a small hotel in Dijon.

« Bonjour. J’ai une réservation au nom de Lefèvre. »
« Bonjour. Chambre quatre-vingt-douze, au quatrième étage. »
« Quatre-vingt-douze. Et le petit déjeuner ? »
« De sept heures à dix heures. Ça fait quatre-vingts euros la nuit. »

Claire pays and takes the key. The lift has a sign on it.

« Le code de la porte ? »
« Soixante et onze, puis la touche verte. »
« Soixante et onze. Merci beaucoup. »

glossary.note: The word on every hotel and restaurant confirmation in France.
A hotel room is always given as chambre plus its number, said as one two-digit shape.
Counted above the ground floor, so the fourth is five flights up.
A price followed by la nuit is the nightly rate, not the total.
Touche is a key or a button on a keypad, never a hotel key.

questions.q: What is Claire’s room number, and which floor is it on?
questions.a: Room ninety-two, on the fourth floor.

questions.q: What does the room cost for one night?
questions.a: Eighty euros.

questions.q: What is the door code?
questions.a: Seventy-one, then the green button.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.back: quatre-vingts. Four twenties, with an S.
quatre-vingt-un. The S is gone and there is no et.
quatre-vingt-dix. Four twenties and ten, never an S.
The ones ending in one, up to seventy-one. Not eighty-one, not ninety-one.
cards.say: vingt et un, soixante et onze

cards.back: quatre-vingt-douze. Douze on the end, not deux.

cards.front: A phone number is read as…
cards.back: …five two-digit numbers, never as ten digits.
cent. The ceiling of this lesson.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have counted to a hundred out loud, taken a phone number in two-digit chunks, and written the two rules that only exist on paper. What is left is the part that tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Four rounds. Miss too many in one and you get its drill before the next round starts.

rounds.label: Twenty-one to sixty-nine
rounds.say: The regular half, and the one written rule inside it.

questions.q: Which of these is twenty-one?
questions.why: A number ending in one takes et and drops its hyphens with it. Both hyphenated spellings are wrong and both are written constantly.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Quarante-cinq is forty then five. Quarante alone stops at forty, and cinquante starts on an S rather than a K.

questions.q: Sixty-two is:
questions.why: Only numbers ending in one take et. Everything from two to nine hyphenates straight on to the ten in front of it.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Trente-huit is thirty then eight. Trente stops short and treize is a single word with no second half at all.

questions.q: Someone has written fifty-one as « cinquante-un ». Write it properly.
questions.why: Fifty-one ends in one, so it takes et and loses its hyphen. So do twenty-one, thirty-one, forty-one and sixty-one.

questions.q: How many tens in French have a word of their own?
questions.why: Vingt, trente, quarante, cinquante and soixante. After sixty the language stops inventing words and starts adding them together.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: One is the only number with a gender, so twenty-one becomes vingt et une in front of a feminine noun. Nothing above it does.

rounds.label: Sixty plus ten
rounds.say: The seventies, where the arithmetic starts.

questions.q: Seventy is written as:
questions.why: Seventy is sixty and ten. Septante is real and standard in Belgium and Switzerland, and it is not what France uses.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Quinze ends on a Z and cinq ends on a K. Seventy-five and sixty-five are separated by that one sound.

questions.q: Which of these takes et?
questions.why: Seventy-one is the last number in the language to take et, because onze stands where un would. Eighty-one and ninety-one refuse it.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Seventy-eight is sixty, ten, eight. Sixty-eight has no dix in the middle, and that syllable is the only thing between them.

questions.q: Write seventy-two in French.
questions.why: Sixty and twelve. The second half is a word you already had, which is true of every number from seventy-one to seventy-nine.

questions.q: What is the second half of soixante-seize?
questions.why: Seize is sixteen, so soixante-seize is seventy-six. Six would make it sixty-six, and a Z on the end is what tells the two apart.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: Seventy-one is sixty and eleven, with et between them. Sixty-one ends on un, which is one nasal syllable rather than two.

rounds.label: Four twenties
rounds.say: The eighties and nineties, and the two rules that only exist on paper.

questions.q: Which is eighty, standing on its own?
questions.why: Eighty takes an S when it is exactly four twenties and nothing follows. The other three spellings are all things people write.

questions.q: Someone has written eighty-one as « quatre-vingts-un ». Write it properly.
questions.why: A number after quatre-vingt takes the S away. Eighty-one, eighty-two and ninety all lose it, and only eighty standing alone keeps it.

questions.q: Ninety-one is:
questions.why: No et, no S, and onze rather than ten plus one. Ninety-one is four twenties and eleven, hyphenated straight through.

questions.q: Listen. Which number is it?
questions.why: Douze ends on a Z and deux ends on a vowel. Ninety-two and eighty-two are one syllable apart, and this is the pair that loses people phone numbers.

questions.q: Ninety-seven decomposes as:
questions.why: Four twenties, ten, seven, in four words. Working that out is worth one reading; recognising the shape without it is worth the whole lesson.

questions.q: Someone has written ninety as « quatre-vingts-dix ». Write it properly.
questions.why: Dix is a number, and any number after quatre-vingt removes its S. Ninety therefore never carries one.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: The S on quatre-vingts is written and never said, so eighty and eighty-one are told apart by the un on the end and by nothing else.

rounds.label: At speed, and out loud
rounds.say: Where all of this actually happens.

questions.q: Listen to the whole number. Which pair comes straight after zéro six?

audio.clip: zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze, quatre-vingt-un, trente-trois

questions.why: Five two-digit chunks, said once at speed, and the second one ends on douze. Nothing repeats it and nothing is written down, which is why the chunk has to be a shape you know.

questions.q: Say it out loud: ninety-two.
questions.why: Four syllables run together, with no pause where the arithmetic would be. A pause in the middle is the sound of somebody adding up.

questions.q: A landlord says « quatre-vingt-quinze euros ». What do you owe?
questions.why: Quatre-vingt-quinze is four twenties and fifteen. Quatre-vingt-cinq would have ended on a K sound rather than a Z.

questions.q: Listen. Which room are you in?
questions.why: Douze on the end, so ninety-two. A room number is said once and there is nothing written in front of you to check it against.

questions.q: Count out loud: seventy, eighty, ninety, a hundred.
questions.why: Three of these four are sums and the last one is not. Cent is the ceiling of this lesson and the only round word left in it.

questions.q: You will hear nonante in Belgium. It means:
questions.why: Nonante is ninety and septante is seventy. They are standard where they are used, so recognise them on sight and keep saying quatre-vingt-dix.

questions.q: The fastest way to catch a number at speed is to:
opts: learn each one as one shape
questions.why: Learn the shape, not the sum. A number you recognise costs nothing. A number you compute costs you the next sentence.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Seven things you did not have this morning, and one line about where the numbers go next.
sections.body: You can count to a hundred, and more usefully you can catch a two-digit number inside a sentence at the speed somebody actually says it. That second thing is what a phone number, a price and a room number all require, and it is the thing no written list of the numbers can hand you.
points: Learn the shape, not the sum. A number you recognise costs nothing, and a number you compute costs the next sentence.
Twenty-one to sixty-nine is a ten and a unit, hyphenated. Forty-nine numbers, one pattern.
Seventy is sixty-ten, eighty is four-twenties, ninety is four-twenties-ten. Three sums, learned as three shapes.
et appears on 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71, and nowhere else. Eighty-one and ninety-one refuse it.
quatre-vingts keeps its S only when nothing follows. quatre-vingt-un and quatre-vingt-dix have none.
Seventy-one to seventy-nine and ninety-one to ninety-nine reuse onze through dix-neuf unchanged, so twenty of the thirty hard numbers were already yours.
In Belgium and Switzerland you will hear septante for seventy and nonante for ninety. They mean exactly what they look like.
The next lesson takes the ceiling off: prices, years and quantities above a hundred.

grammarAssumed: The numbers un to vingt, and un against une
A final consonant sounding, dropping or changing according to the word that follows it
grammarIntroduced: Additive and multiplicative number formation: soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix
The conjunction et in numbers ending in one, and its absence at eighty-one and ninety-one
The plural S on quatre-vingts, and its loss before a following number

overview.introFr: Au-dessus de soixante-neuf, le français calcule à voix haute. Apprenez la forme, pas le calcul.

acts.milestone: You have seen the sum, and seen why doing it is the problem.

acts.title: Twenty-one to sixty-nine
acts.milestone: Forty-nine numbers, one pattern, and the one place French writes and.

acts.title: Sixty plus ten
acts.milestone: The seventies, and the last number in the language that takes et.

acts.title: Four twenties
acts.milestone: All thirty above sixty-nine, and both rules that live only on paper.

acts.milestone: Lesson complete.

errorTriggers.description: Decomposes the number instead of recognising it, and loses the rest of the sentence while doing the arithmetic.
Puts et where it does not belong, or leaves it out where it does: quatre-vingt-et-un, or cinquante-un.
Keeps the S on quatre-vingts when a number follows it, or drops it when nothing does.
Hears one number and takes another, usually a pair one syllable apart: eighty-two for ninety-two, seventy-six for seventy-two.

drills.title: The sum, then the shape
drills.coach: Read the left, say the right out loud. Say it once as a whole, not as the pieces it is made of.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You hear quatre-vingt-dix-sept. What is it?
drills.why: Four twenties, ten, seven. Quatre-vingt-sept would have had no dix in the middle, and that syllable is the whole of the difference.

drills.title: Which ones take et?
drills.coach: A number ending in one takes et, up to seventy-one. Eighty-one and ninety-one are the two that refuse it.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Eighty-one is:
drills.why: Eighty-one takes no et and no S. Twenty-one and seventy-one both take et, which is exactly what makes this one worth remembering.

drills.title: With the S, or without
drills.coach: The S survives only when nothing follows. Put any number after quatre-vingt and it goes.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these carries the S?
drills.why: Only eighty standing as exactly four twenties. Ninety has dix after it and eighty-one has un, and both take the S off.

drills.title: One syllable apart
drills.coach: Listen for the opening. Soixante starts on an S sound and quatre-vingt starts on a K, and that is audible before the ending arrives.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You hear a number ending in douze, opening on a K sound. Which?
drills.why: Quatre-vingt opens on a K and soixante on an S, so the first syllable places it before the ending does. Deux ends on a vowel where douze ends on a Z.

sheets.title: Twenty-one to a hundred, on one screen

sections.title: The tens, and the two rules

rows.v: twenty. Taught in a1.02; everything to twenty-nine is built on it.
thirty.
forty.
fifty.
sixty. The last ten with a word of its own.
seventy. Sixty and ten.
eighty. Four twenties, with an S when nothing follows.
ninety. Four twenties and ten, never an S.
a hundred.
21, 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71 only. No hyphens on those six. Never on 81 or 91.
rows.say: vingt et un, soixante et onze

rows.v: quatre-vingts alone. Gone the moment any number follows it.
Seventy and ninety in Belgium and Switzerland, with huitante for eighty in parts of Switzerland. Recognise them; keep the France forms.

sections.title: What to do with this
sections.body: Do not memorise the middle column. Read it once, then cover it and work down the French, because the sums are how the numbers were built and not how they are used. Notice what the table makes obvious: from seventy-one and again from ninety-one, the second half is onze through dix-neuf, exactly as you already learned them. Twenty of these thirty are a word you own attached to a word you own. Learn the ten that are genuinely new, which are the round three plus seventy-seven, seventy-eight, seventy-nine, ninety-seven, ninety-eight, ninety-nine and eighty-one, and the rest fall out.

arith.title: Where French stops naming numbers and starts adding them
arith.body: Up to sixty-nine every ten has its own word. From seventy it does not. Seventy is sixty-ten, eighty is four-twenties, ninety is four-twenties-ten, and the language expects you to hear the total rather than the parts. The cost is not difficulty, it is time: a listener who computes ninety-two has already missed the next thing the speaker said.

examples.note: Seventy. Sixty, then ten.
Eighty. Four twenties.
Ninety. Four twenties and ten.

etRule.title: The one place French writes the word and
etRule.body: A number ending in one takes the word et, and loses its hyphens with it: vingt et un, trente et un, quarante et un, cinquante et un, soixante et un. Seventy-one takes it too, as soixante et onze, because eleven is standing where one would. Eighty-one and ninety-one do not: quatre-vingt-un, quatre-vingt-onze. That inconsistency is the most common written error in this range.

examples.note: Twenty-one, with et and no hyphens.
Seventy-one. Eleven is standing where one would.
Eighty-one, with no et at all.

theS.title: A letter that appears and disappears in writing only
theS.body: Quatre-vingts takes an S when it stands as exactly four twenties, and loses it the moment another number follows: quatre-vingts euros, but quatre-vingt-un and quatre-vingt-dix. Nothing about the sound changes either way, so this is a rule you will only ever meet on paper: a form, an address, a cheque.

examples.note: Eighty on its own, with the S.
Eighty-one, where the S has gone.

teensBack.title: Two thirds of the hard range is something you already have
teensBack.body: Seventy-one to seventy-nine are sixty plus onze through dix-neuf. Ninety-one to ninety-nine are quatre-vingt plus the same nine words. Nothing new is invented for either: a learner who knows eleven to nineteen already holds twenty of the thirty numbers above sixty-nine, which turns a wall into a pattern.

examples.note: Seventy-two. Sixty, then douze.
Ninety-two. Four twenties, then douze.

chunks.title: Why this range is the one you need for a phone number
chunks.body: A French phone number is said as five two-digit numbers, not as ten digits. Zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze, and so on. Someone who cannot catch quatre-vingt-douze at speed cannot write down a number in France, which makes this range the difference between taking a contact and asking for it in writing.

examples.note: A real number, said the way it is really said.
Ninety-two, the chunk most people lose.

regional.title: The simpler forms you will hear outside France
regional.body: Belgium and Switzerland use septante for seventy and nonante for ninety, and parts of Switzerland use huitante for eighty. They mean exactly what they look like and they are standard where they are used. You do not need to produce them. You do need to have been told they exist, because meeting one with no warning sounds like a word you misheard.

examples.note: The France-standard form of seventy.
And of ninety.

recorded.desc: The tens, then seventy through ninety-nine, then cent. Each number said alone with a clear pause after it, ONE TAKE straight through so the pace does not change between the seventies and the nineties. Do not splice. Also supplies the tapTable rows, the card decks and the flashcard deck.

The contrast pairs, ONE TAKE PER PAIR with both members inside it and no pause longer than a beat: soixante-douze / soixante-seize, then quatre-vingt-deux / quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-treize / quatre-vingt-treize, soixante-quinze / quatre-vingt-quinze, quatre-vingts / quatre-vingt-un, soixante / soixante-dix. Same voice, same speed. Across two takes the members are not comparable and the learner hears the difference between the recordings rather than between the numbers.

The eight listening lines, each read straight through as a whole sentence at natural pace and again at 0.65 from the same take. Never assembled from separately recorded words: the number sits mid-sentence in every one of them and the joins are exactly where the teaching lives.
clipIds: J’ai payé vingt-deux euros cinquante pour ce pull.
Il habite au numéro quarante-sept de la rue.
Le premier ministre a quarante-neuf ans cette année.
Pendant notre voyage, nous avons visité vingt et une villes.
Au mariage, nous avons invité soixante-dix personnes.
Il reste soixante-quinze pages à lire.
Mon voisin a soixante-dix-sept ans mais il court encore.
Nous avons parcouru quatre-vingt-douze kilomètres aujourd’hui.
Pour ce stylo, j’ai payé quatre-vingt-dix-neuf centimes.
Pour le dîner, nous avons dépensé quatre-vingt-quinze euros.

recorded.desc: The stairwell scene. A neutral adult female voice for the landlord, warm and slightly rushed, the way somebody sounds who has one more appointment. The line « Quatre-vingt-douze. Quatre. Vingt. Douze. » is the pivot and must be one take: the whole scene turns on the whole and the parts being audibly the same word.
clipIds: C’est le zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze, quatre-vingt-un, trente-trois.

recorded.desc: The four dictation sentences at natural pace, and again at 0.65 from the same take so the slow version is a slowing rather than a re-reading. Full stops audible; no exaggerated word separation, which would give the tile boundaries away. The phone number keeps its chunk pauses and nothing else.
