Ma sœur a soixante et onze ans.

recorded.desc: The landing exchange, landlord lines only, warm and quick. The number is given at the speed a French speaker gives one, with a beat between chunks and none inside them, because a chunk read as separate words teaches the opposite of the mission.
clipIds: C’est le zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze.
Le loyer, plus quatre-vingt-quinze euros de charges.

segments.text: I am Camille. Today is twenty-one to a hundred, and the part of it that is arithmetic rather than vocabulary.
You could learn eighty words from a list. Catching one of them at speed is a different skill, and above sixty-nine it is the only one that matters.
Quatre-vingt-douze.
Ninety-two. Four twenties and twelve, and if you had to work that out just now, we have found the thing to fix.
Quarante-cinq.
Forty, then five. Nothing to work out, and most of this range behaves like it.
Soixante-dix. Quatre-vingts. Quatre-vingt-dix.
Sixty-ten, four twenties, four twenties and ten. Three sums, and none of them is worth doing twice. Learn the shape, not the sum.
The tens first. Say each one after me.
Trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante.
Sixty is the last one with a word of its own. After that the language adds.
Soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix.
And the ceiling, which is the last round word in the language until a thousand.
Cent.
Two numbers one syllable apart. Listen to the end of each.
Quatre-vingt-deux. Quatre-vingt-douze.
Deux ends on a vowel and douze ends on a Z. Eighty-two and ninety-two, and a phone number will hand you both.
Soixante-douze. Soixante-seize.
Now the written rule. Twenty-one takes et. Eighty-one does not, and neither does ninety-one.
Your turn, with nothing in front of you. Say ninety-two.
And seventy-one, which is the one that takes et.
And eighty on its own, where the S is written and never said.
One question. I will give you a number the way somebody would give it to you, and you tell me the middle pair.
Mon numéro est le zéro six, quatre-vingt-douze, soixante-quinze, quatre-vingt-un, trente-trois.
Ninety-two. Said once, at speed, with nothing written down to check it against, which is the only way you will ever get one.
Three things to keep. Seventy is sixty-ten, eighty is four-twenties, ninety is four-twenties-ten.
et appears on twenty-one through seventy-one, and never on eighty-one or ninety-one.
And quatre-vingts keeps its S only when nothing follows it.
À bientôt.

lessons.title: Les grands nombres
lessons.intro: Three words scale every number in French, and all three behave differently. cent takes an S in one position and loses it in the next, mille takes one nowhere, and million takes one everywhere and needs a de as well. None of it is audible, and all of it is on the form.

say.text: Watch this one on the page rather than in the air. Both spellings sound identical, and only one of them is going on the contract.

setting.place: A rental agency, at the desk, with the lease half signed

beats.text: The flat is yours. There is one page left, and one box on it the agent cannot fill in for you.

beats.speaker: The agent
beats.fr: Écrivez la somme en toutes lettres, s’il vous plaît.
beats.en: Write the amount out in words, please.
beats.stage: She turns the form round and puts a pen on the empty line.

beats.text: The figure printed beside the box is 2 500. You have every word you need. deux, mille, cinq, cent.

beats.prompt: You write it out by hand. Which one?

options.en: an S on mille, none on cent
no S on mille, one on cent

followUp.works: Yes. mille has never taken an S, and cent takes one here because nothing follows it.
followUp.breaks: That is the instinct, and it puts the S on the one word that never takes it.

beats.heading: Never on mille.
beats.body: mille never takes an S. cent takes one here, because nothing follows it.

wrong.en: the S on the wrong word

beats.coach: Neither spelling sounds different. The page is the only place it shows.

beats.speaker: The agent
beats.fr: Parfait. Et les charges, cent vingt euros par mois.
beats.en: Perfect. And the charges, one hundred twenty euros a month.
beats.stage: She has the keys on the desk between you.

beats.text: Nobody in that room could have heard which one you wrote. The form could.

closing.text: Three words scale every number in French, and all three behave differently. That is the whole lesson.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. Four things, and the last one is the only one you will ever be marked on.

goals.t: Say any number to a billion
goals.s: cent, mille, million and milliard, and what goes in front of each.

goals.t: Say a price the way it is said
goals.s: The cents arrive as a bare number, with no word and no and between the halves.
The two forms the 1900s take, and the one the 2000s take.
The S that comes and goes on cent, the one mille never takes, and the de after million.

sections.title: Three Words, Two Kinds
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: Three words do all the scaling in French. Two of them behave one way and the third does not, and that is not a detail.

cards.label: The first two
cards.head: They attach directly
cards.body: Two hundred inhabitants, with nothing between the number and the thing counted. cent and mille sit straight against their noun the way an English number does, and there is no extra word to remember.

cards.label: The third one
cards.head: It needs a word to reach
cards.body: Eight million visitors, and the de is not optional. Take it out and the sentence is wrong in the way a missing preposition is wrong: understood, and audibly not French.

cards.label: Why
cards.head: Two kinds, not three rules
cards.body: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. An adjective attaches to what it counts. A noun needs de to reach it, and pluralises like any other noun. Everything else in this lesson falls out of that one line.

sections.title: The S On Cent
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: One letter, three situations, and you will never hear it in any of them.

cards.label: It has one
cards.head: Multiplied, and last
cards.body: A number stands in front of cent and nothing stands after it. That is the only situation in which the S exists. trois cents and cinq cents behave the same way.

cards.label: It loses it
cards.head: A number follows
cards.body: Put anything behind cent and the S goes, whatever the number in front is doing. deux cent cinquante, trois cent trente, six cent cinquante. Same word, same sound, no letter.

cards.label: It never had one
cards.head: Nothing multiplies it
cards.body: One hundred thousand. There is no number in front of cent, so there is nothing to make it plural and no S to lose. A bare cent is always spelled cent.

sections.title: Six Rows, One Rule
sections.say: Read the third column down the page before you read anything else. The pattern is in it and it takes about four seconds.

detail.title: cent
detail.body: A hundred on its own. Nothing multiplies it, so there is nothing to agree with and never an S.

detail.title: deux cents
detail.body: Two hundreds, and nothing after them. Both conditions are met, so this is one of the few forms that carries the letter.

detail.title: deux cent cinquante
detail.body: Still two hundreds, but cinquante is behind it now. The S goes the moment any number follows, and nothing about the sound changes.

detail.title: trois cent trente
detail.body: The height of the Eiffel Tower in metres, and the form people write with an S more often than any other. trente follows, so there is none.

detail.title: cinq cents
detail.body: Five hundreds, nothing after them, so the S is back. Add one euro to it and it becomes cinq cent un, with none.

detail.title: cent mille
detail.body: A hundred thousand. Here cent is the multiplier rather than the thing multiplied, which is the third situation and the one people forget.

sections.title: Cent, Inside Sentences
sections.say: Four lines, and the spelling of cent is different in three of them. You will not hear a single one of those differences, which is the point of doing this now.

lines.fr: Le petit village compte à peine deux cents habitants.
lines.en: The small village has barely two hundred inhabitants.

lines.fr: La tour Eiffel mesure trois cent trente mètres.
lines.en: The Eiffel Tower is three hundred thirty metres tall.

lines.fr: La bibliothèque possède plus de cent mille livres.
lines.en: The library holds more than a hundred thousand books.

lines.fr: Pour deux cent cinquante euros, elle a acheté cette bague.
lines.en: For two hundred fifty euros, she bought this ring.

questions.q: How many people live in the village?
questions.why: deux cents is two hundred, and it is written with an S because nothing follows it. deux mille would have ended on a different word entirely.

questions.q: Which of the four lines spells cent with an S?
questions.why: Only the village line has a number in front of cent and nothing behind it. The tower has trente behind it, the ring has cinquante, and the library never multiplied cent at all.

questions.q: How much did the ring cost?
questions.why: deux cent cinquante is two hundred fifty. The S has gone from cent because cinquante follows it, and no listener could have told you that.

sections.title: Mille Never Moves
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: This is the shortest rule in the lesson and the one most often broken, and those two facts are related.

cards.label: Never
cards.head: No S, in any position
cards.body: Two thousand. Multiplied, final, both at once, neither: mille is spelled the same way in every situation there is. There is no case to learn because there is no exception.

cards.label: Not even here
cards.head: Where cent would take one
cards.body: Eighty thousand, and quatre-vingts has lost its own S because mille follows it. Two rules on one line, and the word in the middle is the only one that never changes.

cards.label: The trap
cards.head: The S you will want to write
cards.body: Eighteen forty. cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. An adjective may agree, and mille is the one that never does. You have just learned an S on cents, and this is where it will follow you.

sections.title: What Each One Is Made Of
sections.say: The middle column is here once, so that you can stop needing it. Tap a row to hear the whole number said as one run.

detail.title: mille
detail.body: A thousand. Said as one syllable, with no un in front of it: French does not say a thousand, it says thousand.

detail.title: deux mille
detail.body: Two thousand, and the form every year from 2000 onward is built on. Written with no S and no hyphen.

detail.title: dix mille
detail.body: Ten thousand. The X of dix goes silent in front of the M, so this is said dee MEEL and not deeks MEEL.

detail.title: quatre-vingt mille
detail.body: Eighty thousand. quatre-vingts drops the S it would carry alone, because mille is a number and follows it. mille adds none of its own.

detail.title: cent mille
detail.body: A hundred thousand. cent multiplies mille here rather than being multiplied itself, so it carries no S either.

detail.title: deux cent mille
detail.body: Two hundred thousand. cent is multiplied by deux now, but mille follows it, so the S still does not appear.

detail.title: mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-dix-neuf
detail.body: Nineteen ninety-nine. Six words, and every rule in this lesson is in it: mille bare, cent with no S because a number follows, and a1.27 doing the last two.

sections.title: Mille, At Full Speed
sections.say: The number is never the last word in these, so there is no pause afterwards to work anything out in.

lines.fr: Le stade peut accueillir quatre-vingt mille spectateurs.
lines.en: The stadium can hold eighty thousand spectators.

lines.fr: Ce professeur a formé plus de deux mille étudiants.
lines.en: This teacher has trained more than two thousand students.

lines.fr: Depuis mille huit cent quarante, ce moulin tourne sans arrêt.
lines.en: Since eighteen forty, this mill has turned without stopping.

lines.fr: Ce camion a parcouru plus de deux cent mille kilomètres.
lines.en: This lorry has covered more than two hundred thousand kilometres.

questions.q: How many people fit in the stadium?
questions.why: quatre-vingt mille is eighty times a thousand. huit mille would have been eight thousand, and the two open on completely different syllables.

questions.q: The mill line gives a year. Which?
questions.why: mille huit cent quarante is a thousand, nine hundred less than two thousand, and forty. Years before 2000 are built on mille or on the century, never on anything else.

questions.q: How far has the lorry travelled?
questions.why: deux cent mille is two hundred thousand: deux multiplies cent, and cent multiplies mille. Dropping either word changes the answer by a factor of a thousand.

sections.title: Million Is A Noun
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: One word behaves differently from the other two, and once you know why, both of its oddities stop being oddities.

cards.label: It takes de
cards.head: A noun cannot touch what it counts
cards.body: A million inhabitants. The de is what reaches the thing being counted, and in front of a vowel it becomes d’. cent and mille need nothing at all in that gap.

cards.label: It agrees
cards.head: And it pluralises
cards.body: Eight million visitors. millions carries an S in every plural, with no condition attached: not only when it is final, not only when multiplied. It behaves like the noun it is.

cards.label: And milliard
cards.head: Same word class, same two habits
cards.body: Two billion bottles. cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. milliard is a noun too, so it takes the S and the de for exactly the same reason, and you learn it for free.

sections.title: Five Sentences, Five Sizes
sections.say: Each of these is roughly ten times the one before it. Read the French, hear it, then say what size it is before you grade yourself.

sections.title: The Whole Ladder
sections.say: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. Six rungs, and the last two are the ones that behave like things rather than like numbers.

detail.title: cent
detail.body: The rung you arrived with. a1.27 taught it as a ceiling and this lesson uses it as a floor.

detail.title: mille
detail.body: A thousand, said with no article in front of it and spelled the same way for ever.

detail.title: dix mille
detail.body: Ten thousand. French has no single word for it, which English does not either, so nothing new is being asked of you here.

detail.title: cent mille
detail.body: A hundred thousand, and the last rung before the words change class. Everything up to here is an adjective.

detail.title: un million
detail.body: A million, and here it takes un in front of it where mille did not. That is your first sign it is a noun rather than a number word.

detail.title: un milliard
detail.body: A thousand million, which is the English billion. Be careful with the French word billion, which is a thousand times larger again and almost never what you want.

sections.title: Which Rung Was That?
sections.say: These do not sound alike when you meet them one at a time. In a sentence, mille and million share their opening and are three noughts apart.

sections.title: Three Traps
sections.say: One per rule, and all three are written mistakes. Nobody will ever hear you make any of them.

errors.wrong: Writing two thousand as « deux milles », with the S carried over from cents.
errors.right: Writing it as « deux mille », which is how it is spelled in every position.
errors.why: mille has no plural form. The S you just learned belongs to cent and only to cent, and this is the first place it will follow you across.

errors.wrong: Writing three hundred thirty as « trois cents trente », with the S left on.
errors.right: Writing it as « trois cent trente », with no S at all.
errors.why: cent keeps its S only when nothing follows it. trente follows, so it goes. This is the exact shape of the quatre-vingts rule you already met.

errors.wrong: Saying « huit millions visiteurs », with nothing between the two.
errors.right: Saying « huit millions de visiteurs », with the de in place.
errors.why: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. A noun reaches what it counts through de, and dropping it is the one mistake in this lesson a listener actually notices.

sections.title: A Price Is One Run
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: The cents are the part nobody teaches, and they are the part that arrives last and fastest.

cards.label: The shape
cards.head: Currency, then a bare number
cards.body: Twenty-two euros fifty, written 22,50. There is no word for centimes in a shop and no et joining the halves. Waiting for either means the sentence ends before you have understood it.

cards.label: A longer one
cards.head: The same shape, six words
cards.body: One hundred twenty-four euros eighty, written 124,80. It arrives as one run at one speed, and the only clue that the price has finished is that the speaker stops.

cards.label: On the label
cards.body: The same price, printed. French writes the decimal as a comma and separates thousands with a space, so this is a hundred and twenty-four euros rather than twelve thousand. The comma is never said aloud.

sections.title: Four Prices, Said Once
sections.say: The question opens over the line rather than beside it, which is what a counter does too.

lines.fr: Ce billet de train coûte cent vingt-quatre euros quatre-vingts.
lines.en: This train ticket costs one hundred twenty-four euros eighty.

lines.fr: Le boulanger vend des baguettes à un euro vingt.
lines.en: The baker sells baguettes at one euro twenty.

lines.fr: Sophie a payé son loyer, six cent cinquante euros, hier matin.
lines.en: Sophie paid her rent, six hundred fifty euros, yesterday morning.

lines.fr: Mon salaire mensuel est de deux mille cinq cents euros.
lines.en: My monthly salary is two thousand five hundred euros.

questions.q: What does the train ticket cost?
questions.why: quatre-vingts on the end is the cents, said as a bare number with no word in front of it. Nothing in the sentence marks where the euros stop and the cents start except the word euros.

questions.q: Which of the four is the largest?
questions.why: deux mille cinq cents is 2 500, against 650 for the rent. mille is what puts the salary an order of magnitude above everything else in the list.

questions.q: A baguette at un euro vingt costs:
questions.why: The bare number after the currency is always the cents. Read as digits it is 1,20, and the comma is what an English reader has to remember not to treat as a thousands mark.

sections.title: What The Label Actually Says
sections.say: Nothing to practise here. Read it once, then check the comma before you check the digits for the rest of your life.

detail.title: The space is the thousands mark
detail.body: Where English puts a comma, French puts a space or a narrow gap. A gap in a price is never a decimal point and never a typing error.

detail.title: The comma is the decimal point
detail.body: This is the misreading that costs real money, because it moves the size by a factor of a hundred in the direction that makes a bargain look like a mistake.

detail.title: A price with cents
detail.body: Written with the comma, said with nothing in its place. The comma has no spoken form at all in a price, only in a measurement.

detail.title: The two conventions together
detail.body: No thousands gap because there are no thousands, and a comma because there are cents. This is the price from the last two missions, on paper.

rows.say: mille deux cent trente-quatre euros cinquante-six

detail.title: Both marks in one figure
detail.body: A space for the thousands and a comma for the cents, in the same number. Once you have read this one, every French price tag is readable.
detail.say: mille deux cent trente-quatre euros cinquante-six

sections.title: Two Ways To Say A Year
sections.say: Anything before 2000 has two spoken forms and both are correct. Anything after it has one.

detail.body: Both forms are current. The mille form works for every year in every century, which is why it is the one to reach for when you are not sure.
The dix-neuf cent form is the one most people use in speech for the twentieth century, and it is the one you will hear from anyone born in it.
cent has no S in either form, because quinze follows it both times. The two forms differ only in how the century is named.
From 2000 the second form stops existing. There is no vingt cent, and nobody has ever said one.
Three words, and mille sits bare in the middle of them as it always does. English says twenty ten and French does not.
This year. Every year of your life from here is deux mille plus a number you learned in the last two lessons.

sections.title: The Words Themselves
sections.say: Four decks, split where the grammar splits rather than where the numbers do. Open whichever you want first.

cards.en: a hundred, and the one you arrived with
a million inhabitants, with the de

sections.title: Flip And Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French out loud, and spell it in your head, before you flip.

sections.title: Say The Ladder Out Loud
sections.say: From a hundred to two billion, one card at a time. The two at the end are the ones with a de in them, so say the whole phrase.

sections.title: Write What You Hear
sections.say: Five sentences, one for each claim this lesson makes. Build each from the word tiles, and some of the tiles do not belong in it.

sections.title: Six You Will Meet This Month

sections.title: Signing For The Flat
sections.say: The exchange the opening scene went wrong in, and this time you have the pen and the rule.
sections.setting: Back at the agency desk, with the form the right way round.

turns.ai: Alors, le loyer est de huit cent cinquante euros par mois.
turns.en: So, the rent is eight hundred fifty euros a month.
turns.user: Huit cent cinquante euros. D’accord.
turns.userEn: Eight hundred fifty euros. All right.

alts.fr: Huit cent cinquante par mois, c’est noté.
alts.en: Eight hundred fifty a month, noted.

alts.fr: Huit cent cinquante ? C’est dans mon budget.
alts.en: Eight hundred fifty? That's within my budget.

turns.ai: Et le dépôt de garantie, deux mille cinq cents euros.
turns.en: And the deposit, two thousand five hundred euros.
turns.user: Deux mille cinq cents. Je l’écris en toutes lettres ?
turns.userEn: Two thousand five hundred. Shall I write it out in words?

alts.fr: Deux mille cinq cents euros, d’accord.
alts.en: Two thousand five hundred euros, all right.

alts.fr: Deux mille cinq cents, en une fois ?
alts.en: Two thousand five hundred, in one payment?

turns.ai: Oui, s’il vous plaît. Et les charges, cent vingt euros.
turns.en: Yes, please. And the charges, one hundred twenty euros.
turns.user: Cent vingt euros de charges. C’est noté.
turns.userEn: One hundred twenty euros of charges. Got it.

alts.fr: Cent vingt euros par mois aussi ?
alts.en: One hundred twenty euros a month as well?

alts.fr: D’accord, cent vingt euros de charges.
alts.en: All right, one hundred twenty euros of charges.

turns.ai: L’immeuble date de mille neuf cent trente-huit.
turns.en: The building dates from nineteen thirty-eight.
turns.user: Mille neuf cent trente-huit. Il est beau.

alts.en: It dates from nineteen thirty-eight? Magnificent.

sections.title: At The Ticket Desk
sections.say: Read it once for the shape. Tap any word you do not know.
sections.text:
It is a Tuesday in October and Marc is buying tickets at a museum in Paris.

« Bonjour. Deux billets, s’il vous plaît. »
« Bonjour. Ça fait trente-quatre euros cinquante. »
« Trente-quatre euros cinquante. Vous prenez la carte ? »
« Bien sûr. Le musée reçoit huit millions de visiteurs par an. »

Marc pays and looks at the leaflet she gives him.

« Le bâtiment date de mille cinq cent quarante-six ? »
« Oui. Et la pyramide, de mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-neuf. »
« Mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-neuf. Merci beaucoup. »

glossary.note: Also a banknote: un billet de cinquante euros is a fifty-euro note.
The standard way a total is announced at any counter in France.
A bank card. Vous prenez la carte is the question you will ask most often.
Followed by a year, said in either of the two forms this lesson teaches.
The glass entrance in the courtyard, opened in nineteen eighty-nine.

questions.q: What do the two tickets cost?
questions.a: Thirty-four euros fifty, written 34,50.

questions.q: How many visitors does the museum get in a year?
questions.a: Eight million, and the sentence needs de after millions to say so.

questions.q: In which year was the pyramid built?
questions.a: Nineteen eighty-nine, said as mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-neuf.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: When does cent take an S?
cards.back: Only when a number multiplies it and nothing follows: deux cents.

cards.front: When does mille take an S?
cards.back: Never, in any position, in any quantity.

cards.front: What does million need that cent does not?
cards.back: de, before what it counts: huit millions de visiteurs.
deux cent cinquante. No S, because cinquante follows.
cent mille. No S on either word.
deux milliards de bouteilles. An S and a de, like any noun.
vingt-deux euros cinquante. No word for the cents.
One and a quarter. The comma is the decimal point.
mille neuf cent trente-huit, or dix-neuf cent trente-huit.
deux mille dix. After 2000 there is only one form.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have said every multiplier out loud, read five quantities that climb by a factor of ten, and written the three rules that only exist on paper. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Four rounds, one per rule and one for where they get used. Miss too many in a round and you get its drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The S on cent
rounds.say: One letter, three situations, and no sound at all.

questions.q: Which of these carries the S?
questions.why: deux cents is multiplied by deux and nothing follows it, which is the only situation the S survives. The other three each fail one half of that.

questions.q: Someone has written five hundred as « cinq cent ». Write it properly.
questions.why: cinq multiplies cent and nothing comes after it, so the S belongs. Add anything at all behind it, as in cinq cent un, and it goes again.

questions.q: Three hundred thirty is written:
questions.why: trente follows cent, so there is no S, and French numbers below a hundred take hyphens while the multipliers above them do not.

questions.q: Listen. Which did you hear?
questions.why: Two hundred, with the S nobody can hear. The other three are the same opening followed by another word, and each of them is a different order of magnitude.

questions.q: Write two hundred fifty in French.
questions.why: No S, because cinquante follows cent. This is the form the corpus had no card for until this lesson, and the one people write with an S.

questions.q: cent mille has no S on cent. Why?
questions.why: There is no number in front of cent here, so it was never made plural and had no S to lose. cent is multiplying mille rather than being multiplied.

questions.q: Someone has written a hundred fifty euros as « cents cinquante euros ». Write it properly.
questions.why: Nothing multiplies cent here, so there is no S even before you notice that cinquante follows it. Both halves of the rule refuse it.

rounds.label: Mille, which never moves
rounds.say: The shortest rule here, and the one you are most likely to break.

questions.q: In how many situations does mille take an S?
questions.why: None at all. mille has no plural form, which makes it the one thing in this lesson that has to be memorised rather than worked out.

questions.q: Someone has written ten thousand as « dix milles ». Write it properly.
questions.why: The S came across from cents, which is where it belongs and the only place it does. dix mille is spelled this way whatever comes before or after it.

questions.q: Write the year 1840 out in words, the form that works for any century.
questions.why: mille takes no S and cent loses its own because quarante follows. dix-huit cent quarante is also correct, and the mille form is the one that never lets you down.

questions.q: Listen. How many spectators?
questions.why: Eighty thousand. Without mille the same opening is eighty, and the syllable that separates them is the only thing standing between the two figures.

questions.q: quatre-vingt mille has no S on quatre-vingt. Why?
questions.why: mille is a number and it follows quatre-vingt, which takes the S off exactly as un does in quatre-vingt-un. That is a1.27 rule meeting this one on a single line.

questions.q: As a quantity, 1 999 is written:
questions.why: mille bare, cent with no S because a number follows, and quatre-vingt with none for the same reason. The dix-neuf cent form exists but it is for years, not quantities.

questions.q: Say it out loud: two hundred fifty thousand.
questions.why: Four words with no S anywhere in them, because a number follows cent and mille never carries one. Said as one run, the way a figure is given.

rounds.label: Million, and the word after it
rounds.say: One word class, two habits, and both of them are visible.

questions.q: Eight million visitors is:
questions.why: The S because millions is a plural noun, and de because a noun cannot touch what it counts. des would make it some of the visitors rather than that many.

questions.q: Someone has written « trois millions utilisateurs ». Write it properly.
questions.why: The de is missing, and in front of the vowel of utilisateurs it elides to d’. This is the one mistake in the lesson a French listener actually hears.

questions.q: Why does deux cents habitants have no de in it?
questions.why: An adjective attaches straight to its noun and needs nothing in between. Only million and milliard, which are nouns, have to reach across a de.

questions.q: Write two billion in French.
questions.why: milliard is a noun, so the plural S is unconditional: it does not wait for the word to be final the way cent does. A French milliard is the English billion.

questions.q: Listen. How many bottles?
questions.why: Two billion. million and milliard open on the same two syllables and separate only at the end, which is a thousandfold difference decided by one sound.

questions.q: A French milliard is:
questions.why: A thousand million, which is what English calls a billion. The French word billion means a thousand times more again and is almost never the one you want.

questions.q: Which two words attach straight to what they count, with nothing in between?
questions.why: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. That is the whole prediction: two of them behave like adjectives and need no de, and the third behaves like a thing and does.

rounds.label: Prices, years and the page
rounds.say: Where all of this actually happens, which is a counter and a shelf.

questions.q: The label says 1,25 €. That is:
opts: one thousand two hundred fifty euros
questions.why: The comma is the decimal point in France and the space is the thousands mark. Read the other way round, a bargain looks like a mistake.

questions.q: Listen. What does the ticket cost?
questions.why: The bare number after euros is the cents. There is no word marking the boundary, so the word euros itself is the only signal that the second half has started.

questions.q: « vingt-deux euros cinquante » means:
questions.why: Twenty-two euros and fifty cents, said with no word for the cents and no et. A speaker expecting either is still waiting when the price is over.

questions.q: Someone wrote « sept euros et cinquante centimes ». Write it the way it is actually said.
questions.why: Understandable and not what anybody says. The currency is named once and the cents follow it as a bare number, which is what makes a price one run rather than two.

questions.q: 2010 said aloud is:
questions.why: From 2000 there is one form and it is built on deux mille. There is no vingt cent, and no et in any number above a hundred.

questions.q: Write the price 124,80 the way it is said, in words.
questions.why: cent with no S because a number follows, then the cents as a bare number, and quatre-vingts keeps its own S because nothing comes after it.

questions.q: Say the price out loud: 124,80 euros.
questions.why: One run at one speed, with no pause where the comma is. A pause in the middle is the sound of somebody reading the label rather than saying the price.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Eight things you did not have this morning, and one of them is a comma.
sections.body: You can say any number in French up to a billion, which sounds larger than it is: the numbers were never the difficulty. What you actually have is the three spelling rules that separate a form filled in correctly from one that has to be done again, and a way of reading a price tag that does not put the decimal point in the wrong place.
points: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun. An adjective attaches to what it counts and a noun reaches it through de.
cent takes an S only when a number multiplies it and nothing follows: deux cents, but deux cent cinquante and cent mille.
mille never takes an S, in any position, in any quantity. This is the one to memorise outright.
million and milliard are nouns: an S in every plural, and de before what they count. huit millions de visiteurs, and d’ before a vowel.
A price names the currency and then says the cents as a bare number: vingt-deux euros cinquante is 22,50.
French writes a space for thousands and a comma for the decimal, so 1 234,56 and never 1,234.56.
Years before 2000 have two spoken forms, mille neuf cent and dix-neuf cent. From 2000 there is only deux mille.
A French milliard is the English billion. The French word billion is a thousand times larger and rarely what you want.

grammarAssumed: Every number from un to cent, including the S on quatre-vingts and where et appears
A final consonant sounding, dropping or changing according to the word that follows it
grammarIntroduced: The agreement of cent when multiplied and final, and its loss before a following number
The invariability of mille in every position
million and milliard as nouns of quantity: plural agreement, and de before the noun counted
The French decimal comma and space-separated thousands, and how a price is said aloud

overview.introFr: Trois mots multiplient tous les nombres français, et les trois ne se comportent pas de la même façon. Rien ne s’entend, tout s’écrit.

acts.title: mille, which never moves
acts.milestone: The shortest rule in the lesson, and the one you will not now break.

acts.title: million, and the word after it
acts.milestone: All three rules, and the whole ladder from a hundred to a billion.

acts.title: Prices, years, and out loud

acts.milestone: Lesson complete.

lessons.reframe: cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun.

errorTriggers.description: Keeps the S on cent when a number follows it, or drops it when nothing does, or adds one to a cent that was never multiplied.
Writes mille with an S, carrying the plural across from cents. The corpus contains no example of this, so the lesson has to stage it.
Drops the de after million or milliard, or leaves the plural S off it, treating a noun as if it were a number-adjective.
Hears a price as two separate numbers, or reads a written decimal comma as a thousands separator and gets the size wrong by a factor of a hundred.

drills.title: With the S, or without
drills.coach: The S survives only when a number multiplies cent AND nothing follows it. Both halves, every time.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these carries the S?
drills.why: Only deux cents. The first has cinquante behind it and the third has no number in front of cent at all.

drills.title: mille, in every position
drills.coach: Read the left, say and spell the right. Look at the middle word every time and notice that it never changes.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Ten thousand is:
drills.why: mille has no plural form at all. The S you are reaching for belongs to cent, and to nothing else in this lesson.

drills.title: What comes after the number
drills.coach: million and milliard are nouns, so they reach what they count through de. cent and mille sit straight against it.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Eight million visitors is:
drills.why: The S because it is plural, and the de because a noun cannot touch what it counts. Both, or the sentence is wrong.

drills.title: Written, and said
drills.coach: Read the figure on the left, say the price on the right. The comma is never spoken and the space is never a decimal point.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: A shelf label reads 2,50 €. What does it cost?
drills.why: The comma is the decimal point in France. Read as a thousands mark it turns a two-euro item into a two-hundred-euro one.

sheets.title: The three rules, on one screen
contains: Every case of the S on cent

sections.title: Every case, side by side
cols: Why it is spelled that way
rows: Nothing multiplies it, so no S.
Nothing multiplies it, and un follows. No S twice over.
Multiplied, and nothing follows. The S.
Multiplied, but cinquante follows. No S.
Multiplied, but trente follows. No S.
Multiplied, and still no S. There is no case where it has one.
mille takes the S off quatre-vingts and adds none itself.
cent is the multiplier here, not the multiplied. No S.
cent is multiplied but mille follows it. No S.
A noun, so it reaches its noun through de, elided to d’.
A plural noun: the S is unconditional and the de is required.
milliard is a noun too, with exactly the same two habits.

sections.title: What to do with this
sections.body: Read the third column down the page once, then cover it and work down the first. Two of the fourteen rows carry an S on cent and both of them end on cent, which is the whole rule in a sentence: the S needs a number in front and nothing behind. Not one row carries an S on mille, and every million and milliard row carries both an S and a de. If you remember only one thing from this sheet, make it that mille is invariable, because it is the rule with no logic underneath it and the only one you cannot reconstruct from the reframe.

sheets.title: What the page says and the voice does not

sections.title: The comma and the space
sections.body: French writes the decimal point as a COMMA and separates thousands with a space, often a narrow gap. English does exactly the reverse, so the same figure is 1 234,56 in France and 1,234.56 at home. That gap is never a typing error, and that comma is never a thousands mark. Reading it the English way moves the size by a factor of a hundred or a thousand, in the direction that makes a cheap thing look expensive and an expensive thing look like a bargain. It is the one convention on this sheet that costs real money, and there is nothing to practise: check the comma before you check the digits.

sections.title: Saying a price
sections.body: 124,80 € is said cent vingt-quatre euros quatre-vingts. The comma has no spoken form at all in a price: the currency is named once and the cents follow it as a bare number, with no word between them and no et. The word centimes does exist and is used on official documents and almost nowhere else, so nobody at a till will say it and you never need to. The euro sign goes AFTER the figure with a space in front of it, as in 12,50 €. In front of the figure is the English habit.

sections.title: Saying a measurement
sections.body: Outside a price the comma IS said, and the word for it is virgule. 1,25 litre is un virgule vingt-cinq litre, and 1,25 % is un virgule vingt-cinq pour cent. So the same written mark is silent on a price tag and spoken on a fuel pump, a set of scales or a weather forecast. If what follows the figure is money, say nothing; if it is a unit, say virgule.

sections.title: Both forms of a year
sections.body: Any year before 2000 has two spoken forms and both are correct: mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-quinze, or dix-neuf cent quatre-vingt-quinze. The mille form works for every century and is the one to reach for when you are not sure; the century form is what most people say for the twentieth. From 2000 the second form stops existing and there is only deux mille sept, deux mille dix, deux mille vingt-six. There is no vingt cent and nobody has ever said one. On a contract or a cheque you will also see years spelled mil neuf cent, with one L. It is an old legal convention, it is not wrong, and that is the only place you will meet it.

multiplier.title: The three words that decide the size of everything in front of them
multiplier.body: cent, mille and million are the only words in French that scale a number. Everything else you have learned counts up to ninety-nine and stops. These three take that ninety-nine and make it a hundred times, a thousand times or a million times larger, and the number in front of them says how many of the multiplier there are. Two of them behave one way and the third behaves another, which is the entire difficulty of this lesson.

examples.note: Two hundreds.
Two thousands.
Two millions, and this one is a noun.

centS.title: A letter that appears only when cent is both multiplied and last
centS.body: cent takes an S in exactly one situation: a number stands in front of it AND nothing stands after it. deux cents, trois cents, cinq cents. Put any number behind it and the S is gone, as in deux cent cinquante and trois cent trente. Leave the front empty and there was never one to lose, as in cent mille. Nothing about the sound changes in any of the three, so this is a rule you will only ever meet on paper.

examples.note: Multiplied and final, so the S is there.
Multiplied, but cinquante follows, so the S has gone.
Not multiplied at all, so there was never one.

invariable.title: mille, which has never taken an S in the history of the language
invariable.body: mille is spelled the same in every position and every quantity. deux mille, dix mille, cent mille, and a year like mille huit cent quarante. There is no situation, none at all, in which it takes an S. Learners over-generalise the S they just learned on cents and write it anyway, which is the single most common written error in this range, and it is the one thing here that has to be memorised rather than worked out.

examples.note: Two thousand, and no S.
Ten thousand, and still no S.
A hundred thousand, and neither word carries one.

nounNumber.title: Why million needs a word to reach what it counts, and cent does not
nounNumber.body: million and milliard are nouns, not number-adjectives, so they behave like any other French noun of quantity. They take an S in the plural and they need de before the thing they count: huit millions de visiteurs, deux milliards de bouteilles. In front of a vowel that de becomes d’. cent and mille attach straight to their noun with nothing in between, which is why deux cents habitants has no de in it and huit millions de visiteurs must.

examples.note: The de, elided to d’ before a vowel.
Eight millions, and then de before what they are.
milliard does exactly the same thing.

bareCents.title: How a French price says the part after the comma
bareCents.body: French names the currency and then says the cents as a plain number with nothing in front of them. vingt-deux euros cinquante is 22,50. There is no word for centimes in ordinary speech and no et joining the halves, so the whole price arrives as one run at one speed. Somebody waiting for "euros and fifty cents" will still be waiting when the sentence is over.

examples.note: 124,80. Six words, one price, no pause anywhere in it.

decimalComma.title: The punctuation mark that means the opposite of what you expect
decimalComma.body: French writes the decimal point as a COMMA and separates thousands with a space or a narrow gap. So 1 234,56 is one thousand two hundred thirty-four point five six, and 1,25 is one and a quarter rather than a thousand two hundred fifty. An English speaker reading a shelf label straight off gets the size wrong by a factor of a thousand, in the direction that makes cheap things look expensive. This is reading knowledge and there is nothing to practise: see it once, and check the comma before you check the digits.

examples.note: Written 124,80 and said with no comma in it at all.

recorded.desc: The multiplier ladder from cent to deux milliards, each said alone with a clear pause after it, ONE TAKE straight through so the pace does not change between the hundreds and the billions. Do not splice. Also supplies the three tapTables and the card decks.

The contrast pairs, ONE TAKE PER PAIR with both members inside it and no pause longer than a beat: deux cents / deux cent cinquante, deux mille cinq cents / deux mille cinq cents read twice identically for the scene break, mille / million, cent mille / un million. Same voice, same speed. The scene-break pair is deliberately the SAME utterance twice: the learner is being shown that the two spellings are phonetically identical, so any difference between the takes would teach the opposite.

The prices. Each one is ONE UTTERANCE AT NATURAL SPEED with no pause anywhere inside it, and specifically none between the currency and the cents: vingt-deux euros cinquante is a single run and a gap after euros teaches the opposite of the mission it sits in. Read each again at 0.65 from the same take so the slow version is a slowing rather than a re-reading.

recorded.desc: The years, each in BOTH forms back to back where both exist, one take per year: mille huit cent quarante then dix-huit cent quarante, and so on. The two forms must be comparable, which they are not across two takes. The three years from 2000 are read once each, because they have no second form.

The twelve listening lines, each read straight through as a whole sentence at natural pace and again at 0.65 from the same take. Never assembled from separately recorded words: the number sits mid-sentence in every one of them and the joins are exactly where the teaching lives.

segments.text: I am Camille. Today is the numbers above a hundred, and the part of them that is grammar rather than size.
Three words do the scaling in French, and all three spell themselves differently. None of that is audible, which is why it is worth twenty minutes.
Deux cents. Deux mille. Deux millions de.
One of those has an S you cannot hear, one has none anywhere, and one needs a word after it. That is the lesson.
Deux cents habitants.
Two hundred inhabitants. cent is multiplied and nothing follows it, so it takes an S.
Deux cent cinquante euros.
Same word, and the S has gone, because cinquante is behind it now. cent and mille are adjectives. million is a noun.
The hundreds first. Say each one after me.
Deux cents. Trois cents. Cinq cents.
Now the thousands, and listen for a letter that is not there.
Mille. Deux mille. Cent mille.
And the two that are nouns, which need a word before what they count.
Un million d’habitants. Deux milliards.
Two figures three noughts apart. Listen to the middle of each.
Cent mille. Un million.
A hundred thousand and a million. In a sentence they open on the same sound and separate at the end.
Now a price, which arrives as one run. There is no word for the cents.
Cent vingt-quatre euros quatre-vingts.
A hundred twenty-four euros eighty, written with a comma you will never hear.
Your turn, with nothing in front of you. Say two hundred fifty.
Now a hundred thousand, where neither word takes an S.
And a million inhabitants, with the word that reaches them.
One question, and it is the only rule here a listener can hear you break. I will say a quantity and you tell me the word that sits between the number and the thing.
Le musée du Louvre reçoit huit millions de visiteurs par an.
de. Leave it out and the sentence is still understood and audibly not French, which is the only mistake in this lesson anybody will notice out loud.
Three things to keep. cent takes an S only when a number multiplies it and nothing follows.
mille never takes one, in any position. That is the one to memorise rather than work out.
And million and milliard take an S and a de, because they are nouns.
À bientôt.

lessons.title: Les articles indéfinis
lessons.intro: Anyone can learn that un is masculine and une is feminine. What stays hard is knowing which article a sentence wants at all, and that is not a fact about the noun. It is a fact about what the person listening already knows.

say.text: Watch this go wrong on a word you already know. Nothing here is mispronounced and nothing here is rude.

setting.place: A square outside the station

beats.text: Seven in the evening in Annecy. Your train was late and you have nowhere to sleep.
A woman is closing up a flower stall in the square. You know every word you need.

beats.prompt: You have one sentence. Which one?

options.en: asking where the hotel is
saying you are looking for a hotel

followUp.works: Yes. You do not have a hotel in mind, and un is how you say so.
followUp.breaks: Every word is correct. Watch what it does anyway.

beats.speaker: The woman
beats.stage: She waits for a name you do not have.

beats.heading: You asked for one she knew
beats.body: The article carries information English hides in tone. Le says the two of you are already thinking of the same hotel. She was not, so the question had no answer and she had to stop and ask.

wrong.en: the hotel, the one we both know

right.en: a hotel, any hotel, I have none in mind

beats.coach: Same noun, same street, one syllable different. One of them is a question she can answer.

beats.speaker: Second try
beats.en: I am looking for a hotel.

beats.speaker: The woman
beats.fr: Il y a un hôtel derrière la gare.
beats.en: There is a hotel behind the station.
beats.stage: She is already pointing.

beats.speaker: The woman
beats.fr: L'hôtel est petit, mais il est bon.
beats.en: The hotel is small, but it is good.
beats.stage: Now that she has named it, it is the hotel for both of you.

beats.text: She said un, then le, about the same building, four seconds apart.

closing.text: Un introduces it. Le assumes you already know it. She used both, about one building, inside one exchange.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Un introduces it. Le assumes you already know it. By the end of this lesson you will know which of the two a sentence is asking for, and the four places your English will tell you the wrong one.

goals.s: Bring a thing into a conversation the way French brings it in, so the other person can follow you.
Switch to le, la or les the moment they know which one you mean, and hear when somebody does it to you.
Put a word where your English puts nothing, which is the one form you have no instinct for.
Generalisations, jobs, negatives and plurals: the four places the transfer from English quietly fails.

sections.title: Three Words, One Job
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: Three forms, one job between them. The job is the interesting part, so meet the forms quickly.

cards.label: The job
cards.head: What all three do
cards.sub: a · a · some, in the sense English leaves out
cards.body: Un introduces it. Le assumes you already know it. Every card after this one is that sentence in a different situation.

cards.label: Singular
cards.head: un and une
cards.body: Which of the two is decided by the noun, and you settled that in the gender lesson. Nothing new is being asked of you here.

cards.label: Plural
cards.head: des
cards.body: The plural of both. English has no word here at all, which is why this is the form that goes missing.

sections.title: Un or Une?
sections.say: Revision, not teaching. Twelve nouns you have already met, and the only question is which article.

groups.label: Read the noun, say the article

sections.title: The One English Throws Out
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: This is the form with no English twin, and the one you will drop for months if nobody points at it.

cards.label: The gap
cards.head: English has nothing here
cards.body: Read the English again. There is no word in front of apples, so there is nothing in your own language reminding you that French wants one.

cards.label: In a sentence
cards.head: It is not optional
cards.body: Leave des out and the sentence is wrong, not casual. French does not have a bare plural noun the way English does.

cards.label: Not only food
cards.head: des amis
cards.body: Friends are not a quantity of anything, which is what makes this the clearest example. Des is simply the plural of un and une.

cards.label: Already yours
cards.head: Three you know
cards.body: You have met these as vocabulary and never asked why they came with a word attached. This is why.

sections.title: Same Noun, Two Articles
sections.say: Un introduces it. Le assumes you already know it. Tap any row to hear both halves back to back.

detail.title: un hôtel · l’hôtel
detail.body: Say un hôtel to someone who has none in mind. Say l’hôtel once one of you has named it. Ask for l’hôtel too early and you get asked which one.
detail.say: Je cherche un hôtel. L'hôtel est complet.

detail.title: une chambre · la chambre
detail.body: Il reste une chambre, and one line later, je prends la chambre. Nothing about the room changed. What changed is that it is now in the conversation.
detail.say: Il reste une chambre. Je prends la chambre.

detail.title: des croissants · les croissants
detail.body: Il y a des croissants puts them on the table. Les croissants sont pour moi asks about the ones now sitting there. Des would be asking about croissants everywhere.
detail.say: Il y a des croissants. Les croissants sont pour moi ?

detail.title: un livre · le livre
detail.body: Je cherche un livre is a request anybody can help with. Je cherche le livre is a request that needs you to already know which book.

detail.title: une voiture · la voiture
detail.body: J'ai une voiture introduces it. La voiture est dehors assumes you have already been told about it. Both are ordinary; only one of them can go first.
detail.say: J'ai une voiture. La voiture est dehors.

sections.title: A Room for One Night
sections.say: Un introduces it. Le assumes you already know it. Three nouns arrive in this passage and every one of them comes back. Watch the article change.
sections.text: It is seven in the evening in Annecy and Marc has nowhere to sleep. He stops a woman closing up a stall in the square. « Pardon madame. Je cherche un hôtel. » She points past the station without looking up. « Il y a un hôtel derrière la gare. » Ten minutes later he is standing at the desk of that same hotel. « Bonsoir. L'hôtel est complet ? » The woman behind the desk turns the book round so he can see it. « Non. Il reste une chambre. » He does not ask to see it first. « Je prends la chambre. » The next morning she puts a plate down in front of him. « Il y a des croissants. » He has not paid for breakfast and he says so with his eyebrows. « Les croissants sont pour moi ? » She is already walking away. « Bien sûr. »

glossary.note: Any hotel. Neither of them has one in mind, and that is what un says.
The one behind the station. She named it, so now there is only one.
It arrives here. Nobody has mentioned a room before this line.
One line later. It is the room now, because they have both heard about it.
English has nothing in front of croissants. French has des, every time.
The ones on the plate between them. Des would ask about croissants in general.
What a hotel is when there is nothing left. The opposite of il reste une chambre.

questions.q: Marc says un hôtel and so does the woman. Why does neither of them say l’hôtel?
questions.a: Neither has a particular hotel in mind, and un is how French says that.

questions.q: What changes between « Il reste une chambre » and « Je prends la chambre »?
questions.a: Nothing about the room. It is now in the conversation, so they both know which one.

questions.q: Why « Les croissants sont pour moi ? » rather than « Des croissants »?
questions.a: The croissants are on the plate in front of him. Des would be asking about croissants in general.

sections.title: Two Words, One Vowel
sections.say: Un against une, and des against les. Both pairs are one vowel apart and both carry the whole meaning.

lines.en: I am looking for a hotel.
The hotel is full.
There are croissants.
Are the croissants for me?

questions.q: In the first line, has the speaker got a particular hotel in mind?
opts: Yes, one they have stayed in
Yes, the one by the station
questions.why: Un is the whole answer. It says the listener has no way of knowing which one, and does not need to.

questions.q: The second line uses l’. What must have happened before it?
opts: Nothing, l’ can open a conversation
questions.why: Le and la point at something both people already have. Something has to put it there first.

questions.q: Which pair is the harder one to tell apart at normal speed?
opts: both, and for the same reason
questions.why: Each pair differs by one vowel and nothing else, so the ear has no consonant to hold on to. Slow the audio down and both separate cleanly.

sections.title: Six Moments This Week
sections.say: Six real moments. In every one of them the article is doing the work, not the noun.

cases.situation: Asking for somewhere to stay, in a town you do not know
cases.en: I am looking for a hotel.

cases.situation: Asking about the hotel they have just recommended
Telling someone what you saw on the table
cases.fr: Il y a des livres sur la table.
cases.en: There are books on the table.

cases.situation: Ordering at a counter, for the first time
Saying what you like, in general, forever
Saying what you do for a living

sections.title: Which One Goes Here?
sections.say: One question. Read both halves before you answer, because the first half is what decides it.

check.q: You have just said « Il y a une chambre libre. » Now you want to take it. Which?
check.why: You put the room into the conversation one sentence ago, so you are both thinking of the same one. Une would introduce a second, different room.

sections.title: Liking the Whole Thing
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: The single most common mistake an English speaker makes with French articles, and it is not the one you would guess.

cards.label: The trap
cards.head: I like coffee
cards.body: Not "I like the coffee". English puts nothing in front of coffee and French names the whole of it, so the article that looks wrong is the right one.

cards.label: Why le
cards.head: The ultimate known thing
cards.body: Un introduces it. Le assumes you already know it. A whole category is the most known thing there is, so it takes le.

cards.label: The test
cards.head: Try adding "in general"
cards.body: If the English still makes sense with "in general" on the end, French wants le, la or les. If it does not, you probably want un.

sections.title: What Your Job Takes
sections.say: English requires a word here and French forbids it, so this error is guaranteed and it is audible. Tap any line.

examples.note: Nothing in front of the job. Je suis un professeur is the sentence to unlearn.
Same after il est and elle est. The gap is the grammar.
And after tu es and vous êtes. Every form of être behaves the same way.
Médecin does not change for a woman. Only the article would have, and there is none.
The one place it comes back. C’est points at a person; il est describes one.

sections.title: Say No and Watch
sections.say: Negate a sentence and un, une and des all turn into the same word. The definite article does not move at all.

rows.say: J'ai une voiture. Je n'ai pas de voiture.

detail.title: une becomes de
detail.body: Not pas une voiture, and not pas la voiture. Under a negative the indefinite collapses to de and the noun is left bare behind it.

rows.say: J'ai un stylo. Je n'ai pas de stylo.

detail.title: un becomes de
detail.body: The same word, whatever the gender was. De does not agree with anything, which is one fewer thing to get right.

rows.say: J'achète des pommes. Je n'achète pas de pommes.

detail.title: des becomes de
detail.body: All three indefinites go the same way. The plural noun stays plural; only the word in front of it changes.

rows.say: J'aime le café. Je n'aime pas le café.

detail.title: le does not move
detail.body: This is the half that makes the rule usable. If the article survives the negative it was le, la or les. If it collapsed to de it was un, une or des.

rows.say: Elle a un portable. Elle n'a pas de portable.

detail.title: One more, from the corpus
detail.body: You have met this sentence before as vocabulary. It is the same rule you have just watched three times.

sections.title: Four Traps
sections.say: Four sentences an English speaker produces in their first month. One per screen.

errors.wrong: Saying « J’aime café » for "I like coffee".
errors.right: Saying « J’aime le café » for "I like coffee".
errors.why: English leaves the slot empty when you talk about a thing in general. French names the whole of it, and naming the whole of it takes le.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je suis un professeur » for "I am a teacher".
errors.right: Saying « Je suis professeur » for "I am a teacher".
errors.why: After être a job goes in bare. English needs the article and French forbids it, so this is the one place a correct English instinct is always wrong.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je n’ai pas une voiture » for "I do not have a car".
errors.right: Saying « Je n’ai pas de voiture » for "I do not have a car".
errors.why: Un, une and des all collapse to de under a negative. Le, la and les do not move, which is how you can tell afterwards which one you had used.

errors.wrong: Saying « J’achète pommes » for "I am buying apples".
errors.right: Saying « J’achète des pommes » for "I am buying apples".
errors.why: Your English has nothing in front of apples, so nothing reminds you that French wants des. A bare plural noun is not a thing French has.

sections.title: The Words Themselves
sections.say: Three decks. Every card carries its article, because the article is the half you are here for.

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French, article and all, before you flip.

cards.front: a hotel (you have none in mind)
I do not have a car
I am looking for a hotel

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Six sentences. The tiles include articles you did not hear, so put the right one where it belongs.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: Fourteen nouns, said with their articles. The article is the part the mic is listening for.

sections.title: Your Turn at the Desk
sections.say: The same hotel, and this time you hold up the whole exchange. Watch your own articles change.
sections.setting: The small hotel behind the station in Annecy, half past seven in the evening.

turns.ai: Bonsoir monsieur. Je peux vous aider ?
turns.en: Good evening sir. Can I help you?
turns.user: Bonsoir. Je cherche une chambre.
turns.userEn: Good evening. I'm looking for a room.

alts.fr: Bonsoir. Vous avez une chambre libre ?
alts.en: Good evening. Do you have a room free?
Good evening, I'd like a room.

turns.ai: Pour combien de nuits ?
turns.en: For how many nights?
turns.user: Pour une nuit, s’il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: For one night, please.

turns.ai: Il reste une chambre au deuxième étage.
turns.en: There is one room left on the second floor.
turns.user: Je prends la chambre.
turns.userEn: I'll take the room.

alts.fr: Très bien. C’est une grande chambre ?
alts.en: Very good. Is it a big room?

turns.ai: Le petit-déjeuner est à sept heures.
turns.en: Breakfast is at seven.
turns.user: Il y a des croissants ?
turns.userEn: Are there croissants?

turns.ai: Bien sûr. Voici la clé.
turns.en: Of course. Here is the key.
turns.user: Merci beaucoup. Bonne soirée !
turns.userEn: Thank you very much. Good evening!

alts.en: Thank you very much, see you tomorrow.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: Which article does something new to the listener take?
cards.back: Un introduces it. Le assumes you already know it. So un, une or des.

cards.front: You mentioned a room last sentence. Now?
cards.back: la chambre. It is in the conversation, so it is the room.
des pommes. The gap in English is not a gap in French.
J'aime le café. The whole of it, so le.
Je suis professeur. Nothing after être.

cards.front: J'ai une voiture. Now say you do not.
cards.back: Je n'ai pas de voiture. Un, une and des all become de.

cards.front: J'aime le café. Now say you do not.
cards.back: Je n'aime pas le café. Le does not move.

cards.front: You ask « où est l’hôtel » in a town of forty hotels
cards.back: You get « Lequel ? », because le claimed you both knew which one.

cards.front: The one place the article comes back after a job
cards.back: C'est un professeur. C’est points; il est describes.

cards.front: How do you tell which article a sentence had?
cards.back: Negate it. If it collapsed to de it was indefinite. If it survived it was not.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a question fail on one word, read a passage where three nouns arrive and come back, sorted the nouns you already knew, met the four places your English points the wrong way, spelled the sentences and said them out loud. What is left is the part that tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Five rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round’s drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: Which of the three
rounds.say: The forms, quickly.

questions.q: You want a book. Any book. You have not said anything about books yet.
questions.why: Nothing about books is in the conversation yet, so the listener has no way of knowing which one. That is exactly what un is for.

questions.q: Which article does voiture take the first time you mention it?
questions.why: Voiture is feminine, which you settled in the gender lesson. This lesson only decides indefinite against definite; the noun decides the rest.

questions.q: Fix this. « J’achète pommes. »
questions.why: English has nothing in front of apples so nothing reminds you. French has no bare plural noun: des is the plural of un and une and it is not optional.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: Un and une are one vowel apart and there is no consonant to hold on to. Slow it down and the rounded ü of une separates cleanly.

questions.q: Write the plural of « un croissant ».
questions.why: Both halves change: the article becomes des and the noun takes its s. English would give you croissants and nothing in front of it.

rounds.label: First mention, second mention
rounds.say: The rule the whole lesson is about.

questions.q: You are new in town and you stop a stranger. « Excusez-moi, je cherche ___ hôtel. »
questions.why: They have no way of knowing which hotel you mean, and you do not mean a particular one. Ask for the hotel and you get asked which one.

questions.q: She has just told you there is a hotel behind the station. You ask: « ___ hôtel est loin ? »
questions.why: She named it one sentence ago, so you are both thinking of the same building. Le and la become l apostrophe in front of a vowel sound.

questions.q: Fix the second sentence. « Il reste une chambre. Je prends une chambre. »
questions.why: Une a second time introduces a second, different room. The room is already in the conversation, so it is the room now.

questions.q: The croissants are on the plate between you. Complete: « ___ croissants sont pour moi ? »
questions.why: You can both see them, so you can both point at the same ones. Des would be asking about croissants in general.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: Des and les are the same pair of problems as un and une: one vowel, no consonant, and the whole meaning riding on it.

rounds.label: The whole of it
rounds.say: Where English leaves the slot empty.

questions.q: Fix this. « J’aime café. »
questions.why: You are talking about coffee as a whole, and French names the whole of it. A category is the most known thing there is, so it takes le.

questions.q: "I like coffee" in French is:
questions.why: Le café here is not "the coffee". It is coffee itself, which is what English says with no article at all.

questions.q: Which of these is about coffee in general rather than one cup of it?
opts: Il y a des cafés ici.
questions.why: The other three are all one cup or several places. Only the fourth is a statement about coffee itself, and that is the one that takes le.

questions.q: You hate tomatoes. All of them, always. Complete: « Je déteste ___ tomates. »
questions.why: Hating, liking, loving and preferring all name the whole category, and a whole category takes le, la or les. Des would be some particular tomatoes.

questions.q: Fix this. « Elle aime un thé. »
questions.why: Un thé is one cup, which nobody likes in general. Aimer takes the whole of the thing, so le.

rounds.label: Jobs and negatives
rounds.say: Two rules English gives you no help with.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je suis un professeur. »
questions.why: After être a job goes in bare. English needs the article and French forbids it, so a correct English instinct is wrong every time here.

questions.q: Which one is right?
questions.why: Nothing between est and the job. The third would mean she is the lawyer you have both already been talking about.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je n’ai pas une voiture. »
questions.why: Un, une and des all collapse to de under a negative. De agrees with nothing, so there is only one form to remember.

questions.q: « J’aime le café. » Now say you do not.
questions.why: Le does not move under a negative. That asymmetry is what lets you work out afterwards which article you had used.

questions.q: You are pointing at someone across the room and telling a friend what they do.
questions.why: C'est points at a person and takes the article back. Il est describes one and takes nothing. Those are the only two shapes.

rounds.label: Put it together
rounds.say: All of it, mixed.

questions.q: You have mentioned no hotel and neither has she. Fix this. « Je cherche l’hôtel. »
questions.why: L apostrophe claims the two of you already have the same building in mind. She does not, so the question has no answer and she has to stop and ask.

questions.q: « J’ai une voiture. » Write it again, saying you do not.
questions.why: Une goes to de, not to pas une and not to pas la. The car never entered the conversation, so there is nothing for la to point at.

questions.q: Say it out loud, to a stranger in a town you do not know.
questions.why: Un runs straight into hôtel and the two become one three-syllable block. A gap between them is what makes it sound like two separate words.

questions.q: Fix this. « Il y a livres sur la table. »
accept: Il y a des livres sur la table.
questions.answer: Il y a des livres sur la table.
questions.why: The books are new to the listener so they take des. The table is one you can both see, which is why la is already right.

questions.q: What does the choice between un and le actually depend on?
opts: Whether the noun is masculine or feminine
Whether the thing is one or many
Whether the sentence is a question
Whether the person listening already knows which one you mean
questions.why: It is a fact about the conversation rather than about the noun. Gender decides un against une; this decides un against le, and it is the part that stays hard.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Five things you did not have this morning.
sections.body: You can bring something into a French conversation and hand it over properly, which is most of what an article is for. The four traps below are worth more to you than the forms are: the forms take a morning and the traps take a year, and you have just had them all named.
points: Un introduces it. Le assumes you already know it.
Des is the plural of both, and English puts nothing where French puts des.
Talking about a thing in general takes le, la or les. J’aime le café.
After être a job takes nothing at all. Je suis professeur.
Under a negative un, une and des become de. Le, la and les do not move.

grammarAssumed: Every noun carries a gender, and the article in front of it is the choice that gender makes
Elision of le and la to l apostrophe in front of a vowel
grammarIntroduced: The indefinite article un, une and des, including the plural English has no equivalent for
First mention against second mention: which article a sentence wants is decided by what the listener already knows
Generalisation takes the definite article in French where English takes none
No article at all after être in front of a profession, and its exception after c’est
Under negation un, une and des all reduce to de, while le, la and les are unchanged

overview.introFr: Un, une, des : le choix ne dépend pas du nom, mais de ce que votre interlocuteur sait déjà.

acts.title: The three you choose between
acts.milestone: You have watched one word decide whether a question could be answered.

acts.title: First mention, second mention
acts.milestone: You can hear the moment a thing stops being new.

acts.title: Where English misleads you
acts.milestone: Four habits named, before they cost you a year.

acts.title: Banked, and used
acts.milestone: You have spelled them, said them and held a whole exchange with them.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete.

lessons.reframe: Un introduces it. Le assumes you already know it.

errorTriggers.description: Leaves the plural bare, because English has nothing in front of it to translate.
Uses le, la or les on a first mention, so the listener is asked to know something they do not.
Drops the article when talking about a thing in general, the way English does.
Puts un or une in front of a job after être, because English requires it there.
Keeps un, une or des under a negative instead of collapsing all three to de.

drills.title: The word English leaves out
drills.coach: Read the English on the left. Say the French on the right, out loud, and do not let the article go missing.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are telling someone what is on the table. There are books.
opts: Il y a livres sur la table.
Il y a des livres sur la table.
Il y a le livre sur la table.
drills.why: French has no bare plural noun. The books are new to the listener, so des.

drills.title: New to them, or already theirs?
buckets: They do not know it yet
drills.coach: Read each line and ask one question: could the other person point at it yet? If not, it is un, une or des.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You have just said there is a room free. Now you take it.
drills.why: You put the room into the conversation yourself one sentence ago. Une would introduce a second one.

drills.title: In general, or just this one?
drills.coach: Add "in general" to the English. If it still makes sense, French wants le, la or les.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: "I like coffee." Which one?
drills.why: Coffee as a whole. English leaves the slot empty and French names the category, which takes le.

drills.title: After être, nothing
drills.coach: The left is what English gives you. Say the French before you flip, and leave the gap where English wants a word.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Someone asks what you do. You teach.
drills.why: Nothing between suis and the job. The third one says you are the teacher they were expecting.

drills.title: Say no and watch it move
drills.coach: Say the negative out loud before you flip. Three of these collapse to de and one does not move at all.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which sentence has an article that did NOT change under the negative?
drills.why: Le, la and les survive a negative untouched. Only un, une and des collapse to de.

sheets.title: Every choice in this lesson, on one screen

sections.title: New to them, or already known
The four places English points the wrong way

rows.v: J'aime le café, not J'aime café. A whole category takes le, la or les.
Je suis professeur, not Je suis un professeur. Nothing after être.
C'est un professeur. The one place the article comes back.
Je n'ai pas de voiture. Un, une and des all become de.
Je n'aime pas le café. Le, la and les do not move.
J'achète des pommes, not J'achète pommes. French has no bare plural noun.

sections.title: What this lesson does not cover
sections.body: Des has a second life as a quantity word, in sentences about how much of something there is rather than how many things. That belongs with its own family and it is a whole lesson, so it is not started here. Everything above treats des as exactly one thing: the plural of un and une. Where you have seen it in front of food in this lesson, it is still that.

introducing.title: The article for something new to the listener
introducing.body: Use these the first time a thing comes into the conversation, when the person you are talking to has no way of knowing which one you mean and does not need to. Un for a masculine noun, une for a feminine one, des for more than one. English does the same thing with a and an, so you already have the instinct. The half English does not give you is des, because English simply leaves the gap empty.

examples.note: Any hotel. That is the point of the question.
Croissants she has not mentioned before.

known.title: The article that assumes you both know which one
known.body: Use these once the thing is already in the conversation, or when there is only one of it, or when you are talking about the whole category rather than any particular example. It is a claim about the listener as much as about the noun: le says you can both point at the same thing. Say it too early and you get asked which one you mean.

examples.note: The hotel she just named. Now there is only one.
Coffee as a whole. Nobody has to ask which coffee.

secondMention.title: The moment the article changes
secondMention.body: A thing arrives on un, une or des and stays on le, la or les for the rest of the conversation. Nothing about the noun changed; what changed is that the other person now knows about it. This is why a single sentence cannot show you the rule, and why the passage in this lesson says every noun twice.

examples.note: It arrives.
One line later it is the room, for both of you.

noArticle.title: What a job takes after être
noArticle.body: After je suis, tu es, il est and elle est, a job goes in bare: je suis professeur, elle est avocate. English requires a and French forbids it, so this error is guaranteed and it is audible.
