The one place the article comes back is after c’est, which points at a person rather than describing one: c’est un professeur.

examples.note: Nothing in front of the job.
The exception, and the only one: c'est takes the article.

deUnderNo.title: What un, une and des become under a negative
deUnderNo.body: Say you do not have something and all three collapse into de. J’ai une voiture becomes je n’ai pas de voiture, never pas une voiture. The definite article does not do this: j’aime le café becomes je n’aime pas le café, unchanged. That asymmetry is the whole rule, and it is the fastest way to hear which article you were using.

examples.note: Une went to de.
Le stayed exactly where it was.

wholeThing.title: Liking a thing in general
wholeThing.body: J’aime le café is "I like coffee", not "I like the coffee". When you like, love, prefer or hate something, French names the whole of it and that takes le, la or les. English puts nothing there, which is why this is the single most common mistake an English speaker makes with French articles. If the sentence would work with the words "in general" after it, you want le.

examples.note: Coffee in general, for the rest of your life.
Open-air markets as a category, not one market.

recorded.desc: Twelve nouns with their articles, six on un and six on une, read in ONE TAKE by ONE voice at ONE speed. The whole contrast is a single unstressed syllable, so a pair split across two takes has the learner comparing two performances instead of two articles. Do not over-articulate un: its vowel is nasal, and a careful reading that lets the n through removes the only thing separating it from une.

The two minimal pairs, un against une and des against les, each pair recorded BACK TO BACK IN ONE TAKE by the same voice at the same speed, in the same way sons.07 pins rec-h-pairs. Both pairs are one vowel apart. Also the four passage lines at natural pace, then again at 0.65, so the learner can hear where un ends and hôtel begins without a gap being inserted between them.

The four English-speaker traps, wrong form then right form, with a clear beat between them so the learner hears the difference rather than a correction. J’aime café / J’aime le café. Je suis un professeur / Je suis professeur. Je n’ai pas une voiture / Je n’ai pas de voiture. J’achète pommes / J’achète des pommes. Read the wrong version plainly, not comically.

lessons.title: Les articles définis
lessons.intro: French has four ways to say the, and which one you need depends on the noun's gender, its number and the sound it starts with. The harder half is that English lets you use none of them and French never does.

say.text: Watch this happen. You know both words, you say both words, and the sentence still is not French.

setting.place: A friend's kitchen table

beats.text: Lunch is finished and the plates are still on the table. Claire is filling the cafetière and asking everyone what they want.

beats.speaker: Claire
beats.fr: Et toi, qu'est-ce que tu aimes ?
beats.en: And you, what do you like?

beats.text: You have known the word for coffee since your first week. This is the easiest question anyone will ask you all afternoon.

beats.prompt: You answer her. Which one?

options.en: the words you actually need
the same words, and one more

followUp.works: Right, and the extra word is not politeness or emphasis. French has no version of that sentence without it.
followUp.breaks: Every word there is a real French word, and the sentence is not French. Watch what Claire does next.

beats.speaker: Claire
beats.stage: She says it back to you with the word you left out, gently, the way you would to a child.

beats.heading: The word you left out
beats.body: Every word you said was a French word. The sentence was not, because English lets you drop the article in front of a general idea and French has no way to do that at all.

wrong.en: what you said

beats.coach: Nobody misunderstood you. They heard a learner.

beats.speaker: Claire
beats.fr: Le matin, le café. Le soir, le thé.
beats.en: Coffee in the morning. Tea in the evening.
beats.stage: Four nouns in one breath, and every one of them arrives with a word English would not have used.

beats.text: You were not misunderstood, and you were not corrected. You were repeated back to.

closing.text: When English says nothing, French says le. That is the decision, and you make it before you open your mouth.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: When English says nothing, French says le. By the end of this you will hear the gap before you fall into it.

goals.s: Put the article where English gives you nothing, which is where you currently lose the sentence.
Choose le, la, l apostrophe or les for any noun you know, in three questions.
Two of those three questions never ask what a1.03 taught you to store.
Tell l heure from le hibou, which is the only place the difference ever shows.

sections.title: Where English Says Nothing
sections.frSub: Là où l'anglais ne dit rien
sections.hint: Swipe through the five cards.
sections.say: When English says nothing, French says le. Here is what that looks like in four sentences you would get wrong today.

cards.label: A thing in general
cards.head: Coffee, all coffee
cards.fr: Elle aime le café au lait.
cards.body: English says coffee. French says le café. The English sentence has nothing at all in front of the noun, and that empty slot is the whole problem, because there is no gap on the page for you to notice.

cards.label: A whole category
cards.head: Cats, meaning cats
cards.fr: Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
cards.sub: Cats love sleeping in the sun
cards.body: Not these cats. Cats as a species. English marks that by removing a word and French marks it by keeping one, which is the same idea running in opposite directions.

cards.label: A subject you study
cards.head: A language, a skill
cards.body: Languages, school subjects, sports and instruments all behave this way. Le français, les mathématiques, le tennis, le piano. English drops the word in front of every one of them.

cards.label: The other direction
cards.head: Where French drops it
cards.fr: Elle est infirmière et elle travaille la nuit.
cards.sub: She is a nurse and she works nights
cards.body: This one runs both ways in a single sentence. French refuses an article in front of a job after être, where English insists on one, and then adds la in front of a time where English gives nothing. a1.11 owns the first half.

cards.label: What le stands for
cards.head: One line, four words
cards.body: When English says nothing, French says le. Le there is shorthand for whichever of the four the noun actually takes. Working out which is the next act, and it is the easy half.

sections.title: The Rule In Twelve Lines
sections.say: Read the English first, then the French. Every English line is missing a word the French line has.

examples.note: A language. English has nothing in front of it and French has le.
Feminine, so la. The English still has nothing.
Plural in French, singular in English, and only French marks it at all.
An activity. Same shape, same missing word.
Sports take the article every time, and English never gives them one.
A type of food rather than particular plates on a table.
Preferring a kind of thing is the most common place this catches people.

examples.fr: Je préfère le sport en équipe.
examples.note: English plural, French singular, and the article arrives anyway.

examples.fr: Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
examples.en: Cats love sleeping in the sun.
examples.note: A whole species as the subject of the sentence.

examples.fr: Les abricots sont chers cette semaine.
examples.note: Apricots as a thing you buy, not the ones in your bag.

examples.fr: Les oiseaux volent vers le sud en hiver.
examples.note: Birds in general. Two articles here, and English has neither.

examples.fr: Le sport rend les enfants plus forts.
examples.note: Two bare nouns in the English and two articles in the French, in one short line.

sections.title: Le, La, L' and Les
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Four cards, one form each. This is the part you will have from a single reading, and it is the smaller half of the lesson.

cards.label: Masculine singular
cards.head: le
cards.body: For a masculine noun that starts on a consonant sound. This is the form the corpus shows you most: nearly eight hundred entries in this app begin with it, which is why it feels like the default even though it is one of four.

cards.label: Feminine singular
cards.head: la
cards.body: For a feminine noun that starts on a consonant sound. Nothing in the word maison tells you it is feminine, which is a1.03's whole subject and the reason you were asked to store the article with the noun.

cards.label: Before a vowel sound
cards.head: l'
cards.body: Le and la both shorten to this in front of a vowel sound, and the two become one word. Water is feminine and the card no longer says so, which is exactly the concealment a1.03 warned about.

cards.label: Any plural
cards.head: les
cards.body: Put those two in the plural and both take les. The sun is masculine and the moon is feminine for no reason anyone can give you, and les is the one form that never asks.

sections.title: Three Questions In Order
sections.say: Three questions, and you stop at the first one that answers yes. Two of the three never ask about gender.
steps: Is the noun plural? Then it is les, whatever its gender. You are done, and you never had to know whether it was masculine or feminine.
Does the noun start on a vowel sound? Then it is l apostrophe, whatever its gender. Done again, and again the gender never came up.
Neither? Then it is le or la, and only now do you need the gender you stored in a1.03. This is the one branch of the three that asks.

sections.title: The Grid, Row By Row
sections.say: The same four forms as a table. Tap any row for the case it covers and the one it does not.

detail.title: le
detail.body: The third question, masculine answer. You reach this row only after the noun turned out to be singular and to start on a consonant sound, which is why the gender matters here and nowhere else.

detail.title: la
detail.body: The third question, feminine answer. The same row as le with the other answer, and the only thing separating them is a fact about the noun that you cannot see on the page.

detail.title: l'
detail.body: The second question. School is feminine and the card will not tell you, because la and le both arrive here as the same two letters. Store it as une école the moment you meet it.

detail.title: les
detail.body: The first question, and the shortest route through. Masculine, feminine or a mixture, it makes no difference. The S on the end of the noun is usually silent, so les is the only part a listener hears carrying the plural.

sections.title: When Les Takes Over
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: One form, and it is the only place in the language where the gender you worked to store is simply not consulted.

cards.label: Masculine plural
cards.head: les
cards.body: Masculine, and it takes les. Nothing about the article records that, and nothing later will ask you to.

cards.label: Feminine plural
cards.head: les again
cards.body: Feminine, and it takes exactly the same word. Put those two cards side by side and there is no way to tell which is which, which is the point of this mission.

cards.label: The one you hear
cards.head: Where the plural lives
cards.body: The S on the end of a French noun is usually silent, so les is doing all the work out loud. Drop it and a listener hears one friend. Nothing else in the phrase corrects that.

sections.title: Plurals, Both Genders
sections.say: Two decks. The line under each word is the gender it is hiding, and les is identical on both sides.

sections.title: Hearing The Plural
sections.say: Nothing on screen to work it out from. Listen for what happens at the join between the two words.

lines.en: the books
the friends
the parents
the children

questions.q: In « les livres », how many separate sounds do you hear before the noun?
opts: The noun starts with a Z
questions.why: Livres starts on a consonant, so les ends and livres begins. Two words, two starts, nothing joining them.

questions.q: In « les amis », what do you hear between the two words?
questions.why: Amis starts on a vowel, so the silent S of les wakes up as a Z and is said with the noun rather than with the article.

questions.q: You hear a Z at the join. What does that tell you about the noun?
opts: It starts on a vowel sound
questions.why: Only a vowel sound pulls that Z out. It says nothing about gender, because les never did.

sections.title: When Le And La Vanish
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: Two forms collapse into one, and the thing they were carrying goes with them.

cards.label: Both become one
cards.head: le and la, gone
cards.body: The flat is masculine and the school is feminine, and in front of a vowel sound both articles shorten to the same two letters. The words are now indistinguishable and the gender is still there, unrecorded.

cards.label: Sound, not letter
cards.head: What counts as a vowel
cards.body: This is about the SOUND the noun starts on, not the letter it is spelled with. Heure begins with an h on the page and with a vowel in the mouth, so it shortens. The next mission is where that bites.

cards.label: The habit
cards.head: Convert it as it arrives
cards.body: a1.03 asked you to switch a new l apostrophe noun to un or une in your head before storing it. This is where that pays: oil is feminine, you will need la for it eventually, and nothing on this card says so.

sections.title: The Letter H, Two Ways
sections.say: Same letter, two behaviours, and no rule joining them. These are two lists to recognise, not a pattern to work out.

sections.title: Which H Is It?
sections.say: The bare noun on the front. Say the whole thing, article included, before you flip it.

sections.title: Three Traps
sections.say: Three, and the first one is the one you will make today.

errors.wrong: « J'aime café »
errors.why: When English says nothing, French says le. English lets a general noun stand bare and French does not, so this is not a missing flourish, it is a missing part of the sentence.

errors.wrong: « le eau »
errors.why: Two vowel sounds cannot sit next to each other here, so the e of le drops out and the two words join. This is not optional and there is no version of French that says le eau.

errors.wrong: « les ami »
errors.why: The S of the noun is silent, so les is carrying the plural alone. Say it in front of a vowel and the S of LES comes back as a Z, joined onto the noun.

sections.title: Flip And Recall
sections.say: English on the front, and it gives you no article at all. Supply the French one before you flip.

sections.title: Write What You Hear
sections.say: Six sentences, built from word tiles, and some of the tiles do not belong. The article is a tile like any other, so you have to place it.

sections.title: Say The Whole Thing
sections.say: Sixteen nouns, and none of them is a word on its own. Say the article and the noun as one piece.

sections.title: Six Moments This Week
sections.say: Six real moments, and in five of them English would have given you nothing to say.

cases.situation: Someone asks what you drink
Saying what you are learning
Turning down a whole food group
Asking where something is
Ordering the thing on the counter
Asking for the bill

sections.title: Your Turn At The Counter
sections.say: A café in the middle of the afternoon. Every line you say has an article in it, and one of them is the one you would drop.
sections.setting: A café counter in Bordeaux, mid-afternoon.

turns.ai: Bonjour ! Qu'est-ce que je vous sers ?
turns.en: Hello! What can I get you?
turns.user: Bonjour. Le café au lait, s'il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: Hello. The café au lait, please.

alts.fr: Bonjour. Le thé, s'il vous plaît.
Bonjour, je prends le café au lait.
alts.en: Hello, I'll have the café au lait.

turns.ai: Et avec ça ? Nous avons des tartes.
turns.en: Anything with that? We have tarts.
turns.user: Non merci. Je n'aime pas les tartes.
turns.userEn: No thank you. I don't like tarts.

alts.fr: Non merci, je préfère les croissants.
alts.en: No thank you, I prefer croissants.

turns.ai: Très bien. Vous êtes en vacances ?
turns.en: Very good. Are you on holiday?
turns.user: Non, j'apprends le français ici.
turns.userEn: No, I'm learning French here.

alts.en: Yes, I like the city a lot.

turns.ai: Ah, bravo ! C'est difficile, le français.
turns.en: Ah, well done! French is hard.
turns.user: Oui, mais j'aime la langue.
turns.userEn: Yes, but I love the language.

alts.fr: C'est vrai, mais j'adore le français.
alts.en: That's true, but I love French.

turns.ai: Voilà votre café. L'addition est sur la table.
turns.en: Here is your coffee. The bill is on the table.
turns.user: Merci beaucoup.
turns.userEn: Thank you very much.

alts.en: Thank you! Have a good day.

sections.title: The Flat Above The Bakery
sections.say: Read it once for the shape. Tap any word you do not know, and notice how few nouns arrive on their own.
sections.text: Marc has just moved into a flat above a bakery in Toulouse, and his neighbour Sylvie has come up with two cups. She wants to know how he is settling in. « Alors, l'appartement te plaît ? » He says it is small, and then he says the part he actually likes. « Oui, beaucoup. La cuisine est petite, mais j'aime la lumière. » Sylvie points at the floor and grins, because everyone in the building asks this eventually. « Et le pain ? Tu entends le boulanger à quatre heures ? » He admits that he does, every single morning. « Je l'entends. Mais j'aime le pain, alors ça va. » She asks whether he has met anyone on the stairs yet. « Tu connais les voisins ? » He has met the two from the third floor and nobody else. « Les voisins du troisième, oui. Ils sont gentils. » Sylvie stands up to leave and gives him the one piece of advice that matters in this building. « Une chose. L'été, ouvre les fenêtres tôt. Après huit heures, il fait trop chaud. »

glossary.note: Masculine, and the card refuses to say so. Store it as un appartement, the way a1.03 asked.
The baker is masculine and the shop downstairs is la boulangerie, which is feminine. Nobody can tell you why.
Plural, so les, and the gender never entered into it.
The passage says l'été. The noun on its own is été, and the article in front of it is the word an English speaker would not have said at all.
Feminine and plural. Les does not care which, which is the whole of that mission in two words.

questions.q: What does Marc like about the flat, and what does he not?
questions.a: He likes the light. The kitchen is small.

questions.q: In « j'aime le pain », why is there a word there that English would not have?
questions.a: Because it means bread in general, and French keeps the article where English drops it.

questions.q: The passage says l'été. What is the noun on its own, and what is its gender?
questions.a: The noun is été, and it is masculine. The article hides that.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.back: J'aime le café. English gives you nothing; French needs le.
Is it plural? If yes, les, and stop.
Does it start on a vowel sound? If yes, l apostrophe.
Only now, le or la, and only now do you need the gender.
Two of them. les always, and l apostrophe in the singular.
l'heure. The h behaves like a vowel.
le hibou. The same letter, behaving like a consonant.
les haricots verts. Plural, so les settles it either way.

cards.front: Cats love sleeping in the sun.
cards.back: Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
cards.say: Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.

cards.front: What does the S in les do before a vowel?
cards.back: It comes back as a Z and joins onto the noun.
le soleil et la lune. Arbitrary, opposite, and worth storing together.
Elle est infirmière. Here French drops what English keeps.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have put the article where English gave you nothing, worked the three questions in order, and found the one letter that behaves two ways. What is left is the part that tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Four rounds. Most of these ask you to write the answer rather than pick it, because picking was never the hard part.

rounds.label: The missing word
rounds.say: The half of this lesson that is not about which article. It is about whether there is one.

questions.q: Write in French: I like coffee.
questions.why: When English says nothing, French says le. Coffee in general still takes le, and without it this is not a sentence.

questions.q: Fix this: « Nous aimons français. »
questions.why: A language is a general idea, so French keeps the article. English drops it, which is why the gap is invisible.

questions.q: Cats love sleeping in the sun. What does the French sentence start with?
questions.why: Cats as a species is the general case. French marks that by keeping a word where English removes one.

questions.q: Write in French: I am learning French.
questions.why: School subjects, languages, sports and instruments all take the article, and English gives none of them one.

questions.q: Fix this: « Elle aime musique. »
questions.why: Music is feminine, so la, but the reason a word is needed at all has nothing to do with gender.

questions.q: English says "Sport makes children stronger". How many articles does the French have?
questions.why: Le sport and les enfants. Both nouns are general, and English happens to mark neither of them.

rounds.label: Le or la
rounds.say: The third question, and the only one of the three that needs the gender.

questions.q: Maison is feminine. Write "the house".
questions.why: Feminine, singular, and it starts on a consonant sound, so you reach the third question and answer it with la.

questions.q: You need the gender of a noun in order to choose:
questions.why: Les and l apostrophe both settle it without asking. Only the third branch needs the gender.

questions.q: Livre is masculine. Write "the book".
questions.why: Masculine, singular, consonant sound. The one branch of the three where what a1.03 taught you is doing the work.

questions.q: Fix this: « le maison »
questions.why: Nothing in the word maison says it is feminine. That is why the article is stored with it.

questions.q: Lune is feminine and soleil is masculine. Write "the sun and the moon".
questions.why: Two everyday things with opposite genders and no reason behind either. This pair is worth storing as one card.

rounds.label: When gender stops counting
rounds.say: Two branches, and neither of them asks you a thing about the noun's gender.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: The Z at the join gives it away. It appears only when the noun starts on a vowel sound.

questions.q: Toilettes is feminine and plural. Write "the toilet".
questions.why: Plural, so the first question already answered it and the gender was never consulted.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: Livres starts on a consonant, so the two words stay apart and there is no Z. Le livre would be one word shorter.

questions.q: École is feminine. Which is right?
questions.why: A vowel sound follows, so la shortens and the gender goes invisible before you needed it.

questions.q: Eau is feminine. Write "the water".
questions.why: La cannot sit in front of a vowel sound, so it shortens. There is no French that says la eau.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: One word, not two. Heure starts on a vowel sound despite the h, so the article shortens and joins onto it.

rounds.label: The two kinds of h
rounds.say: A closed list, not a rule. The article is the only place the difference is ever visible.

questions.q: Write "the owl". Hibou is masculine.
questions.why: This h behaves like a consonant, so le stays whole. Nothing on the page distinguishes it from the other kind.

questions.q: Both hôtel and hibou start with h. Why does only one take l apostrophe?
opts: There is no rule; the two are separate lists
questions.why: The split is a leftover of where the words came from. It is two lists, and gender is not in it.

questions.q: Fix this: « le heure »
questions.why: Heure behaves like a vowel, so the article shortens. Store the pair together and you never have to work it out.

questions.q: Write "the green beans".
questions.why: It is plural, so the first question settles it and the h never gets a chance to matter.

questions.q: Say it out loud: I like coffee.
questions.why: When English says nothing, French says le. If you said three words, the missing one is this lesson.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Six things, and one that a later lesson finishes for you.
sections.body: You can pick the right article for any noun you know, in three questions, and two of those three never ask you about gender. More usefully, you can hear the place where English gave you nothing and French wants a word, which is the error that marks a beginner more reliably than any accent does.
points: When English says nothing, French says le. Say it to yourself before a general noun and you will stop losing the sentence.
Plural takes les, whatever the gender. A vowel sound takes l apostrophe, whatever the gender.
Only le and la need the gender, which makes it one branch of three rather than the whole decision.
Every French h is silent, and only the article ever tells you which kind you are holding.
Store the noun with its article, the way a1.03 asked. This lesson is where that habit gets paid.
The Z you heard in les amis is a system of its own, and the sons track has a whole lesson on it.
du, au and aux are these same articles wearing a disguise. a1.29 takes them apart.

grammarAssumed: Every noun carries a gender, and it is stored with the noun rather than derived from it
The indefinite articles un and une, as the form gender is stored in
grammarIntroduced: The definite articles le, la, l apostrophe and les, and the order of the three questions that choose between them
The definite article in front of a general noun, where English uses no article at all
Nouns beginning with h splitting into two groups, distinguishable only by the article they take

overview.introFr: Le français a quatre façons de dire the, selon le genre, le nombre et le son du nom. Le plus dur, c'est que l'anglais peut n'en mettre aucun et le français jamais.

acts.title: The word English leaves out
acts.milestone: You have seen the mistake you cannot see from inside English.

acts.title: Which one to reach for
acts.milestone: Four forms, and three questions that pick between them.

acts.title: Where gender stops counting
acts.milestone: Les settles the plural without ever asking about gender.

acts.title: The sound, and the letter that lies
acts.milestone: You can tell l heure from le hibou, which nothing else in the language will tell you.

acts.title: Banked, and used
acts.milestone: You have written them, said them, ordered with them and read them.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete.

lessons.reframe: When English says nothing, French says le.

errorTriggers.description: Leaves a general noun bare, the way English does: J'aime café, Les chats becomes Chats, Le français becomes Français.
Reaches the third question and answers it with the wrong gender: le maison, la livre.
Keeps le or la where the noun is plural or starts on a vowel sound: le eau, la école, le parents.
Guesses at an h word rather than recognising which list it is on: l'hibou, le heure.

drills.title: The word that is not there
drills.coach: Read the English. It has nothing in front of the noun. Say the French, which does.
pairs: Cats love sleeping in the sun.
Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
Les oiseaux volent vers le sud en hiver.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: English says "I like tea". The French is:
drills.why: Tea in general takes le. J'aime un thé would mean one particular cup, which is not what the English said.

drills.title: Which one is it?
drills.coach: Nothing in the word tells you. This is the fact you stored in a1.03, being asked for.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Table is feminine. You want "the table".
drills.why: Feminine, singular, starts on a consonant sound, so the third question applies and the answer is la.

drills.title: Plural, vowel, or neither
drills.coach: Ask them in order. Plural first, vowel sound second, and only then reach for the gender.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: A noun is feminine, singular, and starts on a vowel sound. Which article?
drills.why: The second question fired before the third one could. A vowel sound takes l apostrophe whatever the gender is.

drills.title: Two lists, one letter
drills.coach: There is nothing to work out here. Either you have stored it with its article or you have not.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these keeps its article whole?
drills.why: Le hibou. Heure and homme both behave like vowels and take l apostrophe, and only the article ever shows you the difference.

sheets.title: The four forms, on one screen

sections.title: How to read it
sections.body: Read the table by column rather than by row and the lesson falls out of it. The right-hand column is one word twice, and the bottom row is one word twice, so five of the six cells are settled before gender is mentioned. Only the top two cells of the left-hand column need it, which is why the three questions are asked in the order they are: plural first, vowel sound second, gender last and only if the first two came back no. Most textbooks draw this as a two by two grid with gender along the top, which puts the one thing you cannot see on the page in charge of a decision that usually does not need it.

sheets.title: The h words, both lists
contains: The h that lets the article shorten

rows.v: the hotel. Behaves like a vowel.
the hour. Behaves like a vowel.
history. Behaves like a vowel.
the oil. Behaves like a vowel.
the clock. Behaves like a vowel.
the man. Behaves like a vowel.
the hospital. Behaves like a vowel.
the habit. Behaves like a vowel.
the owl. Behaves like a consonant.
the hamster. Behaves like a consonant.
hockey. Behaves like a consonant.
the lobster. Behaves like a consonant.
the hip. Behaves like a consonant.
chance. Behaves like a consonant.
the hero. Behaves like a consonant.
the green beans. Consonant, and plural anyway.

sections.title: Why there is no rule
sections.body: Every h in French is silent, so nothing you can hear in the noun itself separates these two columns. The split is historical: one group came into French from Latin, where the h had already stopped being pronounced, and the other arrived later from Germanic and Frankish words where it still was. That h is gone now too, but the behaviour it left behind is not, and no feature of the modern spelling records it. So this is a list, and the reason it is a short and manageable list is that the second group is small. The practical consequence is the one this lesson keeps returning to: the article is the only place the difference is ever visible, so a noun stored on its own has thrown the fact away. Store le hibou, not hibou.

zero.title: Why the mistake is invisible from the inside
zero.body: English has three ways to introduce a noun and French has two. Where English says "the coffee" French says le café, and both languages agree. Where English says "a coffee" French says un café, and they agree again. But where English says plain "coffee", meaning coffee in general, French has no matching form: it still says le café. That third English option is the one with no French equivalent, and because it is the option an English speaker reaches for without thinking, the gap never announces itself. Nothing feels missing. The sentence simply is not French.

examples.note: We like French. Four words in English, four in French, and one of them has no English counterpart at all.
Cats in general. English marks the general case by removing a word; French marks it by keeping one.

pick.title: The order that saves you the gender
pick.body: There are four forms and three questions, asked in this order. Is the noun plural? Then it is les, and the gender does not enter into it. Does it start with a vowel sound? Then it is l apostrophe, and again the gender does not enter into it. Only when both answers are no does the third question arrive, and only then do you need to know whether the noun is masculine or feminine. Most courses present this as a two by two grid, which puts gender first and makes it look like the thing every choice depends on. In practice two of the three branches never reach it.

examples.note: Plural, so the first question already answered it.
A vowel sound, so the second one did.
Neither, so this is the one where the gender is finally needed.

plural.title: The form that ignores the question a1.03 taught you to ask
plural.body: Les is the plural for everything. Masculine, feminine, mixed, it makes no difference, and this is the one place in the language where the gender you worked to store is simply not consulted. It is also the form you will have met least: this app teaches nouns in the singular almost everywhere, so les gets a fraction of the exposure le does, and a learner can finish several lessons having barely seen it. Worth knowing too that the S on the end of the noun is usually silent, so les is the only part of the phrase a listener hears carrying the plural.

examples.note: Feminine, and it takes les like everything else.
Masculine, and it takes exactly the same word.

vowelSound.title: Not a vowel letter, which is where the shipped rule was wrong
vowelSound.body: Le and la both shorten to l apostrophe in front of a noun that STARTS ON A VOWEL SOUND. The distinction between sound and letter looks pedantic and costs a learner a whole category of nouns, because the letter h is written and never pronounced, so whether it counts depends on the word and not on the spelling. l heure and le hibou are both spelled with an h and only one of them shortens. a1.03 taught you that l apostrophe conceals the gender and that you should convert it to un or une before storing it. This lesson is the other half: how to know it was coming.

examples.note: A vowel letter and a vowel sound, so it shortens.
An h on the page, a vowel sound in the mouth, so it shortens too.
The same letter, and it does not shorten. Nothing on the page says why.

hSplit.title: A closed list to recognise, not a rule to work out
hSplit.body: Every French h is silent. What splits them is whether the word behaves as though it begins with a vowel or as though it begins with a consonant, and there is no rule that predicts which: the two groups are a leftover of where the words came from. So this is learned as two lists rather than derived, and the good news is that the article is the only place the difference is ever visible. A learner who has stored le hibou has stored the whole fact, and one who stored hibou on its own has stored nothing they can use.

examples.note: Behaves like a vowel.
Behaves like a consonant, and keeps la in full.
Plural and consonant-behaving, and les is unbothered by either.

storeIt.title: The habit a1.03 started, and what this lesson adds to it
storeIt.body: a1.03 asked you to store every noun with un or une in front of it, because the gender is not recoverable from the word. Keep doing that. What this lesson adds is that the definite article is where the storage gets tested: it is the form you reach for most, it is the one the h words only reveal themselves in, and it is the one English will keep tempting you to leave out. Nearly every noun in this app already carries an article in its own entry, so a card showing you the bare word has quietly taught you to store it bare.

examples.note: Stored the way you will need it.
And its opposite number, whose gender is just as arbitrary.

recorded.desc: The central contrast: « J'aime café » then « J'aime le café », in that order, one voice, one speed, ONE TAKE. The wrong version must be read at the same natural pace as the right one and not slowed or flagged, because the whole point is that it sounds almost fine. Do NOT over-articulate le; it is a schwa and it should half disappear, which is exactly why learners leave it out.

The four forms on their example nouns: le fromage, la maison, l'eau, les parents, then le livre, la table, l'école. ONE TAKE straight through so the pace is even and the four articles are directly comparable. le and la differ by one unstressed vowel and across two takes that difference is not audible.

The plural pairs, each pair in ONE TAKE: les livres then les amis, les parents then les enfants. The join is the entire teaching, so les amis must be said as one piece at natural speed and never separated into two words for clarity. Also supplies the listening mission.

l'appartement, l'école, l'heure, l'huile, and for contrast le appartement is NOT to be recorded: there is no such thing and a clip of it would be teaching a form that does not exist. One take, natural pace, and the article and noun joined as a single word throughout.

The two h lists as PAIRS, one take per pair, so each contrast is comparable: l'heure then le hibou, l'hôtel then le hockey, l'homme then le homard, l'huile then la hanche. Every h is silent in all of them, so nothing should be aspirated; the difference the learner is listening for is whether the article joins on or stands alone.

The twelve example sentences, each read straight through at natural conversational pace and again at 0.65 from the same take. Never assembled from separately recorded words: the article runs into the noun and that join is what the mission is showing.
clipIds: Je préfère le sport en équipe.
Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
Les abricots sont chers cette semaine.
Les oiseaux volent vers le sud en hiver.
Le sport rend les enfants plus forts.

recorded.desc: The kitchen scene. A warm adult female voice for Claire, unhurried and friendly rather than corrective: the line « Ah, tu aimes le café. » is the pivot of the whole lesson and it must not sound like a telling-off. She is repeating it back, not marking it wrong. « Le matin, le café. Le soir, le thé. » is four articles in one breath and should be said at full speed, so they are as small as they really are.
clipIds: Et toi, qu'est-ce que tu aimes ?
Le matin, le café. Le soir, le thé.

recorded.desc: The three traps, wrong then right for each, ONE TAKE per pair: « J'aime café » then « J'aime le café », « le eau » then « l'eau », « les ami » then « les amis ». The wrong readings must be spoken naturally rather than mangled, because the point is that a learner cannot hear their own error.

The six dictation sentences at natural pace, and again at 0.65 from the same take so the slow version is a slowing rather than a re-reading. No exaggerated word separation, which would give the tile boundaries away, and specifically no pause after the article: the learner has to hear that les chats is two words without being handed the gap.
clipIds: Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
Les enfants adorent le sport collectif.
Elle aime le café au lait.
Nous allons à la plage demain.
J'achète du pain à la boulangerie.

recorded.desc: The café counter exchange, server lines only, brisk and friendly. « C'est difficile, le français. » carries the article on a subject noun in a throwaway aside, which is the most natural example in the lesson, so it must sound offhand rather than demonstrated.
clipIds: Bonjour ! Qu'est-ce que je vous sers ?
Et avec ça ? Nous avons des tartes.
Très bien. Vous êtes en vacances ?
Ah, bravo ! C'est difficile, le français.
Voilà votre café. L'addition est sur la table.

segments.text: I am Camille. Today is the four little words in front of French nouns, and the reason you keep leaving them out.
J'aime le café.
Four words. In English that sentence has three, and the one you do not have is the one we are here for.
English gives you three ways to introduce a noun. The coffee. A coffee. And plain coffee, meaning coffee in general.
French has the first two and not the third. When English says nothing, French says le. That is the whole lesson.
Les chats adorent dormir au soleil.
Cats, meaning cats everywhere. English marks that by taking a word away and French marks it by keeping one.
Now which one. Three questions, and you stop at the first yes. Is it plural?
Les parents. Les toilettes.
One of those is masculine and one is feminine and you could not tell, because les never asks.
Second question. Does the noun start on a vowel sound?
L'eau. L'école. L'appartement.
Again the gender is hidden, and again you did not need it. Only if both answers were no do you reach the third question.
Le fromage. La maison.
One letter behaves two ways, and the article is the only place you will ever see it. Listen.
L'heure. Le hibou.
Both spelled with an h, both silent, and only one of them lets the article shorten. There is no rule. Store the pair.
Your turn, with nothing in front of you. Say that you like coffee.
Now the green beans. Careful, this one answers two questions at once.
And the school. It is feminine, and I want to know whether that changed anything.
One question. I will say a sentence and you tell me what English would have left out.
Nous aimons le français.
Le. In English you would have said we like French, with nothing in front of it, and that gap is the one thing no course points at.
Three things to keep. When English says nothing, French says le.
Plural takes les and a vowel sound takes l apostrophe, and neither of them asks about gender. Only le and la do.
And the h words are two lists, not a rule. Store the article with the noun and you never have to choose.
À bientôt.

lessons.title: Les articles partitifs
lessons.intro: Anyone can learn that du is masculine and de la is feminine; that takes five minutes and the noun decides it anyway. What stays hard is a line English never makes you draw. Un café and du café are both correct, they order different things, and nothing will correct you.

sections.title: The Loaf He Did Not Want

say.text: Watch this go wrong on a word you already know. Nothing here is mispronounced and nothing here is rude.

setting.place: A bakery on a corner, two streets from the market

beats.text: Saturday morning in Lyon. You are cooking for two people tonight and you need bread for the table.
There is a queue behind you and the baker is already looking up. You know every word you need.

beats.prompt: One sentence, and the queue is waiting. Which one?

options.fr: Je voudrais un pain, s'il vous plaît.
options.en: asking for a loaf

options.fr: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.
options.en: asking for bread

followUp.works: Yes. You want bread rather than a particular object, and du is how you say so.
followUp.breaks: Every word is correct. Watch what she reaches for.

beats.fr: Je voudrais un pain, s'il vous plaît.

beats.speaker: The baker
beats.en: A big one or a small one?
beats.stage: Her hand is already on a round loaf the size of a dinner plate.

beats.heading: You ordered an object
beats.body: A pain is a thing, sold by the piece, with a price of its own. Du pain is bread: an amount, cut to whatever you need. She was not confused for a second, and that is the problem.

wrong.en: one loaf, the round kind, wrapped and paid for

right.en: bread, as much or as little as you need

beats.coach: Same shop, same noun, one syllable different. One of them is a thing and one of them is an amount.

beats.speaker: Second try
beats.fr: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.
beats.en: I would like some bread, please.

beats.speaker: The baker
beats.en: Half a baguette, will that do?
beats.stage: She has already left the round loaves alone.

beats.text: She heard the difference before you finished the sentence, and served a different thing.

closing.text: Un is one of them. Du is some of it. She served the second one without being asked twice.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Un is one of them. Du is some of it. By the end of this lesson you will know which of the two a sentence wants, and the four places your English will hand you the wrong one.

goals.s: Order bread, coffee, water or cheese without accidentally ordering one whole object of it.
Hear the difference between a cup of coffee and coffee, and say which one you meant.
Name a quantity or a container and know that the word in front of the noun now goes.
Spot the du that is about an amount and the du that is nothing of the kind.

sections.title: The Fourth One Is Yours
sections.frSub: Du, de la, de l', des
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: You already own one of these four and nobody told you. Start there rather than with a table.

cards.label: Already yours
cards.head: You have been saying this
cards.body: Last lesson des was the plural of un and une, and it is. It is also the plural of the three words on the next card, and it has been doing that job the whole time.

cards.label: The other three
cards.head: One word, three shapes
cards.body: Du in front of most nouns, de la in front of the ones that take la, and de l apostrophe when the next word starts with a vowel sound.

cards.label: Revision, not teaching
cards.head: The noun decides, not you
cards.sub: pain takes le, soupe takes la
cards.body: Which of the three you use is settled by the noun, and you settled that two lessons ago. Nothing new is being asked of you here, so it gets one screen and one drill.

cards.label: The whole lesson
cards.head: What all four are for
cards.body: Un is one of them. Du is some of it. Every card after this one is that sentence in a different situation.

sections.title: Say the Amount
sections.say: Ten amounts, one per screen. The noun tells you which shape to use, so the only work is saying it.

sections.title: One Cup, or Coffee
sections.say: Un is one of them. Du is some of it. Both columns are correct French. Tap any row to hear the two of them back to back.

detail.title: un café · du café
detail.body: Un café is one cup, on a saucer, at a counter. Du café is coffee: what is in the pot, what you want rather than tea, an amount nobody has measured. Order the first and one arrives.
detail.say: Je prends un café. Je prends du café.

detail.title: un pain · du pain
detail.body: Un pain is a loaf, the big round kind, sold by the piece. Du pain is bread, cut to whatever you need. This is the pair the bakery scene turns on and it is the one you will meet first.
detail.say: Je voudrais un pain. Je voudrais du pain.

detail.title: un fromage · du fromage
detail.body: Un fromage is a whole cheese, the wheel on the board behind the counter. Du fromage is cheese, the thing you eat some of after a meal. Ask for the first at a market stall and you will be taken seriously.
detail.say: Un fromage entier ? Non, du fromage.

detail.title: une salade · de la salade
detail.body: Une salade is a dish somebody brings you. De la salade is salad, the leaves, some of what is in the bowl. Salade takes la, so its amount form is de la rather than du. That is the only difference.
detail.say: Je prends une salade. Je fais de la salade.

detail.title: un bruit · du bruit
detail.body: Not food, and it is the same choice exactly. Un bruit is one noise, a single sound you heard once. Du bruit is noise, the kind the neighbours make. Nothing about this rule is about eating.
detail.say: J'entends un bruit. Il y a du bruit.

sections.title: Saturday at the Market
sections.say: Un is one of them. Du is some of it. One noun in this passage arrives both ways in the same breath, and somebody says out loud what changed.
sections.text: It is Saturday morning and Claire is buying lunch for three people. The bakery smells of the ovens at the back, and there is a queue. « Bonjour madame. Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît. » The baker reaches past the round loaves and picks up a half baguette instead. « Voilà. Et avec ça ? » Claire crosses the road to the cheese stall, where a man is already holding a knife. « Je voudrais du fromage. » He puts a whole wheel of comté on the board, the size of a car wheel, and waits. « Un fromage entier ? » Claire looks at it, and then says the sentence that fixes everything. « Non, pas un fromage. Du fromage. Une tranche, s'il vous plaît. » He cuts a slice and wraps it, and she remembers who she is cooking for tonight. « Il ne mange pas de fromage, lui. De la salade, alors. » The man laughs and reaches for the salad without putting the knife down. « Et de l'eau ? Il y a de l'eau à côté du pain. » Claire takes a bottle from the shelf beside the bread and pays for all of it. « Une bouteille d'eau. Merci beaucoup. »

glossary.note: Bread, cut to whatever she needs. Not a loaf, which would be un pain.
Cheese, an amount of it. The man hears something else, and that is the next line.
One cheese, the entire wheel. A real thing to order, and not what she meant.
Name the quantity and the article in front of the noun goes: une tranche de fromage.
Say no and du collapses to de. The same rule you met last lesson on un and des.
Salade takes la, so its amount form is de la. The noun decides, as always.
Eau opens on a vowel sound, so de la shortens to de l apostrophe.
This du is not about an amount of anything. It is de and le stuck together, meaning of the.
A container is a quantity with a shape, so it takes bare de, and d apostrophe before the vowel.

questions.q: Claire asks for « du fromage » and the man puts a whole wheel on the board. What did he hear?
questions.a: He heard the question as being about one cheese rather than an amount of one, which is why she corrects it to du fromage in the next line.

questions.q: What is different about « un fromage » and « du fromage »?
questions.a: Nothing about the cheese. Un fromage is one whole object you could carry out; du fromage is some of it, cut to size.

questions.q: The word « du » appears in the last exchange and it is not about an amount. Where, and what is it doing?
questions.a: « à côté du pain » means next to the bread. That du is de and le squeezed together, and it says where the water is rather than how much bread there is.

sections.title: Du, De, or Deux?
sections.say: Du against de, and du against deux. All three are one vowel and all three change what the sentence asks for.

lines.en: I would like some bread.
I would like a loaf.
I drink coffee.
I drink a lot of coffee.

questions.q: In the first line, how much bread is being asked for?
opts: All the bread in the shop
questions.why: Du is the whole answer. It says the speaker wants bread without saying how much, and the baker decides the rest.

questions.q: What separates the third line from the fourth, at speed?
opts: The fourth names a quantity, so du goes
questions.why: Beaucoup already says how much, so French drops the word in front of the noun. Beaucoup du café is never said.

questions.q: Which pair is hardest to tell apart when somebody speaks quickly?
opts: both, and for the same reason
questions.why: Each pair differs by one rounded vowel and nothing else, so the ear has no consonant to hold on to. Slow the audio and all three separate cleanly.

sections.title: Six Moments This Week
sections.say: Six real moments. In every one of them the choice is between a thing and an amount, and the noun is the same either way.

cases.situation: At a counter, ordering one cup to drink standing up
At a table, when somebody is holding the pot
At the bakery, buying bread for tonight
Asked what you want to drink with your meal
Telling a waiter what you cannot eat
cases.fr: Je ne mange pas de fromage.

cases.situation: At a stall, once you have decided how much

sections.title: Which One Do You Want?
sections.say: One question. The situation is what decides it, so read the first half before you look at the options.

check.q: Somebody is standing over you with a coffee pot, asking if you want any. What do you say?
check.why: They are offering an amount out of a pot rather than a cup off a shelf. Un café would be ordering a fresh one, which is a different request.

sections.title: Name It and It Vanishes
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: The most counterintuitive rule in this lesson, and the most regular. Say how much and the article goes.

cards.label: The rule
cards.head: Say how much, lose the word
cards.sub: [boh-KOO duh ka-FAY] · a lot of coffee
cards.body: Je bois du café becomes je bois beaucoup de café. The du is gone, not shortened. Beaucoup du café is never said by anybody.

cards.label: All four
cards.head: It is not just beaucoup
cards.fr: un peu de · assez de · trop de
cards.body: Every quantity word behaves the same way. Un peu de sel, assez de pain, trop de sucre, moins de bruit. There are no exceptions to find.

cards.label: Before a vowel
cards.head: de becomes d
cards.body: De shortens in front of a vowel sound, exactly the way le and la do. Beaucoup d apostrophe eau, un peu d apostrophe huile.

cards.label: Why it feels wrong
cards.head: English keeps its word
cards.body: English says "a lot of the coffee" and keeps everything. French takes the article out the moment the quantity is named. Un is one of them. Du is some of it. Say how much, and neither one is needed.

sections.title: A Kilo, a Slice, a Bottle
sections.say: A container is a quantity with a shape, so it does exactly what beaucoup does. Tap any line.

examples.note: Not un kilo des tomates. The kilo says how much, so nothing else needs to.
One card ago this was du fromage. Name the slice and the du goes.
De shortens to d apostrophe in front of eau, the same as everywhere else.
Comté is a particular cheese and it changes nothing. The container is what matters.
Compare du vin, which is wine without a glass named around it.
The one English speakers guess wrong, because part sounds like it needs the.

sections.title: Say No and It Shrinks
sections.say: You met this rule last lesson on un and des. It is the same rule, and there is nothing extra to learn.

rows.say: Je mange du pain. Je ne mange pas de pain.

detail.title: du becomes de
detail.body: Je mange du pain becomes je ne mange pas de pain. Not pas du pain, and not pas le pain. The negative eats the article and leaves the noun bare behind it.
detail.say: Je ne mange pas de pain.

rows.say: Je fais de la soupe. Je ne fais pas de soupe.

detail.title: de la becomes de
detail.body: The la disappears with it. De does not agree with anything, which is one fewer thing to get right rather than one more.
detail.say: Je ne fais pas de soupe.

rows.say: Je bois de l'eau. Je ne bois pas d'eau.

detail.title: de l apostrophe becomes d apostrophe
detail.body: De still meets a vowel sound, so it still shortens. That is why this one looks different: it is the same de, wearing the same shortening you already know.

rows.say: Je mange des légumes. Je ne mange pas de légumes.

detail.title: des becomes de
detail.body: This is the half you already met. Last lesson des was the plural of un and une and it collapsed to de under a negative. It does the same here for the same reason.
detail.say: Je ne mange pas de légumes.

rows.say: J'aime le pain. Je n'aime pas le pain.

detail.title: le does not move
detail.body: This is the half that makes the rule usable. If the word survives the negative it was le, la or les. If it collapsed to de, it was one of this lesson.

sections.title: Four Traps
sections.say: Four sentences an English speaker produces in their first month. One per screen.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je mange pain » for "I eat bread".
errors.right: Saying « Je mange du pain » for "I eat bread".
errors.why: Your English has nothing in front of bread, so nothing reminds you that French wants a word there. A bare noun after a verb is not a thing French has, and this is the error that sounds most obviously wrong to a French ear.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je voudrais un café » when you meant coffee rather than one cup.
errors.right: Saying « Je voudrais du café » when you meant coffee rather than one cup.
errors.why: Both are correct French, which is why nothing corrects you. Un asks for one countable thing and du asks for an amount, so this is the only trap here that gets you served the wrong item rather than a puzzled look.

errors.wrong: Saying « beaucoup du café » for "a lot of coffee".
errors.right: Saying « beaucoup de café » for "a lot of coffee".
errors.why: English keeps the whole phrase in "a lot of the coffee" and French does not. Once the quantity is named the article in front of the noun disappears, and this holds for every quantity word and every container.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je ne mange pas du pain » for "I do not eat bread".
errors.right: Saying « Je ne mange pas de pain » for "I do not eat bread".
errors.why: Du, de la and de l apostrophe all collapse to de under a negative, exactly as un, une and des did last lesson. Le, la and les do not move, which is how you can work out afterwards which word you had used.

sections.title: The Other Du
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Most of the du you have read since your first lesson is not this word at all. Here is how to tell.

cards.label: Four in five
cards.head: This one is not an amount
cards.sub: [preh dü LEE] · next to the bed
cards.body: There is no quantity of bed involved. This du is de and le squeezed into one word, which French does automatically, and you have been reading it since your first lesson.

cards.label: On every menu
cards.head: The dish of the day
cards.sub: [luh pla dü ZHOOR] · the dish of the day
cards.body: Le plat du jour, l'odeur du pain, à côté du salon, à la fin du repas. Every one of them is of the, and not one of them is about how much of something there is.

cards.label: The test
cards.head: Try putting "some" in
cards.sub: [lo-DEUR dü PAⁿ] · the smell of the bread
cards.body: Some bread works, so je mange du pain is this lesson. Some the bread does not work, so l apostrophe odeur du pain is the other one. That test takes a second and it never fails.

cards.label: Away from the table
cards.head: The real one, off duty
cards.body: Faire du sport, jouer de la guitare, entendre du bruit. Same word, same job, no food anywhere near it. Un is one of them. Du is some of it. This is a rule about French, not a rule about restaurants.

sections.title: The Words Themselves
sections.say: Three decks. Every card carries its article, because the article is the half you are here for.

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French, article and all, before you flip.

cards.back: Je ne mange pas de pain.
cards.say: Je ne mange pas de pain.

cards.front: I would like some bread, please
cards.back: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.
cards.say: Je voudrais du pain, s'il vous plaît.

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Six sentences. The tiles include articles you did not hear, so put the right one where it belongs.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: Fourteen amounts, said out loud. The word in front is the part the mic is listening for.

sections.title: Your Turn at the Counter
sections.say: The same market, and this time you hold up the whole exchange. Watch your own articles move.
sections.setting: A covered market in Lyon on a Saturday morning, at the cheese and bread end.

turns.ai: Bonjour ! Qu’est-ce que je vous sers ?
turns.en: Hello! What can I get you?
turns.user: Bonjour. Je voudrais du pain, s’il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: Hello. I'd like some bread, please.

alts.fr: Bonjour. Du pain, s’il vous plaît.
Bonjour, je prends du pain et du beurre.
alts.en: Hello, I'll have some bread and some butter.

turns.ai: Voilà. Et avec ça ?
turns.en: Here you are. And with that?
turns.user: Du fromage. Une tranche, pas plus.
turns.userEn: Some cheese. One slice, no more.

alts.fr: Je voudrais aussi de la confiture.

turns.ai: Du comté, ça vous va ?
turns.en: Comté, does that suit you?
turns.user: Oui, très bien. Et de l’eau ?
turns.userEn: Yes, very good. And some water?

alts.fr: Oui, parfait. Vous avez de l’eau ?
alts.en: Yes, perfect. Do you have any water?

alts.fr: Volontiers. Et de la crème, vous en avez ?
alts.en: Gladly. And cream, do you have any?

turns.ai: Les bouteilles sont derrière vous.
turns.en: The bottles are behind you.
turns.user: Une bouteille d’eau, alors. Merci.
turns.userEn: A bottle of water, then. Thank you.

turns.ai: Ça fait neuf euros cinquante.
turns.en: That comes to nine euros fifty.
turns.user: Voilà. Bonne journée !
turns.userEn: Here you go. Have a good day!

alts.en: Here's nine euros fifty. Thank you.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: You want bread for the table, not a loaf
cards.back: Je voudrais du pain. Un is one of them. Du is some of it.

cards.front: Somebody is holding the coffee pot
cards.back: Du café, oui, merci. Un café would be ordering a fresh one.

cards.front: Soupe takes la. So an amount of it is…
cards.back: de la soupe. The noun decides which shape, and it always has.

cards.front: Eau starts with a vowel sound. So…
cards.back: de l'eau. De la shortens the same way la does.

cards.front: « Je bois du café. » Now say you drink a lot of it.
cards.back: Je bois beaucoup de café. Name the quantity and the du goes.

cards.front: How do you ask for a kilo of tomatoes?
cards.back: Un kilo de tomates. A container is a quantity with a shape.

cards.front: « Je mange du pain. » Now say you do not.
cards.back: Je ne mange pas de pain. The same collapse you met on un and des.
cards.say: Je ne mange pas de pain.

cards.front: « J'aime le pain. » Now say you do not.
cards.back: Je n'aime pas le pain. Le does not move under a negative.

cards.front: Is « près du lit » about an amount of bed?
cards.back: No. That du is de and le stuck together. Try putting "some" in front of the English.

cards.front: You do sport three mornings a week
cards.back: Je fais du sport. Same word, and no food anywhere near it.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a baker hand over the wrong thing, read a passage where one noun arrives both ways in the same breath, met the four shapes, learned what a quantity does to them, and separated the du that is about an amount from the du that is not. What is left is the part that tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Five rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round’s drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The four shapes
rounds.say: The shapes, quickly.

questions.q: You are at a table and you want bread. There is none on the table yet.
questions.why: You want an amount of bread rather than one loaf or all the bread there is. Du is the word for an amount nobody has counted yet.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je mange pain. »
questions.why: English has nothing in front of bread so nothing reminds you. French does not leave that slot empty after a verb, and du is what goes in it.

questions.q: Soupe takes la. So an amount of it is:
questions.why: The noun decides the shape, and you settled that in the gender lesson. Soupe takes la, so its amount form keeps the la and adds de in front.

questions.q: Water starts with a vowel sound. Write "some water" in French.
questions.why: De la shortens in front of a vowel sound exactly the way la does on its own. That is one rule you already have rather than a new one.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: Du and deux are one rounded vowel apart and there is no consonant to hold on to. Slow it down and the tighter ü of du separates cleanly.

rounds.label: One of them, or some of it
rounds.say: The choice the whole lesson is about.

questions.q: You are standing at a counter and you want one cup of coffee to drink now.
questions.why: One cup is a thing you can count, and a thing you can count takes un. Du café would ask for coffee rather than a serving of it.

questions.q: Somebody is holding the pot and asking whether you want any. You do.
questions.why: They are offering an amount out of a pot rather than a fresh cup, so the answer is about how much and not how many. Un café orders a new one.

questions.q: You wanted cheese for the table, not one whole cheese. Fix this. « Je voudrais un fromage. »
questions.why: Un fromage is a whole wheel, a real thing a stall will hand you. Du fromage is an amount of it, which is what somebody buying lunch means.

questions.q: The waiter asks what you would like, and you want bread on the table. Complete: « Je voudrais ___ pain. »
questions.why: Bread on the table is an amount rather than a countable object, and pain takes le, so the amount form is du.

questions.q: What actually decides between un café and du café?
opts: Whether the listener has heard about it before
Whether you mean one thing you can count or an amount of something
Whether the sentence is a question
questions.why: Both are new to the listener, so newness cannot be it. What separates them is whether the thing is countable, which is the line English never makes you draw.

rounds.label: Once a quantity is named
rounds.say: Where the article disappears.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je bois beaucoup du café. »
questions.why: Beaucoup already says how much, so the word in front of the noun is not needed and French takes it out. Beaucoup du café is never said.

questions.q: A kilo is a quantity. So which is right?
questions.why: A container behaves exactly like beaucoup: it names the quantity, so bare de is all that is left between it and the noun.

questions.q: Fix this. « Une tranche du fromage, s’il vous plaît. »
accept: Une tranche de fromage, s’il vous plaît.
Une tranche de fromage, s'il vous plaît.
questions.answer: Une tranche de fromage, s’il vous plaît.
questions.why: The slice is the quantity, so the du goes. One card earlier the same cheese was du fromage, and naming the slice is exactly what changed.

questions.q: « Je bois de l’eau. » Now say you drink a lot of it. Complete: « Je bois beaucoup ___ eau. »
questions.why: The quantity takes the article out and leaves de, and de shortens in front of a vowel sound the same way le and la do.

questions.q: Fix this. « Elle met un peu du sel dans la soupe. »
accept: Elle met un peu de sel dans la soupe.
questions.answer: Elle met un peu de sel dans la soupe.
questions.why: Un peu de is a quantity word like beaucoup de, so it behaves the same way. The un in front belongs to peu and changes nothing about the noun.

rounds.label: Saying no
rounds.say: The rule you already met, one noun-class further on.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je ne mange pas du pain. »
accept: Je ne mange pas de pain.
questions.answer: Je ne mange pas de pain.
questions.why: Under a negative du, de la and de l apostrophe all collapse to de, which is the same thing un, une and des did last lesson.

questions.q: « Je bois de l’eau. » Now say you do not.
opts: Je ne bois pas de l’eau.
Je ne bois pas de eau.
questions.why: The collapse to de happens first and the shortening in front of a vowel happens second, so what is left is d apostrophe rather than de l apostrophe.

questions.q: Which sentence has a word in front of the noun that did NOT change under the negative?
opts: Je ne mange pas de fromage.
Je ne bois pas de café.
Je ne veux pas de soupe.
questions.why: Le, la and les survive a negative untouched. That asymmetry is what lets you work out afterwards which kind of word you had used.

questions.q: « Je mange du fromage. » Write it again, saying you do not.
accept: Je ne mange pas de fromage.
Je ne mange pas de fromage
questions.answer: Je ne mange pas de fromage.
questions.why: Du goes to de, not to pas du and not to pas le. The cheese was never a particular one, so there is nothing for le to point at.

questions.q: Say it out loud, to a waiter, before the cheese board arrives.
questions.target: Je ne mange pas de fromage.
questions.why: Pas de runs together into one short block. A gap between them is what makes it sound like two separate words rather than one negative.

rounds.label: Which du is it?
rounds.say: Four in five of them are not this word.

questions.q: Which of these du is about an amount of something?
opts: Le chargeur est près du lit.
Quel est le plat du jour ?
Le serveur apporte du pain frais.
questions.why: Only the third one would work with "some" in front of the English. The other three are of the: of the bed, of the day, of the bread.

questions.q: « à côté du salon » means "next to the living room". What is du doing there?
opts: Naming an amount of living room
Standing in for de and le together
questions.why: French squeezes de and le into du automatically, and the result looks identical to the word this lesson teaches. Only the meaning tells them apart.

questions.q: Somebody is offering you the pot and you want some. Fix this. « Je prends un café. »
questions.why: Un café orders a fresh cup, which is not what is being offered. When the coffee is already made and in front of you, what you want is an amount of it.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: All four are the same word agreeing with a different noun, so the ear has to catch the shape rather than the meaning. The vowel after de is what separates them.

questions.q: Fix this. « Il y a beaucoup du monde au marché. »
accept: Il y a beaucoup de monde au marché.
questions.answer: Il y a beaucoup de monde au marché.
questions.why: The quantity is already named, so nothing goes between it and the noun. This one catches people because monde takes le and the du looks plausible.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Five things you did not have this morning.
sections.body: You can ask for an amount of something without accidentally buying one whole object of it, which is most of what this word is for. The last two points below are worth more to you than the shapes are: the shapes take five minutes and those two take a year, and you have just had them both named.
points: Un is one of them. Du is some of it.
Du, de la and de l apostrophe are one word agreeing with the noun. Des is the plural, and you already had it.
Name a quantity or a container and the article goes: beaucoup de café, un kilo de tomates.
Say no and it collapses to de, exactly as un, une and des did. Le, la and les do not move.
Four in five of the du you read is de and le stuck together. Try putting "some" in front of the English.

grammarAssumed: Every noun carries a gender, and the article in front of it is the choice that gender makes
The definite article le, la, les, and its use in front of a general noun
Elision of le and la to l apostrophe in front of a vowel sound
The indefinite article un, une and des, and its collapse to de under a negative
grammarIntroduced: The partitive article du, de la and de l', for an unspecified quantity of an uncountable noun
The countable/uncountable distinction as the choice between un and du on the same noun
Des as the partitive plural, extending the indefinite plural already taught in a1.11
Bare de after an expression of quantity or a container, and its elision to d apostrophe
The partitive reducing to de under negation, extending the same rule from the indefinite
The formal identity of the partitive du with the contracted preposition de + le, and how to tell them apart

overview.introFr: Un café ou du café ? Les deux sont corrects, et ils ne commandent pas la même chose.

acts.title: A word you already own
acts.milestone: You have watched one syllable decide what somebody handed you.

acts.title: One of them, or some of it
acts.milestone: You can hear the difference between a thing and an amount of it.

acts.title: When the article disappears
acts.milestone: Two rules that both end in a bare de, and one that does not move at all.

acts.title: The other du, and the words banked
acts.milestone: You have separated two identical words, spelled them and said them out loud.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete.

lessons.reframe: Un is one of them. Du is some of it.

errorTriggers.description: Leaves the noun bare after a verb, because English puts nothing in front of it to translate.
Asks for one countable thing when they meant an amount, or the other way round. Both are correct French, so nothing corrects them.
Keeps du after a quantity word or a container: beaucoup du café, un kilo des tomates.
Keeps du, de la or de l apostrophe under a negative instead of collapsing all three to de.
Reads every du as an amount, including the four in five that are de and le squeezed together.

drills.title: The word English leaves out
drills.coach: Read the English on the left. Say the French on the right, out loud, and do not let the word in front go missing.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are telling somebody what you eat in the morning. Bread.
opts: Je mange du pain le matin.
Je mange le pain le matin.
drills.why: French does not leave the slot empty after a verb. An amount of bread takes du.

drills.title: A thing, or some of a thing?
drills.coach: Read each line and ask one question: could you count what is being asked for? If not, it is du, de la or de l apostrophe.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want cheese for the table. Not a whole cheese.
drills.why: Un fromage is one whole wheel and a stall will hand you one. Du fromage is an amount of it.

drills.title: Say how much, lose the word
drills.coach: The left is the sentence without a quantity. Say the right out loud, and notice what is no longer in it.
pairs: Je mets un peu de sel.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: "A lot of coffee" in French is:
drills.why: Beaucoup already says how much, so nothing goes between it and the noun.

drills.title: Say no and watch it shrink
drills.coach: Say the negative out loud before you flip. Four of these collapse to de and one does not move at all.
pairs: Je ne mange pas de pain.
Je ne fais pas de soupe.
Je ne mange pas de légumes.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which sentence has a word in front of the noun that did NOT change?
opts: Je ne mange pas de pain.
drills.why: Le, la and les survive a negative untouched. Only du, de la, de l apostrophe and des collapse to de.

drills.title: An amount, or of the?
drills.coach: Put "some" in front of the English. Some bread works, so that one is an amount. Some the bed does not.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one is NOT about an amount of something?
opts: Il ajoute du sel dans la soupe.
La cuisine est à côté du salon.
drills.why: À côté du salon is of the living room. There is no quantity of living room in it.

sheets.title: Every choice in this lesson, on one screen
contains: One of them against some of it

sections.title: One of them, some of it, all of it
The four places English points the wrong way

rows.v: Je mange du pain, not Je mange pain. French does not leave that slot empty.
Un café is a cup. Du café is coffee. Both correct, and they order different things.
beaucoup de café, un peu de sel, trop de sucre. Never beaucoup du café.
un kilo de tomates, une tranche de fromage, une bouteille d’eau.
Je ne mange pas de pain. Du, de la, de l' and des all become de.
rows.say: Je ne mange pas de pain.

rows.v: Je n'aime pas le pain. Le, la and les do not move at all.

sections.title: Telling the two du apart
sections.body: Across the a1 corpus, roughly four rows in five holding du, de la or de l apostrophe are not about an amount at all. They are de and le squeezed together, and they turn up after a preposition (près du lit, à côté du salon), between two nouns (l odeur du pain, le plat du jour, la fin du repas), and in fixed compounds you already own (l emploi du temps). The test is one second long: put "some" in front of the English. Some bread works, so je mange du pain is this lesson. Some the bed does not, so près du lit is the other one. Nothing else in French depends on getting this right, but everything you READ does, because you will otherwise be looking for a quantity in four sentences out of five that do not have one.

someOfIt.title: The word for an amount nobody has counted
someOfIt.body: Use these when you mean some of a thing rather than a number of them. Du in front of most nouns, de la in front of the ones that take la, and de l apostrophe in front of a word starting with a vowel sound. English usually puts nothing here, or the word "some" when it wants to be careful, so there is nothing in your own language reminding you that French wants a word at all.

examples.note: Bread, not a loaf. Nobody has weighed it.
Water, not a bottle. De l apostrophe because eau opens on a vowel sound.

oneOfThem.title: The word for a thing you can count
oneOfThem.body: Use these when you mean one of something: one cup, one loaf, one apple. This is the half English gives you for free, because English has a and an and uses them in the same place. The trap is that it also works in front of the same nouns: un café and du café are both correct and they are two different orders.

examples.note: One cup, on a saucer, at a counter.
One whole loaf, wrapped and paid for.

namedQuantity.title: What is left once a quantity is named
namedQuantity.body: Say how much and the article in front of the noun disappears. Beaucoup de café, un peu de sel, trop de sucre, and never beaucoup du café. Containers behave the same way, because a container is a quantity with a shape: un kilo de tomates, une bouteille d apostrophe eau, une tranche de fromage. This is completely regular and it is the opposite of what an English speaker expects, since English keeps "of the" in "a lot of the coffee".

examples.note: The same sentence as Je bois du café, with a quantity named.
A kilo is a quantity, so the noun goes in bare behind it.

deUnderNo.title: What is left once you say no
deUnderNo.body: Je mange du pain becomes je ne mange pas de pain. You met this rule one lesson ago on un, une and des, and it is the same rule here with nothing added: say no and what was in front of the noun collapses to de. Before a vowel sound it shortens again, to d apostrophe. The one that does not move is le, la and les, which is how you can work out afterwards which word you had used.

examples.note: Du went to de. Not pas du pain, and not pas le pain.
The sentence you need on your first day if you do not eat meat.

otherDu.title: The same three letters doing a different job
otherDu.body: Près du lit, le plat du jour, l apostrophe odeur du pain. None of these is about an amount of anything: they are de and le squeezed together, which French does automatically, and you have been reading them since your first lesson. Four out of five of the du in this corpus are this one. The test is whether you could put "some" in front of the English: some bread yes, some the bed no.

examples.note: Near the bed. There is no amount of bed involved.
The smell of the bread. The bread is a particular one, on a particular morning.

inGeneral.title: The word for the whole of something
