inGeneral.body: J'aime le café is I like coffee, all of it, for the rest of your life. That is a1.04's rule and it is here only so you can see it is not the answer to this lesson's question. Le names the whole category or the particular one you have both been talking about. Du names part of it, right now, on this table. Both look wrong to an English speaker and only one of them is what you meant.

examples.note: Some of what is in the pot, now.
Buying cheese, so an amount of it, even though aimer is in the sentence.

recorded.desc: The ten amounts of the group drill, read in ONE TAKE by ONE voice at ONE speed. The learner is comparing four shapes of the same word, so a set split across takes has them comparing four performances instead. Keep du tight and rounded: it is /y/, not /u/ and not /ø/, and a relaxed reading of it lands on deux.

The two minimal pairs this lesson turns on, un against du and du against de, each pair recorded BACK TO BACK IN ONE TAKE by the same voice at the same speed, in the same way sons.07 pins rec-h-pairs and a1.11 pins rec-a1-11-pairs. Both pairs are one vowel and both carry the whole meaning. Then the four listening lines at natural pace and again at 0.65. The warning that matters: DO NOT OVER-ROUND du. Lengthened or relaxed it becomes deux, which is a real word a learner could plausibly have heard, and the exercise stops being about articles.

The four English-speaker traps, wrong form then right form, with a clear beat between them so the learner hears the difference rather than a correction. Je mange pain / Je mange du pain. Je voudrais un café / Je voudrais du café. Beaucoup du café / Beaucoup de café. Je ne mange pas du pain / Je ne mange pas de pain. Read the wrong version plainly, not comically: two of these four are things a French speaker says.

lessons.title: Le verbe être
lessons.intro: Six forms, no pattern behind them, and one of them in almost every sentence you will say. This is the verb that introduces you: who you are, what you do, where you are from and how you are, all on the same six words.

sections.title: The Word She Left Out
sections.frSub: Le mot qu'elle n'a pas dit

say.text: A first meeting, and you will be understood throughout. Watch the one word that goes missing.

setting.place: A conference badge table

beats.text: A badge table at a conference in Lyon. You have the greetings. What nobody gave you is the sentence that comes after them.

beats.speaker: Sylvie
beats.fr: Bonjour ! Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
beats.en: Hello! Are you here for the conference?

beats.stage: That lands. She nods and points at the man beside her.

beats.prompt: He is a doctor. What goes back?

options.en: the one English hands you
the one with nothing in the middle

followUp.works: Yes, and nothing between est and médecin. Watch why the other one is so hard to shake.
followUp.breaks: You will be understood. Watch what happens next anyway.

beats.speaker: Sylvie
beats.fr: Ah, il est médecin. Très bien.
beats.en: Ah, he is a doctor. Very good.
beats.stage: Nobody corrects you. She just says it back without the un.

beats.heading: She dropped a word
beats.body: English needs a word in front of a job and French forbids one. Nobody corrects this, because you were understood. That is why it lasts.

wrong.en: understood, and not French

beats.coach: The one place it comes back is the last act.

beats.text: Four sentences into a first meeting and you have used the verb three times. That is the whole case for learning it outright.

closing.text: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation. You met three of the six in that exchange without being taught one of them.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation. By the end you will have all six and know which sentence wants which.

goals.s: Give your name, and point at someone else without reaching for the wrong word.
Name your job the way French does it, with nothing in front of it.
Both ways, and know which of the two has to agree with you.
By one mechanical test you can run in the moment, not by feel.

sections.title: This One Has No Pattern
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Read this one properly. It decides what you should be doing for the next twenty minutes.

cards.label: What you already have
cards.head: The left column is done
cards.body: You met the nine subject pronouns last lesson, and that il, elle and on share one form while ils and elles share another. Nothing here re-teaches that.

cards.label: The usual deal
cards.head: Most verbs give you a stem
cards.body: Learn one pattern and hundreds of verbs come with it. That is the deal French offers almost everywhere.

cards.label: The exception
cards.head: This one gives you nothing
cards.body: These three are not versions of one word. There is nothing to derive, and looking for it wastes the time you could spend memorising.

cards.label: The trade
cards.head: and pays you back immediately
cards.body: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation. Six words to learn outright, and you will use one of them in almost every sentence you say this week.

sections.title: The Six, In One Table
sections.say: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation. Six rows for nine pronouns, because two rows are shared. Tap any row to hear it.

cells: Je suis ici pour la conférence.
rows.say: Je suis ici pour la conférence.

detail.title: je suis
detail.body: The form you will say more than all the others together, because most of what a beginner says is about themselves. It shortens to j'y and j'en later; with être it never elides, because suis starts on a consonant.

cells: Tu es ici pour la conférence ?
rows.say: Tu es ici pour la conférence ?

detail.title: tu es
detail.body: Two letters and no S sound. It is said exactly like est, so the only thing separating tu es from il est out loud is the pronoun in front.

cells: Il est ici pour la conférence.
rows.say: Il est ici pour la conférence.

detail.title: The row that does the work
detail.body: Three pronouns, one form, and the T is silent. on means we and still takes this form, which is the mismatch a1.05 spent a mission on.

cells: Nous sommes ici pour la conférence.
rows.say: Nous sommes ici pour la conférence.

detail.title: nous sommes
detail.body: The doubled m really is pronounced, so this is not a nasal vowel: it ends on a clear M. Out loud, most rooms use on and est instead.
detail.say: Nous sommes trois à la terrasse.

cells: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
rows.say: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?

detail.title: vous êtes
detail.body: The only row where the pronoun and the verb bind out loud. The silent S of vous wakes up in front of the vowel and the two are said as one word.

cells: Ils sont ici pour la conférence.
rows.say: Ils sont ici pour la conférence.

detail.title: ils sont
detail.body: A nasal vowel and a silent T. Hold this one carefully: ils ont is a different verb entirely and the two are separated by a single sound.

sections.title: One At A Time
sections.hint: Swipe. Say each one out loud before you move on.
sections.say: Six screens, one form each. Say it out loud before you swipe, every time.

cards.label: 1 of 6
cards.body: I am.

cards.label: 2 of 6
cards.body: You are. No S sound.

cards.label: 3 of 6
cards.body: He is. No T sound.

cards.label: 4 of 6
cards.body: We are.

cards.label: 5 of 6
cards.body: You are. One word out loud.

cards.label: 6 of 6
cards.body: They are. No T sound.

sections.title: Which Form Goes With Which
sections.say: Read the pronoun, say the form, then check. No pattern will help you here, which is the point.

check.q: Which of these is the form that follows on?
check.why: on means we and takes the form il takes, so it is est. That collapse was a1.05's and it holds for every verb.

check.q: You are speaking to one stranger, politely. Which form?
check.why: vous takes êtes whether it is one person politely or a whole group. The word alone never tells you which job it is doing.

sections.title: The Join In Vous Êtes
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: One form in the six behaves differently out loud, and it is the one you cannot hear yourself get wrong.

cards.label: The rule
cards.head: The silent S wakes up
cards.fr: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
cards.body: vous ends in a silent S. êtes starts on a vowel. The S comes back as a Z and the two words are said as one.

cards.label: The error
cards.head: A gap that marks you
cards.body: Said with a pause it is still understood, and it is the kind of error nobody mentions and nobody misses either.

cards.label: Where you meet it
cards.head: You already know this one
cards.body: At the door of every restaurant in France. You have heard it as one word since your first week without knowing it was two.

sections.title: Two Verbs, One Syllable Apart
sections.say: Two of these are not this verb at all. The difference is one sound and it is the whole meaning.

lines.en: They are late.
They have an appointment.

lines.fr: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
lines.en: Are you here for the conference?

lines.fr: Tu es ici pour la conférence ?
lines.en: Are you here for the conference?

questions.q: « Ils sont » and « ils ont » differ by one sound. Which one?
opts: An S at the start of the verb
questions.why: ils sont starts on an S. ils ont has a Z join instead, carried over from the silent S of ils. One sound, and a different verb.

questions.q: You hear « voo ZET » as a single word. What are the two words?
questions.why: The Z is the silent S of vous waking up in front of the vowel. It is one word out loud and two on the page.

questions.q: Out loud, « tu es » and « il est » end on the same sound. What separates them?
opts: The T at the end of est
The S at the end of es
questions.why: Both verbs are said the same way: the S of es and the T of est are silent. Only the pronoun does the telling.

sections.title: Saying Who Someone Is
sections.say: Yourself takes one shape and somebody else takes another. Tap any row to hear it.

detail.title: je suis plus a name
detail.body: A name is already as specific as a word can be, so nothing goes in front of it. This is the same shape as je suis architecte.

detail.title: c'est plus a name
detail.body: Introducing somebody is pointing at them, and pointing takes c'est. Il est Marc is not how this is said.

detail.title: c'est plus my something
detail.body: ma, mon, ton and votre are all little words in front of the noun, and any one of them puts the sentence on c'est. This is the test act 5 turns into a rule.

detail.title: ce sont
detail.body: The plural of c'est, and the form almost everyone forgets exists. c'est mes parents is what a beginner says and it is not right.

sections.title: What A Job Takes After Être
sections.say: Nothing. English needs a word here and French forbids one, so this error is guaranteed and it is audible. Tap any line.

examples.note: No un. The gap after suis is the grammar.
a1.11 taught you this one. It holds for every form of the verb, not only for je suis.
Same after elle est. The job noun changes for a woman; nothing appears in front of it.
And after tu es. Being a student counts as a job for this rule.
And after vous êtes, with the liaison running straight into it.

sections.title: Three Ways The Job Goes Wrong
sections.say: Three mistakes, and all three come from English being helpful.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je suis un architecte. »
errors.why: English cannot say "I am architect" and French cannot say the other one. The word you want to insert is the word to leave out.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je suis un français. »
errors.why: A nationality behaves like a job here: nothing in front of it. It is an adjective, and an adjective never took an article in the first place.

errors.wrong: Writing « Je suis Français. » with a capital F.
errors.right: Writing « Je suis français. » with a small f.
errors.why: English capitalises the adjective and French does not. The capital is kept for the noun, as in un Français, which is a different sentence.

sections.title: Where You Are From, Two Ways
sections.say: One question, two answers, and only one of them changes depending on who is speaking. Tap any row.

rows.say: Je suis français. Je suis française.

detail.title: The nationality
detail.body: français for a man, française for a woman, and here you can hear the difference: the e wakes the s. Lowercase f, always.

detail.title: The town
detail.body: de plus wherever you are from. It does not agree with anything and never changes, whoever is saying it.

detail.title: A whole group
detail.body: The adjective takes the group with it. The s is silent, so this agreement exists only on the page.

detail.title: How to ask
detail.body: de plus où, elided to d'où. It is the question that gets you either answer, and it is worth having ready.

sections.title: The E You Sometimes Hear
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: You already do this. a1.01 had you writing enchantée with an extra e and saying nothing different.

cards.label: Already yours
cards.head: You met this in lesson one
cards.body: An adjective agrees with whoever it describes. Nothing new is being asked, only applied to a longer list of words.

cards.label: Silent
cards.head: Often you hear nothing
cards.body: Identical out loud to the masculine. The agreement is real, it matters in writing, and your ear gets no help at all.

cards.label: Audible
cards.head: and sometimes you do
cards.body: Here the e wakes the d and you can hear it. Grand and grande are genuinely different sounds.

cards.label: The rule of thumb
cards.head: A consonant before the e wakes up
cards.body: If the masculine ends on a silent consonant, adding the e sounds it. If it ends on a vowel, nothing changes.

sections.title: How You Are Right Now
sections.say: The fourth thing this verb does, and the smallest. Same agreement as the last screen, different words.

examples.note: A man says this. A woman writes fatiguée and says the same thing.
And here the agreement sounds: the e wakes the d.
You met this in a1.05. It was this use of the verb all along.
en retard does not agree with anyone. Not every state is an adjective.

examples.fr: Tu dois te reposer si tu es fatigué.
examples.en: You should rest if you are tired.
examples.note: One of only four tu es sentences in the whole corpus, and it hides inside a longer one.

sections.title: One Test, Not A Feeling
sections.hint: Swipe through the five cards.
sections.say: This is the part of the lesson you will still be using in two years. One question, asked of the words after the verb.

cards.label: The question
cards.head: Look at what follows the verb
cards.body: Not at the meaning, and not at whether it is a person. Look at whether a little word sits in front of the noun.

cards.label: Little word
cards.head: There is one, so c'est
cards.body: un, une, le, la, mon, ma, votre. Any one of them and the sentence takes c'est.

cards.label: Bare noun
cards.head: There is none, so il est
cards.body: Same doctor, same fact, and no little word. That is what il est is for.

cards.label: Adjective
cards.head: An adjective counts as bare
cards.body: Describing rather than naming, so il est or elle est. This is the half a1.11 could not reach.

cards.label: The one to remember
cards.head: A name is already specified
cards.sub: so it behaves like a little word
cards.body: A name cannot be made more specific, so pointing at Marc takes c'est rather than il est.

sections.title: The Same Person, Twice
sections.say: Read across, not down. Same person and same job on each row, and only one thing moves.

rows.say: C'est un médecin. Il est médecin.

detail.title: The doctor, twice
detail.body: One man, one job, two sentences, both correct. The left one has a little word in front of the noun and the right one does not. Nothing else differs.

rows.say: C'est le directeur. Il est directeur.

detail.title: The definite one counts too
detail.body: The test is any little word, not the indefinite one specifically. le, la, mon and ma all put the sentence on c'est.

rows.say: C'est un professeur. Je suis professeur.

detail.title: The pair you already met
detail.body: a1.11 gave you these two as a fact about professions. They are really one instance of the little-word test, which also covers things, ideas and names.

sections.title: Where C'est And Il Est Go Wrong
sections.say: Four, and the first is the one the scene opened on.

errors.wrong: Saying « Il est un médecin. »
errors.why: A little word appeared with il est, which is the one thing il est does not take. Either drop the un, or keep it and switch to c'est un médecin.

errors.wrong: Saying « Il est Marc. »
errors.why: A name is already fully specified, so it behaves like a noun with a little word in front. Pointing at a person takes c'est.

errors.wrong: Saying « Il est une bonne idée. »
errors.why: il est needs somebody or something to refer back to. An idea, a situation or a general verdict always takes c'est.

errors.wrong: Saying « C'est mes parents. »
errors.why: The verb still has to agree. More than one person takes sont, and ce sont is the form almost everyone forgets exists.

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: The situation is on the front. Say the whole sentence before you flip.

cards.front: How many forms, and how much pattern?
cards.back: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation. suis, es, est, sommes, êtes, sont.

cards.front: A woman saying where she is from, by country
Anyone saying where they are from, by town
He is a doctor, with nothing in front
That is a doctor, pointing across the room
Asking one stranger politely if they are here for it
cards.back: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
cards.say: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?

cards.front: Telling a group they are late

cards.back: est. on means we and takes the il form.

sections.title: Say The Whole Sentence
sections.say: Each one as a single movement. A form on its own proves nothing, so the pronoun comes with it every time.

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Seven sentences. The silent letters are the whole difficulty: es, est and sont all end on something you will not hear.

sections.title: Your Turn At The Badge Table
sections.say: The same conference, an hour later. Every answer is one of the four uses.
sections.setting: The coffee stand at the Lyon conference. Somebody you have not met turns towards you with a cup in each hand.

turns.ai: Bonjour ! Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
turns.en: Hello! Are you here for the conference?
turns.user: Oui, je suis architecte.
turns.userEn: Yes, I'm an architect.

alts.fr: Oui, nous sommes ici pour la conférence.
alts.en: Yes, we're here for the conference.

turns.ai: Ah, très bien. Vous êtes d'où ?
turns.en: Ah, very good. Where are you from?
turns.user: Je suis de Lyon. Et vous ?
turns.userEn: I'm from Lyon. And you?

turns.ai: Je suis espagnole, mais j'habite ici. Et lui, c'est votre collègue ?
turns.en: I am Spanish, but I live here. And him, is that your colleague?
turns.user: Oui, c'est mon collègue. Il est ingénieur.
turns.userEn: Yes, that's my colleague. He's an engineer.

alts.fr: Non, c'est un ami. Il est professeur.
alts.en: No, that's a friend. He's a teacher.

turns.ai: Vous êtes prêts pour la présentation ?
turns.en: Are you ready for the presentation?
turns.user: Non, nous sommes en retard !
turns.userEn: No, we're late!

alts.fr: Presque ! Elle est prête, moi non.

turns.ai: Alors allez-y. Bonne chance !
turns.en: Then off you go. Good luck!
turns.user: Merci beaucoup.
turns.userEn: Thank you very much.

sections.title: Four People, One Badge Table
sections.say: Read it once for the shape. Every one of the six forms is in here. Tap any word you do not know.
sections.text: Nine in the morning at the badge table. Sylvie is already there. « Bonjour, vous êtes ici pour la conférence ? » « Oui. Je suis architecte, et je suis de Lyon. » A man arrives behind you and puts down two cups. « C'est mon collègue. Il est ingénieur. » Sylvie looks at the badges and then at the clock. « Ah, vous êtes les deux de Lyon. Elle est espagnole, elle. » She points at a woman by the door who is holding a folder. « Ce sont les organisateurs ? » « Non, ils sont en retard aussi. »

glossary.note: Bare after il est, like every job. C'est un ingénieur would need the un.
The adjective agreeing. A man would be espagnol, with no e and no L sound.
Plural and pointed at, so ce sont rather than c'est.
En retard is a state, not an adjective, so nothing agrees with anybody.
mon is the little word in front, which is what puts this sentence on c'est.

questions.q: The passage says « Il est ingénieur » and « C'est mon collègue » about the same man. Why do the two sentences take different forms?
questions.a: mon is a little word in front of collègue, so that sentence takes c'est. Ingénieur stands bare, so that one takes il est. Same man, and the test is only about the words after the verb.

questions.q: « Ce sont les organisateurs ? » Why ce sont and not c'est?
questions.a: The verb still agrees. More than one person takes sont, so the plural of c'est is ce sont.

questions.q: Two people say where they are from and one of them agrees with the speaker. Which, and why?
questions.a: Espagnole is an adjective and takes an e because a woman is speaking. De Lyon is a preposition plus a place and never changes for anybody.

sections.title: The Whole Verb, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card objectively. Again, hard, or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: How many forms, and how much pattern behind them?
cards.back: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation. There is nothing to derive, so all six are learned outright.
suis, es, est, sommes, êtes, sont.
cards.say: Je suis ici pour la conférence.

cards.front: What goes between être and a job?
cards.back: Nothing at all. Je suis architecte, never je suis un architecte.

cards.front: The one place the little word comes back
cards.back: After c'est. C'est un médecin, and il est médecin.

cards.front: A little word in front of the noun means…
cards.back: c'est. A bare noun or an adjective means il est.
C'est Marc. A name is already specified, so it takes c'est.

cards.front: You are pointing at two people
cards.back: Ce sont mes parents. The verb agrees even here.

cards.front: A woman saying she is French
cards.back: Je suis française. The e wakes the s and you can hear it.

cards.front: Anyone saying they are from Lyon
cards.back: Je suis de Lyon. De never agrees with anyone.
as one word, voo-ZET. The silent S of vous wakes up in front of the vowel.
cards.say: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?

cards.back: One is this verb and one is the next lesson. An S against a Z.

cards.front: A woman writing that she is tired
cards.back: Je suis fatiguée. The extra e is real and it is silent.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have met all six forms, sorted them by pronoun, heard the two that hide behind silent letters, said them out loud and spelled them from sound alone. You have used the verb for all four of the things it does. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Five rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get a drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The six forms
rounds.say: Six rooms, six forms. No pattern will help you.

questions.q: You are telling someone your job. Which form of être opens the sentence?
questions.why: je takes suis. It is the form you will say more than the other five together, because most of what you say is about yourself.

questions.q: Write the form of être that goes with nous.
questions.why: nous takes sommes, and the doubled m really is pronounced. Nothing in suis or es could have told you that.

questions.q: Three of you have just arrived and you want to say so the way it is actually said out loud. Which form?
questions.why: on means we and takes the form il takes, so it is est. The meaning pulls one way and the form goes the other.

questions.q: Fix this. You are speaking to one stranger, politely: « Vous es ici pour la conférence ? »
accept: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence
questions.answer: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
questions.why: vous takes êtes whether it is one person politely or a group. es belongs to tu and to nowhere else.

questions.q: Fix this. You are speaking about yourself and a colleague: « Nous êtes en retard. »
questions.why: nous takes sommes. êtes is the vous form, and the two are neighbours in the table and nowhere else.

questions.q: Which of these is true of the six forms of être?
opts: They all share the stem êt-
Four of them are built from suis
They are six separate words with no shared stem
questions.why: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation. There is nothing to derive, which is why the correct strategy here is memorising rather than pattern-hunting.

rounds.label: The gap after être
rounds.say: English wants a word here. French does not.

questions.q: You are an architect. Write the sentence.
questions.why: No un. English cannot say "I am architect" and French cannot say the other one, which is what makes this error automatic.

questions.q: Fix this. She works as a nurse: « Elle est une infirmière. »
questions.why: A job after être stands bare. Keeping the une would mean switching the front of the sentence to c'est une infirmière.

questions.q: Fix this. A man saying where he is from: « Je suis un français. »
questions.why: A nationality here is an adjective, and an adjective never took an article. It behaves exactly like a job.

questions.q: Which of these is written correctly?
questions.why: Small f and nothing in front. English capitalises the adjective and French keeps the capital for the noun, as in un Français.

questions.q: You are asking somebody politely whether they are an engineer. Which is right?
questions.why: êtes for vous, and no article in front of the job. Both halves of this lesson in one four-word question.

questions.q: What goes between a form of être and a job noun?
questions.why: Nothing. a1.11 gave you this as a fact about professions; it is really a fact about what follows être.

rounds.label: Where you are from
rounds.say: Two shapes, and only one of them agrees with you.

questions.q: A woman is saying she is French. Write the sentence.
questions.why: The adjective agrees, and here you can hear it: the e wakes the s, so française and français are genuinely different sounds.

questions.q: A woman is saying she is from Marseille. What changes compared to a man saying it?
opts: An e is added to Marseille
questions.why: de plus a place is a preposition and never agrees with anybody. Only the adjective shape of origin moves.

questions.q: Fix this. A group of Canadians, and there is a man among them: « Ils sont canadien. »
questions.why: The adjective takes the group with it, so it needs the plural s. The s is silent, so this one exists only on the page.

questions.q: Which pair sounds identical when said out loud?
questions.why: fatigué ends on a vowel, so adding the e changes nothing you can hear. The other three end on a consonant that the e wakes up.

questions.q: Tap the letter you do not say.
questions.why: The plural s is silent, which is why the agreement on a nationality is often invisible to the ear and only real in writing.

questions.q: How do you ask somebody where they are from?
questions.why: de plus où, elided to d'où. It is the one question that gets you either shape of answer.

rounds.label: c'est or il est
rounds.say: One test, run on the words after the verb.

questions.q: Fix this. He works as a doctor: « Il est un médecin. »
questions.why: il est takes the noun bare. The other repair is just as good: keep the un and it becomes c'est un médecin.

questions.q: You are pointing across the room at your sister. Which is right?
questions.why: ma is a little word in front of the noun, so the sentence takes c'est. Any of mon, ma, ton or votre does the same.

questions.q: Fix this. You are introducing a friend called Marc: « Il est Marc. »
questions.why: A name cannot be made more specific, so it behaves like a noun that already has its little word. Pointing at a person takes c'est.

questions.q: What decides between c'est and il est?
opts: Whether it is a person or a thing
Whether a little word sits in front of the noun
questions.why: A determiner in front of the noun takes c'est. A bare noun, or an adjective, takes il est. It is a question about the words, not about the meaning.

questions.q: Fix this. You are pointing at both your parents: « C'est mes parents. »
questions.why: The verb agrees even here. More than one person takes sont, and ce sont is the form almost everyone forgets exists.

questions.q: Somebody proposes meeting at eight. You want to say that is a good idea. Which is right?
questions.why: il est needs somebody or something to point back to. A verdict on a situation always takes c'est.

rounds.label: By ear
rounds.say: The letters you cannot hear are the ones doing the work.

questions.q: Listen. Which sentence is it?
questions.why: sont starts on an S. ils ont would give you a Z instead, and that single sound is the difference between this verb and the next lesson.

questions.q: Listen. Is this one person or a group?

audio.clip: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?

opts: You cannot tell from the sound
questions.why: vous êtes is the same out loud either way. It is the polite singular and the plain plural at once, and only the room settles it.

questions.q: Listen. How is it said?
opts: With a pause between vous and êtes
With the S said as an S
With the final S of êtes sounded
questions.why: The silent S of vous wakes up as a Z in front of the vowel and the two words are said as one. A gap there is understood and marks you.

questions.q: Say it out loud, the way you would answer at a badge table.
questions.target: Je suis architecte, et je suis de Lyon.
questions.ipa: /ʒə sɥi aʁ.ʃi.tɛkt e ʒə sɥi də ljɔ̃/
questions.why: Two uses in one breath and no article in either. Say it as two phrases, not seven separate words.

questions.q: Out loud, « tu es » and « il est » end on the same sound. Why?
opts: The S of es and the T of est are both silent
Both end on a nasal vowel
The verb changes to match the pronoun
questions.why: Two different forms with two different silent letters, landing on one sound. Only the pronoun in front separates them.

questions.q: Write what you would say to point at your colleague across the room.
questions.why: mon is the little word in front, so the sentence takes c'est. Il est mon collègue is the version to unlearn.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then the lesson that picks this up.
sections.body: You can now introduce yourself completely: who you are, what you do, where you are from and how you are, all on one verb. The next unit is avoir, and it is irregular in exactly the same way and for exactly the same reason. These two are the most broken verbs in French because they are the most used, and no other verb will ask this of you again. One thing to carry across: ils sont belongs to this lesson and ils ont belongs to that one, and a single sound separates them.
points: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation. suis, es, est, sommes, êtes, sont, and nothing derives from anything.
Nothing goes between être and a job. Je suis architecte, never je suis un architecte.
A little word in front of the noun takes c'est. A bare noun or an adjective takes il est.
A nationality agrees with you and de plus a town never does.

grammarAssumed: The nine subject pronouns, and the six verb forms they sit behind, introduced in a1.05
on takes third-person-singular agreement, introduced in a1.05
Gendered agreement on a bare adjective, introduced in a1.01 on enchanté and désolé
No article after être in front of a profession, introduced in a1.11
The indefinite and definite articles, introduced in a1.04 and a1.11
grammarIntroduced: The full present tense of être, as six forms with no derivable stem
être for identity, profession, origin and description
The determiner test: a little word in front of the noun takes c'est, a bare noun or an adjective takes il est
ce sont as the plural of c'est
Nationality adjectives, which agree, against de plus a place, which does not
The obligatory liaison in vous êtes

overview.introFr: Six formes, aucun modèle, et l'une d'elles dans presque chaque phrase que vous direz.

acts.title: The verb that gives you nothing
acts.milestone: You know there is no pattern here, and why that is the good news.

acts.title: The six forms
acts.milestone: You have all six, and you can hear the two that hide behind silent letters.

acts.title: Who you are, and what you do
acts.milestone: You can name yourself, name your job, and point at somebody else.

acts.title: Where you are from, and how you are
acts.milestone: You know which half of origin agrees with you and which half never moves.

acts.title: c'est against il est
acts.milestone: You have a test you can run in the moment instead of a feeling.

acts.title: Out in the world
acts.milestone: You have said all six out loud and spelled them from sound alone.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. avoir is next, and it breaks the same way.

lessons.reframe: No pattern. Six forms. Every conversation.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong row of the table: êtes for nous, es for vous, sommes for on.
Puts un or une in front of a job or a nationality, because English requires one there.
Leaves a nationality unagreed, or tries to agree de plus a place with the speaker.
Uses il est where a determiner is present, or c'est where the noun is bare. The error that survives into B1.
Cannot separate es from est, or ils sont from ils ont, because the letters that differ are silent.

drills.title: Pronoun in, form out
drills.coach: The pronoun is on the left. Say the form out loud before you turn the card.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You and one colleague are late. Which form?
drills.why: nous takes sommes. êtes is the vous form, and they sit next to each other in the table and nowhere else.

drills.title: Does anything go in front?
buckets: A little word goes in front
drills.coach: A job or a nationality after être takes nothing. Anything on a c'est sentence takes its little word.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: She works as a lawyer. Which is right?
drills.why: Nothing in front of a job after être. The un would only be correct with c'est in front instead.

drills.title: Does it agree, or not?
drills.coach: A nationality is an adjective and moves. de plus a place is a preposition and does not.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: A woman says she is from Marseille. What does she say?
drills.why: de plus a place never agrees with anybody. Only the nationality adjective would have moved.

drills.title: c'est, or il est?
drills.coach: Read what comes after the verb and ask one question: is there a little word in front of the noun?

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are pointing at the director across the room. Which is right?
drills.why: le is a little word in front of the noun, so the sentence takes c'est. Il est directeur, with nothing in front, would also be correct.

drills.title: What did the ending do?
drills.coach: Read the written form, then say what your ear actually gets from it.
pairs: no S sound, same as est
no T sound, same as es
a real M, and it sounds

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You hear a Z between the two words. Which did you hear?
drills.why: The silent S of vous wakes up as a Z in front of the vowel. ils sont starts on a clear S instead.

sheets.title: être, in full
contains: All nine pronouns with their form

sections.title: The full paradigm
rows: they are, any group with a man in it

sections.title: The letters you do not say
sections.body: Four of the six end in something silent. The S of es and the T of est are both mute, which is why tu es and il est land on the same sound and only the pronoun separates them. The T of sont is mute and the vowel before it is nasal, so it is [SOHⁿ] and never [SONT]. The final S of vous is mute on its own and comes back as a Z in front of êtes, which is the one place in the paradigm where the pronoun and the verb are said as a single word. Only sommes ends on a consonant you really pronounce, and that is because the m is doubled in the spelling: a single m there would have made a nasal vowel instead.

sections.title: What carries into avoir
sections.body: avoir is the next unit and it breaks in exactly the same way: six forms, no stem to lean on, nothing derivable from anything. That is not a coincidence. être and avoir are the two most used verbs in French and they are the two most broken, because a form said a hundred times a day is never smoothed out by analogy the way a rare verb is. One pair is worth keeping apart from the start, because it belongs to both lessons at once: ils sont opens on a clear S, and ils ont has a Z carried over from the silent S of ils. Everything else in the language after these two has a stem and endings, so this is the last time you will be asked to learn a verb outright.

sheets.title: The four uses, and the c'est test
contains: The full c'est against il est table
What counts as a little word

sections.title: What être is for
rows: A name takes nothing in front of it
Pointing takes c'est, never il est
An adjective, and it agrees with you
A preposition, and it never moves
An adjective, and it agrees again

sections.title: c'est against il est, in full
rows: un or une plus a noun
le, la or les plus a noun
mon, ma or votre plus a noun
A thing, an idea, a verdict

sections.title: Why the test works
sections.body: c'est points and il est describes. Everything in the table follows from that, but a learner in the middle of a sentence has no time to decide whether they are pointing or describing, so the mechanical version is the one to carry: look at the words after the verb and ask whether a little word sits in front of the noun. If it does, c'est. If the noun stands bare, or if what follows is an adjective, il est or elle est. A name counts as having one, because a name is already as specified as a word can be. The reason this is worth learning as a test rather than as a feeling is that it is the confusion that survives longest: learners who can hold a conversation still get it wrong, because at speed the meaning-based version is too slow to run and the mechanical one is not.

etre.title: The verb with no stem
etre.body: To be, and the first verb worth memorising outright. Every regular verb hands you a stem and a set of endings, so parler gives parl- plus six endings and with it come hundreds of other verbs. être gives you nothing to build on: the six forms are six separate words. Learn them as six words and the cost is paid once.

examples.note: suis, the form you will say most.
sommes, which shares no letters with it at all.

sixForms.title: suis, es, est, sommes, êtes, sont
sixForms.body: Six forms for nine pronouns, because il, elle and on share one and ils and elles share another. That collapse is a1.05's and it holds for every verb in the language. What is particular to être is that the six cannot be derived from each other, so this is the one table you memorise rather than work out.

examples.note: est, the form three of the nine pronouns take.
sont, the form the other two share.

determinerTest.title: How to choose between c'est and il est
determinerTest.body: Look at what comes after the verb. If there is a little word in front of the noun, a un, une, le, la, mon or ma, the sentence takes c'est. If the noun stands bare, or if what follows is an adjective, it takes il est or elle est. A name is already as specified as a word can be, so it counts as having one: c'est Marc.

examples.note: un in front of the noun, so c'est.
The same doctor with nothing in front, so il est.

noArticle.title: What a job takes after être
noArticle.body: Nothing. Je suis professeur, elle est avocate, il est boulanger. English requires a word there and French forbids it, which makes this the one grammatical error a beginner produces out loud in the first minute of every introduction. You met this in a1.11 as a rule about professions; it is really a rule about what follows être.

examples.note: No un before architecte.
a1.11's sentence, and the one c'est is the exception to.

originShapes.title: français against de Lyon
originShapes.body: Where you are from has two shapes and they behave differently. A nationality is an adjective and agrees with you: français for a man, française for a woman. de plus a place is a preposition and never moves at all, whoever is speaking. Both answer the same question and only one of them can be got wrong.

examples.note: The adjective, agreeing, and audibly so.
The preposition, which is the same for everyone.

vousLiaison.title: The join you cannot hear yourself miss
vousLiaison.body: The one form in the six where the pronoun and the verb bind out loud. The silent s of vous wakes up in front of the vowel and the two words are said as one: voo-ZET, with no gap. Saying them separately is understood and marks you immediately, and it is the kind of error a learner cannot hear in their own mouth.

examples.note: The paradigm row, with the join in it.
a1.05's question, which you have already heard in a restaurant.

silentAgreement.title: An e you write and never say
silentAgreement.body: An adjective after être agrees with whoever it describes, and often that agreement makes no sound. fatigué and fatiguée are one word out loud and two on the page, exactly like enchanté and enchantée in a1.01. Sometimes it is audible instead: the e in grande wakes the d, and the one in française wakes the s.

examples.note: Written agreement, no sound.
The same rule, and here you can hear it.

recorded.desc: THE SIX FORMS AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, IN PARADIGM ORDER, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE SPEED. This is the single most important instruction in this lesson. Six forms recorded in six sessions are six performances, and the learner is trying to hear a SET: any drift in pace, pitch or emphasis between them teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read them at conversational pace with no pause for teaching between the rows, then the six full sentences in the same take. Do not stress the verb: these are the most frequent words in the language and they are never leaned on in speech.
clipIds: Je suis ici pour la conférence.
Tu es ici pour la conférence ?
Il est ici pour la conférence.
Nous sommes ici pour la conférence.
Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
Ils sont ici pour la conférence.

recorded.desc: vous êtes WITH ITS LIAISON INTACT, never as two words with a gap. The S of vous must arrive as a Z bound to the front of êtes so the pair is one phonetic word, [voo-ZET]. Do not articulate the two halves separately even for the slow take: the slow version must be the same join stretched, not the join taken apart, because a learner who hears it separated once will produce it separated forever. Do not sound the final S of êtes.
clipIds: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?

recorded.desc: ils sont AND ils ont RECORDED IN THE SAME TAKE, back to back, by one voice at one speed, so the contrast is real rather than an artefact of two sessions. ils sont opens on a clear S; ils ont carries a Z over from the silent S of ils. That single sound is the whole difference between this lesson and a1.07, so the two must be comparable against each other and not against a memory of a different recording. Do not sound the S of ils in either, and do not sound the T of sont.
clipIds: Ils sont ici pour la conférence.

recorded.desc: The c'est and il est pairs, each PAIR in one take back to back so the appearing and disappearing determiner is audible against itself: « C'est un médecin. » then « Il est médecin. », then « C'est le directeur. » then « Il est directeur. » Both halves must sound like ordinary speech; the difference being taught is a word, not a level of care. Run est straight into the following noun with no pause, because a gap there is exactly where a learner inserts the un.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of one woman in her forties at an ordinary conference-lobby pace. The beat where she says it back (« Ah, il est médecin. Très bien. ») must be warm and passing rather than corrective: the whole point of the scene is that nobody tells the learner they were wrong, so any hint of emphasis on médecin would destroy it.
clipIds: Bonjour ! Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
Ah, il est médecin. Très bien.

recorded.desc: The origin set. français and française must be recorded in ONE take back to back, because the whole teaching is that the e wakes the s and the two are audibly different; recorded apart, the learner hears two words rather than one contrast. Same for fatigué and fatiguée, where the point is the opposite: they must be INDISTINGUISHABLE, so do not let a second take drift them apart and do not lean on the ending of either.

lessons.title: Les pronoms sujets
lessons.intro: French makes you say who the sentence is about before you say anything else, and it gives you nine words to do it with. The useful part is that the nine sit behind only six forms of the verb, which is what makes the next two lessons possible.

sections.title: The Word She Used Instead
sections.frSub: Le mot qu'elle a dit à la place

say.text: Watch this one. Nothing you say is wrong, and the room still tells you something.

setting.place: A shared kitchen, four flatmates

beats.text: Three weeks in the flat, and this is the first Saturday anyone has asked you along.

beats.speaker: Chloé
beats.fr: On est au marché à dix heures. Vous êtes libres ?
beats.en: We are at the market at ten. Are you two free?

beats.text: You are free. Sam is free. You want to say so, and you want to say it the way she just did.

beats.prompt: What goes back across the table?

options.en: the we a course teaches first
the we she just used

followUp.works: Yes. She said on, and on is what a French kitchen actually speaks.
followUp.breaks: Nothing in that is wrong. Watch what it does anyway.

beats.en: (correct, and one register above the room)

beats.speaker: Chloé
beats.fr: Super. On est là à dix heures alors.
beats.en: Great. So we are there at ten.
beats.stage: Nobody corrects you. She just says it back.

beats.heading: She changed one word, and the verb went with it
beats.body: Nous is correct and it is what a course hands you. In a kitchen, French says on. Same meaning, one register down, and a different form of the verb behind it.

wrong.en: the we from the book

beats.coach: Nous took sommes. On took est, which is the form il takes. That is the trade.

beats.text: One word smaller, one register closer, and a different verb form riding along with it.

closing.text: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms. On is the clearest place to see why: it means we and it borrows the form il uses.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms. By the end of this you will know which of the nine a sentence needs, and which of them share a form.

goals.s: Decide who the sentence is about before you start it, the way French makes you.

goals.t: Use on the way French does
goals.s: Say we the everyday way, and take the verb form that comes with it.
Know why the pronoun tells you nothing, and what does the telling instead.
Meet the next lesson with the subject half of the table already settled.

sections.title: Nine Words, Six Jobs
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: This is the one idea worth carrying out of here. Three cards, and then the table it comes from.

cards.label: The count
cards.head: Nine in, six out
cards.body: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms. Nine words go in front of the verb. Behind them, a verb only ever has to do six different things.

cards.label: The three
cards.head: il, elle and on share one
cards.body: Whatever the verb is, these three take exactly the same form of it. Three pronouns, one ending, nothing to choose between.

cards.label: The two
cards.head: ils and elles share another
cards.body: Same again at the plural end. The spelling of the pronoun changes and the verb after it does not move at all.

sections.title: The Whole Set, One Table
sections.say: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms. Six rows for nine words, because two of the rows are shared. Tap any row to hear it.

detail.title: je
detail.body: The one you use most. It stays lowercase in the middle of a sentence, unlike the English I, and it drops its e in front of a vowel sound: j'ai, j'attends.

cells: one person you are close to

detail.title: tu
detail.body: One person, and someone you already have permission to be close to. A friend, a child, family. If you are not sure whether you have that permission, you do not have it yet.

rows.say: Il est là. Elle est là. On est là.

detail.title: The row that does the work
detail.body: Three pronouns, one form. il is he, elle is she, and on is the we French speaks out loud. All three take the same form of the verb.

rows.say: Nous sommes trois à la terrasse.

detail.title: nous
detail.body: Correct everywhere, and still what you write. Out loud, in most rooms, on has taken its place. nous is never wrong; it simply sits a register above where the conversation is.

cells: one person politely, or any group

detail.title: vous
detail.body: One word doing two jobs. It is the polite singular, and it is also the plain plural for any group at all, however close you are to them. The word alone will not tell you which.

rows.say: Ils sont là. Elles sont là.

detail.title: The other shared row
detail.body: Two pronouns, one form. elles is for a group that is all women. ils covers everything else, including a group of ninety-nine women and one man.

sections.title: The Four You Say Most
sections.hint: Swipe through the five cards.
sections.say: je, tu, il, elle. Four words, and one of them changes shape before it will let a vowel past.

cards.label: je
cards.head: You, speaking
cards.body: Lowercase in the middle of a sentence, unlike the English I. Only a capital when it opens one.

cards.label: tu
cards.head: One person, close
cards.body: Never for a group and never for a stranger. tu is a permission, and it is given rather than taken.

cards.label: il
cards.head: He, and sometimes nobody
cards.fr: Il est au comptoir du café.
cards.body: He, for a person. It also runs a whole family of sentences about nobody at all, which is two missions from here.

cards.label: elle
cards.head: She
cards.fr: Elle est en terrasse ce matin.
cards.body: The same form of the verb as il, in the same frame, with one word changed. Nothing else moves.

cards.label: j'
cards.head: Before a vowel, je shrinks
cards.body: You already do this with le and la. je behaves identically: the e drops, an apostrophe closes the gap, and the two words are said as one.

sections.title: The Plural Side
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: nous, vous, ils, elles. Two of them are not quite what they look like.

cards.label: nous
cards.head: We, on paper
cards.fr: Nous sommes trois à la terrasse.
cards.body: The we you will read and write. Out loud you will hear it far less often than the next card.

cards.label: on
cards.head: We, out loud
cards.fr: On est trois à la terrasse.
cards.body: Same meaning as nous, and the verb drops to the il form. This one has a mission to itself, because that swap is where everyone slips.

cards.label: vous
cards.head: You, one or many
cards.body: The question at the door of every restaurant in France. Here vous is plainly plural and nothing polite is happening.

cards.label: ils · elles
cards.head: They, twice
cards.fr: Ils sont là. Elles sont là.
cards.body: elles only when every single one of them is a woman. Otherwise ils, and the verb does not care which you picked.

sections.title: Two Words, One Sound
sections.say: il and ils are the same sound. So are elle and elles. Something else has to tell you, and something else does.

lines.en: He is here.
They are here.
She is here.
They are here.

questions.q: il and ils are the same sound on their own. What tells you which one you heard?
opts: The verb that comes after it
questions.why: The S on ils is silent, so the pronoun carries no clue at all. est against sont is the whole difference.

questions.q: You hear « Elles sont là. » How many people, and what do you know about them?
opts: Two or more, all of them women
Two or more, at least one man
questions.why: sont makes it plural, and elles rather than ils makes it a group with no man in it.

questions.q: Which pair sounds identical when the two words are said on their own?
questions.why: il and ils are said the same way, and so are elle and elles. The plural is audible only in the verb that follows.

sections.title: On Means We, and Behaves Like He
sections.frSub: On, le « nous » de tous les jours
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: This is the one the unit is named for. Two facts, and they pull in opposite directions.

cards.label: The meaning
cards.head: on is we
cards.fr: On est trois à la terrasse.
cards.body: In spoken French on has almost entirely taken over from nous as the subject. Around a table it is what you will hear every time.

cards.label: The form
cards.head: and it takes the il form
cards.body: The verb behaves as though on were he. So a we idea comes out on a he form, and that is the mismatch to hold on to.

cards.label: The pair
cards.head: The same sentence, twice
cards.fr: On est là. · Nous sommes là.
cards.body: Neither is wrong. The first is what gets said, the second is what gets written, and a course hands you the second one first.

cards.label: The slip
cards.head: Where everyone trips
cards.body: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms. on sits in the same row as il, so it can never take the nous form, however much it means we.

sections.title: Three Ways On Goes Wrong
sections.say: Three mistakes, and all three come from knowing what on means.

errors.wrong: Saying « On sommes d'accord. »
errors.why: on means we and takes the form il takes. The meaning pulls one way and the verb goes the other, which is exactly why this gets its own screen.

errors.wrong: Writing « On est d'accord. » at the end of a job application.
errors.right: Writing « Nous sommes d'accord. » at the end of a job application.
errors.why: on is spoken register. It is not slang and nobody will correct you for it, but written French still reaches for nous, and an application is not a kitchen.

errors.wrong: Hearing « On est là. » and looking for one person.
errors.right: Hearing « On est là. » and counting the people in front of you.
errors.why: The verb is singular and the meaning is not. Nothing in the form will ever tell you that, so it is learned once and then it is done.

sections.title: The Il That Is Nobody
sections.say: A quarter of the il sentences you will meet are not about a man at all. Better to know that now than to spend a month looking for him.

examples.fr: Il y a une table dans le salon.
examples.en: There is a table in the living room.
examples.note: The most common sentence frame in the language, and its il is nobody.
Weather takes il, the same way English weather takes it.
Literally it makes beautiful. Nobody is making anything.

examples.fr: Il est huit heures et demie.
examples.note: Every clock time in French starts here.
il faut is how French says one has to. It never has a subject you could point at.

sections.title: One Word, Two Jobs
sections.say: You already choose between tu and vous. What nobody mentions is that vous is doing a second job at the same time. Tap any row.

detail.title: One person, close
detail.body: The only room in this table that takes tu. One person, and someone who has already offered you the closeness.

detail.title: One person, polite
detail.body: The vous you already know. One person, kept at a distance, and the verb takes the plural form even though there is only one of them.

detail.title: A group, close
detail.body: Nothing polite is happening here. You would say tu to each of them alone, and together they are vous, because French has no plural of tu. It sounds exactly like the row above: the S on prêts is silent.

detail.title: A group you do not know
detail.body: Polite and plural at the same time, in one word. This is the question at the door of every restaurant in France, and the answer is a number.

sections.title: Ils Swallows Elles
sections.frSub: Ils, même avec un seul homme
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: One rule, stated plainly, and then the reason elles turns up so seldom.

cards.label: All women
cards.head: elles
cards.fr: Elles sont en terrasse ce matin.
cards.body: elles is the group with no man in it. Not mostly and not nearly: none.

cards.label: Add one man
cards.head: ils
cards.fr: Ils sont au comptoir du café.
cards.body: One man joins and the whole group becomes ils. That is the rule French uses, and it holds at any size of group.

cards.label: The consequence
cards.head: elles is genuinely rare
cards.body: Because ils takes every mixed group, elles only survives where the group is entirely women. You will read it far less often than the other eight.

cards.label: The verb
cards.head: and the form does not move
cards.fr: Ils sont là. · Elles sont là.
cards.body: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms. These two share the second of the shared rows, so picking the wrong one never changes the verb.

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: The room is on the front. Say the pronoun before you flip.

cards.back:
je
Je suis à la terrasse.

cards.front: You, speaking, in front of a vowel
We, said out loud at a table
Nobody at all, as in the weather

sections.title: Who Is In the Room?
sections.say: No text this time. The verb is the only thing telling you how many people there are.

sections.title: Say the Whole Phrase
sections.say: Say each one as one movement. A pronoun on its own proves nothing, so the verb comes with it every time.

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Six sentences in three pairs. You cannot spell the pronoun until you have heard the verb, so listen to the end of each one.

sections.title: Your Turn at the Table
sections.say: The same terrace, a week on. The waiter uses vous and you answer with on, which is exactly how this goes in real life.
sections.setting: A café terrace in Toulouse, Saturday at noon. You arrived first and two friends are on their way.

turns.ai: Bonjour ! Vous êtes combien ?
turns.en: Hello! How many of you are there?
turns.user: On est trois.
turns.userEn: There are three of us.

alts.fr: On est trois, mais ils arrivent.
alts.en: Three of us, but they're on their way.

turns.ai: Parfait. Vous êtes prêts à commander ?
turns.en: Perfect. Are you ready to order?
turns.user: Pas encore. Ils arrivent.
turns.userEn: Not yet. They're on their way.

alts.en: Not yet, they're on their way.
No, we're waiting for two friends.

turns.ai: Très bien. Et elle, elle prend quelque chose ?
turns.en: Very good. And her, is she having something?
turns.user: Elle prend un café.
turns.userEn: She's having a coffee.

alts.fr: Oui, elle prend un café au lait.
alts.en: Yes, she's having a café au lait.

turns.ai: Et vous ?
turns.en: And you?
turns.user: J'ai soif. Une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: I'm thirsty. A jug of water, please.

turns.ai: Je vous apporte ça.
turns.en: I will bring you that.
turns.user: Merci beaucoup.
turns.userEn: Thank you very much.

sections.title: Four People, One Table
sections.say: Read it once for the shape. Every pronoun in this lesson is in here somewhere. Tap any word you do not know.
sections.text: It is noon on the terrace. Léa is there first. Sam and Chloé arrive together. « On est là ! » « Vous êtes en avance. » « Non, tu es en retard. » The waiter comes over to the table. « Vous êtes combien ? » « On est trois. Il arrive dans dix minutes. » Two women at the next table stand up to leave. « Elles sont pressées. » « Elles sont toujours pressées. »

glossary.note: The waiter is counting the table, so this vous is plural.
En avance is early. It is said to the two who just arrived, so vous.
En retard is the opposite. Said to one person, so tu.
The extra e agrees with elles. A group with a man in it would take pressés.
Sits between the verb and what follows it, where English puts it before the verb.

questions.q: The waiter says vous and Léa answers with on. Why does neither of them use nous?
questions.a: The waiter is addressing the whole table, so vous is plural, not polite. Léa answers for the table, and on is what a French speaker says out loud for we.

questions.q: Two women get up from the next table and the line is elles, not ils. What does that tell you about them?
questions.a: Every one of them is a woman. One man among them and the whole group would be ils.

questions.q: The last two lines both open « Elles sont ». How do you know that is more than one person?
questions.a: From sont. elles on its own is the same sound as elle, so the verb is doing all the work.

sections.title: The Whole Set, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card objectively. Again, hard, or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: How many pronouns, and how many forms behind them?
cards.back: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms. il, elle and on share one row; ils and elles share another.
we, in everyday spoken French. And it takes the form il takes.
never said. on sits in the il row, so it is « On est là. »

cards.front: A group of women, plus one man
cards.back: ils. One man is enough to take the whole group.

cards.front: You are speaking to two friends at once
cards.back: vous. French has no plural of tu.

cards.front: You are speaking to one stranger
cards.back: vous again, doing its other job.
identical. The verb after them is the only difference you can hear.
cards.say: Il est là. Ils sont là.

cards.front: je, in front of a vowel
cards.back: j'. The same drop you already make with le and la.
Nobody. il also runs the clock and il y a.

cards.front: Writing an email rather than talking at a table
cards.back: nous, not on. Same meaning, one register up.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have met all of them, watched a scene turn on one of them, heard the two pairs your ear cannot separate, spelled the sentences where only the verb tells you how many people there are, and said them out loud. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Every question describes a room and asks who is in it. Miss too many in a round and you get a drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: Who is in the room
rounds.say: Five rooms. Say who is in each one.

questions.q: You are telling a colleague where your manager is. She is at the counter. Write the pronoun that opens the sentence.
questions.why: elle is the one woman. il would make her a man, and on would fold you into the group with her.

questions.q: You are writing to a landlord on behalf of yourself and your flatmate. Which one belongs in the letter?
questions.why: Both on and nous mean we. Written French reaches for nous, and a letter to a landlord is written French.

questions.q: Two women are at the next table and nobody else is with them. Write the pronoun for them.
questions.why: Every one of them is a woman, so the group takes elles. One man among them and it becomes ils.

questions.q: You are about to say « ai soif ». Which goes in front of it?
questions.why: ai starts on a vowel sound, so je drops its e: j'ai. The same drop you already make with le and la.

questions.q: How many subject pronouns does French have, and how many forms does a verb take behind them?
questions.why: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms. il, elle and on share one form, and ils and elles share another.

rounds.label: The everyday we
rounds.say: The word that means we and behaves like he.

questions.q: Fix this. Three of you have just arrived at the terrace: « On sommes là. »
questions.why: on means we and takes the form il takes, so the verb is est. sommes belongs to nous and to nowhere else.

questions.q: You are at a table with two friends and the waiter asks how many. Which is what a French speaker actually says?
questions.why: On est trois is the everyday answer. Nous sommes trois is correct and reads as written French, and On sommes is not a form at all.

questions.q: Rewrite this for an email: « On est d'accord. »
questions.why: Same meaning, one register up. The verb has to move with the pronoun, because nous takes sommes.

questions.q: In « On est là », what is the verb form following?
opts: Nothing, on takes no verb form
The number of people on means
The pronoun on, which behaves as third-person singular
questions.why: The form follows the pronoun and not the meaning. That gap is the whole difficulty, and it never closes.

questions.q: Say it out loud, the way you would answer a waiter.
questions.why: Said as one movement: the nasal of on carries straight into est. There is no pause anywhere in it.

rounds.label: One word, two jobs
rounds.say: How many people, and how close.

questions.q: You are asking one close friend whether they are ready. Write the pronoun that opens the question.
questions.why: One person, and someone close. tu is the only row in the table that fits both of those at once.

questions.q: You are speaking to two close friends at once. Which pronoun?
questions.why: French has no plural of tu. Two friends together take vous, and nothing polite is being signalled by it.

questions.q: A waiter looks at your group of four and asks how many you are. Write the pronoun he uses.
questions.why: vous is the plain plural here, doing its second job. Nothing about the question is formal.

questions.q: You read « Vous êtes prêt ? » with no S on prêt. What do you know?
opts: You cannot tell from the spelling
It is one person, addressed politely
questions.why: The singular prêt is the only thing marking it, and only on the page. Out loud prêt and prêts are the same sound.

questions.q: Fix this. You are asking both of your flatmates at once: « Tu es prêt ? »
questions.why: French has no plural of tu, so two people together take vous, and the verb goes to êtes with them.

rounds.label: Ils and elles
rounds.say: Who counts as they, and what it costs the verb.

questions.q: A hundred women and one man are waiting. Which pronoun covers them?
questions.why: One man is enough to take the whole group to ils. That is the rule French uses, at any size of group.

questions.q: Fix this. The group is three women and one man: « Elles sont à la table du fond. »
accept: Ils sont à la table du fond
questions.answer: Ils sont à la table du fond.
questions.why: elles needs a group with no man in it. One man and the whole group is ils, however many women are in it.

questions.q: Which of these is genuinely rare in French?
questions.why: Because ils takes every mixed group, elles only survives where every single member is a woman.

questions.q: Two women and nobody else are at the next table. Write the sentence that says they are there.
questions.why: elles for the all-women group, and sont because it is plural. Both halves have to move together.

questions.q: A group of four women is joined by one man, so elles becomes ils. What happens to the verb?
opts: It changes from sont to est
Nothing at all, it stays sont
It changes from est to sont
questions.why: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms. ils and elles share one of the six, so swapping the pronoun never touches the verb behind it.

rounds.label: By ear
rounds.say: The pronoun will not tell you. Something else will.

questions.q: Listen. How many people?
questions.why: sont is plural and it is the only clue. ils and il are the same sound, so the pronoun tells you nothing.

questions.q: Listen. Which sentence is it?
questions.why: est against sont is what you are listening for. elle and elles are identical when the word is said on its own.

questions.q: Listen. Which one did you hear?

audio.clip: On est trois à la terrasse.

opts: Nous sommes trois à la terrasse.
On est trois à la terrasse.
Il est trois à la terrasse.
Elles sont trois à la terrasse.
questions.why: on and il take the same form, so est alone does not settle it. The word at the front is what does.

questions.q: Listen. Is this about one man or about a group?

audio.clip: Il est au comptoir du café.

questions.why: est is singular. Had it been a group you would have heard sont, whatever the pronoun sounded like.

questions.q: Tap the letter you do not say.
questions.why: The S on ils is silent, which is why ils and il are one sound. Only the verb after it separates them.

rounds.label: The il that is nobody
rounds.say: A quarter of the il sentences you will meet are these.

questions.q: In « Il y a une table dans le salon », who is il?
questions.why: il y a, il pleut and il est huit heures all use an il that refers to no one. This is a frame, not a person.

questions.q: Which of these sentences has a real person behind its il?
opts: Il est au comptoir du café.
questions.why: Weather and il faut never have anyone behind them. Only the third is about somebody you could point at.

questions.q: Write the three little words French uses for both there is and there are.
questions.why: il y a covers both, and its il is nobody. Whether it means is or are lives in whatever follows it.

questions.q: The impersonal il, as in « Il pleut », takes which form of the verb?
opts: The same form as the il that means he
It takes no verb at all
questions.why: It sits in exactly the same row as the il that means he, so nothing new has to be learned to use it.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the frames where il means nobody?
questions.why: The first three never have anyone behind them. The fourth is a man arriving, so that il is a person.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Five things, and then the two lessons that pick this up.
sections.body: You can now put the right word in front of a verb, which is the half of a French sentence that has to be settled before the verb exists. The next unit is être and the one after it is avoir. Both of them are verb tables, and you are walking in with the left-hand column already learned and with six rows to fill rather than nine.
points: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms. il, elle and on share one; ils and elles share another.
on means we, out loud, and takes the form il takes. Never « On sommes ».
One man in a group of women, and the whole group is ils.
vous is the polite singular AND the plain plural, and the word will not tell you which.
il and ils are one sound, and so are elle and elles. The verb is what you listen for.

grammarAssumed: The tu / vous distinction, introduced in a1.01
Elision of le and la before a vowel sound, introduced in a1.03
grammarIntroduced: The nine subject pronouns, and the six verb forms they sit behind
on as the everyday subject for nous, taking third-person-singular agreement
ils for any mixed group, and elles only for a group that is entirely women
vous as both the polite singular and the plain plural
Impersonal il, in il y a, il faut and the weather and clock frames
Elision of je to j' before a vowel sound

overview.introFr: Neuf pronoms, six formes du verbe. C'est ce qui rend la conjugaison possible.

acts.title: Who is in the room
acts.milestone: You have seen why nine words are only six decisions.

acts.title: The whole set, in one look
acts.milestone: You can find any of the nine on the table, and you know which two rows are shared.

acts.title: The everyday we
acts.milestone: on means we and takes the il form, and you know which il means nobody.

acts.title: One, or more than one
acts.milestone: You can tell vous doing one job from vous doing the other, and elles from ils.

acts.title: Out in the world
acts.milestone: You have heard all nine, said them out loud and spelled the ones only a verb separates.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. être is next.

lessons.reframe: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong row of the table: il for a woman, tu for a group, nous where the room wants on.
Knows on means we and gives it the nous form, producing « On sommes ».
Reads every vous as the polite singular and answers for one person when a group was addressed.
Uses elles for a group that has a man in it, usually because the women are the majority.
Hears il/ils or elle/elles and guesses from the pronoun, which carries no information at all.
Reads « Il y a » or « Il pleut » as being about a man, and looks for one in the sentence before it.

drills.title: Read the room, then pick
drills.coach: The room is on the left. Say the pronoun out loud before you turn the card.
pairs: You and one other person, at a table
You and one other person, in a letter
Two friends you are speaking to

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are speaking to your neighbour and her husband, both at the door. Which pronoun?
drills.why: You are addressing them, so it is vous. ils would be for talking ABOUT them to somebody else.

drills.title: on takes the il form
drills.coach: on goes with il and elle, not with nous. The meaning is no help here, so use the row.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Three of you have arrived. Which is said?
drills.why: on sits in the same row as il, so it takes est. The other two are not forms anyone uses.

drills.title: Which job is vous doing?
drills.coach: Count the people in the room, not the politeness. vous is the same word either way.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: A waiter says « Vous êtes prêts ? » to your table of four. What is vous doing?
drills.why: The S on prêts marks the plural. Out loud you would not hear it, and the table in front of him would settle it.

drills.title: elles, or ils?
drills.coach: Read the sentence and ask one question: could there be a man in this group? If yes, it is ils.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Nine women and one man are in the queue. Which pronoun?
drills.why: One man takes the whole group to ils. The proportion never matters.

drills.title: Count from the verb
drills.coach: Read the verb, then say how many people. The pronoun is no help and you should stop looking at it.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You hear « Elles sont en terrasse. » How many people?
drills.why: sont is the plural form. elles on its own sounds exactly like elle, so the verb is doing all the work.

drills.title: Is there a man in this sentence?
drills.coach: Weather, the clock and il y a never have anyone behind them. Everything else does.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these il sentences has a person in it?
opts: Il est au comptoir du café.
drills.why: Only the middle one is about somebody. The other two use the il that refers to no one at all.

sheets.title: The nine, the six, and the verb
contains: Every pronoun with its form of être
The other set of pronouns, named so you can put it down

sections.title: All nine, in paradigm order
rows: he is, or it is (weather, the clock)
you are, one person politely or any group
they are, any group with a man in it

sections.title: What shares what
sections.body: Nine rows above, six distinct forms in the middle column. il, elle and on all take est, which is why the third row of the in-lesson table holds three pronouns. ils and elles both take sont. Every other pronoun has a form to itself. This is not a fact about être: the same collapse happens on every verb in the language, which is why it is worth more than any single conjugation. When you meet the être table in the next lesson, the left-hand column is already learned and there are six endings to fill rather than nine.

sections.title: moi, toi, lui, eux, and why they are not here
sections.body: You have already met « et toi ? » and « et vous ? », and toi is not the same kind of word as tu. moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux and elles are STRESSED pronouns: they turn up after a preposition (avec moi), alone as an answer (Qui ? Moi.), and for emphasis (Moi, je prends un café). They are not subjects and they do not choose the verb form, so they are deliberately out of scope here. Note that nous, vous and elles appear in both sets and are spelled identically, which is why the two are easy to confuse and worth keeping apart until the stressed set gets its own lesson.

subjectPronoun.title: The word that says who is doing it
subjectPronoun.body: The little word in front of the verb that names who the sentence is about. French has nine of them and uses them far more strictly than English does: a French verb almost never stands without one, so leaving it out is not brevity, it is an unfinished sentence. Choosing it is the first decision you make, before the verb exists.

examples.note: je, and the form of the verb that comes with it.
vous, and a different form again.

sixForms.title: Why the nine are not nine
sixForms.body: il, elle and on all take one form of the verb. ils and elles both take another. So nine pronouns sit behind six forms, and two of the six do triple and double duty. That is the arithmetic that makes a verb table learnable, and it is true of every verb in the language rather than only of être.

examples.note: il takes est.
ils takes sont, and so does elles.

on.title: We, said out loud
on.body: In spoken French on has almost entirely replaced nous as the subject. It means we and it takes the form il takes, so a we idea comes out on a he form. Both halves have to be held at once: knowing only the meaning produces « On sommes », and knowing only the form leaves you translating it as one or people.

examples.note: The everyday version, and what you will hear.
The same sentence with nous, which is what you will write.

vous.title: One word, two jobs
vous.body: vous is the polite singular you already know, and it is also the plain plural for any group at all, however close you are to them. French has no plural of tu, so two friends together are vous with nothing polite being signalled. The word alone will not tell you which job it is doing; only the room will.

examples.note: One person, kept at a distance.
A group. Identical out loud, and the silent S is the only difference.

ils.title: The rule that makes elles rare
ils.body: elles is for a group in which every single member is a woman. Add one man, at any group size, and the whole group becomes ils. That is the rule French uses. It is also why elles turns up so seldom: the corpus behind this app holds eighteen sentences with it against ninety-five with ils, and that ratio is the language, not the sample.

examples.note: Every one of them a woman.
One man among them and it is this.

impersonalIl.title: The il that is nobody
impersonalIl.body: il y a, il faut, il pleut, il est huit heures. In all of these il refers to no one at all, the way English uses it in "it is raining".
