A quarter of the il sentences in this app are this kind, so you will meet one within minutes of being told il means he. It takes exactly the same verb form as the il that means he.

examples.note: There is, there are. The most common frame in the language.
Every clock time in French starts here.

jApostrophe.title: je, in front of a vowel
jApostrophe.body: je drops its e and becomes j' whenever the next word starts on a vowel sound: j'ai, j'attends, j'habite. You already make this drop with le and la, so nothing new is being asked of you. The two words are then said as one, with no gap where the apostrophe is.

examples.note: je + ai.
je + attends, and the H of an h muet counts as a vowel too.

etre.title: A carrier, not the lesson
etre.body: Every pronoun on these screens arrives with a form of être attached, because a pronoun said on its own proves nothing: il and ils are the same sound and only the verb separates them. Take the forms as vocabulary that comes with the pronoun rather than as a table to learn. être itself is the next lesson, and avoir is the one after it.

examples.note: je suis.
elle est, the form three of the nine share.

recorded.desc: The four contrast shorts, in two pairs, each pair recorded in ONE take by one voice at one speed with no gap between the halves: « Il est là. » then « Ils sont là. », then « Elle est là. » then « Elles sont là. ». Do not record the pronouns on their own, ever: il and ils are the same sound and a bare clip teaches nothing. Do not over-articulate the S of ils or elles; it is silent and making it audible would teach a pronunciation that does not exist. Also carries the six dictée sentences, which may be separate takes.
clipIds: Il est au comptoir du café.
Ils sont au comptoir du café.
Elle est en terrasse ce matin.
Elles sont en terrasse ce matin.

recorded.desc: The nine paradigm sentences, one per pronoun, read in paradigm order in ONE take at conversational pace. Every clip carries its verb, because a pronoun alone cannot be identified by ear. Keep je, tu and on unstressed and quick: they are small function words and reading them carefully teaches a weight they never have in speech.
clipIds: Il est au comptoir du café.
Elle est en terrasse ce matin.
On est trois à la terrasse.
Nous sommes trois à la terrasse.
Ils sont au comptoir du café.
Elles sont en terrasse ce matin.

recorded.desc: The on/nous minimal pairs, each pair in ONE take back to back so the register difference is audible against itself rather than across two sessions: « On est là. » then « Nous sommes là. », and « On est trois à la terrasse. » then « Nous sommes trois à la terrasse. ». The on version should sound like speech and the nous version should sound like speech too, not like reading: the difference being taught is register, not care.
clipIds: On est trois à la terrasse.
Nous sommes trois à la terrasse.

recorded.desc: The register trio in ONE take: « Tu es prêt ? », « Vous êtes prêt ? », « Vous êtes prêts ? ». The last two must be indistinguishable, which is the whole teaching, so do not let a second take drift them apart and do not over-articulate the silent S on prêts.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of one woman in her thirties speaking at an ordinary kitchen pace. The beat where she says it back (« Super. On est là à dix heures alors. ») must be warm rather than corrective: nobody in this scene is being told they were wrong.
clipIds: On est au marché à dix heures. Vous êtes libres ?
Super. On est là à dix heures alors.

lessons.title: Le verbe avoir
lessons.intro: Six forms, no pattern behind them, and a verb that spends most of its time not meaning have. This is how you say your age, how you say you are hungry, cold, right or afraid, and how you read the sentences where it has stopped meaning have at all.

say.text: One question, twice, and nothing you said was mispronounced. Watch which word was missing.

setting.place: A flat above a bakery, at a birthday

beats.text: A flat in Nantes on a Saturday evening. It is your friend Léa's birthday and you have met nobody here before.
Her grandmother has taken the chair beside you and turned it to face you properly. She is going to ask you something.

beats.prompt: You are twenty. What goes back?

options.en: the one English hands you
the one with a different verb in it

followUp.works: Yes, and the verb is the whole of it. Watch what the other one does to the room.
followUp.breaks: Every word in that is a real word. Watch what happens next anyway.

beats.speaker: Léa's grandmother
beats.stage: She says it again, slower, and glances at Léa while she waits.

beats.heading: She did not hear a mistake
beats.body: She heard "I am twenty years" and waited for the rest of it. There was nothing to guess at, so she asked again instead of correcting you. That is why this error survives: it never gets fixed for you.

wrong.en: I am twenty years, and then it stops

right.en: I have twenty years, which is how French says it

beats.coach: One verb, and it is the same swap on eleven other sentences you will need this week.

beats.speaker: Léa's grandmother
beats.fr: Ah, vingt ans. Vous avez faim ?
beats.stage: She has already turned to reach for a plate.

beats.text: Her next question uses the same verb again, and you have not been taught it yet.

closing.text: French has it. English is it. She used the same verb again before you had put your coat down.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: French has it. English is it. By the end you will have the six forms and the fourteen sentences that use them.

goals.s: Ask it and answer it, with numbers you already had before this lesson started.
Hungry, cold, afraid, right, lucky, and eleven more, all on one verb.
All six forms, including the four that bind to the pronoun in front of them.
Spot the sentences where this verb has stopped meaning have at all.

sections.title: The Second Set Of Six
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: You have met this arithmetic before and you have already filled it in once. This is the second time.

cards.label: Two lessons ago
cards.head: Nine pronouns. Six verb forms.
cards.body: You counted the nine and were shown the six slots they sit in, and nothing filled them. il, elle and on share one; ils and elles share another. That has not changed and it is not re-taught here.

cards.label: Last lesson
cards.head: One set filled
cards.body: être took the first of those two sets. You learned its six outright because nothing could be derived from anything, and that is the deal for exactly two verbs in the language.

cards.label: This one
cards.head: The second, and the last
cards.body: avoir is the other one. Six forms, no stem, and after this every verb you meet has a pattern behind it. Ten minutes of memorising and the closed set is closed.

cards.label: What is actually hard
cards.head: Not the six
cards.body: The forms are the easy half and they are on one screen. French has it. English is it. That is the half that will still be catching you in a year, so it gets five missions and the forms get three.

sections.title: The Six, In One Table
sections.say: Six rows for nine pronouns, exactly as last time. Tap any row to hear the whole sentence.

detail.title: j'ai
detail.body: Je never survives in front of this one. Ai starts on a vowel, so je loses its e and the two are written as one word. You have made that drop since your first lesson on le and la, and here it is compulsory.

rows.say: Tu as un cadeau pour Léa ?

detail.title: tu as
detail.body: Two letters and the s is silent, so out loud this is the same sound as the il form. Only the pronoun in front separates them, which is why the pronoun is never dropped.

rows.say: Il a un cadeau pour Léa.

detail.title: The row that does the work
detail.body: One letter, and it takes no accent: à with an accent is a different word meaning to or at. Three pronouns share this form, and on means we and still takes it, which is the mismatch a1.05 spent a mission on.

rows.say: Nous avons un cadeau pour Léa.

detail.title: nous avons
detail.body: The first of the four that bind. Avons starts on a vowel, so the silent s of nous wakes up as a z and the two words are said as one. Never noo, then a-VOHⁿ.

rows.say: Vous avez un cadeau pour Léa ?

detail.title: vous avez
detail.body: The same join you learned on vous êtes, on a different verb. If you can already say that one you can say this one, and the two are the most common openings to a question you will hear in a shop.

rows.say: Ils ont un cadeau pour Léa.

detail.title: ils ont
detail.body: A nasal vowel, a silent t, and a z carried over from the silent s of ils. Hold this one carefully: ils sont is a different verb and one consonant is the whole difference between them.

sections.title: One At A Time
sections.hint: Swipe. Say each one out loud before you move on.
sections.say: Six screens, one form each. Say it out loud before you swipe, every time.

cards.label: 1 of 6
cards.body: I have. Je and ai are one word.

cards.label: 2 of 6
cards.body: You have. The s is silent.

cards.label: 3 of 6
cards.body: He has. One letter, no accent.

cards.label: 4 of 6
cards.body: We have. Joined by a z.

cards.label: 5 of 6
cards.body: You have. Joined by a z.

cards.label: 6 of 6
cards.body: They have. Joined by a z.

sections.title: Pronoun, Then Form
sections.say: Read the pronoun, say the form, then check. Nothing derives from anything, which is the point.

check.q: Which of these is the form that follows on?
check.why: on means we and takes the form il takes, so it is a. That collapse was a1.05's and it holds for every verb in the language.

check.q: You hear a z between the pronoun and the verb. How many of the six do that?
check.why: Four: nous avons, vous avez, ils ont and elles ont. Every form starting on a vowel pulls the silent consonant in front of it back to life.

sections.title: Two Verbs, One Consonant
sections.say: Two pairs, and each of them is one consonant. Slow the audio down before you answer.

lines.en: They have white sheets of paper.
They are in the room.

lines.fr: Il a un cadeau pour Léa.
lines.en: He has a present for Léa.

lines.fr: Ils ont un cadeau pour Léa.
lines.en: They have a present for Léa.

questions.q: What separates ils ont from ils sont, out loud?
questions.why: Both end on the same nasal vowel with a silent t. The s of ils comes back as a z in front of ont, and sont brings its own s. That is the whole of it.

questions.q: Lines three and four differ by more than the verb. What else moved?
opts: The pronoun, from one person to several
questions.why: il became ils, and that is the only clue you get in writing, because the s of ils is silent. In speech the z is what tells you.

questions.q: Which pair is harder to separate at speed?
questions.why: The first pair differs by a liaison that either exists or does not; the second by which consonant that liaison produces. Slowed down both separate cleanly.

sections.title: The Swap
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Read this one properly. It is the reason twelve separate things in this lesson are one thing.

cards.label: The line
cards.head: Six words for twelve rules
cards.body: French has it. English is it. Your English puts am in front of hungry. French puts have in front of hunger, and the second word is a thing rather than a description.

cards.label: It is about English
cards.head: The trouble is on your side
cards.body: Nothing about the French here is irregular. English is the odd one: it uses be for states that most languages treat as things you carry. Translate word by word and you get something that is not a sentence.

cards.label: Test it on yourself
cards.head: Say the English literally
cards.body: Before you say any of these, put the English into the shape French wants: I have hunger, I have twenty years, he has fear. If that reads as odd English, it is right French.

cards.label: How far it goes
cards.head: Eleven, plus your age
cards.body: Eleven of the fourteen expressions in this lesson work this way and so does every age anybody will ever tell you. Three of the fourteen do not, and they get their own screen so you know which three.

sections.title: How Old Are You
sections.say: French has it. English is it. You already own every number in this table. What is new is the frame around it, and there is one.

detail.title: Twenty years, had
detail.body: The number came from the counting lessons and nothing about it changes here. What changes is that French counts years as something you hold, so the verb is avoir and the word ans is never dropped. Twenty on its own is not an age.

detail.title: The same on somebody else
detail.body: This sentence was written for the numbers lesson, where sixty was the thing being taught. You already read it once and never asked why the verb was there. It is the same rule and it holds for every person.

detail.title: The question, both ways
detail.body: Quel âge as-tu to somebody you would call tu, and quel âge avez-vous to anybody else. The register split is a1.01's and nothing here changes it. Answer either one the same way.

cells: Elle a six ans et demi.
She is six and a half
rows.say: Elle a six ans et demi.

detail.title: The half year, free
detail.body: Et demi after ans, and it is the sentence every parent of a small child says. Nothing about the rule moves for it. This one was already in the corpus and no course teaches it.

cells: Le chien de mon grand-père a treize ans.
rows.say: Le chien de mon grand-père a treize ans.

detail.title: Anything with an age
detail.body: A dog, a building, a bottle of wine. If it has an age, it has years, and the verb does not change because the thing is not a person. This is where a learner stops expecting avoir and reaches for être again.
detail.say: Mon voisin a soixante-dix-sept ans mais il court encore.

sections.title: The Eleven
sections.say: Eleven screens. Every one of them is the same swap, so there is one thing to remember and eleven places to use it.

sections.title: Cold, Or A Cold Room?
sections.say: One question, and the difference between the two wrong answers is the whole of the next mission.

check.q: You are cold. What do you say?
check.why: Cold is something you have here. Je suis froid describes your personality rather than your temperature, and il fait froid is about the room.

sections.title: The Three That Differ
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Three of the fourteen do not follow the line above. Knowing which three is worth more than knowing the eleven.

cards.label: Not a swap
cards.head: These land somewhere else
cards.fr: besoin de · envie de · mal à
cards.body: The eleven all turn English am into French have. These three turn into need, want and hurt instead, so there is no be to swap out and nothing to translate literally.

cards.label: de, twice
cards.head: Two of them take de
cards.body: Besoin and envie both carry de, and it shortens to d apostrophe in front of a vowel sound. Leave the de out and the sentence stops: j ai besoin eau is not French.

cards.label: à, once
cards.head: The third takes à
cards.body: Mal takes à, and the à then merges with whatever the body part wants: au dos, à la tête, aux dents. This is the commonest of the fourteen in real speech by a distance.

cards.label: Why it is worth naming
cards.head: Three, not fourteen
cards.body: A learner told there are fourteen expressions memorises fourteen. A learner told there are eleven of one kind and three of another has a shape, and a shape survives a week off.

sections.title: Which Kind Is It?
sections.say: One question. The little word after the expression is what the answer turns on.

check.q: You want to say you need a pen. Which is right?
check.why: Besoin always carries de, and de shortens in front of the vowel of un. The verb is avoir, so the third option is wrong twice over.

sections.title: Hot Rooms And Hot People
sections.frSub: J'ai chaud ou il fait chaud
sections.say: French has it. English is it. And when it is the weather rather than you, French uses neither of them.

detail.title: J'ai chaud · il fait chaud
detail.body: The first says you are too warm. The second says the weather is. They are not interchangeable and swapping them produces two different mistakes: il a chaud about the weather, and je suis chaud about yourself, which means something else entirely.
detail.say: Elle a chaud dans la salle d'attente.

rows.say: Tu as froid ? Il fait froid ?

detail.title: The same pair, on cold
detail.body: Tu as froid asks about the person in front of you. Il fait froid asks about outside. Get the pair right on chaud and froid comes with it, because the split is identical and there is nothing extra to learn.
detail.say: Il a froid dans le bureau.

detail.title: The one to avoid
detail.body: Je suis chaud is real French and it is not about temperature at all: in everyday speech it means you are keen or up for something. Said in a warm room it will be understood as an answer to a question nobody asked.

sections.title: When Have Stops Meaning
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Nearly a quarter of the sentences you will meet with this verb are not about having anything. Here is how to see it coming.

cards.label: Almost a quarter
cards.head: Not a possession
cards.fr: J'ai perdu mes clés ce matin.
cards.sub: I lost my keys this morning
cards.body: There is no having in that sentence. J ai is there, and what follows it is another verb, and the pair of them together is a past tense you have not met yet.

cards.label: The test
cards.head: Look at the next word
cards.fr: Elle a pris le bus ce matin.
cards.sub: She took the bus this morning
cards.body: One noun after the form means having. Another verb after the form means the past. That is the whole check and it takes a second.

cards.label: The one that fools people
cards.head: A noun turns up anyway
cards.fr: Nous avons réservé une table pour six personnes.
cards.sub: We reserved a table for six
cards.body: There is a table in it, so it looks like a possession. Read the word straight after avons: it is a verb, so this is the past and nobody currently owns a table.

cards.label: What to do now
cards.head: Recognise, do not use
cards.fr: Ils ont pris le premier bus du matin.
cards.body: You are not learning this tense yet. What you need today is to stop reading it as possession, so that a page of French stops looking like a list of things people own.

sections.title: Saying No, Two Ways
sections.say: The same negative on two sentences, and it leaves a different thing behind each time.

rows.say: J'ai une voiture. Je n'ai pas de voiture.

detail.title: A thing you could count
detail.body: Une collapses to de under the negative, which is the rule you met on un, une and des one lesson ago. Not pas une voiture and not pas la voiture. Nothing new is being asked of you here.

rows.say: J'ai faim. Je n'ai pas faim.

detail.title: An expression, with no article
detail.body: Faim never had a word in front of it, so there was nothing for the negative to collapse. It is pas faim and never pas de faim. This is the half nobody teaches, and it catches the learner who took the first half seriously.

rows.say: Je n'ai pas de voiture. Je n'ai pas faim.

detail.title: What the answer tells you
detail.body: This works backwards too. If the de turned up, you were talking about a countable thing. If it did not, you were using one of the fourteen. That is the ground the negation unit builds on, and you have it before you get there.

sections.title: Four Traps
sections.say: French has it. English is it. Four sentences an English speaker produces in their first month, one per screen.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je suis vingt ans » for "I am twenty".
errors.right: Saying « J'ai vingt ans » for "I am twenty".
errors.why: This one costs the most, because it lands in the first sentence you say about yourself and it is not a near miss. Je suis vingt ans says "I am twenty years" and stops, so a listener has nothing to repair and asks again instead.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je suis faim » for "I am hungry".
errors.right: Saying « J'ai faim » for "I am hungry".
errors.why: The same swap on a different noun, and the same shape of failure. Faim is hunger, a thing, so French puts have in front of it. This holds for eleven of the fourteen expressions in this lesson and there is nothing to memorise beyond that.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je suis chaud » when the room is warm.
errors.right: Saying « J'ai chaud » when the room is warm.
errors.why: Wrong twice. Warmth is had here, and je suis chaud is a real sentence meaning you are keen or up for something, so it is understood as an answer to a question nobody asked. Il fait chaud is the version for the weather.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je n'ai pas de faim » for "I am not hungry".
errors.right: Saying « Je n'ai pas faim » for "I am not hungry".
errors.why: A rule applied one noun too far. De turns up under a negative only where an article had to be removed, and faim never had one. Je n ai pas de voiture is right for that same reason: it had a une in it.

sections.title: Sunday At Her Grandmother's
sections.say: Six sentences in this passage use the verb and not one of them means have. Tap any underlined word.
sections.text: It is Sunday and Claire is at her grandmother's table for the first time. Her grandmother pours the wine and looks at her over the top of her glasses. « Vous avez quel âge ? » Claire has practised this one on the train, twice, out of the window. « J'ai vingt ans. » Her grandmother nods and passes the bread without saying anything else about it. « Et vous avez faim ? » Claire has not eaten since seven in the morning. « Oui, j'ai très faim. » Her cousin leans across the table and says the sentence Claire has been dreading all week. « Moi, j'ai mal à la tête. Je n'ai pas faim. » Nobody offers him anything, and nobody asks him to explain himself. Her grandmother turns back and points at the window with the knife she is holding. « Tu as chaud ? Il fait chaud aujourd'hui. » Claire looks at those two questions and works out that only one of them was about her. « Non, ça va. Mais j'ai soif. »

glossary.note: The polite form of the question. Quel âge as-tu to somebody you would call tu.
Twenty years, had. Je suis vingt ans is not a sentence, and it is the error this lesson opens on.
The same verb again, on a different noun. Hunger is a thing you have.
Très goes in front of the noun rather than in front of a description, because faim is a noun.
One of the three that take a little word after them. Mal takes à, and à plus la is à la.
No de anywhere, because faim never had an article for the negative to remove.
About the person. This is the question she is really asking.
About the weather, and a different verb entirely. The two sit in the same breath here on purpose.
Thirst, had. The eleventh of the eleven, and the last one in the passage.

questions.q: Claire's grandmother asks two questions in one breath near the end. What is the difference between them?
questions.a: The first is about Claire and uses avoir. The second is about the weather and uses a different verb, faire, so only the first one needs an answer about how she feels.

questions.q: The cousin says two things and both use the same verb. Why is there no « de » in the second one?
questions.a: Because faim never had an article in front of it, so the negative had nothing to collapse. If he had said he did not have a car, the une would have become de.

questions.q: Count the sentences in the passage where this verb means have. What did you find?
questions.a: None of them. Every use of avoir here is an age, a state or a pain, which is the whole point: the verb is called "to have" and most of what a beginner does with it is something else.

sections.title: The Fourteen, Banked
sections.say: Two decks and the split between them is the lesson. Eleven behave one way, three behave another.

themes.title: the three with a word after them

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French out loud, verb and all, before you flip.

cards.front: I am hot (the person, not the room)
I am afraid of the dark
I do not have a car
They have a present for Léa
cards.back: Ils ont un cadeau pour Léa.
cards.say: Ils ont un cadeau pour Léa.

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Seven short lines. Two of the three forms you will hear sound identical, so the spelling is the exercise.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: Twenty-five lines out loud. The verb at the front is the part the mic is listening for.

sections.title: At The Chemist
sections.say: One exchange, and you hold up your half of it. Four of the fourteen turn up without being asked for.
sections.setting: A pharmacy on a corner in Nantes, late on a Monday morning, with one person ahead of you.

turns.ai: Bonjour. Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ?
turns.en: Hello. What seems to be the matter?
turns.user: Bonjour. J'ai mal à la tête depuis ce matin.
turns.userEn: Hello. My head has been hurting since this morning.

alts.fr: Bonjour. J'ai mal à la tête.
J'ai très mal à la tête, depuis ce matin.
alts.en: My head hurts a lot, since this morning.

turns.ai: Vous avez de la fièvre ?
turns.en: Do you have a fever?
turns.user: Je ne sais pas. J'ai chaud, oui.
turns.userEn: I do not know. I am hot, yes.

alts.fr: Je ne sais pas, mais j'ai chaud.
alts.en: I do not know, but I am hot.
Maybe. I have been hot since yesterday.

turns.ai: Vous avez soif aussi ?
turns.en: Are you thirsty as well?
turns.user: Oui, très soif. Et j'ai sommeil.
turns.userEn: Yes, very thirsty. And I am sleepy.

alts.fr: Oui, j'ai soif et j'ai sommeil.
alts.en: Yes, I am thirsty and I am sleepy.

turns.ai: Quel âge avez-vous ?
turns.en: How old are you?
turns.user: J'ai vingt ans.
turns.userEn: I am twenty.

turns.ai: Prenez ça deux fois par jour.
turns.en: Take this twice a day.
turns.user: Merci. J'ai besoin d'eau, alors.
turns.userEn: Thank you. I need water, then.

alts.en: Thank you very much. Do I need water?

alts.fr: D'accord, merci. Avec de l'eau, alors.
alts.en: All right, thank you. With water, then.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: Somebody asks how old you are. You are twenty.
cards.back: J'ai vingt ans. French has it. English is it.

cards.front: You have not eaten since seven this morning.
cards.back: J'ai faim. Hunger is a thing you have, not a way you are.

cards.front: The room is too warm for you personally.
cards.back: J'ai chaud. Il fait chaud would be about the room instead.

cards.front: Your friend has just proved they were correct.
cards.back: Tu as raison. Never tu es raison.

cards.front: You want to say you need a pen.
cards.back: J'ai besoin d'un stylo. Besoin always carries de.
J'ai mal à la tête. Mal takes à, and à plus la is à la.

cards.front: The nous form, with its join.
cards.back: nous avons, said as one word with a z in the middle.

cards.front: You hear a z, then a nasal vowel. Which verb?
cards.back: ils ont. With an s instead of the z it would be ils sont.

cards.front: « J'ai une voiture. » Now say you do not.
cards.back: Je n'ai pas de voiture. Une collapsed to de.

cards.front: « J'ai faim. » Now say you do not.
cards.back: Je n'ai pas faim. Nothing collapsed, because nothing was there.

cards.front: « J'ai perdu mes clés. » Is that a possession?
cards.back: No. A second verb follows the form, so it is a past tense and nothing is owned.

cards.front: How do you ask a stranger their age?
cards.back: Quel âge avez-vous ? With somebody you call tu it is quel âge as-tu.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a question get asked twice, filled in the second set of six verb forms, and found out that eleven expressions and every age you will ever give are the same rule wearing different nouns. You have separated the three that behave differently, the two ways a negative can land, and the sentences where this verb has stopped meaning have. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Seven rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The six forms
rounds.say: The forms, quickly.

questions.q: You and one colleague have the tickets. Which form?
questions.why: nous takes avons. avez is the vous form, and the two sit next to each other in the table and nowhere else in the language.

questions.q: Write the form that goes with on.
questions.why: on means we and takes the form il takes, which is a with no accent on it. That collapse was settled two lessons ago and holds for every verb.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: A z between the two words means the s of ils has woken up in front of a vowel, so the verb starts on one. ils sont brings its own s instead.

questions.q: Fix this. « Vous avons un rendez-vous. »
questions.why: avons belongs to nous. The two plural forms are the pair most often swapped, because both start on the same vowel and both bind to their pronoun.

rounds.label: French has it, English is it
rounds.say: The swap the whole lesson is about.

questions.q: You have not eaten all day. What do you say?
questions.why: Faim is hunger, a thing, so French puts have in front of it. Your English puts am in front of hungry, and that is what makes the wrong one feel right.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je suis froid. »
questions.why: Cold is something you have here. Je suis froid is a real sentence and it describes what kind of person you are rather than how warm you feel.

questions.q: Somebody has just proved their point. Fix this. « Tu es raison. »
questions.why: Being right is having reason in French. There is no adjective in this sentence at all, which is why the verb cannot be être.

questions.q: How many of the fourteen expressions work this way?
opts: Only the ones about the body
questions.why: Eleven swap English be for French have. The other three land on need, want and hurt instead, and knowing which three is what stops the rule being applied where it does not go.

questions.q: Say it out loud, to somebody holding a plate.
questions.why: Two words, and the second is nasal: the m is not pronounced and the vowel carries it. A spoken m at the end is the commonest thing to get wrong here.

rounds.label: How old are you
rounds.say: The half of the canDo that is a number you already had.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je suis vingt ans. »
questions.why: An age is a number of years you hold, so it takes avoir. The wrong version says "I am twenty years" and stops, which is why nobody corrects it: there is nothing to guess at.

questions.q: Complete it. « Elle ___ quarante ans. »
questions.why: The elle row shares its form with il and on, and the form is a with no accent. À with an accent is a different word meaning to or at.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a way to give an age?
opts: Elle a six ans et demi.
questions.why: Two things are wrong with the last one: the verb, and the missing word ans. A bare number is never an age in French, however the sentence starts.

questions.q: You are asking a stranger, politely. Write the question.
questions.why: The vous form, because you would not call a stranger tu. Quel âge as-tu is the same question for somebody you are on tu terms with, and the answer is identical either way.

rounds.label: The three that need a word after them
rounds.say: Eleven behave one way. These do not.

questions.q: Fix this. « J'ai besoin un stylo. »
questions.why: Besoin always carries de, and de shortens in front of a vowel sound. Without it the sentence has two nouns in a row and no way to connect them.

questions.q: Which little word does mal take?
questions.why: Mal takes à, and the à then merges with whatever the body part wants: au dos, à la tête, aux dents. Besoin and envie take de instead, which is the split worth holding.

questions.q: Your back hurts. Write it.
questions.why: À plus le is au, which is the merge you already make everywhere else. Le dos becomes au dos, and à la tête stays as it is because la does not merge.

questions.q: Which one does NOT map onto English "be"?
questions.why: Envie de lands on want or feel like, not on be. It is one of the three that behave differently, and all three of them carry a little word the other eleven do not.

rounds.label: Hot rooms and hot people
rounds.say: One noun, two sentences, and neither of them is the other.

questions.q: The weather is warm today. Which is right?
questions.why: The weather takes neither of this lesson's verbs. Il a chaud would say that some particular man is too warm, which is a sentence about a person.

questions.q: You personally are too warm. Fix this. « Je suis chaud. »
questions.why: Je suis chaud is real French and it means you are keen or up for something, so this is not a small error. Warmth in a person is had, exactly like hunger and cold.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: Two of these are about a person and one is about the room. The opening is what separates them, and it arrives before the noun does.

questions.q: Somebody says « Elle a chaud dans la salle d'attente. » What is warm?
questions.why: Avoir attaches the warmth to the person. To say the room was warm you would need il fait chaud, and the sentence would stop being about her.

rounds.label: Saying no, two ways
rounds.say: Where the de goes, and where it does not.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je n'ai pas de faim. »
questions.why: De only turns up under a negative where an article had to be removed, and faim never had one. Je n ai pas de voiture is right for exactly that reason: there was a une in it.

questions.q: « J'ai une voiture. » Now say you do not.
questions.why: Une collapses to de under a negative, which is the rule you met on un, une and des one unit ago. It has not changed for arriving on a new verb.

questions.q: You own no pen at all. Complete: « Je n'ai pas ___ stylo. »
questions.why: A pen is a thing you could count, so the un in front of it collapses to de. If the sentence had been about hunger there would be nothing here at all.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je n'ai pas de soif. »
questions.why: Soif is one of the fourteen and it never carried an article, so there is nothing for the negative to reduce. The de belongs only where a un, une or des had to go.

rounds.label: When have stops meaning have
rounds.say: Nearly a quarter of what you will read.

questions.q: Which sentence is NOT about having something?
opts: Tu as un stylo pour moi ?
J'ai perdu mes clés ce matin.
questions.why: Look at the word straight after the form of avoir. One noun means having; another verb means a past tense, and there is nothing being owned in that sentence.

questions.q: « Nous avons réservé une table. » There is a table in it. Is anybody holding one?
questions.why: This is the one that fools people, because a noun does turn up. Réservé is a verb and it sits directly after avons, so the pair is a past tense and the table belongs to a restaurant.

questions.q: Roughly how much of what you read that opens on this verb is a past tense?
questions.why: About a quarter, which is enough that a learner who reads every j ai as a possession misreads a page. Recognising it is the whole job for now; using it is a later unit.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can give your age and ask for somebody else's, say how you feel in fourteen different ways, and say what you have with all six forms. Two of those are things you will use before the end of the week. The last point below is worth more than the other three: it is what stops a page of French reading as a list of things people own, and it is also the ground the negation unit stands on.
points: French has it. English is it. Eleven expressions and every age you will ever give.
Six forms, and four of them bind to the pronoun in front. ils ont has a z; ils sont has an s.
Besoin and envie carry de. Mal carries à. The other eleven carry nothing.
A noun after the verb is having. Another verb after it is a past tense, and nothing is owned.

grammarAssumed: The nine subject pronouns, and the six verb forms they sit behind, introduced in a1.05
on takes third-person-singular agreement, introduced in a1.05
The six forms of être, introduced in a1.06, and the liaison in vous êtes
The numbers from one to a hundred, introduced in a1.02, a1.27 and a1.28
The indefinite article un, une and des, and its collapse to de under a negative, introduced in a1.11
Elision of le, la and je in front of a vowel sound
grammarIntroduced: The full present tense of avoir, as six forms with no derivable stem
The obligatory liaison in nous avons, vous avez, ils ont and elles ont
avoir for age, with the obligatory noun ans
The fourteen fixed expressions built on avoir, and the eleven that render English predicative be
avoir besoin de, avoir envie de and avoir mal à, and the complement each requires
il fait plus an adjective for the weather, against avoir for a person
The absence of a partitive de under negation after an article-less expression
Recognition only of the passé composé with avoir as auxiliary, as a reading skill

overview.introFr: Six formes, et un verbe qui passe le plus clair de son temps à ne pas vouloir dire avoir.

acts.title: The second set of six
acts.milestone: You have watched one verb decide whether a sentence existed at all.

acts.title: The forms, and the join
acts.milestone: You have all six, and you can hear the z that separates two verbs.

acts.title: French has it, English is it
acts.milestone: Twelve separate things turned out to be one thing, and three turned out not to be.

acts.title: Where English points the wrong way
acts.milestone: You can read a page of this verb without looking for possessions that are not there.

acts.title: Say it, spell it, use it
acts.milestone: You have said all fourteen out loud and spelled three forms that sound like two.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. Negation is next, and it is built on your last two missions.

lessons.reframe: French has it. English is it.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong row of the table: avez for nous, avons for vous, ont for il.
Uses être where French uses avoir: Je suis faim, Je suis froid, Tu es raison. The error the reframe exists to kill.
Gives an age with être, or gives a bare number with no ans behind it.
Drops the de after besoin or envie, or the à after mal, because the other eleven carry nothing.
Says il a chaud about the weather, or je suis chaud about themselves. One noun, two wrong verbs.
Writes pas de faim, or drops the de from pas de voiture. The rule applied one noun too far, or not far enough.
Reads every j'ai as a possession, including the 23% of them that are a past tense.

drills.title: Pronoun in, form out
drills.coach: The pronoun is on the left. Say the form out loud before you turn the card, and join it up where it joins.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You and one colleague have an appointment. Which form?
drills.why: nous takes avons. avez belongs to vous, and the two are the pair most often swapped because both bind to their pronoun.

drills.title: Have it, do not be it
drills.coach: Read the English on the left. Say the French on the right out loud, and notice which verb you reached for first.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You have not eaten since breakfast. What do you say?
drills.why: Faim is hunger, a thing, so it is had rather than been. The English am in front of hungry is what makes the wrong one feel right.

drills.title: A number of years, held
drills.coach: Every line here is a real age sentence. Say each one out loud and listen for the two things that are never missing: the verb, and the word ans.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: She is forty. Which is right?
drills.why: The verb is avoir and the word ans is never dropped. The third option gives a number with nothing to count, which is not an age in French.

drills.title: What comes after it?
drills.coach: Three buckets and eleven of the fourteen belong in the last one. Put each line where the word after the expression tells you it goes.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You need a pen. Which is right?
drills.why: Besoin always carries de, and de shortens in front of a vowel sound. Mal is the one that takes à, and the other eleven take nothing at all.

drills.title: The person, or the room?
drills.coach: Read each one and ask who is warm. If it is somebody, the verb is avoir. If it is the day, the verb is neither of the two you have learned.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: The weather is warm today. Which is right?
drills.why: The weather takes neither of this lesson's verbs. Il a chaud would say that a particular man is too warm, which is a sentence about a person.

drills.title: What does the no leave behind?
drills.coach: Say the negative out loud before you flip. Half of these leave a de behind and half of them leave nothing.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one is right for "I am not hungry"?
drills.why: Faim never had an article, so the negative had nothing to collapse to de. The de only appears where a un, une or des had to be removed.

drills.title: Having, or something else?
drills.coach: Read the word straight after the form of avoir. A noun means somebody has something. Another verb means a past tense, and nothing is owned.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one is NOT about having something?
opts: J'ai perdu mes clés ce matin.
drills.why: Perdu is a verb and it sits directly after the form of avoir, so the pair is a past tense. Nothing is being owned in that sentence.

sheets.title: avoir, in full
contains: All nine pronouns with their form

sections.title: The full paradigm
rows: they have, any group with a man in it

sections.title: The four that join up
sections.body: Four of the six start on a vowel, and every one of them pulls the silent consonant in front of it back to life. Nous ends in a silent s and avons starts on an a, so the s returns as a z and the two words are said as one: noo-za-VOHⁿ. The same happens with vous avez, ils ont and elles ont. Je is the fifth case and it behaves differently: rather than binding, it disappears, because ai starts on a vowel and je loses its e and is written j apostrophe. Only tu as and il a stand apart with nothing joining them, and those two happen to be the pair that sound identical, since the s of as is silent. So the six forms produce five distinct sounds, and the pronoun is what tells you which of the two identical ones you are hearing. That is why French never drops a subject pronoun the way English drops one in a list.

sections.title: Against être, which you already have
sections.body: These are the two most used verbs in French and they are the two most broken, for the same reason: a form said a hundred times a day is never smoothed out by analogy the way a rare verb is. You have now learned both outright and no other verb will ask this of you again. One pair is worth keeping apart from the start because it belongs to both lessons at once: ils sont opens on a clear s and means they are, while ils ont carries a z over from the silent s of ils and means they have. Slowed down they are obvious. At conversational speed the z against the s is the only thing separating them, and there is no other clue in the sentence, because both are followed by whatever comes next with no pause. The written forms are further apart than the spoken ones, so reading them will not train your ear. That is what the listening mission is for.

sheets.title: The fourteen, and the two rules around them

sections.title: The four places English points the wrong way

rows.v: J'ai vingt ans, never Je suis vingt ans. And ans is never left off.
J'ai faim, J'ai froid, J'ai peur. Eleven of them, all the same swap.
Il fait chaud for the room. J'ai chaud for the person.
besoin de, envie de, mal à. The other eleven carry nothing.
Je n'ai pas de voiture. The une collapsed to de.
Je n'ai pas faim. Nothing collapsed, because nothing was there.

sections.title: The sentences where it stops meaning have
sections.body: Across the a1 corpus, 119 of the 522 rows that open on a form of avoir are not about having anything, which is 23 out of every hundred. J ai perdu mes clés is I lost my keys. Elle a pris le bus is she took the bus. Nous avons réservé une table is we booked a table, and the table belongs to a restaurant. In every one of them the form of avoir is doing a job you have not been taught yet, and the word straight after it is what gives it away: one noun means somebody has something, another verb means a past tense. The reason this matters now rather than later is that you will read four or five times as much French as you produce for the next year, and a learner who meets j ai only as I have will read almost a quarter of what they meet as a possession that is not there. You are not being asked to use this. You are being asked to see it and move on.

haveNotBe.title: The swap English makes you get wrong
haveNotBe.body: English puts "am" in front of hungry, cold, afraid, right and twenty. French puts "have" in front of all five, and the word after it is a thing rather than a description: hunger, cold, fear, reason, years. So the sentence is not built the way yours is, and translating it word by word gives you something that is not French at all. This is the single most audible beginner error there is, because it lands in the first sentence anyone says about themselves.

examples.note: Hunger, had. Not hungry, been.
Twenty years, had. Je suis vingt ans is not a sentence.

ageRule.title: Years are something you have
ageRule.body: An age in French is a number of years that belong to you, so it takes avoir and the word ans is never left off. You already own every number you need for this: they were the whole of three earlier lessons, and nothing about counting changes here. What changes is the frame the number sits in, and there is exactly one of them. Ask it with quel âge and answer it with a form of avoir plus a number plus ans.

examples.note: The number is the part you already had.
The question that gets you the answer, in the tu form.

sixForms.term: ai, as, a, avons, avez, ont
sixForms.title: Six forms, and three of them join up out loud
sixForms.body: Nine pronouns sit behind six forms, which is the arithmetic you were given two lessons ago and which holds here unchanged. What is new is that four of the six start on a vowel, so the pronoun in front binds to them: nous avons is said as one word with a Z in the middle, and so are vous avez, ils ont and elles ont. That join is not optional and it is the thing that separates ils ont from ils sont.

examples.note: noo-za-VOHⁿ, one word out loud.
eel-ZOHⁿ. The S of ils wakes up, exactly as it did in vous êtes.

withComplement.term: besoin de, envie de, mal à
withComplement.title: The three that behave differently
withComplement.body: Eleven of these expressions are a straight swap of have for be. These three are not: they land on need, want and hurt rather than on be, and all three carry a little word after them that has to come too. Besoin and envie take de, which shortens to d apostrophe in front of a vowel. Mal takes à, and then the à joins whatever article the body part wants: au dos, à la tête, aux dents. Learn them as a group of three and the other eleven stay simple.

examples.note: need, and the de that has to come with it.
hurt, and the à that merged with le to make au.

pastAmbush.term: j'ai in front of a verb
pastAmbush.title: When have stops meaning have
pastAmbush.body: Nearly a quarter of the sentences in this course that open on a form of avoir are not about having anything. J ai perdu mes clés is I lost my keys, not I have lost-keys. When the word after the form of avoir is another verb, the pair is a past tense and the have has gone. You are not learning that tense yet. What you need now is to recognise it on sight, so that a sentence you meet in the wild does not get read as a possession that is not there.

examples.note: Lost, in the past. There is no having in this sentence.
A real possession, for comparison. One noun after the form, no second verb.

noArticleUnderNo.term: pas de, and pas on its own
noArticleUnderNo.title: Two ways a negative can land
noArticleUnderNo.body: Say no to a thing you could count and the word in front of it collapses to de: j ai une voiture becomes je n ai pas de voiture. Say no to one of these expressions and nothing collapses, because there was never an article there to lose: j ai faim becomes je n ai pas faim. Both halves are on the same screen for a reason. Which one you get tells you which kind of sentence you were in, and it is the whole of what the negation unit will ask you to do.

examples.note: une became de. The rule you met on un, une and des.
Nothing to collapse, so nothing collapsed. Never pas de faim.

recorded.desc: THE SIX FORMS AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, IN PARADIGM ORDER, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE SPEED. Six forms recorded in six sessions are six performances, and the learner is trying to hear a SET: any drift in pace, pitch or emphasis between them teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read the bare forms first, then the six full sentences in the same take. THE FOUR LIAISONS ARE THE POINT AND THEY ARE NOT OPTIONAL: nous avons, vous avez and ils ont are each ONE phonetic word with a z in the middle, and the slow take must be that join stretched rather than the join taken apart. A learner who hears them separated once will produce them separated forever. Do not sound the s of as, the t of ont, or the final s of ils.
clipIds: Tu as un cadeau pour Léa ?
Il a un cadeau pour Léa.
Nous avons un cadeau pour Léa.
Vous avez un cadeau pour Léa ?
Ils ont un cadeau pour Léa.

recorded.desc: The two minimal pairs this lesson turns on, EACH PAIR RECORDED BACK TO BACK IN ONE TAKE by the same voice at the same speed, in the way sons.07 pins rec-h-pairs and a1.11 pins rec-a1-11-pairs. ils ont against ils sont is a liaison z against an s and it is the same take or it is nothing: recorded apart, the learner compares two performances instead of two verbs. il a against ils ont is a liaison that exists against one that does not, and the temptation is to lean on the ils to make it clearer. DO NOT. The whole difficulty is that nobody leans on it in speech. Then the four listening lines at natural pace and again at 0.65.
clipIds: Il a un cadeau pour Léa.
Ils ont un cadeau pour Léa.

recorded.desc: The scene break and the swap deck. « Je suis vingt ans. » must be read PLAINLY and at ordinary pace, not comically and not hesitantly: the entire teaching of the scene is that it sounds like a normal sentence right up until it stops, and any performance signalling that it is wrong destroys that. Then « J'ai vingt ans. » in the same take at the same pace, so the only audible difference is the verb. Run the verb straight into the number with no pause, because a gap there is exactly where a learner inserts être.

The eleven expressions as ONE TAKE in the order the drill shows them, one voice, one speed, no teaching pause between them. The learner is being shown that eleven separate things are one thing, and eleven separately recorded clips would teach eleven separate things. Keep the nasals closed: faim ends on a nasal vowel with NO m sound, raison ends on a nasal vowel with NO n sound, and honte likewise. Those three are the ones a reader will over-articulate.

The four English-speaker traps, wrong form then right form, with a clear beat between them so the learner hears the difference rather than a correction. Je suis vingt ans / J'ai vingt ans. Je suis faim / J'ai faim. Je suis chaud / J'ai chaud. Je n'ai pas de faim / Je n'ai pas faim. Read every wrong version plainly rather than comically: two of these four are real French sentences that mean something else, and a performance that marks them as errors removes the reason they are dangerous.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of one woman in her seventies at an ordinary kitchen-table pace. The beat where she asks again (« Pardon ? Vous avez quel âge ? ») must be patient and unbothered rather than corrective or impatient: the whole point of the scene is that she is not correcting anybody, she simply did not receive a sentence, so any edge on it turns the moment into a telling-off and the teaching is lost.
clipIds: Ah, vingt ans. Vous avez faim ?

lessons.title: Les jours de la semaine
lessons.intro: Seven short words, and one that decides whether you meant one day or every one of them. This is how you name the days, say what your week looks like, and make a plan for a particular Saturday without accidentally describing your year.

say.text: One question, one answer, and nothing you said was wrong. Watch which word was doing the damage.

setting.place: A tram going north, and a phone in your hand

beats.text: A Thursday evening in Lyon. Your phone goes while you are still on the tram home.
It is Chloé, who you met at a language exchange three weeks ago and have been meaning to see again.

beats.prompt: You are free this Saturday, and you want to see her. What goes back?

options.en: the one with the little word in it
the one without it

followUp.works: Yes, and that is a yes. Watch what the other one does to her evening.
followUp.breaks: Every word in that is correct French. Watch what happens next anyway.

beats.speaker: Chloé
beats.fr: Ah, d'accord. Bon, une autre fois alors.
beats.en: Ah, all right. Another time then.
beats.stage: She does not ask again. The three dots appear once and stop.

beats.heading: She did not hear a yes
beats.body: She asked about one Saturday and you answered about all of them. That is a fact about your week, not an acceptance, so she read it as a polite way of not saying yes. Nothing was mispronounced and nothing got corrected.

wrong.en: I am free on Saturdays, as a rule

right.en: I am free this Saturday, which is a yes

beats.coach: Le makes it every week. One word, and it decides whether you have made a plan or described a habit.

beats.speaker: Chloé
beats.stage: She has already sent a second message with a place in it.

beats.text: One word separated a plan from a description, and it is the same word on all seven days.

closing.text: Le makes it every week. That is the whole of the next twenty minutes.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Le makes it every week. By the end you will have the seven names and the one word that decides how often.

goals.s: In order, starting where a French calendar starts, which is not where an English one does.

goals.t: Say what you do every week
goals.s: One article turns one day into all of them, on all seven days, with no exceptions.

goals.t: Make a plan for one day
goals.s: Accept an invitation for a Saturday without accidentally describing your whole year.
Lowercase, with nothing in front of it, which is two habits English gives you and French does not want.

sections.title: Where The Week Starts
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Four cards before any of the seven words, because the shape of the week decides how you read all of them.

cards.label: The row
cards.head: Monday first, Sunday last
cards.body: A printed French calendar starts its week on Monday. Lundi sits in the first column and dimanche in the last, so the two days at the right-hand edge are the weekend.

cards.label: Why it matters
cards.head: You will read one before you say one
cards.body: The first French calendar you meet will be a shop notice or a timetable, and counting the columns from the wrong end puts every appointment one place out.

cards.label: The weekend
cards.head: At the end, not around it
cards.body: Borrowed straight from English, hyphenated, and masculine. It sits at the end of the row rather than wrapping from one week into the next.

cards.label: What is actually hard
cards.head: Not the seven
cards.body: Seven short words is an afternoon and there is no pattern to teach. Le makes it every week. That is the half that will still be catching you in a year, so it gets eight missions and the names get three.

sections.title: The Seven, In Order
sections.say: Seven rows in week order. Tap any one to hear it, and tap again for where the name came from.

detail.title: lundi
detail.body: Latin lunae dies. The same moon as English Monday and Spanish lunes. Said out loud it is [luhⁿ-DEE], and every one of the seven takes the stress on its last syllable.

detail.title: mardi
detail.body: Latin martis dies. English swapped the Roman god for the Norse one, Tiw. Said out loud it is [mar-DEE], and every one of the seven takes the stress on its last syllable.

detail.title: mercredi
detail.body: Latin mercurii dies. English took Woden instead, which is why it is Wednesday. Said out loud it is [mehr-kruh-DEE], and every one of the seven takes the stress on its last syllable.

detail.title: jeudi
detail.body: Latin jovis dies. English took Thor, so Thursday and jeudi are the same god twice over. Said out loud it is [zheu-DEE], and every one of the seven takes the stress on its last syllable.

detail.title: vendredi
detail.body: Latin veneris dies. English took Frigg, and both are the goddess of love. Said out loud it is [vahⁿ-druh-DEE], and every one of the seven takes the stress on its last syllable.

detail.title: samedi
detail.body: Latin sabbati dies. Not a planet: this one comes from the rest day. Said out loud it is [sam-DEE], and every one of the seven takes the stress on its last syllable.

detail.title: dimanche
detail.body: Latin dies dominica. English kept the sun and French did not. Said out loud it is [dee-MAHⁿSH], and every one of the seven takes the stress on its last syllable.

sections.title: One At A Time
sections.hint: Swipe. Say each one out loud before you move on.
sections.say: Seven screens, one day each. Say it out loud before you swipe, every time.

cards.label: 1 of 7
cards.body: Monday.

cards.label: 2 of 7
cards.body: Tuesday.

cards.label: 3 of 7
cards.body: Wednesday.

cards.label: 4 of 7
cards.body: Thursday.

cards.label: 5 of 7
cards.body: Friday.

cards.label: 6 of 7
cards.body: Saturday.

cards.label: 7 of 7
cards.body: Sunday.

sections.title: Five, Then Two
sections.say: Read each one, say it, then check. The split is five working days and two at the end.

groups.label: The five that carry the week

check.q: Which day sits between mardi and jeudi?
check.why: mercredi. It is the longest of the seven and the one in the middle, which is the pair of facts that makes it easy to place once you have noticed them.

check.q: A French calendar puts which day in its first column?
check.why: lundi. The week runs Monday to Sunday, so the weekend is the two columns at the right-hand edge rather than one at each end.

sections.title: Two That Collide
sections.say: One pair here is genuinely hard at speed. Slow the audio down before you answer.

lines.en: Tuesday
Thursday

lines.fr: J'ai piscine le mardi et le jeudi.
lines.en: I have swimming on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

lines.fr: Nous partons jeudi et nous revenons dimanche.
lines.en: We're leaving on Thursday and coming back on Sunday.

questions.q: Which two of the seven are hardest to separate at conversational speed?
opts: none of them, they are all distinct
questions.why: Both are two syllables ending in the same DEE, and the opening consonant is the only difference. At speed the m and the zh are the whole of it, which is why an arrangement gets made for the wrong day.

questions.q: Line three names two days. Does it mean two particular days or every week?
opts: Neither, it is about the past
questions.why: Every week. There is a le in front of each day, and that is the only signal there is. Nothing else in the sentence says how often.

questions.q: Line four names two days and neither has a le. What does that tell you?
questions.why: One trip, out on Thursday and back on Sunday. A bare day is one day, and which one the conversation has already settled.

sections.title: The Word That Means Every
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Read this one properly. It is the reason the rest of the lesson is eight missions rather than one.

cards.label: You already have this
cards.head: The same le as le café
cards.body: a1.04 taught this le: coffee in general rather than one cup, where English uses no article at all. A day works the same way, and this lesson is that rule pointed at a Monday.

cards.label: The line
cards.head: One word, two meanings
cards.body: Le makes it every week. Take the le away and you are talking about one Monday instead, the one the conversation is already about.

cards.label: It is about English
cards.head: Yours marks it somewhere else
cards.body: English puts a plural S on the day. French puts a singular article in front of it. There is nothing to carry across, which is why this one never arrives by accident.

cards.label: Singular, not plural
cards.head: Never les lundis
cards.fr: Le magasin est fermé le mardi.
cards.body: Reaching for the English plural gives you les lundis, which is real French meaning Mondays as a set of days. It is not how you say every Monday.

sections.title: Every Week, Or One Day
sections.say: Le makes it every week. Left column has it, right column does not. Tap either side of a row to hear the pair.

detail.title: le lundi · lundi
detail.body: With the article it is every Monday, as a rule about your week. Without it, it is one, and which one the conversation has already decided. Out loud the difference is one unstressed syllable, so it is easy to hear and easy to leave out.

detail.title: le mardi · mardi
detail.body: With the article it is every Tuesday, as a rule about your week. Without it, it is one, and which one the conversation has already decided. Out loud the difference is one unstressed syllable, so it is easy to hear and easy to leave out.

detail.title: le mercredi · mercredi
detail.body: With the article it is every Wednesday, as a rule about your week. Without it, it is one, and which one the conversation has already decided. Out loud the difference is one unstressed syllable, so it is easy to hear and easy to leave out.

detail.title: le jeudi · jeudi
detail.body: With the article it is every Thursday, as a rule about your week. Without it, it is one, and which one the conversation has already decided. Out loud the difference is one unstressed syllable, so it is easy to hear and easy to leave out.

detail.title: le vendredi · vendredi
detail.body: With the article it is every Friday, as a rule about your week. Without it, it is one, and which one the conversation has already decided. Out loud the difference is one unstressed syllable, so it is easy to hear and easy to leave out.

detail.title: le samedi · samedi
detail.body: With the article it is every Saturday, as a rule about your week. Without it, it is one, and which one the conversation has already decided. Out loud the difference is one unstressed syllable, so it is easy to hear and easy to leave out.

detail.title: le dimanche · dimanche
detail.body: With the article it is every Sunday, as a rule about your week. Without it, it is one, and which one the conversation has already decided. Out loud the difference is one unstressed syllable, so it is easy to hear and easy to leave out.

sections.title: Seven Pairs, Said Out Loud
sections.say: Sixteen sentences in eight pairs. Read a pair across, not down, and say both halves before you move on.

items.fr: Le magasin est fermé le mardi.
items.en: The shop is closed on Tuesdays.

items.fr: Elle est à Paris le jeudi.

sections.title: A Plan, Or A Habit?
sections.say: One question, and it is the one the opening scene turned on.

check.q: A friend asks if you are free on Saturday. You are, this week. What do you answer?
check.why: She asked about one Saturday, so answer about one Saturday. With le you have described your usual week, which is true and is not a yes.

sections.title: Which One Did You Mean
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: The bare day is one day. These four cards are how you make sure it is the one you meant.

cards.label: The default
cards.head: The nearest one
cards.fr: Samedi, je fais les courses au marché.
cards.body: A bare day means the closest one that makes sense. Said on a Wednesday, samedi is in three days. Nothing marks it because there is only ever one close enough to mean.

cards.label: Being certain
cards.head: prochain and dernier
cards.body: Put prochain after the day for the one coming and dernier for the one gone. Both go after, never before, and neither takes an article.

cards.label: Looking back
cards.head: The one just gone
cards.body: Vendredi dernier is the Friday just gone. You will read far more of these than you say for now, so recognising the shape is enough.

cards.label: The over-correction
cards.head: Do not add it back
cards.fr: Jeudi prochain, nous partons en voyage.
cards.body: Once the article rule lands, the temptation is to put le in front of everything. A day carrying prochain or dernier never takes one.

sections.title: Two Habits To Drop
sections.frSub: Ce que le français ne veut pas
sections.say: Two things English makes you add and French does not want. Tap either row for why.

detail.title: Nothing in front of the day
detail.body: English needs on and French needs nothing. Sur is physically on top of something, and à lundi is how you say goodbye until Monday. Neither says when. This is the one error here that leaves a listener with nothing to repair.

rows.say: Ce n'est pas lundi, c'est mardi.

detail.title: A small letter, always
detail.body: French treats a day as an ordinary noun, so it takes a capital only where any word would: at the start of a sentence. This is inaudible, which is why it survives for years in the writing of people who speak well.
detail.say: Lundi, je commence un nouveau travail.

detail.title: The one place a word IS wanted
detail.body: Le makes it every week. French does put a word in front of a day, just never the one English reaches for. This one is an article and it changes the meaning. A preposition would only have been grammar.

sections.title: Four Traps
sections.say: Le makes it every week. Four sentences an English speaker produces in their first month, one per screen.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je suis libre samedi » when you mean every Saturday.
errors.right: Saying « Je suis libre le samedi » when you mean every Saturday.
errors.why: This one costs the most, because it lands while somebody is making a plan with you. A bare day is one day, so you have answered about this week when you meant your whole year, or the other way round.

errors.wrong: Saying « On se voit sur samedi ».
errors.why: English needs on and French needs nothing at all. Sur means physically on top of, so this asks to meet standing on a Saturday and there is nothing for a listener to repair. À lundi is real, and it means see you Monday.

errors.wrong: Writing « Je viens Lundi ».
errors.why: Days are ordinary nouns in French and take a capital only at the start of a sentence. Nobody will hear this and everybody will read it, which is why it survives for years in the writing of people who speak the language well.

errors.wrong: Saying « J'ai cours les lundis » for every Monday.
errors.right: Saying « J'ai cours le lundi » for every Monday.
errors.why: The English plural, moved across. Les lundis is real French meaning Mondays as a set, so nothing marks it wrong and it never gets corrected. The habitual form is singular. Tous les lundis is where the plural belongs.

sections.title: The Note On The Door
sections.say: Every day in this passage is lowercase and half of them carry an article. Tap any underlined phrase.
sections.text: There is a printed card taped inside the window of the bakery on the corner, and under it somebody has stuck a second one, handwritten. The printed one has been there for years. « Le magasin est fermé le mardi. » The handwritten one went up this morning, in biro, slightly crooked. « Le magasin est fermé mardi. » Read quickly they are the same sentence and one word apart, and the difference between them is a week of your shopping. The printed card is about every Tuesday, for ever, which is when this baker takes his day off. The handwritten one is about one Tuesday, the one coming, because something is happening that week. Underneath both, in the same biro, he has added the part that matters to his regulars. « On se voit mercredi. » Nobody needs telling which Wednesday.

glossary.note: Every Tuesday, for ever. The article is the whole difference, and this is what a printed sign means.
One Tuesday, the one coming. This is what the handwritten one means.
Masculine, so le rather than la. Nothing to do with the day rule.
Read this as a whole phrase. The verb behind it is not one you have been given yet.
Lowercase, and with nothing in front of it. Both are the French default, and a bare day is the nearest one.

questions.q: The two signs are one word apart. What does that word change?
questions.a: How often. The printed one has le in front of mardi and means every Tuesday, which is the baker's regular day off. The handwritten one has no article and means one Tuesday, the one coming.

questions.q: Which of the two signs would you expect to come down next week, and why?
questions.a: The handwritten one. It is about a single Tuesday, so once that Tuesday has passed it says nothing. The printed one describes a habit and stays up for years.

questions.q: Why does nobody need telling which Wednesday he means?
questions.a: Because a bare day is always the nearest one that makes sense. The conversation has already settled which week everyone is in, so the day on its own is enough.

sections.say: Five lines. Two of them offer you a word you must decide not to use, which is the whole exercise.

sections.say: The seven, the week around them, and the pairs. The little word in front is what the mic is listening for.

sections.title: Making A Plan
sections.say: One exchange, and you hold up your half. Every turn turns on whether you meant one day or all of them.
sections.setting: A message thread with Chloé, the evening after the language exchange, working out when you are both free.

turns.ai: Salut ! Tu es libre cette semaine ?
turns.en: Hi! Are you free this week?
turns.user: Salut ! Je suis libre jeudi et samedi.
turns.userEn: Hi! I am free on Thursday and Saturday.

alts.fr: Salut ! Oui, je suis libre jeudi.
alts.en: Hi! Yes, I am free on Thursday.

alts.fr: Oui ! Jeudi ou samedi, ça va.

turns.ai: Ah, moi j'ai cours le jeudi. Samedi alors ?
turns.en: Ah, I have class on Thursdays. Saturday then?
turns.user: Samedi, oui. Je suis libre samedi.
turns.userEn: Saturday, yes. I am free on Saturday.

turns.ai: Super. Le musée est gratuit le dimanche, mais samedi c'est bien aussi.
