sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: A friend asks if you are free this Saturday. You are.
cards.back: Je suis libre samedi. Le makes it every week.

cards.front: Your timetable puts a class on every Monday.
cards.back: J'ai cours le lundi. The article is doing all the work.

cards.front: The shop shuts every Tuesday, for ever.
cards.back: Le magasin est fermé le mardi. This is what a printed sign says.
cards.say: Le magasin est fermé le mardi.

cards.front: The shop shuts this coming Tuesday only.
cards.back: Le magasin est fermé mardi. Same sentence, one word shorter.

cards.front: How do you say "on Monday" in French?
cards.back: lundi. There is no word for on, and adding one breaks the sentence.

cards.front: Which day is between mardi and jeudi?
cards.back: mercredi. The longest of the seven and the one in the middle.

cards.front: You want to write "I am coming Monday" in a message.
cards.back: Je viens lundi. Lowercase l, because French days are ordinary nouns.

cards.front: You reach for "les lundis" for every Monday. What is wrong?
cards.back: The form that means every week is singular: le lundi. Les lundis is Mondays as a set.

cards.front: Which day does a French calendar put first?
cards.back: lundi. The week runs Monday to Sunday and the weekend is the last two columns.

cards.front: You want to be certain it is the Saturday coming.
cards.back: samedi prochain. After the day, never before, and never with an article.

cards.front: Every Saturday, said as strongly as it can be said.
cards.back: tous les samedis. This is the one place the plural belongs.

cards.front: The two days easiest to confuse at speed.
cards.back: mardi and jeudi. Two syllables, same ending, and only the first consonant apart.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a plan quietly fail over one word, learned the seven names in the order a French calendar prints them, and found out that the difference between every Monday and one Monday is an article your last-but-four lesson already taught you. You have seen both halves of that rule side by side on one screen, met the two written habits English hands you and French does not want, and read a shop door where one word was a week of your shopping. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The seven names
rounds.say: The names, quickly.

questions.q: A French calendar has seven columns. Which day is in the first one?
questions.why: lundi. The French week runs Monday to Sunday, so the weekend is the last two columns rather than one at each end. Counting from the wrong end puts every appointment one place out.

questions.q: Write the day that comes between mardi and jeudi.
questions.why: mercredi, from Mercury. It is the longest of the seven and sits in the middle of the week, which is the pair of facts that makes it easy to place.

questions.q: Listen. Which day is it?
questions.why: jeudi. It and mardi are two syllables ending in the same DEE, and the opening consonant is the whole difference. At speed that is what sends somebody to a meeting two days early.

questions.q: Five of the seven are named after planets. Which one is not?
questions.why: samedi, from the Sabbath, and dimanche from the Lord's day. The other five are the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter and Venus, and they are the same five planets behind the English names.

rounds.label: Every week
rounds.say: The article, and what it does.

questions.q: Your timetable puts a class on every Monday. How do you say it?
questions.why: Le makes it every week. A bare day is one day, so the first option describes a single Monday. The article is the only thing in the sentence saying how often.

questions.q: You mean every Saturday. Fix this. « Je suis libre samedi. »
questions.why: Without the article this is about one Saturday, which is an answer to an invitation rather than a fact about your week. Adding le turns one Saturday into all of them.

questions.q: Which lesson taught you this same le already?
questions.why: The definite articles taught le in front of a general noun, where English uses none at all: j'aime le café is coffee in general. A day works the same way, so this is one idea rather than two.

questions.q: You are closed every Tuesday. Write the two words for "on Tuesdays".
questions.why: le mardi. Singular, with the article, and that is what goes on a printed sign because it is true for ever rather than for one week.

rounds.label: One day
rounds.say: The bare day, and which one it is.

questions.q: Somebody asks if you are free on Saturday. You are, this week. What answers them?
opts: Je suis libre tous les samedis.
questions.why: She asked about one Saturday, so answer about one Saturday. The other three all describe your usual week, which is true and is not a yes, and that is how a plan quietly fails.

questions.q: One Thursday, the one coming. Write the French for "on Thursday".
questions.why: jeudi, on its own. No article, because it is one day, and no preposition, because French does not use one. Two things to leave out and nothing to add.

questions.q: The museum is free this Sunday only, because of an event. Fix this. « Le musée est gratuit le dimanche. »
questions.why: With the article this says every Sunday, which is a standing arrangement rather than a one-off. Take it away and you have one Sunday, the nearest one.

questions.q: Say it out loud: you are free this coming Saturday.
questions.why: No article and no preposition. The mic is listening for what is NOT in front of the day, which is the hardest thing to hear yourself leave out.

rounds.label: Singular, not plural
rounds.say: The English plural, and where it does belong.

questions.q: You are writing your timetable out for a friend. Which form means "every Monday"?
questions.why: le lundi, singular. English marks this with a plural S and French marks it with a singular article, so there is nothing to carry across and the English instinct gives you the wrong one every time.

questions.q: Fix this. « J'ai cours les lundis. »
questions.why: Les lundis is real French and means Mondays as a set of days, so nothing marks it as an error and nobody corrects it. The form that means every week is singular.

questions.q: Fix this. « Elle est à Paris les jeudis. »
accept: Elle est à Paris le jeudi.
elle est a paris le jeudi
questions.answer: Elle est à Paris le jeudi.
questions.why: The same swap on a different day, and the same reason: the habitual form is le plus a singular day. It holds for all seven with no exceptions.

questions.q: Where does a plural day belong?
questions.why: tous les samedis, every Saturday, said as strongly as it can be said. That is the one frame where the day goes plural, and it is a reinforcement of the rule rather than an exception to it.

rounds.label: No word for on
rounds.say: The word English makes you add.

questions.q: How do you say "on Monday" in French?
questions.why: lundi, with nothing in front of it. Sur is physically on top of, and à lundi is how you say goodbye until Monday rather than a way of saying when something happens.

questions.q: Fix this. « On se voit sur samedi. »
questions.why: Sur asks to meet standing on top of a Saturday, so there is nothing for a listener to repair and they ask again instead. This is the one error here that stops the sentence making sense rather than shifting its meaning.

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous avons une réunion à vendredi. »
questions.why: The day needs nothing in front of it. À vendredi is a real phrase and it means see you Friday, so putting it here says goodbye in the middle of a sentence about a meeting.

questions.q: French does put one word in front of a day. Which, and what for?
opts: le, and it means every week
en, and it marks the future
questions.why: Le makes it every week. It is an article rather than a preposition, and it changes the meaning rather than just being grammar. That is why leaving it out is not a small error.

rounds.label: On the page
rounds.say: What only shows in writing.

questions.q: You are writing a message. Which is spelled correctly?
questions.why: Days are ordinary nouns in French, so lundi takes a small letter mid-sentence. Je keeps its capital because it opens the sentence, which is the only reason any word gets one here.

questions.q: Prochain never takes an article. Fix this. « Je suis libre le dimanche prochain. »
questions.why: Prochain already picks out one Sunday, so the article has nothing left to do and would contradict it. This is the over-correction that arrives once the every-week rule has landed.

questions.q: A printed sign reads « Fermé le mardi ». A handwritten one reads « Fermé mardi ». Which comes down next week?
questions.why: The handwritten one is about a single Tuesday, so it says nothing once that Tuesday has passed. The printed one describes a habit and stays up for years.

questions.q: Write the French for "the week".
questions.why: la semaine, feminine. It runs lundi to dimanche here, which is a different seven days from the one an English calendar draws even though both have seven.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can name all seven days in the order a French calendar prints them, say what you do every week, and make a plan for one particular day without accidentally describing your year. The second and third of those are the same rule read in two directions, and it is one you already had before this lesson started: it is the le from the definite articles, pointed at a day. Months are next, and they inherit every habit on this list.
points: Le makes it every week. Take it away and you are talking about one day instead.
No word for on. Lundi, never sur lundi, and à lundi is a goodbye.
Lowercase, always, except where any word would take a capital.
The habitual form is singular: le lundi. Les lundis is Mondays as a set.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong day, most often mardi for jeudi: two syllables, the same ending, and one consonant apart.
Says a bare day when they mean every week. The error the reframe exists to kill, and the one the opening scene turns on.
Says le plus a day when they mean one particular day. The over-correction that arrives once the first half of the rule has landed.
Writes les lundis for every Monday, carrying the English plural across. Real French, wrong meaning, and nothing corrects it.
Puts sur, à or en in front of a day, because English needs on. The one error here that stops a sentence making sense.
Writes Lundi mid-sentence. Inaudible, so nobody corrects it, and it survives for years in the writing of people who speak well.

drills.title: English in, French out
drills.coach: The English is on the left. Say the French out loud before you turn the card, and keep the stress on the last syllable.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which day comes straight after mercredi?
drills.why: jeudi. mardi is the day before mercredi, and the two that sound alike sit on either side of it, which is what makes this order worth saying out loud rather than reading.

drills.title: One day, or all of them?
drills.coach: Read the word straight in front of the day. If there is a le, it is every week. If there is nothing, it is one day, and the conversation has already decided which.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You have a class every Monday. Which is right?
drills.why: Le lundi, singular, with the article. A bare day is one Monday and the plural is Mondays as a set, so only the middle one says every week.

drills.title: Take it away again
drills.coach: Read the habit on the left. Say the version on the right, which is about one day, and notice that the only thing you did was delete a word.
pairs: Le magasin est fermé le mardi.
Le musée est gratuit le dimanche.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: A friend asks if you are free this Saturday. What is a yes?
opts: Je suis libre tous les samedis.
drills.why: She asked about one Saturday. The other two describe your usual week, which is true and is not an acceptance, so she has no way of knowing whether you are coming.

drills.title: Where the plural belongs
drills.coach: Two shapes mean every week: le plus a singular day, and tous les plus a plural one. Everything else is one day. Sort on that and nothing here is ambiguous.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these does NOT mean every Saturday?
drills.why: Les samedis is Saturdays as a set of days, which is real French and is not how you say every Saturday. The article does that job on its own, in the singular.

drills.title: Nothing in front of it
drills.coach: Read the English on the left. Say the French on the right, and count how many words are in front of the day. The answer is always zero or one.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one means "we are meeting on Saturday"?
drills.why: Nothing in front of the day. Sur is physically on top of something, and à samedi means see you Saturday, which is a goodbye rather than a statement about when.

drills.title: Small letters
drills.coach: Every line here is correct French, which is the point: look at where each capital falls. A day only ever gets one because it opened the sentence, never because it is a day.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is written the way French writes it?
drills.why: The day takes a small letter and the sentence takes a capital. The third option gets the day right and drops the capital that any first word would have.

rows.v: The week, running lundi to dimanche. Feminine.
Borrowed from English, hyphenated, masculine, and at the END of the row.
The day, as a unit. Masculine.
Yesterday and tomorrow. Neither takes an article or a preposition.
The calendar, which starts its week on Monday here.
Every day. The plural is correct here, after tous les.

sections.title: Five planets and two days off
sections.body: Five of the seven carry a planet and they are the same five planets behind the English names, which is why this is worth thirty seconds rather than a mission. Lundi is the moon, as Monday is. Mardi is Mars, where English took the Norse god Tiw instead. Mercredi is Mercury, where English took Woden. Jeudi is Jupiter, and English took Thor, so Thursday and jeudi are the same god arriving by two different roads. Vendredi is Venus, and English took Frigg, and both are the goddess of love. That leaves the two at the end of the row, which are not planets at all: samedi comes from the Sabbath and dimanche from dies dominica, the Lord's day. English kept the sun in Sunday and French did not. The reason this sticks is that it is checkable. You can hold the French list against the English one and watch five of them line up, and a fact you verified yourself is a different kind of memory from a fact you were handed.

sheets.title: Every week, or one day
contains: Both halves on all seven days
The four errors, and which are audible

sections.title: The four errors, and which you can hear

rows.v: Je suis libre samedi for every Saturday. Audible, and it costs you a plan.
Je suis libre le samedi for this Saturday. Audible, and it reads as a polite no.
sur lundi, en lundi. Audible, and the sentence stops making sense.
les lundis for le lundi. Audible only in writing, since both sound the same.
Je viens Lundi. Inaudible, so nothing ever corrects it.

rows.k: The one plural that is right
rows.v: tous les samedis. Every Saturday, said as strongly as it can be said.

sections.title: Why there is nothing to carry across
sections.body: English and French both mark the difference between one Monday and every Monday, and they mark it in different places with different machinery, which is the whole reason this is hard. English uses a plural on the noun: on Monday against on Mondays. French uses a singular article in front of it: lundi against le lundi. So the English signal is at the end of the word and the French signal is a separate word in front of it, and the French form is singular exactly where the English one is plural. A learner translating word by word from English arrives at les lundis, which is a real phrase meaning Mondays as a set of days, so nothing about it looks wrong and no listener repairs it. That is why this error survives years of otherwise good French. The fix is not to translate the mechanism but to replace it: decide first whether you mean every week or one day, then put le in front or leave it off. The article is the same one you learned in front of a general noun, and it is doing the same job it does there. J'aime le café is coffee in general rather than one cup. Le lundi is Mondays in general rather than one Monday. It is one idea pointed at two different kinds of word, not two rules to keep apart.

everyWeek.term: le, in front of a day
everyWeek.title: The article that means every week
everyWeek.body: Put le in front of a day and you have stopped talking about one day and started talking about all of them. Le lundi is every Monday, as a rule, the way your week is arranged. This is the same le you met in front of a general noun a few lessons ago: j'aime le café is coffee in general rather than one cup, and le lundi is Mondays in general rather than one Monday. It is one idea you already have, pointed at a day.

examples.note: Every Monday. It is what your timetable says.
Every Saturday. A fact about your week, not a plan.

oneDay.title: The bare day, which is one day
oneDay.body: A day with nothing in front of it is one particular day, and which one is decided by the conversation you are already in. Said on a Wednesday, samedi is this coming Saturday. Said about the past, it is the one just gone. Nothing marks it and nothing needs to, because there is only ever one Saturday close enough to mean. Prochain and dernier are there when you want to be certain: samedi prochain, samedi dernier.

examples.note: This Saturday. An answer to an invitation.
Prochain, when being certain is worth two extra syllables.

noPreposition.title: French does not need on
noPreposition.body: English needs a preposition in front of a day and French does not. On Monday is lundi, and there is nothing in front of it. Neither sur lundi nor a bare à lundi is a way of saying when something happens: sur means physically on top of, and à lundi is a way of saying goodbye until Monday. The urge to put a small word there is strong and it is the one error in this lesson that produces something a listener cannot repair, because the sentence stops making sense rather than shifting meaning.

examples.note: On Monday, and nothing in front of it.
Two bare days in one sentence, neither with a preposition.

lowercase.title: Days are lowercase in French
lowercase.body: English capitalises the days and French does not. A day name is an ordinary noun here and takes a capital only where any word would: at the start of a sentence. This is inaudible, which is why it survives for years in the writing of people who speak well. It is worth fixing now rather than later, because every message you send is written and the habit is easier to break in the first week than in the fifth year.

examples.note: A capital, and only because it opens the sentence.
Two days mid-sentence, and both are lowercase.

weekStartsMonday.title: What a French calendar looks like
weekStartsMonday.body: A printed French calendar starts its week on Monday and ends it on Sunday, so the two days at the right-hand edge are the weekend. Lundi is le premier jour de la semaine and nobody says so out loud because nobody needs to. It matters the first time you read a timetable, a shop notice or a diary and count the columns from the wrong end, and it is why le week-end sits where it does rather than wrapping around.

examples.note: Next week, which starts on a Monday and not on a Sunday.
Every day, which is the whole row rather than one column of it.

recorded.desc: THE SEVEN DAYS AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, IN WEEK ORDER STARTING ON MONDAY, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE SPEED. Seven days recorded in seven sessions are seven performances, and the learner is memorising a SEQUENCE: any drift in pace, pitch or emphasis between them teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read the seven straight through with an even beat, the way somebody counts, then again slowly in the same take. EVERY ONE TAKES THE STRESS ON ITS LAST SYLLABLE and none of them is stressed on the first, which is the single most common thing an English speaker does to these words. Keep the nasals closed: lundi opens on one with NO n sound, vendredi carries one with NO n sound, and dimanche carries one in the middle with NO n sound. Those three are the ones a reader over-articulates.

The contrast this lesson exists for. EACH PAIR IS ONE TAKE: « le lundi » immediately followed by « lundi » by the same voice at the same pace, so the ONLY difference the learner hears is the article. Recorded apart, they compare two performances instead of two meanings, and the whole teaching is lost. Do not lean on the le to make it clearer: it is an unstressed syllable in ordinary speech and a learner who hears it emphasised will never recognise it at conversational speed. All seven pairs, in week order, then the four sentence pairs (« Je suis libre le samedi » / « Je suis libre samedi », and the same for the other three). SEPARATELY, and this is the other half of this recording: mardi and jeudi ADJACENTLY IN THE SAME TAKE, because they are the pair that genuinely collides at speed, and the m against the zh is the whole of the difference. Do not slow that pair down on the natural-pace take.

The frame words, one take, one voice: la semaine, le week-end, le jour, hier, demain, le calendrier, tous les jours. le week-end is borrowed from English and must be read as FRENCH, with the stress on the second half and no English diphthong on the week: a reader who says it the English way teaches the learner to code-switch mid-sentence. Keep the nasal in calendrier closed.

The four English-speaker traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them so the learner hears a difference rather than a correction. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically: three of the four are real French sentences that mean something else, and a performance that marks them as errors removes the reason they are dangerous. « Je suis libre samedi » is not a mistake at all out of context, which is the point of the first one. « On se voit sur samedi » is the only one that is not a sentence, and it still gets read straight.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of a woman in her twenties reading messages at an ordinary texting pace rather than a teaching pace. The beat where she gives up (« Ah, d'accord. Bon, une autre fois alors. ») must be light and unbothered rather than hurt or pointed: the whole point of the scene is that nobody is upset and nobody is corrected, the plan simply does not happen. Any edge on that line turns it into a telling-off and the teaching is lost.
clipIds: Ah, d'accord. Bon, une autre fois alors.

lessons.title: Les mois de l'année
lessons.intro: Twelve short words, and two small ones that decide whether you named a month or a day inside it. This is how you name the months, say when something is happening, and give a date somebody can write down and meet you on.

say.text: One question, one answer, and nothing you said was wrong. Watch which word was missing.

setting.place: A kitchen table, a laptop, and a flight open in another tab

beats.text: A Tuesday night, and you are finally booking the trip you have been talking about since winter.
Karim has a spare room in Marseille and has offered it twice. You have the flight open in another tab.

beats.prompt: The flight is on the twelfth. You know the day. What goes back?

options.en: the one that names the month

options.fr: Mon vol est le douze juin.
options.en: the one that names the day

followUp.works: Yes, and that is a date he can write down. Watch what the other one does to his week.
followUp.breaks: Every word in that is correct French. Watch what happens next anyway.

beats.speaker: Karim
beats.fr: Ah, super ! Dis-moi quand tu sais.
beats.en: Ah, great! Tell me when you know.
beats.stage: He does not book the day off. There is nothing in that message he could book it against.

beats.heading: You told him a month
beats.body: He asked which day and you answered which month. Both sentences are correct French and only one of them is a date, so he read yours as not booked yet and waited. Nothing was mispronounced and nothing got corrected.

wrong.en: My flight is in June, somewhere

right.fr: Mon vol est le douze juin.
right.en: My flight is on the twelfth, which he can meet

beats.coach: En for a month, le for a date. Two extra syllables, and one of them is the whole arrangement.

beats.speaker: Second try
beats.fr: Mon vol est le douze juin.
beats.en: My flight is on the twelfth of June.

beats.speaker: Karim
beats.fr: Parfait, je pose ma journée. Je serai à l'aéroport.
beats.en: Perfect, I am taking the day off. I will be at the airport.
beats.stage: He has already put it in his calendar.

beats.text: One small word separated a month from a day, and it works the same way on all twelve.

closing.text: En for a month, le for a date. That is the whole of the next twenty-five minutes.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the last two are the same rule read in opposite directions.

goals.s: In order, lowercase, and with the four that are genuinely hard to say sorted out from the eight that are not.

goals.t: Say which month something is in
goals.s: One small word in front, and it is not the one the days lesson taught you.
The day, the month, and the article that cannot be dropped, in the order French puts them.

goals.t: Write a date the way French writes it
goals.s: No capital letter, no extra word inside it, and the one day of the month that counts differently.

sections.title: Two Ways To Answer When
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Four cards before any of the twelve words, because these two frames decide how you use all of them.

cards.label: The question
cards.head: When is it?
cards.body: There are two true answers to this and they are not interchangeable. One names a month. The other names a day inside one. French marks the difference with the small word in front, and English does not mark it at all.

cards.label: The month
cards.head: en, and nothing else
cards.body: En plus the bare month. No article, no number, nothing added. This is what you say when the day is not known, not decided, or not the point.

cards.label: The day inside it
cards.head: le, then the number, then the month
cards.fr: Mon vol est le douze juin.
cards.sub: [luh DOOZ ZHWEHⁿ] · on the twelfth of June
cards.body: En for a month, le for a date. The le is not optional. It is the only thing marking this as one day rather than the whole month, which is what the opening scene turned on.

cards.label: What is actually hard
cards.head: Not the twelve
cards.body: Twelve short words is an afternoon and there is no pattern to teach, so they get three missions. Choosing between these two frames is what will still be catching you in a year, and it gets the rest.

sections.title: Twelve, One At A Time
sections.hint: Swipe. Say each one out loud before you move on.
sections.say: Twelve screens, one month each. Say it out loud before you swipe.

cards.label: 1 of 12
cards.body: January.

cards.label: 2 of 12
cards.body: February.

cards.label: 3 of 12
cards.body: March.

cards.label: 4 of 12
cards.body: April.

cards.label: 5 of 12
cards.body: May.

cards.body: June.

sections.title: Four Groups, Not Twelve Rows
sections.say: The twelve, split four ways. Every group is a real group, so the split is worth remembering.

check.q: Both of these open the same way. Which one is June?
check.why: juin is one syllable and juillet is two. They open identically, so the ending is the whole difference, and a holiday booked on the wrong one is a month out.

groups.label: Three that end the same, and one that does not

check.q: Three of these four rhyme. Which one does not?
check.why: octobre. The other three all end -embre and sound identical from the middle onward, and octobre sits between two of them without rhyming, which is exactly the shape that gets it misfiled.

groups.label: Two that sound their last letter

check.q: French usually leaves a final consonant silent. Which of these breaks that?
check.why: Both. Mars sounds its s and avril sounds its l, so the silent-final-consonant habit is wrong on both. The silent letters lesson already filed avril as a CaReFuL L you do pronounce.

groups.label: The four that give no trouble

check.q: Which of these four is the shortest to say?
check.why: août is one short sound, close to the English word oot. It is the shortest month name in French and the one learners most often stretch into two syllables that are not there.

sections.title: Two Pairs That Collide
sections.say: Two clusters here are genuinely hard at speed. Slow the audio down before you answer.

lines.en: June
July
September
November
December
October

questions.q: Which two months are hardest to separate at conversational speed?
questions.why: Both open on the same sound and the ending is the whole difference. They are also next to each other in the year, so a booking made on the wrong one is a month out rather than obviously absurd.

questions.q: Three of the last four lines end the same way. What does that ending sound like?
opts: a clear em, then a separate ruh
one nasal, then a quick br with no vowel
questions.why: The vowel is nasal and the -bre behind it is one quick sound with no vowel of its own. Adding a vowel there is what makes septembre come out with four syllables instead of three.

questions.q: Line six sits between two of the others in the year. Does it rhyme with them?
opts: No, octobre is the odd one out
questions.why: octobre ends -obre rather than -embre and carries no nasal. Being the only one of the four that does not rhyme, while sitting in the middle of them, is what makes it easy to misfile.

sections.title: The Word The Days Did Not Want
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Read this one properly. It is the place the last lesson's rule stops holding.

cards.label: This is new
cards.head: A day took nothing. A month takes en.
cards.body: The days lesson taught that a day needs no word in front of it, and that was true of days. Months are where it stops. A month always takes en, and leaving it out is the error that rule hands you.

cards.label: The frame
cards.head: en, then the bare month
cards.body: Nothing else goes in. No article in front of the month, no number, and no second small word. En janvier, en juin, en octobre, all twelve the same way with no exceptions.

cards.label: What it means
cards.head: The month, and nothing smaller
cards.fr: Le magasin est fermé en août.
cards.body: En names the month and stops. Which day is either not known, not decided, or not worth saying. That is exactly right for a birthday month or a holiday, and exactly wrong for a flight.

cards.label: The over-correction
cards.head: Never le janvier
cards.body: En for a month, le for a date. Once the date frame lands, the pull is to put le in front of everything. A month on its own never takes one, and le janvier is not a thing anybody says.

sections.title: The Month, Or A Day In It
sections.frSub: En juin ou le douze juin
sections.say: En for a month, le for a date. Left column is the month, right column is one day in it. Tap either side to hear the pair.

detail.body: Mon anniversaire est en janvier. names the month. Mon anniversaire est le premier janvier. names one day inside it. Nothing else in the two moved, so the frame carries the whole difference.
detail.say: Mon anniversaire est en janvier. Mon anniversaire est le premier janvier.

detail.title: en mars · le douze mars
detail.body: Nous sommes en mars. names the month. Nous sommes le douze mars. names one day inside it. Nothing else in the two moved, so the frame carries the whole difference.

detail.title: en juin · le douze juin
detail.body: Mon vol est en juin. names the month. Mon vol est le douze juin. names one day inside it. Nothing else in the two moved, so the frame carries the whole difference.
detail.say: Mon vol est en juin. Mon vol est le douze juin.

detail.title: en juillet · le quatorze juillet
detail.body: Le concert est en juillet. names the month. Le concert est le quatorze juillet. names one day inside it. Nothing else in the two moved, so the frame carries the whole difference.
detail.say: Le concert est en juillet. Le concert est le quatorze juillet.

detail.title: en août · le premier août
detail.body: Le magasin est fermé en août. names the month. Le magasin est fermé le premier août. names one day inside it. Nothing else in the two moved, so the frame carries the whole difference.

detail.say: La rentrée scolaire est en septembre. La rentrée scolaire est le premier septembre.

detail.title: en octobre · le trois octobre
detail.body: L'anniversaire de mon père est en octobre. names the month. L'anniversaire de mon père est le trois octobre. names one day inside it. Nothing else in the two moved, so the frame carries the whole difference.
detail.say: L'anniversaire de mon père est en octobre. L'anniversaire de mon père est le trois octobre.

detail.title: en décembre · le douze décembre
detail.body: J'ai un examen en décembre. names the month. J'ai un examen le douze décembre. names one day inside it. Nothing else in the two moved, so the frame carries the whole difference.
detail.say: J'ai un examen en décembre. J'ai un examen le douze décembre.

sections.title: A Month, Or A Day?
sections.say: One question, and it is the one the opening scene turned on.

check.q: A friend asks which day your flight lands. You know: the twelfth of June. What do you answer?
opts: Mon vol est le douze juin.
Mon vol est en douze juin.
Mon vol est le juin douze.
check.why: He asked which day, so answer with a day. The first names the month and is true without being an answer, and the other two mix the two frames into something French does not use.

sections.title: The Shape Of A Date
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Three parts, in this order, with nothing else in it. Four cards.

cards.label: The order
cards.head: Number first, month second
cards.body: English says March twelfth and French says the twelve March, so the two change places. Reaching for the English order gives you mars douze, which is not a date in either language.

cards.label: The article
cards.head: le cannot be dropped
cards.fr: J'ai un examen le douze décembre.
cards.body: English has no word here at all, so there is nothing to translate and the instinct is to leave it out. Without it there is no date, only a number sitting next to a month.

cards.label: Nothing in between
cards.head: Never le douze de mars
cards.body: The number and the month sit straight against each other. Spanish and Portuguese both want a small word between them, so this one arrives with anybody who has either, and it survives because the sentence still parses.

cards.label: The month, named
cards.head: le mois de, and what happens before a vowel
cards.fr: Pendant le mois d'août, nous campons à la campagne.
cards.body: To name the month itself rather than date something in it, use le mois de. Before a vowel the de loses its e, exactly as the elision lesson showed: le mois de mai, but le mois d'août.

sections.title: The First, And All The Rest
sections.say: One day of the month counts differently. Tap any row for why.

rows.say: Le magasin est fermé le premier janvier.

detail.title: le premier, the only one
detail.body: En for a month, le for a date. And the first of the month is the single day that takes a first-second-third word rather than a plain number. Le premier janvier, le premier mai, le premier août.
detail.say: Le magasin est fermé le premier janvier.

detail.title: From the second onward, just count
detail.body: Le deux, not le deuxième. From here to the end of the month you use the same word you would use for the number on its own, which means you already have all thirty of them.
detail.say: le deux, le trois, le quatre

rows.say: Mon vol est le douze juin.

detail.title: The one the scene turned on
detail.body: Le douze, not le douzième. English puts an ordinal ending on every day of the month and French puts one on exactly one, so the English habit is wrong thirty times out of thirty-one.
detail.say: Mon vol est le douze juin.

rows.say: Chaque année, le feu d'artifice a lieu le quatorze juillet.

detail.title: The date everybody knows
detail.body: Le quatorze juillet is the national holiday, and it is a plain fourteen. Hearing it said often is the fastest way to stop reaching for an ordinal ending on the other thirty days.
detail.say: Chaque année, le feu d'artifice a lieu le quatorze juillet.

detail.title: The last day, and still a plain number
detail.body: Le trente et un décembre. The numbers from twenty-one to a hundred are the lesson you did four units ago, so every day of every month is already in your hands.

sections.title: Five Traps
sections.say: En for a month, le for a date. Five sentences an English speaker produces in their first month, one per screen.

errors.wrong: Saying « Mon vol est en douze juin ».
errors.right: Saying « Mon vol est le douze juin ».
errors.why: En is the frame for a whole month and it cannot hold a day. Putting a number inside it produces something no French speaker says, and the listener has to guess whether you meant the month or the day.

errors.wrong: Saying « Le concert est le juillet ».
errors.right: Saying « Le concert est en juillet ».
errors.why: The over-correction, and it arrives the week after the date rule lands. A month on its own never takes an article. Le juillet is not a thing, so this one stops the sentence rather than shifting it.

errors.wrong: Writing « Je pars en Juillet ».
errors.why: Months are ordinary words in French and take a capital only at the start of a sentence. You met this on the days already and it holds here unchanged. Nobody will hear it and everybody will read it.

errors.wrong: Saying « le douze de mars ».
errors.why: The number and the month sit straight against each other with nothing between. Spanish and Portuguese both want that small word, so this arrives with anybody who has either, and the sentence still parses, which is why it survives.

errors.wrong: Saying « le un janvier » for the first of January.
errors.why: The first of the month is the one day that takes premier rather than a counting number. Every other day is the plain number, so this is the single exception and it runs the opposite way to the English habit.

sections.title: The Notice In The Window
sections.say: Every month here is lowercase, and two of the notices say different things about the same shop.
sections.text: The bakery on the corner has two notices taped inside the window, and they have been arguing with each other since June. The printed one is old, curled at the edges, and says what the shop does every year. « Le magasin est fermé en août. » The handwritten one went up last week, in the same biro the baker uses for everything. « Le magasin est fermé le premier août. » Read quickly they are the same sentence, and the difference between them is four weeks of somebody's bread. The printed one means the whole month, which is what a great many French shops do and why cities empty out. The handwritten one means one day, the first, because this year he has decided to stay open and take a single day instead. Underneath both, smaller, he has added the part his regulars actually came to read. « On se voit lundi deux août. » Nobody needs telling which August.

glossary.note: The whole month. En plus the bare month, which is what a printed sign means.
One day. The article and the number together make it a date rather than a month.
Masculine, so le rather than la. Nothing to do with the date rule.
Read this as a whole phrase. The verb behind it is not one you have been given yet.
A full date with a day in it. The day comes first and the number stays a plain two.

questions.q: The two notices are a few words apart. What does that difference change?
questions.a: How long the shop is shut. The printed one says en août, which is the whole month. The handwritten one says le premier août, which is one day, and this year he has decided to close for a single day instead of the usual four weeks.

questions.q: Which of the two notices would you expect to come down first, and why?
questions.a: The handwritten one. It is about a single day, so once the second of August has passed it says nothing. The printed one describes what the shop does every year and goes back up each summer.

questions.q: The last line gives a full date. What order are its parts in?
questions.a: The day name first, then the number, then the month: lundi deux août. The number sits straight against the month with nothing between them, and it is a plain two rather than a second.

sections.title: The Year, Banked
sections.say: Three decks. The twelve names, the words around them, and the two frames.

themes.title: the month, or a day in it

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French out loud, small word and all, before you flip.

cards.front: My flight is on the twelfth of June.
cards.back: Mon vol est le douze juin.
cards.say: Mon vol est le douze juin.

cards.front: Today is the twelfth of March.
The shop is closed in August.

turns.ai: Alors, c'est confirmé ? Tu arrives quel jour ?
turns.en: So, is it confirmed? Which day do you get in?
turns.user: Mon vol est le douze juin.
turns.userEn: My flight is on the twelfth of June.

alts.en: I get in on the twelfth of June.

turns.ai: Parfait. Et tu repars quand ? Fin juin ?
turns.en: Perfect. And when do you leave? End of June?
turns.user: Non, je suis là en juillet aussi.
turns.userEn: No, I am here in July as well.

alts.en: No, I am staying in July.

alts.fr: Je suis là en juin et en juillet.
alts.en: I am here in June and in July.

turns.ai: Ah super ! Il y a le feu d'artifice le quatorze juillet, tu seras là ?
turns.en: Ah great! There are fireworks on the fourteenth of July, will you be here?
turns.user: Oui ! Le quatorze juillet, je suis à Marseille.
turns.userEn: Yes! On the fourteenth of July, I am in Marseille.

alts.fr: Oui, je suis là le quatorze juillet.
alts.en: Yes, I am here on the fourteenth of July.

alts.fr: Bien sûr, le quatorze juillet je suis là.
alts.en: Of course, on the fourteenth of July I am here.

turns.ai: Génial. Et ton anniversaire, c'est quand déjà ?
turns.en: Great. And your birthday, when is it again?
turns.user: Mon anniversaire est en janvier.
turns.userEn: My birthday is in January.

alts.fr: C'est en janvier, il faut attendre.
alts.en: It is in January, you have to wait.

turns.ai: Janvier ! Bon, on fêtera ça en juin alors. Le douze ?
turns.en: January! Well, we will celebrate it in June then. The twelfth?
turns.user: Le douze juin, oui. Le jour de mon arrivée.
turns.userEn: The twelfth of June, yes. The day I arrive.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a trip quietly fail to get booked over one small word, learned the twelve names in four groups that each mean something, and found out that the days lesson's rule about needing no word in front stops exactly here. You have seen both frames side by side on one screen, on nine different months, met the one day of the month that counts differently from the other thirty, and read a shop window where a few words were four weeks of somebody's bread. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The twelve names
rounds.say: The names, quickly.

questions.q: Listen. Which month is it?
questions.why: juillet. It and juin open on the same sound and the ending is the whole difference, which is what sends a holiday booking a month out from where it was meant.

questions.q: Listen. Which month is it?
questions.why: novembre. Three of these four end -embre and sound identical from the middle onward, so the opening syllable is the only thing telling them apart.

questions.q: Write the month that comes between février and avril.
questions.why: mars, and it is one of the two months that sound their final consonant. It is the same word as the planet, which is worth knowing because the planet is where the name came from.

questions.q: Which of these four does NOT rhyme with the other three?
questions.why: octobre ends -obre and carries no nasal. It sits between two months that do rhyme, which is exactly the position that gets it misfiled when somebody is reciting the year at speed.

rounds.label: En for a month
rounds.say: The month frame, and the word that carries it.

questions.q: Somebody asks when your birthday is. It is in January and the day does not matter here. What do you say?
questions.why: En for a month, le for a date. A month on its own takes en and nothing else. The third option is the habit the days lesson gives you, and months are exactly where that rule stops holding.

questions.q: You are telling a friend the shop shuts for the whole of August. Fix this. « Le magasin est fermé le août. »
accept: Le magasin est fermé en août.
le magasin est fermé en aout
questions.answer: Le magasin est fermé en août.
questions.why: A whole month never takes an article. This is the over-correction that arrives once the date rule has landed, and it stops the sentence rather than shifting its meaning.

questions.q: The days lesson taught that a day needs no word in front of it. What happens with a month?
opts: The same: a month needs nothing either
questions.why: Months are where that rule stops. A day takes nothing and a month takes en, with no exceptions across the twelve. Carrying the days rule across gives you a bare month, which is the most common error here.

questions.q: Your holiday is somewhere in July and you have not booked a day yet. Write the two words for "in July".
questions.why: en juillet. The month, bare, with en in front. That is the right answer precisely because the day is not settled, and it is what you would say about a birthday month too.

rounds.label: Le for a date
rounds.say: One day inside a month.

questions.q: Your flight lands on the twelfth of June and a friend is meeting you. What do you tell them?
opts: Mon vol est en douze juin.
Mon vol est le douze juin.
questions.why: They asked which day, so the answer has to be a day. The first is true and is not a date, and the other two mix the two frames into something French does not use.

questions.q: You mean one particular day. Fix this. « Le concert est en quatorze juillet. »
accept: Le concert est le quatorze juillet.
le concert est le quatorze juillet
questions.answer: Le concert est le quatorze juillet.
questions.why: En is the frame for a whole month and cannot hold a number. A day inside a month takes le, then the number, then the month, and nothing else changes in the sentence.

questions.q: Somebody asks what the date is today. It is the twelfth of March. Say it out loud.
questions.why: The mic is listening for the le in front of the number. It is unstressed and easy to swallow, and it is the only thing making this a date rather than a month with a number beside it.

questions.q: Write the French for "on the twelfth of December".
questions.why: le douze décembre. Article, then number, then month. The number goes in front of the month, which is the opposite of the order English uses.

rounds.label: The first, and the rest
rounds.say: One day of the month counts differently.

questions.q: New Year's Day. Which is right?
questions.why: le premier janvier. The first of the month is the single day that takes a first-second-third word, and it is the only one, so this is an exception you learn once and apply everywhere.

questions.q: Your father's birthday is the third of October. Fix this. « L'anniversaire de mon père est le troisième octobre. »
accept: L'anniversaire de mon père est le trois octobre.
l anniversaire de mon pere est le trois octobre
questions.answer: L'anniversaire de mon père est le trois octobre.
questions.why: trois, not troisième. English puts an ordinal ending on every day of the month and French puts one on exactly the first, so the English habit is wrong on thirty days out of thirty-one.

questions.q: Write the French for "on the first of August".
questions.why: le premier août. The one ordinal in the French month, on the month with the shortest name. Note there is nothing between premier and août.

questions.q: The last day of the year. Which is right?
opts: le trente et un de décembre
questions.why: A plain counting number, nothing between it and the month, and the number before the month. Every day but the first works this way, and you already had the numbers to a hundred four units ago.

rounds.label: What English adds
rounds.say: The word English puts in, and the order it puts things in.

questions.q: You have Spanish or Portuguese behind you and it wants a small word here. Fix this. « Mon vol est le douze de juin. »
accept: Mon vol est le douze juin.
mon vol est le douze juin
questions.answer: Mon vol est le douze juin.
questions.why: Nothing goes between the number and the month in French. Both those languages want that word, so this arrives with anybody who has either, and the sentence still parses, which is why nobody corrects it.

questions.q: You have reached for the English order. Fix this. « Nous sommes mars douze. »
questions.why: English says March twelfth and French says the twelve March, so the two change places and the article appears in front. Two things move at once, which is why this one needs saying out loud a few times.

questions.q: How many parts does a French date have, and in what order?
opts: Two: the month, then the number
Three: le, the month, the number
Three: le, the number, the month
Four: le, the number, de, the month
questions.why: le douze mars. Three parts, in that order, with nothing added. The fourth option is the one Spanish and Portuguese speakers reach for and the third is the English order with a French article on it.

questions.q: You want to name the month itself in front of a vowel. Write the French for "the month of August".
questions.why: The de loses its e in front of a vowel, exactly as the elision lesson showed. It is le mois de mai but le mois d'août, and août starts on a vowel sound despite the way it is spelled.

rounds.label: On the page
rounds.say: What only shows in writing.

questions.q: You are writing a message. Which is spelled correctly?
questions.why: Months are ordinary words in French, so juillet takes a small letter mid-sentence. Je keeps its capital only because it opens the sentence, which is the one reason any word gets one here.

questions.q: A printed notice reads « Fermé en août ». A handwritten one reads « Fermé le premier août ». How long is the shop shut, according to each?
opts: The whole month, and one day
One day, and the whole month
questions.why: En names the month, so the printed one is four weeks. Le plus a number names one day, so the handwritten one is the first of August only. That difference is a month of somebody's shopping.

questions.q: Which month name is spelled correctly?
questions.why: février, with an accent on the first e and none on the second, and a small f in the middle of a sentence. It is the month most often misspelled and the one with the fewest days.

questions.q: Write the French for "in December".
questions.why: en décembre, with the accent on the first e. The month takes en and no article, and the accent is the part a spellchecker will not put back for you.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can name all twelve months, say which month something is in, and give a full date that somebody can write down and meet you on. The second and third of those are the same choice made in two directions, and it is the choice the whole unit exists for. Seasons and the weather are next, and they use a small word in front of them too, which is worth knowing before you meet it.
points: En for a month, le for a date. The month takes nothing else, and the date cannot lose its le.
The first of the month is le premier. Every other day is a plain number.
Number in front of the month, and nothing at all between them.
Lowercase, always, except where any word would take a capital.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong month: juin for juillet, or one of the three -embre months for another.
Says le plus a bare month, or drops the small word entirely. The days lesson's rule carried across, plus the over-correction that follows the date rule.
Says en plus a number plus a month when they mean one day. The error the reframe exists to kill, and the one the opening scene turns on.
Writes le un janvier for the first, or puts an ordinal ending on every other day of the month, carrying the English habit across.
Puts a de inside the date, or leaves the number and the month in the English order. Both survive because the sentence still parses.
Writes Juillet mid-sentence. Inaudible, so nobody corrects it, and it survives for years in the writing of people who speak well.

drills.title: English in, French out

drills.q: Which month comes straight after juin?
drills.why: juillet. It is also the month juin is hardest to tell apart from, so the two sitting next to each other in the year is worth saying out loud rather than reading.

drills.title: The month takes en
drills.coach: Read the words in front of the month. If it is just en, the whole month is meant. If there is a le and a number, one day is meant.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Your birthday is in January and the day does not matter. Which is right?
drills.why: A month on its own takes en. The first puts an article on a whole month, which French never does, and the third is the days rule carried across to a word that does not want it.

drills.title: Put the day back in

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Your flight lands on the twelfth of June and a friend is meeting you. What do you tell them?
opts: Mon vol est le douze juin.
Mon vol est en douze juin.
drills.why: They need a day, so the answer has to carry one. The first names the month and is true without being an answer, and the third puts a number inside a frame that cannot hold one.

drills.title: The first, and everything after it
drills.coach: Read the English on the left. Say the French on the right, and notice that only the first one gets a word of its own.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these is the way French writes the third of a month?
drills.why: A plain counting number. premier is the only day of the month that takes a first-second-third word, so from the second onward you use the number you already know.

drills.title: Three parts, nothing else
drills.coach: A date has three parts in one order: le, the number, the month. If a sentence names a month with en and no number, it is naming the month rather than dating anything in it.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one means "on the twelfth of March"?
drills.why: Nothing goes between the number and the month, and the number comes first. The first option is the shape Spanish and Portuguese want, and the third is the English order.

drills.title: Small letters
drills.coach: Every line here is correct French, which is the point: look at where each capital falls. A month only ever gets one because it opened the sentence, never because it is a month.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is written the way French writes it?
drills.why: The month takes a small letter and the sentence takes a capital. The third option gets the month right and drops the capital that any first word would have.

sections.title: The four sounds worth thirty seconds
sections.body: Four things in the twelve are genuinely hard and the other eight are not, so it is worth knowing which four. First, juin and juillet open on exactly the same sound and the ending is the whole difference. They are also next to each other in the year, so confusing them books a holiday a month out from where it was meant rather than somewhere obviously absurd. Say them as a pair, out loud, several times, because that is the only way the difference becomes automatic. Second, septembre, novembre and décembre all end the same way: a nasal vowel followed by a quick br with no vowel of its own. Three months, one ending, and octobre sits in the middle of them without rhyming at all, which is exactly the shape that makes it get misfiled. Learn the trio as a trio and let octobre be the odd one out on purpose. Third, mars sounds its final s and avril sounds its final l, which breaks the habit that French leaves a final consonant silent. Both are already filed as exceptions elsewhere in this app: avril is the CaReFuL L exemplar in the silent letters lesson, where gentil is compared against it. Fourth, août is one short sound and it is the shortest month name in French. It is often stretched into two syllables that are not there, and this app teaches one pronunciation of it and does not show you the others, because an A1 learner needs a word to say rather than a debate to follow.
