The five errors, and which are audible

sections.title: The five errors, and which you can hear

rows.k: The month frame with a day in it
rows.v: en douze juin. Audible, and it is not French.

rows.k: An article on a bare month
rows.v: le juillet. Audible, and it stops the sentence.

rows.k: The missing article on a date
rows.v: douze mars. Audible, and it is a number beside a month rather than a date.
le douze de mars. Audible, and the sentence still parses, so nobody corrects it.
mars douze. Audible, and it is not a date in either language.

rows.k: An ordinal on the wrong day
rows.v: le douzième juin. Audible. Only premier works that way.
en Juillet. Inaudible, so nothing ever corrects it.

sections.title: Why there is nothing to carry across
sections.body: English marks the difference between a month and a day inside it with the same word twice, and French marks it with two different ones, which is the whole reason this is hard. English says in January and on the twelfth of March, and both of those small words are doing the job of pointing at a time. A learner reaching for a translation finds that in and on both come out as one French word in other contexts, and picks whichever comes first. French does not work that way here. A whole month takes en and nothing else, and a day inside a month takes le, then the number, then the month. There is no overlap between the two frames and no sentence where either would do. That is actually good news, because it means the choice is never a matter of taste: decide first whether you are naming a month or a day, and the frame follows with no judgement involved. The second thing worth knowing is that the two errors point in opposite directions and the second one arrives after the first is fixed. A learner who has only been told to use le for dates starts putting le in front of bare months within a week, which is why every drill in this lesson sorts both ways rather than only asking you to add the article. Finally, the article in a date is not optional and has no English equivalent at all, so there is nothing to translate and the instinct is to leave it out. Without it you have a number sitting next to a month, which is not a date, and the listener has to work out what you meant.

rows.v: Compulsory. English has nothing here, so there is nothing to translate and it is the part most often left out.
A plain counting number on every day but the first. You had all of these four units ago.
Straight after the number, with nothing between them, and always lowercase.

rows.k: a day name, if you want one
rows.v: It goes at the front: lundi deux août. That is the days lesson rather than this one.

monthFrame.term: en, in front of a month
monthFrame.title: The frame for a whole month
monthFrame.body: Put en in front of a month and you have named the month and nothing smaller. En janvier is somewhere in January, en août is somewhere in August, and which day is either not known or not the point. Nothing else goes with it: no article, no number, and no other small word. This is the frame you want for a birthday month, a holiday, a season of work, and anything where the answer to when is a month rather than a day.

examples.note: A birthday month. Nobody needs the day to send a card in the right week.
A flight somewhere in June, which is not enough for anyone to meet you.

dateFrame.term: le, in front of a date
dateFrame.title: The frame for one day inside a month
dateFrame.body: A day inside a month takes le, then the number, then the month: le douze mars. The le is not optional and it is not decoration, because it is the only thing marking this as one day rather than the whole month. Swapping en for le plus a number is the difference between a month you might travel in and a day somebody can meet you on. Out loud it is two extra syllables, which is a small price for the only precise answer there is.

examples.note: One day in June, and now the plan can happen.
Today, given as a date. This is how a French speaker says what the date is.

firstOnly.title: The first is the only one that counts differently
firstOnly.body: The first of a month is le premier: le premier janvier, le premier mai, le premier août. Every other day is a plain counting number, the same word you would use for the number itself. Le deux, le trois, le douze, le trente et un. English does the opposite and puts a first, second, third ending on all of them, so the instinct is to reach for one every time. There is exactly one place in the French month where that instinct is right, and it is the first.

examples.note: The first, and the only day of the month that gets its own word.
trois, not troisième. The third of October takes a plain counting number.

dateShape.title: Number first, and nothing between
dateShape.body: English says March twelfth and French says le douze mars, so the number and the month change places. There is also nothing between them: le douze mars, never le douze de mars. That extra small word is the one Spanish and Portuguese speakers bring with them, because both their languages want it, and it is the error most likely to survive here. Three parts, in this order, with no fourth: le, the number, the month.

examples.note: The number in front of the month, and nothing sitting between the two.
A date inside a longer sentence, and the three parts are still in that order.

lowercase.title: Months are lowercase in French
lowercase.body: English capitalises the months and French does not. A month name is an ordinary word here and takes a capital only where any word would: at the start of a sentence. You met this on the days a lesson ago and it holds for the months with no change. It is inaudible, which is why it survives for years in the writing of people who speak well, and it is worth fixing now because every message you send is written.

examples.note: Inside the name of a national holiday, and mai still takes a small letter.
A famous date, and novembre is lowercase in the middle of it.

recorded.desc: THE TWELVE MONTHS AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, IN CALENDAR ORDER STARTING AT JANVIER, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE SPEED. Twelve months recorded in twelve sessions are twelve performances, and the learner is memorising a SEQUENCE: any drift in pace, pitch or emphasis between them teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read the twelve straight through with an even beat, the way somebody counts, then again slowly in the same take. JUIN AND JUILLET MUST BE ADJACENT AND IN THIS SAME TAKE, in calendar order, because they are the pair that genuinely collides and the learner has to hear them against each other rather than four minutes apart. Do not slow that pair down on the natural-pace pass and do not lean on the ending of juillet to separate them: a learner who only recognises the difference when it is exaggerated will not recognise it at conversational speed. SEPTEMBRE, OCTOBRE, NOVEMBRE AND DÉCEMBRE MUST ALSO SIT TOGETHER IN THIS TAKE, in that order, so the three that rhyme and the one that does not are heard against each other: octobre in the middle without the -embre ending is the whole teaching of that group. Keep every nasal closed: janvier opens on one with NO n sound, juin is a single nasal syllable with NO n sound, and septembre, novembre and décembre each carry one in the middle with NO n sound and a quick br behind it that has no vowel of its own. Those five are the ones a reader over-articulates. mars sounds its final s and avril sounds its final l, both deliberately, and août is ONE short sound: do not give it two syllables and do not use any pronunciation other than the one this app teaches, which is the oot form.

The contrast this lesson exists for. EACH PAIR IS ONE TAKE: « en juin » immediately followed by « le douze juin » by the same voice at the same pace, so the ONLY difference the learner hears is the frame. Recorded apart, they compare two performances instead of two meanings, and the whole teaching is lost. Do not lean on the le to make it clearer: it is an unstressed syllable in ordinary speech and a learner who hears it emphasised will never recognise it at conversational speed. All nine pairs, in the order the contrast table shows them, then the four full sentence pairs (« Mon vol est en juin » / « Mon vol est le douze juin », and the same for the août, juillet and décembre pairs). The bare-frame pairs and the sentence pairs are both needed: the first shows the difference with nothing around it and the second shows it surviving inside a sentence, which is where the learner has to hear it.
clipIds: Mon vol est le douze juin.
Le magasin est fermé en août.
Le magasin est fermé le premier août.

recorded.desc: The date shape, one take: le premier, le deux, le trois, le onze, le douze, le quatorze, le vingt et un, le trente et un, read as a list so the learner hears premier as the ONE that is shaped differently and the rest as plain counting. Then the same numbers attached to a month with NO PAUSE between the number and the month: « le douze mars », « le trois octobre », « le trente et un décembre ». That gap is the whole point, because a reader who breathes between them teaches the learner that something belongs there, and the error this lesson fights hardest is a de inserted in exactly that position. Also record « le mois de mai » and « le mois d'août » adjacently in one take, so the elision is heard as the same phrase changing rather than two phrases.

The five English-speaker traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them so the learner hears a difference rather than a correction. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically. Two of the five are real French sentences that mean something else, and a performance that marks them as errors removes the reason they are dangerous: « Mon vol est en juin » is not a mistake at all out of context, which is the point of the first one, and « le douze de mars » parses perfectly well to a listener, which is why nobody corrects it. « Le concert est le juillet » is the one that genuinely stops, and it still gets read straight.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of a man in his thirties reading messages at an ordinary texting pace rather than a teaching pace. The beat where he accepts the vague answer (« Ah, super ! Dis-moi quand tu sais. ») must be warm and genuinely pleased rather than disappointed or pointed: the whole point of the scene is that nobody is upset and nobody is corrected, the day simply never gets booked. Any edge on that line turns it into a telling-off and the teaching is lost. The final line, where he says he will take the day off, is the one place warmth is allowed to show, because that is the reward for having given him a date.
clipIds: Ah, super ! Dis-moi quand tu sais.
Parfait, je pose ma journée. Je serai à l'aéroport.

lessons.title: L'heure
lessons.intro: Twelve short hours, a noun English throws away, and one small word that decides whether you are telling somebody the time or arranging to meet them. This is how you say what time it is, read a timetable that counts to twenty-four, and make a plan without answering a question nobody asked.

sections.title: The Answer That Booked Something
sections.frSub: Il est midi, ou à midi

say.text: Somebody asks you the time and you have every word they need. Watch which one gets in the way.

setting.place: Outside the station, with a coffee going cold

beats.text: You are outside the station with a coffee. A man about your age stops, taps his bare wrist, and looks at you hopefully.

beats.speaker: A stranger
beats.en: Excuse me, what time is it?
beats.stage: He has no watch and no phone in his hand.

beats.text: You know this. Your phone says twelve exactly. You have met midi, you have read it in a dozen sentences this week, and you have the verb in full.

beats.prompt: Your phone says twelve. What do you say back?

options.en: it is noon
it is at noon

followUp.works: That is it, and the small word you did not say is the reason it worked.
followUp.breaks: Every word was one you know. One of them turned your answer into a different sentence.

beats.heading: One word, and you answered a different question
beats.body: À midi means at noon, which is when something happens. He did not ask when anything happens. He asked what time it is, and that sentence has no à in it at all.

wrong.en: It is at noon, which is an answer about a schedule

right.en: It is noon, which is an answer about the clock

beats.coach: Il est says the time. À books it. You have read à in front of an hour far more often than you have read il est, so it is the one that arrives first.

beats.speaker: A stranger
beats.fr: Midi ! Merci, je suis en retard.
beats.stage: He is already walking.

beats.text: He got his answer on the second try, and the thing standing between the two tries was one letter.

closing.text: Il est says the time. À books it. That is the whole of the next half hour.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Il est says the time. À books it. By the end you will have both frames and know which one a question is asking for.

goals.s: All twelve hours, plus the two that take no number, in the frame that never changes.

goals.t: Say half past and quarter to
goals.s: Four phrases that hang off the back of an hour, one of which carries an article for no reason at all.
The printed clock runs to twenty-four and says its minutes as a plain number, and it never borrows from the spoken one.
Two ways to ask, one of them memorised whole, and the small word that turns a time into a plan.

sections.title: The Frame That Never Changes
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Four cards, and then every hour you will ever say fits into them.

cards.label: The shape
cards.head: Two fixed words, then a number
cards.body: Il est, then the hour, then the word for hours. The first two words never change and the last one never leaves. Only the number in the middle moves.

cards.label: The subject
cards.head: The il is nobody
cards.body: You learned il as he, and here it points at nothing. French wants a subject in front of a verb even when there is nothing to put there. The verb itself you already have in full.

cards.label: The word English drops
cards.head: Never il est huit
cards.fr: il est huit heures · il est huit
cards.body: English says it is eight and throws the noun away. French cannot. Leave it off and you have not said something wrong, you have stopped in the middle.

cards.label: One, then the rest
cards.head: Singular once, plural after
cards.sub: [ü-NUHR] · one, and the only singular one
cards.body: Une heure is one hour so the noun is singular. From two upward it is heures. Midi and minuit take neither, which is act two.

sections.title: The Word You Will Leave Off
sections.say: Four rows. The left column is what English hands you and the right is what French wants. Tap either for why.

detail.title: The noun is compulsory
detail.body: English lets the number stand alone and French does not. Il est huit is not a shorter way of saying it, it is an unfinished sentence. A listener waits for the rest rather than correcting you, which is why it survives.

detail.title: The only singular hour
detail.body: One hour, so heure has no s. Every other hour on the clock is plural. Said out loud the s changes nothing, so this is a writing habit rather than a sound, and it is the one place the noun looks different.

detail.title: Midi takes nothing at all
detail.body: No heures and no article. Il est midi heures is not said and neither is il est le midi. Midi and minuit are the two exceptions to the rule on the row above, and they are taught next rather than saved up.

rows.say: Il est huit heures et quart.

detail.title: French builds a time hour-first
detail.body: English puts the minutes in front and French hangs them off the back. Read a French time left to right and the hour always arrives before you find out what is being done to it. Translating in order is what produces quart huit heures.
detail.say: Il est huit heures et quart.

sections.title: One Hour Per Screen
sections.hint: Swipe. Say each one out loud before you move on.
sections.say: Twelve screens, one hour each. Say it out loud before you swipe, every time.

cards.label: 1 of 12
cards.body: one o'clock

cards.label: 2 of 12
cards.body: two o'clock

cards.label: 3 of 12
cards.body: three o'clock

cards.label: 4 of 12
cards.body: four o'clock

cards.label: 5 of 12
cards.body: five o'clock

cards.label: 6 of 12
cards.body: six o'clock

cards.label: 7 of 12
cards.body: seven o'clock

cards.label: 8 of 12
cards.body: eight o'clock

cards.label: 9 of 12
cards.body: nine o'clock

cards.label: 10 of 12
cards.body: ten o'clock

cards.label: 11 of 12
cards.body: eleven o'clock

cards.label: 12 of 12
cards.body: twelve hours

sections.title: Where The Hour Ends
sections.say: Read down each group. The hour never ends where its spelling says it does, and these are the three ways it moves.

groups.label: The ones that grow a Z
The ones that grow a T
One F becomes a V, and three just carry on

sections.title: Which One Changes Its Letter?
sections.say: One question, and it is the only genuine exception in the twelve.

check.q: One hour does not just add a sound before heures, it changes a letter it already had. Which?
check.why: neuf heures. The f is said as a v, so it is neu-VUHR and not neuf-UHR. Neuf does this before heures and before ans and nowhere else in the language, which is why it is worth knowing by name rather than by rule.

sections.title: Two That Collide
sections.say: One pair here is genuinely hard at speed. Slow the audio down before you answer.

lines.en: two o'clock
twelve hours
It's exactly two o'clock.
It's nine o'clock.

questions.q: Which two of the twelve are hardest to separate at speed?
questions.why: Both end in the same ZUHR and the opening consonant is the whole difference. At speed a d against a d-oo is very little, which is how somebody arrives ten hours early, and it is the one pair worth slowing an audio clip down for.

questions.q: Line four is neuf heures. What has happened to the f?
opts: It is said as a v
It is said as an f, as usual
questions.why: It is said as a v. This is the one hour that changes a letter it already had rather than growing a new sound, and neuf only does it in front of heures and ans.

questions.q: Why does every hour in this lesson run into the next word?
opts: Because heure begins with a vowel sound
questions.why: Heure opens on a written h that is never said, so the word begins on a vowel and the consonant in front of it has somewhere to go. That is why every one of the twelve links and none of them stands alone.

sections.title: The Two With No Number
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Two words that break the rule you just learned. They come now rather than later, because they break it in the same place.

cards.label: Noon
cards.head: No heures, no article
cards.body: Not il est midi heures and not il est le midi. Midi is the hour and the noun at once, so nothing else is wanted in front of it or behind it.

cards.label: Midnight
cards.head: The same, twelve hours later
cards.body: Minuit works exactly as midi does. Between them they cover both ends of the day, which is why douze heures is almost never a time of day.

cards.label: The one that reads wrong
cards.head: Midi is not the afternoon
cards.body: The word for afternoon has midi inside it, so a learner who has just met one misreads the other. Cet après-midi is this afternoon and has nothing to do with twelve.

cards.label: They still bend
cards.head: The quarters work on both
cards.body: Midi et quart, minuit et demi. Everything act three is about hangs off these two as readily as off a number. Only the noun is missing, not the rest of the clock.

sections.title: Four Ways To Bend An Hour
sections.frSub: Et quart, et demie, moins le quart
sections.say: Four phrases. Each one goes on the back of an hour, and one of them carries a word the other three do not.

items.fr: Il est trois heures et quart.
Il est huit heures et demie.
Il est sept heures moins le quart.
Il est cinq heures moins dix.

groups.label: The same hour, worked both ways

items.fr: Il est huit heures et quart.
Il est huit heures moins le quart.
Il est cinq heures et demie.

sections.title: Past On One Side, To On The Other
sections.say: A clock face has two halves and so does this. Left is past the hour, right is counting down to the next.

rows.say: Il est huit heures et quart. Il est huit heures moins le quart.

detail.title: Quarter past eight, quarter to eight
detail.body: Both name eight and they are half an hour apart. On the left you have gone past it. On the right you are counting down to it, so the hour named is the one still coming. That is the half a learner reads backwards.
detail.say: Il est huit heures et quart. Il est huit heures moins le quart.

rows.say: Il est cinq heures et demie. Il est cinq heures moins dix.

detail.title: Any number works on the right
detail.body: Moins takes a plain minute count as readily as it takes the quarter. Moins dix, moins vingt, moins cinq. The left half is the other way about: past the hour you have et quart and et demie and then you say the minutes plainly.
detail.say: Il est cinq heures moins dix.

detail.title: One of the four carries le
detail.body: Et quart has nothing in front of the quarter. Moins le quart has an article, and it is the only one of the four that does. There is no rule behind it, so learn it as one piece of sound.

detail.title: The exceptions take both halves
detail.body: Midi and minuit have no number and no noun and they still bend exactly like an hour. Only the word for hours is missing; everything on this table works on them unchanged.

detail.title: The half only goes one way
detail.body: Half past exists and half to does not. Thirty minutes before the hour is the same moment as thirty minutes after the one before it, so French says the earlier hour and et demie. There is no moins la demie to learn.

sections.title: The One That Carries Le
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Four cards on one small word. It is arbitrary, and that is exactly why it needs a screen.

cards.label: Three without
cards.head: Nothing in front of the number
cards.fr: et quart · et demie · moins dix
cards.body: Three of the four phrases put nothing between the joining word and what follows it. Read them together and the shape looks completely regular.

cards.label: One with
cards.head: And then this
cards.body: An article, in exactly one of the four, and no reason behind it. It is a fixed phrase. Say the three words as one piece and the question never arises.

cards.label: What you will write
cards.head: The regularised version
cards.body: A learner who has met et quart first generalises from it and drops the article. That is the most common written error in this lesson and nothing in speech corrects it, because it is a short unstressed word in the middle of a phrase.

cards.label: The tell
cards.head: Quart is a noun here
cards.body: Le quart is a thing, a quarter of something, and you have met it in the numbers unit. Moins le quart is minus the quarter. That is not a rule you can apply anywhere else, but it does make the le stop looking random.

sections.title: With, Or Without?
sections.say: One question, and it is the one this act exists for.

check.q: It is 7:45 and you are telling somebody the time. Which is right?
opts: Il est huit heures moins quart.
Il est huit heures moins le quart.
Il est sept heures moins le quart.
Il est huit heures et quart.
check.why: Quarter to eight, so the hour named is the one coming, and moins le quart is the one phrase of the four that carries an article. The third option is a quarter to seven, which is an hour earlier.

sections.title: Demie, Or Demi
sections.say: Four rows, and nothing here is audible. This one lives entirely on the page.

rows.say: Il est huit heures et demie.

detail.title: The e is there after an hour
detail.body: Half agrees with the thing it is half of, and that thing is heure. So after any numbered hour it is written demie, with an e. Eleven of the twelve take this form, so it is the one you will write most.
detail.say: Il est huit heures et demie.

detail.title: The e goes after noon
detail.body: Midi is masculine, so the e comes off. This is the trap: midi looks like it should take the feminine because every other time expression in the lesson does, and it does not. Nothing is audible, which is why it survives for years.

detail.title: Midnight behaves like noon
detail.body: Minuit takes the same masculine form, for the same reason and with the same silence. Learn the pair together rather than one at a time, because they are the only two words on the clock that do this.

rows.say: Elle a six ans et demi.

detail.title: The same rule off the clock
detail.body: An is masculine, so six ans et demi has no e either. That is worth seeing, because it shows this is agreement doing an ordinary job rather than a quirk of telling the time, and it is the same decision every time.
detail.say: Elle a six ans et demi.

sections.title: The Same Moment, Twice
sections.say: Read across, not down. Each row is one moment said two ways, and the only thing that changes is which clock you are on.

rows.say: Le film commence à huit heures et demie. Le film commence à vingt heures trente.

detail.title: At the cinema
detail.body: Le film commence à huit heures et demie. is what you say. Le film commence à vingt heures trente. is what is printed. Same moment, two registers. The printed one never takes et demie and the spoken one never runs past twelve.
detail.say: Le film commence à huit heures et demie. Le film commence à vingt heures trente.

rows.say: Le train part à quatre heures dix. Le train part à seize heures dix.

detail.title: On the departure board
detail.body: Le train part à quatre heures dix. is what you say. Le train part à seize heures dix. is what is printed. Same moment, two registers. The printed one never takes et demie and the spoken one never runs past twelve.
detail.say: Le train part à quatre heures dix. Le train part à seize heures dix.

rows.say: Le magasin ferme à six heures du soir. Le magasin ferme à dix-huit heures.

detail.title: On the shop door
detail.body: Le magasin ferme à six heures du soir. is what you say. Le magasin ferme à dix-huit heures. is what is printed. Same moment, two registers. The printed one never takes et demie and the spoken one never runs past twelve.
detail.say: Le magasin ferme à six heures du soir. Le magasin ferme à dix-huit heures.

rows.say: Le rendez-vous est à deux heures de l'après-midi. Le rendez-vous est à quatorze heures.

detail.title: In the diary
detail.body: Le rendez-vous est à deux heures de l'après-midi. is what you say. Le rendez-vous est à quatorze heures. is what is printed. Same moment, two registers. The printed one never takes et demie and the spoken one never runs past twelve.
detail.say: Le rendez-vous est à deux heures de l'après-midi. Le rendez-vous est à quatorze heures.

sections.title: Reading The Printed One
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Four cards, and then a timetable stops being a wall of numbers.

cards.label: The minutes
cards.head: Said as a plain number
cards.fr: Le film commence à vingt heures trente.
cards.sub: [vehⁿ-TUHR TRAHⁿT] · eight thirty in the evening
cards.body: Twenty hours, thirty. No et, no quart, no demie. The printed clock says the minutes the way you would read them off a display, and you already own every number it needs.

cards.label: The hours
cards.head: Thirteen to twenty-four
cards.fr: Le rendez-vous est à quatorze heures.
cards.body: Past midday the printed clock keeps counting. Quatorze is fourteen, which is two. Your numbers unit already gave you every one of these, so this is arithmetic rather than vocabulary.

cards.label: Where you meet it
cards.head: Anything with a schedule
cards.fr: Le musée est ouvert de neuf heures à dix-huit heures.
cards.sub: from nine to six in the evening
cards.body: Timetables, cinema listings, opening hours, tickets, appointment cards, official invitations. If it is printed rather than spoken, expect this one. Nobody says it in a café.

cards.label: Which half of the day
cards.head: Only the spoken clock needs it
cards.fr: Il est huit heures du soir.
cards.body: The spoken clock has twelve hours, so it adds du matin, de l'après-midi or du soir when it matters. The printed one has twenty-four and never needs to say which.

sections.title: Six Sentences You Will Produce
sections.say: Il est says the time. À books it. Six sentences an English speaker produces in their first month, one per screen.

errors.wrong: Saying « Il est huit » for it is eight.
errors.right: Saying « Il est huit heures » for it is eight.
errors.why: English throws the noun away and French cannot. This is the commonest error in the lesson and it is invisible to the ear: somebody who leaves the noun off has not said something wrong, they have stopped in the middle.

errors.wrong: Saying « Il est huit heures moins quart ».
errors.right: Saying « Il est huit heures moins le quart ».
errors.why: Three of the four phrases take no article and this one does. There is no rule behind it, so it cannot be reasoned back: it is a fixed phrase and the fix is to say all three words as one piece rather than assembling them.

errors.wrong: Saying « Le film commence à vingt heures et demie ».
errors.right: Saying « Le film commence à vingt heures trente ».
errors.why: Half of each clock. Past twelve you are on the printed one, and it says its minutes as a plain number. This is the sentence that marks a beginner in a station.

errors.wrong: Writing « Il est midi et demie ».
errors.right: Writing « Il est midi et demi ».
errors.why: Midi is masculine, so the half loses its e. Midi looks like it should take the feminine because every other time expression around it does. Nothing is audible here, which is why it lives for years in the writing of people who speak well.

errors.wrong: Answering « Il est à huit heures » when asked the time.
errors.right: Answering « Il est huit heures » when asked the time.
errors.why: Il est says the time. À books it. À plus an hour says when something happens, so this answers a question nobody asked. You read à in front of an hour far more often than il est, so it arrives first.

errors.wrong: Saying « Il est midi heures ».
errors.why: Midi is already the hour and the noun together, so nothing goes after it and nothing goes in front. This one comes from applying the rule you just learned correctly, which is why it is worth naming rather than assuming it away.

sections.title: Two Ways To Ask
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: One of these you memorise whole and one you can see inside. Both are worth having on your first day.

cards.label: The ordinary one
cards.head: Take it whole
cards.body: Four words, one shape, no parts to assemble. The machinery that makes this work is two units further on, so learn it the way you learned bonjour and come back for the grammar later.

cards.label: The transparent one
cards.head: This one you can see inside
cards.fr: Vous avez l'heure, s'il vous plaît ?
cards.sub: [voo-za-VAY LUHR] · do you have the time
cards.body: The verb you met a few lessons ago, with the hour as its object, and a rising voice at the end. Nothing here is hidden, and it is just as ordinary in the street as the first one.

cards.label: Who you are asking
cards.head: Tu, or vous
cards.sub: the same question, to somebody you know
cards.body: Vous avez l'heure to a stranger, tu as l'heure to a friend. Quelle heure est-il carries no register at all, which makes it the safe one when you are not sure.

cards.label: Asking about a plan
cards.head: À quelle heure, for when
cards.body: Put à in front and you have stopped asking the time and started asking about a schedule. À quelle heure ouvre le musée. That is the next mission, and the à is doing the same job it does there.

sections.title: À Books It
sections.say: Il est says the time. À books it. Five rows, and every one of them is about when rather than about now.

rows.say: Nous avons rendez-vous à dix heures.

detail.title: À plus the hour, and nothing else
detail.body: One small word turns a time into a plan. Nous avons rendez-vous à dix heures. The hour behind it is built exactly as it was in act one, so there is no second system to learn here, only a word in front.
detail.say: Nous avons rendez-vous à dix heures.

detail.title: Vers, for around
detail.body: Vers trois heures is around three, and it is what you say when you do not want to promise a minute. It replaces à rather than joining it, so there is never a vers à.

detail.title: Pile, and précises
detail.body: Pile goes after the hour and means on the dot. Précises does the same job in writing and on an invitation: à quatorze heures précises. Both say the time is not a suggestion.
detail.say: La réunion commence à quatorze heures précises.

detail.title: À l'heure, and en retard
detail.body: Être à l'heure is to be on time and être en retard is to be late. These are the two words attached to every appointment you make, and the second one is the reason the first matters.

rows.say: Le cours de français dure deux heures.

detail.title: The same word, a different question
detail.body: Le cours dure deux heures is how long it lasts, not when it starts. Same noun, and the sentence is answering a different question entirely. Une heure, un quart d'heure and une demi-heure are all lengths rather than times.

sections.title: Where You Will Say This
sections.say: Five situations you will be in this month, and the line each one wants.

cases.situation: Outside a shop with the shutters half down
Outside a museum, working out whether to wait
Arriving at a reception desk with a card in your hand
cases.fr: Bonjour, j'ai un rendez-vous à quatorze heures.
cases.en: Hello, I have an appointment at two o'clock.

cases.situation: Agreeing a time in a message, off a listing you just read
cases.fr: Ça marche, on se voit à dix-huit heures.
cases.en: Sounds good, we'll see each other at six.

cases.situation: Somebody stops you in the street with no watch on
cases.en: Excuse me, what time is it?

sections.title: The Card In The Cinema Window
sections.say: Every time in this passage is on one clock or the other. Tap any underlined phrase.
sections.text: The card taped inside the cinema window is printed, so every time on it runs past twelve. « Le film commence à vingt heures trente. » Under it somebody has written the week's other showing in biro, and the shop next door has its own notice up. « Le magasin ferme à dix-huit heures. » You are standing there working out whether you have time to eat first, and the man behind the counter reads the same card out loud to somebody on the phone. He does not say what is printed on it. « Le film commence à huit heures et demie. » Nothing on the card changed and nothing he said was different, which is the part worth noticing: one clock is what gets printed and the other is what gets spoken, and a French speaker moves between them without thinking about it. A woman comes out of the shop, sees you reading, and asks the one question everybody asks. « Excusez-moi, quelle heure est-il ? » You look at your phone and you have the answer, and it is not the one on the card.

glossary.note: The printed clock. Past twelve the hours keep counting, and the minutes are said as a plain number with no et.
The spoken clock, and the same moment. Twelve hours, and the half hangs off the back of the hour.
Eighteen hundred. On a shop door, because a printed notice never uses the spoken clock.
The frozen question. Four words, taken whole, and the grammar behind it is two units away.
Read this as a whole phrase. The verb behind it is not one you have been given yet.

questions.q: The card and the man behind the counter give the same time. Why do they not sound the same?
questions.a: They are on different clocks. The card is printed so it uses the twenty-four hour system and says vingt heures trente. He is speaking, so he uses the twelve hour one and says huit heures et demie. Neither is more correct and a French speaker moves between them without noticing.

questions.q: The shop notice says dix-huit heures. What would somebody say out loud instead?
questions.a: Six heures du soir. The spoken clock only has twelve hours, so it has to say which half of the day it means. The printed one has twenty-four and never needs to.

questions.q: Why is « vingt heures et demie » not in this passage anywhere?
questions.a: Because it takes half of each clock and neither system allows it. Past twelve you are on the printed clock, and the printed clock says its minutes as a plain number: vingt heures trente.

sections.title: The Clock, Banked
sections.say: Three decks. The twelve hours, the four phrases that bend them, and the words around an appointment.

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French out loud, noun and all, before you flip.

cards.back: Il est huit heures et demie.
cards.say: Il est huit heures et demie.

cards.front: it is a quarter to eight
cards.back: Il est huit heures moins le quart.
cards.say: Il est huit heures moins le quart.

cards.front: it is half past noon (watch the ending)

cards.back: Vous avez l'heure, s'il vous plaît ?
cards.say: Vous avez l'heure, s'il vous plaît ?

cards.front: we have an appointment at ten
cards.back: Nous avons rendez-vous à dix heures.
cards.say: Nous avons rendez-vous à dix heures.

cards.back: Le film commence à vingt heures trente.
cards.say: Le film commence à vingt heures trente.

cards.front: the film starts at half past eight (spoken)

cards.say: Le film commence à huit heures et demie.

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Five lines. Four of them hand you a word you must decide not to use, which is half the exercise.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: The twelve hours, then the phrases that bend them. The join between the number and the noun is what the mic is listening for.

sections.title: Booking It
sections.frSub: On se voit à quelle heure ?
sections.say: One exchange, and you hold up your half. Every turn turns on which clock the other person is using.
sections.setting: A message thread with Yannick, working out when to meet for a film he has read the listing for and you have not.

turns.ai: Salut ! Le film commence à vingt heures trente. Ça te va ?
turns.en: Hi! The film starts at 20:30. Does that work for you?
turns.user: Vingt heures trente, donc huit heures et demie ?
turns.userEn: Twenty thirty, so half past eight?

alts.fr: Huit heures et demie, oui, ça me va.
alts.en: Half past eight, yes, that works for me.

alts.fr: Donc à huit heures et demie ?

turns.ai: Oui, c'est ça. On se retrouve devant à huit heures et quart ?
turns.en: Yes, that is it. Shall we meet outside at a quarter past eight?
turns.user: Huit heures et quart, parfait. Je serai à l'heure.
turns.userEn: A quarter past eight, perfect. I will be on time.

alts.fr: Oui, à huit heures et quart devant le cinéma.
alts.en: Yes, at a quarter past eight outside the cinema.

alts.fr: Parfait, à huit heures et quart.
alts.en: Perfect, at a quarter past eight.

turns.ai: Super. Et le magasin à côté, il ferme à dix-huit heures je crois.
turns.en: Great. And the shop next door closes at 18:00 I think.
turns.user: Six heures du soir, donc c'est fermé. Tant pis.
turns.userEn: Six in the evening, so it is closed. Never mind.

alts.fr: À six heures du soir ? Alors c'est fermé.
alts.en: At six in the evening? Then it is closed.

alts.fr: Six heures, oui. On ira une autre fois.
alts.en: Six, yes. We will go another time.

turns.ai: Exactement. Tu as l'heure là, au fait ? Ma montre est arrêtée.
turns.en: Exactly. Do you have the time right now, by the way? My watch has stopped.
turns.user: Il est sept heures moins le quart.
turns.userEn: It is a quarter to seven.

alts.fr: Oui, il est sept heures moins le quart.
alts.en: Yes, it is a quarter to seven.

turns.ai: Ah, on a le temps alors. À tout à l'heure !
turns.en: Ah, we have time then. See you shortly!
turns.user: À tout à l'heure. Je ne serai pas en retard.
turns.userEn: See you shortly. I will not be late.

alts.fr: À huit heures et quart, alors.
alts.en: At a quarter past eight, then.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: Somebody stops you in the street. It is eight.
cards.back: Il est huit heures. Il est says the time. À books it.

cards.front: Why is « Il est huit » not an answer?
cards.back: The noun is compulsory in French. Without it the sentence has stopped rather than finished.
Il est midi. No heures and no article, because midi is both at once.

cards.front: Which hour changes a letter before heures?
cards.back: neuf heures. The f is said as a v, and only before heures and ans.

cards.front: The two hours easiest to confuse at speed.
cards.back: deux heures and douze heures. Same ending, one consonant apart.

cards.front: It is 8:15 and you are telling somebody.
cards.back: Il est huit heures et quart. No article on this one.
cards.say: Il est huit heures et quart.

cards.front: It is 7:45 and you are telling somebody.
cards.back: Il est huit heures moins le quart. The hour named is the one coming, and this one takes le.
cards.say: Il est huit heures moins le quart.

cards.front: You wrote « moins quart ». What is missing?
cards.back: The article. Moins le quart is the only one of the four phrases that carries one, and there is no rule behind it.

cards.front: A listing reads 20:30. What is printed on it?
cards.back: Le film commence à vingt heures trente. Minutes as a plain number, and never et demie.
cards.say: Le film commence à vingt heures trente.

cards.front: You say the same showing out loud.
cards.back: Le film commence à huit heures et demie. Twelve hours, and the half on the back.
cards.say: Le film commence à huit heures et demie.

cards.front: Why is « vingt heures et demie » wrong?
cards.back: It takes half of each clock. Past twelve you are on the printed one and it says its minutes plainly.
cards.say: Le film commence à vingt heures trente.

cards.back: Il est midi et demi. Midi is masculine, so the half loses its e.
Il est huit heures et demie. Heure is feminine, so the e is there.
cards.say: Il est huit heures et demie.

cards.front: You want to ask a stranger the time.
cards.back: Quelle heure est-il ? Four words, taken whole, no parts to assemble.

cards.front: The other way to ask, the one you can see inside.
cards.back: Vous avez l'heure ? The verb from a1.07, with the hour as its object.
cards.say: Vous avez l'heure, s'il vous plaît ?

cards.front: You are arranging to meet at ten.
cards.back: Nous avons rendez-vous à dix heures. Il est says the time. À books it.
cards.say: Nous avons rendez-vous à dix heures.

cards.front: You do not want to promise a minute.
cards.back: Vers trois heures. Around three, and it replaces à rather than joining it.

cards.front: The class lasts an hour. Is that a time?
cards.back: La classe dure une heure. Same noun, and it answers how long rather than when.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched one small word turn an answer into a schedule, learned the frame that every hour drops into and the noun English throws away, and met all twelve hours as sounds rather than as numbers, including the one that changes a letter. You have the four phrases that bend an hour and you know which of them carries an article for no reason at all. You have seen the same moment written on both clocks, side by side on one screen, which is the only place the rule against mixing them can actually be seen. And you can ask, two ways, and turn a time into a plan. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The frame
rounds.say: The shape every hour drops into.

questions.q: Somebody asks you the time and it is eight exactly. What do you say?
questions.why: The noun is compulsory and it is plural above one. The first option stops in the middle, the third answers a question about a schedule, and the fourth is the singular that only une heure takes.

questions.q: Fix this. « Il est sept. »
questions.why: English throws the noun away and French cannot. Nothing about this sounds wrong, which is the problem: a listener waits for the rest of the sentence rather than correcting you.

questions.q: What is the il in « Il est midi » pointing at?
questions.why: Nothing. French wants a subject in front of a verb even where there is nothing to put there, so il holds the seat. The verb is the one you already conjugate in full, so only the subject is unusual.

questions.q: Which of these is the only hour written in the singular?
questions.why: Une heure is one hour, so the noun has no s. Everything from two upward is plural. Midi is not an answer to this because it takes no noun at all.

rounds.label: The twelve
rounds.say: The hours, by ear.

questions.q: Listen. Which hour is it?
questions.why: Neuf heures, and the f is said as a v, so it comes out as neu-VUHR. That is why it can be mistaken for a word ending in -ve, and it is the only hour in the twelve that changes a letter it already had.

questions.q: Listen. Which hour is it?
questions.why: Douze heures. It and deux heures end in the same ZUHR and the opening is the whole difference, which is the pair that genuinely collides at speed and the reason to slow a clip down before answering.

questions.q: Why does every hour in this lesson run straight into the next word?
opts: It is a rule about plurals
Heure begins on a vowel sound
questions.why: The h of heure is written and never said, so the word starts on a vowel and the consonant in front of it has somewhere to go. That is what makes the join happen on all twelve rather than on some of them.

questions.q: Say what time it is when the clock reads nine exactly.
questions.why: The scored part is the join. Neuf heures is neu-VUHR with the f said as a v, and saying the two words apart is what makes an ordinary hour hard to understand.

rounds.label: Past and to
rounds.say: The four phrases, and the one with an article.

questions.q: It is 7:45 and you are telling somebody the time. Which is right?
opts: Il est sept heures et quart.
Il est huit heures moins le quart.
Il est sept heures moins le quart.
Il est huit heures moins quart.
questions.why: Counting down, so the hour named is the one still coming, which is eight. The last option drops the article, and moins le quart is the only one of the four phrases that carries one.

questions.q: Fix this. « Il est neuf heures moins quart. »
accept: Il est neuf heures moins le quart.
il est neuf heures moins le quart
questions.answer: Il est neuf heures moins le quart.
questions.why: The article is missing. Three of the four phrases take nothing, so generalising from et quart is exactly what produces this, and no rule will get it back for you: it is a fixed phrase.

questions.q: It is 3:15. Write the two words that go after « Il est trois heures ».
questions.why: Et quart, with nothing between et and quart. This is the half of the pair that takes no article, and it is the one a learner writes correctly and then copies onto the other.

questions.q: Which of these does French not say?
questions.why: Half past exists and half to does not, because thirty minutes before an hour is the same moment as thirty minutes after the one before it. French says the earlier hour and et demie, so there is nothing to learn on that side.

questions.q: Fix this. « Il est quart huit heures. »
accept: Il est huit heures et quart.
il est huit heures et quart
questions.answer: Il est huit heures et quart.
questions.why: French builds a time hour-first and hangs the rest off the back of it. English puts the minutes in front, so translating in order is what produces this, and waiting for the hour before you say anything is the habit that fixes it.

rounds.label: Two clocks
rounds.say: Which one you are on, and staying on it.

questions.q: Fix this. « Le film commence à vingt heures et demie. »
accept: Le film commence à vingt heures trente.
le film commence à vingt heures trente
questions.answer: Le film commence à vingt heures trente.
questions.why: Half of each clock. Past twelve you are on the printed one, and the printed one says its minutes as a plain number. This is the hybrid that marks a beginner in a station.

questions.q: A cinema listing reads 16:10. Write what somebody says out loud, starting with the hour.
questions.why: Speaking, so twelve hours. Seize heures dix is what is printed rather than said, and quatre heures moins dix would be ten to four, which is twenty minutes earlier.

questions.q: Where would you expect to read « à dix-huit heures » rather than hear it?
opts: On the phone to a friend
questions.why: Anything printed with a schedule on it: notices, timetables, listings, tickets, appointment cards. The twenty-four hour clock is what gets written down, and nobody uses it across a table.

questions.q: Why does the spoken clock sometimes add « du soir » and the printed one never does?
opts: The printed one uses it in writing instead
It only has twelve hours, so it has to say which half of the day
questions.why: Twelve hours cover half a day twice over, so six could be either. The printed clock counts to twenty-four and dix-huit heures can only be one moment, which is why it never needs to say more.

rounds.label: Demie, or demi
rounds.say: The ending nobody can hear.

questions.q: Fix this. « Il est midi et demie. »
questions.why: Midi is masculine, so the half loses its e. It looks like it should take the feminine because every other time expression around it does, and nothing in speech will ever tell you otherwise.

questions.q: Which of these is written correctly?
questions.why: Heure is feminine so the half takes an e after an hour. Minuit and midi are masculine and take demi with none, so the first and last are the wrong way round and the second is too.

questions.q: What does the half agree with in « six ans et demi »?
questions.why: An, which is masculine, so there is no e. Seeing it away from the clock is what shows this is ordinary agreement doing an ordinary job rather than a quirk of telling the time.

questions.q: Write the French for half past eleven, starting with « Il est ».
accept: Il est onze heures et demie.
il est onze heures et demie
questions.answer: Il est onze heures et demie.
questions.why: Eleven hours, feminine, so the half keeps its e. The noun is plural because it is above one, and neither of those is audible, which is why this is a writing question rather than a speaking one.

rounds.label: Telling, or booking
rounds.say: Which of the two jobs the sentence is doing.

questions.q: Somebody asks « Quelle heure est-il ? » and it is eight. Fix this answer. « Il est à huit heures. »
questions.why: Il est says the time. À books it. The à turns the answer into a statement about when something happens, which is not what was asked, so the question goes unanswered rather than answered wrongly.

questions.q: You are arranging to meet somebody at ten. Which is right?
opts: On se voit il est dix heures.
On se voit à dix heures.
On se voit est dix heures.
questions.why: À is the word that turns a time into a plan, and the hour behind it is built exactly as it was when you were telling the time. Nothing else changes, which is why this is one small word rather than a second system.

questions.q: Which question asks about a schedule rather than about now?
opts: À quelle heure ouvre le musée ?
questions.why: The à in front is doing the same job it does in an answer: it moves the question from what time it is to when something happens. The other three all ask for the time right now.

questions.q: Which of these is a length of time rather than a time of day?
opts: Il est deux heures et demie.
questions.why: Dure asks how long rather than when. The noun is the same word in all four and the sentence around it is answering a different question, which is worth noticing once so it never confuses you again.

questions.q: Write the French for « at half past nine », as you would say it to a friend.
questions.why: À books it, the hour comes first, and the half keeps its e because heure is feminine. Three of this lesson's rules in five words, and the join in neuf heures is the part to say out loud.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Five things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can say what time it is on all twelve hours plus the two that take no number, bend an hour four ways, read a printed timetable without converting it in your head, ask two different ways, and turn any of it into a plan. The last of those is one small word, and it is the same word that made the man outside the station ask you twice. Everything here is said out loud far more often than it is written, and the two things nobody can hear are the two you will be correcting longest.
points: Il est says the time. À books it. One word, and it decides which question you answered.
Heures never leaves. Il est huit is not a shorter sentence, it is an unfinished one.
Three of the four phrases take no article, and moins le quart takes one for no reason.
Two clocks, and they never borrow from each other. Vingt heures trente, never vingt heures et demie.
Demie after an hour, demi after midi and minuit, and neither is audible.

grammarAssumed: The numbers from one to a hundred, introduced in a1.02 and a1.27
The full present of être, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07
le, la and les in front of a noun, introduced in a1.04
The nine subject pronouns, introduced in a1.05
The tu and vous split, introduced in a1.01
grammarIntroduced: The impersonal il, as a subject that refers to nothing
il est plus a number plus heures, as the frame for telling the time
The obligatory noun heures, singular after une and plural above it
midi and minuit, which take neither the noun nor an article
et quart, et demie and moins plus a minute count, hung off the back of the hour
moins le quart, and that it is the only one of the four carrying an article
The agreement of demi with heure, midi and minuit
The twenty-four hour clock as a separate register, with minutes as a plain number
à plus a time, marking when something happens rather than what time it is
Quelle heure est-il and Vous avez l'heure, as fixed question chunks

lessons.reframe: Il est says the time. À books it.

errorTriggers.description: Leaves the noun off: « il est huit » for it is eight. The highest-frequency error in the lesson and inaudible, because the learner stops early rather than saying something wrong.
Says the hour and the noun apart, or reaches for the wrong one of deux and douze. Neuf heures is the one that changes a letter and the one most often said as written.
Writes « moins quart » without the article, generalising from et quart. The most common written error in act 3, and nothing in speech corrects it.
Takes half of each clock: « vingt heures et demie ». What meeting both systems without being told they are separate registers produces.
Writes « midi et demie » with the feminine, because every other time expression in the lesson is feminine and midi is not. Entirely inaudible.
Answers the time with a booking: « il est à huit heures ». The error the reframe exists to kill, and the one the opening scene turns on.

drills.title: Finish the sentence
drills.coach: The English is on the left and it stops where English stops. Say the French out loud and notice that it does not.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: It is six o'clock. Which is a whole sentence?
drills.why: The noun is compulsory and it is plural above one. The first stops in the middle and the third is the singular that only une heure takes.

drills.title: Where the hour ends
drills.coach: Say each one out loud before you sort it. The question is what you hear between the number and the noun, not what is written there, because nothing is written there at all.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: How does « neuf heures » come out?
drills.why: The f is said as a v. Neuf does this before heures and before ans and nowhere else, so it is worth knowing by name rather than looking for a rule behind it.

drills.title: With, or without
drills.coach: One of these four phrases carries an article and three do not. There is no rule to work it out from, so read each one and remember which pile it went in.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one is written the way French writes it?
drills.why: Moins le quart carries the article and et quart does not. The third puts one where it does not belong, which is what over-correcting after this drill produces.

drills.title: Which clock is this?
drills.coach: Look at the hour first. Anything past twelve is the printed clock and says its minutes as a plain number. Anything with et quart or et demie in it is the spoken one.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: A listing reads 20:30. Which of these is never said?
drills.why: It takes half of each clock. The first is what is printed and the second is what is spoken, and both are correct for the same moment.

drills.title: Where the e goes
drills.coach: Read what comes before the half, not the half itself. If it is an hour the e is there, and if it is midi, minuit or a year it is not.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is written correctly?
drills.why: Midi is masculine so the half has no e, and midi takes no noun after it either. The first is the trap and the third adds a word that never goes there.

drills.title: Telling, or booking
drills.coach: Read the situation on the left and say the French on the right. Every pair here turns on one small word, and it is the same word every time.
pairs: Somebody asks you the time. It is eight.
You are arranging to meet at eight.
Somebody asks you the time. It is noon.
Asking what time it is now.
À quelle heure ouvre le musée ?

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Somebody asks « Quelle heure est-il ? » What answers them?
drills.why: They asked what time it is, so the answer has no à in it. The other two both say when something happens, which is a different question and leaves theirs unanswered.

sheets.title: The twelve hours, in full
contains: What the liaison does to each

sections.title: The frame, and what never leaves it

rows.v: The whole frame. Only the number in the middle ever moves.
The only singular. Everything from two upward is heures.
No heures and no article. Both are the hour and the noun at once.
rows.say: Il est midi. Il est minuit.

rows.v: Which half of the day, when twelve hours are not enough. De l'après-midi for the afternoon.
rows.say: Il est sept heures du matin.

rows.v: On the dot. Pile after any hour in speech, précises in writing.
Around, when you do not want to promise a minute. Replaces à rather than joining it.

sections.title: Why every hour runs into the next word
sections.body: Heure is spelled with an h and the h is never said, so the word begins on a vowel. French does not like a consonant sitting in front of a vowel with a gap between them, so the consonant moves across and joins it. That is all a liaison is, and it is why not one of the twelve hours ends where its spelling says it does. Six of them grow a z that is written but silent on its own: the x of deux and dix, the s of trois, the z already in onze and douze. Two grow a t the same way, the t of sept and of huit, both silent when the word stands alone. Three simply carry on, because une, quatre and cinq end in a sound that was already going to be pronounced. And one is genuinely exceptional. Neuf ends in an f everywhere else in the language and says a v here, so neuf heures is neu-VUHR. It does the same thing in front of ans and nowhere else at all, which means there is no rule to derive it from and no other word it applies to. Learn that one by name. The practical consequence is worth stating plainly, because it is the difference between being understood and not: an English speaker reading these words says the number, stops, and then says heures, and a French listener hears two words that do not belong together rather than a time. Say the join and the whole thing lands.

sections.title: The same moment, both clocks
rows: Le film commence à huit heures et demie.
Le film commence à vingt heures trente.
Le train part à quatre heures dix.
Le train part à seize heures dix.
Le magasin ferme à six heures du soir.
Le magasin ferme à dix-huit heures.
Le rendez-vous est à deux heures de l'après-midi.

sections.title: The six errors, and which you can hear

rows.v: il est huit for il est huit heures. Audible, and the sentence stops rather than finishes.
moins quart for moins le quart. Audible, barely: it is one short unstressed word in the middle.
vingt heures et demie. Audible, and it is the one that marks a beginner in a station.
rows.say: Le film commence à vingt heures trente.

rows.v: midi et demie for midi et demi. Inaudible, so nothing ever corrects it.
il est à huit heures. Audible, and it answers a question nobody asked.
il est midi heures. Audible, and it comes from getting the main rule right.

sections.title: Why the two clocks never mix
sections.body: French runs two ways of saying a time and they are not formal and informal versions of one another. They are two systems with different hours and different minutes, and each is complete on its own. The spoken one has twelve hours and bends them with et quart, et demie and moins le quart, and because twelve hours cover half a day twice over it adds du matin, de l'après-midi or du soir when it matters which. The printed one runs to twenty-four, needs no such marking because dix-huit heures can only be one moment, and says its minutes as a plain number: vingt heures trente, seize heures dix, quatorze heures. It has no et quart and no moins le quart at all. A learner who meets both without being told they are separate takes the hours from one and the minutes from the other and produces vingt heures et demie, which is the single most recognisable beginner sentence in a French station. The fix is not a rule about which to use, because both are ordinary and a French speaker moves between them a dozen times a day without noticing. The fix is to decide which clock you are on before the sentence starts and finish on the same one. If the hour is above twelve you are on the printed clock and the minutes are a number. If it is twelve or below you are on the spoken one and the minutes can be a phrase. That is the whole of it, and it is checkable mid-sentence, which is what makes it usable rather than merely true.

heuresStays.title: The word English throws away
heuresStays.body: English says "it is eight" and drops the noun. French cannot: il est huit heures, with the word for hours still in it. There is no shorter version of this sentence, and il est huit is not a sentence at all. The trap is that nothing corrects it, because a learner who leaves it off simply stops early and the listener hears an unfinished line rather than a wrong one. Two smaller rules ride on the same word: une heure is singular because it is one, and everything from two upward is plural.

examples.note: One, so the noun is singular. It is the only hour that is.
Seven, so heures is plural, and it is still there.

hourFirst.title: French builds a time hour-first
hourFirst.body: English puts the minutes in front: quarter past eight, ten to five. French puts the hour first and hangs everything else off the back of it: huit heures et quart, cinq heures moins dix. Read a French time left to right and you always meet the hour before you find out what is being done to it. This is why a learner translating in order arrives at quart huit heures, and why waiting for the whole phrase before deciding what you heard is the habit worth building.

examples.note: Eight first, the quarter second. English says it the other way round.
Five first, and only then that you are taking ten off it.

noArticleExcept.term: et quart, but moins LE quart
noArticleExcept.title: One of the four carries an article
noArticleExcept.body: Et quart, et demie and moins dix take nothing in front of the quarter or the number. Moins le quart takes le, and it is the only one of the four that does. There is no rule behind this and inventing one will cost you later: it is a fixed phrase and it is worth learning as a single piece of sound rather than as three words. A learner who has generalised from et quart writes moins quart, which is the most common written error in this lesson.

examples.note: The article is there, and it belongs to this phrase alone.
The same shape one hour earlier, and no article at all.

twoClocks.title: The conversational one and the printed one
twoClocks.body: French runs two systems. The one you speak uses one to twelve and bends them with et quart, et demie and moins le quart. The one you read on a timetable, a cinema listing or a ticket uses thirteen to twenty-four and says the minutes as a plain number: vingt heures trente. They do not mix. Vingt heures et demie is the sentence that marks a beginner in a station, because it has taken half of each. Pick which clock you are on before you start the sentence and finish on the same one.

examples.note: The printed clock. Twenty hours, thirty, and no et anywhere.
The spoken clock. Eight, and a half hung off the back of it.

demiAgrees.title: The half agrees with what it follows
demiAgrees.body: Heure is feminine, so after an hour the half is written demie: huit heures et demie. Midi and minuit are masculine, so after either of them it is demi with no e: midi et demi. Nothing is audible here, which is why it survives in writing for years. The trap is that midi looks like it should take the feminine, because every other time expression in this lesson does, and it does not. The same masculine form turns up outside the clock: six ans et demi.

examples.note: After heure, which is feminine, so the e is there.
After midi, which is not, so the e is gone.

frozenQuestion.title: A question you memorise rather than build
frozenQuestion.body: This is the ordinary way to ask, and the machinery that makes it work is two units further on than you are. Take it whole, the way you took bonjour: four words, one shape, no parts to assemble. Vous avez l'heure ? is the second form and that one you can see inside, because it is the verb you met a few lessons back with the hour as its object. One memorised and one transparent is both the accurate position and the useful one, and you need an answer to this on your first day.

examples.note: The frozen one. Say it as a single piece.
The transparent one, built on a verb you already have.

nobodyIl.title: There is no he in il est huit heures
nobodyIl.body: You learned il as he, and here it points at nothing at all. Nothing in the room is eight o'clock. French wants a subject in front of a verb even when there is nothing to put there, so it uses il as a placeholder and the sentence means what it would mean with no subject in English. The verb itself is one you already have in full, so this is a small thing to accept rather than a new form to learn: only the subject is strange, and it is strange in exactly one way.

examples.note: No he, no it, nothing. The il is holding a seat.
The same placeholder with the verb you already conjugate.

recorded.desc: THE TWELVE HOURS AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, IN CLOCK ORDER FROM UNE HEURE TO DOUZE HEURES, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE SPEED. Twelve hours recorded in twelve sessions are twelve performances, and the learner is memorising a SEQUENCE of JOINS: any drift in pace between them teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read them straight through with an even beat, then again slowly in the same take. EVERY ONE IS ONE PHONETIC WORD. There must be no gap, no glottal stop and no breath between the number and heures on any of the twelve: a reader who separates them is teaching the error this lesson exists to stop. NEUF HEURES IS RECORDED IN ISOLATION AS WELL, AND SLOWLY, because the f becoming a v is the one exception in the set and it is the card a learner will replay. DEUX HEURES AND DOUZE HEURES GO ADJACENTLY IN THE SAME TAKE, at natural pace and not slowed, because that is the pair the ear actually fails on and slowing it removes the difficulty being taught.

The frame, and the pair the lesson turns on. « Il est midi » immediately followed by « Il est à midi » BY THE SAME VOICE AT THE SAME PACE IN ONE TAKE, so the only thing the learner hears is the à. Recorded apart they compare two performances instead of two meanings and the whole teaching is lost. Do not lean on the à to make it clearer: it is unstressed in ordinary speech and a learner who hears it emphasised will never catch it at conversational speed. Then the same pair on eight: « Il est huit heures » against « Il est à huit heures ». SEPARATELY, and this is the other half of this recording: « il est huit » read as a complete utterance and then « il est huit heures », so the learner hears what stopping early sounds like. Read the truncated one PLAINLY and without a trailing rise, because a reader who performs it as obviously unfinished removes the reason it is dangerous.

The four phrases that bend an hour. « et quart » and « moins le quart » ADJACENTLY IN THE SAME TAKE, because the article is the whole difference between them and two separate recordings are two performances. The le is short, unstressed and easy to swallow, and it MUST NOT be leaned on: the learner has to hear it as it really sounds, which is almost nothing, or they will not recognise it in the wild and will not miss it when it is gone. Then all four in order, then each worked on a real hour. « il est midi » and « il est minuit » ALSO GO ADJACENTLY IN THE SAME TAKE: they are close in sound, opposite in meaning, and the difference is one syllable in the middle.

The two clocks, and this is the recording the whole of act 4 rests on. THE SAME MOMENT IN BOTH SYSTEMS, ONE TAKE PER PAIR, spoken half first and printed half second with a clear beat between them: « huit heures et demie » then « vingt heures trente », and the same for the other three pairs. The only thing changing is the register, so the voice, the pace and the emphasis must not change with it. In particular do NOT read the printed clock in an announcement voice: it is what an ordinary person says reading a listing out loud, not a station tannoy, and performing it as official teaches a difference in formality that is not the difference being taught. All four pairs are complete sentences rather than bare times, because the sentence is what makes them the same event.
clipIds: Le film commence à huit heures et demie.
Le film commence à vingt heures trente.
Le train part à quatre heures dix.
Le train part à seize heures dix.
Le magasin ferme à six heures du soir.
Le magasin ferme à dix-huit heures.
Le rendez-vous est à deux heures de l'après-midi.
Le rendez-vous est à quatorze heures.

recorded.desc: The two questions and the booking frame. « Quelle heure est-il ? » read as ONE PHONETIC WORD with no break between quelle and heure, because it is taught as a frozen chunk and a reader who separates the words invites the learner to parse it. « Vous avez l'heure ? » on a rising intonation, and « Tu as l'heure ? » after it in the same take so the register shift is audible against a fixed voice. Then the booking rows: à, vers and pile on real hours, with vers read genuinely casually, since its whole job is to sound like somebody not committing to a minute.
clipIds: Vous avez l'heure, s'il vous plaît ?

recorded.desc: The six traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them so the learner hears a difference rather than a correction. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically: three of the six are real French that means something else, and a performance that marks them as errors removes the reason they are dangerous. « Il est à huit heures » is a perfectly good sentence out of context, which is the point of the fifth one. « Il est midi et demie » and « il est midi et demi » ARE THE SAME SOUND and must be read identically: that pair exists to demonstrate that the ear cannot settle it, so any audible difference between the two takes would be actively false.

The opening scene, French only, two voices. The stranger is a man in a hurry who is not annoyed and never becomes annoyed: he asks, does not get an answer he can use, and simply asks again. Any edge on the second ask turns the scene into a telling-off and the teaching is lost, because the whole point is that nobody is upset and nobody corrects anybody. His last line (« Midi ! Merci, je suis en retard. ») is already half walking away and should sound like it. The learner's two attempts are the same voice, the same pace and the same confidence: the second is not a sheepish correction, it is the same person saying a slightly different sentence.
clipIds: Midi ! Merci, je suis en retard.

lessons.title: Les couleurs
lessons.intro: Twelve colours, and the first describing word in this course that changes shape depending on what it is describing. This is how you name a colour, make it match the thing, know which endings you will ever hear, and leave the two that were something else alone.

say.text: One post, two colours, and only one of them wanted an ending. Watch which.

setting.place: A phone, a pile of clothes on the bed, and a neighbourhood selling group

beats.text: You are clearing out a wardrobe, and two things are going in the neighbourhood group where everybody sells everything.
A green jacket and a pair of brown shoes. You have the photos. All that is left is to say what colour they are.

beats.speaker: Your post
beats.stage: That one is right, and it took an ending because the jacket is feminine.

beats.prompt: Now the shoes. They are brown. Which line goes in the post?

options.en: the one that follows the pattern
the one that leaves the colour alone

followUp.works: Yes, and it looks wrong precisely because everything else in the post took an ending. Watch what the other one does.
followUp.breaks: That is the pattern you just used on the jacket, applied again. Watch what a reader does with it.

beats.speaker: Your post
beats.en: (The shoes are brown, with an ending that should not be there)

beats.speaker: Salomé
beats.fr: Les marrons ? Pardon, tu vends des chaussures ou des marrons ?
beats.en: The chestnuts? Sorry, are you selling shoes or chestnuts?
beats.stage: She is teasing, and she is also not entirely joking. Des marrons is a bag of chestnuts.

beats.heading: The one letter a French reader notices
beats.body: Every other colour in your post took an ending, so adding one here looked like being careful. It is the one colour that must not have it, because marron is a chestnut being used as a colour, and the chestnut keeps its own shape.

wrong.en: The shoes are brown, with an s that turns the colour back into a nut

beats.coach: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. Both lines sound identical, which is why only a reader ever catches it.

beats.speaker: Salomé
beats.fr: Ah, les chaussures ! Je les prends. Et la veste verte aussi.
beats.en: Ah, the shoes! I will take them. And the green jacket too.
beats.stage: Both items sold, in one message, and nothing else about the post changed.

beats.text: One colour took an ending and one refused it, and knowing which is which is the whole of this lesson.

closing.text: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. That sentence is the next twenty-five minutes.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the fourth is the one people get wrong for years.

goals.s: The set you will actually use, each one attached to something you already know the word for.

goals.t: Make the colour match the thing
goals.s: Four shapes for most colours, and a way of working out which one without guessing.

goals.t: Know which endings you can hear
goals.s: Some of them change the sound and most of them do not, and knowing which is which stops you listening for something that is not there.
Not as two exceptions to memorise, but as one idea that also covers every colour made of two words.

sections.title: The Word That Changes Shape
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Four cards before any colour, because this idea decides how you use all twelve of them.

cards.label: What you already have
cards.head: Things have a gender
cards.body: You met this already: every thing in French is either the un kind or the une kind, and the small word in front follows it. A bag is one, a jacket is the other, and there is nothing about either object that explains why.

cards.label: What is new
cards.head: The describing word follows too
cards.fr: Mon sac est vert. · Ma veste est verte.
cards.body: This is new, and nothing before now has asked it of you. The colour changes shape to match the thing it describes. Same colour, same sentence, and the only reason the second grew an e is that a jacket is the une kind.

cards.label: Where it sits
cards.head: After the thing, not before
cards.sub: She is wearing a green skirt.
cards.body: English puts the colour first and French puts it after. Une jupe verte, the skirt then its colour. That holds for every colour you will meet, so it is worth getting used to now rather than translating word by word and rearranging afterwards.

cards.label: What is actually hard
cards.head: Not the twelve names
cards.body: Twelve short words is an afternoon. Deciding which shape the colour takes is what will still be catching you in a year, and two of the twelve refuse to change at all. Colours agree. Things that became colours do not.

sections.title: Twelve, One At A Time
sections.hint: Swipe. Say each one out loud before you move on.
sections.say: Twelve screens, one colour each. Say it out loud before you swipe.

cards.label: 1 of 12
cards.body: red.

cards.label: 2 of 12
cards.body: blue.

cards.label: 3 of 12
cards.body: green.

cards.label: 4 of 12
cards.body: yellow.

cards.label: 5 of 12
cards.body: black.

cards.label: 6 of 12
cards.body: white.

cards.label: 7 of 12
cards.body: grey.

cards.label: 8 of 12
cards.body: pink.

cards.label: 9 of 12
cards.body: orange.

cards.label: 10 of 12
cards.body: purple.

cards.label: 11 of 12
cards.body: brown.

cards.label: 12 of 12
cards.body: beige.

sections.title: A Colour On A Thing
sections.hint: Twelve things you can already name.
sections.say: The same twelve, this time stuck to something. The colour comes after the thing, every time.

cards.label: red
cards.head: rouge
cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. This one already ends in an e, so the feminine asks nothing new of it.

cards.label: blue
cards.head: bleu
cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. Notice the ending: it is there because of the thing, not because of the colour.

cards.label: green
cards.head: vert
