cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. Notice the ending: it is there because of the thing, not because of the colour.

cards.label: yellow
cards.head: jaune
cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. This one already ends in an e, so the feminine asks nothing new of it.

cards.label: black
cards.head: noir
cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. Notice the ending: it is there because of the thing, not because of the colour.

cards.label: white
cards.head: blanc
cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. Notice the ending: it is there because of the thing, not because of the colour.

cards.label: grey
cards.head: gris
cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. Notice the ending: it is there because of the thing, not because of the colour.

cards.label: pink
cards.head: rose
cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. This one already ends in an e, so the feminine asks nothing new of it.

cards.label: orange
cards.head: orange
cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. This is one of the two that never changes shape, whatever it is stuck to.

cards.label: purple
cards.head: violet
cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. Notice the ending: it is there because of the thing, not because of the colour.

cards.label: brown
cards.head: marron
cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. This is one of the two that never changes shape, whatever it is stuck to.

cards.label: beige
cards.head: beige
cards.body: The thing first, then the colour. This one already ends in an e, so the feminine asks nothing new of it.

sections.title: Four Groups, Not Twelve Rules
sections.say: The twelve, split by what the feminine does. Every group is a real group, so the split is worth remembering.

check.q: These four already end in an e. What does the feminine add?
check.why: Nothing. A colour already ending in e is the same word for either kind of thing: un sac rouge, une veste rouge. Four of the twelve are free this way, which is worth knowing before you start worrying about the other eight.

check.q: All four add an e for the feminine. On how many of them can you HEAR it?
check.why: Two. Vert and gris end in a sleeping consonant that the e wakes up, so verte and grise sound different from their plain forms. Bleu and noir end in a vowel sound already, so bleue and noire are identical to bleu and noir.

check.q: Blanc does not become blance. What is the feminine?
check.why: blanche. The c at the end turns into a ch, which no other colour does, and you hear it clearly. Violet is the other one in this group and it doubles its t: violette, not violete.

check.q: Why do these two never change?
opts: They are both borrowed from English
They were both something else before they were colours
They are too short to take an ending
They are irregular and have to be memorised
check.why: A marron is a chestnut and une orange is a fruit. Both are things that got used as colours, and a thing borrowed this way keeps the shape it had. That is one idea rather than two exceptions, and it covers the two-word colours too.

sections.title: One Colour, Four Shapes
sections.hint: The same colour on four different things.
sections.say: One bag, one jacket, then more than one of each. Only the ending moves.

cards.label: one masculine thing
cards.head: vert
cards.body: The plain form, and the t at the end is silent.

cards.label: one feminine thing
cards.head: verte
cards.body: The noun is feminine, so the colour adds an e. Here you HEAR it: the sleeping t wakes up.

cards.label: more than one, masculine
cards.head: verts
cards.body: The s is written and never said. This is the same sound as the singular.

cards.label: more than one, feminine
cards.head: vertes
cards.body: Feminine and plural, so both endings are there. It sounds exactly like the singular verte.

cards.label: the whole idea
cards.head: The thing decides
cards.fr: Mon sac est vert. → Mes vestes sont vertes.
cards.sub: from one masculine thing to several feminine ones
cards.body: Nothing about the colour changed between those four sentences. The bag became a jacket and one became several, and the colour followed each time. That is the whole mechanism, and it works the same way on every colour that changes at all.

cards.label: one sentence, both shapes
cards.head: The only thing that changed is the noun
cards.fr: Mon sac est noir et ma veste est noire.
cards.sub: [NWAR] · [NWAR] · My bag is black and my jacket is black.
cards.body: One sentence, one colour, two shapes of it, and the only difference between them is which thing is being described. Noir and noire also sound exactly the same, so this is a difference you can only see.

sections.title: The Same Three Colours, Four Ways
sections.say: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. Tap any cell to hear it. The bottom row never moves.

detail.title: vert: four shapes
detail.body: Mon sac est vert. Ma veste est verte. Mes sacs sont verts. Mes vestes sont vertes. Four things and four spellings. You can hear the feminine here: the t at the end wakes up. You cannot hear either plural.
detail.say: Mon sac est vert. Ma veste est verte. Mes sacs sont verts. Mes vestes sont vertes.

detail.title: bleu: four shapes
detail.body: Mon sac est bleu. Ma veste est bleue. Mes sacs sont bleus. Mes vestes sont bleues. Four things and four spellings. You can hear none of it. All four of these sound exactly the same out loud.
detail.say: Mon sac est bleu. Ma veste est bleue. Mes sacs sont bleus. Mes vestes sont bleues.

detail.title: marron: one shape
detail.body: Mon sac est marron. Ma veste est marron. Mes sacs sont marron. Mes vestes sont marron. Four different things and one spelling, because marron was a chestnut before it was a colour. Nothing you can do to the noun will make this word change.
detail.say: Mon sac est marron. Ma veste est marron. Mes sacs sont marron. Mes vestes sont marron.

sections.title: Which Shape Does It Take?
sections.say: Four things, four decisions. Say the whole phrase out loud before you check.

items.en: She is wearing a green skirt.

check.q: All three describe one feminine thing. What do all three colours have in common?
check.why: All three ended in an e, because the thing being described was the une kind. Two of them also changed sound when the e arrived, which is what the next mission is about.

check.q: Two of these carry both an e and an s. Why does the first carry only an s?
opts: rouge already ends in e, so there is nothing to add
it is a mistake in the sentence
check.why: rouge already ends in an e, so the feminine asks nothing of it and only the plural s gets added. Noires and blanches needed both, because noir and blanc do not end in e on their own.

items.en: The brown table comes from Italy.

check.q: One feminine thing and two plurals. How many times did marron change?
check.why: Not once. A feminine table, plural shoes and plural eyes, and the colour is spelled identically in all three. This is what the rule looks like in real sentences rather than in a table.

groups.label: The one that doubles a letter

items.fr: Le ballon des enfants est violet.
Les fleurs des champs sont violettes.

check.q: Violet becomes violette in the feminine. What happened to the t?
opts: It doubled, and now you say it
check.why: It doubled and woke up. Violet ends in a silent t, and the feminine e both doubles it in writing and makes it pronounced. Violete would be wrong twice over: wrong spelling and wrong sound.

sections.title: Now Without The Table
sections.say: Same decisions, nothing to look at. This is the one that tells you whether it landed.

check.q: Une veste, and the colour is orange. What do you write?
check.why: orange, unchanged. It is a fruit being used as a colour, so it keeps the shape it has as a fruit, and a feminine noun in front of it changes nothing at all.

check.q: You hear somebody say « mes vestes sont bleues » out loud. What tells you it is plural?
opts: nothing in the colour, only the words before it
the way the speaker stresses the ending
check.why: Nothing in the colour. Bleu, bleue, bleus and bleues are one identical sound, so mes and vestes are carrying the whole message. This is why listening cannot tell you which ending to write.

check.q: La porte, and the colour is blanc. What do you write?
check.why: blanche. It is the one colour whose feminine changes more than the ending, and unlike most of the others you can hear it: the silent c becomes a ch you say out loud.

check.q: You are describing two feminine things and the colour is bleu. What do you write?
check.why: bleues. Feminine, so an e, and more than one, so an s, in that order. It sounds exactly like bleu, so there is nothing in the audio to help you and the decision has to come from the thing being described.

sections.title: Can You Hear The Difference?
sections.say: Seven pairs. On five of them something changes and on two nothing does. Slow the audio down.

lines.en: you hear a difference: the t at the end wakes up
you hear a difference: the s wakes up as a z
you hear a difference: the c turns into a ch
you hear a difference: the t wakes up, and the spelling doubles it
you hear a difference: the nasal collapses into a plain n
these two are the same sound
these two are the same sound

questions.q: Two of those seven pairs are the same sound twice. Which two?
opts: none of them, all seven differ
questions.why: bleu / bleue and noir / noire. Both end in a vowel sound already, so there is no sleeping consonant for the feminine e to wake up and nothing at all changes. The other five all bring a letter back to life.

questions.q: On the five pairs where you DO hear something, what is making the sound?
opts: The e itself is being pronounced
A consonant that was silent is now being said
The speaker is stressing the ending
questions.why: The consonant. The e is not itself a sound: it stops the letter in front of it being last in the word, so that letter gets pronounced again. Vert hides its t and verte says it, which is what the silent letters lesson showed you.

questions.q: None of those seven pairs was a plural. Why not?
opts: Plurals were covered in an earlier lesson
The plural s is never pronounced, so there would be nothing to hear
The recording only had singular forms available
questions.why: There is nothing to hear. The plural s on a colour is silent without exception, so vert and verts are one sound and an ear question on them would be asking you to hear something that is not in the recording at all.

sections.title: Heard, Or Only Written
sections.say: Tap both cells in a row and listen. Five rows change and two do not.

detail.title: vert → verte
detail.body: [VEHR] becomes [VEHRT], so the t at the end wakes up. The letter sat there silently in the plain form and the e behind it brought it back. Same mechanism as the silent letters lesson.

detail.title: gris → grise
detail.body: [GREE] becomes [GREEZ], so the s wakes up as a z. The letter sat there silently in the plain form and the e behind it brought it back. Same mechanism as the silent letters lesson.

detail.title: blanc → blanche
detail.body: [BLAHⁿ] becomes [BLAHⁿSH], so the c turns into a ch. The letter sat there silently in the plain form and the e behind it brought it back. Same mechanism as the silent letters lesson.

detail.title: violet → violette
detail.body: [vyoh-LEH] becomes [vyoh-LET], so the t wakes up, and the spelling doubles it. The letter sat there silently in the plain form and the e behind it brought it back. Same mechanism as the silent letters lesson.

detail.title: brun → brune
detail.body: [BRUHⁿ] becomes [BRÜN], so the nasal collapses into a plain n. The letter sat there silently in the plain form and the e behind it brought it back. Same mechanism as the silent letters lesson.

detail.title: bleu → bleue
detail.body: [BLUH] becomes [BLUH]. Not a typo: the two are one sound, and the e is written and never said. No way to hear which one somebody used, and no amount of practice will change that.

detail.title: noir → noire
detail.body: [NWAR] becomes [NWAR]. Not a typo: the two are one sound, and the e is written and never said. No way to hear which one somebody used, and no amount of practice will change that.

sections.title: The Ending Nobody Can Hear
sections.hint: Four cards about the half of this that is invisible.
sections.say: The plural is never pronounced. Not quietly: never. This card is here so you stop listening for it.

cards.label: The plural s
cards.head: Written, never said
cards.fr: Mon sac est vert. · Mes sacs sont verts.
cards.body: One bag and several bags, and the colour is the same sound in both. The s exists only on the page. This is true of every colour without exception, so there is nothing to learn here beyond knowing not to listen for it.

cards.label: And with the feminine too
cards.head: Still nothing
cards.fr: Ma veste est verte. · Mes vestes sont vertes.
cards.body: One jacket and several jackets. Verte and vertes are one sound, exactly as vert and verts were. So of the four shapes a colour takes, your ear can separate at most two of them, and on some colours it cannot separate any.

cards.label: All four the same
cards.head: bleu, bleue, bleus, bleues
cards.body: Bleu is the extreme case. Four different spellings, one sound, and nothing in any recording that could tell them apart. A native speaker writing this sentence is working it out from the jacket, not from what they heard.

cards.label: What this means for you
cards.head: You will not hear your mistakes
cards.body: If you have been slowing recordings down to catch these endings, stop. The information is not in the sound, and concluding your listening is bad would be the wrong lesson. Work the ending out from the thing, then write it. Everybody does.

sections.title: The Fruit And The Colour
sections.say: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. Left is the fruit doing its ordinary job. Right is the same word used as a colour.

detail.title: The same word, two jobs
detail.body: On the left it is a fruit you could eat. On the right it is only telling you the colour of a skirt. Same word, two jobs, and the endings reach it in one job and not the other.

detail.title: More than one, both ways
detail.body: Le client demande le prix des oranges. Several fruits, so oranges takes an s. Elle aime les fleurs orange. Several flowers, and the colour takes nothing: the flowers are what is plural, not the oranges.
detail.say: Le client demande le prix des oranges. Elle aime les fleurs orange.

rows.say: Cette orange est bien mûre. Les rideaux sont orange.

detail.title: The proof, in one sentence
detail.body: Cette orange est bien mûre. Look at what happens beside the fruit: mûre took an e, because that is what describing words do here. So orange is not a word French refuses to touch. It is the thing being described.

sections.title: Marron Is A Chestnut
sections.hint: The same idea, on the colour from the opening scene.
sections.say: Four cards, and the last one is the sentence that cost you a sale at the start of this lesson.

cards.label: What it was first
cards.head: A nut, then a colour
cards.body: Un marron is a chestnut you can hold. Somebody used the word for the colour of one, it stuck, and the word never stopped being a nut. That is the entire explanation, and it is why the ending rules do not reach it.

cards.label: On a feminine thing
cards.head: Still marron
cards.sub: The brown table comes from Italy.
cards.body: La table is the une kind, so a colour like vert would be verte here. Marron is not, and it does not become marronne, which is not a word. The thing being described has no effect on it at all.

cards.label: On several things
cards.head: Still marron
cards.body: Several shoes, and the colour still takes nothing. Compare that with les chaussures rouges, where the same shoes made rouge take an s. Same noun, same sentence shape, and only one of the two colours moved.

cards.label: The one that got you
cards.head: Never marrons
cards.body: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. Adding the s here is the most noticeable written error in the lesson, because des marrons is a real thing and it is a bag of chestnuts. Nobody hears it and every reader sees it.

cards.label: And two-word colours, free
cards.head: vert pomme, vert foncé
cards.fr: Les murs sont vert pomme. Ses yeux sont vert foncé.
cards.body: Both describe plural things and neither colour moved. A colour built from two words has stopped being a plain colour, the same way marron is really a nut, so the same rule reaches it.

sections.title: Five Traps
sections.say: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. Five things an English speaker writes in their first month, one per screen.

errors.wrong: Writing « des chaussures marrons ».
errors.why: The highest-value one in the lesson. Marron is a chestnut used as a colour, so it keeps the shape it had as a nut. Nobody will hear the s and every French reader will see it, which is why this one survives for years.

errors.wrong: Writing « une jupe vert ».
errors.why: The colour has to match the thing, and a skirt is the une kind. This one you can also hear: verte says its final t and vert does not, so leaving the e off changes the sound as well as the spelling.

errors.wrong: Writing « une robe orangée » for an orange dress.
errors.why: Orangée exists and means something closer to orange-ish, so this is not simply wrong, it is a different word. The colour orange itself never changes, because it is the fruit being borrowed.

errors.wrong: Writing « une porte blance ».
errors.why: Blanc is the one colour whose feminine changes more than the ending: the silent c becomes a ch you pronounce. Blance is not a word and does not sound like anything, so this one gets noticed immediately.

errors.wrong: Writing « des yeux verts foncés ».
errors.why: Once a colour is built from two words it stops changing, so neither half takes an ending. This looks like being careful twice over, and it is the same instinct that puts the s on marron.

sections.title: The Lost Property Board
sections.say: Four notices, and the colour is the only word doing any work in any of them.
sections.text: The lost property board by the pool entrance is the only place in the building where everybody writes in full sentences, because a colour is the only thing separating one lost jacket from another. « La veste verte est à moi. » That one has been there three weeks and nobody has claimed it, which is either very sad or means the owner has moved away. Underneath it somebody has pinned a note about a bag, and they have been careful with it. « Mon sac est marron. » No ending on the colour, which is right, and it is the detail that tells you the writer has been here a while. A third note is about shoes, and whoever wrote it added an s to the colour the way you would to anything else. « Les chaussures sont marrons. » Nobody has corrected it, nobody will, and the shoes will find their owner regardless, because the s changes nothing you can hear. The last one is the shortest and the only one with a phone number on it. « Les gants sont violets. »

glossary.note: A jacket is the une kind, so the colour took an e. You can hear this one: verte says its t.
No ending, and that is correct. Marron never changes, whatever it is describing.

glossary.en: are brown (with an ending that should not be there)
glossary.note: The s should not be here. It is inaudible, so only a reader ever catches it.
Gloves are masculine and plural, so violet takes an s. The s is silent, as every plural s is.

questions.q: Two of the four notices are about brown things. What is different about how they are written?
questions.a: The bag note leaves marron with no ending, which is correct. The shoes note adds an s. Marron is a chestnut being used as a colour and keeps the shape it had as a nut, so it never takes an ending no matter how many shoes there are.

questions.q: Could you tell the two brown notices apart if somebody read them out loud to you?
questions.a: No. The s on marrons is silent, exactly like every other plural s on a colour, so the two sentences are identical in sound. This is why the error survives: nobody hears it, so nobody corrects it.

questions.q: The first and last notices both have endings on the colour. Why are they different endings?
questions.a: The jacket is one feminine thing, so verte takes an e. The gloves are several masculine things, so violets takes an s. The ending comes from the thing being described, not from the colour.

sections.title: The Colours, Banked
sections.say: Three decks. The twelve names, the feminines worth knowing, and the two that never move.

cards.en: vert → verte, and you hear it
gris → grise, and you hear it
blanc → blanche, and you hear it
violet → violette, and you hear it
brun → brune, and you hear it

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French out loud, ending and all, before you flip.

cards.front: My bag is black and my jacket is black.
cards.back: Mon sac est noir et ma veste est noire.
cards.say: Mon sac est noir et ma veste est noire.

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Five lines. On four of them the ending you write is one you cannot hear, and on two of them there is no ending at all.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: The twelve, the four feminines and the whole grid. Half of these sound identical to each other, which is the point.

sections.title: Selling The Rest Of It
sections.say: One exchange, and you hold up your half. Every turn turns on which shape the colour takes.
sections.setting: The same neighbourhood group, a week later. Salomé is back, and this time she wants the rest of the wardrobe.

turns.ai: Salut ! Tu vends encore des choses ? Je cherche une veste.
turns.en: Hi! Are you still selling things? I am looking for a jacket.
turns.user: Oui. Ma veste est verte.
turns.userEn: Yes. My jacket is green.

alts.en: Yes, I have a green jacket.

turns.ai: Parfait. Et le sac sur la photo, il est de quelle couleur ?
turns.en: Perfect. And the bag in the photo, what colour is it?
turns.user: Mon sac est marron.
turns.userEn: My bag is brown.

turns.ai: Marron, d'accord. Et tu as des chaussures aussi ? De quelle couleur ?
turns.en: Brown, alright. And do you have shoes as well? What colour?
turns.user: Les chaussures sont marron.
turns.userEn: The shoes are brown.

turns.ai: Et les vestes, il y en a d'autres ? Bleues, peut-etre ?
turns.en: And the jackets, are there others? Blue ones, maybe?
turns.user: Oui, mes vestes sont bleues.
turns.userEn: Yes, my jackets are blue.

turns.ai: Je prends tout. Tu es sur que les chaussures ne sont pas marrons ?
turns.en: I will take everything. Are you sure the shoes are not marrons?
turns.user: Marron, sans s. Les marrons, ça se mange.
turns.userEn: Marron, without an s. Marrons are something you eat.

alts.fr: Sans s ! Les marrons sont des fruits.
alts.en: Without an s! Marrons are a fruit.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: A jacket is feminine. What happens to the colour vert?
cards.back: Ma veste est verte. It takes an e, and you hear the t wake up.

cards.front: Several jackets, and the colour is bleu. What do you write?
cards.back: Mes vestes sont bleues. An e and an s, and neither one is audible.

cards.front: Several shoes, and the colour is marron.
cards.back: Les chaussures sont marron. Colours agree. Things that became colours do not.
It is a chestnut being used as a colour, and the nut keeps its own shape.
Same reason. It is a fruit, and une orange is still a thing you can eat.

cards.front: Can you hear the plural s on a colour?
cards.back: Never. Not on any colour, not ever. It exists only on the page.

cards.front: Which two of the twelve have a feminine you cannot hear at all?
cards.back: bleu and noir. Bleue and noire are identical to bleu and noir.
blanche, not blance. The silent c turns into a ch you say out loud.
violette. The t wakes up and the spelling doubles it.
grise. The silent s comes back as a z sound.

cards.front: What happens to a colour made of two words, like vert pomme?
cards.back: Les murs sont vert pomme. Nothing. Two-word colours never change.

cards.front: Where does the colour go, before or after the thing?
cards.back: Elle porte une jupe verte. After it, every time.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a sale nearly fall through over one silent letter, learned twelve colours attached to things you can already name, and met the idea that a describing word changes shape to match what it describes, which nothing before this lesson has asked of you. You have seen one colour take four shapes and another take none, found out that most of those shapes sound identical and that no amount of listening will separate them, and worked out why two of the twelve refuse to move at all. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The twelve names
rounds.say: The names, quickly.

questions.q: Listen. Which colour is it?
questions.why: jaune. It is the one colour in this lesson whose n is a real consonant you pronounce rather than a nasal ending, so it sounds closer to the English word zone than to anything nasal.

questions.q: Which of these is the word for white?
questions.why: blanc. Its final c is silent and the vowel is nasal, so it sounds like blahn with no n you actually say. Bleu is blue and beige is beige, and both start the same way, which is what makes this cluster worth a second look.

questions.q: Write the French word for red.
questions.why: rouge. It is one of the four colours that already end in an e, so the feminine asks nothing of it and only a plural s is ever added to it.

questions.q: Which colour is named after something you can eat?
questions.why: orange, and marron is the other one. Both were things before they were colours, which is exactly why neither of them ever takes an ending.

rounds.label: Making it match
rounds.say: The thing decides the shape.

questions.q: Une jupe is feminine. You want to say the skirt is green. What do you write?
questions.why: Une jupe verte. The colour takes an e because the skirt is the une kind, and it sits after the thing rather than in front of it the way English would put it.

questions.q: Fix this. « Les voitures sont noir. »
questions.why: Several feminine things, so the colour takes an e and an s. Neither of them is audible, which is why this sentence sounds completely correct as it stands and is still wrong on the page.

questions.q: Mes vestes are feminine and plural, and the colour is bleu. Write the colour.
questions.why: bleues. The e is for the jackets being the une kind and the s is for there being more than one, in that order. All four shapes of bleu sound identical, so this had to be worked out rather than heard.

questions.q: What decides which ending a colour takes?
opts: Where the colour sits in the sentence
Whether you can hear the ending
questions.why: The thing being described. Nothing about the colour has any say in it, which is why the same colour appears in four different shapes across four sentences that are otherwise identical.

rounds.label: The feminines that change more
rounds.say: Four of the twelve do something extra.

questions.q: La porte is feminine and the colour is blanc. Write the colour.
questions.why: blanche. It is the only colour here whose feminine changes the consonant rather than adding to it, and unlike most feminines you can hear this one clearly. blance is not a word.

questions.q: Write the feminine of violet.
questions.why: violette, with two t letters. The silent t of violet wakes up and the spelling doubles it, so violete would be both misspelled and mispronounced.

questions.q: Fix this. « Sa chemise est gris. »
questions.why: grise. A shirt is the une kind, so the colour takes an e, and here the e wakes the sleeping s into a z sound. This is one of the few agreement errors you can actually hear.

questions.q: Which of these feminines does NOT change the sound of the word?
questions.why: noire. It sounds exactly like noir. The other three all wake a letter that was silent: verte says its t, grise says its s as a z, and blanche turns its c into a ch.

rounds.label: What you cannot hear
rounds.say: Half of this lesson is invisible to your ear.

questions.q: Listen to these two: « bleu » then « bleue ». What is the difference?
opts: The second one ends in a soft sound
There is no difference, they sound identical
questions.why: They are identical. Bleu ends in a vowel sound already, so the feminine e adds nothing your ear can pick up. If you thought you heard a difference, that is the spelling you were expecting rather than the sound.

questions.q: How many of the four shapes of vert can you tell apart by ear?
questions.why: Two. Vert and verts are one sound, verte and vertes are another, and the plural s is never pronounced on any of them. So your ear separates the masculine from the feminine and can do nothing at all about the number.

questions.q: Mes sacs are masculine and plural, and the colour is vert. Write the colour.
questions.why: verts. It sounds exactly like vert, because the plural s on a colour is never pronounced, so the only reason to write it is that there is more than one bag.

questions.q: You are listening carefully and still cannot hear whether somebody said bleue or bleues. What does that mean?
opts: The information is not in the sound at all
The speaker was not articulating clearly
You need to slow the recording down further
questions.why: The information is genuinely not there. A native speaker cannot hear it either, and works the ending out from the thing being described exactly as you have to. Slowing the audio down will never help with this one.

rounds.label: The two that never change
rounds.say: The half of the lesson people remember wrongly.

questions.q: You are writing an ad for brown shoes. What goes in it?
questions.why: marron, with nothing added. Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. It is a chestnut being used as a colour, and the s on the first option is the single most noticeable written error in this lesson.

questions.q: Fix this. « Les rideaux sont oranges. »
questions.why: orange, unchanged. The fruit takes an s when you are counting fruit, but the colour is the fruit being borrowed and there is nothing to count, so it stays exactly as it is.

questions.q: Why does « des oranges » take an s while « des fleurs orange » does not?
opts: The first is a thing being counted, the second is a colour
The first is feminine and the second is masculine
The second is an exception with no reason behind it
The second is plural and the first is singular
questions.why: The first counts fruit, so it behaves like any other thing you can count. The second uses the fruit as a colour, and the flowers are what is plural rather than the oranges, so there is nothing for the s to attach to.

questions.q: La table is feminine and the colour is marron. Write the colour.
questions.why: marron, unchanged. A feminine thing in front of it makes no difference at all, and marronne is not a word. This is the same answer you would give for a masculine thing, a plural, or anything else.

rounds.label: Colours made of two words
rounds.say: The last round, and you already know the answer to all of it.

questions.q: Fix this. « Les murs sont verts pommes. »
questions.why: Neither half takes an ending. Once a colour is built from two words it has become a description of a thing rather than a plain colour, so the same rule that stops marron moving stops this one too.

questions.q: Say this out loud: the shoes are brown.
questions.why: Nothing in the sound tells anybody whether you wrote the s or not, which is exactly why this is the error that survives. Saying it correctly and writing it correctly are two separate skills here.

questions.q: Write the French for dark green eyes. The word for eyes is yeux.
questions.why: Neither half changes. Adding the endings looks like being careful, and it is the same instinct that puts an s on marron: a rule applied in the one place it does not reach.

questions.q: What do marron, orange and vert pomme have in common?
opts: They are all shades of brown
They are all borrowed from other languages
They are all irregular and must be memorised separately
None of them is a plain colour word, so none of them changes
questions.why: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. A nut, a fruit and a description of an apple. None of the three is a plain colour word, so the endings never reach them. One idea, not three things to memorise.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can name twelve colours, make them match the thing they describe, tell which endings you will ever hear, and leave the two that were something else alone. The second of those is the first time in this course that a describing word has changed shape, and it is not the last: the same mechanism is waiting for you on every adjective you meet from here. Basic adjectives are next, and everything in this lesson transfers to them unchanged.
points: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not. A nut and a fruit keep the shape they had.
The thing being described decides the ending, never the colour itself.
The plural s is never pronounced, and on bleu and noir the feminine e is not either.
The colour comes after the thing, and colours made of two words never move at all.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that un and une follow it, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, introduced in a1.04
The plural of a noun, introduced in a1.03
The full present of être, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07
mon, ma and mes, introduced in a1.05
That a final consonant is usually silent, and that a following e wakes it, introduced in sons.06
The nasal vowels and the fact that a following vowel blocks them, introduced in sons.03
grammarIntroduced: Adjective agreement, introduced here for the first time in the course, through colour
The feminine -e on an adjective, and the four colours where it is audible
The plural -s on an adjective, which is never pronounced
The combined feminine plural -es
Irregular feminine formation: blanc to blanche, violet to violette
Invariable colour adjectives derived from nouns: marron and orange
Invariable compound colour adjectives: vert pomme, vert foncé, bleu clair
The postposition of colour adjectives, stated as a fact and not as a system

overview.introFr: Douze couleurs, et le premier mot de ce cours qui change de forme selon ce qu'il décrit.

acts.title: Your first describing word
acts.milestone: You have watched one silent letter nearly cost a sale.

acts.title: The colours
acts.milestone: Twelve colours, each stuck to something, in four groups that each mean something.

acts.title: Four shapes
acts.milestone: One colour in four shapes, and one that has only ever had the one.

acts.title: What you hear, what you write
acts.milestone: You know which endings reach your ear and which are only ever on the page.

acts.title: The two that never change
acts.milestone: Not two exceptions. One idea, and it covers the two-word colours as well.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. Basic adjectives are next, and all of this transfers to them.

lessons.reframe: Colours agree. Things that became colours do not.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong colour name, most often inside the blanc / bleu / beige cluster or between violet and rose.
Leaves the colour in its plain form on a feminine or plural thing. The default error, and the one every learner starts with because English never asks for this.
Regularises a feminine that changes more than its ending: writes blance for blanche, or violete for violette.
Believes the silent endings should be audible and concludes their listening is at fault. Costs confidence rather than accuracy, which is why it gets its own drill.
Puts an ending on marron or orange. The highest-value error in the lesson: inaudible, so nobody corrects it, and it is the first thing a French reader sees.
Agrees one or both halves of a two-word colour: writes des yeux verts foncés. The same instinct as the s on marron, arriving one step later.

drills.title: English in, French out
drills.coach: The English is on the left. Say the French out loud before you turn the card, and keep the stress on the last syllable.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these means white?
drills.why: blanc. All three start with a b and the first two start with bl, which is what makes them worth saying out loud as a group rather than reading.

drills.title: Match the colour to the thing
drills.coach: Look at the thing being described, not at the colour. One of it or several? The un kind or the une kind? The ending follows from those two answers and from nothing else.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Mes vestes are feminine and plural. Which shape of bleu do they take?
drills.why: bleues. An e for the jackets being the une kind and an s for there being more than one. None of it is audible, so it has to come from the thing.

drills.title: What does the feminine do?
drills.coach: Say the feminine out loud before you place each one. If nothing changes it is already an e word; if you add an e it is the second group; if the word itself changes shape it is the third; and two of them never move at all.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: What is the feminine of blanc?
drills.why: blanche. The c becomes a ch, which is the only feminine in this lesson that changes a consonant rather than adding to it, and you can hear it clearly.

drills.title: Heard, or only written
drills.coach: Say the plain form, then the feminine, then the plain form again. If a letter arrived that was not there before, it goes on the left. If you said the same word twice, it goes on the right.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: How much of a colour's plural can you hear?
opts: some of it, on some colours
drills.why: None of it, on any colour, without exception. The plural s on a colour is never pronounced, so nothing in a recording could ever tell you a colour was plural.

drills.title: The thing, or the colour?
buckets: doing its job as a thing
drills.coach: Ask what the word is naming. If it is naming a fruit you could eat or a nut you could hold, it behaves like any other thing and takes its endings. If it is only telling you what colour something else is, it keeps the shape it had and takes nothing.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: How do you write "brown shoes"?
drills.why: marron, with nothing added. It is a chestnut being used as a colour and the nut keeps its own shape, so no thing in front of it will ever make it move.

drills.title: One word, or two?
drills.coach: Every one of these describes more than one thing, so the number is not what decides it. Count the words in the colour. One word and it agrees; two words and it has stopped being a plain colour, so it does not.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: How do you write "dark green eyes"?
drills.why: Neither half moves. Once the colour is two words it works the same way marron does, so adding endings to either part is the same error in a new place.

sheets.title: All twelve, in four forms
contains: Every colour in all four shapes
What the feminine does to each

rows.v: rouge, jaune, rose, beige. The feminine asks nothing of these; only the plural s is ever added.
bleu, vert, noir, gris. Add an e for the feminine. You hear it on vert and gris and not on bleu or noir.
blanc, violet. blanc becomes blanche and violet doubles its t to become violette. Both are audible.
orange, marron. Never change, in any position, because both were things before they were colours.
gris already ends in s, so the masculine plural adds nothing: un sac gris, des sacs gris. The feminine still adds its own e.

sheets.title: What you can hear
contains: Why the plural is always silent
What to do instead of listening

sections.title: Can you hear the feminine?
rows: yes, the t at the end wakes up
yes, the s wakes up as a z
yes, the c turns into a ch
yes, the t wakes up, and the spelling doubles it
yes, the nasal collapses into a plain n

sections.title: Why half of this is invisible
sections.body: French stopped pronouncing most of its final consonants a long time ago and kept writing them, which is the single fact behind almost everything strange about French spelling. The plural s on a colour is one of those. It is never pronounced, on any colour, in any position, so a recording of a plural colour and a recording of its singular are the same recording. Nothing about listening more carefully will change this, and a learner who believes the difference is there and that they simply cannot hear it will spend months concluding something untrue about their own ears. The feminine e is a different case and it is worth understanding rather than memorising. An e written after a consonant makes that consonant get pronounced again, because it is no longer at the end of the word. That is why vert is said without its t and verte says the t clearly, why gris hides its s and grise brings it back as a z, and why violet doubles and sounds its t in violette. It also explains the two that do nothing: bleu and noir already end in a vowel sound, so there is no sleeping consonant for the e to wake up, and bleue and noire are identical to bleu and noir in every way except on the page. You met this exact mechanism in the silent letters lesson, where a final consonant sits quiet until something turns up behind it. The practical rule is short. Work the ending out from the thing being described, then write it. That is what a native speaker does, and it is why they make this mistake too when they are typing quickly.

rows.v: Never marrons. Des marrons is a bag of chestnuts, which is where the colour came from.
Never marronne, which is not a word at all. A feminine thing changes nothing here.
Never oranges. Des oranges is the fruit, and it takes an s only when you are counting fruit.
Never orangée. Orangée is a real word meaning orange-ish, so this one is a different word rather than a misspelling.
Neither half moves. Two-word colours have stopped being plain colours.
Same again. Apple green is a description of an apple, and you are not counting apples.
A feminine thing and neither word moves, which looks wrong and is right.

sections.title: One idea, not a list
sections.body: Most courses hand you marron and orange as two exceptions and tell you to memorise them, which works for about a fortnight. There is a reason behind both of them and it is worth thirty seconds. Un marron is a chestnut and une orange is a fruit. Neither word started life as a colour: somebody described something as being the colour of a chestnut, the phrase got shortened, and the word carried on being a nut the whole time. So when you write des chaussures marron, what you are really writing is shoes the colour of a chestnut, and there is only one chestnut in that phrase no matter how many shoes there are. That is why the ending never arrives. The same reasoning covers every colour built out of two words, which is the part that makes this worth learning as an idea rather than a pair. Vert pomme is apple green, and the apple in it is one apple. Bleu clair is light blue, and clair is describing the blue rather than the thing. In both cases the colour has become a small description rather than a plain colour word, and descriptions of that kind do not take endings. Once you have this, you never have to ask whether a new compound colour agrees, because none of them do and you know why. The one thing worth watching is that both words also still exist in their original jobs, and there they behave completely normally. Des oranges takes an s because you are counting fruit. Des marrons glacés takes an s because you are counting nuts. If the word is naming a thing, it agrees like anything else; if it is standing in for a colour, it does not move.

agreement.term: the colour follows the noun it describes
agreement.title: The describing word changes shape
agreement.body: This is new. Until now the only words that changed shape were the small ones in front of a noun: un or une, le or la. From here the describing word changes too, and it changes to match the thing it is describing rather than anything about you or the sentence. A bag is masculine, so the colour on it takes the plain form. A jacket is feminine, so the colour takes an e. Two jackets, and it takes an e and an s. Nothing about the colour itself decides this. The noun decides, and the colour follows.

examples.note: A masculine thing, so the colour is in its plain form.
The same colour on a feminine thing, and now it carries an e.

borrowedNoun.title: Two colours that were something else first
borrowedNoun.body: A marron is a chestnut and une orange is a fruit. Both got used as colours, and both kept the shape they had as things. That is why they never take an e or an s when they are describing something: underneath, des chaussures marron means shoes the colour of a chestnut, and you would not put the shoes ending on the chestnut. This is not a pair of exceptions to memorise. It is one idea, and it also covers every colour built out of two words, like bleu clair or vert pomme, which stay unchanged for the same reason.

examples.note: The fruit, doing its ordinary job, and taking an s like any other thing.
The same word as a colour, in front of a plural, and refusing the s.

writtenNotHeard.term: endings you write and never say
writtenNotHeard.title: Half of this is invisible to your ear
writtenNotHeard.body: The s on a plural colour is never pronounced. Not sometimes, not softly: never. Vert and verts are one sound, and so are verte and vertes. The e for a feminine is heard only when it wakes up a letter that was asleep, which happens on some colours and not others. Vert becomes verte and the t arrives. Bleu becomes bleue and nothing at all changes. So listening will not tell you which ending to write, and no amount of practice will make it tell you. You work it out from the thing being described, then you write it.

examples.note: The s is written here and is not in the sound. This is the singular sound.
The e is written and changes nothing. Say it beside the masculine and hear that.

wakesUp.title: When you CAN hear the feminine
wakesUp.body: Some colours end in a letter that stays silent on its own and starts being pronounced once an e is added behind it. Vert ends in a silent t, and verte says that t. Gris ends in a silent s, and grise says it as a z. Violet doubles its t and says it. Blanc does the strangest one and turns into blanche. You met this exact mechanism in the silent letters lesson, where a final consonant sits quiet until something comes along behind it. This is the same thing, and the something is the feminine e.

examples.note: The t at the end of vert is silent until this e turns up behind it.
The silent s of gris comes back as a z sound.

afterTheNoun.title: The colour comes after the thing
afterTheNoun.body: English puts the colour first and says a green jacket. French puts it after and says une veste verte. That order holds for every colour in this lesson and every colour you will meet, with nothing to remember and no cases to sort out, so it is worth getting used to now rather than translating word by word and then rearranging. When the colour comes after a verb instead, as in ma veste est verte, nothing changes about the ending: it still matches the thing being described.

examples.note: The skirt first, then its colour. English would give you those the other way round.
The shoes, then the colour, and the colour is one that never changes shape.

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. EVERY MASCULINE / FEMININE PAIR IS ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, the masculine immediately followed by its feminine with no gap and no reset: vert / verte, gris / grise, blanc / blanche, violet / violette, brun / brune. The ONLY difference the learner may hear is the ending. Recorded separately these become two performances and the learner hears the performance rather than the language. THE SILENT PAIRS MUST ALSO BE RECORDED AS PAIRS, IN THIS SAME TAKE: bleu / bleue and noir / noire. This matters MORE than the audible ones, not less, because the whole teaching is that NOTHING CHANGES. A reader who records bleue in a separate session will drift in pitch or length and invent a difference that is not in the language, and the learner will spend a year listening for it. Read bleu / bleue as if reading the same word twice, because that is what it is. Do not lengthen the second, do not add a breathy release, do not lift the pitch. The same applies to noir / noire. Keep every nasal closed: blanc is a nasal vowel with NO n sound behind it, and brun is a nasal that COLLAPSES in brune into a plain n plus a vowel, which is the most dramatic change in the set and should be read plainly rather than demonstrated.

The twelve colours as ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE by one voice at one speed, in the deck order: rouge, bleu, vert, jaune, noir, blanc, gris, rose, orange, violet, marron, beige. Twelve colours recorded in twelve sessions are twelve performances, and any drift in pace or pitch teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read them straight through with an even beat, then again slowly in the same take. JAUNE IS THE ONE TO WATCH: its n is a REAL CONSONANT and the word has no nasal vowel at all. It rhymes with the English zone. Do not nasalise it. The app respells it ZHON deliberately and a nasalised reading would contradict the card. blanc, marron and orange DO carry genuine nasal vowels and must be read with NO n or m sound behind them at all.

THE PLURALS, AND THEY MUST NEVER BE RECORDED IN ISOLATION. A lone plural clip teaches nothing and implies a difference exists. Every plural here is recorded ONLY as the second half of a pair with its own singular, in one take, so the learner hears that nothing changed: vert / verts, verte / vertes, bleu / bleus, bleue / bleues. Read the two members of each pair as the same word twice, because they are the same word twice. There is no s sound in any of these and there must be no hint of one: no lengthening, no release, no breath. If a reader cannot resist marking the plural somehow, record the singular twice and use it for both, because that is a more truthful clip than a performed difference. Also record the four-way set bleu / bleue / bleus / bleues as one continuous take, which is the clip the card about all four sounding alike depends on.

marron and orange recorded AS COLOUR PHRASES, NOT BARE, so the invariability is heard in context: « mon sac est marron », « ma veste est marron », « mes sacs sont marron », « les chaussures sont marron », « les rideaux sont orange », « elle aime les fleurs orange ». All four marron sentences are ONE TAKE, read one after another, because the entire teaching is that the colour is identical in all four and only the words around it move. Do not vary the colour at all between them. Then the contrast the lesson turns on, also one take: « le prix des oranges » immediately followed by « elle aime les fleurs orange », so the fruit taking its s and the colour refusing one sit next to each other in the same voice. Finally « cette orange est bien mûre », where mûre agrees and orange does not, in the same sentence. Read every one of these plainly. Nothing here should sound like a demonstration.
clipIds: Le client demande le prix des oranges.

recorded.desc: The twelve colours attached to a thing, one take, one voice: les tomates rouges, les yeux bleus, les haricots verts, le citron jaune, les olives noires, la farine blanche, la souris grise, les fleurs roses, les rideaux orange, le raisin violet, les chaussures marron, le manteau beige. The thing comes first and the colour after it in every one, which is the pattern being absorbed rather than taught, so keep the phrasing even and do not pause between the noun and the colour. Several of these carry an agreement ending that is completely silent (rouges, bleus, verts, noires, roses): do not mark them.

The five written traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically. FOUR OF THE FIVE ARE ACOUSTICALLY IDENTICAL TO THEIR CORRECTION, which is the whole reason they are traps: « des chaussures marrons » and « des chaussures marron » are the same sound, and so are the compound pair and the orange pair. Do not try to make the wrong one sound wrong. Read both members of those pairs identically and let the screen carry the difference, because a reader who performs a distinction that does not exist teaches the learner to listen for something that will never be there. Only the « une jupe vert » / « une jupe verte » pair genuinely differs in sound, and it should be read straight.

The four-form grid, three colours, ONE TAKE EACH, read across the row: « mon sac est vert, ma veste est verte, mes sacs sont verts, mes vestes sont vertes », then the same four for bleu, then the same four for marron. Reading a row in one take is the entire point: the learner has to hear that the vert row changes once (at verte) and never again, that the bleu row never changes at all across four different spellings, and that the marron row is four identical words. Do not record these twelve sentences separately and do not vary the pace between rows, because the comparison is between rows as much as within them.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of a woman in her thirties reading messages at an ordinary texting pace rather than a teaching pace. The beat where Salomé asks about the chestnuts (« Les marrons ? Pardon, tu vends des chaussures ou des marrons ? ») must be WARM AND AMUSED rather than corrective or pointed. She is teasing a neighbour, not marking homework, and any edge on that line turns the scene into a telling-off and loses the teaching. The final line, where she buys both items, is where warmth is allowed to show, because that is the reward for having fixed it.
clipIds: Les marrons ? Pardon, tu vends des chaussures ou des marrons ?
Ah, les chaussures ! Je les prends. Et la veste verte aussi.

lessons.title: Les saisons & la météo
lessons.intro: One adjective, three verbs, and English gives you no help choosing between them. This is how you name the seasons, say what the weather is doing, and ask somebody else the same thing.

say.text: Four words, and you know three of them. That is what makes this one worth watching.

setting.place: A roof terrace six floors up, one door, and a view over the street

beats.text: Nadia has a flat with a roof terrace, and she has been promising to show you it since March.
Six floors up, one door, and a view over the whole street. She pushes it open and stops on the step.
You have four words of that and you know three of them. Il means he. So somebody is doing something.

beats.speaker: Nadia
beats.stage: She laughs, points at the sky, and you spend a while working out what just happened.

beats.text: It is warm out here, and the sun is straight on you. You want to say so before she offers you a jumper.

beats.prompt: You are the one who is hot, not the terrace. What goes out?

options.en: the one built the English way
the one that says you have hot

followUp.works: Yes. A person HAS hot in French, and that is two words you can reuse forever.
followUp.breaks: Every word in that is a real French word. Watch what the sentence turns into.

beats.heading: Two sentences, and neither was about what you meant
beats.body: She said the weather and you heard a man. Then you reached for the word English uses and said something about yourself that you did not mean. Nothing was mispronounced, and nothing got corrected either time.

wrong.en: Says something about you that is not the temperature

right.en: I am hot, which is what you meant

beats.coach: Weather makes, people have, things are. Three verbs, one adjective, and English hands you the wrong one twice.

beats.speaker: Nadia
beats.fr: Oui, il fait chaud ici. On rentre ?
beats.en: Yes, it is hot here. Shall we go in?
beats.stage: She says the weather version straight back at you, and now you can hear the difference.

beats.text: One adjective, three sentences, and which one you want depends on what is hot.

closing.text: Weather makes, people have, things are. That is the whole of the next twenty-five minutes.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the third one is where almost everybody goes wrong.

goals.s: And the small word each one takes, because three take the same one and spring does not.

goals.t: Say what the weather is doing
goals.s: Two words in front, and they never change no matter what follows them.

goals.t: Say who is hot and what is hot
goals.s: Three ways to build the same sentence, and English gives you no help choosing.
The one question that opens more conversations in French than anything else you know.

sections.title: The Sentence With Nobody In It
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Read this one properly. It undoes something the pronouns lesson taught you, in one place only.

cards.label: This is new
cards.head: il, pointing at nothing
cards.sub: [EEL FEH BOH] · the weather is nice
cards.body: The pronouns lesson taught you that il means he, and that is true everywhere except here. In a weather sentence il points at nobody: not a man, not a thing, not something said earlier. It is holding a space open.

cards.label: The frame
cards.head: il fait, then what it is like
cards.sub: [EEL FEH SHOH] · it is hot today
cards.body: Two words in front, then the word for what the weather is like. Il fait chaud, il fait froid, il fait beau, il fait frais. Nothing agrees with anything and nothing changes.

cards.label: It never changes
cards.head: There is only ever il fait
cards.body: This is the only shape this verb has when it is talking about the weather. There is no other person and no plural, so you can learn these two words as one block and use them for the rest of your life.

cards.label: What comes later
cards.head: You will meet this verb properly
cards.body: The verb behind il fait has other shapes, and they are taught in their own lesson higher up. You need none of them for the weather, which only ever uses this one. Learn the block now and the rest will fit around it later.

sections.title: Same Four Words, Two Different Sentences
sections.say: Read a row across, not down. The word after du is the only thing telling you who this is about.
cols: A person, il is a man

rows.say: Il fait du vent dehors. Il fait du yoga tous les matins.

detail.title: [EEL FEH DÜ VAHⁿ] · [EEL FEH DÜ yoh-GAH]
detail.body: Il fait du vent dehors. is the sky. Il fait du yoga tous les matins. is a man in a room. Four words of identical shape, and the noun at the end is the entire difference between them.
detail.say: Il fait du vent dehors. Il fait du yoga tous les matins.

rows.say: Il fait du brouillard ce matin. Il fait de la pêche près de la rivière.

detail.title: It is not a one-off
detail.body: Il fait du brouillard ce matin. is fog. Il fait de la pêche près de la rivière. is a man with a rod. Both are ordinary, both are common, and neither one marks itself.
detail.say: Il fait du brouillard ce matin. Il fait de la pêche près de la rivière.

rows.say: Il pleut, en plus il fait du vent. Il fait du sport tous les jours.

detail.title: When there is nothing after it
detail.body: Il pleut, en plus il fait du vent. has two weather sentences in it and no person anywhere. Il fait du sport tous les jours. is a man who exercises. Read to the end before you decide who il is.
detail.say: Il pleut, en plus il fait du vent. Il fait du sport tous les jours.

rows.say: Il fait froid en hiver. Il a froid dans le bureau.

detail.title: [EEL FEH FRWAH] · [ee-LAH FRWAH]
detail.body: Il fait froid en hiver. is the season. Il a froid dans le bureau. is a man who wants his coat. Here il really is a person, and the verb is what tells you so.
detail.say: Il fait froid en hiver. Il a froid dans le bureau.

sections.title: Four Seasons, One Screen Each
sections.hint: Swipe. Say each one out loud.
sections.say: Four screens, one season each, and the small word is part of the card rather than a footnote.

cards.label: 1 of 4
cards.body: In spring. The only au.

cards.label: 2 of 4
cards.body: In summer. One of the three en.

cards.label: 3 of 4
cards.body: In autumn. One of the three en.

cards.label: 4 of 4
cards.body: In winter. One of the three en.

sections.title: Three En, And One Au
sections.say: All four here together on purpose. The odd one out is only obvious while you can see the other three.

detail.title: au printemps · in spring
detail.body: The one that is different, and the only one to remember separately. Le village est très joli au printemps. Il fait bon vivre ici au printemps.

detail.title: en été · in summer
detail.body: Like the other two that take en. Say it as one piece rather than two words. Les jours sont chauds en été.

detail.title: en automne · in autumn
detail.body: The n at the end is real and the m is silent. Il pleut beaucoup en automne. Il pleut souvent en automne.

detail.title: en hiver · in winter
detail.body: The h is silent, so en runs straight into it. Il fait froid en hiver. Il fait nuit tôt en hiver. Il neige beaucoup en hiver à Québec.

rows.say: au printemps, en été, en automne, en hiver

detail.title: A hook for exactly these four words
detail.body: The three that take en all begin on a vowel sound, and printemps begins on a consonant. That is completely reliable for these four and it is not a rule about French generally, so use it to hold the set and nothing wider.
detail.say: au printemps, en été, en automne, en hiver

detail.title: The m in automne is not there
detail.body: Written au-t-o-m-n-e and said with no m at all: it comes out close to oh-TONN. The n at the end is a real n that you do pronounce, which is unusual and worth thirty seconds on its own.

sections.title: Which Season Is Different?
sections.say: One question, and it is the only thing about the seasons you can get wrong.

check.q: You are telling somebody the garden is best in spring. Which one is right?
check.why: au printemps. Spring is the one season that does not take en, and the version with en is the one nobody says, so it is the one worth fixing now while there are only four words to hold.

sections.title: Three Ways To Say Hot
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: One adjective, three sentences. English uses is for all three, so there is nothing to carry across.

cards.label: The weather
cards.head: il fait chaud
cards.sub: [EEL FEH SHOH] · it is hot out
cards.body: Weather makes, people have, things are. The sky, the street, the day: all of it takes il fait, and the il is nobody. This is the one you want when you are talking about being outside.

cards.label: A person
cards.head: j'ai chaud
cards.body: A person HAS hot in French. You met this in the avoir lesson as a fixed expression and nothing about it changes here. J'ai chaud, tu as froid, elle a chaud.

cards.label: A thing
cards.head: le café est chaud
cards.sub: [luh ka-FAY eh SHOH] · the coffee is hot
cards.body: An object is what it is, so this one takes être and matches English word for word. That is exactly why it gets used in the other two places, where it is wrong.

cards.label: The one that stings
cards.head: Never je suis chaud
cards.body: Weather makes, people have, things are. Reaching for être about yourself produces a sentence that is real French and means something else entirely. Nobody will explain why they are laughing, so it is worth getting now.

sections.title: One Adjective, Three Frames
sections.say: Weather makes, people have, things are. Read across. Only the verb moves, and the adjective sits still.

rows.say: il fait chaud. J'ai chaud. Le café est chaud.

detail.title: chaud, three times, three verbs
detail.body: il fait chaud is the day. J'ai chaud. is you. Le café est chaud. is the cup. One adjective, and the verb carries the whole meaning.
detail.say: il fait chaud. J'ai chaud. Le café est chaud.

rows.say: il fait froid. J'ai froid aux pieds. Le vent est froid.

detail.title: [zhay FRWAH] · [luh VAHⁿ eh FRWAH]
detail.body: J'ai froid aux pieds. is about you rather than the room. Le vent est froid. is the wind itself, which is a thing. Swap the adjective and nothing else about the rule moves.
detail.say: il fait froid. J'ai froid aux pieds. Le vent est froid.

detail.title: The three, named
detail.body: Weather makes, people have, things are. That line decides every sentence in this lesson and a great many it never shows you. Ask what is hot before you start, and the rest follows with no judgement in it.

rows.say: Elle a chaud dans la salle d'attente. Le café est chaud et le thé est froid.

detail.title: All three in one room
detail.body: Elle a chaud dans la salle d'attente. is a person, so avoir. Le café est chaud et le thé est froid. is two things, so être twice. The room itself would take il fait, and none of the three can borrow another one's verb.
detail.say: Elle a chaud dans la salle d'attente. Le café est chaud et le thé est froid.

sections.title: il fait, il a, il est
sections.say: These three all start the same and none of them is stressed. Slow the audio down before you answer.

lines.en: it is hot out
he is hot
it is hot, said about a thing
it is cold out
he is cold
it is raining

questions.q: Lines one and two are one syllable apart. Which one is about a person?
questions.why: il a chaud. The verb is the only thing carrying that information, it is unstressed, and it is the shortest word in the sentence, which is exactly the combination that makes it easy to miss.

questions.q: Line three is the one a learner produces about the weather by mistake. What is it actually about?
questions.why: A thing. Il est chaud is a perfectly good sentence about an object, which is what makes it dangerous: it does not fail, it just stops being about the weather and starts being about something else.

questions.q: Line six has nothing after the verb at all. Who or what is it about?
questions.why: Nobody. Il pleut is the whole sentence and its il points at nothing. There is no other way to say this in French, which is why the verb only ever appears in this one shape.

sections.title: Who Or What Is Hot?
sections.say: Read down each column and say what the sentence is about before you read the verb.

items.fr: Elle a chaud dans la salle d'attente.
items.en: She is hot in the waiting room.

items.fr: Il a froid dans le bureau.
items.en: He is cold in the office.

items.fr: Le café est chaud et le thé est froid.
items.en: The coffee is hot and the tea is cold.

items.fr: Il pleut depuis ce matin, et le ciel est gris.
items.en: It has been raining since this morning, and the sky is grey.

sections.title: Which One Do You Want?
sections.say: One question, and it is the one the opening scene turned on.

check.q: You have just come in from the snow and you want to say that YOU are cold. What do you say?
check.why: A person has cold in French. The third is true about the weather and is not an answer about you, and the first and fourth are the two ways an English speaker builds this sentence out of être.

sections.title: Four Shapes, Not One
sections.say: Four ways to build a weather sentence, then the question that gets you any of them.

groups.label: il + one word that is the whole thing

items.fr: Il neige beaucoup en hiver à Québec.
items.en: It snows a lot in winter in Quebec.

groups.label: il y a + du, de la or des

items.fr: Il y a du brouillard sur la route.
items.en: There is fog on the road.

items.fr: Il y a de l'orage cette nuit.

groups.label: the same first shape, with a number in it

items.fr: Il fait moins cinq degrés ce matin.
items.en: It is minus five degrees this morning.

groups.label: and how to ask for any of them

items.en: What is the weather like today?

items.fr: Fait-il beau à Paris en ce moment ?
items.en: Is the weather nice in Paris right now?

items.fr: Est-ce qu'il y a du vent aujourd'hui ?

sections.title: Two Of Them Overlap
sections.frSub: Il fait du vent ou il y a du vent
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Two of the four shapes say the same thing, and you need telling before you meet both.

cards.label: Both are right
cards.head: il fait du vent · il y a du vent
cards.sub: [EEL FEH DÜ VAHⁿ] · [eel yah DÜ VAHⁿ]
cards.body: These two mean the same thing and both are ordinary French. Nobody prefers one. If you meet both and nobody says so, you will assume one of them is a mistake and spend a year avoiding it.

cards.label: What follows
cards.head: A thing, not a describing word
cards.fr: Il y a du soleil aujourd'hui.
cards.sub: [eel yah DÜ soh-LAY] · it is sunny
cards.body: Both of these shapes take du or de la and then a thing: du vent, du soleil, du brouillard. That is the small word the partitive lesson gave you, doing exactly the job it was taught for.

cards.label: The short shape
cards.head: il pleut · il neige
cards.body: Two of them are the whole sentence on their own. Nothing goes in front and nothing goes after, and there is no version of these with il fait attached to them.

cards.label: The trap
cards.head: Never il fait pleut
cards.body: Welding the first shape onto the third is what a learner produces after being told that il fait is the weather phrase. It is one or the other, never both, and this is the error worth being warned about in advance.

sections.title: Five Traps
sections.say: Weather makes, people have, things are. Five sentences an English speaker produces in their first month, one per screen.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je suis chaud » when you are too warm.
errors.why: A person has hot in French. The version with être is a real sentence about something else, so nobody corrects it and nobody forgets it either. This is the one that actually embarrasses people.

errors.wrong: Saying « Il est chaud aujourd'hui » about the weather.
errors.why: Être belongs to things. Used about the day it turns a weather report into a remark about some object nobody has mentioned, and it survives because the sentence still parses perfectly well.

errors.wrong: Saying « En printemps, il fait doux ».
errors.right: Saying « Au printemps, il fait doux ».
errors.why: Three seasons take en and spring takes au. Nobody says the version with en, so this one stops rather than shifting, and it is the only thing about the four seasons you can get wrong.

errors.wrong: Saying « Il fait pleut depuis ce matin ».
errors.right: Saying « Il pleut depuis ce matin ».
errors.why: Il pleut is the whole sentence already. Bolting il fait onto it is what comes out after a lesson that teaches il fait as the weather phrase, and it is one shape or the other, never both.

errors.wrong: Hearing « Il fait du vent » as a man doing something.
errors.right: Hearing it as the sky, with nobody in the sentence.
errors.why: The pronouns lesson taught you that il means he and this is the place it stops. Read the noun at the end before you decide: vent is the weather and yoga is a man, and nothing else in the two sentences differs.

sections.title: Asking About It
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: One question, learned as a block. It opens more conversations in French than anything else you have.

cards.label: The question
cards.head: Quel temps fait-il ?
cards.sub: [KEHL TAHⁿ feh-TEEL] · what is the weather like?
cards.body: Learn these four words as one block, the way you learned il fait. The pieces of it are taken apart in a later lesson and you do not need any of that to use it today.

cards.label: The answer
cards.head: Any shape you like
cards.fr: Il fait beau et il y a du soleil.
cards.body: All four shapes are legal answers and this one uses two of them in a single sentence. There is nothing to match and nothing to agree with, so answer with whichever comes to you first.

cards.label: Why it is worth it
cards.head: The most useful small talk there is
cards.fr: Ça dépend du temps qu'il fait.
cards.body: Weather is what people talk about when there is nothing to say, which makes it the one subject you can raise with anybody on your first day. This is a question you will use more than any sentence in the last three lessons.

sections.title: The Balcony Downstairs
sections.say: Three people, one building, and all three frames in the space of a morning.
sections.text: The woman on the second floor puts her plants out the same week every year and takes them in again the same week every autumn. She has a sentence for it that she says to anybody on the stairs. « Au printemps, je sors les plantes. » This morning she is out there at seven, and it is not warm. « Il fait frais ce matin. » The man from the flat above her comes down in a coat and disagrees with her about it, in the way neighbours do. « Moi, j'ai froid. » Both of them are describing the same eleven degrees and neither of them is contradicting the other, because they are not talking about the same thing. She is describing the morning and he is describing himself, and French makes you choose which one you meant before you open your mouth. Then the coffee arrives from somewhere upstairs, and the third sentence turns up on its own. « Le café est chaud. » Three sentences, three verbs, and one thermometer between them.

glossary.note: The one season that takes au. The other three take en.
The weather, and the il here points at nobody at all.
A person, so avoir. He is describing himself and not the morning.
A thing, so être. This is the frame English speakers already have.
Read this as a whole phrase. The verb behind it is not one you have been given yet.

questions.q: Two neighbours describe the same morning and use different verbs. Are they disagreeing?
questions.a: No. She says il fait frais, which is about the morning, and he says j'ai froid, which is about himself. Both can be true at once, and French makes you decide which one you mean before you start the sentence.

questions.q: Three sentences in this passage use three different verbs on the same kind of adjective. What decides which verb?
questions.a: What the sentence is about. The weather takes il fait, a person takes avoir, and a thing takes être. The adjective does not change and neither does the temperature; only the subject does.

questions.q: The woman says au printemps rather than en printemps. Would en have worked?
questions.a: No. Spring is the only one of the four seasons that takes au, and en printemps is not something a French speaker says. Summer, autumn and winter all take en.

sections.title: The Weather, Banked
sections.say: Three decks. The four seasons, the frames, and the words for what is actually outside.

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French out loud, verb and all, before you flip.

cards.back: il fait du vent · il y a du vent
cards.say: il fait du vent, il y a du vent

cards.front: It rains a lot in autumn.

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Five lines, and between them all three verbs. One of them offers you a word you must decide not to use.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: The four seasons, the frames, and both halves of the contrast. The mic is listening for the verb.

sections.title: Back On The Roof
sections.say: One exchange, and you hold up your half. Every turn turns on which of the three you mean.
sections.setting: The same roof terrace, a week later, and this time you know which il is which.

turns.ai: Alors, tu montes ? Quel temps fait-il chez toi ?
turns.en: So, are you coming up? What is the weather like where you are?
turns.user: Il fait beau, il y a du soleil.
turns.userEn: The weather is nice, it is sunny.

alts.fr: Il fait chaud et il y a du soleil.
alts.en: It is hot and it is sunny.

turns.ai: Ici aussi. Mais il fait du vent sur le toit, attention.
turns.en: Here too. But it is windy on the roof, careful.
turns.user: Du vent ? Personne, alors.
turns.userEn: Wind? Nobody, then.

alts.fr: Ah, le vent. Pas un homme.
alts.en: Ah, the wind. Not a man.

alts.fr: Oui, il fait du vent, je sais.
alts.en: Yes, it is windy, I know.

turns.ai: Tu as froid ? Je prends une veste pour toi ?
turns.en: Are you cold? Shall I bring a jacket for you?
turns.user: Non, j'ai chaud. C'est le soleil.
turns.userEn: No, I am hot. It is the sun.

alts.en: No thanks, I am hot here.

turns.ai: J'ai fait du café. Attention, il est très chaud.
turns.en: I made coffee. Careful, it is very hot.
turns.user: Le café est chaud, oui. Merci !
turns.userEn: The coffee is hot, yes. Thank you!

alts.en: Thank you! The coffee is hot.
All right, the coffee is hot.

turns.ai: En hiver, c'est impossible ici. Et au printemps ?
turns.en: In winter it is impossible up here. And in spring?
turns.user: Au printemps, il fait doux. Parfait.
turns.userEn: In spring it is mild. Perfect.

alts.en: In spring the weather is nice.

alts.fr: Au printemps c'est parfait, il fait doux.
alts.en: In spring it is perfect, it is mild.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: You have just come in from the snow and you are cold. Say it.
cards.back: J'ai froid. A person has cold, not is cold. Weather makes, people have, things are.

cards.front: You want to say the day is cold. Say it.
cards.back: il fait froid. The weather makes cold, and the il is nobody.

cards.front: You want to warn somebody about a cup of coffee.
cards.back: Le café est chaud. A thing is what it is, so être.

cards.front: Which season takes au rather than en?
cards.back: au printemps. The other three take en, and this is the only exception.
en automne. The m is silent, so it ends on a plain n sound.

cards.front: Somebody says « Il fait du vent ». Who is doing something?
cards.back: Nobody. It is the sky. « Il fait du yoga » is the one with a man in it.
cards.say: il fait du vent, il fait du yoga

cards.front: Two ways to say it is windy.
cards.back: il fait du vent, and il y a du vent. Both are ordinary and neither is preferred.
cards.say: il fait du vent, il y a du vent

cards.front: You reach for « il fait pleut ». What is wrong with it?
cards.back: il pleut is already the whole sentence. It is one shape or the other, never both.

cards.front: You want to ask somebody what it is like outside.
cards.back: Quel temps fait-il ? Four words, learned as one block.

cards.front: Why is « je suis chaud » worth avoiding?
cards.back: It is real French about something else. A person has hot: j'ai chaud.

cards.front: How do you say it is twenty degrees?
cards.back: Il fait vingt degrés aujourd'hui. The weather frame, carrying a number.
