sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a conversation quietly go sideways because a word that means he meant nobody at all, then watched it go sideways again over a verb English does not have. You have the four seasons and the one that is different, you have seen the same adjective sitting in three sentences with three verbs on one screen, and you have sorted four ways of building a weather sentence that a lot of people carry around as one. You can also ask somebody what it is like outside, which is the sentence that will actually start conversations. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The sentence with nobody in it
rounds.say: The frame the weather uses, and who is in it.

questions.q: You are texting a friend about the day you are having outside. It is hot. What do you send?
questions.why: Weather makes, people have, things are. The weather takes il fait and the il points at nobody. The other three are all real French sentences about a thing, a man, or something nobody has mentioned.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: il fait chaud. The verb is one short unstressed syllable and it is the only thing in the sentence carrying who this is about, which is exactly the combination the ear loses at speed.

questions.q: In « il fait beau », who or what does the word il refer to?
questions.why: Nothing. It is holding a space open because a French sentence needs something in that position. The pronouns lesson taught you il means he, and this is the one place that stops being true.

questions.q: Somebody asks what it is like outside and the weather is nice. Write the three words.
questions.why: il fait beau. Two words of frame that never change, then the word for what the weather is like. You now have a sentence that works for every kind of weather there is.

rounds.label: Three en, and one au
rounds.say: Four seasons, and only one thing to get wrong.

questions.q: You are telling somebody the village is at its best in spring. Which is right?
questions.why: au printemps. It is the only one of the four that does not take en, and nobody says the version with en, so this stops the sentence rather than shifting what it means.

questions.q: Your holiday is in summer. Fix this. « Je pars au été. »
questions.why: Summer takes en, like autumn and winter. Only spring takes au, so carrying au across to the other three is the over-correction that arrives the week after the exception lands.

questions.q: Write the French for "in autumn".
questions.why: en automne. The m in automne is silent, so it comes out ending on a plain n sound, and that is the part a learner gets wrong long after the spelling is solid.

questions.q: Three of the four seasons take the same small word. What do those three have in common?
opts: They all begin on a vowel sound
questions.why: été, automne and hiver all open on a vowel sound and printemps does not. That is completely reliable for these four words and it is not a rule about French generally, so use it to hold this set and nothing wider.

rounds.label: A person has
rounds.say: When it is you who is hot.

questions.q: You have just come in from the snow and you want to say that you are cold. What do you say?
questions.why: Weather makes, people have, things are. A person has cold. The second is true about the weather and is not an answer about you, and the first and third are the two ways an English speaker reaches for être here.

questions.q: You are the one who is too warm. Fix this. « Je suis chaud. »
questions.why: A person has hot in French. The version with être is real French about something else, which is why nobody corrects it and why it is the error people remember having made.

questions.q: Listen. Is this about the weather or about a person?
questions.why: A person. Il a froid is a man who wants his coat, and il fait froid is the season. One short unstressed word apart, and that word is the only thing telling you which.

questions.q: A friend asks « Tu as froid ? » and you are fine. Which answer is built correctly?
opts: Non, je ne suis pas froid.
Non, il ne fait pas froid pour moi.
Non, ça va, je n'ai pas froid.
Non, je ne fais pas froid.
questions.why: The question was built with avoir, so the answer is too. The others swap in être or il fait, and the second one is about the weather rather than about you, which was what you were asked.

rounds.label: A thing is
rounds.say: The one that matches English, and the two places it does not belong.

questions.q: You want to warn somebody that the coffee will burn them. What do you say?
questions.why: Weather makes, people have, things are. A cup of coffee is a thing, so it takes être, and this is the one of the three that matches English word for word. That is also why it gets borrowed for the other two.

questions.q: The wind itself is cold, not the day. Fix this. « Le vent fait froid. »
questions.why: The wind is a thing here rather than the weather, so it takes être. Il fait du vent is a weather report; le vent est froid is a remark about the wind you are standing in.

questions.q: Which sentence in this list is about a THING rather than the weather or a person?
questions.why: Le thé est froid. A cup of tea is an object, so être. The first and last are the weather with nobody in them, and the second is a person, which is the whole three-way split this lesson turns on.

questions.q: Write the French for "the coffee is hot".
questions.why: le café est chaud. A thing, so être, and the accent on the e is the part a spellchecker will not put back for you.

rounds.label: Four shapes, not one
rounds.say: Four ways to build it, and one way to build it wrong.

questions.q: It has been raining all morning. Fix this. « Il fait pleut depuis ce matin. »
questions.why: Il pleut is already the whole sentence. Welding il fait onto it is what comes out after being told that il fait is the weather phrase, and it is one shape or the other, never both.

questions.q: It is raining right now. Say it out loud.
questions.why: Two words and nothing else. The mic is listening for the fact that you stopped, because the commonest thing to add here is a word this shape does not take.

questions.q: Somebody tells you « Il fait du vent » and somebody else tells you « Il y a du vent ». Which is right?
opts: Only il y a du vent
Neither, you need le vent est fort
questions.why: Both are ordinary French and mean the same thing. If nobody tells you that, meeting both makes you assume one is a mistake and avoid it, which costs you a sentence you had already learned.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT how French builds a weather sentence?
opts: il fait plus a word for what it is like
il fait du plus a thing
il plus one word that is the whole sentence
il est plus a word for what it is like
questions.why: The last one. Être belongs to things, so il est chaud is a remark about some object rather than about the day. The other three are the shapes this lesson sorted, and they all work.

rounds.label: Who is it about?
rounds.say: The four words that mean two completely different things.

questions.q: You hear « Il fait du yoga tous les matins. » What is this about?
questions.why: A man. The shape is identical to il fait du vent and the noun at the end is the entire difference, which is why you read to the end of the sentence before deciding who il is.

questions.q: Listen. Is the il in this sentence a person, or nobody at all?
opts: you cannot tell from the sound
questions.why: Nobody. This is the sky, and the sentence has no person in it anywhere. Il fait du yoga sounds the same for four words and then does not.

questions.q: You want to ask somebody what it is like outside. Fix this. « Quel temps il fait ? »
questions.why: The two words swap round and take a hyphen between them. Learn the four as one block: it is the question that will start more conversations for you than any sentence in the last three lessons.

questions.q: Write the French for "I am hot", meaning you personally.
questions.why: j'ai chaud. A person has hot. Reaching for the English verb here produces a sentence that is real French about something else, and nobody will explain to you why it is funny.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can name the four seasons with the small word each one takes, describe what the weather is doing four different ways, put the right verb in front of the right subject, and ask somebody what it is like outside. The third of those is the one that matters most and the one nobody would ever correct you on, which is why it is worth having drilled. Telling the time is next, and it uses a frame with nobody in it too.
points: Weather makes, people have, things are. Ask what is hot before you start the sentence.
il fait never changes. Two words, one shape, every kind of weather.
Three seasons take en. Spring takes au, and that is the whole exception.
il fait du vent is the sky. il fait du yoga is a man. Read to the end.

grammarAssumed: The full present of être, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, and its fixed expressions including avoir chaud and avoir froid, introduced in a1.07
du, de la and de l' in front of an uncountable noun, introduced in a1.29
il, elle and the rest of the subject pronouns, introduced in a1.05
The numbers from one to twenty, introduced in a1.02
The numbers from twenty-one to a hundred, introduced in a1.27
le, la, l' and les, introduced in a1.04
grammarIntroduced: The impersonal expression il fait plus an adjective, taught as one frozen form and never conjugated
The impersonal subject pronoun il, referring to no antecedent
The impersonal verbs pleuvoir and neiger in the third person singular
il y a plus a partitive article as a weather expression, and its overlap with il fait du
The preposition en in front of été, automne and hiver, and au in front of printemps
The three-way split between impersonal faire, avoir and être for one predicate adjective
The set question Quel temps fait-il, taught as an unanalysed block

overview.introFr: Un adjectif, trois verbes, et un « il » qui ne désigne personne du tout.

acts.title: Weather makes, people have, things are

acts.title: Four shapes, not one

acts.title: Say it, spell it, use it

lessons.reframe: Weather makes, people have, things are.

errorTriggers.description: Says « il est chaud » or « c'est chaud » about the weather. Reaches for être because English uses is, and produces a sentence about some object instead.
Says « en printemps », or carries au across to the other three seasons once the exception has landed.
Says « je suis chaud » or « je suis froid » about themselves. The error that actually embarrasses people, because it is real French about something else.
Says « le café fait chaud » or « le vent fait froid ». The over-correction that arrives once il fait has landed, and it spreads to objects that never wanted it.
Welds the first shape onto the third and produces « il fait pleut ». Exactly what a learner says after being taught il fait as the weather phrase.
Reads « il fait du vent » as a man doing something, because a1.05 taught that il means he and nothing has said where that stops.
The mirror of the one above: reads « il fait du yoga » as the weather once the empty il has landed, and loses the man in the sentence.

drills.title: What the weather takes
drills.coach: Look at what the sentence is about rather than at the adjective. If it is the day or the sky, it takes il fait. If it is an object sitting somewhere, it takes être.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are describing the day you are having outside. Which is right?
drills.why: The weather takes il fait, and the il in it points at nobody. The other two are real sentences about an object that nobody has mentioned.

drills.title: en, or au
drills.coach: Three of the four take en and spring takes au. If you are stuck, say the season out loud: the three that take en all open on a vowel sound.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: The garden is at its best in spring. Which is right?
drills.why: Spring is the only one of the four that takes au. Nobody says the version with en, so this one stops the sentence rather than changing what it means.

drills.title: A person has
drills.coach: Read the English on the left. Say the French on the right, and notice that every one of them is built on avoir rather than on the verb English uses.
pairs: She is hot in the waiting room.
Elle a chaud dans la salle d'attente.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You have just come in from the snow and you are cold. Which is right?
drills.why: A person has cold in French. The third one is true about the weather and is not an answer about you, and the first is the sentence English hands you.

drills.title: A thing is what it is
drills.coach: Every line here is correct French, which is the point. Ask what the sentence is about: a cup and the wind are things, and a day and a season are the weather.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want to warn somebody that the coffee will burn them. Which is right?
drills.why: A cup of coffee is a thing, so it takes être. This is the one of the three frames that matches English word for word, which is also why it gets borrowed for the other two.

drills.title: Four shapes, one sentence
drills.coach: Il pleut and il neige are already whole sentences and take nothing in front of them. Il fait and il y a both want something after them. Pick one shape and finish it.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: It has been raining all morning. Which is right?
opts: Il fait pleut depuis ce matin.
Il y a pleut depuis ce matin.
drills.why: Il pleut is the whole sentence already. Both of the others bolt a second shape onto the front of it, which is what comes out after being told that il fait is the weather phrase.

drills.title: Who is il?
drills.coach: Every line opens the same way, so the opening tells you nothing. Read to the noun at the end: if it is something in the sky, il is nobody, and if it is something a person does, il is a person.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You hear « Il fait du vent ». Who is doing something?
drills.why: Nobody. Il fait du yoga is the one with a man in it, and the two are identical for four words. The noun at the end is the whole difference.

il est chaud aujourd'hui. Audible, and it turns a weather report into a remark about an object.
le café fait chaud. Audible, and it is the over-correction that follows the weather rule.
il fait pleut. Audible, and it is not French at all, so it stops.
hearing il fait du vent as a man. Silent, because nothing about it is wrong, so nobody corrects it.
il fait chaud [EEL FEH SHOH] · il fait froid [EEL FEH FRWAH]

rows.k: a person, as a set phrase

j'ai chaud [zhay SHOH] · j'ai froid [zhay FRWAH]

rows.say: le café est chaud, le vent est froid

sections.title: Why there is nothing to carry across
sections.body: English uses one verb for all three of these and French uses three, which is the whole reason this is hard rather than merely new. English says it is hot, I am hot and the coffee is hot, and the verb is the same word every time, so a learner reaching for a translation finds one French verb and uses it in all three places. It happens to be the wrong one twice. The weather takes il fait and the il in front of it refers to nothing whatsoever: not a man, not a thing, not something said earlier. A person takes avoir, which you already met as a fixed expression, and the useful way to hold it is that a person HAS hot rather than being it. A thing takes être, and that is the one that lines up with English, which is exactly why it gets borrowed for the other two. The good news is that the choice is never a matter of taste. Decide what the sentence is about before you start it and the verb follows with no judgement involved: the sky, a person, or an object. The second thing worth knowing is that the two errors run in opposite directions and the second one arrives after the first is fixed. A learner told to use il fait for the weather starts putting it in front of cups of coffee within a week, which is why the drills here sort both ways rather than only asking you to add il fait. Finally, the empty il is not a quirk of the weather. French uses the same trick elsewhere and you will meet it again, so the habit of asking who il actually is, rather than assuming, is worth more than this lesson alone.

sections.title: The four, both ways
rows: one n sound links the two words
the m is silent, the n is real
the h is silent, so en links straight in

rows.v: The three that take en all open on a vowel sound. printemps does not. Reliable for these four words only.
rows.say: au printemps, en été, en automne, en hiver

rows.v: Written with an m and said with none: [oh-TONN]. The n at the end is a real n you do pronounce.
Two nasal sounds and a silent ps at the end: [luh prehⁿ-TAHⁿ].
The h is silent, so en runs straight into it and the two words come out as one piece.
au printemps is the only one. There is no reason behind it and no wider rule to learn.

sections.title: Why two of the four say the same thing
sections.body: Il fait du vent and il y a du vent both mean it is windy, both are ordinary, and neither is preferred by anybody. That is worth saying out loud because a learner who meets both without being told will assume one of them is a mistake and spend a year avoiding a sentence they already knew how to build. The same is true of du soleil and du brouillard: either opening works. What the two shapes have in common is what comes after them, which is du or de la and then a thing rather than a word describing what the weather is like. That small word is the one the partitive lesson gave you and it is doing exactly the job it was taught for, so there is nothing new to learn here beyond noticing that the weather is a place it turns up constantly. The two shapes that do not overlap with anything are the first and the third. Il fait takes a describing word straight after it with no small word in between, and il pleut and il neige take nothing at all, because each of those is already a complete sentence on its own. That last point is the one worth holding, because the commonest error in this whole lesson is bolting il fait onto the front of il pleut, and it comes from exactly the right instinct applied one step too far.

weatherFrame.title: The frame the weather uses
weatherFrame.body: The weather takes il fait and then the word for what it is like: il fait chaud, il fait froid, il fait beau. Nothing in that sentence is a person or a thing, and nothing agrees with anything. Il fait never changes: there is no other form of it anywhere in this frame, so you can learn these two words as one block and reuse them for every kind of weather there is. English uses is here and French does not, which is why this has to be learned rather than worked out.

examples.note: Today, described. This is the sentence the whole lesson is built to get right.
The same two words, a different season, and nothing else moved.

personFrame.title: A person has hot, they are not hot
personFrame.body: When it is a person who is hot or cold, French uses avoir: j'ai chaud, tu as froid, elle a chaud. You met this in the avoir lesson as one of the fixed expressions and it is unchanged here. What is new is that it now sits beside a weather sentence built on the same adjective, so the two are easy to swap. Saying je suis chaud instead of j'ai chaud is the error that gets remembered, because it does not mean nothing in French. It means something else.

examples.note: The person, not the room. Two words, and it is avoir rather than être.
A man is cold in an office. This il is a person, and the frame shows it.

thingFrame.title: A thing is what it is
thingFrame.body: A cup of coffee, the wind, the water: an object takes être, exactly the way the être lesson taught it. Le café est chaud. Le vent est froid. This is the one of the three that matches English word for word, which makes it the one a learner reaches for by default and uses in the two places it does not belong. It is correct about things and wrong about both the weather and people, so the useful skill is noticing which of the three you are talking about before you start the sentence.

examples.note: A thing, so être. The same adjective as the weather sentence and a different frame.
The wind itself is a thing. Il fait du vent is the weather; le vent est froid is the wind.

seasonIn.title: Three take en, one takes au
seasonIn.body: To say what happens in a season: en été, en automne, en hiver, and au printemps. Three of the four take the same small word and spring takes a different one, with no meaning behind the difference. There is a hook that works for exactly these four: the three that take en all begin with a vowel sound, and printemps is the one that begins on a consonant. That is reliable for these four words and it is not a rule about French generally, so use it to remember the set and nothing wider.

examples.note: The exception, and the only one. Spring is the season you have to remember separately.
The pattern the other three follow. Summer, autumn and winter all take the same word.

emptyIl.title: This il refers to nothing at all
emptyIl.body: In il fait beau, the il points at no one. Not a man, not a thing, not something mentioned earlier: nothing. It is there because a French sentence needs something in that position, and it carries no meaning of its own. The pronouns lesson taught you that il means he, and that is true everywhere except here. The test is what comes after it: il fait du vent is the weather, and il fait du yoga is a man in a room, and those two sentences are the same four words of shape.

examples.note: Nobody is doing anything. This il is a placeholder and the sentence is about the sky.
Same opening, and now it is a man. The word after du is the whole difference.

recorded.desc: THE THREE FRAMES AS ONE TAKE PER ADJECTIVE, BY ONE VOICE AT ONE PACE. « Il fait chaud », « J'ai chaud » and « Le café est chaud » spoken CONSECUTIVELY IN THE SAME TAKE, in that order, so the only thing the learner hears changing is the verb. Recorded apart they compare three performances instead of three meanings and the whole teaching is lost. Then the same three on froid: « Il fait froid », « J'ai froid », « Le vent est froid ». Do not lean on the verb to make it clearer. Fait, ai and est are all unstressed in ordinary speech, and a learner who only hears the difference when it is emphasised will not hear it in a café. ALSO IN THIS TAKE, adjacent and in this order: « il fait chaud », « il a chaud », « il est chaud ». Those three are the listening mission and the quiz round built on it, they differ by one short unstressed syllable, and they must be one performance or the exercise is testing the recording rather than the ear.

« IL FAIT DU VENT » AND « IL FAIT DU YOGA » ADJACENT IN THE SAME TAKE, in that order, because the pair IS the lesson and two recordings are two performances. Read BOTH completely straight and at the same pace: the entire teaching is that they are identical for four words and then are not, so any difference in delivery before the final noun destroys it. Do NOT pause before the noun and do not lean on it. Then the same treatment for « Il fait du brouillard ce matin » against « Il fait de la pêche près de la rivière », and for « Il fait froid » against « Il a froid », which is the same collision one letter apart. The scene line « Il fait du vent dehors » is Nadia speaking to somebody she likes, standing in wind, and it should sound like a remark rather than a demonstration.
clipIds: Il fait du yoga tous les matins.
Il fait du brouillard ce matin.
Il fait de la pêche près de la rivière.

recorded.desc: THE FOUR SEASONS IN CALENDAR ORDER, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, WITH THE PREPOSITION ATTACHED: « au printemps », « en été », « en automne », « en hiver ». Four bare nouns teach nothing this lesson needs, and the small word in front is the entire content of the mission. Read them with an even beat, the way somebody lists things, then again slowly in the same take. « au printemps » comes FIRST so the exception is heard against the three that follow it rather than buried among them. Keep every nasal closed: printemps carries TWO nasal vowels and NO n sound in either, and en carries one in all three of the others. The liaison in « en été », « en automne » and « en hiver » is a real linking n and it should sound like one smooth piece rather than two words. SEPARATELY IN THIS TAKE, RECORD « automne » SLOWLY ONCE IN ISOLATION. The m is SILENT and the n at the end is a REAL PRONOUNCED CONSONANT, close to oh-TONN with no nasal vowel anywhere in the word. That is the pronunciation the learner will get wrong, the deck is the only place the word is heard alone, and a reader who nasalises it teaches the opposite of what this lesson says.

The four shapes, grouped by shape rather than by weather, so the learner hears the STRUCTURE repeating. First « il fait beau », « il fait chaud », « il fait froid », « il fait frais » straight through with the same two opening words each time and no pause after them: the frame is one block and a reader who breathes between fait and the adjective teaches the learner that something belongs there. Then « il fait du vent », « il fait du soleil », « il fait du brouillard ». Then « il pleut » and « il neige », both short and both complete, with a clear silence after each so it is audible that nothing follows. Then « il y a du vent », « il y a du soleil », « il y a des nuages », « il y a de l'orage ». FINALLY, adjacent and in one breath: « il fait du vent » immediately followed by « il y a du vent », at the same pace and with no emphasis on either, because the learner has to hear that these are two ordinary ways of saying one thing rather than a correction of one by the other.

« Quel temps fait-il ? » as ONE BLOCK at ordinary conversational speed, the way somebody actually asks it, then once more slowly in the same take. It is four words and the learner is being taught it as a single unit, so do not separate them and do not put a rise on temps. The t of fait links into il and that link is the reason this sounds like three syllables rather than four: keep it. Then « Quel temps fait-il aujourd'hui ? » and « Fait-il beau à Paris en ce moment ? » so the shape is heard surviving inside a longer question. Finish with two ordinary answers, « Il fait beau et il y a du soleil » and « Il fait vingt degrés aujourd'hui », read as replies rather than as examples.
clipIds: Fait-il beau à Paris en ce moment ?
Il fait beau et il y a du soleil.

recorded.desc: The five traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them so the learner hears a difference rather than a correction. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically. Three of the five are real French sentences that mean something else, and a performance that marks them as errors removes the reason they are dangerous: « Je suis chaud » is grammatical and lands somewhere the learner did not intend, « Il est chaud aujourd'hui » parses perfectly as a remark about an object, and hearing « Il fait du vent » as a man is not an error of production at all. « Il fait pleut » and « En printemps » are the two that genuinely stop, and they still get read straight.

The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of a woman in her thirties on her own roof, talking to a friend rather than to a class. The beat where she explains that nobody is doing anything (« Qui ? Personne. Le vent ! ») must be AMUSED AND WARM rather than corrective or exasperated: the whole point of the scene is that the misunderstanding costs nothing socially and is simply funny, and any edge on that line turns it into a telling-off. The closing line, where she says the weather version straight back at the learner, is the one that has to be perfectly ordinary, because the learner is meant to notice they can now hear it.
clipIds: Oui, il fait chaud ici. On rentre ?

lessons.title: Les adjectifs de base
lessons.intro: Six describing words you will use every day, and the first thing to know about them is that they do not go where the colours went. This is how to put them in front of the thing, get the feminine right on all six, and use the two extra shapes that appear in front of a vowel.

say.text: One sentence, every word correct, and the conversation switches to English. Watch why.

setting.place: An estate agent's office, a folder of listings, and twenty minutes

beats.text: You have twenty minutes with an estate agent and a list of three places to see. You have the words for all of it.
You want somewhere big with a small garden. Last lesson taught you where a describing word goes, so you are not worried about this bit.

beats.speaker: Nadia
beats.fr: Alors, qu'est-ce que vous cherchez exactement ?
beats.en: So, what exactly are you looking for?
beats.stage: She has a folder open and a pen already moving.

beats.prompt: A big house. Which one comes out of your mouth?

options.en: the one that follows last lesson
the one that puts the word first

followUp.works: Yes, and it is the order English would give you, which is the one thing about this that is easy. Watch what the other line does.
followUp.breaks: That is where a colour goes, and you built the habit last lesson. Watch what it costs.

beats.speaker: You
beats.en: I am looking for a big house, with the words in last lesson's order.

beats.speaker: Nadia
beats.fr: Ah, a big one. No problem, I have three.
beats.en: She has answered in English, and she is going to stay there.
beats.stage: Nothing was misunderstood. She just decided which language this was going to be.

beats.heading: Nothing went wrong, and that is the problem
beats.body: Every word was right and she understood you completely. She answered in English anyway, because the order told her more about your French than the words did. Nobody corrected anything, so nothing tells you it happened.

wrong.en: a big house, with the word where a colour would go

beats.coach: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. Both lines mean the same thing, which is exactly why nobody will ever tell you.

beats.speaker: Second try
beats.fr: Je cherche une grande maison, avec un petit jardin.
beats.en: I am looking for a big house, with a small garden.

beats.speaker: Nadia
beats.fr: Un petit jardin, d'accord. J'ai exactement ça, dans une vieille rue très calme.
beats.en: A small garden, alright. I have exactly that, on a very quiet old street.
beats.stage: She stayed in French, and she is now telling you about a street you have not seen.

beats.text: The same words, the same meaning, and one of them moved. That is the whole difference between the two halves of that conversation.

closing.text: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. That sentence is the next twenty-five minutes.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the first one is the one nobody will ever correct you on.

goals.t: Put these six in front of the thing
goals.s: Which is not where the colours went, and is the one difference a listener notices without ever mentioning it.

goals.t: Name six words you will use daily
goals.s: Big, small, beautiful, old, good and bad. Between them they describe most of what you will want to describe.

goals.t: Get the feminine right on all six
goals.s: Three of them follow the rule you already have. Three of them do something else, and nothing about the word tells you which.

goals.t: Say bel and vieil in front of a vowel
goals.s: A third shape that beau and vieux take and almost nothing else does, used constantly and taught late everywhere else.

sections.title: Which Side Of The Thing
sections.say: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. Tap any cell to hear it. The same thing is being described on both sides.

rows.say: une maison bleue, une grande maison

detail.title: The house, twice
detail.body: Elle habite dans une grande maison. The colour goes behind the house and the size goes in front of it. Nothing about the house changed between the two, and nothing about the two words is different except where they sit.
detail.say: Elle habite dans une grande maison.

rows.say: une jupe verte, une petite robe

detail.title: The same sentence opening, both ways
detail.body: Elle porte une jupe verte. Elle porte une petite robe rouge. Two real sentences that start with the same three words. In the first the describing word is last. In the second there are two of them, one at each end.
detail.say: Elle porte une jupe verte. Elle porte une petite robe rouge.

rows.say: un chien blanc, un petit chien

detail.title: The dog, twice
detail.body: J'ai un petit chien blanc. That sentence has both in it: the size in front of the dog and the colour behind it. Say it out loud and notice that you never had to think about the order in English.

rows.say: une robe bleue, une belle robe

detail.title: And both at once
detail.body: Elle porte une belle robe bleue. One dress, two describing words, and one of them at each end. This is what the pattern looks like when it is finished, and it is a published sentence rather than a made-up one.
detail.say: Elle porte une belle robe bleue.

sections.title: One Phrase, Both Orders
sections.hint: Four cards. Each one has both in it.
sections.say: The clearest proof of this is one sentence with a word at each end. Here are three of them.

cards.label: What a1.13 gave you
cards.head: The colour goes last
cards.sub: [pə-TEET] · She is wearing a green skirt.
cards.body: This is the sentence you finished the last lesson able to write. The skirt, then its colour. Hold on to it, because the next card starts exactly the same way and does something different.

cards.label: The same opening
cards.head: And now a size, in front
cards.fr: Elle porte une petite robe rouge.
cards.sub: [pə-TEET] · She is wearing a small red dress.
cards.body: Three identical words, then two describing words in one phrase, one at each end. The size is in front of the dress and the colour is behind it, and both are correct in the same breath.

cards.label: Again, with a different pair
cards.head: Beautiful in front, blue behind
cards.fr: Elle porte une belle robe bleue.
cards.sub: [BEL] · She is wearing a beautiful blue dress.
cards.body: One dress, one sentence, and the two words sitting on opposite sides of it. Nobody chose this to make a point: it is a published corpus sentence and this is simply what French does.

cards.label: The whole idea
cards.head: Where, not whether
cards.sub: [pə-TEE] · I have a small white dog.
cards.body: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. Both words are describing the same dog and they are not competing for the same slot. There is nothing to decide between them: one goes in front and one goes behind.

sections.title: Six, One At A Time
sections.hint: Swipe. Say each one out loud before you move on.
sections.say: Six screens, one word each. Say it out loud before you swipe, and put it in front of something.

cards.label: 1 of 6
cards.body: It goes in front of the thing it describes.

cards.label: 2 of 6
cards.body: It goes in front of the thing it describes.

cards.label: 3 of 6
cards.body: It goes in front of the thing it describes.

cards.label: 4 of 6
cards.body: It goes in front of the thing it describes.

cards.label: 5 of 6
cards.body: It goes in front of the thing it describes.

cards.label: 6 of 6
cards.body: It goes in front of the thing it describes.

sections.title: Each One On Something Real
sections.hint: Six published sentences, one per word.
sections.say: The same six, this time attached to something. Every sentence here is one somebody has already written.

cards.label: big, tall
cards.head: grand
cards.body: The plain form, which is what you use for one thing of the un kind. The feminine is coming, and for this one it changes the sound.

cards.label: small, little
cards.head: petit
cards.body: The plain form, which is what you use for one thing of the un kind. The feminine is coming, and for this one it changes the sound.

cards.label: beautiful, good-looking
cards.head: beau
cards.body: The plain form, which is what you use for one thing of the un kind. The feminine is coming, and for this one it changes the sound.

cards.label: old
cards.head: vieux
cards.body: The plain form, which is what you use for one thing of the un kind. This one already ends in the letter a plural would add, which matters later.

cards.label: good
cards.head: bon
cards.body: The plain form, which is what you use for one thing of the un kind. The feminine is coming, and for this one it changes the sound.

cards.label: bad
cards.head: mauvais
cards.body: The plain form, which is what you use for one thing of the un kind. This one already ends in the letter a plural would add, which matters later.

sections.title: One Word, Four Shapes
sections.hint: The same word on four different things.
sections.say: One boy, one girl, then more than one of each. Only the ending moves, and last lesson already taught you why.

cards.label: one of the un kind
cards.head: grand
cards.body: The plain form, and the d at the end is silent.

cards.label: one of the une kind
cards.head: grande
cards.body: The thing is the une kind, so an e arrives and the sleeping d wakes up with it. You can hear this one clearly.

cards.label: more than one, un kind
cards.head: grands
cards.body: The s is written and never said. This is the same sound as the plain form, exactly as it was with the colours.

cards.label: more than one, une kind
cards.head: grandes
cards.body: Both endings are there. It sounds identical to the one before it, because the s adds nothing to any word ever.

cards.label: nothing here is new
cards.head: You already have this rule
cards.fr: Ce garçon est très grand. Les filles sont grandes.
cards.sub: from one thing of the un kind to several of the une kind
cards.body: That is the same four-shape grid the colours had, doing the same job for the same reason. The thing being described decides, the describing word follows, and the plural is silent. None of it has changed.

sections.title: All Six, Both Shapes
sections.say: Tap any row to hear both halves. Every single one of these six changes sound, which the colours did not.

detail.title: grand to grande
detail.body: [GRAHⁿ] becomes [GRAHⁿD], so the d at the end wakes up. Ce garçon est très grand. Cette fille est très grande. Les garçons sont grands. Les filles sont grandes.
detail.say: Ce garçon est très grand. Cette fille est très grande. Les garçons sont grands. Les filles sont grandes.

detail.title: petit to petite
detail.body: [pə-TEE] becomes [pə-TEET], so the t at the end wakes up. Elle a un petit chien. Il a une petite voiture. Nous avons de petits problèmes. Elle porte de petites chaussures.
detail.say: Elle a un petit chien. Il a une petite voiture. Nous avons de petits problèmes. Elle porte de petites chaussures.

detail.title: beau to belle
detail.body: [BOH] becomes [BEL], so the word is replaced outright. C'est un beau jardin. C'est une belle maison. Ce sont de beaux tableaux. Ce sont de belles fleurs.
detail.say: C'est un beau jardin. C'est une belle maison. Ce sont de beaux tableaux. Ce sont de belles fleurs.

detail.title: vieux to vieille
detail.body: [VYUH] becomes [VYEY], so the word is replaced outright. Mon grand-père est vieux. Ma grand-mère est vieille. Ce sont de vieux amis. Ce sont de vieilles photos.
detail.say: Mon grand-père est vieux. Ma grand-mère est vieille. Ce sont de vieux amis. Ce sont de vieilles photos.

detail.title: bon to bonne
detail.body: [BOHⁿ] becomes [BON], so the nasal collapses into a plain n. Le repas était très bon. La soupe est bonne. Les résultats sont bons. Les nouvelles sont bonnes.
detail.say: Le repas était très bon. La soupe est bonne. Les résultats sont bons. Les nouvelles sont bonnes.

detail.title: mauvais to mauvaise
detail.body: [moh-VEH] becomes [moh-VEHZ], so the s wakes up as a z. Ce film est mauvais. Cette idée est mauvaise. Les temps sont mauvais. Les odeurs sont mauvaises dans la cuisine.
detail.say: Ce film est mauvais. Cette idée est mauvaise. Les temps sont mauvais. Les odeurs sont mauvaises dans la cuisine.

sections.title: Three Groups, Not Six Rules
sections.say: The six, split by what the feminine actually does. Two of last lesson's four groups are empty here, which is worth noticing.

groups.label: Adds an -e, exactly like last lesson

check.q: These three add an e and nothing else. On how many of them can you HEAR it?
check.why: All three. grande says its d, petite says its t, mauvaise says its s as a z. That is the difference from last lesson, where four of the twelve colours changed sound and the rest did not.

check.q: bon does not become bone. What is the feminine?
check.why: bonne, with two n letters. The doubled n has to be there because a single one would leave the vowel nasal, which is the thing that stopped being true. You met this in the nasal lesson: an n followed by a vowel blocks it.

check.q: The feminine of beau is belle. What happened to beau?
opts: It was replaced by a different word
check.why: It was replaced. belle shares almost nothing with beau and vieille shares almost nothing with vieux, so these two are not the rule going wrong, they are two shapes to know. There is no way to work them out.

sections.title: The One That Changes Most
sections.hint: Four cards on the biggest sound change of the six.
sections.say: One word, and the vowel itself changes. Slow the audio down on this one.

cards.label: the plain form
cards.head: bon
cards.body: One sound, and there is no n in it at all. The n on the page is there to tell you the vowel is nasal, and it is never itself pronounced.

cards.label: the une kind
cards.head: bonne
cards.body: Two n letters and now you say one of them. The vowel stops being nasal and becomes a plain o. This is the largest change any of these six makes and it is impossible to miss.

cards.label: why it doubles
cards.head: A single n would not work
cards.body: The nasal lesson taught this exact mechanism: an n with a vowel behind it stops making the vowel nasal and starts being a consonant you say. Doubling the n is how the spelling gets a vowel behind the first one.

cards.label: what not to write
cards.head: Never bone
cards.body: bone with one n would be a different sound and is not a word. The doubling is not decoration and it is the only one of the six that does this, so it is worth writing out by hand once.

sections.title: You Can Hear All Six
sections.say: Six pairs, and something changes in every single one. That is not what happened last lesson.

lines.en: you hear a difference: the d at the end wakes up
you hear a difference: the t at the end wakes up
you hear a difference: the s wakes up as a z
you hear a difference: the nasal collapses into a plain n
you hear a difference: the word is replaced outright
you hear a difference: the word is replaced outright

questions.q: How many of those six pairs sounded identical?
questions.why: None. Every one of these six changes sound for the une kind, which is the opposite of the colours: bleu and bleue were the same word twice and four others already ended in an e. Here your ear is telling you the truth.

questions.q: On grand, petit and mauvais, what is making the sound?
opts: The e itself is being pronounced
A letter that was silent is now being said
The speaker is stressing the ending
questions.why: The consonant. The e is not itself a sound: it stops the letter in front of it being last in the word, so that letter gets said again. grand hides its d and grande says it, which is the silent letters lesson doing its job.

questions.q: None of those six pairs was a plural. Why not?
opts: Plurals were covered in an earlier lesson
Plural forms of these words are rare
The plural s is never pronounced, so there would be nothing to hear
The recording only had singular forms
questions.why: There is nothing to hear. The plural s is silent on all six, exactly as it was on every colour, so grand and grands are one sound. Your ear separates the two kinds here and can do nothing about the number.

sections.title: Now Without The Table
sections.say: Same decisions, nothing to look at. This is the one that tells you whether it landed.

groups.label: One thing of the une kind

check.q: Ma grand-mère, and the word is vieux. What do you write?
check.why: vieille. It is one of the two that get replaced rather than added to, so there is nothing to work out and nothing that would have told you. vieuxe is not a word and never was.

check.q: Several old friends, all of them the un kind. What do you write?
check.why: de vieux amis, unchanged. vieux already ends in an x and French will not stack a plural on top of it, so the singular and the plural are the same word on the page as well as in the air.

groups.label: The other one that does not move

check.q: Les temps, and the word is mauvais. What do you write?
check.why: mauvais, exactly as it was. The s is already there, so there is nothing to add. This is the same situation as vieux and they are the only two of the six it happens to.

check.q: Les filles, and the word is grand. What do you write?
check.why: grandes. The une kind, so an e, and more than one, so an s, in that order. You can hear the e and not the s, so half of that decision came from your ear and half from the girls.

sections.title: A Third Shape, Before A Vowel
sections.hint: Five cards. These two are used constantly.
sections.say: Two of the six have a shape you have not met, and it only exists in front of a vowel sound.

cards.label: the problem
cards.head: Two vowels, touching
cards.sub: [BOH] · a vowel sound at the start of the next word
cards.body: beau ends in a vowel sound and homme starts with one, and French will not run two of them together like that. You met the same pressure in the elision lesson, where le became l' for exactly this reason.

cards.label: the answer
cards.head: bel
cards.body: beau becomes bel, and the l gives the vowel something to land on. It sounds exactly like the feminine belle, and it is not the feminine: this is a man, and the word in front of him is un.

cards.label: the same thing again
cards.head: vieil
cards.fr: Mon grand-père a un vieil ami à Lyon.
cards.sub: [VYEY] · My grandfather has an old friend in Lyon.
cards.body: vieux becomes vieil for the same reason, and it sounds exactly like vieille. un vieil ami is one of the most common phrases in the language and almost every course leaves it until much later.

cards.label: on a thing rather than a person
cards.head: It is not about people
cards.body: arbre starts with a vowel, so the same thing happens. Nothing here is about whether the thing is a person: it is only ever about the first sound of the word that comes next.

cards.label: and the other one
cards.head: un vieil immeuble
cards.body: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. And when one of them lands in front of a vowel, it changes shape again. These two forms are worth more than anything else in this lesson because you will need them today.

sections.title: The Same Sentence, One Sound Apart
sections.say: Two rows, four real sentences, and the same opening on all four. Only the next word changed.
cols: next word starts with a consonant
next word starts with a vowel

rows.say: C'est un beau jardin. C'est un bel arbre.

detail.title: beau and bel
detail.body: C'est un beau jardin. C'est un bel arbre. Identical up to the describing word, and then one of them has to change because of a letter in the word after it. It's a beautiful garden. It's a beautiful tree.
detail.say: C'est un beau jardin. C'est un bel arbre.

rows.say: C'est un vieux château. C'est un vieil immeuble.

detail.title: vieux and vieil
detail.body: C'est un vieux château. C'est un vieil immeuble. Identical up to the describing word, and then one of them has to change because of a letter in the word after it. It's an old castle. It's an old building.
detail.say: C'est un vieux château. C'est un vieil immeuble.

sections.title: Five Traps
sections.say: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. Five things an English speaker writes in their first month, one per screen.

errors.wrong: Writing « une maison grande ».
errors.why: The highest-value one here, and the only one nobody will ever mention. It is understood perfectly, so it survives for years and marks every sentence you say. These six go in front, and the colours you learned last time do not.

errors.wrong: Writing « des vieuxs vélos ».
errors.why: vieux already ends in an x, so there is nothing to add and vieuxs has never been a word. mauvais does the same thing with its s. These two are the only place in this lesson where the careful move is to leave it alone.

errors.wrong: Writing « un beau homme ».
errors.why: homme starts with a vowel sound, and beau ends in one, so the two would collide. bel exists to stop that. It sounds identical to belle and it is not the feminine: the word in front is still un.

errors.wrong: Writing « la soupe est bone ».
errors.why: bonne doubles its n, and the doubling is doing real work: a single n would leave the vowel nasal, which is what bon is. Two n letters is what makes the o plain and the n audible.

errors.wrong: Writing « ma grand-mère est vieuxe ».
errors.why: vieux is one of the two that get replaced rather than added to. Applying last lesson's rule to it produces something that is not a word, and there is nothing about vieux that would have warned you. It has to be learned.

sections.title: The Board At The Bakery
sections.say: Four notices, and one of them has the describing word where English would have left it.
sections.text: The board inside the bakery door is where this part of town advertises itself, and most of it is people trying to let a room. « Grande chambre dans une vieille maison. » Whoever wrote that got both words into the right place, and the room has almost certainly gone already. Under it somebody is selling a bicycle and the whole notice is five words long. « Un vieux vélo, bon état. » Nothing on the end of either word, and nothing needed: one bicycle, and both words are the un kind. A third card is looking for a flatmate, and the writer has left the describing word exactly where English would put it. « Je cherche une personne calme dans un appartement grand. » Everybody who reads that will understand it, nobody will correct it, and every French reader will notice. The last one is the shortest thing on the board and it is selling the flat above the bakery. « Belle vue, petit loyer. »

glossary.note: In front of the room, which is where these six go. The d is pronounced here because of the e.
The une kind, so vieux is replaced by vieille rather than gaining an ending.
The un kind and one of it, so the plain form. A second bicycle would change nothing at all.

glossary.en: a big flat, with the words the wrong way round
glossary.note: This should be un grand appartement. It is understood, and it is the thing this lesson exists to stop.
The une kind, so beau becomes belle. In front of the view, as always.

questions.q: Three of the four notices put the describing word in the same place. Which one does not, and what should it say?
questions.a: The flatmate notice says « un appartement grand ». It should say « un grand appartement ». All six of the words in this lesson go in front of the thing, and this one has been left where English would put it.

questions.q: The bicycle notice says « un vieux vélo ». What would it say for two bicycles?
questions.a: Exactly the same thing: « de vieux vélos ». vieux already ends in an x, so the plural adds nothing to it. Only the word for bicycle changes, and even that change is silent.

questions.q: Would a French reader notice the mistake in the flatmate notice if somebody read the board out loud?
questions.a: Yes, and this is the one error in the lesson you can hear, because word order is the one thing that is never silent. Every other mistake here is about an ending, and endings are half inaudible. An order is always audible.

sections.title: The Six, Banked
sections.say: Three decks. The six plain forms, the six feminines, and the two that change again in front of a vowel.

cards.en: grand becomes grande, and the d at the end wakes up
petit becomes petite, and the t at the end wakes up
mauvais becomes mauvaise, and the s wakes up as a z
bon becomes bonne, and the nasal collapses into a plain n
beau becomes belle, and the word is replaced outright
vieux becomes vieille, and the word is replaced outright
beau becomes bel in front of a vowel sound
vieux becomes vieil in front of a vowel sound

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French out loud, and put it on the correct side of the thing before you flip.

cards.front: big, tall, describing one thing of the une kind
small, little, describing one thing of the une kind
beautiful, good-looking, describing one thing of the une kind
old, describing one thing of the une kind
good, describing one thing of the une kind
bad, describing one thing of the une kind
She is wearing a small red dress.
cards.back: Elle porte une petite robe rouge.
cards.say: Elle porte une petite robe rouge.

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Six lines. On four of them the ending you write is one you can hear, which is new, and on one of them it is not.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: Fourteen words and three sentences. Every feminine here sounds different from its plain form, so this one your ear can actually check.

sections.title: Back At The Agency
sections.say: One exchange, and you hold up your half. Every turn needs one of the six in the right place.
sections.setting: The same office, three days later. Nadia wants to know which of the three you want, and she has stayed in French this time.

turns.ai: Alors, vous avez vu les trois. Laquelle vous a plu ?
turns.en: So, you have seen all three. Which one did you like?
turns.user: La grande maison, dans la vieille rue.
turns.userEn: The big house, on the old street.

alts.fr: La grande maison, s'il vous plaît.

turns.ai: Ah oui, celle-là. Et le jardin, il vous convient ?
turns.en: Ah yes, that one. And the garden, does it suit you?
turns.user: C'est un petit jardin, mais il est beau.
turns.userEn: It is a small garden, but it is beautiful.

alts.fr: Oui, un petit jardin, c'est parfait.
alts.en: Yes, a small garden is perfect.

alts.fr: Le jardin est petit et très beau.
alts.en: The garden is small and very beautiful.

turns.ai: Et le bâtiment à côté ? Vous l'avez regardé ?
turns.en: And the building next door? Did you look at it?
turns.user: Oui. C'est un vieil immeuble, mais il est beau.
turns.userEn: Yes. It is an old building, but it is beautiful.

alts.fr: Un vieil immeuble, oui, et il me plaît.
alts.en: An old building, yes, and I like it.

turns.ai: Bien. Et l'appartement au centre, qu'est-ce que vous en pensez ?
turns.en: Good. And the flat in the centre, what do you think of it?
turns.user: Ce n'est pas un mauvais appartement, mais il est trop petit.
turns.userEn: It is not a bad flat, but it is too small.

alts.fr: Il est trop petit pour moi.
alts.en: It is too small for me.

alts.fr: C'est un petit appartement, un peu trop petit.
alts.en: It is a small flat, a little too small.

turns.ai: Donc la maison. Vous êtes sûr ?
turns.en: So the house. Are you sure?
turns.user: Oui. Une grande maison, un beau jardin, une bonne rue.
turns.userEn: Yes. A big house, a beautiful garden, a good street.

alts.fr: Oui, la grande maison avec le beau jardin.
alts.en: Yes, the big house with the beautiful garden.
Certain. It is a good house.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: A big house. Where does the word for big go?
cards.back: une grande maison. In front of the house, which is not where a colour goes.

cards.front: A green skirt. Where does the colour go?
cards.back: Elle porte une jupe verte. Behind the skirt, and that has not changed.
Elle est grande. grande, and the silent d wakes up so you can hear it.
petite, and the silent t wakes up.
mauvaise, and the silent s comes back as a z.
C'est une bonne idée. bonne, with two n letters, and the vowel stops being nasal.
Ils achètent une belle maison. belle. It is not beau with an ending, it is a different word.
vieille. Also a different word, and vieuxe has never existed.

cards.front: un ___ homme, and the word is beau.
cards.back: C'est un bel homme. bel, because homme starts with a vowel sound.

cards.front: un ___ ami, and the word is vieux.
cards.back: Mon grand-père a un vieil ami à Lyon. vieil, for the same reason.
cards.say: Mon grand-père a un vieil ami à Lyon.

cards.front: Several old friends, all the un kind.
cards.back: Ce sont de vieux amis. vieux does not change, because the x is already there.

cards.front: Can you hear the plural on any of these six?
cards.back: Never. The s is silent on all six, exactly as it was on every colour.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a conversation quietly switch to English over one word order, learned six describing words you will use every day, and found out that three of their feminine forms follow the rule you already had and three of them replace the word instead. You have met a third shape that beau and vieux take in front of a vowel and that almost nothing else in the language has, and you have discovered that unlike the colours, every one of these six can be heard changing. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: Which side of the thing
rounds.say: Word order, which is the one thing in this lesson that is never silent.

questions.q: Your sister has a big house. Which line do you write?
questions.why: Elle a une grande maison. The word goes in front of the house, and it takes an e because a house is the une kind. The first option is the one a listener understands perfectly and never corrects.

questions.q: A green skirt, and a small dog. Which pair puts both words where French wants them?
opts: une jupe verte, un petit chien
une verte jupe, un chien petit
une jupe verte, un chien petit
une verte jupe, un petit chien
questions.why: The colour goes behind the skirt and the size goes in front of the dog. Those are two different rules operating at once and both of them are already yours: one from last lesson and one from this one.

questions.q: Write the French for a big house. The word for house is maison, and it is the une kind.
questions.why: une grande maison. In front of the house and carrying an e. Word order is the half of this that a French listener hears immediately, and the ending is the half they only see.

questions.q: In « Elle porte une petite robe rouge », why is one word in front of the dress and one behind it?
opts: Because petite is one of the six that come first and rouge is a colour
Because rouge has more letters than petite
Because petite matches the dress and rouge does not
Because the two could be swapped without changing anything
questions.why: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. Both words describe the same dress and neither is competing for the other's place. That sentence is a published one, not an invented example, which is what makes it worth remembering.

rounds.label: The six words
rounds.say: The names, quickly.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.why: mauvais. Its final s is silent, so it ends on the vowel and sounds like moh-VEH. It is the least frequent of the six and the one most likely to slip away, which is why it is here.

questions.q: Which one means the opposite of bon?
questions.why: mauvais. These six come in opposite pairs and it is worth using that: grand against petit, and bon against mauvais. Two of them are already the other one's answer, which halves what there is to remember.

questions.q: Write the French for old. Use the form for one thing of the un kind.
questions.why: vieux, ending in an x. That x is why the plural adds nothing to it later, and it is one of only two words in this lesson that behaves that way.

questions.q: Le repas était très bon. What is being said about the meal?
questions.why: It was good. bon is the plain form because a meal is the un kind, and here it sits after the verb rather than in front of a noun, which is the one position where all six behave like any other describing word.

rounds.label: The feminine
rounds.say: Three of the six follow the rule you already have. Three do not.

questions.q: Ma grand-mère, and the word is vieux. Write the word.
questions.why: vieille. It replaces vieux rather than adding to it, which is the half of this lesson that cannot be worked out from the plain form. vieuxe is what the rule from last lesson would have produced and it is not a word.

questions.q: Cette idée, and the word is mauvais. Write the word.
questions.why: mauvaise. This one is the plain rule doing its job: add an e. The reward is that the sleeping s wakes up as a z, so unlike most of last lesson you can hear that you got it right.

questions.q: Fix this. « La soupe est bone. »
questions.why: bonne, with two n letters. The doubling is what stops the vowel being nasal, so bone would be a different sound as well as a misspelling. This is the same mechanism the nasal lesson taught with brun and brune.

questions.q: Which of these feminines is NOT the plain form with an e added?
questions.why: belle. grande, petite and mauvaise are all their plain form plus an e, exactly as the colours were. belle is a different word from beau, and so is vieille from vieux, and there is nothing in either plain form that says so.

rounds.label: In front of a vowel
rounds.say: The shape almost nothing else in the language has.

questions.q: Un ___ homme. Which one goes in the gap?
questions.why: bel. homme starts with a vowel sound and beau ends in one, so the two would collide and French will not have it. bel sounds exactly like belle, and belle would be wrong here because the word in front is un.

questions.q: Un ___ ami. Write the word for old that fits.
questions.why: vieil. Same pressure as bel, same solution, and un vieil ami is one of the most common phrases you will hear. It sounds identical to vieille and it is not the feminine.

questions.q: C'est un beau jardin, but C'est un bel arbre. What decided which one to use?
opts: The first sound of the word that comes next
Whether the thing is the un kind or the une kind
Whether the speaker is being polite
questions.why: The first sound of the next word. jardin starts with a consonant and arbre starts with a vowel, and that is the whole of it. Nothing about gardens or trees comes into it, and nothing about people does either.

questions.q: Fix this. « C'est un vieux immeuble. »
questions.why: vieil immeuble. immeuble starts with a vowel sound, so vieux changes shape in front of it. This is the same thing the elision lesson showed you when le turned into l' before a vowel.

rounds.label: What does not move
rounds.say: Two of the six already end in the letter a plural would add.

questions.q: Several old friends, all of them the un kind. Which one do you write?
questions.why: de vieux amis. vieux already ends in an x and French does not stack a plural on top of it, so the word is spelled the same for one friend and for six. vieuxs has never existed.

questions.q: Fix this. « Les temps sont mauvaiss. »
questions.why: mauvais, unchanged. The s is already on the end of the word, so the plural adds nothing. mauvais and vieux are the only two of the six this happens to, and it happens for the same reason both times.

questions.q: Les garçons, and the word is grand. Write the word.
questions.why: grands. It sounds exactly like grand, because the plural s on a describing word is never pronounced, so the only reason to write it is that there is more than one boy. That much is unchanged from last lesson.

questions.q: Now the same thing about les filles. Write the word.
questions.why: grandes. An e for the girls being the une kind and an s for there being several, in that order. You can hear the e clearly and you cannot hear the s at all, which is the split this whole lesson turns on.

rounds.label: Heard, or only written
rounds.say: The last round, and this is the half that is different from the colours.

questions.q: Listen to these two: « bon » then « bonne ». What changed?
opts: Nothing, they are the same sound
The n is now pronounced and the vowel is plain
questions.why: The n arrives and the vowel stops being nasal. This is the biggest change any of these six makes, and it is the opposite of bleu and bleue last lesson, which were the same sound twice.

questions.q: Listen. Is the speaker describing one thing of the un kind, or one thing of the une kind?
questions.why: The une kind. You can hear the d on the end, and the d only arrives when the e is there. On these six the ear genuinely answers this question, which it could not do for bleu or noir.

questions.q: Say this out loud: my grandmother is old.
questions.why: vieille sounds nothing like vieux, so this is one of the few places in either lesson where getting it right out loud proves you also know what to write. Most agreement is not like this.

questions.q: You hear « Les garçons sont grands » and « Le garçon est grand ». What tells you the first one is about several boys?
opts: The way the speaker stresses the ending
The e sound at the end
Nothing in the describing word, only the words in front of it
questions.why: Nothing in the describing word. grand and grands are one sound, so les and garçons and sont are carrying the whole message. The feminine you can hear on these six; the plural you never can, on any word, ever.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can put six of the most useful describing words in the language in front of the thing they describe, get the feminine right on all six including the three that do not follow the rule, and use bel and vieil in front of a vowel, which most courses leave for much later. You also know that on these six your ear is worth trusting for the feminine and worth ignoring for the plural. Adjective placement is next, and it takes the fact this lesson stated and turns it into the system behind it.
points: Colours follow the noun. These six come first. That is the sentence to keep.
Three of the six add an e. bon doubles first, and beau and vieux are replaced outright.
In front of a vowel sound, beau becomes bel and vieux becomes vieil.
vieux and mauvais already end in the plural letter, so for several things they do not move.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that un and une follow it, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, introduced in a1.04
un, une and des, introduced in a1.11
The full present of être, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07
mon, ma and mes, introduced in a1.05
Adjective agreement, the four forms, and the silent plural -s, introduced in a1.13
That a final consonant is usually silent, and that a following e wakes it, introduced in sons.06
The nasal vowels and the fact that a following vowel blocks them, introduced in sons.03
That French avoids two vowel sounds meeting, introduced in sons.07
grammarIntroduced: The prenominal position of a closed set of six common adjectives, stated as a fact about these six and not as a system
Irregular feminine formation by suppletion: beau to belle, vieux to vieille
Feminine formation with consonant doubling: bon to bonne, and the denasalisation it produces
The third masculine form before a vowel: bel and vieil
Invariance of the masculine plural on adjectives already ending in -s or -x: vieux, mauvais
That the feminine of all six is audible, in contrast with a1.13, while the plural remains silent

overview.introFr: Six mots que vous utiliserez tous les jours, et ils ne se placent pas là où allaient les couleurs.

acts.title: Which side of the thing
acts.milestone: You have watched a conversation switch to English over one word order.

acts.title: The six words
acts.milestone: Six words, each one attached to a sentence somebody has already written.

acts.title: Her form
acts.milestone: Three of them follow the rule you had, three replace the word, and you can hear all six.

acts.title: Before a vowel
acts.milestone: bel and vieil, which almost nothing else in the language has and everybody uses.

acts.title: Say it, write it, use it
acts.milestone: You have read them on a real board and said all fourteen out loud.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. Adjective placement is next, and it starts where this one stopped.

lessons.reframe: Colours follow the noun. These six come first.

errorTriggers.description: Puts one of the six behind the noun, the way a colour goes. The default error on this lesson, because a1.13 taught the opposite order on every screen and nobody ever corrects this one out loud.
Reaches for the wrong one of the six, most often between bon and beau, which start the same way and mean nothing like each other.
Applies a1.13's rule to the half of this set it does not reach: writes vieuxe for vieille, beaue for belle, or bone for bonne.
Writes un beau homme or un vieux ami. Not a mistake a learner can hear themselves make, because both are perfectly pronounceable, and the correct forms are almost never taught this early.
Writes vieuxs or mauvaiss. The learner has just internalised "add an s" and applies it to the two words that already end in the letter.

Carries a1.13's conclusion across unchanged and stops listening, or listens for the plural and concludes their ear is at fault. Costs confidence rather than accuracy, which is why it gets its own drill.

drills.title: Which side does it go on?
drills.coach: Say the whole phrase out loud before you turn the card. If the word is one of these six it goes in front, and if it is a colour it goes behind.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: A big house. Which one?
drills.why: une grande maison. In front of the house, which is not where the colours went, and nobody will ever tell you if you get it wrong.

drills.title: English in, French out
drills.coach: The English is on the left. Say the French out loud before you turn the card, and put it in front of something.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one means bad?
drills.why: mauvais. bon and beau both start with a b and mean nothing like each other, which is what makes this trio worth saying out loud as a group rather than reading.

drills.title: What does the feminine do?
buckets: Adds an -e, exactly like last lesson
drills.coach: Say the feminine out loud before you place each one. If you added an e it is the first group; if you doubled a letter first it is the second; and if you said a completely different word it is the third.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: What is the feminine of vieux?
drills.why: vieille. It replaces the word rather than adding to it, and so does belle. Those two are the ones there is no way to work out.

drills.title: Which shape, in front of this word?
drills.coach: Ignore the describing word entirely and look at the word after it. If it starts with a vowel sound the describing word had to change, and if it starts with a consonant nothing happened.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: un ___ ami. Which one?
drills.why: vieil. ami starts with a vowel sound. It sounds exactly like vieille and it is not the feminine: the word in front is still un.

drills.title: Does the plural add anything?
drills.coach: Look at the last letter of the plain form. If it is already an s or an x, French will not put another one behind it, and the word for several things is the word you are looking at.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Several old friends, all the un kind. Which one?
drills.why: de vieux amis. The x is already there and nothing goes behind it. mauvais does the same, and they are the only two of the six.

drills.title: Heard, or only written
drills.coach: Say each one, then say it again with the plain form of the describing word. If the two versions sound different it goes on the left. If you said the same thing twice it goes on the right.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: How much of the plural can you hear on these six?
opts: some of it, on some words
drills.why: None of it. The plural s is silent on every one of these six, exactly as it was on every colour. The feminine is the half you can hear, and that part is new.
