contains: The six in all four shapes
What the feminine does to each

sections.title: In front of a vowel sound

rows.v: beau becomes bel. Never un beau homme: two vowel sounds would collide.
The same thing on a thing rather than a person. It is only ever about the next sound.
vieux becomes vieil. One of the most common phrases in the language.
Same again. bel and vieil sound exactly like belle and vieille and are not the feminine.
The feminine is unaffected by any of this: belle is belle in front of anything.

rows.k: Adds an -e, exactly like last lesson
rows.v: grand, petit, mauvais. Add an e, and on all three of them you can hear the last letter wake up.
bon. bonne doubles the n, which is what makes the vowel plain and the n audible.
beau, vieux. belle and vieille replace the word. There is nothing to work out and nothing that would have told you.

rows.k: vieux and mauvais for several things
rows.v: Both already end in the letter the plural would add, so the un kind never changes: un vieux vélo, des vieux vélos.
rows.say: un vieux vélo, des vieux vélos

rows.v: In front of the thing they describe, which is the opposite of where a colour goes. That is the one thing a listener hears immediately.
rows.say: une grande maison, une jupe verte

sheets.title: What you can hear
contains: Why the plural is still silent
How this differs from the colours

sections.title: Can you hear the feminine?
rows: the d at the end wakes up
the t at the end wakes up
the s wakes up as a z
the nasal collapses into a plain n

sections.title: Why this lesson sounds different from the last one
sections.body: The colour lesson spent an act teaching that most of agreement is invisible, and it was right about colours. Four of the twelve already ended in an e and were the same word for either kind of thing. Two more, bleu and noir, added an e that changed nothing you could hear. Only four of the twelve did anything audible at all, and the practical advice was to stop listening for the ending and work it out from the thing instead. That advice was correct and it does not transfer here. Every one of these six changes sound for the une kind, and they do it in three different ways. grand, petit and mauvais all end in a consonant that is silent while it is last in the word, and the feminine e stops it being last, so the d, the t and the s all come back. That is the silent letters lesson doing exactly what it said it would. bon is a different mechanism and a bigger change: the n on the end of bon is not a consonant at all, it is a mark telling you the vowel is nasal, and doubling it in bonne puts a vowel behind the first n, which makes it a real consonant and makes the vowel plain. You met that in the nasal lesson with brun and brune. beau and vieux do not do anything to their ending because they do not keep it: belle and vieille are different words and sound like it. So on these six the ear is a reliable guide to the feminine, which is worth knowing because a learner who took the last lesson at its word will have stopped listening. The plural is the part that has not changed at all. The s on grands, petits, bons and beaux is never pronounced, in any position, on any word, and grand and grands are the same recording. Nothing about listening more carefully will separate them, and a native speaker cannot do it either. So the rule is now in two halves and both of them are short: listen for the feminine and work out the plural.

whereTheySit.title: Not where the last lesson put them
whereTheySit.body: Colours go after the thing they describe, and you have just spent a lesson on that. These six go in front of it instead. Une grande maison, not une maison grande. That is the English order, which makes it easy to say and easy to forget, because the habit you built last lesson pulls the other way. Nobody will correct you if you get it wrong, since the sentence is perfectly understandable either way, and that is exactly why it is worth fixing now rather than later.

examples.note: A colour, sitting behind the thing, which is where every colour sits.
One phrase carrying both: the size in front, the colour behind.

theFeminine.title: Three of them follow the rule and three do not
theFeminine.body: You already know the rule from last lesson: for the une kind of thing, add an e. Grand becomes grande, petit becomes petite and mauvais becomes mauvaise, and nothing new is being asked of you there. Bon doubles its n first and becomes bonne. Beau and vieux do not add anything at all: they turn into belle and vieille, which are different words to look at. Nothing about the plain form tells you which of the three will happen, so these are six shapes to know rather than one rule to apply.

examples.note: The plain rule, doing what it did all last lesson.
And the one that replaces the word instead of adding to it.

beforeAVowel.title: A third shape, in front of a vowel
beforeAVowel.body: Beau and vieux each have a form nothing else in this lesson has. In front of a word starting with a vowel sound they become bel and vieil: un bel homme, un vieil ami. It is the same pressure you met in the elision lesson, where two vowel sounds meeting each other is something French will not do. Beau homme and vieux ami both put two vowels together, so the word in front changes shape to stop it. These two are used constantly and they are worth having now.

examples.note: Homme starts with a vowel sound, so beau cannot stand there.
Ami does the same thing to vieux.

alwaysAudible.title: The opposite of the colours
alwaysAudible.body: Last lesson four of the twelve colours changed sound for the une kind and the rest did not, and on bleu and noir there was nothing to hear at all. These six are the other way round: every one of them sounds different. Grand wakes a d, petit wakes a t, mauvais wakes an s as a z, bon collapses its nasal into a plain n, and beau and vieux become other words entirely. So on these six your ear is worth listening to. The plural is still completely silent, exactly as it was.

examples.note: The biggest change of the six, and the nasal lesson already taught why.
The silent letters lesson authored this one: the d arrives with the e.

noPluralChange.term: vieux and mauvais, for several things
noPluralChange.title: Two of them already end in the plural letter
noPluralChange.body: For more than one thing you add an s, and it is silent, which you know. But vieux already ends in an x and mauvais already ends in an s, and French does not stack a second one on top. Un vieux vélo and des vieux vélos are the same word on the page as well as in the air. Vieuxs and mauvaiss are not words and never have been. This is the one place in the lesson where the careful thing to do is nothing.

examples.note: One old grandfather.
Several old friends, and the word has not moved.

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. EVERY MASCULINE / FEMININE PAIR IS ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, the plain form immediately followed by its feminine with no gap and no reset: grand / grande, petit / petite, mauvais / mauvaise, bon / bonne, beau / belle, vieux / vieille. The ONLY difference the learner may hear is the ending. Recorded apart these become two performances and the learner compares the performances instead of the forms. UNLIKE a1.13, ALL SIX OF THESE PAIRS GENUINELY DIFFER, so there is no silent pair to protect here and the risk runs the other way: do not EXAGGERATE the difference to make it audible. It already is. Read every pair at ordinary conversational pace. bon / bonne is the one to get right. bon is a nasal vowel with NO n sound behind it at all, and bonne is a plain oral o followed by a clearly pronounced n. That is a vowel change and a consonant arriving in one step, it is the largest change in the set, and it must not be softened into a half-nasal. This is the brun / brune shape from sons.03 and should be read the same way. beau / belle and vieux / vieille are not endings and must not be read as though they were: they are two different words and should sound like two different words.

THE THREE-FORM SETS, AND EACH IS ONE TAKE. « beau / bel / belle » read straight through as one continuous take by one voice, then « vieux / vieil / vieille » the same way. The three-form set is this lesson's unique content and it only reads as a set if it is heard as one. bel and belle are the same sound and vieil and vieille are the same sound, and the learner has to hear that rather than be told it, so do not differentiate them: read the second and third members of each set identically. THEN THE PHRASES, AND THESE ARE NEVER BARE. « un bel homme », « un bel arbre », « un vieil ami » and « un vieil immeuble » are recorded AS FULL PHRASES, never as isolated words. The form exists ONLY because of the vowel that follows it, so a lone bel clip teaches nothing and a lone vieil clip is actively misleading. Record each vowel phrase immediately after its consonant partner, in the same take, so the contrast is inside one performance: « un beau jardin » then « un bel arbre », « un vieux château » then « un vieil immeuble ». There is NO liaison to perform in any of these. Do not add one.
clipIds: Mon grand-père a un vieil ami à Lyon.

recorded.desc: THE WORD ORDER PAIR, AND IT IS THE HARDEST THING IN THIS BRIEF TO READ CORRECTLY. « une maison grande » and « une grande maison » are recorded as ONE TAKE, one after the other, with an even beat between them and NOTHING ELSE DIFFERENT. Both must be read as ordinary confident French. Do NOT read the first one hesitantly, do not put a question in the voice, do not mark it as wrong in any way. The entire teaching of this lesson is that the wrong one sounds completely fine, and a reader who performs the error destroys it. Same instruction for « un appartement grand » against « un grand appartement » and for the same reason. Also record the two-order phrases as whole units at conversational pace, with no pause between the noun and either describing word: « une petite robe rouge », « un petit chien blanc », « une belle robe bleue ». The pattern being absorbed is that both words belong to the same phrase, and a pause in the middle would break it into two.
clipIds: Elle porte une petite robe rouge.
Elle porte une belle robe bleue.
Elle habite dans une grande maison.

recorded.desc: The six as ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE by one voice at one speed, in the deck order: grand, petit, beau, vieux, bon, mauvais. Six words recorded in six sessions are six performances, and any drift in pace or pitch teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a difference in French. Read them straight through with an even beat, then again slowly in the same take. grand and bon are NASAL and must be read with no n sound behind the vowel at all. petit and mauvais both end in a silent consonant and must end on the vowel, with nothing after it. THE MASCULINE PLURALS ARE NOT RECORDED IN ISOLATION AND MUST NOT BE. vieux and mauvais are identical in the singular and the plural, and a lone clip of a plural implies a difference that is not there. Where a plural is needed it is recorded as the second half of a pair with its own singular, in one take, so the learner hears that nothing changed: grand / grands, petit / petits, bon / bons, vieux / vieux, mauvais / mauvais. If a reader cannot resist marking the plural somehow, record the singular twice and use it for both, because that is a more truthful clip than a performed difference.

The four-form grid, read ACROSS THE ROW in one take: « Ce garçon est très grand, cette fille est très grande, les garçons sont grands, les filles sont grandes. » Reading a row in one take is the entire point: the learner has to hear that the row changes ONCE, at grande, and never again, because the two plurals are the same sound as the two singulars. Do not record these four sentences separately. Do not vary the pace between them. There is no s sound anywhere in the third or fourth sentence and there must be no hint of one: no lengthening, no release, no breath.

The five written traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically. THREE OF THE FIVE ARE ACOUSTICALLY IDENTICAL TO THEIR CORRECTION: « des vieuxs vélos » and « des vieux vélos » are the same sound, and so is the vieuxe pair once the reader stops trying to mark it. Do not try to make the wrong one sound wrong. Read both members identically and let the screen carry the difference, because a reader who performs a distinction that does not exist teaches the learner to listen for something that will never be there. THE FIRST TRAP IS THE OPPOSITE CASE AND IS THE MOST IMPORTANT CLIP IN THE LESSON. « une maison grande » against « une grande maison » differs audibly, because word order is the one thing that is never silent, and it must still be read WITHOUT any hint that the first is wrong. That combination is the whole lesson: audibly different, and nobody ever mentions it. Only the « un beau homme » / « un bel homme » pair and the « bone » / « bonne » pair genuinely differ in a way the reader should let through, and both should be read straight.

The opening scene. Nadia is an estate agent in her forties with a folder open and twenty minutes, reading at an ordinary working pace rather than a teaching pace. THE BEAT THAT MATTERS IS THE ONE WHERE SHE SWITCHES TO ENGLISH. « Ah, a big one. No problem, I have three. » must be read as HELPFUL AND SLIGHTLY BRISK, never as corrective, never as pointed, and above all never as unkind. She is not marking anybody. She heard a sentence, understood it completely, made a snap judgement about which language would be faster, and moved on. The whole lesson depends on the learner feeling that nothing bad happened, because nothing bad did. Any edge on that line turns it into a telling-off and loses the point entirely. Her final line, where she stays in French and starts describing a street, is where warmth is allowed to show, because that is the reward for having fixed it.
clipIds: Alors, qu'est-ce que vous cherchez exactement ?
Ah, a big one. No problem, I have three.
Un petit jardin, d'accord. J'ai exactement ça, dans une vieille rue très calme.

lessons.title: La famille
lessons.intro: Twenty-two words for the people in a family, and one rule for saying whose they are that runs the opposite way round from the one your own language gave you. This is how you say who is who, name everybody, and introduce your own family out loud.

say.text: One word meant two things and nobody said a word about it. Watch which.

setting.place: A friend's kitchen table, phones out, photos going round

beats.text: Sunday lunch at a friend's place, and somebody has asked to see photos from work.
You scroll to one of the team. You want to point at somebody you work with. Nobody you are related to.

beats.prompt: You mean a woman you work with. Which line do you say?

options.en: the one that uses the word for woman
the one that says a woman rather than the woman

followUp.works: Yes, and the difference is one word. Watch what the other one does, because nobody will tell you.
followUp.breaks: That is the word for woman, and it is also the word for something else. Watch what she hears.

beats.speaker: Salomé
beats.stage: Nothing has been corrected. She has simply understood you, and she is pleased for you.

beats.heading: One word, two meanings, and nobody asks
beats.body: La femme is the word for woman and also the word for wife, and nothing in the sentence separates them. With la in front of it, a French ear reaches for wife first. Une says one of many, and that is the whole difference.

wrong.en: This is the wife

beats.coach: Both lines are correct French. Only one of them says what you meant, and the wrong reading makes enough sense that it never gets questioned.

beats.speaker: Second try
beats.fr: Voici une femme. Elle travaille avec moi.
beats.en: This is a woman. She works with me.

beats.speaker: Salomé
beats.fr: Ah d'accord ! Et lui, c'est le frère de Paul, non ?
beats.en: Ah, right! And him, that is Paul's brother, isn't it?
beats.stage: And there is the rest of the lesson, said by somebody else without thinking about it.

beats.text: Nothing was corrected the first time, and that is the part worth noticing. You were understood, just not the way you meant.

closing.text: Saying exactly who is who is the rest of this lesson, and it starts with something English has and French does not. French has no apostrophe. Turn it around.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the first one is a rule your own language does not have.

goals.t: Say whose mother, whose brother, whose sister
goals.s: One rule, and it runs the opposite way round from English. It works for every relationship in the lesson.
Twenty-two words, and for once you will not have to guess at le or la for most of them.
Three or four words where the friendly rule runs out, told to you rather than found by you later.

goals.t: Introduce your own family out loud
goals.s: How many brothers and sisters you have, and the three words you need for my.

sections.title: French Has No Apostrophe
sections.say: This is the one rule in the lesson, and everything after it is an application of it.
sections.body: English says whose with an apostrophe: Paul's mother. French has none, so it names the relationship first and hangs the owner off the back with de. French has no apostrophe. Turn it around. La mère de Paul. Whatever follows de owns what precedes it.

sections.title: Both Orders, Side By Side
sections.say: French has no apostrophe. Turn it around. Read across each row and watch the two names swap ends.

detail.title: la mère de Paul
detail.body: la mère de Paul is Paul's mother. In French the relationship comes first and the owner comes last. In English the owner comes first and the relationship comes last. Same two people, opposite ends.

detail.title: le père de Marie
detail.body: le père de Marie is Marie's father. In French the relationship comes first and the owner comes last. In English the owner comes first and the relationship comes last. Same two people, opposite ends.

detail.title: le frère de Paul
detail.body: le frère de Paul is Paul's brother. In French the relationship comes first and the owner comes last. In English the owner comes first and the relationship comes last. Same two people, opposite ends.

detail.title: la sœur de Marie
detail.body: la sœur de Marie is Marie's sister. In French the relationship comes first and the owner comes last. In English the owner comes first and the relationship comes last. Same two people, opposite ends.

detail.title: la fille de Paul
detail.body: la fille de Paul is Paul's daughter. In French the relationship comes first and the owner comes last. In English the owner comes first and the relationship comes last. Same two people, opposite ends.

detail.title: le fils de Marie
detail.body: le fils de Marie is Marie's son. In French the relationship comes first and the owner comes last. In English the owner comes first and the relationship comes last. Same two people, opposite ends.

sections.title: Same Two People, Both Ways
sections.say: Two sentences about the same two people. One word moves, and it is not a small one.
sections.hint: Swipe through both, then read them again in order.

cards.label: One way round
cards.head: De points at Paul
cards.fr: Marie est la sœur de Paul.
cards.body: Paul is the one who has a sister, and Marie is the sister. The name sitting immediately after de is the one who owns.

cards.label: The other way round
cards.head: De points at Marie
cards.fr: Paul est le frère de Marie.
cards.body: The same two people, and the sentence now says something different. Nothing moved except which name landed after de and which relationship word went in front of it.

cards.label: What actually moved
cards.head: Two words, and they decide everything
cards.body: Both sentences use the same four ideas. Which of the two people ends up after de is what makes one of them true and the other one a different claim entirely.

cards.label: The test you can run while speaking
cards.head: French has no apostrophe. Turn it around.
cards.body: Whatever sits immediately after de owns whatever sits in front of it. Say the relationship, then de, then whose it is, and you never have to think about it again.

sections.title: Six Pairs, Twelve Words
sections.say: Twelve words in six pairs. The pair is the point.
sections.hint: Swipe through all twelve.

sections.title: The Rest Of The Household
sections.say: The generations either side, the married pair, and the four that arrive with a second marriage.
sections.hint: Swipe through. The grandparents are the ones worth a second look.

cards.label: Learn these two whole
cards.head: One word, not two
cards.body: The first half of each never changes shape, whoever you are talking about. The two halves were welded together centuries ago and have been carried along as single items ever since, so there is nothing to work out here and nothing that applies anywhere else.

cards.label: Saying whose name is what
cards.head: A fixed phrase, for now
cards.body: Take « s'appelle » whole, the way you took « je m'appelle » in the very first lesson. There is a system behind that little se and it is a long way off; today it is just how you say what somebody is called.

sections.title: Generation By Generation
sections.say: Generations down the side. The two columns are the two articles, which is the next act in one picture.

detail.title: Grandparents
detail.body: le grand-père and la grand-mère. Together they are les grands-parents, which is masculine plural whatever the mix.

detail.title: Parents
detail.body: le père and la mère. Together they are les parents, which is masculine plural whatever the mix.

detail.title: Their brothers and sisters
detail.body: l'oncle and la tante. The word takes le for a man and la for a woman, and you never have to guess.

detail.title: You and yours
detail.body: le frère and la sœur. The word takes le for a man and la for a woman, and you never have to guess.

detail.title: Cousins
detail.body: le cousin and la cousine. The word takes le for a man and la for a woman, and you never have to guess.

detail.title: Children
detail.body: le fils and la fille. Together they are les enfants, which is masculine plural whatever the mix.

detail.title: Their children
detail.body: le neveu and la nièce. The word takes le for a man and la for a woman, and you never have to guess.

detail.title: Grandchildren
detail.body: le petit-fils and la petite-fille. The word takes le for a man and la for a woman, and you never have to guess.

sections.title: For Once, The Article Fits
sections.frSub: Le pour lui, la pour elle
sections.say: After the gender lesson, this is a genuine relief. It is also worth knowing where it runs out.
sections.body: The gender lesson said you would mostly have to memorise the article. Family is where you do not. Le for a man, la for a woman, across all twelve paired words. The next screen is where that stops, and it does stop.

sections.title: Where That Rule Stops
sections.say: Five places the friendly rule runs out. Better here than in a fortnight.

errors.wrong: la bébé
errors.why: Masculine whatever the baby is. Nobody switches to la for a girl.

errors.wrong: l'enfante
errors.why: Masculine for a boy or a girl, and the l apostrophe hides the article anyway.

errors.wrong: les parentes
errors.why: Masculine plural over a mother and a father together.

errors.wrong: les enfantes
errors.why: Masculine plural over any mix of children.

errors.wrong: les grand-parents
errors.why: Masculine plural again, over a grandmother and a grandfather.

sections.title: Le Or La, By The Person
sections.say: Two groups, then a check on each. Look at the person, not at the word.

groups.label: The ones that follow the person

check.q: Your father's sister. Which word, and which article?
check.why: La tante. She is a woman, so the word takes la, and you did not have to remember anything about the word itself.

check.q: A baby girl. What does French call her?
check.why: Le bébé, for a girl as much as for a boy. This is one of the handful of family words where the article stops following the person and just sits there.

sections.title: Fils And Fil
sections.say: Two words, one letter apart, and the spelling predicts the wrong sound in one of them.
sections.hint: Listen to each before you turn it over.

cards.label: The son
cards.head: Silent l, sounded s
cards.body: The l says nothing and the s says everything, which is the reverse of almost every rule the silent letters lesson gave you. A final s is usually the one letter you can count on to stay quiet. Not here.

cards.label: The thread
cards.head: Everything behaves
cards.body: The l is pronounced and there is no s to worry about. This is the ordinary word doing the ordinary thing, and it is worth meeting so you can hear what fils is NOT.

cards.label: Together
cards.head: More letters, fewer sounds
cards.body: Say them one after the other. The longer word is the one that drops a sound at the end, and no amount of looking at the spelling would have told you which way round that goes.

cards.label: In a phrase
cards.head: The same sound inside a sentence
cards.body: Said out loud this is [luh FEES duh mah-REE]. The trap does not go away once the word has company, and this is the shape you will actually need it in.

sections.title: Two Words, Two Meanings
sections.say: This is the one from the opening scene, and its partner.
sections.hint: Both of these cost you nothing in grammar and something in meaning.

cards.label: Two meanings, one word
cards.head: woman, and also wife
cards.body: With la in front of it and nothing else, a French ear reaches for wife. Une femme is a woman.

cards.label: Two meanings, one word
cards.head: girl, and also daughter
cards.body: De and a name behind it makes it daughter. La fille de Paul is his daughter, never a girl he knows.

cards.label: The sound will not help
cards.head: Identical either way
cards.body: The same two syllables both times, so there is nothing in the audio to separate them. La reaches for wife and une reaches for woman, and the little word in front is the entire signal.

cards.label: How to be certain
cards.head: De settles it
cards.body: De and a name behind it leave only one reading available: this is his daughter, and nobody can hear it as a girl he happens to know. That is the second thing the rule buys you.

sections.title: The N You Do Not Say
sections.say: Six family words end in a nasal vowel. The n is written and there is no n sound in any of them.

detail.title: les parents
detail.body: les parents is [LAY pah-RAHⁿ]. The raised n marks a nasal vowel: the air goes through your nose and no n is said. Compare la cousine, [LAH koo-ZEEN], where a vowel follows the n so it sounds.

detail.title: la grand-mère
detail.body: la grand-mère is [LAH grahⁿ-MEHR]. The raised n marks a nasal vowel: the air goes through your nose and no n is said. Compare la cousine, [LAH koo-ZEEN], where a vowel follows the n so it sounds.

detail.title: le grand-père
detail.body: le grand-père is [LUH grahⁿ-PEHR]. The raised n marks a nasal vowel: the air goes through your nose and no n is said. Compare la cousine, [LAH koo-ZEEN], where a vowel follows the n so it sounds.

detail.title: les grands-parents
detail.body: les grands-parents is [LAY grahⁿ-pah-RAHⁿ]. The raised n marks a nasal vowel: the air goes through your nose and no n is said. Compare la cousine, [LAH koo-ZEEN], where a vowel follows the n so it sounds.

detail.title: le cousin
detail.body: le cousin is [LUH koo-ZAⁿ]. The raised n marks a nasal vowel: the air goes through your nose and no n is said. Compare la cousine, [LAH koo-ZEEN], where a vowel follows the n so it sounds.

detail.title: l'enfant
detail.body: l'enfant is [lahⁿ-FAHⁿ]. The raised n marks a nasal vowel: the air goes through your nose and no n is said. Compare la cousine, [LAH koo-ZEEN], where a vowel follows the n so it sounds.

sections.title: Hear The Difference
sections.say: Four lines. Two of them are the pair from a moment ago.

lines.en: the son
thread, wire
the wife, or a woman
the cousin (male)

questions.q: Which one has a silent l?
questions.why: Le fils. The l says nothing and the s says everything, which is the opposite of what the spelling suggests.

questions.q: Which one has no n sound at all, despite the n?
questions.why: Le cousin. The n marks a nasal vowel rather than a consonant. Its partner la cousine does have a real n, because a vowel follows it.

questions.q: La femme sounds closest to which English word?
questions.why: Calm, for the vowel. La femme is said FAM. It is the only common French word where the letter e says that sound.

sections.title: How Many Of Each
sections.say: Nothing new here. This is the have verb and the numbers, pointed at people.
sections.body: Nothing new here: the have verb and the numbers, put together. J'ai un frère et deux sœurs, with the s landing on sœurs because two is more than one. If the answer is none, un becomes de: je n'ai pas de frère.

sections.title: Mon, Ma, Mes
sections.say: Three words, taken whole. The system they belong to is the next lesson.
sections.hint: Learn these three as words rather than as a rule.

cards.label: Choosing between them
cards.head: Follow the article you already know
cards.body: Mon goes with the words that take le. Ma goes with the words that take la. Mes goes with anything plural, and there the kind of word stops mattering entirely.

cards.label: What is missing, and where it is
cards.head: The rest arrives next lesson
cards.body: Yours, his, hers, ours and theirs all arrive together next lesson, along with one wrinkle in the ma column that nobody can guess. Until then, if these three will not reach, use de and a name. That always works.

cards.label: Two of them in one sentence
cards.head: Mon and ma, side by side
cards.fr: Mon frère et ma sœur habitent à Lyon.
cards.sub: My brother and my sister live in Lyon.
cards.body: Frère takes le so it takes mon, and sœur takes la so it takes ma. Both choices are made from the article and neither is made from the person.

cards.label: One you already own
cards.head: Age runs on the have verb
cards.sub: My brother is ten years old.
cards.body: French counts age with the have verb rather than the be verb, which you met two lessons ago. Nothing here is new; it is the same verb pointed at a person in your family.

sections.title: A Family, Written Down
sections.say: Six sentences. Every relationship in them is built the French way round.
sections.text: Read this, then answer the three questions. « Voici la famille de Paul. Marie est la mère de Paul. Marie est la sœur de Sophie, et Sophie est la tante de Paul. Marie habite avec le grand-père de Paul. Paul a un frère et deux sœurs. Le fils de Sophie est le cousin de Paul. »

glossary.note: The relationship first, then de, then the owner.
Same shape again. De points at Paul.
Tante is said [LAH TAHⁿT]. The n marks a nasal vowel and is not a sound of its own.
Grand-père is one frozen word, and the first half never changes.
Cousin is said [LUH koo-ZAⁿ]. His female counterpart is la cousine, with a real n.

questions.q: Who is Marie?
questions.a: Paul's mother, and Sophie's sister.

questions.q: Sophie is whose aunt?
questions.a: Paul's.

questions.q: How many brothers and sisters does Paul have?
questions.a: One brother and two sisters.

sections.title: Who Is Who At The Table
sections.say: You are the one being asked this time.
sections.setting: A lunch table, somebody working out how everybody is related

turns.ai: Tu as des frères et sœurs ?
turns.en: Do you have any brothers and sisters?
turns.user: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.
turns.userEn: I have one brother and two sisters.

alts.fr: J'ai deux frères et une sœur.
alts.en: I have two brothers and one sister.
I do not have a brother.

turns.ai: Et elle, sur la photo, c'est qui ?
turns.en: And her, in the photo, who is she?
turns.user: Voici la mère de Paul.
turns.userEn: This is Paul's mother.

turns.ai: Marie a des enfants ?
turns.en: Does Marie have children?
turns.user: Oui, Paul est le fils de Marie.
turns.userEn: Yes, Paul is Marie's son.

alts.fr: Oui, il est le fils de Marie.

turns.ai: Et lui, à côté, c'est qui ?
turns.en: And him, next to her, who is that?
turns.user: C'est le frère de Paul.
turns.userEn: That is Paul's brother.

turns.ai: Et le monsieur derrière eux ?
turns.en: And the gentleman behind them?
turns.user: Voici le grand-père de Marie.
turns.userEn: This is Marie's grandfather.

sections.title: Everything, Once More
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French out loud before you turn it over.

cards.front: How do you say whose something is?
cards.back: The relationship, then de, then the owner. La mère de Paul.

cards.front: Which twelve words never make you guess at le or la?
cards.back: The six pairs. Father and mother, brother and sister, son and daughter, uncle and aunt, and both kinds of cousin, nephew and niece.
le bébé, and it stays masculine.
[LAH FAM]. The only common word where e says that.
mon with le words, ma with la words, mes with plurals.
cards.say: mon père, ma mère, mes parents

cards.front: I have one brother and two sisters
cards.back: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.
cards.say: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.

sections.title: Write What You Hear
sections.say: Five lines. The last one hands you the words and asks you to put them in order, which is the whole rule.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: The twelve, the six relationships and the three words for my.

sections.title: One Last Pass
sections.say: Rate each one. Anything you mark again comes back sooner.

cards.front: Marie est la sœur de Paul.
cards.say: Marie est la sœur de Paul.

cards.front: Paul est le frère de Marie.
cards.say: Paul est le frère de Marie.

cards.back: the wife or a woman, said [LAH FAM]
the grandmother, said [LAH grahⁿ-MEHR], one frozen word
the baby, masculine whoever the baby is

cards.front: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.
cards.back: I have one brother and two sisters.
cards.say: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched somebody be congratulated on a marriage that has not happened, learned a rule for saying whose something is that runs the opposite way round from the one your own language gave you, and picked up twenty-two words for the people in a family. You found out that for twelve of them the article follows the actual person, which is the one place in French that is true, and you were told exactly where that stops rather than being left to discover it. You know that one word here has a silent l and a sounded s, and that two more mean two things each. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: Whose is whose
rounds.say: The rule, four ways.

questions.q: You want to say: Marie's brother. Which one is it?
questions.why: Le frère de Marie. The relationship comes first and the owner comes last, which is the opposite of the order English gave you. Nothing else about the phrase changes.

questions.q: Write the French for: Paul's mother.
questions.why: La mère de Paul. Say the relationship, then de, then whose it is. fold() ignores the accent, so mere is accepted, but the word order is the thing being tested and it is not negotiable.

questions.q: In « la sœur de Paul », who has a sister?
questions.why: Paul. Whatever sits immediately after de is the owner, every time. That single test settles every phrase of this shape.

questions.q: You want to say: Paul is Marie's brother. Fix this. « Paul de le frère est Marie. »
accept: Paul est le frère de Marie.
paul est le frere de marie
Paul est le frère de Marie
questions.answer: Paul est le frère de Marie.
questions.why: Paul est le frère de Marie. The relationship has to come before de and the owner after it. Written the other way round it is not word order a French speaker can repair on the fly.

rounds.label: The people
rounds.say: Twenty-two words. These are the ones worth checking.

questions.q: Your mother's sister is your...
questions.why: La tante. La nièce is the other direction (your sibling's daughter), la cousine is her daughter, and la belle-mère is a mother-in-law or a stepmother.

questions.q: Write the French for: the grandparents.
questions.why: Les grands-parents. The s lands on grands as well as on parents, which is the one thing about this word worth remembering.

questions.q: Write the French for: the nephew.
questions.why: Le neveu, which is your brother's or sister's son. Le petit-fils is your own son's son, a generation further down and a different word entirely.

questions.q: Which of these means the half sister?
questions.why: La demi-sœur. Demi is the half; belle marks the ones that arrive by marriage, which is why la belle-sœur is a sister-in-law.

rounds.label: Le or la
rounds.say: The article, and the places it stops helping.

questions.q: Which article goes with the word for aunt?
questions.why: La tante. She is a woman, so the word takes la, and that is true of all twelve of the paired words without a single one to memorise.

questions.q: A baby girl. What does French call her?
questions.why: Le bébé, for a girl exactly as for a boy. This is one of the handful of words where the article stops following the person and simply sits there.

questions.q: A mother and a father together. Which one?
questions.why: Les parents, masculine plural over a mixed group. That is the ordinary French rule showing through, and you met it on a card in the indefinite articles lesson.

questions.q: Write the French for: the children.
questions.why: Les enfants. Masculine plural whatever the mix of boys and girls, for the same reason as les parents.

rounds.label: What it sounds like
rounds.say: Four you have to hear rather than read.

questions.q: Listen. Which word is it?
questions.why: Le fils, said [LUH FEES]. The l is silent and the s is sounded, so it is the one word here whose spelling points at the wrong sound.

questions.q: Listen. Which word is it?
questions.why: La femme, said [LAH FAM]. It is the only common French word where the letter e says that sound, which is why it never comes out right first time.

questions.q: Which of these has NO n sound in it at all?
questions.why: Le cousin, [LUH koo-ZAⁿ]. The n marks a nasal vowel rather than a consonant. La cousine has a real n, because a vowel follows it, and that is the whole difference between the pair.

questions.q: Tap the letter in « fils » that you do not say.
questions.why: The l. In fils it is silent and the final s is pronounced, which is the reverse of the pattern the silent letters lesson gave you.

rounds.label: Words with two jobs
rounds.say: Two words, four meanings, and no sound to separate them.

questions.q: Somebody points at a photo and says « Voici la femme. » What have they most likely said?
questions.why: This is the wife. La femme is both woman and wife, and with la in front of it a French ear reaches for wife. Nothing in the sentence separates them and nobody will ask you which you meant.

questions.q: You mean a woman rather than a wife. Which word do you change?
questions.why: Change la to une. Une femme is a woman, because une says one of many. The word femme itself is doing nothing wrong.

questions.q: Write the French for: Paul's daughter.
questions.why: La fille de Paul. La fille is girl and also daughter, and de with a name behind it is what settles which. That is the second thing the rule buys you.

questions.q: Fix this so it can only mean a girl, not a daughter. « la fille de Paul »
questions.why: Une fille. Dropping de and the name takes the relationship away, and une says one of many, so both halves of the ambiguity are closed at once.

rounds.label: Your own family
rounds.say: Say it about yourself.

questions.q: Which word goes in front of « mère » for my?
questions.why: Ma mère. Ma goes with the words that take la, and mère is one of them. Mon goes with the le words and mes goes with anything plural.

questions.q: Write the French for: I have one brother and two sisters.
accept: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.
j'ai un frere et deux soeurs
J'ai un frère et deux sœurs
questions.answer: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.
questions.why: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs. The have verb and the numbers, both of which you already own. The s on sœurs is the ordinary plural after a number bigger than one.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je n'ai pas un frère. »
questions.why: Je n'ai pas de frère. After a negative, un and une flatten to de, which is the same shape as je n'ai pas de voiture from the have lesson.

questions.q: Say your own line out loud: how many brothers and sisters you have.
questions.target: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.
accept: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.
J'ai deux frères et une sœur.
questions.answer: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.
questions.why: Any true version of this counts. The shape is the have verb, a number, and the family word, with the plural s appearing on anything above one.

sections.title: What You Have Now
sections.say: Six things, and the first one is the one the rest hang off.
sections.body: You can say whose mother, whose brother and whose sister you mean, which is the half of this unit that a word list could never have given you. French has no apostrophe. Turn it around. Everything else in the lesson was either the people themselves or a place where French quietly says something you did not intend.
points: The relationship first, then de, then the owner. La mère de Paul is Paul's mother, and the two names come out in the opposite order to English.
Twenty-two words for the people in a family, twelve of which never make you guess at le or la.
Le bébé, l'enfant, les parents, les enfants and les grands-parents, where that stops.
Le fils is said with a silent l and a sounded s, and la femme rhymes with calm.
La femme is woman and wife; la fille is girl and daughter. Une and de are what settle them.
Mon, ma and mes, as three words. The rest of that set is the next lesson.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that le and la follow it, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, introduced in a1.04
un and une, and that they become de after a negative, introduced in a1.11
de for quantity, in une bouteille d'eau and beaucoup d'eau, introduced in a1.29
The numbers, introduced in a1.02
The full present of être, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, and its age frame, introduced in a1.07
That a final consonant is usually silent, introduced in sons.06
The nasal vowels, and that a following vowel blocks them, introduced in sons.03
grammarIntroduced: de for possession: the possessed noun first, de second, the possessor last
That French has no genitive apostrophe, and that the constituent order is therefore the reverse of English
Natural gender in kinship terms: le and la tracking the referent rather than the lexeme
The limits of that: epicene le bébé and l'enfant, and masculine plurals over mixed groups
mon, ma and mes as three lexical items, with no paradigm and no vowel-elision rule
The lexicalised compound grand-mère, taken as a frozen form rather than as a failure to agree

overview.introFr: Vingt-deux mots pour la famille, et une règle pour dire à qui ils sont qui marche à l'envers de l'anglais.

acts.title: Who is who
acts.milestone: You can say whose mother, whose brother and whose sister you mean.

acts.title: The people
acts.milestone: Twenty-two words, and a shape to hang them on.

acts.title: Gender that tells the truth
acts.milestone: Twelve words you never have to guess at, and the five places that stops.

acts.title: Saying it out loud
acts.milestone: The one word whose spelling lies to you, and the two that mean two things.

acts.title: Introduce your own
acts.milestone: You can say how many of each you have, and whose everybody is.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. Possessive adjectives are next, and the three you have transfer straight in.

lessons.reframe: French has no apostrophe. Turn it around.

errorTriggers.description: Builds the phrase the English way round, owner first, and either reverses it outright or drops de altogether. The default error, because the learner's own language has a piece of punctuation for this and French does not.
Reaches for the wrong relationship word, most often between neveu and petit-fils, or between the demi- and belle- families, where the two halves of the household look alike.

Guesses at le or la on a family word, having learned in a1.03 that gender mostly has to be memorised, and does not notice that for twelve of these it simply follows the person. The mirror error is applying that rule to le bebe and les parents, where it stops.

Reads the spelling and says the l in fils, or gives femme its ordinary vowel. Both are the natural reading of the letters and both are wrong, and neither gets corrected because the listener usually works out what was meant.

Takes la femme as woman and la fille as girl, and never learns that the listener took them the other way. The highest-value error in the lesson: it costs something socially rather than grammatically and nobody ever corrects it.
Reaches past mon, ma and mes for a possessive this lesson has not given, or picks the wrong one of the three by looking at the person rather than at the article the word takes.

drills.title: English in, French out
drills.coach: The English is on the left. Before you turn the card, say the French out loud, and make yourself start with the relationship rather than with the name.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Marie's father. Which one?
drills.why: Le père de Marie. Relationship, then de, then the owner. The two names come out in the opposite order to the one English put them in.

drills.title: Put each one where it belongs
drills.coach: Work out where the person stands relative to you first, then reach for the word. Neveu and petit-fils are the pair worth slowing down on: both are younger, and only one of them is yours.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Your sister's daughter is your...
drills.why: La nièce. La petite-fille is your own child's daughter, one generation further down.

drills.title: Look at the person, not at the word
drills.coach: For the twelve paired words the article follows the actual person and you never have to remember anything. The third bucket is where that stops, and it is a short list rather than a pattern.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: A baby girl. Which one?
drills.why: Le bébé. It stays masculine for a girl, which is one of the handful of places the friendly rule runs out.

drills.title: Two words your eyes get wrong
drills.coach: Say each one out loud before you turn it. Both of these point at a sound that is not there.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: How is « le fils » said?
drills.why: [LUH FEES]. Silent l, sounded s, which is the reverse of the pattern the silent letters lesson gave you.

drills.title: Which of the two did they hear?
buckets: Says a woman or a girl
Says a wife or a daughter
drills.coach: The word never changes. What changes is what is standing next to it: une says one of many, and de with a name says a relationship.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want to say a woman rather than the wife. What do you say?
drills.why: Une femme. Une says one of many, and that is the entire difference. The word femme is doing nothing wrong.

drills.title: Which of the three?
drills.coach: Mon with the words that take le, ma with the words that take la, mes with anything plural. Look at the article the word already takes rather than at the person.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which word goes in front of « sœur » for my?
drills.why: Ma sœur. Sœur takes la, so it takes ma. The person has nothing to do with it; the article does.

sections.title: Both orders, side by side
rows: Marie est la sœur de Paul.
Paul est le frère de Marie.

sections.title: Mon, ma, mes, and what is not here yet

rows.v: Mon goes with the words that take le.
Ma goes with the words that take la.
Mes goes with anything plural, whichever kind of word it is.
The next lesson. Until then, de and a name always works: la mère de Paul, le frère de Marie.

sections.title: The ones that do not sound like they look

rows.v: [LUH FEES]. Silent l, sounded s. The thread, fil, is [FEEL] and behaves normally.
[LAH FAM]. The only common word where the letter e says that sound.
[LUH koo-ZAⁿ] and [LAH koo-ZEEN]. The masculine has a nasal vowel and no n sound; the feminine has a real n, because a vowel follows it.
[LAH grahⁿ-MEHR]. One frozen word, and the first half never changes shape.

sections.title: Why French turns it around
sections.body: English has a piece of punctuation whose only job is to say whose something is. You put the owner first, add an apostrophe and an s, and put the thing after it. French never developed that piece of punctuation, so it does the job with a small word instead, and a small word has to sit between the two things rather than on the end of one of them. That is the whole reason the order comes out backwards: the thing has to be said first so that de has something to follow, and the owner arrives last. Once you see it that way there is nothing to memorise, because the order is forced by the shape of the tool rather than chosen. The same de turns up all over the language doing the same structural job. A bottle of water is une bouteille d'eau: the container first, then de, then what is in it. A lot of water is beaucoup d'eau: the quantity first, then de, then the stuff. In every one of them the thing being measured or owned comes after de and the thing doing the measuring or being owned comes before it. What changes between them is only what kind of relationship de is naming, and with a person's name behind it the relationship is always ownership. The practical version is short and it works while you are talking. French has no apostrophe. Turn it around. Say the relationship, say de, say whose. If you find yourself starting with the name, you are speaking English with French words, and the sentence will stop rather than merely sound odd.

deOwner.term: de, and who it points at
deOwner.title: De marks the owner, and the owner comes second.
deOwner.body: English marks the owner with an apostrophe and puts them first: Paul's mother. French has no apostrophe at all, so it names the relationship first and hangs the owner off the back of it with de: la mère de Paul. The two names come out in the opposite order, and that is the whole mechanism. Whatever sits immediately after de is the one who owns, and whatever sits in front of de is the relationship. That is why la sœur de Paul and le frère de Marie can describe the same two people and still say different things. You have met de before, in a bottle of water and a lot of water, where it was doing a different job: there it measured out a quantity, and here it names a person. The order rule is the same in both, which is the useful part. Say the thing, then de, then whose it is.

examples.note: De points at Paul, so Paul is the one with a sister.
The same two people, and de now points at Marie instead.

matchesThePerson.term: le and la, for once, match
matchesThePerson.title: With people, the article follows the actual person.
matchesThePerson.body: a1.03 asked you to learn the article with the noun, because for most words nothing about the word tells you which one it takes. Family is the one corner of the language where it does. Le père and la mère, le frère and la sœur, le fils and la fille, l'oncle and la tante, le cousin and la cousine, le neveu and la nièce. Twelve words, six pairs, and you never have to guess at one of them: if the person is a man the word takes le, and if she is a woman it takes la. That is a real saving and it is worth using. It is also worth knowing exactly where it stops, because it does. Le bébé stays masculine for a baby girl, l'enfant stays masculine for any child, and les parents, les enfants and les grands-parents are all masculine plurals covering a mixed group. Those are not exceptions somebody forgot to fix: they are the ordinary French rule showing through in the one place the friendly version runs out.

examples.note: A man, so the word takes le. Nothing had to be memorised.
And where it stops: le bébé stays masculine for a baby girl.

frozenPossessive.title: Three words to use now. The system arrives next lesson.
frozenPossessive.body: You need to say my father and my mother before you need to know how the whole set works, so take three words and use them. Mon goes with the words that take le, ma goes with the words that take la, and mes goes with anything plural whichever kind of word it is. Mon père, ma mère, mes parents. That is enough to introduce your own family and it is all this lesson asks of you. There is more to it, and the next lesson is where it arrives: the full set covers your, his, hers, ours and theirs, and there is one wrinkle in the ma column that nobody can guess and that is not worth meeting today. If you find yourself wanting to say whose something is and mon, ma and mes will not reach, use de and a name instead. That always works and you already have it.

examples.note: Père takes le, so it takes mon.
Plural, so mes, and the kind of word stops mattering.

doubleDuty.title: La femme is woman and wife. La fille is girl and daughter.
doubleDuty.body: Two of the most common words here mean two things, and French does not separate them. La femme is the word for woman and also the word for wife. La fille is the word for girl and also the word for daughter. Nothing in the spelling or the sound tells them apart, and the person listening picks one without noticing they chose. That matters more than it sounds, because the wrong reading usually still makes sense, so nobody corrects it and you never find out. What decides is the company the word keeps. Une femme is a woman, because une says one of many. La femme, standing on its own in a conversation about people you both know, is a wife. La fille de Paul is his daughter, because de and a name make it a relationship. Une fille is a girl. If you want to be certain, add the thing that fixes it rather than hoping the context will.

examples.note: On its own with la, this is a wife far more often than a woman.
De and a name settle it: this is his daughter, not a girl.

fossilised.title: Grand-mère never takes an e. The form stopped moving centuries ago.
fossilised.body: Grand-mère is written grand-mère whoever she is, and the e you would expect on the first half is not a spelling anyone uses. This looks like a mistake and it is not: the two halves were welded together a very long time ago, before the language settled into its current habits, and the pair has been carried forward as a single frozen item ever since. The same is true of grand-père and of les grands-parents, where the s lands on grands and nowhere else. Treat all three as single words you have learned whole, the way you learned aujourd'hui, rather than as two words you assemble. There is nothing to work out and nothing to apply elsewhere. Learn the spelling with the word and you will never have to think about it again.

examples.note: One frozen word, and the first half never moves.
The s lands on grands and nowhere else.

recorded.desc: THE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. « le fils » AND « fil » ARE ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, one pace, said one immediately after the other with no gap and no reset: le fils, fil, le fils, fil. The whole point is that the SPELLING PREDICTS THE WRONG SOUND, and two separate recordings let the speaker drift so the learner hears two performances instead of two words. le fils is FEES: the l is completely silent and the final s IS pronounced. fil is FEEL: the l is pronounced and there is no s. Do not lean on either one, do not slow the fils down to make the point, and do not aspirate the s. Read them as two ordinary words that happen to sit next to each other, because that is what a learner will meet. Then « le fils de Marie » as a whole phrase in the same take, so the trap is heard inside a sentence rather than only in isolation.

« la femme » RECORDED SLOWLY IN ISOLATION ONCE, and then again at ordinary pace, in the same take. It is FAM: the vowel is the one in the English word calm, and it is the only common French word where the letter e says that. This is the pronunciation the learner will get wrong and the deck is the only place it is heard alone, so the slow reading matters more here than anywhere else in the lesson. Then « la femme » and « une femme » AS A PAIR IN ONE TAKE, read IDENTICALLY apart from the little word in front. The teaching is that the two are acoustically the same and only the article separates them, so any difference the reader performs on the noun teaches something untrue. Finally the scene lines: « Voici la femme. » and « Voici une femme. », also one take, also identical on the noun.

EVERY MASCULINE AND FEMININE PAIR IS ONE TAKE, one voice, the masculine immediately followed by its feminine with no gap: le père / la mère, le frère / la sœur, le fils / la fille, l'oncle / la tante, le cousin / la cousine, le neveu / la nièce. Recorded apart, the learner compares two performances instead of two forms, and the whole teaching of this act is that the two members of each pair differ only in the article and the person. LE COUSIN / LA COUSINE IS THE ONE TO WATCH AND IT IS THE ONLY PAIR WHERE THE NOUN ITSELF CHANGES SOUND. le cousin ends in a NASAL VOWEL with NO n consonant behind it at all; la cousine has a REAL n, because a vowel follows it. Read the masculine with nothing after the vowel and the feminine with the n clearly sounded. Do not nasalise la cousine and do not put any n at the end of le cousin. Every other pair should sound identical on the noun.

EVERY de PHRASE IS RECORDED AS A WHOLE PHRASE, NEVER AS THREE WORDS. The rule being taught is about the ORDER, so a clip of de on its own teaches nothing and a phrase assembled from three separate clips teaches the learner to pause where a French speaker does not. « la mère de Paul », « le père de Marie », « le frère de Paul », « la sœur de Marie », « la fille de Paul », « le fils de Marie », each one continuous, with the de completely unstressed and swallowed into the phrase the way it really is. THE MINIMAL PAIR IS ONE TAKE: « Marie est la sœur de Paul. » immediately followed by « Paul est le frère de Marie. » Same voice, same pace, same everything, because the two sentences differ only in which name lands after de and the learner has to hear that as the only change. Do not emphasise either name.
clipIds: Marie est la sœur de Paul.
Paul est le frère de Marie.

recorded.desc: The rest of the household as one continuous take at an even pace: la famille, les parents, la grand-mère, le grand-père, les grands-parents, le petit-fils, la petite-fille, le mari, la femme, le beau-père, la belle-mère, le demi-frère, la demi-sœur. THE NASALS MUST BE CLOSED, WITH NO n SOUND BEHIND THEM AT ALL: les parents, la grand-mère, le grand-père and les grands-parents all carry a genuine nasal vowel and the app respells them with a superscript n deliberately. A reader who sounds the n contradicts the card. In les grands-parents the d of grands is silent and the liaison does NOT happen. In le petit-fils the t of petit is silent and the s of fils IS sounded, which is the same trap as the fils clip.

The three possessives, each attached to its noun and NEVER bare: « mon père », « ma mère », « mes parents ». A bare mon teaches nothing, because the whole question is which noun it goes in front of. One take, in that order. mon carries a nasal vowel with no n sound behind it; mes parents has NO liaison between mes and parents in ordinary speech at this level and should be read without one. Then the avoir lines, also one take: « J'ai un frère et deux sœurs. », « Je n'ai pas de frère. », « Tu as des frères et sœurs ? ». The last one is a question by INTONATION ONLY, with the voice rising at the end and the words in statement order, which is how it is really asked.
clipIds: J'ai un frère et deux sœurs.
Tu as des frères et sœurs ?

recorded.desc: The opening scene, French lines only, in the voice of a woman in her thirties at an ordinary conversational pace rather than a teaching pace. The beat where Salomé congratulates the learner on a marriage that has not happened (« Ah, tu es marié ? Félicitations ! ») must be WARM AND GENUINELY PLEASED, with no hint of correction, teasing or a raised eyebrow. The entire teaching depends on the learner hearing that NOTHING WENT WRONG as far as she is concerned: she has simply understood something that was not said, and any edge on that line turns an invisible error into a visible one and loses the point. The final line, « Ah d'accord ! Et lui, c'est le frère de Paul, non ? », should be equally unremarkable, because it is the rest of the lesson arriving in somebody else's ordinary speech.
clipIds: Ah d'accord ! Et lui, c'est le frère de Paul, non ?

lessons.title: La place de l'adjectif
lessons.intro: French puts the describing word after the thing it describes, and English puts it before, on every single phrase. Ten common words break the pattern, four of them change meaning depending on which side they sit, and this is the lesson where all of that becomes one decision you can make while you are still speaking.

sections.title: The Hotel That Used To Be One

say.text: One sentence, every word correct, and it describes a different building from the one you meant.

setting.place: A message thread, and a hotel with stone stairs somewhere behind it

beats.text: A friend is coming to Bordeaux for a weekend and has asked you where to stay. You know exactly the place: stone stairs, shutters, a hundred and fifty years old and still taking guests.
You have all the words for this. Nothing here is beyond you. You are about to say one of them on the wrong side of the noun.

beats.speaker: Théo
beats.fr: Alors, tu connais un endroit sympa pour deux nuits ?
beats.en: So, do you know a nice place for two nights?
beats.stage: Notice where sympa is sitting. Behind the noun, which is where most of them go.

beats.prompt: You want to say it is an old hotel. Which line do you send?

options.en: the one that puts the describing word first
the one that names the thing first

followUp.works: Yes. Now watch what the other one does, because it is not wrong and that is the difficulty.
followUp.breaks: That is the English order, and it is perfectly good French. Watch what Théo hears.

beats.speaker: You
beats.en: (You meant: it is an old hotel)

beats.speaker: Théo
beats.fr: Ah bon ? Et c'est quoi maintenant ? On peut dormir dedans ?
beats.en: Oh really? And what is it now? Can you sleep in it?
beats.stage: He is not correcting you. He understood every word and is answering the sentence you sent.

beats.heading: Both are correct. They are about different buildings.
beats.body: Nothing was misheard and nothing sounded wrong, so nobody will ever tell you. In front, ancien means it used to be a hotel. Behind, ancien means it is old and still open. The side carried the meaning.

wrong.en: It is a former hotel.

beats.coach: When in doubt, put it after. Théo would have understood either one, which is exactly why this never gets corrected.

beats.text: Four French words behave like that. Every other describing word has one correct side, and working out which side is the next twenty-five minutes.

closing.text: When in doubt, put it after. That sentence decides almost every one of these for you.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the fourth one is the reason this lesson exists at all.

goals.t: Put the describing word on the right side
goals.s: One default that covers almost everything, and a way of deciding in the moment rather than remembering afterwards.

goals.t: Know the ten that go in front
goals.s: A closed group that does not grow, so every new word you meet from here is already sorted.
What happens to des, what happens with two describing words at once, and three shapes that only exist in front.
The only place so far where moving a word changes what you said rather than how good it sounded.

sections.title: The Side Is A Decision
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: Four cards before any list, because this decides how you build every phrase from here.

cards.label: What you already do
cards.head: Colours go after the thing
cards.body: You met this with colours and it is true of every one of them. The house first, then what colour it is. Nothing about that was a fact about colours: it is the general order, and colours were simply the first place you met it.

cards.label: What is new
cards.head: It holds for almost every describing word
cards.fr: Nous habitons dans un quartier calme.
cards.sub: [KALM] · We live in a quiet neighborhood.
cards.body: Calm is not a colour and it goes in the same place. So do easy, difficult, delicious, French, comfortable and every other describing word you will ever look up. The thing first, then what it is like.

cards.label: Why it feels wrong
cards.head: English never does this
cards.body: In English every describing word goes in front: a quiet neighbourhood, a red car, an easy question. So the French order is the reverse of the one your ear expects, on every phrase, which is why this stays awkward long after you understand it.

cards.label: The six you already met
cards.head: They were not six separate facts
cards.fr: C'est une grande ville. · C'est un bon restaurant.
cards.body: The last lesson gave you six that come first: grand, petit, beau, vieux, bon and mauvais. It did not say why. They are not six exceptions. They are most of a small closed group, and this lesson adds the last four.

cards.label: The decision
cards.head: You will not always know
cards.body: Ten words go in front, and you reach for them constantly, so the exception feels bigger than it is. When you cannot remember whether a word is one of them: When in doubt, put it after. Ten against everything else is not a close call.

sections.title: The Thing, Then What It Is Like
sections.hint: Ten sentences. The describing word is always the last one.
sections.say: Ten real sentences. Read each one and notice you never have to decide anything.

sections.title: One Noun, Both Sides
sections.say: When in doubt, put it after. Tap either cell to hear it. The noun never moves.

cells: Nous habitons dans un quartier calme.
rows.say: C'est un joli quartier. Nous habitons dans un quartier calme.

detail.title: quartier, described twice
detail.body: C'est un joli quartier. Nous habitons dans un quartier calme. Same noun, two describing words, each one where it belongs. The word decides the side. The noun has nothing to do with it.
detail.say: C'est un joli quartier. Nous habitons dans un quartier calme.

rows.say: Il a une petite voiture. Mon frère conduit une voiture rouge.

detail.title: voiture, described twice
detail.body: Il a une petite voiture. Mon frère conduit une voiture rouge. Same noun, two describing words, each one where it belongs. The word decides the side. The noun has nothing to do with it.
detail.say: Il a une petite voiture. Mon frère conduit une voiture rouge.

detail.title: maison, described twice
detail.body: C'est une belle maison. Nous avons une maison bleue. Same noun, two describing words, each one where it belongs. The word decides the side. The noun has nothing to do with it.

rows.say: C'est un gros chat gris. Le chat gris dort.

sections.title: Which Side Does It Go?
sections.say: Sixteen words and two slots. Decide before you read the check, every time.

groups.label: In front: the six you already have

check.q: These six all go in front of the noun. What actually puts them there?
opts: They are all about size or quality
They are six of the ten that go in front, and nothing else
They all describe people rather than things
check.why: Membership of the group, and nothing else. Bon is about quality and petit is about size, so meaning does not explain it. Nouveau and mauvais are not short, so length does not either. They go in front because they are on the list.

groups.label: In front: the four that are new

check.q: With these four added, how many words go in front of the noun in French?
opts: ten, and the group takes no more
check.why: Ten, and that is the whole group. This is the useful part: the list is closed, so a describing word you have never seen before is already decided before you look it up.

check.q: None of these six is on the list. Where does each one go?
check.why: Behind, every time, and so does every other describing word in the language. When in doubt, put it after. These six are a sample of a group with no end to it, which is why the ten are worth learning and these are not.

sections.title: Now Without The Groups
sections.say: The same decision with the answer no longer sorted for you. Commit before you check.

items.fr: Le chef prépare un plat délicieux.
items.en: The chef prepares a delicious dish.

check.q: You want to say a difficult question. Where does difficile go?
check.why: une question difficile. Difficile is not one of the ten, so it goes behind. The first option is the English order and it is the mistake this whole lesson exists to stop.

groups.label: One of the ten, and one not

items.fr: Mon frère conduit une voiture rouge.
items.en: My brother drives a red car.
I am reading an easy book.

check.q: You have never met the word « bruyant », meaning noisy. Where do you put it?
opts: you cannot say without looking it up
check.why: Behind. When in doubt, put it after. The ten are closed and bruyant is not one of them, so it goes where every other describing word goes. That is the value of a closed list: a word you have never seen is already sorted.

sections.title: Four Words, Two Meanings Each
sections.say: Four rows. Both halves of each one are correct French, and they mean different things.

cells:
C'est un grand homme.
He is a great man.

C'est un homme grand.
He is a tall man.
rows.say: C'est un grand homme. C'est un homme grand.

detail.title: grand: great, important or tall
detail.body: C'est un grand homme. He is a great man. C'est un homme grand. He is a tall man. In front, grand means great, important. Behind, it means tall. Both are correct French, so nobody will tell you which one you said.
detail.say: C'est un grand homme. C'est un homme grand.

cells:
C'est un ancien hôtel.
It is a former hotel.

C'est un hôtel ancien.
It is an old hotel.
rows.say: C'est un ancien hôtel. C'est un hôtel ancien.

detail.title: ancien: former or old
detail.body: C'est un ancien hôtel. It is a former hotel. C'est un hôtel ancien. It is an old hotel. In front, ancien means former. Behind, it means old. Both are correct French, so nobody will tell you which one you said.
detail.say: C'est un ancien hôtel. C'est un hôtel ancien.

cells:
C'est un pauvre homme.
He is an unfortunate man.

C'est un homme pauvre.
He is a man with no money.
rows.say: C'est un pauvre homme. C'est un homme pauvre.

detail.title: pauvre: unfortunate or with no money
detail.body: C'est un pauvre homme. He is an unfortunate man. C'est un homme pauvre. He is a man with no money. In front, pauvre means unfortunate. Behind, it means with no money. Both are correct French, so nobody will tell you which one you said.
detail.say: C'est un pauvre homme. C'est un homme pauvre.

C'est ma propre chambre.
It is my own room.

C'est ma chambre propre.
It is my clean room.

detail.body: C'est ma propre chambre. It is my own room. C'est ma chambre propre. It is my clean room. In front, propre means own. Behind, it means clean. Both are correct French, so nobody will tell you which one you said.
detail.say: C'est ma propre chambre. C'est ma chambre propre.

sections.title: Eight Sentences, Four Meanings Apart
sections.hint: Each pair is two cards. Read both before you swipe on.
sections.say: The four pairs one screen at a time, so you meet each meaning on its own.

cards.label: grand, in front
cards.head: great, important
cards.body: In front, grand is about importance rather than height. Nothing about the man's size is being said.

cards.label: grand, behind
cards.head: tall
cards.body: Behind, grand is a measurement. Same three words, same order of everything else, and the two sentences describe two different men.

cards.label: ancien, in front
cards.head: former
cards.body: In front, ancien means it used to be one and is not one now. It could be flats today.

cards.label: ancien, behind
cards.head: old
cards.body: Behind, ancien means old. It is still a hotel and you can still book a room in it.

cards.label: pauvre, in front
cards.head: unfortunate
cards.body: In front, pauvre is sympathy. It says nothing at all about money.

cards.label: pauvre, behind
cards.head: with no money
cards.sub: [POHVR] · He is a man with no money.
cards.body: Behind, pauvre is about money and nothing else. English uses the one word poor for both of these, which is why the position has to do the work.

cards.label: propre, in front
cards.head: own
cards.body: In front, propre means it belongs to me and I do not share it.

cards.label: propre, behind
cards.head: clean
cards.body: Behind, propre means clean. Same room either way, and only one of the two sentences is about tidying.

cards.label: the one from the scene
cards.head: In front, ancien is always former
cards.body: If you meant a teacher who is elderly, this sentence did not say it. It says you no longer study with them, and the person you said it to now believes that. Nothing about it sounds wrong, which is why it survives.

cards.label: how many words do this
cards.head: Four, and you have met all four
cards.body: This is not a general property of French. Four common words change meaning by position and the rest do not, so there is no wider system to worry about. Every other describing word has exactly one correct side.

sections.title: Which One Did You Mean?
sections.say: Each check gives you a meaning in English and asks for the side. The word alone cannot answer it.

check.q: You want to tell someone your neighbour is very tall. Which do you say?
check.why: C'est un homme grand. Behind the noun, grand is a measurement. In front it would say he is a great man, which is about importance and says nothing about his height.

items.en: He is a man with no money.

check.q: You share a flat and you want to say the room is yours alone. Which do you say?
opts: You cannot say this with propre.
check.why: C'est ma propre chambre. In front, propre means your own. Behind, it means clean, so the other option tells your flatmate the room has been tidied and says nothing about who it belongs to.

groups.label: The four, with no sentence around them

items.en: great, important in front · tall behind
unfortunate in front · with no money behind

check.q: Somebody hands you the word « ancien » and asks which side of the noun it goes on. What is the answer?
opts: in front, because it is a short common word
behind, because it is not one of the ten
there is no answer until you know which meaning you want
either side, and it makes no difference
check.why: There is no answer yet. These four are the only words in the lesson where the word alone cannot tell you, because both sides are correct and they mean different things. For every other describing word the question does have an answer.

sections.title: Five Things An English Speaker Writes
sections.say: When in doubt, put it after. Five errors, one per screen, and the first one is the whole lesson.

errors.wrong: Writing « une rouge voiture ».
errors.why: The English order applied to French. Rouge is not one of the ten, so it goes behind, and this is the error every English speaker makes on their first day and some make for years.

errors.wrong: Writing « une maison grande » for a big house.
errors.why: The correction over-applied. A learner who has just been told describing words go behind starts putting all of them behind, including the ten that do not. This one arrives about a week after the first.

errors.wrong: Writing « des beaux tableaux ».
errors.why: Once one of the ten moves in front of a plural noun, des shortens to de. Nothing else in the phrase changes and the adjective keeps its own plural ending.

errors.wrong: Writing « un vieux ami ».
errors.why: Ami starts with a vowel sound, and vieux grows a special form in front of one. These three forms exist only in front of the noun, which is another way of noticing which side you are on.

errors.wrong: Saying « un ancien hôtel » when you mean the building is old.
errors.why: The one error nobody will correct, because both are correct French. In front, ancien means it used to be a hotel. Four words behave this way and this is the one you will meet most.

sections.title: When Des Becomes De
sections.hint: Ten sentences, and the same small change in every one.
sections.say: One consequence of the rule you have just learned, and it only ever happens in the plural.

cards.label: the rule
cards.head: One of the ten, in front, and a plural noun
cards.body: The small word in front is de, not des. When one of the ten gets in front of a plural noun the article shortens, the adjective still takes its own plural ending, and nothing else in the phrase moves.

cards.label: you have seen de before
cards.head: This is the second place it happens
cards.body: The indefinite articles lesson showed des shortening to de under a negative: je n'ai pas de voiture. That is a different trigger and worth keeping separate. There, the negative did it. Here, the describing word moving in front does it.

cards.label: 2 of 10
cards.head: de, not des
cards.body: The same shortening again. Nine real sentences in a row and not one of them says des, because every one has a describing word in front of a plural noun.

cards.label: 3 of 10

cards.body: The same shortening again. Nine real sentences in a row and not one of them says des, because every one has a describing word in front of a plural noun.
