sections.title: Three Shapes That Only Exist In Front
sections.hint: Each one beside the ordinary form it replaces.
sections.say: Two of these you met last lesson. The third is new, and all three tell you the same thing about position.

cards.label: beau, consonant behind it
cards.head: beau
cards.body: The ordinary form, because the noun after it starts with a consonant. Nothing unusual happens here.

cards.label: bel, from last lesson
cards.head: bel
cards.body: You had bel last lesson as a shape beau takes. Here it is doing something else as well: it is telling you where in the phrase you are.

cards.label: vieux, consonant behind it
cards.head: vieux
cards.body: The ordinary form, because the noun after it starts with a consonant. Nothing unusual happens here.

cards.label: vieil, from last lesson
cards.head: vieil
cards.body: You had vieil last lesson as a shape vieux takes. Here it is doing something else as well: it is telling you where in the phrase you are.

cards.label: nouveau, consonant behind it
cards.head: nouveau
cards.body: The ordinary form, because the noun after it starts with a consonant. Nothing unusual happens here.

cards.label: nouvel, new
cards.head: nouvel
cards.body: nouveau does the same thing beau and vieux do, and this is the third and last word in the language that does it. Say un nouveau hôtel out loud and you will hear why.

cards.label: why this belongs here
cards.head: A shape that can only happen in front
cards.body: A describing word behind its noun never needs one of these, because there is no noun after it to run into. So meeting bel, vieil or nouvel is a signal: you are in front of the noun, and the word is one of the ten.

cards.label: what not to worry about
cards.head: Two on the same side is a later problem
cards.body: Putting two describing words on the SAME side has its own rules and they are not worth your time yet. If you need it, use two short sentences. Everything on this screen is one from each group.

sections.title: The Flat Listing
sections.say: Four lines from a listing, and one of them is not describing what the person writing it thought.
sections.text: Flat listings are the one kind of French writing where every word is doing paid work, because the person writing them is charging by the month and the person reading them has forty others open. « C'est un ancien hôtel. » That line is the reason four people came to the viewing and left again, because they had all understood that the building used to be a hotel and is something else now. The owner meant the opposite and has never worked out why nobody stays. « Nous avons de beaux appartements. » Correct, and the small word in front of it is the tell: de rather than des, because beaux got in front of the noun. The third line is about the street and it is the easiest sentence on the page. « Nous habitons dans un quartier calme. » Nothing to decide there, because calme is not one of the ten and goes where almost everything goes. The last line is the one worth copying. « C'est une petite ville tranquille. »

glossary.note: In front, ancien means it used to be one. Behind, it would mean the building is old.
de rather than des, because one of the ten got in front of a plural noun.
The default order. Calme is not one of the ten, so it goes behind the noun.
One from each group. Petite in front, tranquille behind, and the town in between.

questions.q: What did the owner mean by the first line, and what does it actually say?
questions.a: They meant the building is old and still a hotel, which would be « un hôtel ancien ». What they wrote says it used to be a hotel and is not one now. Both sentences are correct French, so nobody reading the listing had any reason to think it was a mistake.

questions.q: The second line says « de beaux appartements ». The plural would normally take a longer word in front of it. What shortened it?
questions.a: Beaux is one of the ten and it got in front of a plural noun, which shortens the article to de. The adjective still carries its own plural ending. This is the only place in the listing where a word outside the noun phrase had to change.

questions.q: The last line has two describing words. How did the writer decide where to put them?
questions.a: They did not have to decide anything. Petite is one of the ten so it goes in front, tranquille is not so it goes behind, and the noun ends up between them. Two describing words in one phrase is not a third rule, it is the two rules you already have applied at once.

sections.say: One viewing, and you hold up your half. Every turn is a decision about which side a word goes.
sections.setting: The same building from the listing, a week later. Théo has come to look at it and you are showing him round.

alts.en: It is an old building, yes.

turns.ai: Et l'appartement ? Il est comment ?
turns.en: And the flat? What is it like?
turns.user: C'est une belle maison.
turns.userEn: It is a beautiful house.

alts.fr: Il y a de beaux appartements ici.

turns.ai: Et le quartier ? Il y a beaucoup de bruit le soir ?
turns.en: And the neighbourhood? Is there a lot of noise in the evening?
turns.user: Nous habitons dans un quartier calme.
turns.userEn: We live in a quiet neighbourhood.

alts.fr: Le quartier est calme le soir.
alts.en: The neighbourhood is quiet in the evening.

turns.ai: Parfait. Et la chambre, je la partage avec quelqu'un ?
turns.en: Perfect. And the bedroom, do I share it with someone?
turns.user: Non, c'est ta propre chambre.
turns.userEn: No, it is your own room.

alts.fr: Non, la chambre est à toi.
Non, tu as ta propre chambre.
alts.en: No, you have your own room.

turns.ai: Ah, et tu as dit un ancien hôtel dans l'annonce. C'est encore un hôtel ou pas ?
turns.en: Ah, and you said a former hotel in the listing. Is it still a hotel or not?
turns.user: Pardon, un hôtel ancien. Il est vieux, mais c'est toujours un hôtel.
turns.userEn: Sorry, an old hotel. It is old, but it is still a hotel.

alts.fr: Un hôtel ancien, pas un ancien hôtel.
alts.en: An old hotel, not a former hotel.

alts.fr: Ancien apres le nom. Il est vieux et il marche toujours.
alts.en: Ancien after the noun. It is old and still running.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: Where does a describing word go, if you have no idea?
cards.back: When in doubt, put it after. The group in front is ten words and closed; the group behind is endless.
cards.say: Nous habitons dans un quartier calme.

cards.front: Name the ten that go in front.
cards.back: petit, grand, gros, jeune, vieux, beau, joli, bon, mauvais, nouveau
cards.say: petit, grand, gros, jeune, vieux, beau, joli, bon, mauvais, nouveau

cards.front: You meet a describing word you have never seen. Which side?
cards.back: Behind. The front group is closed and does not take new members.
C'est une grande ville. grande is one of the ten, so it goes in front.
Mon frère conduit une voiture rouge. rouge is not on the list, so it goes behind.
cards.say: Mon frère conduit une voiture rouge.

cards.front: What happens to des when one of the ten moves in front?
cards.back: Ce sont de beaux tableaux. It shortens to de, and nothing else changes.
C'est un grand homme. In front, grand is about importance.
C'est un homme grand. Behind, grand is a measurement.
C'est un ancien hôtel. In front, ancien means it used to be one.
C'est un hôtel ancien. Behind, ancien just means old.
C'est ma propre chambre. In front, propre means it belongs to you.
C'est un homme pauvre. Behind, pauvre is about money and nothing else.

cards.front: Why does beau become bel in un bel arbre?
cards.back: Arbre starts with a vowel sound. These three shapes only ever happen in front of the noun.

cards.front: Two describing words, one on the list and one not.
cards.back: Elle porte une petite robe rouge. Each one takes its own side and the noun sits between them.
cards.say: Elle porte une petite robe rouge.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a message thread go wrong without anybody noticing, learned that French puts the describing word behind the noun and that English does the opposite on every single phrase, and met the small closed group that goes in front instead. You have sorted words into sides with the groups shown and then without them, seen what happens to des when one of the ten moves up, met three shapes that can only ever occur in front of a vowel, and watched four words change meaning depending on which side they sit. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: Which side, by default
rounds.say: The default, on words that are not on the list.

questions.q: You want to say a red car. Which is correct French?
questions.why: une voiture rouge. Rouge is not one of the ten, so it goes behind the noun. The English order puts it in front and is the single most common beginner mistake in French.

questions.q: You have just looked up « bruyant », meaning noisy, and you have never seen it before. Where does it go?
opts: behind the noun, because the front group is closed
in front of the noun, like in English
behind the verb, never inside the noun phrase
either side, because new words have no fixed place
questions.why: Behind. When in doubt, put it after. The ten that go in front are a closed group and take no new members, so any describing word you have not met is already decided.

questions.q: Write the French for a quiet neighbourhood, using quartier and calme.
questions.why: un quartier calme. The thing first, then what it is like. Calme is not on the short list, so there was no decision to make here.

questions.q: Listen, and choose what you heard.
questions.why: un plat délicieux. The dish comes first and the description follows it, which is where almost every describing word in French sits.

rounds.label: The ten that go in front
rounds.say: The exception, and knowing when you are in it.

questions.q: You want to say a big house. Which is correct French?
questions.why: une grande maison. Grand is one of the ten, so it goes in front. This is the mistake that arrives about a week after somebody learns the default, when they start putting every describing word behind.

questions.q: Which of these words is NOT one of the ten that go in front?
questions.why: facile. Joli, gros and mauvais are all on the short list. Facile is an ordinary describing word and goes behind the noun: une question facile.

questions.q: Write the French for a good restaurant, using bon and restaurant.
questions.why: un bon restaurant. Bon is one of the ten. Un restaurant bon is not what a French speaker says, even though it follows the general rule.

questions.q: One of these phrases has the describing word on the wrong side. Write it out corrected.
questions.why: une petite ville. Petit is one of the ten and goes in front. This one is worth saying out loud a few times, because the corrected version is the one that will feel wrong to an English ear.

rounds.label: When the side changes the meaning
rounds.say: Both options are correct French in every question here. The meaning decides.

questions.q: Your neighbour is two metres tall. How do you say he is a tall man?
questions.why: C'est un homme grand. Behind the noun, grand is a measurement. In front it means great or important and says nothing about his height, and both sentences are correct French so nobody would correct you.

questions.q: The building is a hundred years old and still takes guests. How do you describe it?
questions.why: C'est un hôtel ancien. Behind the noun, ancien means old. In front it means former, so the other version tells the listener it used to be a hotel and is something else now.

questions.q: You share a flat and the bedroom is yours alone. How do you say it is your own room?
questions.why: C'est ma propre chambre. In front, propre means your own. Behind it means clean, so the other version tells your flatmate the room has been tidied and nothing about who it belongs to.

questions.q: You feel sorry for someone after a hard week. Which sentence says that, rather than saying he has no money?
questions.why: C'est un pauvre homme. In front, pauvre is sympathy and says nothing about money. Behind, it is about money and nothing else. English uses the one word poor for both, which is why the position has to do the work.

rounds.label: What happens to des
rounds.say: One consequence of the rule, and it only shows up in the plural.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: Ce sont ___ beaux tableaux. Write only the missing word.
questions.why: de. Once one of the ten gets in front of a plural noun, des shortens to de. The adjective keeps its own plural ending and nothing else in the phrase moves.

questions.q: Which of these is correct French for beautiful flowers?
questions.why: de belles fleurs. Belle is one of the ten and it is in front of a plural noun, so des shortens to de. Belles still carries its own plural s.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: Nous avons ___ nouveaux voisins. Write only the missing word.
questions.why: de. Same rule again on a different word. Nouveau is one of the ten, the noun is plural, so des becomes de.

questions.q: Which of these plurals keeps des, because the describing word is NOT in front of the noun?
questions.why: des voitures rouges. Rouge is not on the short list, so it stays behind the noun, nothing moved in front of anything, and des is untouched. The shortening only happens when one of the ten moves up.

rounds.label: The vowel forms, and two at once
rounds.say: Three shapes that only exist in front, and what happens with two describing words.

questions.q: You want to say an old friend, using vieux and ami. Which is correct?
questions.why: un vieil ami. Ami starts with a vowel sound, and vieux takes a special shape in front of one. Say un vieux ami out loud and you will hear the reason it exists.

questions.q: Listen. Which one has the vowel form in it?
questions.why: C'est un bel arbre. Arbre starts with a vowel sound, so beau becomes bel. A describing word sitting behind its noun never needs one of these shapes, because there is no noun after it to run into.

questions.q: Write the French for a small red dress, using petite and rouge.
questions.why: une petite robe rouge. Petite is one of the ten so it goes in front, rouge is not so it goes behind, and the dress sits between them. This is not a third rule, it is the two you already have applied at once.

questions.q: One of these has a describing word on the wrong side. Write it out corrected.
questions.why: un petit chien blanc. Petit is on the list and goes in front, blanc is not and goes behind, and the dog is in the middle. Both describing words were on the wrong side here.

rounds.label: All of it at once
rounds.say: The last round, and every question needs more than one thing from the lesson.

questions.q: Listen carefully. In which one does the d at the end of grand get pronounced?
opts: Mon frère est un grand garçon.
questions.why: C'est un grand homme. Homme starts with a vowel sound, so the silent d at the end of grand wakes up and is said as a t. In front of garçon there is nothing to wake it.

questions.q: Say this out loud: a beautiful house, using belle and maison.
questions.why: une belle maison. Belle is one of the ten, so it goes in front. Say it as one phrase rather than three words, because that is what makes the order stick.

questions.q: Say this out loud: an old hotel that is still open, using hôtel and ancien.
questions.why: un hôtel ancien. Behind the noun, ancien means old. This is the sentence the scene at the start of the lesson needed and did not have.

questions.q: Write the French for a quiet neighbourhood, using quartier and calme, and put the two words in the right order.
questions.why: un quartier calme. When in doubt, put it after. Calme is not one of the ten, so it goes behind, and this is the shape almost every describing phrase in French takes.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can put a describing word on the right side of the noun, name the ten that break the pattern, handle what follows from them, and hear four words change meaning depending on where they sit. The default half of that transfers to every describing word you will ever meet, including all the ones you have not learned yet, which is the part worth keeping. Family vocabulary is next, and the possessives after it, and you will be building noun phrases in both of them from the first screen.
points: When in doubt, put it after. The group in front is ten words and closed. The group behind has no end.
English puts every describing word in front, so the French order is the reverse on every phrase and stays awkward after you understand it.
Once one of the ten moves in front of a plural noun, des shortens to de.
Four words change meaning by position, and both versions are correct, so nobody will tell you which one you said.

le, la, l' and les, introduced in a1.04
un, une and des, and that des becomes de under a negative, introduced in a1.11
The plural of a noun, introduced in a1.03
The full present of être, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07
mon, ma and mes, introduced in a1.05
Adjective agreement, and that a colour follows the noun, introduced in a1.13
That a final consonant is usually silent and a following vowel can wake it, introduced in sons.06 and sons.10
grammarIntroduced: The position of the attributive adjective, introduced here for the first time as a system rather than as a fact about colour
Post-nominal placement as the default for the open class of adjectives
The closed pre-nominal set: petit, grand, gros, jeune, vieux, beau, joli, bon, mauvais, nouveau
Adjectives whose meaning depends on position: grand, ancien, pauvre, propre
The reduction of des to de before a pre-nominal adjective
The pre-vocalic masculine forms bel, vieil and nouvel, taught here as position-bound rather than as a third form
Two adjectives distributed either side of the noun
The liaison of a pre-nominal grand before a vowel-initial noun

overview.introFr: En français, le mot qui décrit se place après la chose. Dix mots font l'inverse.

acts.title: Which side
acts.milestone: You have watched a correct sentence describe the wrong building.

acts.title: The short list
acts.milestone: Ten words in front, everything else behind, and you have sorted both with and without the answer shown.

acts.title: When the side changes the meaning
acts.milestone: Four words, eight meanings, and no way to hear which one you chose.

acts.title: What follows from it
acts.milestone: des becomes de, three shapes exist only in front, and two describing words need no new rule.

acts.title: Sort it, say it, use it
acts.milestone: You have written the order down and said it out loud, rather than recognised it.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. Family vocabulary is next, and you will be building noun phrases in it from the first screen.

lessons.reframe: When in doubt, put it after.

errorTriggers.description: Puts every describing word in front of the noun, the way English does. The default error, and the one every English speaker starts with.
Having learned the default, puts the ten behind the noun as well: writes une maison grande. Arrives about a week after the first error is fixed.
Picks the wrong side of a meaning-changing pair and is understood as saying the other thing. Invisible to the learner, because both versions are correct French and nobody corrects either one.
Leaves des in place when one of the ten moves in front of a plural noun: writes des beaux tableaux.
Uses the plain form in front of a vowel: writes un vieux ami, un beau arbre, un nouveau hôtel.
With two describing words, stacks both in front the way English does: writes une petite rouge robe.

drills.title: The thing, then the description
drills.coach: The English is on the left and it is in the English order. Say the French out loud with the noun first, before you turn the card.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is correct French for a difficult question?
drills.why: une question difficile. Difficile is not one of the ten, so it goes behind the noun like almost every other describing word in French.

drills.title: On the list, or not
drills.coach: Look at the describing word, not at the noun. Is it one of the ten? If you cannot remember, put it behind, because that is right far more often than it is wrong.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is correct French for a small town?
drills.why: une petite ville. Petit is one of the ten and goes in front, even though almost everything else goes behind.

drills.title: Which meaning did you want?
buckets: about importance, or former, or yours, or unlucky
about height, or age, or clean, or money
drills.coach: Read the English on each card before you place it. The French words are the same on both sides of every pair, so the only thing telling you where it goes is what it means.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want to say your friend is tall. Which do you say?
drills.why: C'est un homme grand. Behind the noun, grand is about height. In front it means great or important.

drills.title: des or de
buckets: de, because one of the ten is in front
des, because nothing moved in front
drills.coach: Find the noun, then look at what is immediately in front of it. If one of the ten got there first, des shortens to de. If nothing did, des stays as it is.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is correct French for good results?
drills.why: de bons résultats. Bon is one of the ten and it is in front of a plural noun, so des shortens to de.

drills.title: What is behind the word
drills.coach: Look at the first sound of the noun, not the first letter. If it is a vowel sound, the describing word in front of it changes shape.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is correct French for an old friend?
drills.why: un vieil ami. Ami starts with a vowel sound, so vieux takes its special in-front shape. Say the other one out loud and you will hear why the form exists.

drills.title: One on each side
drills.coach: Take the two describing words one at a time. Each one has its own side and neither one cares what the other is doing. The noun ends up in the middle.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is correct French for a small white dog?
drills.why: un petit chien blanc. Petit is one of the ten so it goes in front, blanc is not so it goes behind, and the dog sits between them.

sections.title: The ten, each in a phrase

rows.k: When in doubt, put it after.
rows.v: The group in front is ten words and closed. The group behind is every other describing word in the language, including all the ones you have not met.
rows.say: Nous habitons dans un quartier calme.

rows.v: The noun first, then the word describing it: un quartier calme, une question facile, un café noir. English does the opposite on every phrase.
petit, grand, gros, jeune, vieux, beau, joli, bon, mauvais, nouveau. They are the words you reach for most, which is why the exception feels bigger than it is.
rows.say: petit, grand, gros, jeune, vieux, beau, joli, bon, mauvais, nouveau

rows.v: Once one of the ten is in front of a plural noun: de beaux tableaux, de bonnes vacances, de vieux amis. The adjective keeps its own plural ending.
In front of a vowel sound: un bel arbre, un vieil immeuble, un nouvel hôtel. These shapes can only ever occur in front of the noun.
rows.say: un bel arbre, un vieil immeuble, un nouvel hôtel

rows.v: One from each group, and the noun in between: une petite robe rouge, un petit chien blanc. No new rule, just the two you already have.
rows.say: Elle porte une petite robe rouge.

sections.title: In front, and behind
rows: C'est un homme pauvre. (with no money)

sections.title: Why this one is invisible
sections.body: Every other mistake in this lesson gets caught eventually, because the wrong version is not French and a listener stumbles over it. Une rouge voiture is not something a French speaker says, so somebody will eventually repeat it back to you the right way round and you will notice. These four are different, and it is worth understanding why rather than just memorising the list. Both versions are grammatical, both are ordinary, and both are things people say every day. When you say un ancien hôtel meaning an old building, nothing has gone wrong from the listener's side at all: they have received a well-formed sentence, understood it correctly, and are now holding a fact about the world that is not true. There is nothing for them to correct. The conversation carries on from the new footing and neither of you finds out. This is why the four are worth learning as four rather than trusting to exposure. Exposure fixes the errors that get corrected, and nobody corrects these. The four are grand, ancien, pauvre and propre, and the pattern across all of them is roughly the same: in front, the word is about something abstract or about the speaker's attitude, and behind, it is about a plain physical fact. A great man is a judgement; a tall man is a measurement. A former hotel is about the building's history; an old hotel is about the building. Your own room is about who it belongs to; a clean room is about the state of it. An unfortunate man is your sympathy; a man with no money is his bank balance. That is not a rule you can apply to a new word, because only four words do this, but it is a way of remembering which of the two you wanted once you know the word is one of the four.

whichSide.title: The describing word usually comes second
whichSide.body: You already do this with colours: une veste verte, the jacket and then its colour. That habit is the general rule, not a rule about colours. Most French describing words sit behind the thing they describe, and English is the odd one out here, because English puts every single one of them in front. So the sentence you are about to build has the words in the opposite order to the one your ear wants, and the fix is not to translate faster. It is to name the thing first and describe it second. Un quartier calme. Une question facile. Un café noir. The thing, then what it is like.

examples.note: The neighbourhood first, then what it is like.
The same order again, on a word that has nothing to do with colour.

theShortList.term: the ten that go in front
theShortList.title: A small closed group, and it does not grow
theShortList.body: Ten words break the pattern and sit in front of the noun instead: petit, grand, gros, jeune, vieux, beau, joli, bon, mauvais, nouveau. They are the words you reach for most often, which is why the exception feels bigger than it is. The useful fact is that this group is closed. New words do not join it. Every describing word you meet from here that is not on this list goes behind the noun, and you can stop wondering about each one as it arrives.

examples.note: grande in front, because grand is one of the ten.
bon in front, for the same reason and no other.

positionCarriesMeaning.term: when the side changes the meaning
positionCarriesMeaning.title: Four words that mean two different things
positionCarriesMeaning.body: This is the only place in the course so far where moving a word changes what a sentence means rather than how good it sounds. Un grand homme is a great man and un homme grand is a tall man. Un ancien hôtel used to be a hotel; un hôtel ancien still is one and is simply old. Both versions are correct French, so nobody corrects you and nothing sounds wrong. The other person just understands you to have said the other thing, and the conversation carries on from there. Four words behave this way and you have met all four: grand, ancien, pauvre, propre.

examples.note: In front: about importance.
Behind: about height. The same three words.

deInFront.title: One small word changes when the adjective moves up
deInFront.body: Once one of the ten moves in front of a plural noun, des shortens to de. Ce sont de beaux tableaux, and the longer form is what an English speaker reaches for. You have seen des shorten to de once before, under a negative, in the indefinite articles lesson: je n'ai pas de voiture. This is a second place it happens and the trigger is different, so it is worth meeting on its own rather than filed with the first. Nothing else in the phrase moves, and the adjective still takes its own plural ending.

examples.note: de, not des, because beaux got in front of the noun.
The same shortening on bons, in an ordinary sentence.

vowelForm.title: Three shapes that exist only in front
vowelForm.body: Beau, vieux and nouveau each grow a third form used in front of a word starting with a vowel sound: un bel arbre, un vieil immeuble, un nouvel hôtel. Every one of them is a mouthful to say the other way, which is the whole reason they exist. They are worth noticing here rather than memorising as three odd words, because they can only ever turn up in front of the noun. A describing word sitting behind its noun never needs one, so meeting them is another way of noticing which side you are on.

examples.note: A consonant behind it, so the plain form.
A vowel behind it, and the same word changes shape.

twoAtOnce.title: Two describing words, one in each place
twoAtOnce.body: When a phrase carries one word from the short list and one from everywhere else, they simply take their own places and the noun sits between them. Une petite robe rouge. Un petit chien blanc. Nothing new is happening and there is no extra rule to learn: each word goes where it was always going to go. This is worth seeing once, because written down it looks like a third pattern and it is not.

examples.note: petite in front, rouge behind, the dress in the middle.
The same shape again with a different pair of words.

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. EVERY MEANING-CHANGING PAIR IS ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, the front version immediately followed by the behind version with no gap and no reset: « C'est un grand homme. C'est un homme grand. », then the ancien pair, then pauvre, then propre. The ONLY difference the learner may hear is where the word sits. Recorded apart these become two performances and the learner compares two readings instead of two meanings, and here the meaning is the entire point of the lesson. DO NOT ACT THE DIFFERENCE. There is a strong temptation to lean on the adjective in the front version to signal that it means something special. It does not sound special in French and a reader who marks it teaches the learner to listen for an emphasis that will never be there. Read all eight sentences as flatly as you would read a shopping list. ONE GENUINE SOUND DIFFERENCE EXISTS AND MUST NOT BE FLATTENED: in « un grand homme » the d at the end of grand is pronounced as a t, because homme starts with a vowel. In « un homme grand » it is silent. That difference is in the language and should be read normally rather than emphasised.

THE LIAISON, AND THE TWO SENTENCES MUST BE ADJACENT IN ONE TAKE: « C'est un grand homme. » immediately followed by « Mon frère est un grand garçon. ». Same word, same position, and the d at the end of grand is said as a t in the first and is silent in the second, because homme begins with a vowel and garçon does not. Recorded in separate sessions the learner hears two readings; recorded together they hear one consonant appear. Then « C'est un homme grand. » in the same take, where grand has nothing behind it at all and the d stays silent. Three sentences, one voice, one breath group each, no pause longer than a beat. This is the ONLY ear question in the lesson. Placement itself is not one: both orders are pronounceable and neither sounds wrong, so an ear test of word order would test nothing.
clipIds: Mon frère est un grand garçon.

recorded.desc: THE de FORM, AND THE ERROR MUST NOT BE RECORDED. Record « de beaux tableaux », « de belles fleurs », « de bons résultats », « de bonnes vacances », « de vieux amis », « de nouveaux voisins », « de petits problèmes », « de petites chaussures », « de jolies fleurs » and « de vieilles photos », one take, one voice, straight through. DO NOT RECORD « des beaux tableaux » OR ANY OTHER des VERSION. The lesson shows the error in writing and must never have a clip of it, because a clip of an error becomes indistinguishable from a model the moment it leaves the card it was authored on. There is no card in this lesson that plays a wrong form and there must not be one. Read de as a short unstressed syllable running into the adjective rather than as a separate word, which is what it sounds like in speech and is the thing that makes the shortening audible at all.
clipIds: Les enfants ont de bons résultats à l'école.
Nous avons passé de bonnes vacances.

recorded.desc: bel, vieil AND nouvel, EACH BESIDE ITS CONSONANT PARTNER IN ONE TAKE, in this order: « C'est un beau jardin. C'est un bel arbre. », then « C'est un vieux château. C'est un vieil immeuble. », then « Il a un nouveau vélo. C'est un nouvel hôtel. » Each pair is one take. Without the partner these are three words to memorise; with it, the learner hears one word reshaping itself in front of a vowel, which is one thing rather than three. Run the adjective straight into the noun with no gap in the vowel versions, because the reason the form exists is that the two words are said as one unit. « un bel arbre » should sound like three syllables, not like two words with a join.

THE TEN, AND NOT ONE OF THEM IS EVER RECORDED IN ISOLATION. A bare « grand » carries no placement information at all, and this lesson is entirely about position, so a clip of the word alone teaches nothing and implies the word can stand on its own. Every one of the ten is recorded INSIDE ITS PHRASE: « une grande ville », « un petit chien », « une grosse valise », « un jeune homme », « un vieux château », « une belle maison », « une jolie robe », « un bon restaurant », « une mauvaise idée », « un nouveau vélo ». One take, one voice, even pace, no pause between the adjective and its noun. The five written errors in s12-errors are NOT recorded at all, for the same reason as the des version above.

THE DEFAULT ORDER, ten sentences as one continuous take by one voice at one speed: « C'est une question facile. », « Elle porte une jupe courte. », « Elle a une voix forte. », « Je lis un livre facile. », « Je prends un café noir. », « Nous habitons dans un quartier calme. », « Le chef prépare un plat délicieux. », « Mon frère conduit une voiture rouge. », « Le chat gris dort. », « Nous avons une maison bleue. » The noun comes first and the describing word after it in every one, which is the pattern being absorbed rather than taught, so keep the phrasing even and do not pause between the noun and the word describing it. Ten sentences recorded in ten sessions are ten performances, and any drift in pace teaches a difference between the recordings rather than a fact about French.
clipIds: Nous habitons dans un quartier calme.
Le chef prépare un plat délicieux.
Mon frère conduit une voiture rouge.

recorded.desc: The opening scene, French bubbles only, in the voice of a man in his late twenties reading messages at an ordinary texting pace rather than a teaching pace. THE BEAT WHERE THÉO ASKS WHAT THE BUILDING IS NOW (« Ah bon ? Et c'est quoi maintenant ? On peut dormir dedans ? ») MUST BE CURIOUS AND SLIGHTLY PRACTICAL, never puzzled and never corrective. He has understood the sentence perfectly and is asking a reasonable follow-up question about a building that used to be a hotel. Any note of confusion in that line turns the scene into the learner being caught out, and the entire teaching is that nobody catches this. He should sound like somebody who is still planning to book it.
clipIds: Alors, tu connais un endroit sympa pour deux nuits ?
Ah bon ? Et c'est quoi maintenant ? On peut dormir dedans ?

lessons.title: Les adjectifs possessifs
lessons.intro: Fifteen words for what English does with five, and the choice between them has nothing to do with you. This is how to pick one by looking at the thing rather than the person, use all six owners, put mon in front of a vowel, and tell leur from leurs.

sections.title: An Hour As Somebody Else's Sister

say.text: One word wrong, nobody corrects it, and the conversation carries on about the wrong person. Watch which word.

setting.place: The back room of a bar, a language exchange, and a table of half-finished glasses

beats.text: A language exchange in a bar back room. You have been here an hour and you are doing well, which is exactly when this happens.
For ten minutes you have been telling everybody about your friend Amélie. Her flat, her job, her brother. Ten minutes of son and sa.

beats.speaker: Hugo
beats.fr: Et toi, tu es venue avec qui ce soir ?
beats.en: And you, who did you come with tonight?
beats.stage: He is refilling glasses and barely looking up. Nothing rides on this.

beats.prompt: You came with your own sister, and she is standing right there. Which line do you say?

options.en: the word you have been using all evening
the word for a thing that is yours

followUp.works: Yes. Watch what the other one does, because it is the one you reach for when you are tired.
followUp.breaks: That is the word you have said about twenty times in the last ten minutes. Watch where it goes.

beats.speaker: You
beats.en: (This is his sister, or hers, and either way it is not yours)

beats.speaker: Hugo
beats.fr: Ah, enchanté ! Vous êtes la sœur d'Amélie, alors ?
beats.en: Ah, nice to meet you! So you are Amélie's sister?
beats.stage: He shakes her hand warmly. Nothing at all has gone wrong yet, as far as anybody in the room can tell.

beats.heading: Every word was a real word
beats.body: Nothing you said was wrong. Sa sœur is correct French and Hugo understood it perfectly, which is the problem: he understood it to mean Amélie's sister, because sa never meant yours in the first place.

wrong.en: This is his sister, or her sister. Somebody else's, either way

beats.coach: Ask what is owned, not who owns it. A sister is a sister in both lines, and it was never the sister that had to change.

beats.speaker: At the door, an hour later
beats.stage: One syllable different, and it is the only syllable in the sentence that was ever about you.

beats.speaker: Hugo
beats.fr: Ta sœur ! Ah, pardon, j'avais compris autre chose. Revenez toutes les deux.
beats.en: Your sister! Oh, sorry, I had understood something else. Come back, both of you.
beats.stage: Nobody minds. An hour of him thinking she was somebody else, and it cost nothing except the hour.

beats.text: One word out of five, and it was the only one carrying anything about you. The next twenty-five minutes are about choosing it.

closing.text: Ask what is owned, not who owns it. That question is the next twenty-five minutes.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the first one is a habit rather than a list.

goals.t: Ask the right question before you speak
goals.s: One question, asked about the thing rather than the person, and it answers all fifteen of these words.
From mon to leurs. Three of the six make you check the thing and three do not, which is most of the good news.

goals.t: Say mon amie without it looking like a mistake
goals.s: A word you have already met twice under a different name, arriving here for the third time.
The one place where an s is counting something other than what you expect.

sections.title: English Marks You. French Marks It.
sections.hint: Four cards before any of the fifteen words.
sections.say: Four cards before any table, because this idea is what the table is for.

cards.label: What you already have
cards.head: Three of these are already yours
cards.fr: mon père · ma mère · mes parents
cards.sub: my father · my mother · my parents
cards.body: The family lesson gave you these three and one rule: mon with the le words, ma with the la words, mes with anything plural. That rule is right and it is about to get a reason. There are twelve more words behind it.

cards.label: What that rule was really about
cards.head: Things have a kind
cards.sub: [LUH FREHR] · [LAH SUHR] · the brother · the sister
cards.body: You met this already: every thing in French is either the un kind or the une kind, and the small word in front follows it. A brother is one, a sister is the other, and nothing about either person explains why.

cards.label: What English does
cards.head: The word changes with the person
cards.body: His bag, her bag. The bag has not moved and the word did, because English is telling you who. That is so automatic for an English speaker that it does not feel like a choice at all, which is why it survives into French unexamined.

cards.label: What French does
cards.head: The word changes with the thing
cards.fr: Voici son frère. · Voici sa sœur.
cards.sub: his brother, or her brother · his sister, or her sister
cards.body: Son and sa, and what separates them is a brother against a sister. Not a man against a woman. Both lines can be said about the same person, and neither tells you anything about who that person is.

cards.label: What that gives you
cards.head: One question, fifteen words
cards.body: You never have to think about the owner again. Look at the thing: which kind is it, and is there one or several? Ask what is owned, not who owns it.

sections.title: The Same French, Twice
sections.say: Ask what is owned, not who owns it. Read across a row. The French is the same word twice and the English is not.

detail.title: his sister, and her sister
detail.body: Il parle avec sa sœur. He is talking with his sister. Elle parle avec sa sœur. She is talking with her sister. One word changed and it was the first. Sa did not move: a sister is the une kind whoever she belongs to.
detail.say: Il parle avec sa sœur. Elle parle avec sa sœur.

detail.title: his brother, and her brother
detail.body: Voici son frère. The same again with the other kind of thing. Son is not the masculine of anybody: it is the word you use in front of a brother, and a brother stays the un kind no matter whose he is.

detail.title: his parents, and her parents
detail.body: Voici ses parents. With more than one thing the question about the kind is never even asked, so ses covers both and covers both owners as well. One word doing four English jobs.

sections.title: Three Words For My
sections.hint: Three cards, one for each shape.
sections.say: English has one word here and French has three. The three are not about you.

cards.label: the un kind
cards.head: mon
cards.body: A brother is the un kind, so the word for my is mon.

cards.label: the une kind
cards.head: ma
cards.body: A sister is the une kind, so the same my becomes ma. Nothing about the speaker changed between this sentence and the one before it.

cards.label: more than one
cards.head: mes
cards.body: More than one thing, so the question about the kind is never asked and mes covers both.

cards.label: the whole idea
cards.head: Nothing here is about you
cards.fr: Mon frère et ma sœur habitent à Lyon.
cards.sub: My brother and my sister live in Lyon.
cards.body: One speaker, one sentence, and the word for my is spelled two different ways inside it. Nobody changed between the brother and the sister. Ask what is owned, not who owns it.

cards.label: and there is nothing else
cards.head: No le in front of it
cards.body: Mon is standing exactly where le would have stood, so the two never appear together. There is no le mon livre and there never will be. Once you have chosen mon you are finished, and nothing else goes in front of the noun.

sections.title: Which One Would You Say?
sections.say: Three decisions, and each one is answered by looking at the thing rather than at yourself.

check.q: You want to say: my brother. Which word goes in front of it?
check.why: mon. A brother is the un kind, and that is the only fact the choice needed. If you found yourself thinking about who was speaking, that is the English habit and it is the one this lesson is here to break.

check.q: You want to say: my sister. Which word goes in front of it?
check.why: ma. A sister is the une kind. A man saying this sentence and a woman saying it produce exactly the same three words, because nothing in the sentence is reporting on the speaker.

check.q: You want to say: my parents. Which word goes in front of it?
check.why: mes. Once there is more than one thing the question about the kind stops being asked at all, so there is one word rather than two. That is true of every owner in this lesson and it is a third of the grid gone.

check.q: You want to say: my sister, and you have spent ten minutes talking about your friend. Which word?
check.why: ma. This is the exact slip from the opening scene and it is worth making twice on purpose. Sa is correct French about somebody else, so nothing about it will feel wrong as you say it and nobody will stop you.

sections.title: The Three That Ask About The Thing
sections.say: Nine cells. Read across a row and only the thing moves. Tap any cell to hear it.

detail.title: je: my
detail.body: Voici mon frère. Voici ma sœur. Voici mes parents. Three sentences, one speaker, and the only thing that moved is what is being pointed at. The word changed twice and the person speaking never did.
detail.say: Voici mon frère. Voici ma sœur. Voici mes parents.

detail.title: tu: your
detail.body: Voici ton frère. Voici ta sœur. Voici tes parents. Three sentences, one speaker, and the only thing that moved is what is being pointed at. The word changed twice and the person speaking never did.
detail.say: Voici ton frère. Voici ta sœur. Voici tes parents.

detail.title: il / elle: his or her
detail.body: Voici son frère. Voici sa sœur. Voici ses parents. Three sentences, one speaker, and the only thing that moved is what is being pointed at. This is the row English speakers lose: English would have used two different words here.
detail.say: Voici son frère. Voici sa sœur. Voici ses parents.

sections.title: The Row That Says Nothing About Who
sections.hint: Four cards on the row that costs English speakers the most.
sections.say: Three words covering six English ones, and none of them reports on the owner.

cards.label: his, and hers
cards.head: One word, two English words
cards.sub: [sa SUHR] · his sister, and her sister
cards.body: No French sentence distinguishes these. If it matters, French says it another way and names the person. The possessive itself will not do it, and waiting for it to is how an evening gets spent on the wrong person.

cards.label: in the wild
cards.head: Somebody already had to choose
cards.fr: Il a mangé ses croissants avec sa sœur.
cards.sub: He ate his croissants with his sister.
cards.body: That English was written by somebody translating this sentence, and they had to pick his or her out of nowhere. They picked his because the sentence starts with il. The French carries no such information and never did.

cards.label: context does the work
cards.head: The sentence around it tells you
cards.fr: Il joue au football avec ses amis le week-end.
cards.sub: He plays soccer with his friends on weekends.
cards.body: Here you know whose friends they are, and it is not ses that told you. It was il, three words earlier. That is how French does it every time: the owner is established once and the possessive never repeats it.

cards.label: the other one
cards.head: son is also a noise
cards.body: Un son is a sound: the same three letters being a different word. You can tell them apart without thinking, because a possessive always has a thing straight behind it. Son frère, son sac. On its own or after le, it is the noise.

sections.title: The Three That Ask Nothing
sections.say: Six cells instead of nine, because these three never ask which kind the thing is.

detail.title: nous: our
detail.body: Voici notre frère. Voici notre sœur. Voici nos parents. The first two are the same word: one in front of a brother, one in front of a sister. Only the count ever changes it.
detail.say: Voici notre frère. Voici notre sœur. Voici nos parents.

detail.title: vous: your
detail.body: Voici votre frère. Voici votre sœur. Voici vos parents. The first two are the same word: one in front of a brother, one in front of a sister. Only the count ever changes it.
detail.say: Voici votre frère. Voici votre sœur. Voici vos parents.

detail.title: ils / elles: their
detail.body: Voici leur frère. Voici leur sœur. Voici leurs parents. The first two are the same word: one in front of a brother, one in front of a sister. The s on leurs counts the parents. There were already several owners without it.
detail.say: Voici leur frère. Voici leur sœur. Voici leurs parents.

sections.title: Does It Ask, Or Not?
sections.say: Four groups. The first three make you look at the thing and the last three do not.

check.q: You want to say: our sister. Which word?
check.why: notre, exactly as it was for our brother. This row does not ask which kind the thing is, so the first two cells of it are the same word and you have one fewer decision than you had a minute ago.

check.q: You want to say: your parents, speaking politely to one person. Which word?
check.why: vos. Politeness is not what the s is about: vos is the plural of votre and it counts the parents. Speaking politely to one person about one thing you would say votre, and about two things you still say vos.

check.q: You want to say: their sister, about two brothers. Which word?
check.why: leur, with no s. There are two owners and one sister, and the s counts sisters. This is the one place in the lesson where an s is answering a question you did not think you were being asked.

items.fr: Notre maison a un grand jardin.
items.en: Our house has a big garden.

items.fr: Nous attendons nos amis au café.
items.en: We wait for our friends at the café.

items.fr: Vous ouvrez vos livres à la page dix.
items.en: You open your books to page ten.

check.q: Two of those four say notre or votre and two say nos or vos. What separates them?
opts: Whether the speaker is being polite
Whether the thing is the un kind or the une kind
Whether the owner is one person or several
check.why: How many things. A house and an address are one each, so notre and votre. Friends and books are several, so nos and vos. Nothing in any of the four sentences depends on the kind of thing or on how many owners there are.

sections.title: Now Without The Tables
sections.say: Same decisions, nothing to look at. This is the one that tells you whether it landed.

check.q: Marie is talking about her own father. Which word does she use?
check.why: son. A father is the un kind, and that settles it. Marie being a woman has nothing to do with the choice, and reaching for sa here is the single most common possessive error an English speaker makes in their first year.

check.q: You want to say: your parents, to a friend. Which word?
check.why: tes. More than one thing, so the kind is never asked about, and a friend takes the tu row rather than the vous row. Votre would be correct French said to somebody you were being careful with.

check.q: Two women are talking about the one flat they share. Which word for their flat?
check.why: leur. Two owners and one flat, and leur counts flats. If they had two flats it would be leurs, and the two women would still be exactly two women either way.

check.q: Before you say a possessive out loud, what should you be looking at?
opts: Whether the owner is a man or a woman
What the thing is, and how many of it
check.why: Ask what is owned, not who owns it. Which kind is the thing, and is there one or several. Those two answers pick the word every time. The owner only chooses which row you are standing in, and you knew that already.

sections.title: The Third Time You Have Met This
sections.hint: Four cards, and the idea in them is not new.
sections.say: One old idea, one new repair. You have watched French dodge this collision twice already.

cards.label: the problem
cards.head: Two vowels meeting
cards.sub: not French, and it never has been
cards.body: Say those two words at ordinary speed and they run into each other. French does not allow it, and the interesting part is that it has more than one way out. You have already seen one of them.

cards.label: the repair you know
cards.head: la amie became l'amie
cards.sub: the small word gets cut short
cards.body: That was the definite articles, and the silent-letters lesson before it. The little word in front loses its vowel and an apostrophe takes the place. Same collision, and the language solved it by taking something away.

cards.label: the repair that is new
cards.head: ma amie becomes mon amie
cards.body: Here nothing is cut. The word is swapped for the other shape, which ends in a sound that carries straight into the vowel behind it. Une amie is still the une kind, and only this one word borrowed the other form.

cards.label: how far it reaches
cards.head: Three words, and only three
cards.body: It reaches mon, ton and son and stops. Notre, votre and leur never change for anything, which that sentence shows: votre sits in front of a vowel and does not move. There is no votr' adresse and there is no swap.

sections.title: Both The Une Kind
sections.say: Left and right are the same kind of thing. Only one of them takes ma. Tap both and listen.

detail.title: Two things of the same kind
detail.body: Ma sœur et mon amie sont ici. My sister and my friend are here. Both are the une kind, and you can check both on cards you have already seen. The only difference is the letter the second one starts with.
detail.say: Ma sœur et mon amie sont ici.

detail.title: The same swap, on a word from the liaison lesson
detail.body: Mon école ouvre tôt. My school opens early. Une école is the une kind and takes mon for the same reason. This sentence was in the corpus long before this lesson existed, so the rule is not a teaching device.

detail.title: Both in one published sentence
detail.body: Mon amie cherche sa trousse. My friend is looking for her pencil case. Mon in front of a vowel and sa in front of a consonant, in one line nobody arranged. Note that sa tells you nothing: the English chose her, the French did not.

sections.title: One Pair Your Ear Can Do
sections.say: Three pairs. Two of them are the same sound twice, and saying so is the point of this screen.

lines.en: these two are one sound, and only the page can tell them apart

lines.fr: Voici leur fille. · Voici leurs filles.
lines.en: these two are one sound as well: the s of leurs is silent here

lines.fr: Ce sont mes amis. · Ce sont ses amis.
lines.en: this pair really does differ, in the vowel of the first syllable

questions.q: mon ami and mon amie. How many sounds is that?
opts: two, and the second is longer
two, and the e is faintly there
questions.why: One sound, said twice. The e on amie is written and never pronounced, so a recording of one is a recording of the other. There is nothing to listen for and no practice will produce it. If you need the difference, you read it.

questions.q: leur fille and leurs filles, said out loud. What separates them?
questions.why: Nothing at all. Both plural endings are silent here, so the two sentences are identical in the air. Leurs only becomes audible in front of a vowel, where its s wakes up as a z: leurs amis. In front of a consonant it never does.

questions.q: mes amis and ses amis. What is different?
opts: the s at the end of mes and ses
the vowel in the first syllable
questions.why: The vowel in the first syllable, and that is all. Both carry the same z liaison into amis and the same stress, so the whole difference is one unstressed vowel. This is the one pair in this lesson your ear can be trained on.

sections.title: Five Traps
sections.say: Ask what is owned, not who owns it. Five things an English speaker writes in their first month, one per screen.

errors.wrong: Saying « sa père » for her father.
errors.why: The highest-value one in the lesson. A father is the un kind and that is the whole decision. Picking sa because the owner is a woman is the English habit arriving intact, and it produces something that is not French at all.

errors.wrong: Saying « son mère » for his mother.
errors.why: The same error going the other way, and the two arrive together. Once you are choosing from the owner you will get both of these wrong on alternate days, which is more confusing than getting them wrong consistently.

errors.wrong: Writing « ma amie ».
errors.why: Two vowels colliding, and French will not have it. This is the same pressure that turned la amie into l'amie, repaired a different way: nothing is cut, the word is swapped. Une amie is still the une kind throughout.

errors.wrong: Writing « leurs enfants » about one child.
errors.why: The s counts the children rather than the parents. There were already several owners before the s turned up, so it cannot be reporting on them. One child and any number of owners gives you leur.

errors.wrong: Writing « le mon livre ».
errors.why: A possessive stands where le would have stood rather than beside it. English hides this, because the my in my book is not visibly replacing anything. Once you have chosen mon there is nothing else to add.

sections.title: The S That Counts Something Else
sections.hint: Four cards on the one that looks like a different question.
sections.say: By the time you reach leur there are already several owners. So the s cannot be about them.

cards.label: one thing
cards.head: leur
cards.body: Several people, one daughter. Leur carries no s, and if you were counting owners that would look wrong, because there are clearly more than one of them.

cards.label: more than one thing
cards.head: leurs
cards.body: The same several people, and now more than one daughter. That is the only thing that changed. Ask what is owned, not who owns it.

cards.label: in the wild, both ways
cards.head: The corpus does it too
cards.fr: Les clients attendent leur commande. Les élèves rangent leurs livres.
cards.sub: The customers are waiting for their order. · The students put away their books.
cards.body: Several customers and one order between each of them, so leur. Several students and several books each, so leurs. Neither sentence has any interest in how many people there are, and both have several.

cards.label: and the other leur
cards.head: A different word you will meet later
cards.body: There is a second leur and it is not a possessive. It sits in front of a verb rather than in front of a thing. You will meet it later. The test is the same as always: a possessive has a thing behind it.

sections.title: Nothing Else Goes In Front
sections.hint: Three cards, and one of them saves a whole class of error.
sections.say: One card, and it prevents something no amount of grid practice touches.

cards.label: the slot
cards.head: mon stands where le stood
cards.body: Le livre is the book. Mon livre is my book. The two little words are competing for one position and only one of them can have it, so le mon livre is not a thing anybody would finish saying.

cards.label: why English hides it
cards.head: my is not replacing anything you can see
cards.body: In English you say the book and my book, and my does not look like it took the place of the. So nothing in your first language warns you off putting both in. In French that position holds one word and always has.

cards.label: what it saves you
cards.head: Once you have chosen, you are finished
cards.fr: Voici mon frère. · Voici nos parents.
cards.sub: This is my brother. · These are our parents.
cards.body: Neither of those has anything in front of the possessive and neither is missing anything. That is the whole rule, it holds for all fifteen words, and it is the only part of this lesson with no exceptions of any kind.

sections.title: The Group Photo
sections.say: One photo, four captions, and every one of them turns on a word two letters long.
sections.text: Somebody has printed a photo from the summer and pinned four captions round the edge of it, each one in a different hand, and between them they use most of what this lesson has covered. « Voici ma sœur. » That one is written by the person on the left, about the person beside her, and it is the only caption on the board that tells you anything at all about who wrote it. Underneath it somebody has added a note about the two people at the back. « Voici leurs parents. » Several people and two parents, so the s is there, and it is counting the parents rather than the children. A third caption is about the man on the right and the woman he is talking to, and it is the one that has caused an argument. « Voici sa sœur. » Half the room reads that as his sister and half reads it as hers, and both halves are correct, because the sentence was never carrying that information. The last one is the shortest and is stuck on with a different colour of tape. « Voici mon amie. »

glossary.note: A sister is the une kind, so ma. A man and a woman writing this caption would write the same two words.
Several owners and two parents. The s is counting the parents; the owners were already several without it.
Both readings are correct and the French does not choose. This is the caption that started the argument.
A woman friend, and une amie is the une kind. It takes mon anyway, to keep two vowels from colliding.

questions.q: Two captions use a word beginning with m and one uses a word beginning with s. What decides between them?
questions.a: Who is doing the owning, and that is the only thing in this lesson that ever depends on the owner. Ma and mon belong to the je row, sa belongs to the il and elle row. What the owner never decides is which shape within a row: that comes from the thing.

questions.q: Why can the room not agree about the third caption?
questions.a: Because sa sœur means his sister and her sister equally, and nothing in the sentence chooses. French marks what is owned rather than who owns it, so the information the room is arguing about was never written down. In English the writer would have been forced to pick one.

questions.q: The last caption says mon amie about a woman. Is that a mistake?
questions.a: No. Une amie is the une kind and would normally take ma, but ma amie would put two vowel sounds against each other and French avoids that. Mon is borrowed here only for the sound. Nothing about the friend has changed kind.

sections.title: The Fifteen, Banked
sections.say: Three decks. The ones that ask about the thing, the ones that do not, and the two that swap.

cards.en: his or her, the un kind
his or her, the une kind
his or her, more than one
our, one thing of either kind
your, one thing of either kind
their, one thing of either kind
my friend, a woman. Same sound, same respelling
his friends, or hers. One vowel from mes amis

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front, and every front names both the owner and the thing. Say the French before you flip.

cards.front: He is talking with his sister.
She is talking with her sister.
My sister and my friend are here.
cards.back: Ma sœur et mon amie sont ici.
cards.say: Ma sœur et mon amie sont ici.

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Five lines. On two of them the word you write is one you have to work out rather than hear.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: Twenty-nine lines, and not one of them is a possessive on its own. The word only means anything with a thing behind it.

sections.title: The Same Party, Going Better
sections.say: One exchange and you hold up your half. Every turn is a possessive with something behind it.
sections.setting: The same back room, a fortnight later. Hugo is on the door again and this time he asks first.

turns.ai: Te revoilà ! Tu es venue accompagnée ce soir ?
turns.en: You are back! Did you come with somebody tonight?
turns.user: Oui. Voici ma soeur.
turns.userEn: Yes. This is my sister.

alts.fr: Oui, je suis venue avec ma soeur.
alts.en: Yes, I came with my sister.

turns.ai: Enchante ! Et Amelie, elle vient aussi ?
turns.en: Nice to meet you! And Amelie, is she coming too?
turns.user: Elle arrive avec son frere.
turns.userEn: She is coming with her brother.

alts.en: She is coming with her brother.

turns.ai: Son frere ? Je ne le connais pas. Il vient avec quelqu'un ?
turns.en: Her brother? I do not know him. Is he coming with anyone?
turns.user: Il vient avec mon amie.
turns.userEn: He is coming with my friend.

alts.en: He is arriving with my friend.

turns.ai: Ah, et les parents d'Amelie, ils sont la aussi ?
turns.en: Ah, and Amelie's parents, are they here as well?
turns.user: Non, leurs parents restent a la maison.
turns.userEn: No, their parents are staying at home.

alts.fr: Non, leurs parents ne viennent pas.
alts.en: No, their parents are not coming.
No. They are staying at home.

turns.ai: Bon. Vous etes combien alors ? Je note vos noms.
turns.en: Right. How many of you are there then? I am writing down your names.
turns.user: Nous sommes cinq. Voici nos noms.
turns.userEn: There are five of us. Here are our names.

alts.fr: Cinq. Je vous donne nos noms.
alts.en: Five. I will give you our names.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: Marie is talking about her own father. Which word?
cards.back: son père. A father is the un kind, and Marie being a woman changes nothing.

cards.front: Marc is talking about his own mother. Which word?
cards.back: sa mère. A mother is the une kind, and Marc being a man changes nothing.

cards.front: You want to say: my sister.
cards.back: Voici ma sœur. The une kind, so ma.

cards.front: You want to say: my brother.
cards.back: Voici mon frère. The un kind, so mon.

cards.front: You want to say: my parents.
cards.back: Voici mes parents. More than one, so the kind is never asked.

cards.front: What does sa sœur tell you about the owner?
cards.back: Nothing at all. It means his sister and her sister equally.

cards.front: A woman friend, and the word for her is the une kind. Why mon amie?
cards.back: Voici mon amie. Ma amie would put two vowels together, so the word swaps.

cards.front: Does votre swap in front of a vowel the way mon does?
cards.back: Vous écrivez votre adresse. No. Only mon, ton and son ever swap.
Voici leur fille. leur, with no s.
Voici leurs filles. leurs. The s counts the daughters.

cards.front: You want to say: our parents.
cards.back: Voici nos parents. nos, and the kind never came into it.

cards.front: You want to say: your parents, politely.
cards.back: Voici vos parents. vos, which is the form tables lose.

cards.front: Can you say le mon livre?
cards.back: No. C'est mon livre. The possessive is standing where le would have stood.

cards.front: mon ami and mon amie, out loud.
cards.back: One sound, said twice. Only the page can tell them apart.

cards.front: What should you look at before saying a possessive?
cards.back: Ask what is owned, not who owns it. Which kind, and how many.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched an evening go past with somebody being introduced as the wrong person, and nothing in the sentence that caused it was wrong. Since then you have taken a grid apart into the half that asks you a question and the half that does not, met a word that borrows the other shape purely to keep two vowels from running together, and found an s that counts something other than what it looks like it counts. Along the way you have seen the same French phrase carry two English meanings on one screen, which is the thing this whole lesson is built around. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: Whose is it
rounds.say: The inversion, five times.

questions.q: Marie is talking about her own father. Which word does she use?
questions.why: son. A father is the un kind, and that is the whole decision. Marie being a woman never enters into it. This is the most common possessive error an English speaker makes and it survives because it is never corrected.

questions.q: Marc is talking about his own mother. Say the two words he uses.
questions.why: sa mère. A mother is the une kind. This is the same error as the question before it, arriving from the other direction, and the two turn up together: once you are choosing from the owner you get both wrong on alternate days.

questions.q: You hear « Voici sa sœur. » Who does the sister belong to?
opts: A man, because sa is the masculine form
A woman, because a sister is feminine
Either. The sentence does not say
questions.why: Either. Ask what is owned, not who owns it. Sa is chosen by the sister and reports nothing about the owner, so his sister and her sister are the same three words. French has other ways to say whose, and this is not one.

questions.q: You want to say, in French: my brother. Write it.
questions.why: mon frère. A brother is the un kind. Written as a whole phrase rather than as a bare word, because a two-letter answer typed on its own is a coin toss rather than a test.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Elle parle avec son mère » about her own mother. Fix the sentence.
questions.why: sa mère. The writer chose son because elle is a woman, which is the English habit exactly. A mother is the une kind and the owner was never being reported on.

rounds.label: Which of the three
rounds.say: The right shape for the thing in front of you.

questions.q: You want to say: my parents. Which word goes in front?
questions.why: mes. More than one thing, so the question about the kind is never asked. That is true for every owner in the lesson and it removes a third of the grid at a stroke.

questions.q: You want to say, to a friend: your sister. Which word?
questions.why: ta. A sister is the une kind, and a friend takes the tu row. Votre would be correct French said to somebody you were being careful with, but it belongs to a different row rather than to a different kind of thing.

questions.q: You want to say: our sister. Which word?
questions.why: notre, exactly as it was for our brother. This row never asks which kind the thing is, so its first two cells are one word and there is one decision fewer to make.

questions.q: You want to say, politely: your parents. Write the two words.
questions.why: vos parents. Vos is the plural of votre and it counts the parents rather than measuring the politeness. It is also the form most tables quietly leave out, which is why it is worth writing rather than picking.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Voici notre parents. » about their own two parents. Fix the sentence.
questions.why: nos parents. More than one thing, so the plural of notre. Nos and vos are the two cells a grid looks complete without, which is why this lesson asks about each of them twice.

rounds.label: What your ear can do
rounds.say: One real pair, and two that are not pairs at all.

questions.q: Listen. Is this my friends or his friends?
questions.why: mes amis. This is the one genuine listening question in the lesson: mes and ses carry the same z liaison into amis and the same stress, so the whole difference is the vowel of the first syllable.

questions.q: You hear somebody say my friend out loud. Can you tell whether the friend is a man or a woman?
opts: Yes, mon amie is slightly longer
Yes, you can hear the e at the end
No. Mon ami and mon amie are the same sound
Only if the speaker slows down
questions.why: No. They are homophones: the e on amie is written and never pronounced, so one recording is the other. Slowing it down adds nothing, because there is nothing in the signal to slow down.

questions.q: Two parents say « Voici leur fille. » and then « Voici leurs filles. » What separates their daughter from their daughters out loud?
questions.why: Nothing at all. Both plural endings are silent in front of a consonant, so the two sentences are identical in the air. Leurs only becomes audible in front of a vowel, where its s wakes as a z: leurs amis.

questions.q: You want to say: his friends, meaning several of them. Write the two words.
questions.why: ses amis. More than one thing, so the kind is never asked, and the s of ses wakes up as a z in front of the vowel. It also means her friends, which the French will not tell you either way.

rounds.label: In front of a vowel
rounds.say: The swap, and how far it reaches.

questions.q: You want to say: my friend, about a woman. Write the two words.
questions.why: mon amie. Une amie is the une kind and would normally take ma, but ma amie would put two vowel sounds together and French avoids that. The word is swapped rather than cut, which is the difference from l'amie.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Voici ma amie. » Fix it.
questions.why: mon amie. Two vowels colliding, repaired by swapping the word rather than cutting it. You have seen the other repair twice: la amie became l'amie, where the little word lost its vowel instead.

questions.q: You want to say, politely: your address. Does votre change in front of the vowel?
opts: No. Votre never changes for anything
questions.why: No. The swap reaches mon, ton and son and stops there. Notre, votre and leur never change, which is why « Vous écrivez votre adresse. » looks exactly as you would expect it to.

questions.q: You want to say my sister and my friend, about a woman. Both nouns are the une kind, so why does only one of them take ma?
opts: Because amie is not really feminine
Because amie starts with a vowel
Because a friend is not family
Because amie can also describe a man
questions.why: Because amie starts with a vowel. That is the only difference between the two, and nothing about the kind of thing has changed: une amie is the une kind before and after the swap, and everything else in the sentence still agrees that way.

rounds.label: leur or leurs
rounds.say: One s, and it is not counting who you think.

questions.q: Two parents, and one daughter between them. Which word for their daughter?
questions.why: leur. Two owners and one daughter, and the s counts daughters. The owners were already several before any s turned up, so it could never have been reporting on them.

questions.q: Two parents, and three daughters between them. Which word for their daughters?
questions.why: leurs. Nothing about the parents changed between this question and the one before it. Only the daughters did, and that is the only thing the s has ever been about.

questions.q: You want to say: their books, about a class of students. Write the two words.
questions.why: leurs livres. Several books, so the s. A whole class of students is several owners either way and would not have changed the answer if there had been one book each.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Les clients attendent leurs commande. » about one order each. Fix it.
questions.why: leur commande. The writer put the s on because les clients is plural, which is exactly the trap. Count the orders rather than the customers: one each, so no s.

rounds.label: Nothing else in front
rounds.say: Two words competing for one position.

questions.q: You want to say: my book. Which of these is French?
questions.why: mon livre. A possessive stands where le would have stood rather than beside it, so the two never appear together. Once you have chosen mon there is nothing else to put in front of the noun.

questions.q: Why does English not warn you off writing le mon livre for my book?
opts: English has the same rule and hides it
The my in my book is not visibly replacing anything
Because my is not a real word class
questions.why: Because my is not visibly replacing anything. You say the book and my book, and nothing on the page shows that the two little words are competing for the same position, so nothing in your first language stops you putting both in.

questions.q: You want to say: this is my book. Say it out loud.
questions.why: C'est mon livre. Nothing in front of mon, and nothing missing either. A book is the un kind, so mon, and the possessive fills the slot on its own.

questions.q: You want to say: our parents. Say it out loud.
questions.why: Voici nos parents. More than one thing, so nos rather than notre, and the kind of thing never came into it. Nos is one of the two forms this lesson asks about twice on purpose.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can pick any of the fifteen words by looking at the thing rather than at the person, use all six owners including the two forms most tables lose, put mon in front of a vowel without it looking like a mistake, and tell leur from leurs by counting the right thing. The habit underneath all of that is the one worth keeping: French tends to mark what is being talked about rather than who is talking. You will meet a second leur in a later unit which is a completely different word, and a way of saying mine without naming the thing a good deal after that. Neither is needed for anything here.
points: Ask what is owned, not who owns it. Which kind is the thing, and is there one or several.
son and sa say nothing at all about the owner, and no French sentence makes them.
mon, ton and son borrow the other shape in front of a vowel. Notre, votre and leur never change.
The s on leurs counts the things. There were already several owners without it.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that un and une follow it, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, and the elision of le and la in front of a vowel, introduced in a1.04
The plural of a noun, introduced in a1.03
mon, ma and mes as three words rather than a system, and the article-based rule for choosing between them, introduced in a1.15
de for possession, and that it always reaches where a possessive will not, introduced in a1.15
The nine subject pronouns, introduced in a1.05
The full present of être, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07
Liaison, and that a silent final consonant attaches to a following vowel, introduced in sons.10
Elision as a repair for two vowels meeting, introduced in sons.07
grammarIntroduced: The possessive adjectives, introduced here for the first time in the course
That a possessive agrees with the thing possessed rather than with the possessor
All six persons across three forms: mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses, notre/nos, votre/vos, leur/leurs
The syncretism of the first and second forms in the nous, vous and ils rows
mon, ton and son in front of a feminine noun beginning with a vowel or a mute h
That the anti-hiatus swap does not reach notre, votre or leur
The number contrast in leur against leurs, where the plural marks the possessum and not the possessor
That a possessive occupies the determiner slot and excludes the definite and indefinite articles
