overview.introFr: Quinze mots pour dire à qui est quelque chose, et le choix ne dépend jamais de la personne.

acts.title: Whose is it
acts.milestone: You have watched an hour go by with somebody introduced as the wrong person.

acts.title: mon, ma, mes
acts.milestone: Three words for one English one, and the thing picks between them.

acts.title: The rest, and the relief
acts.milestone: All six owners, and the bottom three ask you nothing at all.

acts.title: Before a vowel
acts.milestone: mon amie, and the third time you have watched French dodge two vowels.

acts.title: leur, leurs, and the slot
acts.milestone: An s that counts the things, and a position that only holds one word.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. Everything here carries straight into describing people and places.

lessons.reframe: Ask what is owned, not who owns it.

errorTriggers.description: Picks the possessive from the owner's sex rather than from the thing: writes sa père for her father and son mère for his. The default error, and the one every English speaker starts with.
Asks the right question and gets the answer wrong: reaches for the wrong cell of the grid, most often between mon and mes or between notre and nos.
Believes mon ami and mon amie, or leur and leurs, must be audibly different and concludes their listening is at fault. Costs confidence rather than accuracy, which is why it gets its own drill.
Writes ma amie, or repairs it the wrong way with l'amie or m'amie. Also applies the swap where it does not reach, giving votr' adresse.
Puts the s on leur because the owners are plural. The one error in the lesson where the learner is counting carefully and counting the wrong thing.
Writes le mon livre. Invisible to grid practice, because every cell of the grid is correct in isolation and the error is about what sits beside it.

drills.title: What is being owned?
drills.coach: Do not look at who is speaking. Look at the word after the possessive and ask which kind of thing it is. A brother is one kind and a sister is the other, and that is the whole sort.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Marie is talking about her own father. Which word?
drills.why: son. A father is the un kind. Marie being a woman is not information the sentence carries and never was.

drills.title: Find the cell
drills.coach: The English front tells you the owner and the thing. The owner picks the row and the thing picks the shape, in that order, and neither of them can do the other one's job.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want to say: our parents. Which word?
drills.why: nos. More than one thing, so the plural, and the kind of thing was never asked about in this row at all.

drills.title: Same sound, or not?
drills.coach: Say each pair out loud, twice, at ordinary speed. If you find yourself lengthening something to make a difference appear, that is the answer: it is not there. Only one of these three pairs has anything in it.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: How much of the difference between mon ami and mon amie can you hear?
opts: a little, if the speaker is careful
drills.why: None of it. The e is written and never pronounced, so the two are one sound and no recording could separate them. If it matters, you read it or you ask.

drills.title: Which shape in front of this word?
drills.coach: Every thing in this drill is the une kind, so gender will not sort it. Look at the first letter of the noun instead. A vowel behind ma is a collision the language will not make, so the word swaps.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want to say: my friend, about a woman. Which word in front of amie?
drills.why: mon. The word swaps rather than being cut, which is the difference from l'amie. Une amie is still the une kind throughout.

drills.title: Count the things
buckets: more than one thing, so leurs
drills.coach: Every one of these has several owners, so counting people will get you nowhere: they all go in the same pile. Count what is owned instead. One of it and there is no s; more than one and there is.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Two parents and one daughter between them. Which word for their daughter?
drills.why: leur. The s counts daughters and there is one. The parents were already two before the question was asked.

drills.title: What fills the position?
buckets: le, la or les fills it
drills.coach: Look at the position directly in front of the noun and ask what is standing in it. It holds one word and only one, which is why le mon livre is not something anybody would finish saying.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want to say: my book. Which of these is French?
drills.why: mon livre. The possessive is standing where le would have stood, so there is nothing to add in front of it.

sheets.title: All fifteen, in one grid
contains: Every owner in all three shapes
Which rows ask about the thing
What each row is in English

sections.title: What each row is doing
sections.body: mon, ma and mes are my, in three shapes, and the thing picks between them: mon for the un kind, ma for the une kind, mes for more than one. ton, ta and tes are your, to somebody you would say tu to, and they ask exactly the same three questions. son, sa and ses are his AND her, one row covering both, because the possessive never reports on the owner at all; if it matters whose, French says it another way and names the person. notre and nos are our, in two shapes rather than three: notre for one thing of either kind, nos for more than one. votre and vos are your, politely or to several people, in the same two shapes, and the politeness has nothing to do with the s. leur and leurs are their, and by the time you reach them the owners are already several, so the s is counting the things instead: leur fille, leurs filles. One rule holds across every row. A possessive stands where le, la or les would have stood, so there is no le mon livre and there never will be.

sheets.title: The three rules that are not in the grid
contains: mon in front of a vowel
What your ear can and cannot do

sections.title: What to write, and what never to write
Why each of those is wrong
sections.body: ma amie and ma école put two vowel sounds against each other, which French will not do, so mon is borrowed for the sound alone. Both nouns are still the une kind and everything else about them agrees that way. mon sœur is the same rule misfiring in reverse: a consonant follows, so there is nothing to repair and ma is correct. votr' adresse is the swap being applied where it does not reach, because only mon, ton and son have a second shape to reach for and notre, votre and leur never change for anything. leurs fille and leur filles both count the wrong thing: the owners were already several before any s arrived, so the s can only be counting the daughters, and it has to match the noun beside it. le mon livre puts two words in one position: a possessive stands where le, la or les would have stood rather than beside them, so once you have chosen mon you are finished and nothing else goes in front of the noun.

sections.title: What your ear can and cannot do
sections.body: Two of the pairs in this lesson are not pairs at all in the air, and knowing which is which stops you listening for something that was never recorded. mon ami and mon amie are ONE SOUND with two spellings: the e is written and never pronounced, so no recording could separate them and no amount of slowing one down will help. If you need to know which was meant, you read it or you ask. leur fille and leurs filles are the same situation: in front of a consonant both plural endings are silent, so the two are identical out loud. leurs only becomes audible in front of a vowel, where its s wakes up as a z, as in leurs amis. The one pair your ear can genuinely be trained on is mes amis against ses amis. Both carry the same z liaison into amis and both put the stress in the same place, so the whole difference between my friends and his friends is the vowel of the first syllable. That one is worth practising. The other two are worth knowing about so you stop trying.

sections.title: Why mon amie is not an exception
sections.body: Most courses hand you the vowel rule as a fourth thing to memorise, sitting beside the grid and unconnected to anything. It is not a fourth thing. French has a standing objection to two vowel sounds meeting with nothing between them, and you have already watched it deal with that objection twice. The first time was le and la turning into l apostrophe in front of a vowel, which the lesson on the definite articles taught and the silent letters lesson set up before it. The little word loses its own vowel and an apostrophe marks where it went. The second time was the liaison, where a consonant that had been sitting silent at the end of a word wakes up and attaches itself to the front of the next one, so that mon ami comes out as three syllables with an n in the middle of it. This is the third time, and it is the same objection with a third answer. Ma amie would put an a straight against an a, so instead of cutting anything the language reaches for the other shape of the same word, which happens to end in a sound that runs into a vowel without any trouble at all. Ma becomes mon, ta becomes ton, sa becomes son. Nothing else about the sentence moves. Une amie is the une kind before the swap and after it, and every other word in the sentence still treats her that way, which is the part that reassures people who think they have missed something. The rule reaches exactly three words and it is worth knowing where it stops: notre, votre and leur have no second shape to reach for and never change for anything. It applies in front of a vowel and in front of a silent h, which is the same set of words that took l apostrophe, so if you know which nouns those were you already know which nouns these are. The practical version is one sentence. If the noun starts with a vowel sound, use mon, ton or son whatever kind of thing it is.

whatIsOwned.term: the thing decides, not the owner
whatIsOwned.title: English marks the owner. French marks the thing.
whatIsOwned.body: In English the word changes with the person: his bag, her bag. In French it changes with the bag. Son sac is his bag and it is also her bag, and nothing in those two words tells you which. That is not French being vague, it is French answering a different question. English asks who, French asks what. So the moment before you speak, look at the thing you are about to name: is it the un kind or the une kind, and is there one of it or several? Those two answers pick the word for you, and who owns it never comes into it.

examples.note: A man is talking, and the word is sa because a sister is the une kind.
A woman is talking, and the word has not moved. Only the English had to.

beforeAVowel.term: mon in front of a vowel
beforeAVowel.title: Why mon amie is not a mistake
beforeAVowel.body: Ma amie is not French. Two vowel sounds meeting head on is something the language will not do, and it has two ways out of it. You have seen the first one twice already: la amie becomes l'amie, and the little word in front gets cut short. This is the second way, and instead of cutting anything it swaps the word: ma becomes mon, ta becomes ton, sa becomes son. The thing has not changed kind. Une amie is still the une kind and everything else about her still agrees that way. Only this one word borrowed the other shape, and only to keep two vowels apart. It happens before a vowel and before a silent h, and it reaches mon, ton and son and nothing else.

examples.note: Two things of the same kind, one taking ma and one taking mon.
The same swap on a word the learner met in the liaison lesson.

oneOrSeveral.title: The s counts the things, not the people
oneOrSeveral.body: By the time you reach leur there are already several owners, every time, without exception: it is the word for a group. So the s on the end cannot be about them, because they were already plural before it arrived. It counts what is owned. Leur fille is one daughter belonging to several people. Leurs filles is more than one daughter belonging to the same several people. This is the same question the whole lesson asks, arriving in the one place where it looks like a different question. Out loud the two are identical in front of a consonant, so this is a difference you read and write rather than one you hear.

examples.note: Several owners, one daughter, and no s.
The same owners, more than one daughter, and the s arrives.

theSlot.term: it stands where le would have stood
theSlot.title: There is no le mon livre
theSlot.body: A possessive takes the place of le, la and les rather than sitting beside them. Le livre is the book and mon livre is my book, and there is no way to say both at once: le mon livre is not a sentence anybody would finish. English is the odd one here, because the my in my book is not replacing anything you can see. The practical effect is small and saves a whole class of error: once you have chosen mon, you are done, and there is nothing else to put in front of the noun.

examples.note: Nothing in front of mon, and nothing missing either.
The same slot, filled the same way, with a different owner.

theOtherSon.title: son is also a noise
theOtherSon.body: Un son is a sound. It is the same three letters as the son in son frère and it is a completely different word, which you can tell apart every time without thinking about it: a possessive always has a thing behind it. Son frère, son sac, son adresse. On its own, or after le, it is the noise: le son de la télé. Nothing about the two is related and there is no rule to learn here. It is worth thirty seconds only because you have met le son already and would otherwise wonder whether you had missed a connection.

examples.note: A possessive, because there is a thing straight behind it.
The plural of the same word, and still nothing to do with sound.

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. « ma sœur » AND « mon amie » ARE ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, read straight through with no gap and no reset. The swap between them is the rule, and two separate recordings are two performances: a reader who records mon amie in its own session will lean on the mon, and the learner will hear that lean as a change of gender rather than as a change of sound. Read them as if reading one list. Also in this take, immediately after: « Ma sœur et mon amie sont ici. », which carries both halves in one line. THE LIAISON IN mon amie IS A REAL PRONOUNCED N and must be given its full value: the word comes out as three syllables, mohⁿ-na-MEE, with the n on the front of the second syllable rather than closing the first. Do NOT read it as mon, pause, amie. Finally « Vous écrivez votre adresse. » in the same take, because the whole point of that line is that votre does NOT swap in front of a vowel: read it plainly with no elision and no swap.
clipIds: Ma sœur et mon amie sont ici.

recorded.desc: THE THREE PAIRS, AND TWO OF THEM MUST SOUND IDENTICAL. Read every pair as ONE TAKE, one voice. « mes amis » / « ses amis » is the only pair with anything in it: identical z liaison, identical stress, and the whole difference is the vowel of the first syllable. Do not exaggerate it and do not lengthen either word. « mon ami » / « mon amie » MUST BE READ AS THE SAME WORD TWICE, because that is what they are. This matters MORE than the pair that differs, not less. If a reader cannot resist marking the feminine, record mon ami twice and use it for both: that is a more truthful clip than a performed difference, and a learner who hears an invented difference will spend a year listening for it. « Voici leur fille. » / « Voici leurs filles. » is the same instruction again. Both plural endings are silent in front of a consonant and the two sentences are one sound. No lengthening, no release on the s, no breath. Separately, and NOT beside those: « leurs amis », where the s of leurs DOES wake up as a z. That is the one place the pair is audible and it is worth a clip so the learner knows the s is not imaginary.

THE EIGHTEEN GRID SENTENCES, READ ONE ROW AT A TIME AND ONE TAKE PER ROW. « Voici mon frère, voici ma sœur, voici mes parents », then the same three for tu, then for il and elle, then nous, vous and ils. Reading a row in one take is the entire point: the learner has to hear that only the possessive moves within a row, and that in the bottom three rows the first two sentences are the same word twice. Do not record these eighteen separately and do not vary the pace between rows, because the comparison is between rows as much as within them. KEEP EVERY NASAL CLOSED. mon, ton and son are nasal vowels with NO n sound behind them at all, and parents ends in a nasal the same way. The app respells them MOHⁿ, TOHⁿ, SOHⁿ and LAY pah-RAHⁿ deliberately. The s of mes, tes, ses, nos, vos and leurs is SILENT in every one of these eighteen lines, because a consonant follows it every time. Do not sound any of them.

THE INVERSION, AND THE TWO LINES MUST BE ACOUSTICALLY IDENTICAL FROM THE THIRD WORD ON. « Il parle avec sa sœur. » immediately followed by « Elle parle avec sa sœur. », ONE TAKE, one voice. The only difference the learner may hear is il against elle at the very start. Everything after that is the same three words and must be read the same way: no shift in pitch on sa, no emphasis, nothing that would suggest the possessive is doing different work in the two sentences. It is not. That sameness IS the lesson, and a reader who colours the second one teaches the opposite of it. Then, in the same take, « Voici son frère. » and « Voici sa sœur. » back to back, so the learner hears that the change between them tracks the brother and the sister rather than anybody's sex.

« Voici leur fille. » and « Voici leurs filles. » ADJACENT, ONE TAKE, and read as the same sentence twice, because in front of a consonant that is exactly what they are. The difference is on the page and nowhere else. Then the two published lines in the same take: « Les clients attendent leur commande. » and « Les élèves rangent leurs livres. », where the difference is audible only in the noun. Read all four plainly. Nothing here should sound like a demonstration, and no s anywhere in this group is pronounced.

THE SCENE'S CHOICE, AND THE ONE PLACE A BARE FORM COMES CLOSE TO BEING RECORDED ALONE. It is not: every clip here is a possessive WITH ITS THING. « Voici sa sœur. » and « Voici ma sœur. » in ONE TAKE, adjacent, read at the same pace with the same weight, because the whole beat turns on how small the difference is. Do not make the wrong one sound wrong: it is correct French about somebody else and it has to sound like it, or the scene stops being about a slip nobody catches. A BARE POSSESSIVE IS NEVER RECORDED IN THIS LESSON. mon on its own carries no information about the thing and the whole subject is what follows it, so there is no clip anywhere of mon, ma, mes, ton, ta, tes, son, sa, ses, notre, nos, votre, vos, leur or leurs alone. If a request for one arrives, it is a mistake in the request.

The five written traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically. TWO OF THE FIVE ARE ACOUSTICALLY REAL ERRORS and should be read exactly as written: « sa père » and « son mère » are not French and sound wrong, which is the point. « ma amie » should be read with the two vowels genuinely colliding, slowly enough that the learner hears why the language refuses it. « leurs enfants » against « leur enfant » DOES differ audibly, because a vowel follows and the s wakes up as a z: this is the one trap in the group the ear can catch. « le mon livre » should be read flatly and without hesitation, because a learner writing it does not hesitate either.

The opening scene, French bubbles only. Hugo is a man in his thirties running the door at a language exchange, half distracted, refilling glasses. His line « Ah, enchanté ! Vous êtes la sœur d'Amélie, alors ? » MUST BE WARM AND COMPLETELY UNSUSPICIOUS. He has not noticed anything, because there is nothing to notice: the sentence he heard was correct. Any hint of a question in his voice turns the scene into a correction and loses the whole point, which is that the error is undetectable from both sides. His last line, where he realises and does not mind, is where warmth is allowed to show.
clipIds: Et toi, tu es venue avec qui ce soir ?
Ah, enchanté ! Vous êtes la sœur d'Amélie, alors ?
Ta sœur ! Ah, pardon, j'avais compris autre chose. Revenez toutes les deux.

lessons.title: La négation
lessons.intro: Two words rather than one, and they go on either side of the verb. This is how to turn any sentence you can already make into its opposite, what the verb does to the rest of it, and why half of it disappears the moment anybody speaks at normal speed.

say.text: A correct sentence, heard as its own opposite, and nobody in the corridor had any reason to check.

setting.place: A corridor outside an open-plan office, first morning, somebody working down a list

beats.text: The first morning at a new job, in the corridor outside the office, and somebody from the floor below has stopped you with a clipboard.
She is allocating the six parking spaces behind the building. There are eleven people and she is working down a list. This takes forty seconds and then she is gone.

beats.speaker: Salomé
beats.stage: She is already looking at the next name. The corridor is loud and she is not really listening.

beats.prompt: You do not have a car. Which line do you say?

options.en: the way you have heard people say it
the way it is written, with both halves in it

followUp.works: Yes, and notice how much of the sentence is carrying the no. Two words rather than one.
followUp.breaks: That is real French and people say it constantly. Watch what happens to it in a loud corridor.

beats.speaker: You
beats.en: (Every word correct, and the whole meaning is riding on the short one)

beats.speaker: Salomé
beats.fr: Parfait, je vous mets la place numéro quatre. Le badge arrive vendredi.
beats.en: Perfect, I am putting you in space number four. The badge comes on Friday.
beats.stage: She writes it down and moves on. Nothing has gone wrong that anybody in the corridor could point at.

beats.heading: Nobody was corrected
beats.body: You said a real sentence and she heard the opposite of it. With the ne gone, one short unstressed word was carrying the entire no, and in a loud corridor it did not land. She heard a yes.

wrong.en: Correct spoken French, and everything depends on one word arriving

right.en: The same sentence with a second word carrying the same no

beats.coach: Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was. There are two halves for a reason, and this is it.

beats.speaker: Friday, when the badge arrives
beats.en: I do not have a car.
beats.stage: One extra syllable, and it is the one that would have been heard.

beats.speaker: Salomé
beats.fr: Ah, vous n'en avez pas ! Bon, je la donne à quelqu'un d'autre alors.
beats.en: Oh, you do not have one! Right, I will give it to somebody else then.
beats.stage: Four days of a space nobody used, and somebody who needed one walking from the other end of the street.

beats.text: Two words, either side of the verb. The next half hour is how to put them there, and what happens to the rest of the sentence when you do.

closing.text: Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was. That is the whole of the next half hour.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the second one is the only part of this that nobody has told you yet.

goals.t: Turn any sentence you have into its negative
goals.s: Two words, either side of the verb, and it works on every sentence you can already make.

goals.t: Know what the verb does to the rest of it
goals.s: The same sentence gives two different answers depending on which verb is in it. This is the part that catches people.

goals.t: Recognise a negative with half of it missing
goals.s: What you will actually hear, which is not what you will read, and the difference matters more than it sounds.
Two words for no doing two completely different jobs, and English uses one word for both.

sections.title: French Needs Two Words For Not
sections.hint: Four cards before any sentence is turned round.
sections.say: One English word becomes two French ones, and the two go in different places.

cards.label: what English does
cards.head: One word, and it goes after the verb
cards.body: I am not tired. I do not have a car. English puts a single word behind the verb and the job is done. There is nothing in front and nothing to remember about where the other half goes, because there is no other half.

cards.label: what French does
cards.head: Two words, one on each side
cards.sub: /nə/ [nuh] · the first half, and it goes in front
cards.body: French has two and they do not sit together. Ne goes in front of the verb and pas goes behind it, so the verb ends up between them. Neither half is optional in writing and neither one means anything on its own.

cards.label: the verb in brackets
cards.head: Find the verb, then surround it
cards.fr: Je suis fatigué. · Je ne suis pas fatigué.
cards.sub: /ʒə sɥi/ [zhuh SWEE] · /ʒə nə sɥi pɑ/ [zhuh nuh swee PAH]
cards.body: I am tired. becomes I am not tired.. Suis is the verb, so ne went in front of it and pas went behind it. Fatigué did not move and nothing else in the sentence had to.

cards.label: why it is worth the two
cards.head: Two halves, two chances to be heard
cards.body: A negative carried by one short word is a negative that can be missed, which is what happened in the corridor. Two words either side of the verb is harder to lose. Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was.

sections.title: Before And After
sections.say: Read across a row. Two words arrived and nothing else in the sentence moved.

cells:
Je suis fatigué.
I am tired.

Je ne suis pas fatigué.
I am not tired.
rows.say: Je suis fatigué. Je ne suis pas fatigué.

detail.title: The verb is être
detail.body: Je suis fatigué. Je ne suis pas fatigué. Two words arrived and nothing else in the sentence moved. Ne went in front of suis and pas went behind it.
detail.say: Je suis fatigué. Je ne suis pas fatigué.

cells:
Il est là.
He is there.

Il n'est pas là.
He is not there.
rows.say: Il est là. Il n'est pas là.

detail.title: The verb is être
detail.body: Il est là. Il n'est pas là. The same wrap, and ne has lost its e because est starts on a vowel. That is the elision rule from sons.07, not a new one.
detail.say: Il est là. Il n'est pas là.

cells:
Nous sommes prêts.
We are ready.

Nous ne sommes pas prêts.
We are not ready.
rows.say: Nous sommes prêts. Nous ne sommes pas prêts.

detail.title: The verb is être
detail.body: Nous sommes prêts. Nous ne sommes pas prêts. The wrap goes around the conjugated verb whatever person it is in. Sommes is one word, so ne and pas sit either side of it.
detail.say: Nous sommes prêts. Nous ne sommes pas prêts.

cells:
Je n'ai pas soif.
I am not thirsty.
rows.say: J'ai soif. Je n'ai pas soif.

detail.title: The verb is avoir
detail.body: J'ai soif. Je n'ai pas soif. Soif never had a word in front of it, so the negative had nothing to take away. It is pas soif and never pas de soif.
detail.say: J'ai soif. Je n'ai pas soif.

sections.title: Both Verbs, Same Two Words
sections.say: The only two verbs you can conjugate, and the wrap does not care which one it is.

check.q: Where does pas go in « Nous sommes prêts » when you turn it round?
check.why: Straight after sommes. Pas goes behind the verb and ne goes in front of it, so the verb sits between them. Prêts is not the verb and never moves.

items.fr: Je ne suis pas espagnol, je suis portugais.

check.q: Which of these has the two words in the right places?
check.why: Ne in front of suis, pas behind it. The other three have both words on the same side of the verb, which is the shape English speakers reach for because English only has one word to place.

items.fr: Il n'est pas triste, au contraire il est très content.
items.en: He's not sad, on the contrary he's very happy.

check.q: In « Ce chien n'est pas méchant », what is sitting between the two words?
check.why: Est, and it is the verb. Everything else in the sentence is outside the brackets. Finding the verb is the whole of the first step, and on être and avoir it is always the second word or close to it.

check.q: You have a sentence and you want to turn it round. What do you look for first?
opts: the little word in front of the noun
the last word in the sentence
whether the sentence is about you
check.why: The verb, every time, because both words are placed relative to it and nothing else in the sentence tells you where they go. Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was.

sections.title: You Already Have This Rule
sections.hint: Three cards, and none of the ideas in them is new.
sections.say: One old rule arriving on a new word. The elision lesson taught this and it has not changed.

cards.label: the collision
cards.head: ne ai is not something French will say
cards.body: Ne ends in a vowel and ai starts on one, and two vowel sounds meeting head on is something the language will not do. You watched it refuse exactly this in the elision lesson, on le and la and je.

cards.label: the repair
cards.head: ne loses its e and takes an apostrophe
cards.sub: /il nɛ pɑ/ [eel neh PAH] · He is not there.
cards.body: Exactly what happened to le and la. The word is cut short and an apostrophe marks where the vowel went. Ne is on the elision lesson's list alongside je, me, te, se, de and que, and behaves like all of them.

cards.label: when it does not happen
cards.head: A consonant in front, and nothing changes
cards.fr: Je ne suis pas fatigué. · Je ne parle pas allemand.
cards.sub: Nous n'habitons pas à Lyon. · all three start on a consonant
cards.body: Suis, parle and habitons all start on consonants, so ne keeps its e and there is nothing to write. The rule fires on the sound at the start of the verb and nowhere else. The last two use verbs to read rather than say.

sections.title: Which Ones Cut Short
sections.say: Four verbs. Two start on a vowel and two do not, and that is the whole test.

cells:
Je ne suis pas fatigué.
I am not tired.

detail.title: ne keeps its e
detail.body: Je ne suis pas fatigué. No collision, so nothing is cut. This is the shape most of the time, because most French verbs start on a consonant.

cells:
Il n'est pas là.
He is not there.

detail.title: ne becomes n'
detail.body: Il n'est pas là. Est starts on a vowel sound, so ne is cut short exactly as le and la were in the elision lesson.

cells:
Je n'ai pas de frère.
I do not have a brother.

detail.title: the same cut, on avoir
detail.body: Je n'ai pas de frère. Four of the six forms of avoir start on a vowel, so this is the shape you will write most often with that verb.

cells: de, in front of a vowel

Je n'ai pas d'enfants.
I do not have any children.

detail.title: de becomes d' as well
detail.body: Je n'ai pas d'enfants. I do not have any children. The same rule on the other side of the sentence. De is on the same list as ne and cuts short in front of a vowel for the same reason.

sections.title: The Part You Already Know
sections.hint: Four cards, and three lessons have been here before you.
sections.say: You have met this three times. It is here so you can run it rather than read it.

cards.label: where you met it
cards.head: Three lessons have taught you this
cards.sub: I do not have a brother.
cards.body: The lesson on un and une, the one on du and de la, and the one on avoir all taught this: a un, une or des turns into de once a negative arrives. That rule is right and nothing here changes it.

cards.label: the whole rule
cards.head: un, une, des, du and de la all become de
cards.fr: J'ai une voiture. · Je n'ai pas de voiture.
cards.sub: /yn vwa.tyʁ/ [ün vwah-TÜR] · I do not have a car.
cards.body: One word, de, whatever it replaced. There is no feminine version of it and no plural version of it, which makes this the easiest thing in the lesson to get right once you remember to do it at all.

cards.label: in the wild
cards.head: Published French does it constantly
cards.fr: Je ne mange pas de pain. · Je ne mange pas de viande.
cards.sub: I do not eat bread. · I don't eat meat.
cards.body: Both of those had du or de la in them before the negative arrived, and both came out with de. The verb is one you have not learned yet, so read these rather than trying to say them.

cards.label: on avoir, in the wild
cards.head: Somebody else did the same two steps
cards.fr: Elle n'a pas de portable. · Je n'ai pas de stylo.
cards.sub: She does not have a cell phone. · I don't have a pen.
cards.body: Nous n'avons pas de fruits frais. Elle ne mange pas de viande. Two more, one on nous and one on a verb you only read. Each wrapped a verb and then collapsed a little word.

cards.label: the second step
cards.head: It is a second step, and that is the point
cards.body: Turning the sentence round did not do this on its own. You wrapped the verb, and then something else had to change. Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was.

sections.title: Both Changes, One Screen
sections.say: Positive on the left, negative on the right, and two things are different in every row.

cells:
J'ai un frère.
I have a brother.

Je n'ai pas de frère.
I do not have a brother.
rows.say: J'ai un frère. Je n'ai pas de frère.

detail.title: Two things changed
detail.body: J'ai un frère. Je n'ai pas de frère. Two things changed. The wrap went round ai, and then the un became de. A learner who does only the first says Je n ai pas un frère.
detail.say: J'ai un frère. Je n'ai pas de frère.

cells:
J'ai une voiture.
I have a car.

Je n'ai pas de voiture.
I do not have a car.
rows.say: J'ai une voiture. Je n'ai pas de voiture.

detail.title: Two things changed
detail.body: J'ai une voiture. Je n'ai pas de voiture. De agrees with nothing. Une became de, exactly as un did, and there is no de feminine to remember.
detail.say: J'ai une voiture. Je n'ai pas de voiture.

cells:
Elle a des enfants.
She has children.

Elle n'a pas d'enfants.
She does not have children.
rows.say: Elle a des enfants. Elle n'a pas d'enfants.

detail.title: Two things changed
detail.body: Elle a des enfants. Elle n'a pas d'enfants. Des became de like the other two, and then de lost its e in front of the vowel. The same elision, arriving on the other side of the sentence.
detail.say: Elle a des enfants. Elle n'a pas d'enfants.

sections.title: When There Was Nothing To Change
sections.hint: Three cards on the half nobody teaches.
sections.say: A de only turns up where something had to be taken away. Sometimes nothing was there.

cards.label: the case
cards.head: Some sentences have no little word at all
cards.fr: J'ai soif. · Je n'ai pas soif.
cards.body: Soif never had a word in front of it, so the negative had nothing to take away and nothing to replace. It is pas soif and never pas de soif. The avoir lesson taught this on faim and it is the same fact.

cards.label: the one you have already used
cards.head: The avoir lesson got here first
cards.fr: Je n'ai pas faim. · Nous n'avons pas faim.
cards.sub: I am not hungry. · We are not hungry.
cards.body: Both of those are published and both are in the group of expressions avoir uses without any word in front. There was nothing to collapse, so there is no de, and adding one is the rule applied a noun too far.

cards.label: backwards
cards.head: The de tells you what was there
cards.body: This works in reverse and it is worth having. If a de turned up, the sentence had a un, une or des in it. If nothing turned up, it had le, la or les, or it had nothing there at all.

sections.title: One Word, Three Answers
sections.say: The same noun in all three rows. Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was.

cells:
J'ai un livre.
I have a book.

Je n'ai pas de livre.
I do not have a book.
rows.say: J'ai un livre. Je n'ai pas de livre.

detail.title: avoir, and un became de
detail.body: J'ai un livre. Je n'ai pas de livre. Un became de. This is the rule you already have, on the noun the next two cards use as well.
detail.say: J'ai un livre. Je n'ai pas de livre.

cells:
J'ai le livre.
I have the book.

Je n'ai pas le livre.
I do not have the book.
rows.say: J'ai le livre. Je n'ai pas le livre.

detail.title: avoir, and le did not move
detail.body: J'ai le livre. Je n'ai pas le livre. Same verb, same noun, and le did not move. Only un, une, des, du and de la ever collapse. Le, la and les stay exactly where they were.
detail.say: J'ai le livre. Je n'ai pas le livre.

cells:
C'est un livre.
This is a book.

Ce n'est pas un livre.
This is not a book.
rows.say: C'est un livre. Ce n'est pas un livre.

detail.title: être, and un did not move either
detail.body: C'est un livre. Ce n'est pas un livre. The un survived, and the only thing different from the first card is the verb. After être nothing collapses at all.
detail.say: C'est un livre. Ce n'est pas un livre.

sections.title: After Être, Nothing Moves
sections.hint: Four cards on the half of the rule nobody tells you.
sections.say: The rule you have just used three times has a verb it does not apply to.

cards.label: the exception
cards.head: un survives
cards.fr: C'est un livre. · Ce n'est pas un livre.
cards.sub: /sə nɛ pɑ/ [suh neh PAH] · This is not a book.
cards.body: Wrap the verb and stop. The un is still there and nothing became de. Compare that with the first row of the screen before this one, where the same noun with the same word in front of it came out as de livre.

cards.label: and une, and des
cards.head: It reaches all of them
cards.fr: C'est une erreur. · Ce n'est pas une erreur.
cards.sub: Ce sont des amis. · Ce ne sont pas des amis.
cards.body: Une survived and des survived. It is not about the word ce or the phrase ce n'est pas: it is about the verb, and it reaches every person of être you can conjugate.

cards.label: why
cards.head: The two sentences are doing different jobs
cards.body: J'ai un livre is about how many there are, and taking that away leaves nothing to count, which is what de marks. C'est un livre is about what a thing IS, and saying it is not a book leaves you talking about books.

cards.label: in the wild
cards.head: You have already read one of these
cards.fr: Ce n'est pas lundi, c'est mardi. · Non, ce n'est pas mon mari, c'est mon frère.
cards.sub: It's not Monday, it's Tuesday. · No, that's not my husband, that's my brother.
cards.body: Both start with ce n'est pas and neither has anything collapsing behind it. This shape is everywhere in French and it is the single most useful thing in this lesson to be able to say without thinking.

sections.title: Four Things That Can Happen
sections.hint: One card per outcome, and the verb picks between them.
sections.say: Four outcomes. Look at the verb and you know which one you are in.

cards.label: avoir, and a un, une or des
cards.head: It becomes de
cards.sub: /də livʁ/ [duh LEEVR] · I do not have a book.
cards.body: The rule three lessons taught you. Un, une, des, du and de la all collapse to the one word, and de agrees with nothing so there is only ever one form of it.

cards.label: être, and a un, une or des
cards.head: It survives untouched
cards.sub: /sə nɛ pɑ/ [suh neh PAH] · This is not a book.
cards.body: Nothing collapses after être. The same noun with the same word in front of it as the card above, and the only thing different between the two sentences is which verb is in them.

cards.label: le, la or les, on any verb
cards.head: They never move at all
cards.fr: Je n'ai pas le livre. · Il n'aime pas le café.
cards.sub: /lə livʁ/ [luh LEEVR] · I do not have the book.
cards.body: He doesn't like coffee. is on a verb you cannot conjugate yet and it behaves identically. Le, la and les come through a negative unchanged whatever the verb was, and there is no case where they do not.

cards.label: nothing was there
cards.head: Nothing to take away
cards.fr: Je n'ai pas soif. · Je n'ai pas faim.
cards.sub: I am not thirsty. · I am not hungry.
cards.body: A handful of avoir expressions have no word in front of the noun to begin with, so there is nothing for the negative to reduce and no de. Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was.

sections.title: Turn It Round
sections.say: Six sentences, and you run the same two steps on every one of them. Wrap the verb first, then look back at what you wrapped and decide whether anything else has to move.

check.q: Say you do not have one.
opts: Je ne pas ai de livre.
check.why: Both steps. Ne and pas went round ai, and then the un became de because the verb was avoir. Stopping after step one gives Je n ai pas un livre, which is understood perfectly and is the commonest error of a first year.

check.q: Say it is not one.
opts: Ce ne pas est un livre.
check.why: The un stayed. Same noun as two screens ago and the same word in front of it, and this time nothing collapsed, because the verb was être. Reaching for de here is the older rule applied one verb too far.

check.q: Say you do not have it.
opts: Je n'ai pas de le livre.
check.why: Le never moves. The verb was avoir, which does collapse things, and it still did not touch this one, because only un, une, des, du and de la ever collapse. That is the half of the rule with no exceptions in it at all.

check.q: What tells you whether the little word changes?
opts: the verb, and the little word
whether the sentence is about you
check.why: Both, in that order. The verb decides whether anything can change at all, and the little word decides whether it is one of the five that do. Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was.

sections.title: Five Traps
sections.say: Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was. Five sentences an English speaker writes in their first month, one per screen.

errors.wrong: Writing « Je n'ai pas un frère ».
errors.right: Writing « Je n'ai pas de frère. ».
errors.why: The wrap was done and the second step was not. This is the single most common A1 negation error in the language and it survives because it is understood perfectly: nobody stops you, and it simply marks you as new.

errors.wrong: Writing « Ce n'est pas de livre ».
errors.right: Writing « Ce n'est pas un livre. ».
errors.why: The opposite mistake, and it comes from taking the rule seriously. After être nothing collapses, so the un stays exactly where it was. A learner who has just been drilled on de is more likely to write this, not less.

errors.wrong: Writing « Je ne ai pas de temps ».
errors.right: Writing « Je n'ai pas de temps ».
errors.why: Ne and ai are two vowels meeting, which French will not do. The elision lesson put ne on its list alongside je, me, te, se, de and le, and it cuts short here for exactly the reason those do.

errors.wrong: Writing « Je n'aime pas de café ».
errors.right: Writing « Je n'aime pas le café. ».
errors.why: Le, la and les never collapse, on any verb. The de rule reaches un, une, des, du and de la and stops there, so a le in the sentence comes through the negative completely untouched.

errors.wrong: Writing « Je non ai pas de voiture ».
errors.right: Writing « Je n'ai pas de voiture. ».
errors.why: Non answers a question and never goes inside a sentence. Ne goes inside a sentence and never answers a question. English uses one word for both jobs, which is the whole reason this happens.

sections.title: The Half That Disappears
sections.hint: Four cards, and none of them asks you to say anything.
sections.say: One card you need to recognise and never write. The written form keeps both halves.

cards.label: what is written
cards.head: Both halves, every time
cards.sub: /ʒə ne pɑ də ʃjɛ̃/ [zhuh nay pah duh SHYEHⁿ] · I do not have a dog.
cards.body: This is what you write, what you will be marked on, and what you should say while you are still working out where the two words go. Nothing about it is formal or old-fashioned. It is simply the sentence.

cards.label: what is said
cards.head: The ne goes, and it goes constantly
cards.sub: /ʒe pɑ də ʃjɛ̃/ [zhay pah duh SHYEHⁿ] · the same sentence, out loud
cards.body: In ordinary speech the ne is very often just not said, by everybody, all the time. This is not slang and not carelessness. It is what the language does at conversational speed, and half of what you hear will be this shape.

cards.label: why it matters to you
cards.head: One short word left carrying everything
cards.fr: J'ai un chien. · J'ai pas de chien.
cards.sub: /œ̃ ʃjɛ̃/ [uhⁿ SHYEHⁿ] · one word between them
cards.body: With the ne gone, the difference between having a dog and not having one is a single unstressed syllable. Miss it and you hear agreement. That is the corridor from the opening scene and it is the reason this card exists.

cards.label: what to do
cards.head: Hear it. Do not write it.
cards.sub: it's not cheap · published, and this shape is everywhere
cards.body: Learn to catch it, because you cannot follow a conversation without it. Keep writing and saying the full form yourself: the written language keeps the ne every time, and while your pas is still not landing, the ne is what saves the sentence.

sections.title: The One Your Ear Can Miss
sections.say: Three pairs. Two of them your ear does without help, and the third is the one that costs you conversations.

lines.fr: Je suis fatigué. · Je ne suis pas fatigué.
lines.en: two extra syllables, and nobody misses this one

lines.fr: J'ai un livre. · Je n'ai pas de livre.
lines.en: the written negative, and it is comfortably audible

lines.fr: J'ai un chien. · J'ai pas de chien.
lines.en: this pair is one short unstressed word apart, and that is the whole of it

questions.q: Which of these is hardest to catch at conversational speed?
opts: a negative with both halves in it
a negative with the ne dropped
questions.why: A negative with the ne dropped, and it is not close. The full form adds two syllables in front of the verb and one behind it. Drop the ne and one short unstressed word behind the verb is carrying the entire meaning of the sentence.

questions.q: You hear « J'ai pas de chien ». What did the speaker mean?
opts: they do not have a dog
they used to have a dog
it is not clear either way
questions.why: They do not have one. The pas is doing all the work and it is a complete, ordinary negative. Nothing about the missing ne makes the sentence uncertain to a French speaker; it only makes it harder for you.

questions.q: Should you drop the ne when you write?
questions.why: Writing keeps both halves every time. The dropped ne belongs to speech, and while you are still placing the two words it is worth saying the full form too, because it gives the sentence a second word carrying the same meaning.

sections.title: Answering, And Agreeing
sections.hint: Three cards that make this conversational rather than mechanical.
sections.say: Two words for no doing two different jobs, and one reply that makes a negative into a conversation.

cards.label: non answers
cards.head: non stands on its own
cards.body: Non is the answer to a question and that is all it does. Tu as un chien ? Non. It never goes inside a sentence and there is no version of French where je non ai pas is a thing anybody would finish saying.

cards.label: ne wraps
cards.head: ne never stands on its own
cards.fr: Non, je ne suis pas mariée, je suis fiancée.
cards.sub: Bien sûr que non, ce n'est pas grave. · No, I'm not married, I'm engaged.
cards.body: Both words in one line, a few apart, doing completely different jobs. Non answers the question that was asked and then ne wraps the verb of the sentence that follows. English uses one word for both.

cards.label: the reply
cards.head: moi non plus
cards.fr: Je n'aime pas le café. Moi non plus.
cards.sub: /mwa nɔ̃ ply/ [mwah nohⁿ PLÜ] · I don't like coffee. Me neither.
cards.body: Somebody says they do not like something and you agree. Moi non plus is me neither, and it is the reply that turns a negative into an exchange rather than a statement. Note that le café did not collapse: le never does.

sections.title: The Flat Viewing
sections.say: Six sentences, and three of them turn on whether a little word survived.
sections.text: Somebody is being shown a flat and the agent is working through a list of questions, and between them the two of them use most of what this lesson has covered. « Vous avez une voiture ? » The answer comes back with both halves of the negative in it, which is what you would write. « Je n'ai pas de voiture. » The un turned into de, because the verb was avoir and something had to go. Then the agent points at a door at the end of the hall and says something about it. « Ce n'est pas un placard. » Nothing collapsed there at all, and the only difference between that sentence and the one before it is the verb sitting in the middle of it. A neighbour has come in behind them and is talking to somebody on the stairs, quickly and without any ne anywhere. « J'ai pas de chien. » That is the same shape as the first answer with one word missing, and it is what you will hear far more often than the written one. The agent finishes with a question about the coffee machine on the landing and gets the shortest answer of the morning. « Je n'aime pas le café. »

glossary.note: The verb was avoir, so the une became de. Two things changed and neither one was optional.
The verb was être, so the un survived. Same shape as the line above it and the opposite answer.

glossary.en: I do not have a dog
glossary.note: The ne is gone, which is what happens in speech. Recognise it. The written form keeps both halves.
Le never collapses, on any verb. Aimer is a verb you have not learned yet, so read this rather than saying it.

questions.q: Two of those sentences have the same little word in front of the same kind of thing, and only one of them changed. What separates them?
questions.a: The verb. Je n ai pas de voiture is avoir, so the une collapsed to de. Ce n est pas un placard is être, so the un stayed exactly where it was. Nothing else in either sentence decides it, and both are completely ordinary French.

questions.q: The neighbour on the stairs said something without a ne in it. Was that a mistake?
questions.a: No. Dropping the ne is what ordinary spoken French does, by everybody, constantly. It is not slang and it is not careless. What it means for you is that the whole negative is riding on one short unstressed word, so it is much easier to miss than the written form. Keep writing the full one.

questions.q: Why did le café not become de café?
questions.a: Because le, la and les never collapse under a negative, whatever the verb is. Only un, une, des, du and de la ever do. That asymmetry is useful backwards as well: if a de turned up in a sentence, it had one of those five in it before the negative arrived.

sections.title: The Pieces, Banked
sections.say: Three decks. The words that do the wrapping, what the little word turns into, and the two ways to say no.

themes.title: the two halves of the wrap

cards.en: the first half, in front of the verb
the same word when a vowel follows it
the second half, behind the verb
what un, une, des, du and de la turn into
the same de in front of a vowel
le, la and les never move at all
and after être, neither does this

themes.title: the two ways to say no

cards.en: answers a question, and stands on its own
me neither, the reply to somebody else's negative

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Say the French before you flip, and run both steps.

cards.front: I do not have a brother.
I do not have a car.
I do not have a book.
I do not have the book.

cards.back: Ce ne sont pas des amis.
cards.say: Ce ne sont pas des amis.

cards.front: I do not have a dog.

sections.title: Put Them In The Right Places
sections.say: Five lines. You are placing two words either side of a verb, which is the whole of the first step.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: Every line keeps both halves of the wrap, which is what you should be saying while this is still new.

sections.title: The Same Corridor, Going Better
sections.say: One exchange and you hold up your half. Every turn you take is a negative with both halves in it.
sections.setting: The same corridor, a week later. Salomé is reallocating the spaces and this time you are ready.

turns.ai: Rebonjour ! Alors, vous avez une voiture ou pas ?
turns.en: Hello again! So, do you have a car or not?
turns.user: Non, je n'ai pas de voiture.
turns.userEn: No, I do not have a car.

alts.fr: Je n'ai pas de voiture, non.
alts.en: I do not have a car, no.
No, I do not have one.

turns.ai: Ah, d'accord. Et le velo dans le couloir, c'est le votre ?
turns.en: Ah, right. And the bike in the corridor, is that yours?
turns.user: Non, ce n'est pas mon velo.
turns.userEn: No, that is not my bike.

alts.fr: Ce n'est pas le mien, non.
Non, ce n'est pas a moi.

turns.ai: Bon. Vous etes en retard le matin, d'habitude ?
turns.en: Right. Are you usually late in the morning?
turns.user: Non, je ne suis pas en retard.
turns.userEn: No, I am not late.

alts.fr: Je ne suis pas en retard, non.
Non. Je ne suis jamais tres en retard.
alts.en: No. I am not usually very late.

turns.ai: Et les deux personnes du troisieme, ce sont vos collegues ?
turns.en: And the two people from the third floor, are they your colleagues?
turns.user: Non, ce ne sont pas des collegues.
turns.userEn: No, they are not colleagues.

alts.fr: Ce ne sont pas mes collegues, non.
alts.en: They are not my colleagues, no.

alts.fr: Non, je ne les connais pas.
alts.en: No, I do not know them.

turns.ai: Parfait. Vous avez le badge du parking, alors ?
turns.en: Perfect. Do you have the parking badge, then?
turns.user: Non, je n'ai pas le badge.
turns.userEn: No, I do not have the badge.

alts.fr: Je n'ai pas le badge, non.
alts.en: I do not have the badge, no.
No, I do not have it.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: Where do ne and pas go?
cards.back: Je ne suis pas fatigué. Ne in front of the verb, pas behind it.

cards.front: « Il est là. » Now say he is not.
cards.back: Il n'est pas là. Est starts on a vowel, so ne is cut short.

cards.front: « Nous sommes prêts. » Now say you are not.
« J'ai un frère. » Now say you do not.
cards.back: Je n'ai pas de frère. avoir, so un became de.

cards.front: « J'ai une voiture. » Now say you do not.
cards.back: Je n'ai pas de voiture. De agrees with nothing.

cards.front: « Elle a des enfants. » Now say she does not.
cards.back: Elle n'a pas d'enfants. des became de, then de lost its e.

cards.front: « J'ai un livre. » Now say you do not.
cards.back: Je n'ai pas de livre. avoir collapses it.

cards.front: « J'ai le livre. » Now say you do not.
cards.back: Je n'ai pas le livre. le never moves.

cards.front: « C'est un livre. » Now say it is not.
cards.back: Ce n'est pas un livre. être, so the un survives.

cards.front: « Ce sont des amis. » Now say they are not.
cards.back: Ce ne sont pas des amis. des survives after être too.
cards.say: Ce ne sont pas des amis.

cards.front: « J'ai soif. » Now say you are not.
cards.back: Je n'ai pas soif. Nothing was there, so no de.

cards.front: What decides whether the little word changes?
cards.back: Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was. avoir collapses un, une and des. être leaves everything alone.

cards.front: You hear « J'ai pas de chien ». What does it mean?
cards.back: I do not have a dog. (spoken French, with the ne dropped) The ne is dropped in speech. Recognise it, and keep writing both halves.

cards.front: Somebody says they do not like coffee. How do you agree?
cards.back: Moi non plus. Me neither, and it is the reply that makes a negative into a conversation.

cards.front: Can non go inside a sentence?
cards.back: No. Non answers a question and ne wraps a verb, and they never swap jobs.
cards.say: Non, je ne suis pas mariée, je suis fiancée.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a parking space go to the wrong person because one short word did not land in a loud corridor. Since then you have put two words either side of a verb on both of the verbs you can conjugate, watched one of them cut short in front of a vowel for a reason you already had, and run the rule about the little word that three earlier lessons taught you. Then you found the half of it nobody mentions: after être, nothing collapses at all, and the same noun with the same word in front of it comes out two different ways depending only on the verb. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: Two words, one either side
rounds.say: The wrap, four times, on both verbs.

questions.q: Turn this round: « Je suis fatigué. »
questions.why: Ne in front of suis and pas behind it. Two words, one on each side of the verb, and fatigué never moves. This is the whole of the first step and it works on every sentence you can already make.

questions.q: Which one has both words in the right places?
questions.why: Ne in front of sommes and pas behind it. The other three put both halves on the same side of the verb, which is the shape an English speaker reaches for because English has only one word to place.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je suis pas fatigué, mais je ne dors. »
questions.why: The first half is missing from the first sentence and the second half is missing from the last one. In writing both halves are needed every time, and neither one carries the meaning on its own.

questions.q: Turn this round: « J'ai soif. »
questions.why: Wrap ai and stop. Soif never had a word in front of it, so there is nothing for the negative to take away and no de anywhere. The avoir lesson taught this on faim and it is the same fact arriving on a different word.

rounds.label: In front of a vowel
rounds.say: The rule the elision lesson already gave you.

questions.q: Which is written correctly?
opts: Je ne ai pas de frère.
Je n'ne ai pas de frère.
questions.why: Ne and ai are two vowels meeting, so ne is cut short and an apostrophe marks where the e went. This is the same rule the elision lesson taught on je, me, te, se, de and le, and ne was on that list.

questions.q: Fix this. « Il ne est pas là. »
questions.why: Est starts on a vowel sound, so ne cannot keep its e in front of it. Note that the answer key cannot check the apostrophe itself: free text is compared with the punctuation stripped, so this question tests the letters and nothing else.

questions.q: Why does ne keep its e in « Je ne suis pas fatigué »?
opts: because the sentence is about you
because suis starts on a consonant
because fatigué is at the end
questions.why: Suis starts on a consonant, so there is no collision and nothing to repair. The rule fires on the sound at the start of the verb and on nothing else, which is why it reaches ai and est and misses suis and sommes.

questions.q: Turn this round: « Il est là. »
questions.why: Both steps of the wrap and the cut, in one sentence. Ne goes in front of est, loses its e because est starts on a vowel, and pas goes behind. Là is not the verb and does not move.

rounds.label: What happens to the little word
rounds.say: The rule three lessons taught you, on avoir.

questions.q: Turn this round: « J'ai un frère. »
questions.why: Two steps. Ne and pas went round ai, and then the un became de. Doing only the first gives Je n ai pas un frère, which is understood perfectly and is the most common A1 negation error there is.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je n'ai pas une voiture. »
questions.why: Une collapses to de behind a negative on avoir, exactly as un and des do. De agrees with nothing, so there is one form of it rather than three, which makes this the easiest part of the rule once you remember it at all.

questions.q: What does « Elle a des enfants » become?
questions.why: Des became de like the other two, and then de lost its e in front of the vowel of enfants. Two rules in a row, and the second is the same elision that gave you n apostrophe on the other side of the sentence.

questions.q: A de turned up in a negative sentence. What was there before?
opts: un, une, des, du or de la
questions.why: One of those five, because they are the only ones that ever collapse. This works backwards and is worth having: le, la and les come through untouched, and a sentence with nothing in front of the noun stays with nothing.

rounds.label: The verb decides
rounds.say: The same noun, the same little word, and two different answers.

questions.q: Turn this round: « C'est un livre. »
questions.why: The un survived. Wrap est and stop, because after être nothing collapses at all. Compare it with J ai un livre, which is the same noun with the same word in front of it and comes out as de livre.

questions.q: Turn this round: « J'ai un livre. »
questions.why: Here it did collapse, because the verb was avoir. The noun and the little word in front of it are identical to the question before this one, and the verb is the only thing that changed.

questions.q: Fix this. « Ce ne sont pas de amis. »
accept: Ce ne sont pas des amis.
ce ne sont pas des amis
questions.answer: Ce ne sont pas des amis.
questions.why: The verb is sont, which is être, so the des survives and there is nothing to collapse. This is the exception reaching a person other than ce n est pas, which is where most learners stop expecting it.

questions.q: What decides whether the little word changes?
opts: whether the sentence is about you
whether the noun starts on a vowel
questions.why: The verb. avoir collapses un, une, des, du and de la to de. être leaves every one of them exactly where it was. le, la and les never move on either. Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was.

rounds.label: What you will hear
rounds.say: The half that disappears, and what it costs you.

questions.q: You hear this. What does the speaker mean?
opts: they do not have a dog
questions.why: They do not have one. The ne has been dropped, which is what ordinary speech does, so the whole negative is riding on pas. This is the one place your comprehension genuinely fails, and it is worth practising until it does not.

questions.q: Which of these should you write?
questions.why: The written language keeps both halves every time. The first one is completely ordinary spoken French and you will hear it constantly, and it still is not what you write.

questions.q: Is dropping the ne slang?
opts: yes, and it should be avoided
questions.why: It is ordinary speech, from everybody, constantly. Treating it as slang leads people to stop listening for it, and then half of what they hear reads as agreement. Recognise it and keep writing the full form.

questions.q: Say this out loud: I do not have a dog.
questions.why: Both halves, because that is what you should be saying while the placement is still new. The version without the ne is real French and is not what you want to be producing until the two words go where they belong without any thought.

rounds.label: Answering, and agreeing
rounds.say: Two words for no, and the reply that makes it a conversation.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je non ai pas de voiture. »
questions.why: Non answers a question and never sits inside a sentence. Ne sits inside a sentence and never answers a question. English uses one word for both jobs, which is exactly why this gets written.

questions.q: Somebody says « Je n'aime pas le café ». How do you agree?
questions.why: Moi non plus is me neither, and it is the reply to somebody else's negative. Moi aussi agrees with a positive and would mean you do like coffee, which is the opposite of what you meant to say.

questions.q: You hear a question and the answer is no. Which word answers it?
questions.why: Non, and it is the only one of the four that can stand on its own. Ne and pas are two halves of one thing that wraps a verb, and neither of them means anything by itself.

questions.q: Turn this round: « C'est une erreur. »
questions.why: The une survived, because the verb is être. One more of these than you expect to need, and it is the shape that most often gets a de put into it by somebody who learned the collapse properly.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next two units.
sections.body: You can take any sentence you are able to make and turn it round, on either of the two verbs you can conjugate, with the two words in the right places and the right thing happening to everything else. You know that the verb is what decides, which is the part almost nobody is told, and you can recognise a negative with half of it missing, which is most of what you will actually hear. The next two units are questions, and both of them need this: asking somebody whether they do not have something, and the one French answer that only exists in reply to a negative.
points: Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was. avoir collapses un, une and des to de. être leaves them alone.
le, la and les never move under a negative, whatever the verb was.
In writing, both halves every time. In speech the ne very often goes, and you need to hear it.
non answers a question. ne wraps a verb. They never swap jobs.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that un and une follow it, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, introduced in a1.04
un, une and des, and that they collapse to de under a negative, introduced in a1.11
du, de la and de l', and the same collapse, introduced in a1.29
The nine subject pronouns, introduced in a1.05
The full present of être, introduced in a1.06, which never negated it
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07, including pas faim and the collapse on une
Elision as a repair for two vowels meeting, and that ne is on its list, introduced in sons.07
grammarIntroduced: Standard negation with the discontinuous morpheme ne… pas around a finite verb
The elision of ne to n' before a vowel or mute h, applied to a finite verb
That the indefinite and partitive determiners reduce to de under sentential negation
THAT THE REDUCTION DOES NOT APPLY AFTER THE COPULA: ce n'est pas un livre, ce ne sont pas des amis
That the definite article is invariant under negation on any verb
That a noun with no determiner takes no de under negation, extending a1.07
ne-drop in colloquial spoken French, introduced for RECEPTION ONLY and produced nowhere
The distinction between non as a pro-sentence and ne as a preverbal clitic
moi non plus as the negative-polarity agreement reply

overview.introFr: Deux mots autour du verbe, et le verbe décide de ce qui change ensuite.

acts.title: French needs two words for not
acts.milestone: Two words, either side of the verb, on both of the verbs you can conjugate.

acts.title: In front of a vowel
acts.milestone: ne becomes n', which is a rule you already had.

acts.title: What happens to the little word
acts.milestone: The rule three earlier lessons taught you, run rather than read.

acts.title: The verb decides
acts.milestone: One noun, the same little word, and two different answers depending on the verb.

acts.title: What you will actually hear
acts.milestone: The half that disappears in speech, and the reply that makes a negative a conversation.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. Everything here carries straight into asking questions.

lessons.reframe: Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was.

errorTriggers.description: Writes only one of the two words, or puts both on the same side of the verb: « je suis pas fatigué » in writing, « je ne suis fatigué », « je ne pas suis ». The English habit of a single word placed after the verb, arriving intact.
Writes « je ne ai pas » or « il ne est pas », leaving ne whole in front of a vowel. sons.07 taught the rule and this is it failing to transfer to a new word.
Does the wrap and stops: « Je n'ai pas un frère ». The single most common A1 negation error in the language, and it survives because it is understood perfectly and nobody corrects it.

Applies the de rule where it does not reach: « Ce n'est pas de livre », « Je n'aime pas de café ». THE ERROR THIS LESSON EXISTS FOR. It is made by learners who took the earlier rule seriously and it is addressed by nothing else in the course.
Misses a negative whose ne has been dropped and registers agreement. Costs comprehension rather than accuracy, and the learner has no way of finding out, which is why it gets its own drill.
Merges the two words for no: writes « je non ai pas », or answers a question with ne. English uses one word for both jobs and nothing in the learner's first language separates them.

drills.title: Where do the two words go?
buckets: both words, either side of the verb
drills.coach: Find the verb first, then look on both sides of it. A negative has one word in front and one behind, and if you can only see one of them the sentence is not finished.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one has both words in the right places?
drills.why: Ne in front of the verb and pas behind it, with suis between them. Both halves on the same side is the English shape and it is not French.

drills.title: ne or n'?
buckets: the verb starts on a consonant
the verb starts on a vowel
drills.coach: Ignore everything except the first sound of the verb. A vowel there and ne is cut short; a consonant and it is not. Nothing else in the sentence has any say in it.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is written correctly?
opts: Je ne ai pas de frère.
Je n'e ai pas de frère.
drills.why: Ne and ai are two vowels meeting, so ne is cut short and an apostrophe marks the gap. The elision lesson put ne on its list and it behaves like every other word there.

drills.title: What happened to the little word?
drills.coach: Every one of these is avoir, so the verb tells you nothing here. Look at what was in front of the noun before the negative arrived. A un, une or des had to go, and a noun with nothing in front of it had nothing to lose.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: What does « J'ai une voiture » become?
drills.why: Une collapses to de on avoir, and something has to be left in front of the noun, so dropping it entirely is not the answer either.

drills.title: Which verb was it?
drills.coach: The same kind of little word is in every one of these before the negative arrives, so it cannot be what separates them. Find the verb. If it is a form of avoir the word collapsed, and if it is a form of être it did not.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: What does « C'est un livre » become?
drills.why: The un survives, because the verb is être. J ai un livre is the same noun with the same word in front of it and it does collapse, and the verb is the only thing separating the two.

drills.title: Is that a no?
drills.coach: Two of these are negatives with no ne anywhere in them, which is what most spoken negatives look like. Stop looking for ne and look for pas instead. Pas behind the verb is the half that never goes missing.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Somebody says « J'ai pas de chien ». What do they mean?
opts: they do not have a dog
drills.why: They do not have one. The ne is dropped constantly in speech and the pas is carrying the whole negative. Nothing about it is ambiguous to a French speaker.

drills.title: Answering, or wrapping?
drills.coach: Two of these sentences have both words in them, three apart, doing different jobs. Ask what each one is attached to: non is attached to a question somebody asked, and ne is attached to a verb.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these is French?
opts: Je non ai pas de voiture.
Non j'ai pas non de voiture.
drills.why: Non never goes inside a sentence. It answers a question and stops. Ne is the word that goes inside, and it goes in front of the verb.

sections.title: The procedure, in order
sections.body: STEP ONE, AND IT NEVER CHANGES. Find the conjugated verb and put ne in front of it and pas behind it. The verb ends up between the two words like something in brackets, and nothing else in the sentence moves. On être and avoir the verb is almost always the second word of the sentence, so this is quicker than it sounds. If the verb starts on a vowel sound, ne loses its e and becomes n apostrophe: je n ai pas, il n est pas, ce n est pas. That is the elision rule from the sons lesson and ne was already on its list alongside je, me, te, se, de, que and le. Four of the six forms of avoir start on a vowel, so with that verb the cut is the normal case rather than the exception. STEP TWO, AND IT DEPENDS ON THE VERB. Look back at what you just wrapped. If it was avoir, then a un, une, des, du or de la sitting in front of the noun turns into de, and de turns into d apostrophe in front of a vowel. If it was être, nothing happens at all and every word stays exactly where it was. And whatever the verb was, le, la and les never move: they come through a negative completely untouched and there is no case anywhere where they do not. If the noun had nothing in front of it to begin with, as in j ai faim and j ai soif, there was nothing for the negative to take away and no de appears. IN SPEECH, THE NE VERY OFTEN GOES. J ai pas de voiture, c est pas grave. This is ordinary French rather than slang and you need to recognise it, because a negative with its ne gone is one short unstressed word away from the positive. Keep writing both halves yourself.

sheets.title: What happens to the little word
contains: Why the exception is not random

sections.title: Why the verb is what decides
sections.body: Most courses hand you the collapse as a rule and the être case as an exception to memorise beside it, unconnected to anything. It is not random and it is worth thirty seconds. J ai un livre is a sentence about how many books there are, and there is one. Take that away with a negative and there is nothing left to count, which is exactly what de marks: an emptied slot where a number used to be. C est un livre is not a sentence about how many of anything. It is a sentence about what a thing IS, and saying that a thing is not a book still leaves you talking about the category of books, so nothing has been emptied and nothing changes. That is why the split falls on the verb rather than on the little word. avoir counts things and être identifies them. The practical version is one sentence and it is the only thing you actually need at the moment of speaking. If the verb was avoir, a un, une, des, du or de la becomes de. If the verb was être, leave everything exactly where it is. Two things ride along with that. le, la and les never move on either verb, which is useful backwards as well as forwards: if a de turned up in a sentence, the sentence had one of the five collapsing words in it before the negative arrived, and if nothing changed it did not. And a handful of avoir expressions have nothing in front of the noun to start with, j ai faim and j ai soif among them, so there is nothing for the negative to reduce and no de. Writing pas de faim is the rule applied one noun too far, and it is the mistake a learner makes on the day the rule finally sticks.

theWrap.title: French puts not in two places at once
theWrap.body: English has one word and it goes after the verb: I am not tired. French has two and they go round it. Ne slots in front of the verb, pas slots in behind it, and the verb sits between them like something in brackets. Je suis fatigué becomes je ne suis pas fatigué. Nothing else in the sentence moves and nothing else needs to. The two halves are not optional and they are not interchangeable: pas on its own in front of the verb is not French, and ne on its own is not either. Find the verb, put one word on each side of it, and the first half of every negative you will ever make is done.

examples.note: Ne in front of suis, pas behind it, and fatigué has not moved.
The same two words round a different person of the same verb.

theVerbDecides.term: the verb decides what happens next
theVerbDecides.title: The same words, two different answers
theVerbDecides.body: Once the wrap is done, look back at the verb you wrapped, because it decides whether anything else has to change. If it was avoir, a un, une or des in the sentence turns into de. If it was être, nothing turns into anything and every word stays exactly where it was. J'ai un livre becomes je n'ai pas de livre. C'est un livre becomes ce n'est pas un livre. Same noun, same little word in front of it, and the only thing separating the two answers is which verb was in the sentence. This is the step that is worth the half second, because both versions sound completely ordinary and nobody will stop you.

examples.note: avoir, so the un collapsed to de.
être, same noun, same un, and it survived untouched.

whatNeverMoves.term: le, la and les never move
whatNeverMoves.title: The half that has no exceptions
whatNeverMoves.body: Le, la and les come through a negative completely unchanged, whatever the verb was and whatever else is happening. J'ai le livre becomes je n'ai pas le livre. There is no version of this where they collapse and no verb that makes them. That is worth knowing for its own sake and it is also useful backwards: if a de turned up, the sentence had a un, une or des in it, and if nothing changed, it did not. This is the same asymmetry a1.11 and a1.29 pointed at, arriving here with a second reason to trust it.

examples.note: Le survived, and the verb was avoir, which collapses the other kind.
The same survival in an ordinary published sentence.

whatYouWillHear.term: the ne you will not hear
whatYouWillHear.title: Half of it disappears when people talk
whatYouWillHear.body: In ordinary spoken French the ne is very often simply not said. J'ai pas de chien, c'est pas grave. This is not slang and it is not carelessness: it is what the language does at conversational speed, and it reaches everybody. The problem it makes for you is one of listening rather than speaking. A negative with its ne gone is one short word away from the positive, and if you miss the pas you will hear agreement where refusal was meant. So learn to hear it. Do not write it, and do not say it yet: the written language keeps the ne every time, and you are still working out which half you would be dropping.

examples.note: The same sentence as the card above it, said the way it is actually said.
Published, and the only place this turns up in the A1 corpus.

nonAgainstNe.title: Two words for no, and they do different jobs
nonAgainstNe.body: Non answers a question and stands on its own. Ne goes inside a sentence and never stands on its own at all. Tu as un chien ? Non. That is the whole of non. If you then want to say what is not the case, that is a different job and it needs the wrap: non, je n'ai pas de chien. English uses the same word for both, which is why they get merged, and the merge produces sentences like je non ai pas that stop a conversation. Non answers. Ne wraps. They can sit in one sentence and often do, three words apart.

examples.note: Both words in one line: non answers, then ne wraps the verb.
The same shape again, and non is doing nothing to the sentence behind it.
