recorded.desc: EVERY POSITIVE AND ITS NEGATIVE ARE ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, ONE PACE, read straight through with no gap and no reset between them. This is the most important instruction in the lesson and it applies to every pair in it. « J'ai un frère. » then « Je n'ai pas de frère. » Recorded apart, the learner compares two performances instead of two sentences, and BOTH CHANGES ARE SUPPOSED TO BE AUDIBLE IN ONE BREATH: the two words arriving round the verb, and the un becoming de. A reader who records the negative in its own session will lean on the ne and the pas, and the learner will hear that lean as emphasis rather than as the shape of the sentence. NEVER RECORD ne OR pas IN ISOLATION. Both are unstressed particles carrying no meaning alone, and a lone clip invites the learner to pronounce them as stressed words. There is no clip anywhere in this lesson of ne, n apostrophe, pas or de on their own. If a request for one arrives, it is a mistake in the request. Also in this take, and adjacent: « Je n'ai pas de voiture. » against « J'ai pas de voiture. », for the scene. See rec-a1-18-dropped for how that pair must be read.
clipIds: Je suis fatigué. Je ne suis pas fatigué.
Il est là. Il n'est pas là.
Nous sommes prêts. Nous ne sommes pas prêts.
J'ai soif. Je n'ai pas soif.
J'ai un frère. Je n'ai pas de frère.
J'ai une voiture. Je n'ai pas de voiture.
Elle a des enfants. Elle n'a pas d'enfants.
J'ai un livre. Je n'ai pas de livre.
J'ai le livre. Je n'ai pas le livre.
C'est un livre. Ce n'est pas un livre.
C'est une erreur. Ce n'est pas une erreur.
Ce sont des amis. Ce ne sont pas des amis.
J'ai un chien. Je n'ai pas de chien.

recorded.desc: THE THREE-WAY CONTRAST, AND IT IS ONE TAKE FOR ALL SIX SENTENCES. « J'ai un livre. » « Je n'ai pas de livre. » « J'ai le livre. » « Je n'ai pas le livre. » « C'est un livre. » « Ce n'est pas un livre. » In that order, one voice, no pause longer than a breath between pairs. THE POINT IS THAT THE WORD `livre` IS ACOUSTICALLY IDENTICAL IN ALL SIX. Nothing about the noun may change across the take: no lengthening, no shift in pitch, no emphasis on the one in the être sentence. The only things moving are the little word in front of it and the verb. A reader who colours the third pair to mark it as the interesting one teaches the opposite of the lesson, which is that these three sentences are ordinary and indistinguishable except in the one place that matters. DO NOT STRESS `de` OR `un` ANYWHERE IN THIS TAKE. Both are unstressed in ordinary French and the learner has to be able to hear the difference without help, because nobody will help them in a conversation.

THE EXCEPTION, IN ITS THREE PERSONS, ONE TAKE. « Ce n'est pas un livre. » « Ce n'est pas une erreur. » « Ce ne sont pas des amis. » Then their positives immediately after, in the same order. NOTE THAT ne KEEPS ITS e IN THE THIRD ONE and must be read that way: sont starts on a consonant, so there is no elision, and a reader who contracts it out of habit contradicts the screen beside it. The liaison in « ce sont des amis » is real and must be given its full value: day-za-MEE, with the z on the front of the second syllable. Also in this take: « Ce n'est pas lundi, c'est mardi. » and « Non, ce n'est pas mon mari, c'est mon frère. », both published rows the lesson shows beside the authored ones.
clipIds: Ce ne sont pas des amis.
Ce n'est pas lundi, c'est mardi.
Non, ce n'est pas mon mari, c'est mon frère.

recorded.desc: « Je n'ai pas de chien. » AND « J'ai pas de chien. » ADJACENT, IN ONE TAKE, READ AS THE SAME SENTENCE TWICE, because that is what they are. The brief asks for this by name and the reason is precise: recorded apart, the learner hears two different sentences and the whole teaching (that one is the other with a syllable missing) is lost. BOTH MUST BE READ AT ORDINARY CONVERSATIONAL PACE. Do not slow the second one down and do not articulate the pas more clearly in it to compensate for the missing ne. The entire point of the opening scene is that the pas is easy to miss at speed, and a clip that over-articulates it contradicts the lesson's only real listening claim. Then « J'ai un chien. » in the same take, so the learner hears the positive against the ne-less negative: that pair is the one genuine ear question in the lesson and the two are one short unstressed word apart. Finally « c'est pas donné », the published row, read as the fixed expression it is.

THE FOUR ACT-ONE PAIRS, one take per pair, positive then negative with no reset. « Je suis fatigué. » / « Je ne suis pas fatigué. », « Il est là. » / « Il n'est pas là. », « Nous sommes prêts. » / « Nous ne sommes pas prêts. », « J'ai soif. » / « Je n'ai pas soif. » NEITHER ne NOR pas MAY BE STRESSED. Both are unstressed function words and the stress in every one of these sentences falls where it fell in the positive: on the last syllable of the phrase. A reader who marks the two new words is teaching a rhythm French does not have, and the learner will reproduce it. Also in this take, the two published être negatives: « Ce chien n'est pas méchant. » and « Je ne suis pas espagnol, je suis portugais. »
clipIds: Je ne suis pas espagnol, je suis portugais.

recorded.desc: THE CUT, HEARD AGAINST THE UNCUT, IN ONE TAKE. « Je ne suis pas fatigué. » then « Il n'est pas là. » then « Je n'ai pas de frère. » then « Nous ne sommes pas prêts. » The learner has to hear that the first and fourth carry a small extra syllable that the second and third do not. THE ELIDED FORM IS ONE UNBROKEN UNIT. « n'est » is neh, one syllable, and « n'ai » is nay, one syllable. Do not read them as n, pause, est. This is the same instruction the elision lesson gives for its fifteen contractions and it is the one thing a reader most often gets wrong on a particle this short. Also: « Je n'ai pas d'enfants. », where the SAME cut happens on the other side of the sentence, and it should be read in the same take so the learner hears the two as one rule.

THE THREE COLLAPSE PAIRS, one take per pair. « J'ai un frère. » / « Je n'ai pas de frère. », « J'ai une voiture. » / « Je n'ai pas de voiture. », « Elle a des enfants. » / « Elle n'a pas d'enfants. » The third pair carries two changes in the negative and both must be audible: des became de, and then de lost its e in front of the vowel, so it comes out as dahⁿ-FAHⁿ with the d attached to the front of enfants rather than standing alone. DO NOT STRESS de. It is unstressed in every one of these sentences and stressing it to mark the change would teach a rhythm that is not in the language. The change is visible on the page and audible only as a different vowel; that is correct and the recording should not improve on it. Also, and NOT beside those: « Je ne mange pas de pain. » and « Je ne mange pas de viande. », the two published rows the lesson shows as reading exposure. They use a verb the learner cannot conjugate and should be read plainly.
clipIds: Je ne mange pas de pain.
Je ne mange pas de viande.

recorded.desc: non AND moi non plus. « non » MAY be recorded alone, and it is the only word in this lesson that may: it is a complete answer on its own, which is the entire teaching on the card it appears on. IT CARRIES A NASAL VOWEL AND NO n SOUND AT ALL. The app respells it NOHⁿ and this lesson repairs the shipped respelling from NOHN to get there. Do not let any n be heard at the end of it. Then, in one take: « Non, je ne suis pas mariée, je suis fiancée. » and « Bien sûr que non, ce n'est pas grave. », both of which carry non AND ne a few words apart. The two must sound like different words doing different jobs, which they are: non is a complete answer with a small break after it, and ne is glued to the front of the verb with no break at all. Finally « Je n'aime pas le café. Moi non plus. » as one exchange, two voices if possible, because it is a reply rather than a sentence.
clipIds: Non, je ne suis pas mariée, je suis fiancée.
Bien sûr que non, ce n'est pas grave.
Je n'aime pas le café. Moi non plus.

recorded.desc: The five written traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically. TWO OF THE FIVE ARE PERFECTLY PRONOUNCEABLE AND SOUND COMPLETELY NORMAL, and that is the point: « Je n'ai pas un frère » and « Ce n'est pas de livre » are both easy to say and both wrong, and nothing in the sound of either tells you so. Do not signal them. « Je ne ai pas de temps » should be read with the two vowels genuinely colliding, slowly enough that the learner hears why the language refuses it. « Je non ai pas de voiture » should be read flatly and without hesitation, because a learner writing it does not hesitate either.

The opening scene, French bubbles only. Salomé is allocating parking spaces from a clipboard on a Monday morning, half distracted, working down a list of eleven names. HER LINE « Parfait, je vous mets la place numéro quatre. » MUST BE COMPLETELY UNSUSPICIOUS AND SLIGHTLY BRISK. She has not noticed anything because there is nothing to notice: what she heard was a perfectly ordinary sentence. Any hint of a question in her voice turns the scene into a correction and loses the whole point, which is that the failure is invisible from both sides. Her first line « Vous avez une voiture ? » should be read FAST and slightly over the top of the room tone, because the learner needs to believe that a short unstressed word could be lost in it. Her last line, where she works it out and does not mind, is where warmth is allowed to show.
clipIds: Parfait, je vous mets la place numéro quatre. Le badge arrive vendredi.
Ah, vous n'en avez pas ! Bon, je la donne à quelqu'un d'autre alors.

lessons.title: Le genre des noms
lessons.intro: Every course tells you that nouns ending in e are feminine. Measured here it is right seven times in ten, which is often enough to sound wrong and rarely enough to stop trusting. Ten endings do better, and for everything else there is one habit worth building.

say.text: Watch this happen. You know the word, you have known it for a week, and you still have to guess.

setting.place: A second-hand furniture shop

beats.text: A second-hand shop in Lyon, twenty minutes before it closes. You have found the thing you came for.

beats.speaker: The dealer
beats.en: Hello, are you looking for something?

beats.text: Armoire. You learned it on a card last Tuesday and you have not forgotten it.

beats.prompt: You have to say it now. Which one comes out?

options.en: the one your English ear reaches for
the one the word actually takes

followUp.works: Right, and you may not be able to say why. Nothing on the card you learned it from said so.
followUp.breaks: One letter, and it is the first thing a French ear uses to place you. The word was never the problem.

beats.speaker: The dealer
beats.fr: Une armoire ? Elle est au fond, à droite.
beats.en: A wardrobe? It is at the back, on the right.
beats.stage: She says it back with the article corrected, and does not mention it.

beats.heading: The card taught you half a word
beats.body: You learned the noun. The choice that has to be made before you finish saying it was never on the card.

wrong.en: what you learned

beats.coach: Same noun. The word in front of it is the part that was missing.

beats.en: Thank you. I will take the wardrobe.

beats.speaker: The dealer
beats.en: The wardrobe, very good. Eighty euros.
beats.stage: And now even she is not telling you which one it is.

beats.text: You knew the noun all week. The half you needed was on the other side of it.

closing.text: Learn the article, not the noun. Store the pair and this stops happening.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Learn the article, not the noun. By the end of this you will know which nouns tell you and which ones never will.

goals.t: Pick un or une without stopping
goals.s: Reach for the article at the same moment as the noun, rather than a beat after it.

goals.t: Read the article off the ending
goals.s: Use the ten endings that genuinely predict it, and know how often each one is right.

goals.t: Spot the nouns that tell you nothing
goals.s: Notice l apostrophe and ask which article is hiding under it, every time.
Write down une armoire rather than armoire, the way this app already does.

sections.title: One Word, Two Halves
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: Learn the article, not the noun. Here is what that means on one word.

cards.label: Half of it
cards.head: A word you can look up
cards.body: This is what a dictionary gives you and what most cards give you. It is enough to recognise the word when somebody else says it, and it is not enough to say it yourself.

cards.label: All of it
cards.head: A word you can use
cards.body: The article is not decoration on the front. It is a decision you have to make before you finish the first syllable, and there is no time to work it out once you have started.

cards.label: Already the rule here
cards.head: Look at any card in this app
cards.body: Nearly every noun in this app already carries its article. That is not a convention this lesson is proposing. It is one the words were built on, and a card that shows you the bare noun has quietly taught you to store it bare.

sections.title: The Rule You Were Given
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: Every course starts here, and this is the first time anybody has measured it for you.

cards.label: The rule
cards.head: Nouns ending in e are feminine
cards.fr: la table · la porte · la voiture
cards.body: You have almost certainly been given this one. Over the 880 nouns in this app that end in e, it is right 70% of the time.

cards.label: What that costs
cards.head: Wrong about one noun in three
cards.fr: le livre · le fromage · le frère
cards.body: Seven in ten is often enough to sound wrong in every second sentence and rarely enough that you ever stop trusting it. That combination is worse than having no rule at all.

cards.label: What to do with it
cards.head: Keep it as a lean
cards.body: If you have to guess and the noun ends in e, guess feminine. Never let it settle an article you are about to say out loud, and never let it stop you looking the word up.

sections.title: Three Endings To Ignore
sections.say: Three endings that look like rules. Tap a row and you get the same ending going both ways.

detail.title: -e
detail.body: The rule every course gives you. Right seven times in ten, across eight hundred nouns. le livre is masculine and la table is feminine, and nothing on the page separates them.

detail.title: -on
detail.body: Le poisson against la maison. Barely better than guessing, and it looks like a rule. le poisson is masculine and la maison is feminine, and nothing on the page separates them.

detail.title: -é
detail.body: Le café against la clé. A coin toss, so treat it as no information at all. le café is masculine and la clé is feminine, and nothing on the page separates them.

sections.title: Ten Endings That Work
sections.say: Ten endings, 313 nouns between them, right 97 times in a hundred. Tap a row for what breaks it.

detail.title: -ier
detail.body: Fifty-five nouns, no exception here. The feminine of a job is -ière, which is a different word. Worked example: le cahier, notebook. 55 nouns here end this way.

detail.title: -ment
detail.body: No exception either. It is -ment and not -ent: la dent ends in -ent and takes une. Worked example: l'appartement, the apartment. 20 nouns here end this way.

detail.title: -et
detail.body: Twenty-nine nouns, no exception. Two letters more and it flips: -ette takes une. Worked example: le ticket, the ticket. 29 nouns here end this way.

detail.title: -eau
detail.body: Right thirty-four times in thirty-seven. The ones it misses are l’eau and la peau. Worked example: le tableau, the board. 37 nouns here end this way.

detail.title: -age
detail.body: The weakest of the ten, and still nine in ten. La page and la cage are the ones to store. Worked example: le fromage, the cheese. 29 nouns here end this way.

detail.title: -tion
detail.body: Thirty-six nouns, no exception. It is -tion that works and not -on: le poisson takes un. Worked example: la question, the question. 36 nouns here end this way.

detail.title: -ure
detail.body: No exception. The final e does the work: le mur ends in -ur and takes un. Worked example: la voiture, the car. 24 nouns here end this way.

detail.title: -ette
detail.body: Wrong once in thirty-seven, on le squelette. Its partner -et goes the other way: le ticket. Worked example: une baguette, a baguette. 37 nouns here end this way.

detail.title: -ine
detail.body: Twenty-seven of twenty-eight. The one that breaks it is a job: un capitaine. Worked example: la cuisine, the kitchen. 28 nouns here end this way.

detail.title: -ise
detail.body: Seventeen of eighteen. The one that breaks it is a car part: le pare-brise. Worked example: la chaise, the chair. 18 nouns here end this way.

sections.title: The Five That Say Un
sections.say: One noun per screen. Read the ending before you read the word, and the article is already there.

items.note: Ends in -ier, so un. Right 100% of the time here.
Ends in -ment, so un. Right 100% of the time here.
Ends in -et, so un. Right 100% of the time here.
Ends in -eau, so un. Right 92% of the time here.
Ends in -age, so un. Right 90% of the time here.

sections.title: Which One Is It?
sections.say: A word the deck did not show you. The ending is the only thing you have.

check.q: New word: chauffage. Which article?
check.why: It ends in -age, which takes un nine times in ten. La page and la cage are the two to store.

sections.title: The Five That Say Une
sections.say: Five more, the other way. Two of these have never once been wrong in this corpus.

items.note: Ends in -tion, so une. Right 100% of the time here.
Ends in -ure, so une. Right 100% of the time here.
Ends in -ette, so une. Right 97% of the time here.
Ends in -ine, so une. Right 96% of the time here.
Ends in -ise, so une. Right 94% of the time here.

sections.title: Which One Now?
sections.say: Same again, and this one is a word you may never have met.

check.q: New word: lecture. Which article?
check.why: It ends in -ure, which has no exception in this corpus. The final e is what makes it -ure and not -ur.

sections.title: What Breaks The Rules
sections.hint: Swipe through the four cards.
sections.say: A rule without its exception is a rule you will trust in exactly the wrong place.

cards.label: -eau
cards.head: The two you will meet first
cards.body: Thirty-four of the thirty-seven -eau nouns here take un. The ones that do not are water and skin, which is to say the two you will need in your first week.

cards.label: -age
cards.head: A page and a cage
cards.body: Nine -age nouns in ten take un: le fromage, le voyage, le garage. These two go the other way and there is nothing in either word that says so.

cards.label: The rest
cards.head: Three more worth storing
cards.fr: le squelette · un capitaine · le pare-brise
cards.body: One each. Store an exception the same way you store anything else, which is with the article attached to it, because there is nothing to work out and never will be.

cards.label: Not exceptions
cards.head: Words that only look like they qualify
cards.fr: la caissière · la dent · le mur
cards.body: None of these breaks a rule. They fall just outside one and get filed under it anyway. La caissière is -ière, la dent is -ent rather than -ment, and le mur has no final e, so it is not -ure at all.

sections.title: The Article That Hides
sections.hint: Swipe through the three cards.
sections.say: Learn the article, not the noun. And here are two hundred nouns where the card refuses to tell you it.

cards.label: These survive
cards.head: Un and une never change
cards.body: In front of a vowel un stays un and une stays une. The whole distinction is intact, and you can hear it as well as see it.

cards.label: These do not
cards.head: Le and la both become l’
cards.body: One is masculine and one is feminine and they now look identical. More than two hundred nouns in this app are stored this way, so this is not a rare corner.

cards.label: The habit
cards.head: Ask, the moment you see it
cards.body: There is no rule here to learn, only something to do. When a new noun arrives wearing l apostrophe, switch it to un or une in your head before you store it. Nothing later will ask on your behalf.

sections.title: Listen: Which One?
sections.say: Four sentences. The answer is not in any of them, and that is what you are here to notice.

lines.en: The wardrobe is in the bedroom.
The staircase is on the right.
The water is cold this morning.
The computer is on the desk.

questions.q: L’armoire. Which article is under the apostrophe?
questions.why: Armoire is feminine, so it is la, shortened. Nothing you heard or saw said so, which is the whole trap.

questions.q: L’escalier. Which one, and how could you have worked it out?

sections.title: The New Flat
sections.say: Read it once for the shape. Tap any word you do not know.
sections.text: Léa has been in her new flat for three days and she is still learning where things are. Her friend Malik has come to see it. « Voici la cuisine. Le frigo est à gauche. » He points at the tall cupboard by the window. « Et ça, c’est quoi ? » She has to think for a second, because she learned the noun and not what goes in front of it. « C’est une armoire. » Malik opens it, and the bulb above them chooses that moment to go out. « L’ampoule ne marche pas. » Léa writes it on a shopping list she keeps by the door. « L’ampoule, l’huile, le savon. » He reads over her shoulder and notices what she has written. « Tu écris l’article aussi ? » She caps the pen and puts it back. « Oui. Sinon je l’oublie. »

glossary.note: Ends in -ine, which takes une twenty-seven times in twenty-eight here.
No ending rule reaches this one, so the article is stored rather than worked out.
Feminine, and nothing about the written form says so. Une ampoule is what to store.
Also feminine, also hidden. The H is silent, so l apostrophe attaches as if the word began with a vowel.
The word that turns a habit into a reason. Sinon je l’oublie: otherwise I forget it.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have measured the rule you were given, learned the ten endings that beat it, and met the nouns that hide their article entirely. What is left is the part that tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Four rounds. Miss too many in one and you get its drill before the next round starts.

rounds.label: The word and the word in front of it
rounds.say: Learn the article, not the noun. Six questions on what that actually means.

questions.q: You have learned the word « armoire ». What is still missing?
opts: the article that goes with it
questions.why: The choice between un and une is made before you finish the noun, so it has to be stored with it.

questions.q: Write "a wardrobe".
questions.why: Armoire is feminine, and no ending rule tells you that. It is a noun you store rather than derive.

questions.q: Which of these can you actually use in a sentence?
questions.why: Table is a dictionary entry. Une table is something you can say without stopping to decide.

questions.q: Someone wrote « un armoire ». Write it properly.
questions.why: One letter, and it is the fastest thing a French ear uses to place a beginner.

questions.q: You know a noun well and cannot recall its article. What went wrong?
opts: you stored the noun without the article
questions.why: The noun was never the problem. The half that decides un or une was never on the card.

questions.q: Write "the book". Livre ends in e and is masculine.
questions.why: It ends in e and takes le, which is the rule most beginners are given failing in one word.

rounds.label: The part you can work out
rounds.say: Ten endings, and the three that are not worth the trouble.

questions.q: « Nouns ending in e are feminine » is right how often here?
questions.why: Seven in ten across eight hundred nouns, which makes you wrong about one noun in three.

questions.q: Write "a question", using what the ending tells you.
questions.why: -tion has no exception in this corpus across thirty-six nouns. It takes une every time.

questions.q: You meet « le chauffage ». Which ending decided that?
questions.why: -age takes un nine times in ten. La page and la cage are the two worth storing separately.

questions.q: Write "a board", using the ending.
questions.why: -eau takes un thirty-four times in thirty-seven. The ones it misses are l’eau and la peau.

questions.q: Which of these endings tells you nothing worth having?
questions.why: -on is right six times in ten. Le poisson against la maison, with nothing on the page to separate them.

questions.q: Someone wrote « la ticket ». Write it properly.
questions.why: -et takes un across all twenty-nine of them here. Two letters more and -ette flips it to une.

rounds.label: When the article is gone
rounds.say: Nothing on screen will help you here. That is the mission, restated as questions.

questions.q: Listen. Which article is under the apostrophe?
questions.why: Armoire is feminine, so the l’ you heard is la. Nothing in the sound says which one it was.

questions.q: Listen. Which article, and the ending will tell you?
questions.why: Escalier ends in -ier, which takes un across all fifty-five of them here, so the article is le.

questions.q: A new noun is written « l’usine ». What do you know about its gender?
questions.why: Le and la both shrink to l apostrophe before a vowel, so the written form carries nothing.

questions.q: Which of these hides its gender from you?
questions.why: Only l’ hides it. Un and une do not elide, so they keep telling you which one it is.

questions.q: You want one wardrobe rather than the wardrobe. Write it.
questions.why: Un and une never elide, so switching to them is how you check what l’ was covering.

questions.q: Listen. Which article does this one take?
questions.why: Eau is feminine, which -eau does not predict. It is one of the three that break that rule.

rounds.label: Out loud, in a shop
rounds.say: Where all of this actually happens, which is with somebody waiting for you to finish.

questions.q: Say it out loud: one baguette.
questions.why: The article carries the amount and the gender at once. Say the pair, never the noun alone.

questions.q: You are buying cheese. Write "the cheese".
questions.why: -age takes un, so fromage takes le. La page is the exception rather than the rule.

questions.q: A shopkeeper says « la livre ». What did they mean?
questions.why: Le livre is a book and la livre is a pound. Only the article separates the two words.

questions.q: Write "the page", which is the exception to -age.
questions.why: Nine -age nouns in ten take un. La page and la cage are the two to store separately.

questions.q: Why is « des lunettes » no use for practising this?
opts: it is not a real word
des is the same for both genders
questions.why: Les and des say nothing about gender, so a plural-only noun never shows you the choice.

questions.q: The one thing worth storing with every new noun:
opts: the article in front of it
questions.why: Learn the article, not the noun. It is what the next three units all assume you have already done.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Six things you did not have this morning, and one that pays off in the next lesson.
sections.body: You can work out the article for about one noun in five, and more usefully you know which four in five you cannot, so you stop trying and start storing. That is the difference between a learner who has memorised a table and one who can order a coffee without a pause in the middle of it.
points: Learn the article, not the noun. A noun without one is a word you can look up and not one you can say.
Ten endings do real work: -ier, -ment, -et, -eau, -age, -tion, -ure, -ette, -ine, -ise.
The famous rule about a final e is right about seven times in ten. Keep it as a lean, never as a decision.
The exceptions are short and worth storing: l’eau, la peau, la page, la cage, le squelette, le pare-brise.
L apostrophe hides le and la completely. Switch to un or une in your head, because nothing else will ask.
Le livre is a book and la livre is a pound. The article is not decoration.
The article you store here is the same choice a1.04 calls le or la, so the next lesson arrives half done.

sections.title: What to do with this
sections.body: Do not memorise the second table. It is here because a sheet should answer a question you actually have, which is usually about one specific word you are holding, and the fourteen endings on it cover between six and forty-one nouns each. The ten in the first table are the ones worth carrying in your head, and they cover about one gendered noun in five. For the other four in five there is nothing to work out, so the effort belongs on storing the article with the word rather than on a longer table. The floor for anything written down here is ninety percent: two endings that just miss it, -elle and -ie, are deliberately absent rather than shown with a warning, because a rule you half trust is what stops you looking a word up.

sheets.title: The nouns that hide their article

rows.v: un escalier, the staircase
un ordinateur, the computer
un appartement, the apartment
un enfant, the child
un avion, the plane
un oignon, the onion
une armoire, the wardrobe
une eau, the water
une école, the school
une oreille, the ear
une épaule, the shoulder
une huile, the oil

sections.title: How to check a new one
sections.body: There are more than two hundred of these in this app and no list will cover the ones you meet outside it, so the sheet is a worked set rather than a reference. The method is the useful part. Un and une do not elide in front of a vowel, so say the noun to yourself with each of them and one will sound wrong. If neither does, the word is genuinely new and the article has to be looked up, which takes five seconds now and saves the guess you would otherwise make at a counter. The endings help here more than anywhere else, because a noun beginning with a vowel is exactly the case where the front of the word tells you nothing and the back of it may still tell you everything.

pair.title: Why a noun on its own is only half a word
pair.body: A French noun is stored with the word in front of it. Armoire is something you can look up. Une armoire is something you can use, because the choice between un and une is made before you have finished the first syllable and there is no time to work it out mid-sentence. This is not a convention this lesson invented: nearly every noun in this app already carries its article, and a card that shows you the bare noun has quietly taught you to store it bare.

examples.note: The wardrobe, stored the way you will need it.
Water, where the article has been deleted and you still have to know it.

endings.title: The part you can work out
endings.body: Ten endings in French tell you the article, and across the nouns they cover they are right about ninety-seven times in a hundred. Five point to un: -ier, -ment, -et, -eau, -age. Five point to une: -tion, -ure, -ette, -ine, -ise. That is roughly one noun in six. It is a much smaller rule than most courses imply and it is a much better one, because the endings people usually teach are close to a coin toss.

examples.note: A board, and the ending says un before you know the word.
A question, where -tion has never once been wrong here.

finalE.title: The rule you were given, measured
finalE.body: Nouns ending in e are feminine is the first rule most beginners are handed, and over the eight hundred and seventy-one such nouns in this app it is right seven times in ten. Applied confidently it makes you wrong about one noun in three, which is often enough to sound wrong in every second sentence and rarely enough that you never stop trusting it. Le livre, le fromage, le téléphone and le frère all end in e. Keep the rule as a lean, never as a decision.

examples.note: Ends in e, takes le. So does its opposite number, la table.
Ends in e, takes la. Nothing on either card tells you which.

hidden.title: The two hundred nouns that tell you nothing
hidden.body: In front of a vowel, un stays un and une stays une, but le and la both shrink to l apostrophe. More than two hundred nouns in this app show up that way, and the card you learn them from carries no information about gender at all. L’armoire is feminine, l’escalier is masculine, and nothing you can see says so. The fix is a habit rather than a rule: the moment you meet l apostrophe, ask which one it really is, because nothing later will ask for you.

examples.note: Feminine, and the card does not say so.
Masculine, and the card does not say that either.

storage.term: work it out or store it
storage.title: Which of the two you are doing
storage.body: About one noun in six gives its article away through its ending. The rest do not, and no amount of looking at them will change that, so the strategy that survives contact with real French is: work it out where the ending lets you, and store the article with the word everywhere else. That is uncomfortable to be told and it is what actually works. The alternative is a learner who has memorised a table and still stops mid-sentence, which is the failure this lesson exists to stop.

examples.note: Worked out: -age points at un.
Stored: no ending in this lesson reaches it, and none ever will.

agreement.title: Why the article is worth the effort now
agreement.body: Gender is not a label on a noun, it is a choice that spreads. The article you pick is the same choice that decides le or la in the next lesson, du or de la after that, and the ending of every adjective you ever attach to the noun. Get the article stored once and all of those come free. Skip it and each one becomes its own guess, taken under pressure, in the middle of a sentence you are already halfway through.

examples.note: Une baguette now, la baguette next, de la baguette after that.
One decision, reused every time the word comes back.

recorded.desc: The un/une contrasts. Each pair in ONE TAKE, same voice, same speed, no pause longer than a beat: un armoire then une armoire, un table then une table, un escalier then une escalier. Across two takes the learner hears the difference between the recordings rather than between the articles. Do NOT over-articulate un: its vowel is nasal and no N is sounded, and a careful reading that lets the N through removes the only thing separating it from une.

The ten hero nouns, each said alone with a clear pause after it, ONE take straight through so the pace is even. Do not splice. Also supplies the preview table rows and the two word decks: le cahier, l’appartement, le ticket, le tableau, le fromage, la question, la voiture, une baguette, la cuisine, la chaise. « le ticket » and « une baguette » must come from the same take: they are the -et and -ette pair and the mission turns on hearing them side by side.

The elided nouns and the four listening lines. Read each noun naturally, WITHOUT separating the article from the word: the elision is meant to sound like one word, because that is why it hides what it hides. The listening lines are read straight through as whole sentences and again at 0.65 from the same take.

The second-hand shop scene. A neutral adult female voice for the dealer, unhurried and a little brisk, somebody closing up. The line « Une armoire ? Elle est au fond, à droite. » is the pivot: she is repeating the learner back with the article corrected, and it must sound like ordinary speech rather than a correction, because the whole point is that nobody tells you.

recorded.desc: The four dictation sentences at natural pace, and again at 0.65 from the same take so the slow version is a slowing rather than a re-reading. Full stops audible; no exaggerated word separation, which would give the tile boundaries away. « L’ordinateur est sur le bureau. » must keep its elision joined.
clipIds: Vous ouvrez vos livres à la page dix.
Elle va lever la main pendant le cours.
Le professeur pose une question facile.

segments.text: I am Camille. Today is gender, and specifically the part of it nobody measures for you.
You already know more French nouns than you can use, and the reason is the small word in front of each one.
Une armoire.
A wardrobe. You may know armoire. The une is the half that goes missing.
Learn the article, not the noun. That is the whole lesson, and here is why it is not obvious.
Le livre.
Book. It ends in e, and every course you have met says nouns ending in e are feminine. This one is not, and neither is about a third of them.
La table.
Table, feminine, same ending. Nothing on the page separates those two, so the rule is a lean and not a decision.
Now the endings that do work. Five of them point at un.
Le cahier. L’appartement. Le ticket. Le tableau. Le fromage.
Notebook, apartment, ticket, board, cheese. The endings are -ier, -ment, -et, -eau and -age.
And five point at une.
La question. La voiture. Une baguette. La cuisine. La chaise.
Question, car, baguette, kitchen, chair. The endings are -tion, -ure, -ette, -ine and -ise.
Every rule has something that breaks it, and the ones that break these are words you meet immediately.
L’eau. La peau.
Water and skin. Both feminine, and -eau points at masculine thirty-four times in thirty-seven. These are two of the three.
La page.
Page, feminine, against -age. Store an exception the same way you store anything else, which is with the article on it.
Your turn, with nothing in front of you. Ask for one baguette.
Now the cheese, and let the ending decide it for you.
And the hard one. Water, where the ending points the wrong way.
One question. I will say a noun and you tell me which article is hiding in it.
L’armoire.
La. Armoire is feminine, and nothing you heard said so, because le and la both shrink to l before a vowel.
Three things to keep. Learn the article, not the noun.
Ten endings do real work and cover about one noun in five. The famous one about a final e is right seven times in ten.
And when a noun turns up wearing l apostrophe, switch it to un or une in your head, because nothing else will ask.
À bientôt.

lessons.title: Pays & nationalités
lessons.intro: Six small words for what English does with two, and the choice between them was made the day you learned the country. This is how to store a country the way it is used, say where you are going and where you are from, and say what somebody is with nothing in front of it.

beats.speaker: The next morning, same machine
beats.stage: One letter different, and it is the only letter in the sentence that was ever carrying anything.

beats.speaker: Théo
beats.fr: Ah, de France ! Et vous êtes ici depuis longtemps ?
beats.en: Ah, from France! And have you been here long?
beats.stage: He stays in French this time, and neither of you mentions yesterday.

beats.text: One letter, and it was not a letter you could work out in the moment. The next half hour is about where it comes from.

closing.text: Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows. That is the next half hour.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the first is a habit rather than a list.

goals.t: Store a country the way it is used
goals.s: With its article, every time, because that one fact settles everything you will do with it afterwards.
en, au and aux, chosen by the article and by nothing else.
de, du and des, chosen by the same fact all over again. One decision, two systems.
A nationality with nothing in front of it, agreeing the way colours agree, and one capital letter that is not where English puts it.

sections.title: Half A Word Is Not A Word
sections.hint: Five cards before any country list.
sections.say: Five cards before any table, because this habit is what the tables are for.

cards.label: what you already do
cards.head: You have been asked for this before
cards.body: The noun gender lesson asked you to learn the article rather than the noun, and said the payoff would come later. This is later. Countries are where the habit pays for itself inside one sentence.

cards.label: the article is not optional
cards.head: A country is almost never bare
cards.fr: La France est un pays d'Europe.
cards.sub: France is a country in Europe.
cards.body: French says la France where English says France, and the la is not there for emphasis. It is part of how the word is stored and part of how it is used, and it turns up in ordinary sentences nobody wrote to teach you anything.

cards.label: the same, the other kind
cards.head: And le for the others
cards.fr: Le Canada est un grand pays. Les États-Unis sont grands.
cards.sub: Canada is a big country. · The United States are big.
cards.body: Le Canada, and les États-Unis with a plural article because the name is plural. Three kinds of country in three ordinary sentences, and the only thing separating them is the little word in front.

cards.label: the hint
cards.head: Most la countries end in an e
cards.fr: la France · la Belgique · l'Italie · l'Espagne
cards.sub: and so do Allemagne, Chine, Russie, Suisse
cards.body: A good hint, and not a rule. The noun gender lesson measured that ending across the whole app and found it right about seven times in ten. On countries it does better, which is exactly what makes people stop checking.

cards.label: why it matters this much
cards.head: One fact, four words
cards.fr: en France · de France · au Canada · du Canada
cards.body: Going to a country and coming from one are two questions with one answer between them, and the answer is the article. Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows.

sections.title: Which Little Word?
sections.say: Three groups of countries and one question about each. Nothing here is about where they are.

check.q: Four of those five end in an e. Which one does not?
check.why: la France ends in an e as well, so all five do. That is what makes the ending such a good hint here and such a bad rule: it works often enough that you stop checking, and then le Mexique arrives.

check.q: One of those five ends in an e and still takes le. Which one?
check.why: le Mexique. It ends in an e, it takes le, and it is the country most likely to catch you out because the hint is so reliable everywhere else. Le Cambodge and le Zimbabwe do the same thing.

groups.label: the les kind, and the one with a vowel

check.q: les États-Unis takes a plural article. What decides that?
check.why: The name is plural. États-Unis is literally united states, more than one of them, so it takes les the way any plural noun does. That plural follows the country everywhere it goes and gives it its own row in everything this lesson does next.

check.q: You meet a new country word for the first time. What should you write down?
opts: The country and where it is
The country and how to say it
check.why: Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows. Everything this lesson does after this point is decided by that one word, and you cannot work it out later from the country itself. Store it now or guess forever.

sections.title: Two Words, Not One
sections.say: The place on the left and what you are on the right. Two separate words. Tap any cell to hear it.

detail.title: France and French
detail.body: la France [LAH FRAHⁿSS] is the place. français [frahⁿ-SEH] is what a person is. They are stored separately and only one of them carries an article: a nationality never takes one at all.

detail.title: Canada and Canadian
detail.body: le Canada [LUH kah-nah-DAH] is the place. canadien [kah-nah-DYAⁿ] is what a person is. They are stored separately and only one of them carries an article: a nationality never takes one at all.

detail.title: Spain and Spanish
detail.body: l'Espagne [lehs-PAHNY] is the place. espagnol [ehs-pah-NYOL] is what a person is. They are stored separately and only one of them carries an article: a nationality never takes one at all.

detail.title: Japan and Japanese
detail.body: le Japon [LUH zhah-POHⁿ] is the place. japonais [zhah-po-NEH] is what a person is. They are stored separately and only one of them carries an article: a nationality never takes one at all.

sections.title: The Hint And The One That Breaks It
sections.frSub: Le e final n'est qu'un indice
sections.hint: Four cards on an ending you are about to over-trust.
sections.say: A hint worth having, and the country that will make you regret trusting it.

cards.label: the hint working
cards.head: e on the end, la in front
cards.body: Three la countries and all three end in an e. The l apostrophe hides which article it was, which is the same thing the noun gender lesson warned you about, and it is worth saying out loud: those are la words wearing a shortened article.

cards.label: the hint working the other way
cards.head: No e, le in front
cards.fr: le Canada · le Japon · le Sénégal · le Portugal
cards.body: Four le countries and not an e among them. So far the ending has told you the truth eight times out of eight, which is exactly how a hint turns into a habit you stop questioning.

cards.label: the one that breaks it
cards.head: le Mexique
cards.body: Ends in an e and takes le. So do le Cambodge and le Zimbabwe. There are only a few of them and this is the one you will meet, which is why it is on a card of its own rather than in a footnote.

cards.label: what to do about it
cards.head: Guess with the ending, store the article
cards.body: The ending is for the moment somebody says a country you have never met and you have to answer anyway. It is not a substitute for knowing. Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows.

sections.title: Twelve Countries, Banked
sections.say: Three decks. Every card carries the article, because a card without it is half a card.

sections.title: Now Without The Deck
sections.say: Four questions, nothing to look at. This is the one that tells you whether the articles landed.

check.q: Which article goes with Japon?
check.why: le Japon. No e on the end, and the article is the fact everything else in this lesson is about to ask you for.

check.q: You meet la Chine for the first time. Which kind is it?
check.why: the la kind, and the article told you rather than the country. Chine ends in an e as well, so the hint and the article agree here, which is the ordinary case.

groups.label: The one that breaks the hint

check.q: Mexique ends in an e. Which article does it take?
check.why: le Mexique. The ending was wrong here and the article was not, which is the whole argument for storing the article rather than the ending.

check.q: la France is the country. What is the word for a person from there?
check.why: français, with no article at all. A nationality is a different word from the country and it never carries le or la in front of it. The country keeps its article and the nationality never had one.

sections.title: Ask The Article Before The Preposition
sections.hint: Five cards, and one of them is about a verb you are not learning yet.
sections.say: Three words for one English one, and the country picks between them before you open your mouth.

cards.label: the la kind
cards.head: en
cards.sub: [ahⁿ FRAHⁿSS] · I am going to France.
cards.body: la France, so en France. There is no la left in the sentence: en has taken its place, exactly as a possessive takes the place of le. You never say en la France.

cards.label: the le kind
cards.head: au
cards.sub: [oh kah-nah-DAH] · I am going to Canada.
cards.body: le Canada, so au Canada. That au is the le folded into the preposition, which is the same fold you met in the indefinite articles lesson: à plus le is au and it is never written any other way.

cards.label: the les kind
cards.head: aux
cards.sub: [oh-zay-tah-zü-NEE] · I am going to the United States.
cards.body: les États-Unis, so aux États-Unis. The x wakes up as a z in front of the vowel, so this comes out as one long word rather than two. It is worth learning as a single sound.

cards.label: in the wild
cards.head: Nobody arranged these
cards.fr: J'habite au Canada depuis deux ans. Mon frère travaille aux États-Unis.
cards.sub: I have been living in Canada for two years. · My brother works in the United States.
cards.body: Two published sentences with no interest in teaching you a preposition, both doing exactly what the cards above said. The second one is from the liaison lesson, where aux États-Unis is already an example of something else.

cards.label: the verb
cards.head: Je vais is a phrase for now
cards.body: The verb behind this is aller, and you meet it properly a whole band from here. Until then take je vais as one piece, the way you took il fait in the weather lesson. You need one person of it and it is your own.

sections.title: Three Rows, One Column
sections.say: One column for now. The second one arrives in a few minutes and it is the same decision again.

detail.title: la France, so en
detail.body: Je vais en France. [ahⁿ FRAHⁿSS] The article on la France chose that first word and nothing else in the sentence had any say in it. Change the country and only that word moves.

detail.title: le Canada, so au
detail.body: Je vais au Canada. [oh kah-nah-DAH] The article on le Canada chose that first word and nothing else in the sentence had any say in it. Change the country and only that word moves.

detail.title: les États-Unis, so aux
detail.body: Je vais aux États-Unis. [oh-zay-tah-zü-NEE] The article on les États-Unis chose that first word and nothing else in the sentence had any say in it. Change the country and only that word moves.

sections.title: The Sixth Time You Have Met This
sections.hint: Four cards, and the idea in them is not new.
sections.say: One old idea, one new place it turns up. You have watched French dodge this collision five times already.

cards.label: the problem
cards.head: au Iran
cards.sub: not French, and it never has been
cards.body: Say those two at ordinary speed and the o runs straight into the i. French has a standing objection to two vowel sounds meeting with nothing between them, and you have watched it deal with that objection five times now.

cards.label: the five you have seen
cards.head: Always the same objection
cards.fr: l'amie · mon amie · n'ai · est-ce qu'il · combien d'ans
cards.sub: the definite articles, the possessives, the negative, the question, the counting
cards.body: Every one of those was two vowels being kept apart, and each lesson solved it slightly differently: some cut the little word short, one swapped it for another shape. Six rules, one idea behind them.

cards.label: the repair here
cards.head: The le kind borrows en
cards.body: l'Iran is the le kind and ought to take au. It takes en instead, purely for the sound. The n of en arrives on the front of Iran and is fully pronounced, so this is three syllables rather than a pause.

cards.label: how far it reaches
cards.head: Only the going-to column
cards.body: Coming the other way the exception is over. This is the ordinary de of a le country, cut short in front of a vowel like every other de. So one country and one column, not one country and a whole new set of rules.

sections.title: Where Are You Going?
sections.say: Four decisions and each one is answered by the article rather than by the country.

check.q: You are going to Italy, and it is l'Italie. Which word?
check.why: en Italie. The l apostrophe is hiding a la, so this is the la kind and takes en. If you cannot tell which article an l apostrophe country carries, that is the thing to go and look up rather than something to reason out.

check.q: You are going to Portugal, and it is le Portugal. Which word?
check.why: au Portugal. The le has folded into the preposition and disappeared, which is why there is no le anywhere in the finished sentence. Every le country in this lesson does the same.

items.en: I am going to the United States.
My brother works in the United States.

check.q: aux États-Unis, said out loud. How many words does it sound like?
check.why: One long word. The x of aux wakes up as a z and attaches to the front of États, so the whole thing runs together. This is why a recording of aux on its own would teach you nothing at all.

check.q: l'Iran is the le kind. Why is it en Iran rather than au Iran?
opts: Iran is not really a country
Because it starts with a vowel
check.why: Because it starts with a vowel. Au Iran would put two vowel sounds against each other, so the going-to column borrows en. Nothing about the country changed kind: it is still the le kind and it still takes du coming back.

sections.title: The Same Decision, Again
sections.hint: Five cards, and you have already done the hard part of all of them.
sections.say: Three more words, chosen by the fact you already looked up. Nothing new is being asked of you here.

cards.label: the la kind
cards.head: de
cards.body: la France, so de France, and the la disappears exactly as it did with en. This is the sentence from the opening scene and the whole thing turned on one letter of it.

cards.label: the le kind
cards.head: du
cards.body: le Canada, so du Canada. Du is de plus le folded together, the same fold that gave you au, and you met it in the partitive lesson as well. One fold, three places.

cards.label: the les kind
cards.head: des
cards.sub: [day-zay-tah-zü-NEE] · I come from the United States.
cards.body: les États-Unis, so des États-Unis, and the s wakes up as a z for the same reason the x did. Aux and des behave identically here, which is the tidiest thing in the lesson.

cards.label: cut short before a vowel
cards.head: d'Espagne, d'Italie
cards.fr: Je viens d'Espagne. Elle vient d'Italie.
cards.sub: I come from Spain. · She comes from Italy.
cards.body: Both of those are la countries and both take de. In front of a vowel the de is cut short to d apostrophe, which is the ordinary elision you have had since the silent letters lesson rather than anything new here.

cards.label: in the wild
cards.head: The corpus does it without being asked
cards.fr: Je viens du Sénégal. Il vient du Japon. Il vient des États-Unis.
cards.sub: I come from Senegal. · He comes from Japan. · He comes from the United States.
cards.body: du, du and des, on three countries, in three published sentences. The last two use a form of the verb you are not learning here: read them and leave them, because the only thing you need from them is the small word in the middle.

sections.title: Both Columns, One Fact
sections.say: Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows. Read across a row. Both cells were chosen by the same article. Tap any cell to hear it.

detail.title: la France: en and de
detail.body: Je vais en France. Je viens de France. [ahⁿ FRAHⁿSS] [duh FRAHⁿSS] Two sentences, one country, and the same article picked both small words. Read the row above and the row below: only the country moved.
detail.say: Je vais en France. Je viens de France.

detail.title: le Canada: au and du
detail.body: Je vais au Canada. Je viens du Canada. [oh kah-nah-DAH] [dü kah-nah-DAH] Two sentences, one country, and the same article picked both small words. Read the row above and the row below: only the country moved.
detail.say: Je vais au Canada. Je viens du Canada.

detail.title: les États-Unis: aux and des
detail.body: Je vais aux États-Unis. Je viens des États-Unis. [oh-zay-tah-zü-NEE] [day-zay-tah-zü-NEE] Two sentences, one country, and the same article picked both small words. Read the row above and the row below: only the country moved.
detail.say: Je vais aux États-Unis. Je viens des États-Unis.

sections.title: Where Are You From?
sections.say: Four more, and the article you look at is the same one you looked at going the other way.

check.q: You are from Belgium, and it is la Belgique. Which word?
check.why: de Belgique, with nothing between de and the country. This is the sentence the opening scene turned on, on a different country: du Belgique would be understood and it is not something anybody says.

check.q: You are from Mexico, and it is le Mexique. Which word?
check.why: du Mexique. The e on the end of Mexique has nothing to do with it: the article said le, so the answer is du, and this country is the one that will keep testing whether you trusted the ending or the article.

items.en: I come from the United States.
He comes from the United States.

check.q: The country is les États-Unis. Going there was aux États-Unis, so coming from there is which word?
check.why: des États-Unis. Aux and des are the same fold made twice, on à plus les and on de plus les. The s of des wakes up as a z exactly as the x of aux did, so the two are mirror images.

check.q: You looked up an article once. How many of the six small words does it choose for you?
check.why: Two: one for going and one for coming. Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows. That is why the article is worth the two seconds it takes to store, and why working the ending out later never gets you there.

sections.title: Five Traps
sections.say: Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows. Five things an English speaker says in their first month, one per screen.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je viens du France. »
errors.why: The one from the opening scene, and the one that costs the most. Du is right for most countries, which is exactly why it comes out here: the la countries are the smaller group and France is the one you will say most often.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je vais en Canada. »
errors.why: En is the first of the three you meet and it becomes the default. Le Canada is the le kind, so it takes au. This is understood immediately and simply marks you as new: a smaller cost than the first trap, and a commoner mistake.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je vais au Iran. »
errors.why: Iran is the le kind, so this looks right. Two vowel sounds hard against each other is the one thing French will not do, so the going-to column borrows en. Coming back, d apostrophe Iran is the right one.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je vais en la France. »
errors.why: The article has already been used up. En, au, aux, de, du and des have all swallowed the article, which is why none of them is ever followed by one. There is no en la, no au le and no des les.

errors.wrong: Storing a country as France, Canada, Japon.
errors.right: Storing it as la France, le Canada, le Japon.
errors.why: This is the trap behind the other four and it happens weeks before any of them. A country stored without its article cannot tell you anything later, and there is nothing in the word itself to work it out from when you need it.

sections.title: You Already Have This One
sections.hint: Five cards, and four of them are revision.
sections.say: The colours lesson taught how these change and the être lesson taught what goes in front of them. Nothing here is new except one letter.

cards.label: what you already have
cards.head: A nationality behaves like a colour
cards.fr: Il est français. Elle est française.
cards.body: The colours lesson gave you the shape: an e arrives for a woman, and sometimes that e wakes up a letter that had been silent. This is exactly that. The s on the end of français is silent until the e turns up behind it.

cards.label: the other shape
cards.head: And the nasal that collapses
cards.fr: Il est canadien. Elle est canadienne.
cards.body: The colours lesson had this one too, on brun and brune. The nasal vowel at the end of canadien collapses into a plain one with a real n behind it. Two shapes, both of them already met, arriving on a new set of words.

cards.label: in the wild
cards.head: Nobody arranged this one
cards.fr: Elle est canadienne, mais elle habite en France.
cards.sub: She is Canadian, but she lives in France.
cards.body: A published sentence with no interest in teaching you anything, carrying the feminine ending and a country with its own small word in front of it. She is one thing and lives somewhere else, and it needs both halves of this lesson to read.

cards.label: what goes in front
cards.head: Nothing at all
cards.fr: Il est français. Je suis français.
cards.sub: He is French. · I am French. (said by a man)
cards.body: The être lesson said this about jobs and nationalities together, and it holds without exception. English needs an article there and French does not, so a nationality after être stands on its own.

cards.label: the ones that never change
cards.head: belge, for anybody
cards.body: It already ends in an e, so there is nothing for another e to do. Russe, suisse and tchèque are the same. A handful of nationalities are one word for everybody, and they are the ones that already look feminine.

sections.title: The One Pair Your Ear Can Do
sections.say: Three pairs, and every one of them is about the ending rather than about the small word in front.

lines.en: the s wakes up when the e arrives behind it
the nasal collapses and a real n appears
these two share no sound at all, which is why nothing here tests them by ear

questions.q: français and française. What changes?
opts: an s appears at the end
questions.why: An s appears at the end. It was written in français all along and silent; the e behind it wakes it up. This is the same thing the colours lesson called out on gris and grise, so your ear has met it before.

questions.q: canadien and canadienne. What changes?
opts: the nasal at the end turns into a plain vowel with an n after it
the stress moves to the front
questions.why: The nasal collapses. Canadien ends in a sound made through the nose with no n behind it; canadienne has a plain vowel and then a real n. Brun and brune do exactly the same thing and you met them in the colours lesson.

questions.q: en France and au Canada. Is there any point listening carefully to tell en from au?
opts: Yes, if the speaker is careful
No. They share no sound at all
questions.why: No. En and au have nothing in common to confuse, so hearing them apart is not a skill worth building. The decision they come from is the hard part, and that happens before you speak rather than while you listen.

sections.title: One Capital Letter
sections.say: Left is a description and right is a name for a person. Out loud they are identical, so this one is read rather than heard.

rows.say: Il est français. C'est un Français.

detail.title: Small f, and capital F
detail.body: [ee-leh frahⁿ-SEH] [seh-tuhⁿ frahⁿ-SEH] The être lesson already told you this: English capitalises both and French keeps the capital for the person. The left one describes and takes nothing in front. The right one names, so it takes un and a capital.
detail.say: Il est français. C'est un Français.

rows.say: Il est canadien. Je suis canadien.

detail.title: And with a country you have just met
detail.body: Il est canadien. He is Canadian. Je suis canadien. I am Canadian. Both of these describe rather than name, so both take a small letter and nothing in front. That is the ordinary case and the one you will use most.
detail.say: Il est canadien. Je suis canadien.

sections.title: The Form At The Desk
sections.say: Four lines off a form, and every one of them turns on a word two letters long.
sections.text: Somebody at a residence office has a form in front of them with four handwritten answers on it, and between them they use most of what this lesson has covered. « Je viens de France. » That is the first line, and the two letters in the middle of it were decided by an article that is nowhere on the page. Underneath it, in a different hand, somebody has written where they are going next. « Je vais au Canada. » A different country, a different small word, and the same single question answered behind both of them. The third line is the one the clerk had to read twice, because the country in it starts with a vowel and does not do what the others do. « Je vais en Iran. » The last line is not about a place at all, and it is the only one on the form with nothing in front of the word that matters. « Il est français. »

glossary.note: la France is the la kind, so de with nothing after it. Du France is the sentence the opening scene turned on.
le Canada is the le kind, so au, which is à and le folded into one word.
The le kind, taking en because au Iran would put two vowel sounds against each other.
No article in front of a nationality after être, and a small f because this describes rather than names.

questions.q: The first line says de and the second says au. What decided between them?
questions.a: The article each country carries. La France gives de and le Canada gives du or au depending on which direction you are going. Nothing about the countries themselves came into it, and nothing about the person filling in the form did either.

questions.q: Why did the clerk have to read the third line twice?
questions.a: Because Iran is the le kind and would normally take au, and it takes en instead. The reason is only about sound: au Iran puts two vowel sounds hard against each other and French avoids that everywhere. Coming from Iran, it goes back to behaving like every other le country.

questions.q: The last line has no article in it anywhere. Is something missing?
questions.a: No. A nationality after être stands on its own, which the être lesson already covered along with jobs. English needs an article there and French does not. If the word were naming a person rather than describing one, it would take un and a capital letter, and that would be a different sentence.

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Every country front names the article you are being asked for, because a country without one is half a card.

cards.front: the United States, with its article
I am going to the United States.
I come from the United States.

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Five lines. On four of them the word you write is one you have to work out rather than hear.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: Twelve lines, and not one of them is a small word on its own. These words only exist attached to a country.

sections.title: The Same Coffee Machine
sections.say: One exchange and you hold up your half. Every turn is a country with the right small word in front of it.
sections.setting: The same office kitchen, a fortnight later. Théo asks first this time, and stays in French.

turns.ai: Vous venez d'ou, alors ?
turns.en: So where are you from?
turns.user: Je viens de France.
turns.userEn: I come from France.

turns.ai: Ah, et votre collegue ? Il est d'ou ?
turns.en: Ah, and your colleague? Where is he from?
turns.user: Il est canadien.
turns.userEn: He is Canadian.

turns.ai: Et vous partez quelque part cet ete ?
turns.en: And are you going anywhere this summer?
turns.user: Je vais au Mexique.
turns.userEn: I am going to Mexico.

alts.fr: Je vais au Mexique en juillet.
alts.en: I am going to Mexico in July.

turns.ai: Super. Et l'annee prochaine ?
turns.en: Great. And next year?
turns.user: Je vais aux Etats-Unis.
turns.userEn: I am going to the United States.

turns.ai: Vous voyagez beaucoup ! Et votre famille, elle est ou ?
turns.en: You travel a lot! And your family, where are they?
turns.user: Ils sont en Belgique.
turns.userEn: They are in Belgium.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.back: Je vais en France. [ahⁿ FRAHⁿSS] la France, so en.
Je viens de France. [duh FRAHⁿSS] The same article, the other column.
Je vais au Canada. [oh kah-nah-DAH] le Canada, so au.
Je viens du Canada. [dü kah-nah-DAH] du, which is de and le folded together.

cards.front: You are going to the United States.
cards.back: Je vais aux États-Unis. [oh-zay-tah-zü-NEE] A plural name, so aux.

cards.front: You are coming from the United States.
cards.back: Je viens des États-Unis. [day-zay-tah-zü-NEE] des, and the s wakes up as a z.
le Mexique [LUH mehk-SEEK] It ends in an e and takes le anyway.

cards.front: You are going to Iran, and Iran is the le kind.
cards.back: Je vais en Iran. [ahⁿ-nee-RAHⁿ] en, because au Iran would put two vowels together.
Je viens d'Iran. [dee-RAHⁿ] The exception does not reach this column.

cards.front: A man from France, described rather than named.
cards.back: Il est français. Small f, nothing in front.

cards.front: The same man, named rather than described.
cards.back: C'est un Français. Capital F, and un in front of it.
Elle est française. The e wakes the s up.
Elle est canadienne. The nasal collapses and a real n appears.

cards.front: What should you store when you meet a new country?
cards.back: Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows.

cards.front: How many small words does one article choose for you?
cards.back: Two. One for going and one for coming, and you look the article up once.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched a conversation move quietly into English over one letter, and nothing that was said in it was hard. Since then you have stored a set of countries the way they are actually used, taken one fact from each of them and watched it answer two separate questions, met the one country that breaks the ending hint and the one that borrows a word from the other column, and picked up a capital letter that sits somewhere English does not put it. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The article
rounds.say: The fact everything else is built on.

questions.q: Which of these is the way to store a country?
questions.why: la France. Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows. The article is not decoration and it is not something you can work out from the word later, which is the whole reason it goes in with the word rather than beside it.

questions.q: Write the country word for Canada, with its article.
questions.why: le Canada. Written as a whole rather than as a bare article, because a two-letter answer typed on its own is a coin toss rather than a test.

questions.q: la Suisse, la Chine, le Maroc. Which of those three is the odd one out for this lesson?
questions.why: le Maroc, because it is the le kind and the other two are the la kind. None of the three was drilled in this lesson and you could still answer, which is the point: the article told you and the country did not have to.

questions.q: le Mexique ends in an e and takes le. What does that tell you about the ending?
opts: The ending is always wrong on countries
Mexique is not really a country
The ending only works on short words
The ending is a hint rather than a rule
questions.why: A hint rather than a rule. It is right often enough on countries that people stop checking, and le Mexique, le Cambodge and le Zimbabwe are what happens next. Guess with it when you must and store the article anyway.

rounds.label: Going there
rounds.say: en, au and aux, chosen by the article.

questions.q: You are going to Japan, and it is le Japon. Write the two words after Je vais.
questions.why: au Japon. The le has folded into the preposition, which is why there is no le anywhere in the finished sentence. À plus le is au and it is never written any other way.

questions.q: You are going to Spain, and it is l'Espagne. Which word?
questions.why: en Espagne. The l apostrophe is hiding a la, so this is the la kind. If you cannot tell which article an l apostrophe country carries, that is a thing to look up rather than to reason out.

questions.q: You are going to les États-Unis. Write the two words after Je vais.
questions.why: aux États-Unis. The name is plural, so the article is les and the preposition folds with it into aux. Said out loud it is one long word, because the x wakes up as a z in front of the vowel.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Je vais en Canada. » It is le Canada. Fix the sentence.
questions.why: au Canada. En is the first of the three you meet and it becomes the default. Le Canada is the le kind, so it takes au, and this sentence is understood immediately while marking you as new.

rounds.label: Coming from
rounds.say: The same decision, the other direction.

questions.q: You are from Portugal, and it is le Portugal. Say where you are from.
questions.why: Je viens du Portugal. Du is de and le folded together, the same fold that gave you au, and it is the answer for every le country in the lesson.

questions.q: You are from France, and it is la France. Write the two words after Je viens.
questions.why: de France, with nothing between de and the country. This is the sentence the opening scene turned on: du France is understood perfectly and it is not something anybody says.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Je viens du Belgique. » It is la Belgique. Fix the sentence.
questions.why: de Belgique. La Belgique is the la kind, so de with nothing after it. The writer reached for du because du is right for most countries, which is exactly why this error is the common one.

questions.q: The country is les États-Unis. Going there was aux États-Unis, so coming from there is which word?
questions.why: des États-Unis. Aux and des are the same fold made twice, on à plus les and on de plus les, and both wake their last letter up as a z in front of the vowel.

rounds.label: One decision, two systems
rounds.say: Both columns, on countries this lesson never drilled.

questions.q: la Chine is the la kind. You are going there. Write the two words after Je vais.
questions.why: en Chine. This country was never drilled in the lesson and the article still answered it, which is the difference between knowing the rule and having memorised en France as one word.

questions.q: le Brésil is the le kind. You are coming from there. Which word?
questions.why: du Brésil. Another country the lesson never showed you. One article, looked up once, answers both directions for a country you have never used.

questions.q: You look up a country's article once. How many of the six small words does it settle?
questions.why: Two: one for going and one for coming. Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows. That is the return on the two seconds it takes to store, and it is why working the ending out afterwards never gets you there.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Je vais en la France. » Fix the sentence.
questions.why: en France. The article has already been used up: en, au, aux, de, du and des have all swallowed it, so none of them is ever followed by one. There is no en la, no au le and no des les.

rounds.label: The one that borrows en
rounds.say: One country, one column, one old idea.

questions.q: l'Iran is the le kind. You are going there. Which word?
questions.why: en Iran. Au Iran would put two vowel sounds hard against each other and French will not do it, so the going-to column borrows en. En Israël, en Uruguay and en Afghanistan all work the same way.

questions.q: And coming from Iran? Write the two words after Je viens.
questions.why: d'Iran. The exception reaches the going-to column and stops. This is the ordinary de of a le country, cut short in front of a vowel exactly as le and la were in the definite articles lesson.

questions.q: What is the reason for en Iran?
opts: Iran is the la kind after all
questions.why: Two vowel sounds cannot meet. It is the same objection behind l'amie, mon amie, n'ai, est-ce qu'il and combien d'ans. Six rules, one idea, and this is the sixth time you have watched it fire.

questions.q: Say where you are going, for l'Iran.
questions.why: Je vais en Iran. The n of en arrives on the front of Iran and is fully pronounced, so this comes out as three syllables rather than two words with a gap between them.

rounds.label: What you are
rounds.say: The nationality and its ending.

questions.q: Listen. Is this a man or a woman being described?
questions.why: française. The s at the end was written in français all along and silent; the e behind it wakes it up. This is the pair your ear can genuinely be trained on, and it is the colours lesson's idea arriving on a new word.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is this?
questions.why: canadienne. The nasal at the end of canadien collapses into a plain vowel with a real n behind it, which is exactly what brun does when it becomes brune.

questions.q: A woman from Canada. Write the one word that describes her.
questions.why: canadienne. fold() keeps a final e, so this is one of the few places free text can genuinely test an agreement. The nasal at the end of canadien collapses and a real n appears behind the vowel.

rounds.label: The capital letter
rounds.say: A letter shape, and no free-text question can test it.

questions.q: Which of these is written correctly?
questions.why: Il est français, small f and nothing in front. The être lesson already gave you both halves of this: a nationality after être takes no article, and French keeps the capital for the name of a person rather than the description of one.

questions.q: Which of these is written correctly?
questions.why: C'est un Français, with un and a capital F. Here the word names a person rather than describing one, which is the one place French does capitalise it. Out loud this is identical to the sentence with a small f.

questions.q: Why can no dictation ever test the difference between français and Français?
opts: Because the two words mean the same thing
Because the two are identical out loud
Because dictation only tests short words
Because French does not really use capitals
questions.why: Because they are identical out loud. The capital is a written-only difference with no signal in the air at all, exactly like the small letter on the days of the week and the months. It is read and written, never heard.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can store a country the way it is actually used, say where you are going and where you are from using one fact you looked up once, handle the country that breaks the ending hint and the one that borrows a word from the other column, and say what somebody is with nothing in front of it and the right letter at the start. The habit underneath all of that is the one worth keeping: French stores a noun with its article because the article is doing work the noun cannot do. You will meet the verbs behind je vais and je viens properly a whole band from here, and the same two verbs will let you say a good deal more than this. Neither is needed for anything in this lesson.
points: Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows. Which article, and everything else falls out of it.
The la kind takes en and de. The le kind takes au and du. The les kind takes aux and des.
A le country starting with a vowel borrows en for going, and nothing else changes.
A nationality after être takes nothing in front of it, and the capital belongs to the person rather than the description.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that the article in front of a noun is the choice that gender makes, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, and the elision of le and la in front of a vowel, introduced in a1.04
