The full present of être, and that a nationality after it takes no article, introduced in a1.06
That a nationality is written with a small letter when it describes and a capital when it names, introduced in a1.06
Adjective agreement, and that a final e can wake a silent consonant, introduced in a1.13
The nasal that collapses when an e arrives behind it, as in brun and brune, introduced in a1.13
à plus le folding into au, and de plus le folding into du, introduced in a1.11 and a1.29
Elision as a repair for two vowels meeting, introduced in sons.07
Liaison, and that a silent final consonant attaches to a following vowel, introduced in sons.10
grammarIntroduced: en, au and aux with a country name, selected by the country's gender and number
de, du and des with a country name, selected by the same property
That the preposition absorbs the definite article, so no article follows it
en rather than au before a masculine country beginning with a vowel
That the -e ending predicts a feminine country reliably but not without exception
Nationality adjectives as a class, and their agreement applied from a1.13
je vais and je viens as frozen first-person frames, with aller and venir reserved for a2.02

overview.introFr: Un seul fait, appris avec le mot, qui choisit six petits mots à votre place.

acts.title: The article travels with the word
acts.milestone: You have watched a conversation move into English over one letter.

acts.title: The countries
acts.milestone: Twelve countries, each stored the way it is used, and the one that breaks the hint.

acts.title: Going there
acts.milestone: en, au and aux, and the country that borrows one of them.

acts.title: Coming from
acts.milestone: Both columns on one screen, and the same fact chose all six words.

acts.title: What you are
acts.milestone: A nationality with nothing in front of it, and one capital letter.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. Everything here carries straight into talking about where anybody is from.

lessons.reframe: Learn the country with its article. Everything else follows.

errorTriggers.description: Stored the country without its article, so the fact the preposition needs is simply not available and every answer is a guess. The error that happens weeks before any of the others.
Has the article and reaches for the wrong going-to word, most often en for a le country: « Je vais en Canada. » Understood immediately, and it marks the speaker as new.
The same error in the other column, and the expensive one: « Je viens du France. » Du is right for most countries, so it comes out by default on the smaller group, which includes France.

Learns the two columns as two unrelated tables and looks the country up twice, or gets one column right and the other wrong on the same country. Costs confidence rather than accuracy, which is why it has its own drill.
Writes « au Iran », or over-applies the repair and writes « en Portugal », or carries the exception into the other column and writes « de Iran » rather than d apostrophe Iran.

Leaves the nationality unchanged for a woman, or adds an article after être, or capitalises the description. All three were introduced in a1.06 and all three survive into this lesson on a new set of words.
Writes « Il est Français » with a capital, or « C'est un français » without one. A written-only distinction with no audible signal, exactly like the lowercase days and months.

drills.title: Which little word?
drills.coach: Do not sort by the ending. Four of these six end in an e and only three of those four are the la kind. Sort by the word you stored in front of the country, and if you did not store one, that is the finding.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which article goes with Mexique?
drills.why: le Mexique. It ends in an e and takes le anyway, which is the one country in this lesson where the ending and the article disagree.

drills.title: Where are you going?
drills.coach: The front gives you the article. La gives en, le gives au, les gives aux, and a le country starting with a vowel borrows en. Nothing about the country itself is ever consulted.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are going to Japan, and it is le Japon. Which word?
drills.why: au Japon. The le has folded into the preposition and vanished, which is why there is no le left anywhere in the sentence.

drills.title: Where are you from?
drills.coach: The same article, the other column. La gives de, le gives du, les gives des, and in front of a vowel de is cut short to d apostrophe the way le and la always were.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are from France, and it is la France. Which word?
drills.why: de France. Du is right for most countries and France is not one of them, which is exactly why this is the error that costs the most.

drills.title: Same country, both directions
drills.coach: Every country in this drill turns up twice, once in each bucket, so knowing the country will not sort it. Read the small word instead. En, au and aux go one way and de, du and des go the other.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: How many of the six small words does one country's article settle?
drills.why: Two. One for going and one for coming, and you look the article up once rather than twice.

drills.title: Which one in front of this country?
drills.coach: Every country in this drill is the le kind, so the article will not sort it. Look at the first letter of the country instead. A vowel behind au is a collision the language will not make, so the word swaps.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: l'Iran is the le kind. You are going there. Which word?
drills.why: en Iran. The swap is about the sound and nothing else: Iran is still the le kind and still takes d apostrophe Iran coming back.

drills.title: A man or a woman?
drills.coach: The ending carries it and you can hear all four. Français gains an s when the e arrives; canadien loses its nasal and gains a real n. Neither of those is new: the colours lesson taught both shapes.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: A woman from Canada. Which word?
drills.why: canadienne. The nasal collapses into a plain vowel with a real n behind it, which is the same thing brun does when it becomes brune.

drills.title: Describing, or naming?
drills.coach: Ask what the word is doing. After être it is describing somebody, so it takes a small letter and nothing in front. After c'est un it is naming them, so it takes a capital. Out loud the two are identical.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these is written correctly?
drills.why: Il est français. Small f, because this describes rather than names, and nothing in front of it, because a nationality after être never takes an article.

sheets.title: Both columns, and the two exceptions
contains: en, au, aux and de, du, des

sections.title: What each row is doing
sections.body: The la kind takes en for going and de for coming, and neither of them is ever followed by an article: en France and de France, never en la France or de la France. The le kind takes au and du, and both of those already contain the article, because au is à plus le folded into one word and du is de plus le folded the same way. The les kind takes aux and des, folded from the plural article, and both wake their last letter up as a z in front of a vowel, which is why aux États-Unis and des États-Unis each come out as one long word rather than two. l'Iran is the exception and it is a narrow one: it is the le kind, it borrows en for the going-to column only because au Iran would put two vowel sounds against each other, and it goes straight back to behaving like a le country coming the other way. le Mexique is not an exception at all, it just looks like one: it ends in an e, which usually means the la kind, and it takes le. The article is right and the ending is a hint.

sections.title: The nationality, and the one capital letter
sections.body: A nationality is a separate word from the country and it never carries an article of its own. After être it takes nothing in front of it at all, which the être lesson covered alongside jobs: Il est français, not Il est un français. It agrees the way a colour agrees, so an e arrives for a woman and sometimes wakes up a letter that had been silent: français becomes française and you can hear the s arrive, while canadien becomes canadienne and the nasal collapses into a plain vowel with a real n after it. A few nationalities already end in an e and never change at all: belge, russe, suisse, tchèque. The capital letter is the one thing here that is not a rule you already have. French writes the description with a small letter and the name of a person with a capital, so Il est français describes and C'est un Français names, and the two are identical out loud. English capitalises both, which is why this one has to be read rather than reasoned out. It is the same kind of written-only distinction as the lowercase days of the week and the lowercase months.

sections.title: Country, nationality, and both small words
Why the article is stored and the ending is not
sections.body: Most courses hand you the rule as en for feminine and au for masculine and leave it there, which is true and unusable, because the gender is the part you do not have. The gender of a country is not something you can hear, work out or reason towards in the half second before you speak. It is something you either stored or did not. So the practical version of this whole lesson is a habit rather than a rule: when a country word goes into your head, the article goes in with it, attached, as though it were one word. La France. Le Canada. Les États-Unis. Do that and you will never think about en against au again, because the answer arrives with the country. The ending is worth knowing about for the moment somebody names a country you have never met and you have to answer anyway. Most la countries end in an e: France, Belgique, Espagne, Italie, Allemagne, Chine, Russie, Suisse. Most others do not: Canada, Japon, Portugal, Sénégal, Maroc, Brésil. It is a good guess and a bad rule, and the countries where it fails are exactly the ones you will meet: le Mexique, le Cambodge, le Zimbabwe. Use it when you are cornered and store the article the rest of the time. One more thing worth knowing about the six small words: every one of them has already swallowed the article, so none of them is ever followed by another. There is no en la France, no au le Canada and no des les États-Unis, and if one of those is trying to come out of your mouth the fix is to delete the second word rather than to change the first.

articleTravels.term: the article travels with the word
articleTravels.title: Store la France, never France
articleTravels.body: A country in French is almost never said bare. It is la France, le Canada, les États-Unis, and the little word in front is not decoration: it is the one fact that decides everything else you will ever do with that country. If you learn the word without it you have stored half of it, and the missing half is the half you need. This is the same habit the noun gender lesson asked for, arriving on a set of words where the payoff is immediate rather than eventual: two whole systems fall out of it, and neither of them can be worked out from the word itself.

examples.note: la France with its article, in a sentence nobody wrote to teach this.
le Canada doing the same, and the article is the only difference between them.

goingAndComing.title: The same fact answers both questions
goingAndComing.body: Going to a country and coming from one look like two things to learn and are one. The la kind takes en and de; the le kind takes au and du; the les kind takes aux and des. Three rows, six words, and the row is chosen by the article you already stored. Nothing about the country itself is consulted twice: you look once, when you learn the word, and both columns are settled from then on. A learner who knows the article gets four words for free, and a learner who does not is guessing on every sentence in both directions.

examples.note: en, because France is the la kind.
de, from the same fact, in the other direction.

vowelRepair.term: en in front of a vowel
vowelRepair.title: Why it is en Iran and not au Iran
vowelRepair.body: Au Iran would put two vowel sounds hard against each other, and French will not do it. You have watched the language dodge this collision five times already: l'amie instead of la amie, mon amie instead of ma amie, n'ai instead of ne ai, est-ce qu'il instead of est-ce que il, and combien d'ans instead of combien de ans. This is the sixth, and the repair is the simplest of them: the le kind borrows en for the going-to column and nothing else changes. Coming from, the exception is over: d'Iran is the ordinary de of a le country, cut short in front of the vowel like every other de.

examples.note: A le country taking en, purely to keep two vowels apart.
And coming the other way, where the exception does not reach.

theEndingIsAHint.term: the e on the end is a hint
theEndingIsAHint.title: Most la countries end in e, and some le ones do too
theEndingIsAHint.body: France, Belgique, Espagne, Italie, Allemagne, Chine: the la countries almost all end in an e, which is the same hint the noun gender lesson measured across the whole corpus and found right about seven times in ten. On countries it is better than that and still not a rule. Le Mexique ends in an e and takes le, and so do le Cambodge and le Zimbabwe. Treat the ending as a way of guessing when you have to guess, and never as a way of avoiding storing the article. The countries you will actually use are a short list and you will meet each of them many times.

examples.note: Mexique ends in an e and takes au, which is what a hint failing looks like.
And du in the other column, from the same article.

nationalityIsAWord.term: the nationality is a different word
nationalityIsAWord.title: A country and a nationality are two things
nationalityIsAWord.body: La France is a place and français is what you are. They are separate words, they are stored separately, and the small one behaves like the colours lesson said an adjective behaves: it grows an e for a woman, and sometimes that e wakes up a letter that was silent. Français becomes française and you can hear the s arrive; canadien becomes canadienne and the nasal collapses into a plain vowel with a real n after it. Neither of those is new. What is new is the capital letter, which belongs to the person and not to the description.

examples.note: The e on the end, and the s waking up behind it.
The other shape: the nasal collapses and a real n appears.

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. « en France » AND « de France » ARE ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, read straight through with no gap and no reset. Then, in the SAME take, « au Canada » and « du Canada ». The claim the whole lesson rests on is that going and coming are one decision, and two separate recordings are two performances: a reader who records the coming-from column in its own session will lean on the de, and the learner will hear that lean as a difference between the two systems rather than as one system read twice. Then the four whole sentences in the same take: « Je vais en France. », « Je viens de France. », « Je vais au Canada. », « Je viens du Canada. » KEEP EVERY NASAL CLOSED. France is /fʁɑ̃s/ with a nasal vowel and NO n sound behind it: the app respells it FRAHⁿSS deliberately, and a reader who lets an n out of it is teaching the error the opening scene is about.

« aux États-Unis » AND « des États-Unis » RECORDED WHOLE, never as a preposition plus a country. The liaison IS the word: aux États-Unis is /o.ze.ta.zy.ni/ and comes out as one long run of syllables, and a clip of « aux » on its own teaches nothing at all because the sound the learner needs does not exist until the country is attached. Same for des. Both in ONE take, adjacent, so the learner hears that the two behave identically. Then the two whole sentences and the published line: « Je vais aux États-Unis. », « Je viens des États-Unis. », « Mon frère travaille aux États-Unis. » The last of those is fr.sons.liaisons.059 and is already in the seed, so it may already have a clip: if it does, reuse it rather than recording a second performance of the same row.

THE TWO AGREEMENT PAIRS, EACH ADJACENT IN ONE TAKE WITH ONE VOICE. « français » immediately followed by « française », then « canadien » immediately followed by « canadienne ». The whole point is that only the ending changes, so any difference in pace, pitch or weight between the two halves teaches something that is not there. BOTH PAIRS ARE GENUINELY AUDIBLE AND THEY DIFFER IN DIFFERENT WAYS. In français / française an s that was silent WAKES UP: give it full value, and do not lengthen the vowel to compensate. In canadien / canadienne a NASAL VOWEL COLLAPSES: canadien ends /djɛ̃/, through the nose with no n behind it, and canadienne ends /djɛn/, a plain vowel with a real n. Reading the masculine with an n on the end destroys the pair. Then the four sentences, in the same take, in this order: « Il est français. », « Elle est française. », « Il est canadien. », « Elle est canadienne. »

« en France » AND « au Canada » ADJACENT IN ONE TAKE, so the two prepositions are heard against each other in identical frames. This is the only comparison in the going-to column that carries any information: the two words share no sound, and hearing them side by side is what makes that obvious rather than something the learner has to be told. NEVER RECORD A PREPOSITION IN ISOLATION. There is no clip anywhere in this lesson of en, au, aux, de, du or des alone. They are unstressed function words that only exist attached to a country, and a clip of one on its own is a sound the learner will never hear again. If a request for one arrives, it is a mistake in the request. Also in this take: « au Japon », « au Portugal », « en Belgique », « en Espagne », each whole.

« au Iran » AND « en Iran » ADJACENT, ONE TAKE, and the first of them is the error. Read the wrong one slowly enough that the learner hears the two vowels genuinely colliding, which is the whole reason the language refuses it, and then the right one at ordinary pace. THE LIAISON IN « en Iran » IS A REAL PRONOUNCED N and must be given its full value: the phrase comes out as three syllables, ahⁿ-nee-RAHⁿ, with the n on the front of the second syllable rather than closing the first. Do NOT read it as en, pause, Iran. It is the same shape as mon ami from the possessives lesson. Then « d'Iran » and the two whole sentences: « Je vais en Iran. », « Je viens d'Iran. » The second is here so the learner hears that the exception stops at the going-to column.

THE TWELVE COUNTRIES, EACH READ WITH ITS ARTICLE ATTACHED AND NEVER WITHOUT IT. la France, le Canada, la Belgique, les États-Unis, le Sénégal, l'Allemagne, l'Espagne, l'Italie, le Portugal, le Japon, le Mexique, l'Iran. Read as ONE LIST in one take, at an even pace, because the learner is being asked to store the article as part of the word and a pause between the article and the country teaches the opposite. NO COUNTRY IS EVER RECORDED BARE in this lesson. There is no clip of « France » or « Canada » on their own, deliberately: a bare country is the thing the opening scene is about not storing. Then the three published sentences: « La France est un pays d'Europe. », « Le Canada est un grand pays. », « Les États-Unis sont grands. »
clipIds: La France est un pays d'Europe.
Le Canada est un grand pays.

recorded.desc: « Il est français. » AND « C'est un Français. » IN ONE TAKE, AND THEY MUST SOUND THE SAME FROM THE NATIONALITY ONWARDS. The capital letter is invisible to the ear and the whole teaching is that the learner cannot hear it, so a reader who gives the capitalised one any extra weight is inventing a signal the language does not have. Read both plainly at the same pace. Then « Je suis français. » in the same take, which is fr.a1.metiers.264 and is already in the seed: reuse an existing clip if one has been delivered.

The five written traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them. Read EVERY wrong version plainly and at ordinary pace rather than comically, because a learner saying them does not hesitate either. « Je viens du France. » and « Je vais en Canada. » are both perfectly pronounceable and sound completely ordinary, which is the point: nothing about them signals an error, which is why they survive. « Je vais au Iran. » is the one trap in the group that sounds uncomfortable, and it should: read it with the two vowels genuinely meeting. « Je vais en la France. » should be read flatly, with the extra word given no emphasis at all.

The opening scene, French bubbles only. Théo is a colleague in his thirties waiting for a coffee machine, half distracted, being friendly. His switch to English MUST BE WARM AND COMPLETELY UNREMARKABLE. He has not noticed an error and he is not making a point: he heard a learner and decided to make things easier, which is a kindness rather than a judgement. Any hint of correction in his voice turns the scene into a telling-off and loses the whole point, which is that nothing visibly went wrong. His last line the following morning, where he stays in French and neither of them mentions it, is where warmth is allowed to show.
clipIds: Ah, de France ! Et vous êtes ici depuis longtemps ?

lessons.title: Prépositions de lieu
lessons.intro: Nine ways to say where something is, and one rule that splits them in two. Five are single words that sit straight against the noun. Four are phrases ending in de, and leaving that de out is the most common thing an English speaker gets wrong here.

sections.title: Ten Minutes Looking At The Right Table

say.text: One syllable decides where you put your hand. Watch which one, and notice that nobody says anything wrong.

setting.place: A friend's kitchen, a table with a newspaper on it, and two people about to be late

beats.text: A friend's kitchen in Rennes, ten minutes before you both need to leave. You have put your keys down somewhere and you no longer know where.
You ask. She answers without looking up, the way anybody answers a question about keys, at ordinary speed and with no particular care.

beats.speaker: Camille
beats.fr: Les clés sont sous le journal.
beats.en: The keys are under the newspaper.
beats.stage: She is putting her coat on and is already half out of the room. One short word, unstressed, in the middle of a sentence.

beats.prompt: You caught every word except one. Which did she say, and where are you about to look?

options.fr: Les clés sont sur le journal.
options.en: on top of the newspaper, where you can see them

options.fr: Les clés sont sous le journal.
options.en: underneath it, where you cannot

followUp.works: Yes. Now listen to the other one, because at that speed they are one syllable apart and both of them are true sentences.
followUp.breaks: That is the one most people hear. It is also the one that sends you looking at a bare newspaper and finding nothing.

beats.text: You look at the table. There is a newspaper on it, and nothing on top of the newspaper. You look again. You check your coat, then the hall, then your bag.

beats.speaker: You
beats.stage: Said with total confidence, because you looked. You did look. You looked at the exact right table.

beats.heading: You heard four words out of five
beats.body: She said something correct and you heard something correct. Only one syllable separates them, and it is the syllable carrying the entire position. Every other word in that sentence was the same, which is why nothing sounded wrong.

wrong.fr: Les clés sont sur le journal.
wrong.en: On top of it, in plain view

right.fr: Les clés sont sous le journal.

beats.coach: Sur and sous are opposites that sit one syllable apart, and they are the only pair in this lesson your ear has to work at. The rest sound nothing alike.

beats.speaker: Camille
beats.en: Under! Under the newspaper. Lift it up.
beats.stage: She says it twice, louder, which is what anybody does. The second time you hear it perfectly.

beats.text: Five words, one of them two letters long, and it was the only one that decided where to put your hand. The next half hour is about those short words and the one rule that separates them.

closing.text: Five of these words go straight onto the noun. Four others need one more word first, and that is the half of this lesson nobody gets told about.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the second one is the one that separates you from a beginner.

goals.s: Five short words, on one object, in five positions. Most people have these within two screens.
Four more are phrases rather than words, and they end in de. Leaving it out is understood perfectly and marks you as new.

goals.t: Use au and aux without over-using them
goals.s: À and le will not sit side by side. À and la will. Two of the four shapes change and two do not.
The one pair here your ear has to work at, and the one that sends you looking in the wrong place.

sections.title: One Cat, One Box, Five Places
sections.hint: Five cards. Only one word changes.
sections.say: The cat moves and the sentence does not. Read the second word of each line and nothing else.

cards.label: on, on top of
cards.head: sur
cards.fr: Le chat est sur la boîte.
cards.sub: [SÜR] · The cat is on the box.
cards.body: On top of it, touching it, with the box holding it up.

cards.label: under, underneath
cards.head: sous
cards.fr: Le chat est sous la boîte.
cards.sub: [SOO] · The cat is under the box.
cards.body: Underneath it. The opposite of the card before, and the one your ear will lose in fast speech.

cards.label: in, inside
cards.head: dans
cards.fr: Le chat est dans la boîte.
cards.sub: [DAHⁿ] · The cat is in the box.
cards.body: Inside it, which is why the reference point is a box: a chair cannot do this one.

cards.label: in front of
cards.head: devant
cards.fr: Le chat est devant la boîte.
cards.sub: [duh-VAHⁿ] · The cat is in front of the box.
cards.body: On the near side of it, between the box and you.

cards.label: behind
cards.head: derrière
cards.fr: Le chat est derrière la boîte.
cards.sub: [deh-RYEHR] · The cat is behind the box.
cards.body: On the far side of it, hidden from where you are standing.

cards.label: what just happened
cards.head: Four words never moved
cards.fr: Le chat est sur la boîte. · Le chat est sous la boîte.
cards.body: Five sentences, the same four words, one short word swapped into the middle. That word carries the whole position and sits straight against the noun with nothing between them.

sections.title: Read Down The Middle
sections.say: One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first. Read the middle column top to bottom. That is the whole of act one.

cells: The cat is on the box.
rows.say: Le chat est sur la boîte.

detail.title: sur · on, on top of
detail.body: Le chat est sur la boîte. The cat is on the box. The word sits straight against la boîte with nothing in between, which is what makes it one of the five rather than one of the four in the next act.
detail.say: Le chat est sur la boîte.

cells: The cat is under the box.
rows.say: Le chat est sous la boîte.

detail.title: sous · under, underneath
detail.body: Le chat est sous la boîte. The cat is under the box. The word sits straight against la boîte with nothing in between, which is what makes it one of the five rather than one of the four in the next act.
detail.say: Le chat est sous la boîte.

cells: The cat is in the box.
rows.say: Le chat est dans la boîte.

detail.title: dans · in, inside
detail.body: Le chat est dans la boîte. The cat is in the box. The word sits straight against la boîte with nothing in between, which is what makes it one of the five rather than one of the four in the next act.
detail.say: Le chat est dans la boîte.

cells: The cat is in front of the box.
rows.say: Le chat est devant la boîte.

detail.title: devant · in front of
detail.body: Le chat est devant la boîte. The cat is in front of the box. The word sits straight against la boîte with nothing in between, which is what makes it one of the five rather than one of the four in the next act.
detail.say: Le chat est devant la boîte.

cells: The cat is behind the box.
rows.say: Le chat est derrière la boîte.

detail.title: derrière · behind
detail.body: Le chat est derrière la boîte. The cat is behind the box. The word sits straight against la boîte with nothing in between, which is what makes it one of the five rather than one of the four in the next act.
detail.say: Le chat est derrière la boîte.

sections.title: Some Of These Are Not Words
sections.hint: Four cards, and the fourth is the rule.
sections.say: The five you have just met are one shape. There is a second shape, and English gives you no warning about it.

cards.label: what you have
cards.head: One word, straight onto the noun
cards.fr: Le chat est sur la boîte. · Le chat est dans la boîte.
cards.sub: sur la boîte · dans la boîte
cards.body: Five words that behave identically. You say the word, you say the thing, and you are finished. Nothing goes between them and nothing follows.

cards.label: what else there is
cards.head: Two or three words, ending in de
cards.fr: Le chat est à côté de la boîte. · Le chat est près de la boîte.
cards.body: Same cat, same box, same sentence. The only difference is that the position is now a phrase rather than a word, and the last word of that phrase is always de.

cards.label: why it is missed
cards.head: English has nothing here
cards.body: Next to the bank. Near the station. In front of the house. English puts nothing between the phrase and the thing, so there is no habit to bring across and nothing that feels missing when you leave the de out.

cards.label: the rule
cards.head: Which shape are you holding?
cards.fr: Le chat est sur la boîte. · Le chat est à côté de la boîte.
cards.body: One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first. That is one decision, made once, before the noun comes out of your mouth. It covers every position word in this lesson and the four beyond it.

sections.title: The Same Box, Both Ways
sections.say: One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first. Read across a row. Left needs nothing, right needs de, and the box never moved.

rows.say: Le chat est sur la boîte. Le chat est à côté de la boîte.

detail.title: One word against three
detail.body: Le chat est sur la boîte. Le chat est à côté de la boîte. Identical apart from the position, and the one on the right carries a de that cannot be left out.
detail.say: Le chat est sur la boîte. Le chat est à côté de la boîte.

rows.say: Le chat est sous la boîte. Le chat est près de la boîte.

detail.title: Under it, against near it
detail.body: Le chat est sous la boîte. Le chat est près de la boîte. Sous is one of the five. Près de is one of the four, and its de is the last word of the position rather than the first word of the thing.
detail.say: Le chat est sous la boîte. Le chat est près de la boîte.

rows.say: Le chat est devant la boîte. Le chat est en face de la boîte.

detail.title: The pair that means almost the same thing
detail.body: Le chat est devant la boîte. Le chat est en face de la boîte. Close in meaning and opposite in shape, which is the clearest evidence that you cannot work the shape out from the sense.
detail.say: Le chat est devant la boîte. Le chat est en face de la boîte.

rows.say: Le chat est derrière la boîte. Le chat est loin de la boîte.

detail.title: And the last of each
detail.body: Le chat est derrière la boîte. Le chat est loin de la boîte. Four rows, eight positions, and the only thing you ever decide is which column a word lives in.
detail.say: Le chat est derrière la boîte. Le chat est loin de la boîte.

sections.title: Which Column Does It Live In?
sections.say: This is a decision you will make every time you say where something is, so it is worth making it a few times on purpose.

check.q: You want to say that the cat is on the box. How many words go between the position word and la boîte?
check.why: None. Sur is a single word and it sits directly against the noun. All five of these behave the same way, which is why they are worth learning as one group rather than five separate facts.

check.q: You want to say that the café is next to the bank. Which of these is French?
opts: Le café est à côté la banque
Le café est à côté de la banque
Le café est à côté à la banque
Le café est à côté banque
check.why: À côté de la banque. The de is the last word of the position and not an extra. Leaving it out is understood perfectly by everybody, which is exactly why nobody ever corrects it and why it can survive for years.

check.q: Which of these two is missing something?
opts: Le chat est près la boîte
Le chat est sur la boîte
Both of them are missing a word
check.why: Près la boîte is the broken one and needs de. Sur la boîte is complete as it stands. One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first.

sections.title: Three Ways This Goes Wrong
sections.say: Three errors, and the first is the one this whole lesson exists to prevent.

errors.wrong: Le café est à côté la banque.
errors.right: Le café est à côté de la banque.
errors.why: The de is missing. This is the single most common thing an English speaker gets wrong here, and it survives because it works: everybody understands you and nobody repeats it back. It marks you as a beginner for as long as you keep saying it.

errors.wrong: Nous habitons près la gare.
errors.right: Nous habitons près de la gare.
errors.why: The same error on a different phrase. Près, loin, à côté and en face all end in de, and the fix is to learn each one with the de already inside it so there is never a moment where you decide whether to add it.

errors.wrong: Le chat est sur de la boîte.
errors.right: Le chat est sur la boîte.
errors.why: The rule applied where it does not reach. Sur is one of the five that take nothing, and adding de to it is the error a learner makes in the week after this lesson rather than before it. Only the phrases take de.

sections.title: The Sixth Word
sections.hint: Four cards, and one of them is about a missing mark.
sections.say: One more word, and it behaves like none of the five.

cards.label: the word
cards.head: à
cards.body: At, in, or to, depending on what follows. It is the word for being somewhere by name rather than being positioned relative to something, and it is the most common preposition in French.

cards.label: what makes it different
cards.head: It reacts to the word after it
cards.fr: Je suis au bureau. · Je suis à la maison.
cards.body: None of the five did anything to the words around them. This one does. À plus le comes out as au, one word instead of two, and à plus la does not change at all. That is the next screen.

cards.label: the one that is not it
cards.head: à and a are the same sound
cards.fr: il a · il est à Paris
cards.sub: he has · he is in Paris
cards.body: You met a in the avoir lesson: il a is he has. The only difference on the page is the mark, and there is no difference at all out loud. Nobody speaking French is choosing between them, and this is a writing difference only.

cards.label: how to tell them apart
cards.head: Look at what comes next
cards.fr: il a un chat · il est à la maison
cards.sub: a thing being owned · a place
cards.body: A thing after a, a place after à. Once you look past the single letter the two can never be confused, and that is the only test you need. The same mark separates sur from sûr, which is on against sure.

sections.title: Two Change, Two Do Not
sections.say: Four rows. The two that do nothing are as important as the two that do.

detail.title: Two words become one
detail.body: Je suis au bureau. I am at the office. À and le do not appear side by side in French. This is not a shortcut you may choose: the uncontracted version is simply not written or said.

detail.title: The same thing in the plural
detail.body: Je suis aux toilettes. Out loud aux and au are the same sound. The difference is written and it follows the noun. Les enfants jouent aux cartes. shows the same word away from any place at all.

detail.title: Nothing happens
detail.body: Je suis à la maison. Both words stay exactly as they are. Mon frère travaille à la banque. is the same shape in published French. Reaching for a contraction here is the rule applied where it does not go.

detail.title: And nothing here either
detail.body: Je suis à l'école. I am at school. The l' is already the noun's own shortened article, and à leaves it alone. Two of these four rows change and two do not, which is the entire contraction.

sections.title: Does It Contract?
sections.say: Two groups and one control. The control is the one that catches over-application.

items.en: to the, at the (before a le word)
to the, at the (before a plural word)

check.q: You want to say: I am at the office. Le bureau is a le word. Which is French?
check.why: Au bureau. À and le will not stand next to each other, so the two collapse into au. À le bureau is not a thing you may say slowly and carefully instead; it does not exist.

groups.label: These two stay as they are

items.en: to the, at the (before a la word)
to the, at the (before a vowel)

check.q: You want to say: I am at home. La maison is a la word. Which is French?
check.why: À la maison, with both words exactly as they were. Nothing contracts here, and reaching for a shortened form is this rule being applied where it does not reach.

check.q: Somebody has learned that à + le is au and now writes « je suis au école ». What went wrong?
opts: L'école takes à l', and nothing contracts
It should be à le école
check.why: À l'école. The rule was applied to a word it does not cover. Only le and les contract, and l' is neither: it is already a shortened article. This error is commoner after the lesson than before it.

sections.title: You Have Met This Du Before
sections.hint: Four cards, and the first one is a reminder rather than a rule.
sections.say: This is not new. The partitive lesson named it, and here is where it was going.

cards.label: what you already have
cards.head: The partitive lesson said this first
cards.body: When you learned du for some, you were told most du in French is not an amount at all, and you were shown près du lit. That was this. De and le collapse exactly as à and le do.

cards.label: why it turns up here
cards.head: Every phrase in act two ends in de
cards.fr: Le chat est à côté du lit.
cards.sub: The cat is next to the bed.
cards.body: À côté de, près de, loin de, en face de. The moment one meets a le word, the de and the le collapse into du. The same collapse you know, with a place behind it instead of a quantity.

cards.label: the test still works
cards.head: Try putting some in front
cards.fr: Le chat est à côté du lit. · Il revient du travail à six heures.
cards.sub: next to the bed · back from work
cards.body: Some bread makes sense, so je bois du café is the other du. Some the bed does not, so à côté du lit is this one. That test came from the partitive lesson and it still separates them.

cards.label: and the same for des
cards.head: Des collides too
cards.fr: Le chat est près des arbres.
cards.sub: [DAY] · The cat is near the trees.
cards.body: De plus les gives des, which is the same two letters as the des you use for several things. The same test separates these as well, and neither of them is a word you have to choose: both are collapses that happen on their own.

sections.title: The Same Four Rows Again
sections.say: Identical to the à table, one row at a time. If you have one you have both.

rows.say: Le chat est à côté du lit.

detail.title: The one the partitive lesson named
detail.body: Le chat est à côté du lit. The cat is next to the bed. Le chien dort à côté du feu. is the same collapse in published French.
detail.say: Le chat est à côté du lit.

rows.say: Le chat est près des arbres.

detail.title: And it collides with the other des
detail.body: Le chat est près des arbres. The cat is near the trees. The same two letters as the des for several things, doing a different job, and separated by the same test.
detail.say: Le chat est près des arbres.

rows.say: Le chat est à côté de la porte.

detail.title: Nothing happens
detail.body: Le chat est à côté de la porte. The cat is next to the door. Le café est à côté de la banque. is the same shape in published French, and the de is plainly visible in it.
detail.say: Le chat est à côté de la porte.

rows.say: Le chat est à côté de l'arbre.

detail.title: And nothing here either
detail.body: Le chat est à côté de l'arbre. The cat is next to the tree. La pharmacie est à côté de l'école. shows it in the wild. Two collapse and two do not, exactly as with à.
detail.say: Le chat est à côté de l'arbre.

sections.title: One Mark, Two Words
sections.hint: Three cards about a difference you can only see.
sections.say: Two pairs, both of them identical out loud, and both of them worth thirty seconds so you stop worrying about hearing them.

cards.label: the pair
cards.head: à and a
cards.body: One is the verb you met in the avoir lesson and one is the preposition from this one. They sound exactly the same and always will. There is nothing here for your ear to learn, because there is nothing in the sound to catch.

cards.label: the other pair
cards.head: sur and sûr
cards.fr: sur la table · je suis sûr
cards.sub: on the table · I am sure
cards.body: The same again with a different mark. On against sure, and out loud the difference is small enough that context does the work every time. Both of these are writing differences, and you will meet the second one properly much later.

cards.label: what this means for you
cards.head: You will never have to hear it
cards.fr: il a un chat · il est à Paris
cards.body: Because these are identical in speech, no listening exercise can ever test them and none in this lesson does. What separates them is what follows: something owned after a, somewhere after à. That is a reading habit, and it is quick.

examples.en: I go to the market on Saturdays.
examples.note: À or de, meeting the word after it.

examples.fr: Mon frère travaille à la banque.
examples.en: My brother works at the bank.
examples.note: À or de, meeting the word after it.

examples.fr: Il revient du travail à six heures.
examples.en: He comes back from work at six o'clock.
examples.note: À or de, meeting the word after it.

sections.title: Sur, Or Sous?
sections.say: Four lines. Two of them are the sentence from the scene, and this time you know what is coming.

lines.fr: Les clés sont sur le journal.
lines.en: The keys are on the newspaper.

lines.fr: Les clés sont sous le journal.
lines.en: The keys are under the newspaper.
It is on the bed.
It is under the bed.

questions.q: You hear « Les clés sont sous le journal. » Where do you put your hand?
questions.why: Underneath. Sous is under, and this is the sentence from the scene. The two words differ by one vowel and they send you to opposite places.

questions.q: You hear « Il est sur le lit. » Is the thing visible from the doorway?
opts: Yes, it is on top of the bed
No, it is under the bed
No, it is behind the bed
questions.why: Yes. Sur puts it on top, in plain view. Sur has the tight ü sound with rounded lips; sous is a plain oo. Slowly they are obvious, and at speed they are the one pair worth practising.

questions.q: Which of these two pairs actually needs your ear?
questions.why: Sur and sous. Devant and derrière sound nothing alike and never get confused. À and a are the same sound exactly, so no amount of listening will separate them and nothing in this lesson asks you to try.

sections.title: The Flat
sections.say: One short passage. Every position word in it is one you have met, and half of them take de.
sections.text: Voici mon appartement. La cuisine est à côté du salon. Le canapé est devant la fenêtre et la télévision est sur la petite table. Mon sac est sous le lit et les clés sont dans le sac. Le jardin est derrière la maison, et la boulangerie est en face de la gare, tout près de chez moi.

questions.q: Where is the kitchen?
questions.a: Next to the living room. The passage says à côté du salon, with de and le collapsed into du.

questions.q: Where are the keys?
questions.a: In the bag, and the bag is under the bed. Dans le sac and sous le lit, two of the five that take nothing.

questions.q: Which positions in the passage needed a de?
questions.a: À côté du salon, en face de la gare and près de chez moi. The other five go straight onto the noun.

glossary.note: De and le collapsed into du, exactly as à and le collapse into au.
One word, straight onto the noun. No de.
The partner of sur, and the one pair here your ear has to work at.
A three-word phrase and the third word is de. It is never optional.
The same shape again. Près de chez moi is near my place.

sections.title: Two More You Will Meet
sections.hint: Two cards. Neither is on the test.
sections.say: Two words worth recognising now so they do not surprise you later. Neither is examined here.

cards.label: the one that needs two things
cards.head: entre
cards.fr: Le magasin est entre la banque et la poste.
cards.sub: [AHⁿ-truh] · The shop is between the bank and the post office.
cards.body: Between, and the only position word here that cannot work with one reference point. You need both. It goes straight onto the first noun, so it belongs with the five.

cards.label: a second pair
cards.head: two things, every time
cards.fr: Mon école est entre la boulangerie et la pharmacie.
cards.sub: My school is between the bakery and the pharmacy.
cards.body: The same shape again, so the requirement reads as a rule rather than an accident. Entre always has an et behind it somewhere, naming the second thing.

cards.label: the one English has no word for
cards.head: chez
cards.fr: Je vais chez le médecin demain.
cards.sub: [SHAY] · I am going to the doctor's tomorrow.
cards.body: At somebody's place, and it takes a person rather than a building. There is no single English word for it and you will use it constantly.

cards.label: chez without a building
cards.head: chez nous
cards.fr: Nous restons chez nous ce week-end.
cards.sub: We are staying home this weekend.
cards.body: The same word with nobody named at all. Chez moi is my place, chez nous is ours, and the person is the destination rather than the address.

sections.title: Everything In One Place
sections.say: Two groups, and the split is the lesson.

themes.title: What à does to the word after it

cards.en: to the, at the (before a le word)
to the, at the (before a plural word)
to the, at the (before a la word)
to the, at the (before a vowel)

sections.title: The Twelve Words
sections.say: Twelve cards. The four at the end carry their de, because that is how you have to know them.

sections.title: Write What You Hear
sections.say: Six short lines. Two of them differ by one letter, and you have to choose which.

sections.title: Say Where It Is
sections.say: Every line is built on être, which you already have, so the only thing you are choosing is the position.

sections.title: Looking For The Keys
sections.say: The scene again, from the other side. This time you are the one who knows where they are.
sections.setting: Your flatmate is late and cannot find their keys. You can see them from where you are standing.

turns.ai: Tu as vu mes clés ? Je suis en retard !
turns.en: Have you seen my keys? I am late!
turns.user: Elles sont sur la table.
turns.userEn: They are on the table.

alts.fr: Elles sont sur la table de la cuisine.
alts.en: They are on the kitchen table.

turns.ai: Non, il n'y a rien sur la table. J'ai regardé.
turns.en: No, there is nothing on the table. I looked.
turns.user: Elles sont sous le journal.
turns.userEn: They are under the newspaper.

turns.ai: Ah ! Et mon sac, tu sais où il est ?
turns.en: Ah! And my bag, do you know where it is?
turns.user: Il est derrière la porte.
turns.userEn: It is behind the door.

alts.fr: Ton sac est derrière la porte.
alts.en: Your bag is behind the door.

turns.ai: Parfait. Et la boulangerie, c'est loin ?
turns.en: Perfect. And the bakery, is it far?
turns.user: Non, c'est à côté de la gare.
turns.userEn: No, it is next to the station.

alts.fr: C'est à côté de la gare.
alts.en: It is next to the station.

alts.fr: Non, c'est près de la gare.
alts.en: No, it is near the station.

alts.fr: C'est en face de la gare.

turns.ai: Merci ! Je passe au bureau après. À ce soir !
turns.en: Thanks! I am going to the office after. See you tonight!
turns.user: À ce soir !
turns.userEn: See you tonight!

sections.title: Before The Exam
sections.say: Eight cards. Rate each one as you actually found it and the hub will bring the weak ones back.

cards.front: The cat is on the box
cards.back: Le chat est sur la boîte.
cards.say: Le chat est sur la boîte.

cards.front: The cat is under the box
cards.back: Le chat est sous la boîte.
cards.say: Le chat est sous la boîte.

cards.front: The cat is in the box
cards.back: Le chat est dans la boîte.
cards.say: Le chat est dans la boîte.

cards.front: The cat is next to the box
cards.back: Le chat est à côté de la boîte.
cards.say: Le chat est à côté de la boîte.

cards.front: The cat is near the box
cards.back: Le chat est près de la boîte.
cards.say: Le chat est près de la boîte.

cards.front: I am at the office (le bureau)
The cat is next to the bed (le lit)
cards.back: Le chat est à côté du lit.
cards.say: Le chat est à côté du lit.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: Where is it
rounds.say: The five, described in English so there is one answer.

questions.q: The cat is inside the box, with the lid open. Which word?
questions.why: dans. Inside something is dans, and it is the reason the reference point in this lesson is a box: nothing is ever inside a chair. Sur would put the cat on the lid.

questions.q: The keys are underneath the newspaper, out of sight. Which word?
questions.why: sous. Underneath is sous, and this is the sentence the scene turned on. Sur would have you looking at the top of the paper, which is the ten minutes the scene spends.

questions.q: The garden is on the far side of the house, hidden from the street. Write the position word.
questions.why: derrière. Behind is derrière and devant is the near side. These two are opposites that sound nothing alike, so they are a reading and writing pair rather than an ear one.

questions.q: You want to say, in French: the cat is on the box. Write the whole sentence.
accept: Le chat est sur la boîte.
le chat est sur la boite
Le chat est sur la boite
questions.answer: Le chat est sur la boîte.
questions.why: Le chat est sur la boîte. Sur goes straight onto la boîte with nothing between them. Written as a whole sentence rather than a bare word, because a three-letter answer typed on its own is a coin toss rather than a test.

rounds.label: One word or a phrase
rounds.say: The de, and the four phrases that cannot do without it.

questions.q: Fill the gap: « Le café est à côté ___ la banque. »
questions.why: de. À côté is not a finished position word: the de is its last word. Leaving it out is understood perfectly by every French speaker, which is why nobody corrects it and why it survives for years.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Nous habitons près la gare. » Fix the sentence.
accept: Nous habitons près de la gare.
nous habitons pres de la gare
Nous habitons pres de la gare
questions.answer: Nous habitons près de la gare.
questions.why: près de la gare. Près is one of the four that end in de. This is the same error as the question before it arriving on a different phrase, and the two turn up together.

questions.q: Which of these position words does NOT need de after it?
questions.why: devant. It is one of the five single words that sit straight against the noun. The other three are phrases and every one of them ends in de, which is the only split this lesson asks you to keep.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Le chat est sur de la boîte. » Fix the sentence.
accept: Le chat est sur la boîte.
le chat est sur la boite
Le chat est sur la boite
questions.answer: Le chat est sur la boîte.
questions.why: Le chat est sur la boîte. This is the rule applied where it does not reach. Sur takes nothing at all, and adding de to it is the error people make in the week after this lesson rather than before it.

rounds.label: À and what follows it
rounds.say: Two of the four shapes change. Two do not.

questions.q: Fill the gap: « à + le = ___ »
questions.why: au. À and le do not stand side by side in French, so the two collapse into one word. This is not a shortcut you may decline: à le bureau does not exist.

questions.q: You want to say: I am at home. La maison is a la word. Which is French?
questions.why: Je suis à la maison. À plus la does not change at all, and both words stay exactly as they were. Half of this rule is knowing where it stops.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Je suis à le bureau. » Fix the sentence.
questions.why: Je suis au bureau. À and le collapse into au every time, with no exceptions and no slower careful version that keeps them apart.

questions.q: Somebody has learned that à + le is au and writes « je suis au école ». What went wrong?
opts: L'école takes à l', and that does not contract
questions.why: À l'école. The rule was applied to a word it does not cover: only le and les collapse, and l' is already a shortened article that à leaves alone. Over-applying this is more common after the lesson than before it.

rounds.label: The du you already met
rounds.say: The partitive lesson named this one. Here is where it was going.

questions.q: Fill the gap: « Le chat est à côté ___ lit. » Le lit is a le word.
questions.why: du. De and le collapse exactly as à and le do. This is the du the partitive lesson already named as the common one, arriving with a place behind it rather than a quantity.

questions.q: In « à côté du lit », what does du mean?
opts: To the, from à and le collapsing
It is a spelling of due
Of the, from de and le collapsing
questions.why: Of the. The partitive lesson's test still separates them: some bread makes sense, so je bois du café is that one, and some the bed does not, so this is the other.

questions.q: You want to say: the cat is near the trees. Les arbres is plural. Which is French?
opts: Le chat est près de les arbres
Le chat est près du arbres
Le chat est près des arbres
Le chat est près les arbres
questions.why: près des arbres. De and les collapse into des, which is the same two letters as the des you use for several things and a completely different job. Both collapses happen on their own rather than being chosen.

questions.q: Fill the gap: « La cuisine est à côté ___ la salle de bains. » La salle is a la word.
questions.why: de, unchanged. De plus la does not collapse, exactly as à plus la does not. The de is still compulsory; it simply stays as its own word.

rounds.label: The one pair to hear
rounds.say: Sur against sous, and nothing else, because nothing else in this lesson is hard to hear.

questions.q: Listen. Where are the keys?

audio.clip: Les clés sont sous le journal.

questions.why: Underneath. Sous is a plain oo with the lips pushed forward; sur is the tight ü with the tongue high. This is the pair the scene was built on and the only one here worth practising.

questions.q: Listen. Where is it?
questions.why: On the bed. Sur puts it on top and in plain view. Said at speed inside a sentence these two carry no stress of their own, which is what makes them close.

questions.q: Which pair sounds so similar that a French speaker could mishear it?
questions.why: sur and sous. Everything else in this lesson sounds nothing alike and never gets confused. Knowing which pair is genuinely hard means you can stop worrying about the ones that are not.

questions.q: Say it: the cat is under the box.
questions.target: Le chat est sous la boîte.
accept: Le chat est sous la boîte.
le chat est sous la boite
questions.answer: Le chat est sous la boîte.
questions.why: Le chat est sous la boîte. Push your lips forward for sous and keep it short. This is the half of the pair that goes wrong when you are being understood rather than when you are listening.

rounds.label: Say where things are
rounds.say: Everything at once, and one question about a mark you will never hear.

questions.q: Which of these means "he has a cat" rather than a place?
questions.why: Il a un chat, with no mark. A without the mark is the verb from the avoir lesson; à with it is the preposition. They sound identical, so this is a reading difference: a thing follows a, a place follows à.

questions.q: Describe the position: the pen is beside the notebook. Fill the gap: « Le stylo est ___ du cahier. »
questions.why: à côté. Beside is à côté de, and here the de has already collapsed with le into du, which is why the gap takes only the first two words. The phrase is never à côté on its own.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Le jardin est derrière de la maison. » Fix the sentence.
accept: Le jardin est derrière la maison.
le jardin est derriere la maison
Le jardin est derriere la maison
questions.answer: Le jardin est derrière la maison.
questions.why: derrière la maison. Derrière is one of the five and takes nothing after it. This is the over-applied de again, and it is the sign of a learner who has understood the rule and not yet found its edge.

questions.q: The bakery is across the road, facing the station. Which is French?
opts: La boulangerie est en face la gare
La boulangerie est en face à la gare
La boulangerie est face de la gare
La boulangerie est en face de la gare
questions.why: En face de la gare. One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first. En face is a phrase, so it takes the de, and this is the last of the four that behave that way.

sections.title: What You Have
sections.say: Six points, and the second one is the one to carry out of here.
sections.body: Nine ways to say where something is, one rule that separates them, and a collapse that happens on its own whenever à or de meets a le word.
points: Five words go straight onto the noun: sur, sous, dans, devant, derrière. Nothing goes between them and the thing.
One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first.
À côté de, près de, loin de and en face de all end in de, and leaving it out is understood perfectly, which is why nobody will ever correct it for you.
À plus le is au and à plus les is aux. À la and à l' do not change, and knowing where the rule stops matters as much as knowing it.
De plus le is du, which the partitive lesson already named, and de plus les is des. Both collide with words you know and the same test separates them.
Sur and sous are the only pair here your ear has to work at. Entre needs two things and chez needs a person, and you will meet both again.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that un and une follow it, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, and the elision of le and la in front of a vowel, introduced in a1.04
The plural of a noun, introduced in a1.03
The full present of être, which every production surface in this lesson is built on, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, and the a in il a, introduced in a1.07
des as the plural of un and une, introduced in a1.11
du as an amount of something, and that most du in French is not that one, introduced in a1.29
The possessives mon, ma and mes, which appear in imported sentences, introduced in a1.17
grammarIntroduced: The prepositions of place sur, sous, dans, devant and derrière, introduced here for the first time
The preposition à as a locative, beyond its use in fixed expressions
The distinction between simple and compound prepositions of place
That a compound preposition of place terminates in de, which is obligatory
The contraction of à with the definite article: à + le = au, à + les = aux
That à + la and à + l' do not contract, which bounds the rule
The contraction of de with the definite article in a locative rather than a partitive context
The formal identity of the locative du with the partitive du of a1.29, and of the locative des with the indefinite des of a1.11
entre as requiring two reference points, and chez as taking an animate complement

overview.introFr: Neuf façons de dire où se trouve quelque chose, et une règle qui les sépare en deux.

acts.title: Where is it
acts.milestone: One cat, one box, five positions, and you watched ten minutes go by over a single syllable.

acts.title: One word, or a phrase
acts.milestone: The split that separates you from a beginner, and the error it prevents.

acts.title: À, and where it stops
acts.milestone: Au and aux, and the two shapes that do nothing at all.

acts.title: The du you already met
acts.milestone: A collapse you were already taught, arriving with a place behind it.

acts.title: Say where things are
acts.milestone: Published French, the one pair worth hearing, and two words for later.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. Everything here carries straight into describing a house room by room.

lessons.reframe: One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for the wrong one of the five: says sur for sous, or devant for derrière. The ordinary beginner error, and the only one in this lesson that produces a sentence with the wrong meaning rather than a wrong shape.
Drops the de from a compound preposition: à côté la banque, près la gare. The most common error in this area and the one nobody ever corrects, because the meaning survives intact.

Applies the contraction where it does not reach: au école, à l'la maison, or adds de to one of the five. The error of a learner who has understood the rule and not yet found its edge, and it appears AFTER the lesson rather than before it.

Merges the de + le du with the partitive du taught in a1.29, or the de + les des with the indefinite plural des from a1.11. Reads à côté du lit as some of the bed, or simply stops trusting either word.
Mishears sur as sous or the reverse, then searches confidently in the wrong place. Costs nothing in grammar and everything in the moment, which is why it is the scene rather than a trap card.

Believes à and a must be audibly different and concludes their listening is at fault, or writes one for the other. Costs confidence rather than accuracy, which is why it gets its own drill and no ear question anywhere in the lesson.

drills.title: Which position?
pairs: The cat is on the box.
Le chat est sur la boîte.
The cat is under the box.
Le chat est sous la boîte.
The cat is in the box.
Le chat est dans la boîte.
The cat is in front of the box.
Le chat est devant la boîte.
The cat is behind the box.
Le chat est derrière la boîte.
drills.coach: Same cat, same box, five times. The only thing you are choosing is the short word in the middle, and each one puts the cat somewhere different.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: The cat is on the far side of the box, hidden from you. Which word?
drills.why: derrière. The far side is derrière and the near side is devant. These two are opposites that sound nothing alike, so this is a matter of remembering rather than hearing.

drills.title: Does it need de?
drills.coach: Look at the word after the position. If the position is one word, nothing goes between. If it is a phrase, its last word is de and it is not optional.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want to say: the pharmacy is opposite the bakery. Which is French?
opts: La pharmacie est en face la boulangerie
La pharmacie est en face de la boulangerie
La pharmacie est en face à la boulangerie
drills.why: en face de la boulangerie. En face is a phrase and its last word is de. Without it the sentence is still understood, which is exactly why the error lasts.

drills.title: Contract, or leave it?
drills.coach: Only le and les collapse. La stays and l' stays, because l' is already a shortened article. Half of this rule is knowing where it stops.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want to say: I am at school. École takes l'. Which is French?
drills.why: À l'école. L' is not le, so nothing collapses. Reaching for au here is the rule being applied one word too far.

drills.title: Which du is it?
drills.coach: Try putting "some" in front of the English. Some bread works, so that one is an amount. Some the bed does not, so that one is of the, and it is the one this lesson uses.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: In « Le chien dort à côté du feu », what is du doing?
opts: Standing in for de and le
Standing in for à and le
drills.why: De and le. À côté ends in de, the fire is a le word, and the two collapse. The partitive lesson already named this as the commoner of the two du.

drills.title: Sur, or sous?
drills.coach: Sur has the tight ü with your tongue high and your lips rounded. Sous is a plain oo with your lips pushed forward. Say both out loud once and the difference stops being subtle.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are told the keys are sous le journal. Where do you look?
drills.why: Underneath. Sous is under. This is the ten minutes the scene spends, and it is the only pair in the lesson where the ear is doing real work.

drills.title: A place, or a thing?
drills.coach: These sound identical and always will, so stop listening for the mark. What separates them is what follows: something owned after a, somewhere after à.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one means "she is at the office"?
drills.why: Elle est au bureau. A place, so à, and à plus le gives au. The first option puts the verb for having in front of a place, which is where this confusion actually shows up.

sheets.title: Saying where something is
contains: The five that go straight on
The four that end in de

sections.title: The only rule
sections.body: One word goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first. Sur, sous, dans, devant and derrière are single words and they sit straight against the noun. À côté de, près de, loin de and en face de are phrases, and the de is the last word of the phrase rather than the first word of the thing. Leaving it out is understood perfectly and marks you as a beginner, which is why it survives so long: nobody will ever correct it for you.

sections.title: entre and chez
sections.body: Entre needs two reference points rather than one: entre la banque et la poste. It goes straight onto the first noun, so it belongs with the five. Chez takes a person rather than a place and has no single English word: chez le médecin is at the doctor's, chez moi is at my place.

sheets.title: What à and de do to the word after them

sections.title: Where it stops
sections.body: Only le and les collapse. La never does and l' never does, because l' is already a shortened article. Half of this rule is knowing its edge: « au école » and « à l'la maison » are errors made by learners who have understood the rule, not by ones who have not met it.

sections.title: The du you already met
sections.body: The partitive lesson named this first and its test still works. Try putting "some" in front of the English: some bread makes sense, so je bois du café is an amount, and some the bed does not, so à côté du lit is de and le collapsed. Des collides the same way with the des you use for several things, and the same test separates them.

twoShapes.term: one word, or a phrase ending in de
twoShapes.title: Every preposition of place is one shape or the other
twoShapes.body: There are only two kinds here and you can tell them apart by eye. Some are a single word and they sit straight against the noun: sur la table, sous le lit, dans la boîte. Others are two or three words and the last one is always de: à côté de la table, près de la gare, en face de la banque. The de is not decoration and it is not optional. It is the last word of the preposition itself, in the same way that the of in "on top of" is part of the phrase and not something you could drop. Once you have noticed which shape you are holding, the rest of the sentence is the same either way.

examples.note: One word, straight onto the noun. Nothing between them.
The same cat and the same box, and this one needs the de.

theDroppedDe.title: À côté la banque is the error nobody corrects
theDroppedDe.body: This is the most common thing an English speaker gets wrong in this part of French, and the reason it survives is that it works. Say « le café est à côté la banque » and every French speaker in the room understands you perfectly and carries on. Nothing breaks, nobody repeats it back, and you have no way of finding out. It simply marks you as a beginner for as long as you keep saying it. English is what causes it: "next to the bank" has nothing between "to" and "the", so there is no habit to carry over. The fix is to learn the phrase with the de already inside it, as one unit, so there is never a moment where you are deciding whether to add it.

examples.note: The de, in published French, exactly where it belongs.
A different phrase, the same de, doing the same job.

theContraction.title: Two words that will not sit next to each other
theContraction.body: À and le do not appear side by side in French. Where you would expect « à le bureau » you get « au bureau », one word standing in for two, and where you would expect « à les enfants » you get « aux ». This is not something you choose to do and it is not a shortcut: the uncontracted version is simply not written or said. What matters as much as the rule is where it STOPS. À la does not change and à l' does not change, so « je suis à la maison » is exactly as it looks. Two of the four shapes contract and two do not, and a learner who over-applies this makes more errors than one who has never met it.

examples.note: à + le, and the two words are gone.
à + la, and nothing has happened at all.

theOtherDu.title: The partitive lesson named this one first
theOtherDu.body: You have seen du before, and you were told then that most of the du in French is not about an amount of anything. This is that du. De and le will not sit side by side any more than à and le will, so à côté de le lit comes out as à côté du lit, and the du there means of the rather than some. The test you were given still works: try putting "some" in front of the English. Some bread makes sense, so je bois du café is the other one. Some the bed does not, so à côté du lit is this one. Des behaves the same way and collides with the des you use for several things, and the same test separates them.

examples.note: de + le, with a place behind it rather than a quantity.
The same du in published French, meaning from the.

surOrSous.title: The one pair the ear genuinely struggles with
surOrSous.body: These two are opposites and they sound close enough to lose in ordinary speech. Sur ends in the tight ü sound with the tongue high and the lips rounded, and sous is a plain oo with the lips pushed forward. Said slowly they are obviously different. Said at speed inside a sentence, with an unstressed function word carrying no weight of its own, they are the most confusable pair in this lesson. It matters because the two describe opposite places, so mishearing one sends you looking in exactly the wrong spot, and you will not doubt what you heard. Every other pair in the lesson sounds nothing alike.

examples.note: On top of the newspaper, where you would see them.
Underneath it, where you would not.

theAccentPair.title: One is a place, the other is has
theAccentPair.body: À with the mark is the preposition and a without it is the verb: « il a » is he has, and you met that in the avoir lesson. They sound exactly the same, so nobody speaking French is ever choosing between them and nobody listening can tell them apart. This is a writing difference only. What separates them on the page is what comes next: a place or a thing after à, and something being owned after a. « Il a un chat » and « il est à Paris » can never be confused once you look past the single letter. The same is true of sur and sûr, where the mark is the difference between on and sure.

examples.note: The preposition, with the mark, and a place behind it.
The same word before a vowel, and still no contraction.

recorded.desc: THE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. « sur » AND « sous » ARE ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, adjacent, with no gap and no reset between them. This is the pair the learner's ear genuinely fails on and the pair the whole scene is built on. Recorded apart they become two performances and the learner compares the performances rather than the sounds. Read « Les clés sont sur le journal. » immediately followed by « Les clés sont sous le journal. », then « Il est sur le lit. » followed by « Il est sous le lit. » DO NOT LENGTHEN OR STRESS EITHER PREPOSITION. They are unstressed function words and the entire teaching point is that at ordinary speed they are hard to separate. A reader who helpfully clarifies them teaches the opposite of what the scene demonstrates. sur is /syʁ/, the tight ü with the tongue high and the lips rounded. sous is /su/, a plain oo with the lips pushed forward. Both short.
clipIds: Les clés sont sur le journal.
Les clés sont sous le journal.

recorded.desc: THE FIVE PREPOSITIONS RUN OVER ONE IDENTICAL PHRASE IN A SINGLE TAKE. « Le chat est sur la boîte, le chat est sous la boîte, le chat est dans la boîte, le chat est devant la boîte, le chat est derrière la boîte. » One breath group per sentence, one voice, one pace, read straight through as if reading a list. ONLY ONE WORD MOVES and that is the entire point of the hero screen: the learner has to hear that the frame is identical and the position word is the only variable. Do not vary the intonation between sentences and do not record these five separately. KEEP THE NASALS CLOSED. dans is /dɑ̃/ and devant is /də.vɑ̃/, and neither has an n sound behind the vowel at all. The app respells them DAHⁿ and duh-VAHⁿ deliberately, and both rows are repaired by this lesson from a shipped form that spelled a plain n.
clipIds: Le chat est sur la boîte.
Le chat est sous la boîte.
Le chat est dans la boîte.
Le chat est devant la boîte.
Le chat est derrière la boîte.

recorded.desc: EVERY COMPOUND PREPOSITION IS RECORDED AS A WHOLE PHRASE AND NEVER AS PARTS. « à côté de la boîte », « près de la boîte », « loin de la boîte », « en face de la boîte ». The rule this lesson teaches is that the de IS THERE, so a clip of « à côté » on its own teaches the exact error the lesson exists to prevent. Under no circumstances record the preposition without its de, and do not leave a pause before the de: it is unstressed and it belongs to the phrase in front of it, not to the noun behind. Record the contrast pair in ONE take: « Le chat est sur la boîte. » immediately followed by « Le chat est à côté de la boîte. » The frame is identical and the learner has to hear where the extra word sits. NEVER RECORD A PREPOSITION IN ISOLATION anywhere in this lesson. They are unstressed function words that only exist attached to a noun, and an isolated clip gives them a stress they never carry.
clipIds: Le chat est à côté de la boîte.
Le chat est près de la boîte.
Le chat est loin de la boîte.
Le chat est en face de la boîte.

recorded.desc: THE FOUR À ROWS IN ONE TAKE, THEN THE FOUR DE ROWS IN ONE TAKE. « Je suis au bureau. Je suis aux toilettes. Je suis à la maison. Je suis à l'école. » The learner has to hear that the first two are one word and the last two are two words, and that au and aux are the SAME SOUND. Say so by reading them identically: /o/ both times, with nothing on the x. The difference is written only, and a reader who sounds the x of aux invents a distinction French does not have. Then « à côté du lit, près des arbres, à côté de la porte, à côté de l'arbre », same instruction: du is /dy/ and des is /de/, and the last two keep de as its own unstressed word.

À AND A ADJACENT, IN ONE TAKE, AND STATED AS IDENTICAL. « il a » immediately followed by « à la maison », one voice, no gap. They ARE homophones and hearing them from one voice back to back is the only way to prove it to a learner who has been straining to hear a difference. DO NOT DIFFERENTIATE THEM IN ANY WAY. If the reader cannot resist marking the preposition, record the vowel once and use the same audio for both: that is a more truthful clip than a performed difference, and a learner who hears an invented distinction will spend a year listening for it. Then « il a un chat » followed by « il est à Paris », which is the pair that shows what actually separates them: a thing after a, a place after à. Same instruction again for « sur la table » and « je suis sûr », which are close enough that context does the work.

THE TWO DU, ADJACENT, IN ONE TAKE, READ IDENTICALLY. « à côté du lit » immediately followed by « je bois du café ». These are the same two letters doing two different jobs and they are pronounced exactly the same way, /dy/. The learner met the second one in the partitive lesson and this lesson names the first. Read them with no difference at all, because there is none: the separation is grammatical and contextual, never acoustic. Then « près des arbres » followed by « des amis », the same instruction for the des collision. Note that des arbres carries a liaison z onto the vowel and des amis does too, so both are /de.z/ and the parallel is exact.

THE SCENE'S SPOKEN LINES, AT ORDINARY CONVERSATIONAL SPEED. Camille is putting her coat on and half out of the room; she is not delivering a lesson. « Les clés sont sous le journal. » MUST BE READ CASUALLY AND UNSTRESSED, because the whole scene depends on the learner mishearing it. A clear, careful reading destroys the beat. Her later line « Sous ! Sous le journal. Soulève-le. » is the opposite: louder, clearer, slightly impatient, the way anybody repeats themselves. The contrast between the two readings IS the scene.
clipIds: Les clés sont sous le journal.

lessons.title: Questions oui / non
lessons.intro: Three ways to ask the same yes-or-no question, and the choice between them is about the person in front of you rather than the sentence. This is how to ask with your voice, with a block on the front, and by swapping the words round, plus which one to reach for when you cannot tell.

sections.title: The Question That Put A Jacket On
sections.frSub: As-tu faim ou tu as faim ?

say.text: Every word correct, nobody corrects anything, and the evening goes slightly cooler. Watch which form.

setting.place: A narrow kitchen, two people cooking, a chopping board between them

beats.text: Théo's kitchen in Lyon. You have known him a month, you are cooking together, and it is going well.
You want to ask whether he is hungry yet. You know how to do this. You learned the neat version, the one that looked most like proper French.

beats.speaker: Théo
beats.fr: Bon, on mange vers huit heures ?
beats.en: Right, shall we eat around eight?
beats.stage: He is chopping something and not looking up. Nothing rides on this at all.

beats.prompt: You want to ask if he is hungry now. Which line do you say?

options.en: the tidy one you learned from a book
the one you have heard people actually say

followUp.works: Yes. Now watch the other one, because it is the one that looks more correct on paper.
followUp.breaks: Nothing about that is wrong. Watch what it does to the room.

beats.speaker: You
beats.en: (Perfect French. The kind that gets full marks)

beats.speaker: Théo
