beats.stage: He looks up for a second. Then he says merci, which he has not said to you all evening, and goes back to the board.

beats.heading: Nothing you said was wrong
beats.body: As-tu faim ? is correct French and Théo understood it completely. That is the problem. It is the form you would use in a letter, and he heard you put a jacket on.

wrong.en: Correct, careful, and aimed at somebody you are keeping at arm's length

right.en: The same question, asked of a friend

beats.coach: Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. And a friend in a kitchen is one of the two places you would not choose the careful one.

beats.speaker: Théo, later, to somebody else
beats.fr: Tu as faim ? On mange bientôt.
beats.en: Are you hungry? We are eating soon.
beats.stage: Said to his flatmate, three feet away, about the same food. Same question, and it sounds nothing like yours.

beats.text: Both of you asked the same thing. One of you sounded like a friend. The next twenty-five minutes are about which one to reach for.

closing.text: Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. That is the next twenty-five minutes.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the first one is a habit rather than a list.

goals.t: Ask any yes-or-no question three ways
goals.s: One question, three shapes, and all three mean exactly the same thing.

goals.t: Pick the right one for the person in front of you
goals.s: This is the part that is not in the grammar. It is the part the room notices.
A closed list rather than a pattern, because you can only conjugate two verbs so far.

goals.t: Answer with oui, non, peut-être and si
goals.s: Three of those are easy. The fourth only exists because of a question with a not in it.

sections.title: One Question, Three Shapes
sections.hint: Five cards before any table.
sections.say: Five cards, and the third one is the one to hold on to if you only keep one.

cards.label: the same question
cards.head: Three ways to ask one thing
cards.fr: Tu es prêt ? · Est-ce que tu es prêt ? · Es-tu prêt ?
cards.sub: Are you ready? · Are you ready? · Are you ready?
cards.body: Those three lines are the same question. Not similar, not roughly equivalent. Identical in meaning, and a French speaker hearing any of them would answer exactly the same way.

cards.label: so what separates them
cards.head: Who you are saying it to
cards.body: The difference is not what you are asking. It is who is in front of you and how careful you are being with them. That is the whole lesson, and it is the part a table of three forms cannot tell you.

cards.label: the one that always works
cards.head: Est-ce que is never wrong
cards.sub: [ess-kuh tü eh PREH] · Are you ready?
cards.body: Three little words on the front and you have a question. It is correct with a friend, correct in a letter, correct in an exam. Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices.

cards.label: and the other two
cards.head: Both of them say something extra
cards.body: Letting your voice rise says you are relaxed. Swapping the words round says you are being careful. Neither is more correct than the other and neither is more correct than est-ce que. They are choices, and you make them on purpose.

cards.label: what that gives you
cards.head: A safe one and two you reach for
cards.body: You never have to freeze. If you do not know what the situation wants, est-ce que covers it and nobody notices anything. When you do know what it wants, you have two ways to say so without changing a single word of the question itself.

sections.title: The Same Question, Three Ways
sections.say: Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. Read down the first column. Same question every time, and only the shape moves.
cols: who you would say it to

detail.title: Just your voice
detail.body: [tü eh PREH] Nothing moves. This is a plain statement with your voice going up at the end, and it is how most yes-or-no questions get asked out loud. You have been reading these since your first lesson without anybody naming it.

detail.title: The est-ce que block
detail.body: [ess-kuh tü eh PREH] Three words bolted on and nothing inside the sentence moves. Tu es prêt is still sitting there untouched behind them. This one is correct in every situation there is, which is why it is worth making your default.

detail.title: Swapped round
detail.body: [ay-TÜ PREH] The verb and the person change places and a hyphen holds them together. It reads as careful, which is right in a letter and slightly stiff across a kitchen table. This is the one from the scene.

sections.title: The One You Already Use
sections.hint: Five cards, and none of this is new.
sections.say: You have been doing this since your very first lesson. Nobody told you it was a method.

cards.label: you have met this
cards.head: You have been reading these for eighteen lessons
cards.fr: Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ?
cards.sub: Are you here for the conference?
cards.body: That line is from the être lesson, where it is asked four separate times. Nobody there called it a question form. It is one, it is this one, and you have been understanding it without being taught it.

cards.label: what actually happens
cards.head: Nothing moves
cards.fr: Tu es prêt. · Tu es prêt ?
cards.body: Same four words, same order, same sounds. Your voice goes down at the end of the first one and up at the end of the second one. That is the entire difference and there is nothing else to learn here.

cards.label: where it lives
cards.head: Out loud, with people you are relaxed with
cards.body: This is the commonest way a yes-or-no question gets asked in real speech, and the most casual of the three. In writing it turns up in messages to friends and almost nowhere else, because writing is where people are careful.

cards.label: the catch, and it is on the page
cards.head: Written down, one mark separates them
cards.fr: Tu es prêt. · Tu es prêt ?
cards.sub: a full stop · a question mark
cards.body: Out loud you can hear which is which. On the page the only thing between a statement and a question is the mark at the end, and French puts a space before it. Leave it off and you have written a statement.

cards.label: so when not to
cards.head: It is the one that can be missed
cards.body: If your voice stays flat, the question lands as a statement and gets treated as one. That is the one risk this method carries, and it is why the other two exist: they put the question into the words, where it cannot be lost.

sections.title: Up Or Down
sections.say: Three pairs. In every one, the words are identical and only the direction of your voice changes.

lines.fr: Tu es prêt. · Tu es prêt ?
lines.en: a statement, then a question, and the words never move

lines.fr: Tu as faim ? · Tu as besoin d'aide ?
lines.en: two real questions asked with nothing but the voice

lines.fr: Tu es canadien ? · Vous êtes anglais ?
lines.en: the same, to one friend and then to somebody you are being polite with

questions.q: What is the difference between « Tu es prêt. » and « Tu es prêt ? » out loud?
opts: The direction of the voice on the last syllable
The question stresses the first word
Nothing, you can only tell in writing
questions.why: The direction of the voice at the end. Up is a question, down is a statement. No word changes and no word moves, which is what makes this the only method that leaves no trace on the page except the mark at the end.

questions.q: You say a question with a completely flat voice. What happens?
opts: It still works, French marks it another way
It is heard as a statement
It sounds like a different question
questions.why: It is heard as a statement, because here the contour is the only thing carrying the question. That is the one real risk it has, and it is why the other two methods exist: both put the question into the words themselves.

questions.q: In writing, what separates a statement from this kind of question?
opts: A question mark, with a space before it
questions.why: A question mark, and in French a space goes before it. That mark does all the work alone, which is why this method is common in speech and rare in writing, where people reach for a form that shows the question in the words.

sections.title: Statement Or Question?
sections.say: Four decisions. The first three are about your ear and the last one is about the page.

groups.label: The pair that only your ear can split

items.en: Are you ready? (to one person you are close to)

check.q: Somebody says four words to you and their voice rises at the end. Are they telling you something or asking you something?
opts: You cannot tell without more words
check.why: Asking you. A rising voice on the last syllable is a question and nothing else needs to happen. This is the whole of the first method, and it is the one French speakers use most in ordinary conversation.

groups.label: Questions in the wild, with no method bolted on

items.fr: Tu es prêt pour l'examen de demain ?
items.en: Are you ready for tomorrow's exam?

check.q: Neither of those has est-ce que and neither has swapped words. How do you know they are questions?
opts: The verb is in a special form
The mark at the end, and out loud the voice going up
check.why: The mark at the end on the page, and the rising voice out loud. Both of these were published as ordinary French long before this lesson existed, which is the best evidence there is that this method is not a shortcut.

check.q: Both of those use the voice alone. What changed between them?
opts: One is a question and one is not
check.why: Who is being spoken to: tu for somebody you are close to, vous for somebody you are careful with. The method did not move. Choosing tu or vous and choosing a question shape are two separate decisions, and this lesson is about the second.

check.q: You are writing to somebody and you want to ask a question. Why is the voice method a poor choice here?
opts: It is grammatically wrong in writing
A reader has no voice to hear, so only the mark at the end carries it
check.why: A reader has no voice to hear. Everything this method relies on happens in the air, so on paper one small mark does all of it. It is not wrong in writing, only weaker than a form that puts the question into the words.

sections.title: Three Words On The Front
sections.hint: Five cards on the one that always works.
sections.say: Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. Five cards on why that is true.

cards.label: what it is
cards.head: A block, bolted on
cards.fr: Tu es prêt. · Est-ce que tu es prêt ?
cards.sub: a statement · the same statement, asked
cards.body: Take any statement. Put est-ce que in front of it. That is a question now. The statement behind it does not change in any way: same words, same order, still sitting there.

cards.label: nothing inside moves
cards.head: This is why it is the safe one
cards.sub: [ess-kuh voo zet PREH] · Are you ready?
cards.body: The pronoun changed from tu to vous and the block did not care. You do not have to remember a form, work out where a hyphen goes, or decide whether a letter needs adding. You put three words on the front and stop.

cards.label: where it works
cards.head: Everywhere, and that is not an exaggeration
cards.body: Spoken, written, to a friend, to a stranger, in an exam, on a form. There is no situation where est-ce que is wrong, and no other question form in French can be described that way. Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices.

cards.label: in the wild
cards.head: Ordinary French, nobody arranged it
cards.fr: Est-ce que tu es français ? · Est-ce que c'est loin d'ici ?
cards.sub: Are you French? · Is it far from here?
cards.body: Both of those were in the corpus long before this lesson was written. Neither is a teaching example. This is what the form looks like when somebody is simply asking a question and not thinking about which method they are using.

cards.label: one small thing
cards.head: Say it flat and fast
cards.body: It is three unstressed syllables that run together into something like ess-kuh. Nobody leans on it and nobody pauses after it. It exists to get you into the question, and the weight of the sentence lands where it always would, on the end.

sections.title: The Fourth Time You Have Seen This
sections.frSub: Est-ce qu'il, est-ce qu'elle, est-ce qu'on
sections.say: Three words where the e gets cut. Tap any of them, and the reason is one you already have.

detail.title: The e of que is gone
detail.body: [ess-KEEL eh PREH] Est-ce que il would put two vowel sounds head to head, and French will not do it. So the e is cut and an apostrophe marks the place. Nothing else about the sentence moves.

detail.title: The same cut, in front of elle
detail.body: [ess-KEL eh PREHT] In fast speech ess-KEEL and ess-KEL sit very close together, and this is the one pair in the lesson your ear has genuine work to do on. Everything else here you can see.
detail.say: Est-ce qu'il est prêt ? Est-ce qu'elle est prête ?

detail.title: Two things happen at once
detail.body: [ess-kohⁿ-NEH PREH] The e is cut, and then the n of on carries across onto est, so the middle comes out as kohⁿ-NEH. You met the second half of that in the liaison lesson.

cells: You have three of these already
rows.say: Est-ce qu'il y a un supermarché près d'ici ?

detail.title: The same objection, four times over
detail.body: la amie became l'amie: the little word was cut. ma amie became mon amie: the word was swapped. ne ai became n'ai, cut again. And est-ce que il becomes est-ce qu'il, cut again. Four rules, one objection: two vowel sounds may not meet.
detail.say: Est-ce qu'il y a un supermarché près d'ici ?

sections.title: Build It From A Statement
sections.say: Four builds. Each one starts from a statement you can already say.

check.q: You have the statement « Tu es prêt. » and you want the est-ce que question. What do you change inside the statement?
check.why: Nothing at all. That is the whole appeal of this method: the statement goes in untouched and the three words sit in front of it. Every other question form in French asks you to move something.

check.q: You want to ask whether he is ready. Which of these do you write?
check.why: Est-ce qu'il. The e of que is cut and an apostrophe stands where it was. This is the same repair that turned la amie into l'amie, and it happens for the same reason: two vowel sounds cannot sit against each other.

items.fr: Est-ce qu'il y a un supermarché près d'ici ?
items.en: Is there a supermarket near here?

items.fr: Est-ce qu'il y a du vent aujourd'hui ?

check.q: Both of those cut the e of que. What decided it?
opts: They are both questions about weather
The next word starts with a vowel sound
check.why: The next word starts with a vowel sound. It happens to be il in both, but the rule is about the sound rather than the word: anything starting with a vowel does the same, and nothing starting with a consonant does it.

check.q: You are writing to a landlord you have never met and you want to ask whether the flat is available. Is est-ce que acceptable here?
opts: No, it is too casual for writing
Yes. It is correct in every situation there is
Only if you use vous as well
No, writing needs the swapped-round form
check.why: Yes. Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. A landlord would not blink at it. The swapped-round form would also be fine and sound slightly more formal, which is a choice rather than a rule.

sections.title: Swapping Them Round
sections.hint: Five cards on the careful one.
sections.say: Five cards, and the last one is a fact about the corpus rather than about French.

cards.label: what happens
cards.head: The two words change places
cards.body: Tu es becomes Es-tu. The person and the verb swap, and a hyphen joins them into one unit. Everything after that stays exactly where it was.

cards.label: the hyphen
cards.head: It is not optional
cards.body: Without the hyphen this is not a question, it is a typo. The hyphen is what tells a reader that the two words have been deliberately swapped rather than accidentally jumbled, and it is the one part of this method you cannot hear.

cards.label: where it belongs
cards.head: Careful writing, and being formal out loud
cards.sub: Do you have a smaller size?
cards.body: A shop assistant to a customer, a letter, a form, an exam. It is the form that says you are taking care. Said to a friend in a kitchen it lands the way the scene landed it, which is not wrong and is very noticeable.

cards.label: the closed list
cards.head: Twelve forms, and you can learn all of them
cards.body: You can conjugate two verbs so far, so there are exactly twelve of these. That is a list you finish rather than a pattern you extend, and the next screen has all of it. A third verb will swap the same way.

cards.label: and here is the evidence
cards.head: The corpus has none of these
cards.sub: both written for this lesson, because neither existed
cards.body: This app holds twenty-seven thousand sentences of ordinary French, and not one inverts these everyday questions. Es-tu prêt ? and As-tu faim ? had to be written from scratch, while their voice-only twins were already there. That gap is the register, measured.

sections.title: All Twelve
sections.say: Six rows, two verbs. Read across and only the verb changes. Tap any cell to hear it.

detail.title: tu: es-tu and as-tu
detail.body: Es-tu prêt ? As-tu faim ? Neither of these needs anything added. The verb already ends in a consonant, so it runs straight into the pronoun.

detail.title: il: est-il and a-t-il
detail.body: Est-il prêt ? A-t-il faim ? The t in the avoir form means nothing. A ends in a vowel and il starts with one, so a t goes between them. There is no such word as a-il.

detail.title: elle: est-elle and a-t-elle
detail.body: Est-elle prête ? A-t-elle faim ? The t in the avoir form means nothing. A ends in a vowel and il starts with one, so a t goes between them. There is no such word as a-il.

detail.title: nous: sommes-nous and avons-nous
detail.body: Sommes-nous prêts ? Avons-nous faim ? Neither of these needs anything added. The verb already ends in a consonant, so it runs straight into the pronoun.

detail.title: vous: êtes-vous and avez-vous
detail.body: Êtes-vous prêts ? Avez-vous faim ? Neither of these needs anything added. The verb already ends in a consonant, so it runs straight into the pronoun.

detail.title: ils: sont-ils and ont-ils
detail.body: Sont-ils prêts ? Ont-ils faim ? Both of these wake up a t that is silent in the statement. Ils sont is said eel-SOHⁿ and Sont-ils is said sohⁿ-TEEL, so the same two words rearrange completely.

sections.title: Why A-t-il And Not Est-t-il
sections.frSub: Le t qui ne veut rien dire
sections.say: Two rows. One of them needs a t put in and the other already has one. Tap both.

detail.title: est already ends in a consonant. a does not.
detail.body: [eh-TEEL PREH] against [ah-TEEL FAHⁿ]. Est ends in a t of its own, so nothing is added. A ends in a vowel and il begins with one, so a t goes in to keep them apart. It means nothing at all.

detail.title: The same test, on the rest of the list
detail.body: [ah-vohⁿ-NOO FAHⁿ] needs nothing, because avons ends in a consonant and nous begins with one. [ah-TEL FAHⁿ] needs the t for the same reason A-t-il does. Those two are the only places in all twelve forms where anything is inserted.

cells: Y a-t-il des noix dans ce plat ?
rows.say: Y a-t-il des noix dans ce plat ?

detail.title: Somebody asking about a menu
detail.body: Y a-t-il des noix dans ce plat ? Are there nuts in this dish? The same inserted t, in a sentence written for a restaurant lesson rather than for this one. It does exactly the job it does in A-t-il faim ?, and nobody arranged it.
detail.say: Y a-t-il des noix dans ce plat ?

detail.title: You have had this one since the numbers lesson
detail.body: Quel âge a-t-il ? How old is he? The same inserted t again. The first two words of that question are somebody else's lesson and are coming next; the a-t-il in the middle of it is this one.

sections.title: Five Traps
sections.say: Five things people write in their first month with these forms, one per screen.

errors.wrong: Writing « Es tu prêt ? » with no hyphen.
errors.why: The hyphen is compulsory. Without it the two words look accidentally out of order rather than deliberately swapped, and the sentence reads as a typo. You cannot hear this one, which is why it survives so long in writing.

errors.wrong: Writing « A-il faim ? » with no t.
errors.why: A ends in a vowel and il begins with one, so a t goes between them. It means nothing and exists only to keep the two vowels apart. Est-il needs no such thing, because est already ends in a consonant.

errors.wrong: Writing « Est-ce que il est prêt ? ».
errors.why: The e of que is cut in front of a vowel and an apostrophe marks where it went. You have watched French dodge this collision three times before: l'amie, mon amie, n'ai. This is the fourth.

errors.wrong: Writing « Est-ce que es-tu prêt ? », using two methods at once.
errors.right: Writing « Est-ce que tu es prêt ? » or « Es-tu prêt ? ».
errors.why: Pick one. Est-ce que already made it a question, so swapping the words as well is asking twice. This is the commonest thing that happens once all three methods are on the table, and it is the reason the safe default is worth naming.

errors.wrong: Reaching for « Ai-je faim ? » to complete the list.
errors.why: Nobody says ai-je. It is not in a single one of the twenty-seven thousand sentences this app holds, and drilling a form nobody uses builds an instinct you then have to unlearn. The je question goes through est-ce que, which is what it is for.

sections.title: Who Is In Front Of You
sections.say: Four situations. The question is the same every time and the right shape is not.

check.q: You are cooking with a friend and you want to ask if they are hungry. Which do you say?
opts: Both sound the same to a friend
Neither, you need est-ce que here
check.why: Tu as faim ? The swapped-round form is correct French and it is what the opening scene used. It sounds careful, and being careful with a close friend is itself a message. Est-ce que tu as faim ? would also be fine.

groups.label: A letter to somebody you have never met

items.en: Do you have a smaller size?

check.q: You are writing to a landlord you have never met to ask whether the flat is still available. Which shape fits best?
opts: The voice-only one, with a question mark
It does not matter in writing
Only est-ce que is allowed in letters
check.why: The swapped-round one. Writing is where care shows and this is the form that shows it. Est-ce que would be correct too, and plainer. The voice-only one is odd here: in writing there is no voice, and the question rests on one mark.

groups.label: You have no idea what the situation wants

check.q: You are talking to somebody new and you cannot tell how formal to be. Which do you reach for?
opts: The swapped-round one, to be safe
The voice-only one, to be friendly
check.why: Est-ce que. Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. It is the only one that says nothing about how close you are, so it cannot be the wrong temperature. The other two make a claim you are not yet able to make.

check.q: Those two sentences ask the identical thing and both swap the words round. What is different?
opts: One is a question and one is not
Who is being asked: one person you know, or somebody you are being polite with
check.why: Who is being asked. As-tu is the tu form and Avez-vous is the vous form, and both were published as ordinary French. The method did not change between them: choosing tu or vous and choosing a question shape are two separate decisions.

sections.title: Answering
sections.hint: Five cards, and the fourth word is the interesting one.
sections.say: Three of these you already have. The fourth exists only because of questions with a not in them.

cards.label: the two easy ones
cards.head: oui and non
cards.fr: Oui, je suis prêt. · Non, je suis fatigué. · Oui, j'ai faim.
cards.sub: [wee zhuh swee PREH] · [nohⁿ zhuh swee fah-tee-GAY]
cards.body: Either word is a complete answer on its own. Adding a reason is friendlier and is never required. Notice that neither answer needed a negative: saying why is easier than saying not.

cards.label: the realistic third
cards.head: peut-être
cards.body: The answer people actually give most of the time. It is two words joined by a hyphen and it works as a complete reply on its own, exactly like oui and non.

cards.label: the fourth word
cards.head: si, when the question has a not in it
cards.fr: Tu n'es pas prêt ? · Si, je suis prêt.
cards.sub: [tü neh pah PREH] · [see zhuh swee PREH]
cards.body: Somebody asks you a question with a not in it and they have got it wrong. You want to push back. French does not use oui for that: it keeps a separate word, and si is it. Oui there would sound like agreement.

cards.label: and the same three letters twice more
cards.head: si is three different words
cards.body: This si has nothing to do with the si that means if, which you will meet properly later, and nothing to do with the si in si grand, meaning so big. Three separate words wearing the same two letters, with no rule connecting them.

cards.label: the two tags
cards.head: n'est-ce pas ? and non ?
cards.fr: Ton chat miaule toujours le soir, n'est-ce pas ?
cards.sub: [NEHS PAH] · Your cat always meows in the evening, doesn't it?
cards.body: Stick either onto the end of a statement and you are asking the other person to agree. They are tags rather than a fourth method: the sentence in front is still a statement. n'est-ce pas is careful and non ? is casual.

sections.title: All Three, In French Nobody Arranged
sections.say: Six sentences, none written for this lesson. Tap any of them to hear which method it chose.

detail.title: The most ordinary question there is
detail.body: Tu as besoin d'aide ? Do you need help? Four words, nothing added, nothing moved. This is what a question looks like most of the time when nobody is being careful.

detail.title: The safe block, doing its job
detail.body: Est-ce que c'est loin d'ici ? Is it far from here? Three words on the front of c'est loin d'ici, which is a statement you could say on its own.

cells: Est-ce qu'il y a un supermarché près d'ici ?
rows.say: Est-ce qu'il y a un supermarché près d'ici ?

detail.title: And with the e cut
detail.body: Est-ce qu'il y a un supermarché près d'ici ? Is there a supermarket near here? A vowel follows, so the e goes. Nobody wrote this sentence to demonstrate the rule; it is just what the rule looks like when it is not being taught.
detail.say: Est-ce qu'il y a un supermarché près d'ici ?

detail.title: A shop assistant to a customer
detail.body: Avez-vous la taille en dessous ? Do you have a smaller size? Avez-vous rather than Vous avez, because this is somebody being professionally careful with a stranger. That is exactly the situation the form is for.

detail.title: The silent t waking up
detail.body: Sont-ils canadiens ? Are they Canadian? Ils sont is said eel-SOHⁿ with the t silent. Swap them and the t arrives: sohⁿ-TEEL. The letters were there all along.

detail.title: es-tu, outside this lesson
detail.body: Es-tu d'accord avec cette décision ? Do you agree with this decision? One of the twelve, in a sentence nobody wrote for you. Note how much weight it carries: this is a question you would ask when the answer matters.

cells: Avons-nous assez de temps pour visiter le musée ?
rows.say: Avons-nous assez de temps pour visiter le musée ?

detail.title: avons-nous, and it is the rarest of the twelve
detail.body: Avons-nous assez de temps pour visiter le musée ? Do we have enough time to visit the museum? The nous form turns up least often of all twelve, and when it does it usually sounds like this: careful, and about a plan.
detail.say: Avons-nous assez de temps pour visiter le musée ?

cells: Ton chat miaule toujours le soir, n'est-ce pas ?
rows.say: Ton chat miaule toujours le soir, n'est-ce pas ?

detail.title: Not a fourth method
detail.body: Ton chat miaule toujours le soir, n'est-ce pas ? Your cat always meows in the evening, doesn't it? The part before the comma is an ordinary statement. The tag on the end turns it into a request for agreement.
detail.say: Ton chat miaule toujours le soir, n'est-ce pas ?

sections.title: The Viewing
sections.say: One flat viewing, three people asking questions, and each of them picks a different shape.
sections.text: Three people are looking at the same small flat within an hour of each other, and the agent standing by the window hears the same handful of questions all morning. The first is a student who has come straight from a lecture and is already halfway through the kitchen before she asks anything. « Est-ce que le chauffage est compris ? » It is the shape she uses for everything, and it does not tell the agent one thing about how she feels about the flat. The second is a man in his fifties who has brought a folder, and who waits until he is standing still to ask. « Avez-vous une autre visite cet après-midi ? » Nothing about that is warmer or colder than the student, only more careful, and the agent answers it more carefully in turn. The third arrives with a friend and asks the friend rather than the agent, halfway down the corridor and without stopping. « Tu es prêt ? » Later, at the door, the agent tells him the flat has been taken twice this month already and he does not believe it. « Tu n'es pas sérieux ? » And the agent, who is entirely serious, does not say oui. « Si. »

glossary.note: Three words on the front of a statement. Correct with anybody, which is why she uses it for everything.
The swapped-round form, with vous. Careful rather than cold, and the agent matches it.
Voice only, said to a friend on the move. Nothing added and nothing swapped.
The question had a not in it and the agent is disagreeing with the not. Oui would have sounded like agreement.

questions.q: Three people ask questions in three different shapes. What is that telling you about them?
questions.a: How careful each one is being, and nothing else. All three questions are correct French and all three would be understood identically. The student uses the shape that fits any situation, the man with the folder uses the careful one, and the third uses the relaxed one because he is talking to a friend rather than to the agent. The shape reports on the relationship rather than on the question.

questions.q: Why does the agent answer the man with the folder more carefully?
questions.a: Because he asked carefully. Register tends to be matched: a swapped-round question invites a considered answer in the same way that a question asked on the move invites a quick one. Nothing obliges the agent to do this and it happens anyway, which is why choosing the wrong shape has an effect even though nobody comments on it.

questions.q: The agent says si rather than oui at the end. What forced that?
questions.a: The not in the question. « Tu n'es pas sérieux ? » contains a negative, and the agent wants to contradict it. Oui would have read as agreeing that he was not serious. Si is the word French keeps for exactly this and it has no other job: it only appears when there is a negative to push back against.

sections.title: The Shapes, Banked
sections.say: Three decks. The blocks, the twelve swapped forms, and the four answers.

cards.en: put it on the front of anything and it is a question
the same, in front of il, elle and on
on the end of a statement: right? The careful tag
the same job, casual, and what people actually say
have/has il, with the t that means nothing
have/has elle, with the t that means nothing
maybe, and the one people give most
yes, but only when the question had a not in it

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front, and every front says which shape it wants. Say the French before you flip.

cards.front: Are you ready? (est-ce que in front)
Are you hungry? (est-ce que in front)
Are you ready? (est-ce que in front)
Is he ready? (est-ce que, before a vowel)
Is she ready? (est-ce que, before a vowel)
Are we ready? (est-ce que, before a vowel)
You are ready. (a statement, voice down)
You are not ready? (a question with a not in it)
Yes I am, actually. (answering a not)

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Five lines. The first two are the same four words, and one of them is a question.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: Every line is a whole question or a whole answer. The rising voice on the short ones is half the mark.

sections.title: The Same Kitchen, Going Better
sections.say: One conversation and you hold up your half. Every turn is a question or an answer to one.
sections.setting: Théo's kitchen again, a fortnight later. This time you are the one who arrives, and his flatmate is there too.

turns.ai: Salut ! Entre. Tu as faim ?
turns.en: Hi! Come in. Are you hungry?
turns.user: Oui, un peu.
turns.userEn: Yes, a little.

turns.ai: Voici Camille, ma coloc. Vous vous connaissez ?
turns.en: This is Camille, my flatmate. Do you two know each other?
turns.user: Non. Est-ce que vous etes de Lyon ?
turns.userEn: No. Are you from Lyon?

alts.fr: Non, pas encore. Est-ce que vous etes d'ici ?
alts.en: No, not yet. Are you from here?

turns.ai: Non, je suis de Nantes. Et toi, tu es francais ?
turns.en: No, I am from Nantes. And you, are you French?
turns.user: Non, je suis anglais.
turns.userEn: No, I am English.

alts.fr: Non. Et vous, vous etes francaise ?
alts.en: No. And you, are you French?

turns.ai: Ah ! Theo dit que tu n'es pas tres bavard.
turns.en: Ah! Théo says you are not very talkative.
turns.user: Si, je suis bavard !
turns.userEn: Yes I am, actually!

alts.en: Yes I am! I am very talkative.

turns.ai: Bon. On mange dans dix minutes. Vous etes prets ?
turns.en: Right. We are eating in ten minutes. Are you ready?
turns.user: Oui, nous sommes prets.
turns.userEn: Yes, we are ready.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: Which of the three is never the wrong choice?
cards.back: est-ce que. Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices.

cards.front: You want to ask a friend if they are hungry.
cards.back: Tu as faim ? Voice up at the end, nothing else.

cards.front: You are writing to a stranger and want to ask if they are ready.
cards.back: Es-tu prêt ? The careful shape, and writing is where care shows.

cards.front: How do you make a question out of « Tu es prêt. » without moving a word?
cards.back: Tu es prêt ? Let your voice rise, and write a question mark.

cards.front: What happens inside the sentence when you add est-ce que?
cards.back: Nothing at all. The statement goes in untouched.

cards.front: Est-ce que, in front of il.
cards.back: Est-ce qu'il est prêt ? The e is cut and an apostrophe takes its place.

cards.front: Why is there a t in A-t-il faim ?
cards.back: A ends in a vowel and il starts with one. The t keeps them apart and means nothing.

cards.front: Why is there no t in Est-il prêt ?
cards.back: Est already ends in a consonant, so nothing needs adding.

cards.front: Is the hyphen in Es-tu optional?
cards.back: No. Without it the sentence reads as a typo rather than a question.

cards.front: The vous form of the swapped-round être question.
cards.back: Êtes-vous prêts ? The one you will hear most, because vous and care travel together.

cards.front: The nous form of the swapped-round avoir question.
cards.back: Avons-nous faim ? No t needed: avons already ends in a consonant.
No. Nobody says it. Use est-ce que j'ai faim.

cards.front: Somebody asks « Tu n'es pas prêt ? » and you are ready. What do you say?
cards.back: Si, je suis prêt. Not oui, because you are disagreeing with the not.

cards.front: Can you use est-ce que and swap the words round in one question?
cards.back: No. Est-ce que already asked it. Pick one.

cards.front: What decides which of the three you use?
cards.back: Who is in front of you, and how careful you are being. Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched an evening cool by one degree because a question was asked too carefully, and nothing in that sentence was wrong. Since then you have taken one question apart into three shapes that mean exactly the same thing, found that the difference between a statement and a question can be nothing but the direction of your voice, learned a block you can bolt onto anything without moving a word, and closed a list of twelve swapped-round forms including two with a letter in the middle that means nothing at all. You also have a word for yes that only works when somebody has put a not in the question. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: Who is it for
rounds.say: The situation is in every question. The label is in none of them.

questions.q: You are writing to a landlord you have never met, asking whether the flat is still free. Which shape fits best?
opts: Swap the words round: Est-elle libre ?
Let your voice rise: Elle est libre ?
Say it twice to be safe
questions.why: Swap the words round. Writing to a stranger is where the careful shape belongs, and a letter has no voice for a rising contour to live in. Est-ce que would also be correct here and read a shade plainer.

questions.q: You are cooking with a close friend and want to ask if they are hungry. Which of these would sound oddly formal?
opts: None of them, they are identical in feel
questions.why: As-tu faim ? is correct French and it is the one that lands as careful. That is the whole of the opening scene: nothing was wrong, and the room noticed anyway. The other two are both comfortable with a friend.

questions.q: A shop assistant asks a customer whether they have a smaller size. Which shape are they most likely to use, and why?
opts: Voice only, because shops are informal
Swapped round, because they are being professionally careful with a stranger
Est-ce que, because shops require it
Any of them, the situation does not matter
questions.why: Swapped round. « Avez-vous la taille en dessous ? » is a published sentence doing exactly this: a stranger being served, by somebody whose job is to be careful. The corpus agrees: this shape is five times commoner in formal settings than casual ones.

questions.q: Ask a friend, out loud, whether they are ready. Use the shape that suits a friend.
questions.why: Tu es prêt ? with your voice rising at the end. No words moved and nothing was added. Half the mark here is the contour: said flat, this is a statement and it will be heard as one.

rounds.label: What your ear does
rounds.say: Four listens. This is the one method that exists only as a sound.

questions.q: Listen. Is this a statement or a question?
questions.why: A question, and the voice rising on the last syllable is the only thing that says so. The words are identical to the statement « Tu es prêt. » This is the one contrast in A1 that nothing but your ear can settle.

questions.q: Listen. Which shape is this?
questions.why: The est-ce que block. It runs together into something like ess-kuh and nobody leans on it, which is why it can be easy to miss at speed: the sentence you are meant to hear starts after it.

questions.q: Listen. Is this asking about a man or a woman?
questions.why: A woman: est-ce qu'elle. This is the one genuine ear question in the lesson, because ess-KEEL and ess-KEL sit very close together at speed. Everything else here you can see on the page.

questions.q: Listen. Which shape is this?
questions.why: Swapped round: Es-tu. The verb came first. Out loud the two words run together as one, which is what the hyphen is showing you on the page, and it is why the hyphen is not optional.

rounds.label: The safe block
rounds.say: The one that always works, and the one place it changes shape.

questions.q: Turn « Tu es prêt. » into a question using est-ce que. Write the whole thing.
questions.why: Est-ce que tu es prêt ? The statement went in untouched: same words, same order, three more on the front. Nothing inside a sentence ever moves for this method, which is exactly why it is the safe one.

questions.q: You want to ask whether he is ready. Which is correct?
questions.why: Est-ce qu'il. The e of que is cut in front of a vowel and an apostrophe stands where it was. You have watched French refuse to let two vowels meet three times before this: l'amie, mon amie and n'ai.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Est-ce que elle est prête ? ». Fix it.
questions.why: Est-ce qu'elle. A vowel follows, so the e goes and an apostrophe replaces it. The rule is about the sound rather than the spelling: anything starting with a vowel sound does this, and nothing starting with a consonant does.

questions.q: What changes inside the sentence when you put est-ce que on the front of it?
opts: The verb moves to the front
questions.why: Nothing at all. Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. That is precisely why: there is no form to remember, no hyphen to place and no letter to insert, so it cannot go wrong under pressure the way the other two can.

rounds.label: Swapping them round
rounds.say: Twelve forms, one hyphen, and a letter that means nothing.

questions.q: You want to ask, carefully, whether he is hungry. Which is correct?
questions.why: A-t-il faim ? A ends in a vowel and il begins with one, so a t goes between them. It means nothing and exists only to stop the two vowels colliding. This is one of two places in twelve forms where anything is inserted.

questions.q: You want to ask a group, carefully, whether they are ready. Write the two words that start the question.
questions.why: Êtes-vous. The verb comes first and the pronoun second. Note that what you typed cannot show whether you used the hyphen, because the checker ignores punctuation: on paper it is compulsory, and « Etes vous » is a typo rather than a question.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Est-t-il prêt ? ». Fix it.
questions.why: Est-il, with no extra t. Est already ends in one, so there is nothing to keep apart. The insertion only happens when the verb ends in a vowel, which is why a-t-il needs it and est-il does not.

questions.q: Why can you learn all of these as a list rather than working them out?
opts: Because French only has twelve verbs
Because you can conjugate two verbs so far, so there are twelve forms
Because the swapped forms are irregular
Because only être can be swapped
questions.why: Because you can conjugate two verbs so far. Six persons times two verbs is twelve, which is a list you finish rather than a pattern you extend. When a third verb arrives the same swap works on it in the same way.

rounds.label: One method at a time
rounds.say: Three ways to ask, and you use exactly one of them.

questions.q: Which of these is correct French?
questions.why: Est-ce que tu es prêt ? The block already made it a question, so swapping the words as well asks twice. This is the commonest thing that goes wrong once all three methods are available, and the fix is to pick one and stop.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Est-ce que as-tu faim ? ». Fix it.
questions.why: Either « Est-ce que tu as faim ? » or « As-tu faim ? », and both are accepted here. What you cannot do is use both methods in one question. Est-ce que wants an ordinary statement behind it, with the words in their normal order.

questions.q: You want to ask whether you yourself are hungry, out loud, without sounding strange. Write the question.
questions.why: Est-ce que j'ai faim ? The swapped-round je form is ai-je, and nobody says it: it appears in none of the twenty-seven thousand sentences this app holds. When the swap produces a form real speakers avoid, est-ce que covers it.

questions.q: Which one of the three is correct in every situation there is?
questions.why: Est-ce que. Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. The other two are both correct French and both say something about how close you are, so either can be the wrong temperature. Est-ce que says nothing, which makes it safe.

rounds.label: Answering
rounds.say: Four answers, and one of them only exists because of a not.

questions.q: Somebody asks you « Tu n'es pas prêt ? » and you are, in fact, ready. What do you say?
questions.why: Si, je suis prêt. The question has a not in it and you are disagreeing with the not, which is the one job si does. Answering oui there would sound like you were agreeing that you were not ready.

questions.q: Somebody asks you « Tu es prêt ? » with no not in it, and you are ready. What do you say?
questions.why: Oui. Si only turns up when there is a negative to push back against, so using it on an ordinary question is as odd as using oui on a negative one. No not in the question means no si in the answer.

questions.q: Answer « Tu as faim ? » in the affirmative, saying more than one word. Write it.
questions.why: Oui, j'ai faim. The word on its own would have been a complete answer, and adding the reason is friendlier. Note j'ai rather than je ai, for the same reason est-ce qu'il is not est-ce que il.

questions.q: Say the answer you would give if you genuinely did not know yet.
questions.why: Peut-être. It works as a whole reply on its own, exactly like oui and non, and it is the answer people give most often in real conversation. Two words joined by a hyphen, said as one.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can ask any yes-or-no question three ways, choose between them by looking at who is in front of you rather than at the sentence, produce all twelve swapped-round forms including the two with an inserted letter, and answer with oui, non, peut-être or si. The habit underneath all of it is worth keeping: when you are unsure, the safe form exists and costs you nothing. The next unit is about asking for information rather than for a yes or a no, and it is built directly on the block you have just learned, so nothing here is going to be replaced.
points: Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices. The safe one is a real thing and it is worth having.
A statement and a question can be four identical words, separated by your voice going up.
Est-ce que never moves anything inside the sentence. That is the whole reason it is safe.
The swapped-round forms are a closed list of twelve, and nobody says ai-je.
Si is the answer to a question with a not in it, and it has no other job.

grammarAssumed: The nine subject pronouns, introduced in a1.05
The full present of être, introduced in a1.06, which asked nine questions with the voice alone and named none of them as a method
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07, including avoir faim
ne… pas around a finite verb, and the elision of ne, introduced in a1.18
non as a whole answer rather than a piece of a sentence, introduced in a1.18
The rising contour on a final syllable, and that up is a question and down is a statement, introduced in sons.08
Elision as a repair for two vowels meeting, introduced in sons.07
Liaison, and that a silent final consonant attaches to a following vowel, introduced in sons.10
tu against vous as a choice about the listener, introduced in a1.05 and used throughout
grammarIntroduced: The three yes-no interrogative strategies, and the register that selects between them
Rising intonation named as an interrogative strategy for the first time, having been used since a1.01
The est-ce que periphrasis, and that it leaves constituent order untouched
The elision of est-ce que to est-ce qu' before a vowel or mute h
Subject-clitic inversion, restricted to être and avoir as a closed twelve-form paradigm
The obligatory hyphen in an inverted verb-clitic group
Epenthetic -t- between a vowel-final verb and a vowel-initial third-person clitic
That ai-je and suis-je are avoided in real usage and are not taught as production
si as the positive reply to a negative question, against oui after a positive one
n'est-ce pas and non as tag questions, for recognition only

overview.introFr: Trois façons de poser la même question, et le choix dépend de la personne en face de vous.

acts.title: Just your voice

acts.title: The safe block
acts.milestone: Three words on the front of anything, and the one place they change shape.

acts.title: Flipping it round

acts.title: Choosing, and answering
acts.milestone: The choice made on purpose, and four ways to answer.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. The block you learned is what question words are built on.

lessons.reframe: Est-ce que always works. The other two are choices.

errorTriggers.description: Picks a question shape without reference to who is listening: uses the swapped-round form with a close friend, or the voice-only form in a letter. Produces perfectly correct French that lands at the wrong temperature, and nobody ever corrects it.

Says a voice-only question with a flat contour, so it lands as a statement and is answered as one. The one failure mode the first method has, and the learner can eventually hear it, which is why it is a drill rather than a scene.

Writes « Est-ce que il » without cutting the e. The fourth appearance of one anti-hiatus rule, and the first three were all repaired differently, so the learner has three precedents and no reason to prefer this one.
Drops the compulsory hyphen in « Es tu », or gets the inserted t wrong in either direction: « A-il faim ? » with none, « Est-t-il ? » with one it does not need.

Asks the question twice in one sentence: « Est-ce que es-tu prêt ? ». The commonest thing that goes wrong once all three methods are on the table, and unlike the register error it produces something that is not French.
Answers a negative question with oui, which reads as agreeing with the negative rather than contradicting it. Also the reverse: reaching for si on an ordinary question that has no not in it.

drills.title: Who would you say it to?
drills.coach: Every sentence in this drill is correct French, so there is no wrong pile. Ask instead which one you could imagine saying across a kitchen table, and which one you could imagine writing down. The swapped-round ones go in the second pile every time.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are cooking with a close friend and want to ask if they are hungry. Which sounds oddly formal?
drills.why: As-tu faim ? It is correct French and it is the one that puts a jacket on. Being careful with somebody close is itself a message.

drills.title: Up or down?
drills.coach: The first two are the same four words and only the mark at the end separates them. Say each line out loud and let the end of it fall or rise. If a line is asking you something, it goes up.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You say « Tu es prêt ? » with a completely flat voice. What does the other person hear?
drills.why: A statement. With this method the contour is the only thing carrying the question, so a flat one carries nothing and the sentence lands as a piece of news.

drills.title: Does the e get cut?
drills.coach: Look at the first letter of the word straight after the block, and ask whether it is a vowel sound. Tu is a consonant and nothing happens. Il, elle and on are all vowels and the e goes every time. It is about the sound rather than the spelling.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want to ask whether she is ready. Which do you write?
drills.why: Est-ce qu'elle. A vowel follows, so the e is cut and an apostrophe stands where it was. Same objection as l'amie and n'ai, repaired the same way.

drills.title: Does it need a t?
drills.coach: Every one of these is already swapped round, so that will not sort them. Look at the last letter of the verb instead. If it is a vowel and the pronoun starts with one, a t goes in to keep them apart. Everything else takes nothing.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want to ask, carefully, whether he is hungry. Which is correct?
drills.why: A-t-il faim ? A ends in a vowel and il begins with one, so the t goes between them. It means nothing and is there only for the sound.

drills.title: One method, or two?
drills.coach: Read each one and count how many times it asks. The est-ce que block is one. Swapped words is one. A rising voice is one. Any sentence that does two of those at once is asking twice, and none of the six here does, which is the point: correct French never does.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these is correct French?
drills.why: Est-ce que tu es prêt ? The block wants an ordinary statement behind it, with the words in their normal order. Swapping them as well asks the question twice.

drills.title: Oui or si?
buckets: the question has no not: oui
the question has a not: si
drills.coach: Ignore the method entirely: est-ce que, swapped words and a rising voice all make no difference here. Look for a not in the question. If there is one and you want to disagree with it, the answer is si. If there is not, si has no job to do.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Somebody asks « Tu n'es pas prêt ? » and you are ready. What do you say?
drills.why: Si. There is a not in the question and you are contradicting it. Oui would read as agreeing that you were not ready.

sheets.title: The three ways, and when to use each
contains: All three methods on one question

sections.title: One question, three ways
rows: anywhere, spoken or written, and never wrong
writing something careful, or being formal out loud

sections.title: How to choose, in one paragraph
sections.body: All three ask exactly the same thing and all three are correct French, so nothing you choose here can be a grammatical mistake. What separates them is who is listening. Letting your voice rise is the relaxed one and belongs in speech with people you are comfortable with; it is the commonest form in real conversation and the rarest in careful writing, because on paper one small mark is carrying the whole question. Swapping the verb and the person round is the careful one and belongs in letters, on forms, in exams, and out loud when you are being formal with somebody; said to a close friend it is noticeable, and nobody will tell you. Est-ce que sits in neither camp: it is correct everywhere, it says nothing at all about how close you are to the person, and it is the only one of the three you can use without first deciding what the situation wants. That is why it is worth making your default. The measured picture backs this up. Across the questions in this app, swapping the words round is about five times commoner in formal settings than casual ones, and letting your voice rise runs the other way by roughly three to one. Est-ce que barely moves between the two, which is exactly what being unmarked looks like.

sections.title: Where the e gets cut, and why it is not new
sections.body: Est-ce que loses its e in front of il, elle and on, and writes an apostrophe where the e was: est-ce qu'il, est-ce qu'elle, est-ce qu'on. It happens in front of a vowel SOUND rather than a vowel letter, which is the same test you already use for the articles. This is the fourth time you have met one standing objection: French will not let two vowel sounds run into each other with nothing between them. The definite articles solved it by cutting: la amie became l'amie. The possessives solved it by swapping the word for another shape: ma amie became mon amie. The negation lesson cut again: ne ai became n'ai. And this one cuts. Four rules, one objection, and only three different answers between them, so there is less here to remember than it looks. Note what does NOT happen: nothing is cut in front of tu, nous or vous, because those begin with consonants, and nothing about the rest of the sentence changes in any case. Est-ce qu'on carries one extra thing worth knowing: after the e is cut, the n of on carries across onto the following word, so it comes out as kohⁿ-NEH rather than as two separate pieces.

sheets.title: All twelve swapped-round forms
contains: The closed list, être and avoir

sections.title: What to write, and what never to write
Why each of those is wrong
sections.body: Es tu prêt ? is missing the hyphen, which is compulsory: without it the two words look accidentally out of order rather than deliberately swapped, and you cannot hear the difference, so this one survives a long time in writing. A-il faim ? is missing the inserted t. A ends in a vowel and il begins with one, so a t goes between them purely to keep them apart; it carries no meaning at all and there is no such word as a-il. Est-t-il prêt ? has the opposite problem: est already ends in a t of its own, so nothing needs adding, and the insertion only ever happens when the verb ends in a vowel. That is why a-t-il and a-t-elle take one and the other ten forms do not. Est-ce que il est prêt ? has not cut the e in front of a vowel. Est-ce que es-tu prêt ? asks the question twice: the block already made it a question, so the words behind it stay in their ordinary order. And Ai-je faim ? is the one that looks most like completing the set and is the one to avoid: it appears in none of the twenty-seven thousand sentences this app holds, because real speakers do not say it. The je question goes through est-ce que instead, which is one of the things est-ce que is for.

theSafeDefault.term: the one that is never wrong
theSafeDefault.title: Est-ce que works everywhere
theSafeDefault.body: Three little words on the front of a sentence and it is a question. Nothing inside moves, nothing swaps places, nothing needs a hyphen. You can say it to a friend, write it to a landlord, or use it in an exam, and it is never the wrong choice in any of them. That is unusual and it is worth leaning on: when you are tired, or thinking about what you actually want to say rather than how to say it, this is the one to reach for. The other two are things you do on purpose when you want to sound a particular way.

examples.note: The safe form of the question, and it can be said to anybody.
The same three words on the front, and the pronoun change cost nothing.

justTheVoice.title: Your voice going up is a question
justTheVoice.body: Take any statement, let your voice rise on the last syllable, and it is a question. No word changes and no word moves. You have been reading these since your very first lesson without anybody calling it a method: « Vous êtes ici pour la conférence ? » from the être lesson is one, and so is « Tu as froid ? » from avoir. It is the commonest way real French speakers ask a yes-or-no question and it is the most casual. The catch is on the page rather than in the mouth: written down, the only thing separating the question from the statement is the question mark.

examples.note: A statement. The voice goes down.
The same four words with the voice going up, and now it is a question.

flipIt.title: The careful one, and it is a closed list
flipIt.body: Put the verb first, the person second, and a hyphen between them. Es-tu prêt ? As-tu faim ? It sounds careful, and careful is exactly right in a letter, a form or an exam and slightly odd across a kitchen table. Because you can only conjugate two verbs so far, the whole set is twelve short forms and you can learn all of them rather than working them out. Two of the twelve put a t in the middle that means nothing: a-t-il and a-t-elle, where a vowel would otherwise run into a vowel.

examples.note: The two words swapped, held together by a hyphen that is compulsory.
The inserted t, which is there for the sound and means nothing at all.

whoAreYouTalkingTo.term: who is in front of you
whoAreYouTalkingTo.title: The choice is about the person, not the sentence
whoAreYouTalkingTo.body: All three forms ask exactly the same thing and all three are correct French. What separates them is who you are saying it to. A friend across a table gets your voice going up. A stranger, a form, or anything you are being careful about gets the swapped-round one. Everything in between, and everything you are unsure about, gets est-ce que. Getting this wrong does not produce a mistake anybody can point at, which is what makes it hard to notice: the sentence is perfect and the room just goes slightly cooler.

examples.note: The swapped form, said to one person you know. It reads as careful.
The same question to somebody you are being polite with, where it fits.

theSameOldDodge.title: Est-ce qu'il, and the fourth time you have seen this
theSameOldDodge.body: Est-ce que loses its e in front of il, elle and on. That is not a new rule to learn, it is the fourth appearance of one you already have. French will not let two vowel sounds run into each other and it has a few ways out. The articles lesson cut the word short: la amie became l'amie. The possessives lesson swapped the word: ma amie became mon amie. The negation lesson cut it again: ne ai became n'ai. This one cuts, like the first and third. Same objection, four times, and only three answers between them.

examples.note: The e of que is gone, and an apostrophe marks where it went.
The same cut, in a published sentence nobody arranged for this lesson.

theOtherSi.title: Si is three different words
theOtherSi.body: When somebody asks you a question with a not in it, and you want to disagree with the not, French does not use oui. It uses si. « Tu n'es pas prêt ? » gets « Si, je suis prêt. » and that is the only job this si does. The same three letters are also the word for if, which you will meet properly later, and the word for so in front of a description, as in si grand. Nothing connects the three and there is no rule underneath them. It is worth thirty seconds only because you will meet the other two and would otherwise wonder whether you had missed a connection.

examples.note: A question with a not in it, which is the only place si can answer.
Not oui. The not in the question is what makes it si.

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT CLIP IN THIS LESSON, and the only way to teach the first method at all. « Tu es prêt. » AND « Tu es prêt ? » ARE ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, statement first and question immediately after with no reset between them. The words are identical and the ONLY difference the learner may hear is the direction of the voice on the final syllable: down, then up. Two separate recordings are two performances. A reader who records the question in its own session will also make it faster, or lighter, or warmer, and the learner will hear THAT and conclude the contour is not the point. Do not lengthen the question. Do not add a pause before the rise. Do not stress any word differently between the two. Then, in the same take: « Tu as faim ? » and « Tu as besoin d'aide ? », both plainly, both rising, so the learner hears the contour on sentences that are not the demonstration pair.

THE HERO SCREEN, AND ALL THREE METHODS ARE ONE TAKE WITH ONE VOICE. « Tu es prêt ? » then « Est-ce que tu es prêt ? » then « Es-tu prêt ? », read straight through as one list with no gap and no reset. THE VARIABLE THE LEARNER IS JUDGING IS REGISTER, so three separate recordings would be fatal: a reader recording the inversion in its own session will make it crisper and more careful, which is precisely the difference the learner is supposed to be attributing to the FORM rather than to the performance. Read all three at the same pace, the same warmth and the same volume. The forms differ; the delivery must not. Also in this take, immediately after: « As-tu faim ? » followed by « Tu as faim ? », which is the scene's choice beat. Read the inversion PLAINLY and pleasantly. Do NOT make it sound wrong or stiff: it is correct French said by somebody being careful, and if it sounds like a mistake the whole scene stops working.

THE TWELVE FORMS, READ ONE VERB AT A TIME AND ONE TAKE PER VERB. The six être questions in order (es-tu, est-il, est-elle, sommes-nous, êtes-vous, sont-ils), then the six avoir questions in the same order. Reading a verb's six in one take is the point: the learner has to hear that only the person moves down a column. « Est-il prêt ? » AND « A-t-il faim ? » MUST ALSO BE RECORDED ADJACENT, in that order, in one take. That pair is a whole section: the inserted t is audible against a form that does not take one, and separated by so much as a breath the comparison is gone. THE INSERTED t IS AN ORDINARY t AND MUST NOT BE LEANED ON. a-t-il is three light syllables, ah-TEEL, with the t simply beginning the second one. A reader who emphasises it teaches that it means something, and it means nothing at all. THE SILENT t IN sont-ils AND ont-ils WAKES UP AND MUST BE FULLY PRONOUNCED: sohⁿ-TEEL and ohⁿ-TEEL, with the nasal vowel closed and NO n sound behind it. In the statements Ils sont and Ils ont that t is silent, and the contrast is worth a separate clip of each statement for the same take.

EST-CE QUE IS NEVER RECORDED IN ISOLATION. It is an unstressed block that only exists in front of a sentence, and a lone clip invites the learner to stress it and to pause after it. There is no clip anywhere in this lesson of est-ce que on its own, and if a request for one arrives it is a mistake in the request. Every clip here is the block WITH its sentence: « Est-ce que tu es prêt ? », « Est-ce que vous êtes prêts ? », « Est-ce que tu es français ? ». Read the block flat, fast and light, three syllables running together into something like ess-kuh, with the weight of the sentence landing where it always would, at the end. THE THREE ELIDED FORMS ARE ONE TAKE: « Est-ce qu'il est prêt ? », « Est-ce qu'elle est prête ? », « Est-ce qu'on est prêt ? », adjacent and at the same pace. ess-KEEL against ess-KEL is the one genuine listening question in this lesson and it only works if the two are delivered identically apart from the vowel. Do not slow either one down to help. In est-ce qu'on, the n carries across onto est: kohⁿ-NEH, not koh, pause, neh.

THE FOUR ANSWERS, and the si pair is the one that matters. « Tu n'es pas prêt ? » IMMEDIATELY FOLLOWED BY « Si, je suis prêt. », ONE TAKE, because si only means anything as a reply to that question and a clip of it alone teaches nothing. The question rises. The answer is firm but not sharp: si is a correction, not a rebuke, and a reader who makes it sound annoyed teaches the wrong social fact about a very common word. Then, in the same take and for contrast: « Tu es prêt ? » followed by « Oui, je suis prêt. », so the learner hears the same answer shape after a question with no not in it. oui, non and peut-être are each recorded as WHOLE REPLIES rather than as bare words where possible: « Oui, je suis prêt. », « Non, je suis fatigué. », « Oui, j'ai faim. ». peut-être is the one exception and is recorded alone, because it genuinely is a complete reply on its own and is almost always said that way. Two syllables, puh-TEHTR, with no pause at the hyphen.

The six published sentences in s17-wild, read PLAINLY and with no teaching colour at all. These are the evidence that the three methods live in ordinary French rather than in a lesson, and the whole value of the screen is that nobody arranged them. A reader who marks the method in each one turns six pieces of evidence into six demonstrations. Read each at conversational pace, as if it were the only sentence in the room.
clipIds: Est-ce qu'il y a un supermarché près d'ici ?
Ton chat miaule toujours le soir, n'est-ce pas ?

recorded.desc: The five written traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them. FOUR OF THE FIVE ARE INAUDIBLE and must be read as identical pairs, which is itself the teaching: « Es tu prêt ? » and « Es-tu prêt ? » sound exactly the same, because the hyphen is a mark on the page and nothing else. So are « A-t-il faim ? » against a reader's attempt at « A-il faim ? », which is why the wrong one there should be read as written and will sound halting. Do not perform the difference on the hyphen pair. Read both the same and let the card say why. « Est-ce que il est prêt ? » IS audible: read it with the two vowels genuinely colliding, slowly enough that the learner hears why the language refuses it. « Est-ce que es-tu prêt ? » is audible too and should be read flatly and without hesitation, because a learner writing it does not hesitate either. « Ai-je faim ? » should be read correctly and unremarkably. It is not a mispronunciation, it is a form nobody chooses, and making it sound odd would teach the wrong reason for avoiding it.

The opening scene, French bubbles only. Théo is a man in his late twenties, relaxed, cooking, half paying attention. His first line is thrown over a shoulder. HIS REPLY « Oui, merci. Un peu. » IS THE WHOLE SCENE AND MUST NOT SOUND OFFENDED. He is not annoyed, he has not noticed anything, and nothing has gone wrong that he could name. He simply matches the register he was handed: a shade more formal, a shade more distant, and the merci is a word he would not otherwise have used. Warmth drops by one degree and no more. Any hint of a question in his voice turns this into a correction and loses the point, which is that the error is undetectable from both sides. His last line, said to the flatmate rather than to the learner, is where the ordinary warmth comes back, and the contrast between that line and his reply is the only evidence the learner gets.
clipIds: Bon, on mange vers huit heures ?
Tu as faim ? On mange bientôt.

lessons.title: Les mots interrogatifs
lessons.intro: Seven words that decide which answer you get, and one frame that carries all of them. This is how to ask where, when, who, why, how and how many, put quel in front of a thing, and tell the two differences your ear can never reach.

sections.title: The Right Answer To The Wrong Question

say.text: One word wrong, a helpful and correct answer, and a train that leaves without you. Watch which word.

setting.place: The information desk at Gare de Lyon, under a departures board

beats.text: Gare de Lyon, a Friday, and the departures board is showing about forty trains. Yours is one of them.
You know the word for the train and you know the word for the station. What you want to know is what time it goes.

beats.speaker: The man at the information desk
beats.stage: He has done this four hundred times today and he is still pleasant about it.

beats.prompt: You want the departure time. Both of these are real questions. Which one asks for it?

options.fr: Où est-ce que le train part ?
options.en: the first question word most people are sure of

options.fr: Quand est-ce que le train part ?
options.en: the one that asks about time

followUp.works: Yes. Now watch what the other one does, because it is the one you reach for under pressure.
followUp.breaks: That is a real question and he will answer it properly. Watch what he answers.

beats.speaker: You
beats.fr: Où est-ce que le train part ?
beats.en: (This asks where it leaves from, which is not what you wanted to know)

beats.speaker: The man at the information desk
beats.fr: Voie 7. Tout droit, puis à gauche.
beats.stage: He points. He is right, he is helpful, and he has answered exactly what he was asked.

beats.heading: He answered the question you asked
beats.body: Nothing went wrong. Your sentence was correct, his answer was correct, and you now know something true that you did not need. The word at the front chose which fact you got.

wrong.fr: Où est-ce que le train part ?
wrong.en: Where does the train leave from

right.fr: Quand est-ce que le train part ?

beats.coach: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. Four words of those two sentences are the same. The first one is not.

beats.speaker: On platform 7, at 14:14
beats.fr: Quand est-ce que le train part ?
beats.stage: One word different. It is the only word in either sentence that was ever carrying the question.

beats.text: Seven words decide which answer you get. The next half hour is about which one to reach for, and about the frame that carries all seven.

closing.text: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. Which word goes in front is the next half hour.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the first one is a move rather than a list.

goals.t: Ask any question you can think of
goals.s: One frame takes all seven words, and you already know the sentences that go behind it.

goals.t: Pick the word that gets the answer you want
goals.s: Seven words, seven different facts, and the rest of the sentence does not move.

goals.t: Use quel in all four shapes
goals.s: The one word here that is not like the others. It leans on a thing and takes that thing's shape.

goals.t: Tell où from ou, and que from quoi
goals.s: Two distinctions your ear cannot reach. One is an accent and the other is a position.

sections.title: One Frame, And You Already Have It
sections.hint: Five cards before any of the seven words.
sections.say: Five cards before any table, because this move is what the table is for.

cards.label: the frame
cards.head: You already have this one
cards.body: The last lesson gave you this for yes and no questions. It has not changed. Put a word in front of it and the answer stops being yes or no, which is the whole of the next half hour.

cards.label: with nothing in front
cards.head: On its own it asks yes or no
cards.sub: Are you ready? · the frame with nothing added
cards.body: A whole question, and the answer is yes or no. Est-ce que le train part à midi ? is the same shape, published. Everything this lesson does is putting a word in front of it.

cards.label: the move
cards.head: Put your word in front of it
cards.sub: Where are you going? · Your word, then est-ce que. That always works.
cards.body: That is the whole lesson. The word says which fact you want and the frame carries it. Nothing behind the frame has to change when the word does.

cards.label: the two adjustments
cards.head: Two of the seven need one change
cards.body: Que does not stand in front of the frame, it joins it, and the two run together. And quel brings a thing with it. Both still go in the same place. Only the size of what you put there changes.

cards.label: in the wild
cards.head: The corpus was doing this already
cards.sub: Where do you live? · nobody arranged this for you
cards.body: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. This sentence was published long before this lesson existed, and so was the one about being late. The move is not a teaching device.

sections.title: Seven Questions, One Sentence
sections.say: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. Read down the right-hand column. It never changes. Tap any row to hear the whole question.

detail.title: où: Where are you going
detail.body: Où est-ce que tu pars ? Where are you going? The word for where, and everything after it is a sentence you already had. Nothing but the word itself goes in front.

detail.title: quand: When are you leaving
detail.body: Quand est-ce que tu pars ? When are you leaving? One word changed from the sentence above and the answer changed completely. Nothing but the word itself goes in front.

detail.title: pourquoi: Why are you leaving
detail.body: Pourquoi est-ce que tu pars ? Why are you leaving? The only one of the seven whose answer has a grammar of its own: parce que. Nothing but the word itself goes in front.

detail.title: comment: How are you travelling
detail.body: Comment est-ce que tu pars ? How are you travelling? The word the unit description leaves out, and one you have been saying since the first lesson. Nothing but the word itself goes in front.

rows.say: Avec qui est-ce que tu pars ?

detail.title: qui: Who are you going with
detail.body: Avec qui est-ce que tu pars ? Who are you going with? The word for who, with a small word in front of it. It brings avec with it, and the whole thing still goes in the same slot.
detail.say: Avec qui est-ce que tu pars ?

rows.say: Combien de temps est-ce que tu pars ?

detail.title: combien: How long are you going for
detail.body: Combien de temps est-ce que tu pars ? How long are you going for? Combien brings de with it as soon as you name the thing being counted. It brings de temps with it, and the whole thing still goes in the same slot.
detail.say: Combien de temps est-ce que tu pars ?

rows.say: À quelle heure est-ce que tu pars ?

detail.title: quel: What time are you leaving
detail.body: À quelle heure est-ce que tu pars ? What time are you leaving? Quel cannot stand alone. It takes the shape of the thing behind it. It brings a noun with it, and the whole thing still goes in the same slot.
detail.say: À quelle heure est-ce que tu pars ?

sections.title: Five That Never Change
sections.hint: Five cards, one per word, and none of them has a second shape.
sections.say: Five words with no endings, no agreement and no second form. Two missions and they are yours.

cards.label: where
cards.head: où
cards.body: The accent is not decoration. Without it the same three letters are the word for or, and the two sound identical. That is act two of this lesson and it is coming.

cards.label: when
cards.head: quand
cards.body: The d on the end is silent and the vowel is nasal, so this is one sound rather than two. It is the word the man at the station was never asked.

cards.label: how
cards.head: comment
cards.body: You have been saying this since the very first lesson, inside a greeting nobody took apart. Here it is as a word you can use anywhere. The t on the end is silent.

cards.label: why
cards.head: pourquoi
cards.fr: Pourquoi est-ce que tu es en retard ?
cards.body: The only one of the seven whose answer has a word of its own. Ask with pourquoi and you get parce que back, which is act five.

cards.label: who
cards.head: qui
cards.sub: [KEE] · Who are you? · Who do you live with?
cards.body: When the person is the one doing something, qui goes straight in front. When they are not, a small word goes in front of it: avec qui, à qui, pour qui.

cards.label: all five at once
cards.head: Nothing here has a second shape
cards.sub: What is your name? · one form each, always
cards.body: Your word, then est-ce que. That always works. No endings, no agreement, nothing to check before you say them. The word that does have a second shape is the next act, and it is only one word out of seven.

sections.title: Which Word Gets The Answer?
sections.say: Four decisions. Each one is about which fact you want rather than about how to build the sentence.

check.q: You are at a station and you want the departure time. Which word goes in front?
check.why: quand. This is the exact decision from the opening scene and it is worth making twice on purpose. Où is a real question and gets a real answer, which is why nothing about saying it feels wrong.

check.q: You are lost and you want to know where the station is. Which word?
check.why: où, with the accent. Without it the word means or, and the two are one sound, so nothing you can hear will ever tell you which one somebody said.

items.fr: Pourquoi est-ce que tu es en retard ?

check.q: Somebody is late and you want to know the reason. Which word?
check.why: pourquoi. It is the only one of the seven that comes back with a word of its own attached: the answer starts parce que, which is act five of this lesson.
