cards.sub: fehr lah veh-SEHL · to do the dishes
fehr luh LEE · to make the bed
MET-ruh lah TAHBL · to set the table

sections.title: Put It In Its Room
sections.say: Four rooms and one question about each. Nothing here is about the little word in front.

check.q: Three of those wash, cook or cool. Which one holds the plates you are about to use?
check.why: le placard. It is the cupboard, and it is the one word here that turns up in more than one room: the same word covers a kitchen cupboard and a clothes cupboard, so you will meet it again in the bedroom.

check.q: You are describing your bedroom and want to say where your clothes go. Which one?
check.why: l'armoire. A freestanding wardrobe, and the ordinary word rather than a special case: built-in wardrobes are uncommon in French homes, so this is what most people actually have.

check.q: Which of these would you NOT expect to find in a salon?
check.why: le lavabo, the washbasin, which lives behind the bathroom door. The other three are the living room set, and grouping them that way is what makes them stick.

check.q: What is the point of learning these words room by room rather than as one list?
opts: The rooms are easier to spell
Each room is a short set you can walk through in your head
It puts the le words and the la words together
It is the order a dictionary uses
check.why: Each room is a short set you can walk through. Sixty words about a house is a list nobody remembers; the same sixty sorted into four rooms is four sets, and you have stood in all four of them.

sections.title: The One Time You Can Work It Out
sections.hint: Four cards, and one rule that actually predicts.
sections.say: A1 has told you many times that you cannot work this out. Here is the one place you can.

cards.label: the rule
cards.head: A machine named after its job is the le kind
cards.fr: le lave-vaisselle · le sèche-linge · le micro-ondes
cards.body: French names a machine by gluing what it does onto what it does it to. Washes-dishes, dries-laundry, micro-waves. Every one of those is the le kind, and you can apply that to a machine you have never met before.

cards.label: why it works
cards.head: The glue is what decides it
cards.body: Nothing about dishes or laundry comes into it. The word is built as a unit and the unit is the le kind regardless of what is inside it, which is why this is a rule rather than a pattern you have noticed.

cards.label: where it stops
cards.head: And the two that are not built that way
cards.fr: la machine à laver · la cuisinière
cards.body: la machine à laver is a machine for washing rather than a wash-thing, and la cuisinière is not glued together either. Both are the la kind and both have to be stored, which is what makes the rule above a rule rather than a coincidence.

cards.label: the rest of the kitchen
cards.head: le frigo · le four
cards.body: Neither of these is a compound, so neither is covered, and both happen to be the le kind anyway. Store them. The published sentence is the one everybody says at some point on a Sunday evening.

sections.title: You Already Have This One
sections.hint: Four cards and none of them is new.
sections.say: The last unit gave you all of this. What is new is that you now have something to put in the sentence.

cards.label: what changed
cards.head: Last unit you could say where nothing was
cards.fr: Le lit est près de la fenêtre.
cards.sub: The bed is close to the window.
cards.body: You finished the last unit able to say where a thing is and with almost no things to say it about. This sentence is that unit's work and this unit's words, and nothing in it is being taught to you twice.

cards.label: a room inside a room
cards.head: Rooms sit next to rooms
cards.fr: La cuisine est à côté du salon.
cards.sub: The kitchen is next to the living room.
cards.body: Two of the rooms you have just learned, in a published sentence that nobody wrote to teach you anything. The only work left in a sentence like this is picking the right room word, which is what the first act was for.

cards.label: the hallway is how people give directions
cards.head: Down the hall, on the right
cards.fr: La salle de bain est au bout du couloir.
cards.sub: The bathroom is at the end of the hallway.
cards.body: This is the sentence Claire said in the scene, more or less, and it is how anybody in a French home will tell you where something is. The hallway word is doing most of the work.

cards.label: what is in a room
cards.head: And there is a sofa in it
cards.fr: Il y a une table dans le salon. Il y a un canapé dans le salon.
cards.sub: There is a table in the living room. · There is a sofa in the living room.
cards.body: The frame for saying something exists somewhere came from the pronouns unit and you have been using it for weather ever since. Here it is with furniture in it, which is the only thing that has changed.

sections.title: The One Pair Your Ear Can Do
sections.say: One pair worth listening hard to, and one word whose spelling tells you nothing at all.

lines.en: the floor, an open o that stops
the bucket, a closed o that runs on
not a pair, just a warning: see the question below

questions.q: le sol and le seau. What separates them?
opts: the first has a short open vowel and a consonant after it, the second does not
questions.why: The first ends on a consonant and the second does not. Le sol stops on an l; le seau is an open syllable that just ends. The little word in front is the same on both, so it cannot help you here.

questions.q: You hear a word that sounds like pwal. How is it spelled?
questions.why: poêle, with a circumflex on the e. It is the frying pan, and the spelling predicts the sound so badly that this is the one word in the lesson worth meeting written down before you meet it spoken.

questions.q: Is there any point listening carefully to tell salon from balcon?
opts: No. They share one sound at the end and nothing else
questions.why: No. They both end in a nasal and are otherwise nothing alike, so telling them apart is not a skill worth building. The hard part of this lesson happens before you speak rather than while you listen.

sections.title: Where Is It?
sections.say: Three questions, and every one of them is about which room rather than about the small word.

check.q: « La cuisine est à côté du salon. » Which two rooms is this about?
opts: the kitchen and the living room
the dining room and the kitchen
check.why: The kitchen and the living room. Both are rooms you learned in act 2, and the sentence itself was published long before this lesson existed, which is what makes it worth reading.

check.q: « La salle de bain est au bout du couloir. » Where is it?
opts: at the end of the hallway
check.why: At the end of the hallway, which is the sentence Claire more or less said in the scene. The hallway word is how people give directions inside a home, so it is worth more than its length suggests.

groups.label: and one about the thing rather than the room

check.q: « Le lit est près de la fenêtre. » What is being described?
check.why: Where the bed is. The window is the reference point rather than the subject, which is the shape almost every sentence like this takes: the thing you are placing comes first.

sections.title: The Listing
sections.say: A flat listing, four lines of it, and one number that means something different from what it looks like.
sections.text: A flat is advertised online and the whole description is four short lines, every one of which needs a word from this lesson to read properly. « Notre appartement a trois pièces. » That is the first line and it is the one that catches English speakers out, because the number counts the rooms you live in and leaves out the kitchen and the bathroom entirely. « Nous avons deux chambres et une salle de bains. » The second line spells out what those rooms actually are, and it counts the bedrooms separately from the room with the bath in it. « La salle de bains est au premier étage. » The third line tells you which floor that room is on, which matters more than it sounds because the toilet is very often not in the same place. « Le salon a deux fenêtres et une porte. »

glossary.note: The counting word. Three rooms in total, and the kitchen and bathroom are not among them.
Bedrooms specifically. This is the word that only ever means a room with a bed in it.
The room with the bath. Written with an s here and without one on the card, and both are correct French.
Which floor the room is on. The toilet is often on a different one, which is why the listing bothers to say.

questions.q: The listing says trois pièces and then two bedrooms and a bathroom. Is that a contradiction?
questions.a: No. The three rooms are the rooms you live in, which here means two bedrooms and a living room. The kitchen and the bathroom are not counted in that number at all, which is why the second line has to spell them out separately. An English listing would have said two bedrooms and stopped.

questions.q: Why would a listing bother saying which floor the bathroom is on?
questions.a: Because in a lot of French homes the room with the bath and the room with the toilet are two different rooms, and they are not necessarily near each other. Knowing where one of them is does not tell you where the other one is, which is exactly the problem the opening scene turned on.

questions.q: The last line counts windows and a door. What is it telling you?
questions.a: How much light the room gets and how it is laid out. Two windows and one door is a description a French listing gives about a living room as a matter of course, and reading it needs the words for the shell of a room rather than for its furniture.

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Every room front names which kind of room, because room on its own is the question rather than the prompt.

cards.front: "my room", when you sleep in it
"the ___ room", when it is named by what happens there

sections.title: Write What You Hear
sections.say: Five lines, each one about a room you have just learned.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: The rooms, the furniture, the machines and the three things you do. Every one of them scored.

sections.title: Showing Somebody Round
sections.say: One exchange and you hold up your half. Every turn asks you for a room by name.
sections.setting: A friend of a friend is looking at your flat because they might take it over. You are walking them through it.

turns.ai: Merci de me recevoir. Il fait combien de pièces, exactement ?
turns.en: Thanks for having me. How many rooms is it, exactly?
turns.user: Il fait trois pièces.
turns.userEn: It is a three-room flat.

alts.fr: Il fait trois pièces, plus la cuisine.

turns.ai: D accord. Et on dort où ?
turns.en: Right. And where do you sleep?
turns.user: Il y a deux chambres.
turns.userEn: There are two bedrooms.

alts.fr: Il y a deux chambres, au fond.
alts.en: There are two bedrooms, at the back.

turns.ai: Et pour se laver ?
turns.en: And for washing?
turns.user: La salle de bain est au bout du couloir.
turns.userEn: The bathroom is at the end of the hallway.

alts.en: At the end of the hallway.

alts.fr: La salle de bain est juste là.

turns.ai: Ah, et les toilettes sont dedans ?
turns.en: Ah, and is the toilet in there?
turns.user: Non, les toilettes sont à côté.
turns.userEn: No, the toilet is next door.

turns.ai: Parfait. Et la cuisine, elle est équipée ?
turns.en: Perfect. And is the kitchen fitted?
turns.user: Oui, il y a un four et un lave-vaisselle.
turns.userEn: Yes, there is an oven and a dishwasher.

alts.fr: Oui, il y a un frigo et un four.
alts.en: Yes, there is a fridge and an oven.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched somebody be handed a towel over one room name, and nothing said in that scene was hard. Since then you have taken the one English word that covers three French ones and learned which is which, named every room in a home, sorted the furniture and the machines into the rooms they live in rather than into a list, found the one place in this whole level where you can work out a word you have never met, and read a flat listing whose main number does not mean what it looks like. What is left tells you whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: Which room word
rounds.say: The decision everything else rests on.

questions.q: You are in somebody's living room and want to say this room is lovely. Which word?
questions.why: cette pièce. The room you are standing in is a pièce. Chambre would tell them you are in a bedroom and salle does not stand alone. Never say "room". Say which room.

questions.q: A listing says « quatre pièces ». What does the number count?
opts: Only the bedrooms, and nothing else at all
Every room in the flat, kitchen and bathroom included
How many floors the building has above ground
Rooms you live in, not the kitchen or bathroom
questions.why: Rooms you live in, with the kitchen and the bathroom left out. This is why a French flat sounds bigger in the advert than it turns out to be, and it is the number every listing leads with.

questions.q: Write the French for the room you sleep in, with its little word.
questions.why: la chambre. A bedroom and only a bedroom, which is the single most useful thing to know about it: it is not a general word for a room and using it as one puts a bed in the picture.

questions.q: Somebody says « J'ai une grande chambre. » What have they got?
questions.why: A big bedroom. Chambre never widens out to mean a room in general, so there is no reading of this sentence in which they are talking about anything else.

questions.q: This sentence is wrong. Fix it: « Je suis dans la salle. »
questions.why: salle does not stand on its own for a room in a home. It arrives attached to what happens there, as in salle de bain or salle à manger, so the word for the room you are simply in is pièce.

rounds.label: The two rooms
rounds.say: The one from the scene.

questions.q: You are at a dinner party and you need the toilet. What do you ask for?
questions.why: les toilettes. The second option is the room with the bath in it, which is a different door and is how the opening scene ends with a towel. The last option is not French at all.

questions.q: Why is asking for « la salle de bain » a problem when you need the toilet?
opts: It is much too formal for a friend's house
In most French homes they are two rooms
It is the wrong little word in front of it
It only works in a hotel or a hospital
questions.why: They are usually two rooms. You will be shown the one with the bath in it, because that is what you asked for and there is no reason for anybody to think you meant something else.

questions.q: Write the French for the toilet, as a room, with its little word.
questions.why: les toilettes, plural every time. There is no singular of this one for the room, so the s is not optional and dropping it changes the word into something about getting dressed.

questions.q: This is wrong. Fix it: « Où est la toilette ? »
questions.why: The room is always plural, so the verb moves with it. This is the only room in the lesson that behaves this way and it is the one you will need most urgently.

rounds.label: The rooms
rounds.say: Twelve doors.

questions.q: Which of these is the living room?
questions.why: le salon. The others are the kitchen, the hallway and the cellar, and all four are rooms you walked through in act two.

questions.q: Somebody tells you something is « au bout du couloir ». Which part of the home is that?
questions.why: The hallway. It is worth more than its length suggests, because it is how anybody in a French home will tell you where a room is, including the one you need.

questions.q: Say the French for the kitchen.
questions.why: la cuisine. The same word means cooking as an activity, so « j'aime la cuisine » is about food rather than about a room, and context does all the work of separating them.

questions.q: Write the French for the dining room.
questions.why: la salle à manger, the room for eating in. This is salle doing what it always does: arriving attached to what happens in the room rather than standing on its own.

rounds.label: What is in each room
rounds.say: Sorted by where it lives.

questions.q: Which of these would you expect to find in a chambre?
questions.why: l'armoire, the wardrobe. The others belong to the bathroom, the kitchen and the living room, and sorting them that way is what makes sixty words into four short sets.

questions.q: Write the French for the bed, with its little word.
questions.why: le lit. Short, the le kind, and the anchor of the bedroom set: almost everything else in that room is described by where it sits in relation to it.

questions.q: You hear « Les rideaux sont bleus dans le salon. » What is blue?
questions.why: The curtains. Note that they are plural and that the colour has agreed with them, which is the colours lesson still doing its work two units later without being mentioned.

questions.q: Write the French for the armchair, the one that seats a single person.
questions.why: le fauteuil seats one and le canapé seats several, which is the same split English makes between an armchair and a sofa. La chaise is a plain chair with no arms at all.

rounds.label: The machines
rounds.say: The one rule in this lesson that predicts.

questions.q: You meet a machine called « le lave-linge » for the first time. Which little word does it take?
questions.why: le. It is a verb glued onto a noun, washes-laundry, and every machine named that way is the le kind. This is the one word in the whole lesson you can get right without having met it.

questions.q: Why is it « la machine à laver » rather than le?
opts: It is bigger than all of the other ones
It is not built as a verb glued to a noun
It is an older word than the others are
It is used in a different room of the house
questions.why: It is not a compound. It is a machine for washing rather than a wash-thing, so the rule never reaches it and the word has to be stored like every other one.

questions.q: Write the French for the dishwasher, with its little word.
questions.why: le lave-vaisselle. Washes-dishes, glued together, so the le kind by the rule rather than by memory.

questions.q: You hear a kitchen machine named. Which one dries laundry?
questions.why: le sèche-linge, dries-laundry. All three of the first options are compounds and all three are the le kind; only the last one is not built that way, and it is the la kind.

rounds.label: Saying where it is
rounds.say: Last unit's rule on this unit's words.

questions.q: « La cuisine est à côté du salon. » Which two rooms?
opts: the dining room and the garden
the kitchen and the living room
questions.why: The kitchen and the living room. The sentence was published long before this lesson and needed nothing from it except the two room names, which is what act four is for.

questions.q: Say this out loud: there is a sofa in the living room.
questions.target: Il y a un canapé dans le salon.
accept: Il y a un canapé dans le salon.
il y a un canape dans le salon
questions.answer: Il y a un canapé dans le salon.
questions.why: The frame for saying something exists came from the pronouns unit and you have been using it for weather ever since. All that has changed is that there is furniture in it now.

questions.q: Fix this: « Le lit est près de la fenêtre dans la salle. »
accept: Le lit est près de la fenêtre dans la chambre.
le lit est pres de la fenetre dans la chambre
questions.answer: Le lit est près de la fenêtre dans la chambre.
questions.why: A bed is in a chambre. Salle does not stand alone, and the rest of the sentence was already right: the words for where a thing is came from the last unit and have not changed.

questions.q: What is genuinely new in this lesson about saying where something is?
opts: The words for where a thing is have changed
How the little words join up to the room name
The order the words go in inside the sentence
Nothing, except what there is to say it about
questions.why: Nothing about the saying, and everything about what there is to say. The last unit gave you the whole system and almost nothing to point it at; this one filled the sentence in.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can pick the right word for a room before you speak rather than translating and hoping, name every room in a home including the two English keeps confusing, name what is in each of them because you learned them room by room rather than as a list, and say where any of it is using a system you already had. The habit underneath all of that is worth keeping past this lesson: when one English word covers several French ones, the fix is never to pick a favourite and use it everywhere. It is to stop translating and reach for the thing itself. You will meet the same shape again with food, with the body and with the words for time, and each time the answer is the same one.
points: Never say "room". Say which room. Chambre is a bedroom, pièce is a room you count, salle arrives attached to what happens in it.
The bath and the toilet are two rooms with two names, and the toilet is always plural.
A machine named after its job is the le kind, and that stops the moment the name is not glued together.
Saying where a thing is came from the last unit and has not changed. What changed is that you have things to say it about.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that the little word in front is the choice gender makes, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, and the elision of le and la in front of a vowel, introduced in a1.04
Impersonal il, in il y a, introduced in a1.05
The present of avoir, introduced in a1.07
un, une and des, introduced in a1.11
Adjective agreement and adjective placement, introduced in a1.13, a1.14 and a1.16
The possessive adjectives, introduced in a1.17
The prepositions of place sur, sous, dans, devant, derrière and à côté de, and the contraction of à and de with the definite article, introduced in a1.21
grammarIntroduced: The lexical split of English "room" into chambre, pièce and salle, and the semantic conditions on each
chambre as restricted to a sleeping room, against English "room" as unrestricted
pièce as the countable unit of a dwelling, and the French convention of counting rooms excluding kitchen and bathroom
salle as bound in compounds and not free-standing in a domestic register
les toilettes as a plurale tantum in its room sense, against the singular la toilette which is not a room
The gender of verb-plus-noun appliance compounds as invariably masculine, and the boundary at non-compound names

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for chambre for any room, because a bilingual list gave it as the translation of room. Produces a perfectly grammatical sentence about a bedroom the speaker is not in.
Uses salle as a free-standing word for a room, on the strength of having met it in salle de bain. Sounds like the start of a sentence that was not finished.

Asks for la salle de bain when they need the toilet, or says la toilette in the singular. The error the opening scene is built on, and the most expensive one here because it is understood perfectly and sends the speaker to the wrong door.
Has the three-way distinction and does not yet have the room names, so the right word is chosen and the wrong room is named. Costs fluency rather than meaning.
Learns the furniture as one undifferentiated list and cannot retrieve it under time pressure, because there is no room to walk through in their head.
Either misses that a machine named after its job is predictable and stores every appliance separately, or over-applies it and makes la machine à laver masculine.
Believes the last unit's system has changed because the nouns are new, and hesitates over a sentence they could already build. Costs confidence rather than accuracy.

drills.title: Which room word?
buckets: a room with a bed in it
drills.coach: Only one of these is a bedroom. The others are rooms you would count in a listing, and the word for those is pièces. Sort by the room you are picturing, not by the English word you started from.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are in a friend's living room. What word for this room?
drills.why: pièce. The room you are standing in is a pièce unless it has a bed in it, and salle would need something attached to it before it meant anything.

drills.title: Salle never comes alone
drills.coach: Two of these three attach salle to what happens in the room. The third does not use salle at all, because there is nothing to attach it to.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which of these is not something anybody says?
drills.why: la salle on its own. In a home it always arrives attached to what happens in the room, and a bare salle sounds like an unfinished sentence.

drills.title: Which door?
drills.coach: The shower and the bath are behind one door. The toilet is behind the other, and its name is plural. Getting this wrong is understood perfectly and gets you shown the wrong room.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You need the toilet. Which do you ask for?
drills.why: les toilettes, plural. The first is the room with the bath in it and the third is not a room at all.

drills.title: Name the room
drills.coach: Twelve rooms with their little words attached. If a room comes back without its little word you have stored half of it, which the gender lesson warned you about a long time ago.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which one is the hallway?
drills.why: le couloir. The others are the attic, the cellar and the balcony, and the hallway is the one you will hear most because it is how people give directions indoors.

drills.title: Put it in its room
drills.coach: Two per room. Learning them in the room they live in gives you three short sets you can walk through, instead of one long list you have to search.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Where does l'armoire live?
drills.why: la chambre. It is a freestanding wardrobe and it is where the clothes go, which in a French home is usually the ordinary arrangement rather than a built-in cupboard.

drills.title: Glued together, or not?
buckets: named after its job, so the le kind
not built that way, so stored
drills.coach: Three of these five are a verb glued onto a noun and all three are the le kind. The other two are not built that way, and both happen to be the la kind. Sort by how the word is built, not by what the machine does.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: A machine called le lave-linge. Why is it le?
opts: because it is a verb glued onto a noun
because it is in the kitchen
drills.why: Because of how the word is built. Washes-laundry, glued into one unit, and every machine named that way is the le kind whatever it does.

La salle de bain est au bout du couloir.
drills.coach: Nothing in any of these is new except the nouns. The words for where a thing is came from the last unit and have not changed, so the only decision left is which room you mean.
