drills.q: What is new in this lesson about saying where something is?
opts: nothing, only what there is to say it about
drills.why: Only the nouns. The last unit gave you the whole system with almost nothing to point it at, and this one filled the sentence in.

sheets.title: Every room, and the three words for room

sections.title: The word English does not have
rows: my room", when you sleep in it
rooms", when you are counting them
the ___ room", when it is named by what happens there

sections.title: Why this is three words and not one
sections.body: English uses room for a bedroom, for a room you are counting, for a room in a museum and for a room named after what happens in it, and lets the sentence around it work out which was meant. French decides first. A chambre has a bed in it and never means anything else, so calling a living room a chambre does not read as an approximation, it reads as a different room. A pièce is a room as a unit, which is why every flat listing is written in them: trois pièces counts the rooms you live in and leaves out the kitchen and the bathroom, so it is smaller than an English ear expects. A salle is named by what happens in it and almost never stands alone in a home, arriving instead as salle de bain or salle à manger. The practical version of all of this is not three definitions to memorise. It is to stop translating: picture the room you actually mean, and the French word for that room is the one you want. The other thing worth carrying out of this lesson is that the room with the bath in it and the room with the toilet in it are two different rooms in most French homes, with two different names, and that the second of them is always plural. There is no singular of it for a room at all.

sections.title: Room by room
rows: le frigo, le four, le micro-ondes
le canapé, le fauteuil, la table
la douche, la baignoire, le lavabo

sections.title: The machines, and how they are built
Learn them in the room, and the one rule that predicts
sections.body: Sixty words about a house is a list and nobody remembers a list. The same sixty sorted into the rooms they belong to is four short sets, each of which you can walk through in your head because you have stood in the room. The fridge, the oven and the plates belong together because they are in one place, not because they start with the same letter, and this is also the order in which you will actually meet them: nobody hands you a whole house at once, they show you one room at a time. The second thing on this sheet is the only place in the whole of A1 where you can work out a word you have never met. French names a machine by gluing what it does onto what it does it to, and the result is always the le kind: le lave-vaisselle washes dishes, le sèche-linge dries laundry, le micro-ondes does the waves, and a lave-linge you have never seen before is the le kind before anybody tells you. The rule stops the moment the name is not glued together. La machine à laver is a machine for washing rather than a wash-thing, and la cuisinière is not built that way either, so both are the la kind and both have to be stored like every other noun in this level. That boundary is what makes it a rule rather than a coincidence you have noticed.

whichRoom.term: English has one word and French has three
whichRoom.title: chambre, pièce, salle
whichRoom.body: English says room for all of them and lets the sentence sort it out. French makes you choose before you open your mouth. A chambre is a bedroom and only ever a bedroom. A pièce is a room as a unit, the thing a listing counts when it says trois pieces. A salle is a room named by what happens in it, and it almost never turns up on its own: it arrives already attached, as salle de bain or salle a manger. None of the three is a translation of the others, and picking the wrong one is not a small error in a sentence that is otherwise fine. It is the sentence.

examples.note: The one that means bedroom, and nothing else.
The counting one, in the sentence a listing would actually print.

twoRooms.term: the bath and the toilet are two rooms
twoRooms.title: Where the towel comes from
twoRooms.body: In most French homes the bath is in one room and the toilet is in another, and the two have separate names because they are separate places. La salle de bain has the bath, the shower and the basin in it. Les toilettes has the toilet. Asking for the first when you want the second is understood perfectly and sends you to the wrong door, and the person helping you will assume you meant what you said. Note the s on the end of toilettes as well: this one is always plural and there is no singular of it, which is unlike every other room in the lesson.

examples.note: The room with the bath in it.
The other room, always plural, never shortened.

roomByRoom.term: store the thing with the room it lives in
roomByRoom.title: A kitchen word is easier than a house word
roomByRoom.body: Sixty words about a house is a list and nobody remembers a list. The same sixty words sorted into the four rooms they belong to is four short sets, each of which you can walk through in your head because you have stood in the room. The fridge, the oven and the plates go together because they are in one place, not because they are alphabetically near each other. This is also how you will meet them: nobody hands you the whole house at once, they show you one room at a time.

examples.note: A kitchen word, learned in the kitchen set.
And a living room one, in a sentence that puts it there.

machinesAreMasculine.term: a machine named after its job is masculine
machinesAreMasculine.title: The one place gender is predictable
machinesAreMasculine.body: A1 has told you many times that you cannot work out whether a word is the le kind or the la kind, and that is true almost everywhere. Here is the exception. When French names a machine by what it does, it glues a verb onto a noun and the result is always the le kind: le lave-vaisselle washes dishes, le seche-linge dries laundry, le micro-ondes does the waves. That is a rule you can apply to a word you have never met. It stops the moment the name is not a compound: la machine a laver is a machine for washing rather than a wash-thing, and la cuisiniere is not built that way either, so both go back to being stored.

examples.note: Verb plus noun, glued, so the le kind without being told.
Not a compound, so the rule does not reach it.

youAlreadyHaveThis.term: you already know how to say where it is
youAlreadyHaveThis.title: Nothing new here, on purpose
youAlreadyHaveThis.body: The last unit gave you the whole set of words for where a thing is, and it gave you what happens when one of them meets a le word. That has not changed and none of it is retaught here. What is new is that you now have something to put in the sentence: the rooms and the furniture. A learner who finished the last unit and could not name a single room could say where nothing was. This is the other half of that, and the only work left is choosing the right room word.

examples.note: Last unit's rule, this unit's words, in a published sentence.
The same again, with a room this lesson taught you to pick.

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. « la chambre », « les pièces » and « la salle » ARE ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, read straight through with no gap and no reset. The claim the whole lesson rests on is that these are three different rooms rather than three ways of saying one word, and three separate recordings are three performances: a reader who records them in separate sessions will give one of them more weight and the learner will hear that weight as a difference in importance rather than in meaning. KEEP THE NASAL IN « chambre » CLOSED. It is /ʃɑ̃bʁ/ with a nasal vowel and NO n sound behind it: the app respells it lah SHAHⁿBR deliberately, and a reader who lets an n out of it teaches a sound that is not in the word. Then, in the same take, the two whole sentences: « Notre appartement a trois pièces. » and « Il y a cinq pièces dans la maison. »
clipIds: Il y a cinq pièces dans la maison.

recorded.desc: « la salle de bain » AND « les toilettes » ADJACENT IN ONE TAKE, one voice. This is the pair the opening scene turns on and the learner has to hear them as two rooms rather than as two registers of one. Read both plainly and at the same pace: any hint that the second is more colloquial or more delicate than the first invents a difference the language does not have. Both are the ordinary words. GIVE « les toilettes » ITS PLURAL FULLY. The s is silent but the les is not, and a reader who lets it slide toward « la toilette » is recording the error the lesson is about. Then, in the same take: « Où est la salle de bain ? » and « Où sont les toilettes ? », so the learner hears the verb move with the plural.
clipIds: Où est la salle de bain ?

recorded.desc: « le sol » AND « le seau » ADJACENT, ONE TAKE, AND THIS IS THE ONLY GENUINE EAR CONTRAST IN THE LESSON. The two differ in the vowel and in whether the syllable closes, and a gap of even a few seconds between the two recordings lets the reader reset their vowel. Read them back to back, at the same pitch, with the same little word in front of both. ALSO IN THIS TAKE: « la poêle », which is /pwal/. THIS IS NOT A TYPO AND MUST NOT BE "CORRECTED" LATER. The oê spelling predicts the sound so badly that the whole reason the word is in this lesson is that a learner has to be told. Anybody reading it as a spelling pronunciation is recording the trap rather than the word. NEVER RECORD « salle » IN ISOLATION. There is no clip anywhere in this lesson of salle on its own, deliberately: it does not occur alone in a home and a clip of it teaches a word the learner will never need by itself. If a request for one arrives, it is a mistake in the request.

THE TWELVE ROOMS, EACH READ WITH ITS LITTLE WORD ATTACHED AND NEVER WITHOUT IT. Read as ONE LIST in one take at an even pace, because the learner is being asked to store the little word as part of the room and a pause between the two teaches the opposite. EVERY NASAL CLOSED, and there are five of them in this list: la maison, le salon, le jardin, le balcon and la salle à manger. All five are respelled with a superscript in the app and all five were shipped wrong until this build. A reader who lets an n out of any of them undoes the repair. Then the four published sentences: « Il y a un canapé dans le salon. », « Nous avons deux chambres et une salle de bains. », « La salle de bain est au bout du couloir. », « Le salon a deux fenêtres et une porte. »
clipIds: Il y a un canapé dans le salon.
Nous avons deux chambres et une salle de bains.
La salle de bain est au bout du couloir.
Le salon a deux fenêtres et une porte.

recorded.desc: The furniture, read GROUPED BY ROOM rather than as one alphabetical run, with a clear beat between groups. The whole organising idea of act three is that these come in room-sized sets, and a flat list of eleven read at one pace destroys it. Living room, then bedroom, then the soft things, then the things that hold things. Then the three published sentences in the same take: « Il y a un grand lit dans la chambre. », « Le chat dort sur le grand lit blanc. », « Les rideaux sont bleus dans le salon. »
clipIds: Il y a un grand lit dans la chambre.
Le chat dort sur le grand lit blanc.
Les rideaux sont bleus dans le salon.

recorded.desc: THE THREE COMPOUNDS FIRST, TOGETHER, AS A GROUP: « le lave-vaisselle », « le sèche-linge », « le micro-ondes ». Then a beat. Then the two that are not compounds: « la machine à laver », « la cuisinière ». The grouping IS the teaching, and reading all five as one list makes the rule invisible. EACH COMPOUND READ AS ONE WORD, not as two words with a hyphen between them. lave-vaisselle is one unit and the whole point is that the unit is what carries the gender; a reader who pauses at the hyphen is arguing with the lesson. « le sèche-linge » ENDS IN A NASAL, respelled luh sehsh-LAⁿZH, and it was one of the rows this build repaired. Keep it closed. Then « Le frigo est vide. »

The four published sentences act four is built on, read PLAINLY and at ordinary conversational pace: « Le lit est près de la fenêtre. », « La cuisine est à côté du salon. », « La salle de bain est au bout du couloir. », « Il y a une table dans le salon. » DO NOT STRESS THE SMALL WORDS. près de, à côté du, au bout du and dans belong to the previous unit and are deliberately not taught here, so a reader who leans on them turns act four into a preposition lesson, which is exactly what this lesson is forbidden from being. The NOUNS carry the weight in every one of these.
clipIds: Le lit est près de la fenêtre.
La cuisine est à côté du salon.
La salle de bain est au bout du couloir.
Il y a une table dans le salon.

recorded.desc: The five written traps, wrong version then right version, with a clear beat between them. Read EVERY wrong version PLAINLY and at ordinary pace rather than comically, because a learner saying them does not hesitate either. « Où est la salle de bain ? » is a perfectly ordinary French sentence and sounds like one, which is the entire point: nothing about it signals an error, which is why it survives and why it costs. « la toilette » in the singular should be read with no special emphasis on the missing s, because the learner cannot hear it and pretending otherwise teaches a signal that is not there.

The opening scene, French bubbles only. Claire is hosting a dinner, in her thirties, warm and slightly busy. HER OFFER OF A TOWEL MUST BE COMPLETELY UNREMARKABLE AND GENUINELY HELPFUL. She has not noticed an error and she is not making a point: she heard a request for the room with the bath in it and answered it, and offering a towel is simply what you do for somebody who wants to wash. Any hint of amusement or correction in her voice turns the scene into a telling-off and loses the whole point, which is that nothing visibly went wrong. Marc's single line at the end is a different speaker and should be flatter and quicker: it is the version where nothing happens, and it should sound like nothing happening.
clipIds: Bien sûr, au fond du couloir. Prends une serviette si tu veux.
Juste à côté, la porte à droite.

lessons.title: Le corps
lessons.intro: You already know the words for the body. What stops the sentence working is the shape around them, and it is one shape that covers both saying what hurts and describing how someone looks.

sections.title: The Word Was Not The Problem

say.text: You will know every word in this scene. Watch it go wrong anyway.

setting.place: A pharmacy on a corner, late afternoon, one person ahead of you

beats.text: Your back has been bad for three days. There is a pharmacy on the corner and you have looked up the word.
You know it. Le dos. You have said it out loud twice on the way there.

beats.prompt: You want to say that your back hurts. Which one do you say?

options.en: the one built the way English builds it
the one that puts you in the verb

followUp.works: Yes. Watch what the other one does, because it is the one almost everybody reaches for.
followUp.breaks: Every word in it is correct. Watch what happens anyway.

beats.speaker: You
beats.stage: He understands you. That is not the problem.

beats.speaker: Le pharmacien
beats.fr: Ah. Your back. One moment, please.
beats.en: Ah. Your back. One moment, please.
beats.stage: He switches to English, slowly, and reaches for something behind the counter.

beats.heading: You had the word. You did not have the frame.
beats.body: Nothing you said was wrong as vocabulary. What marked you was the shape: English hangs the person on the noun and puts the hurting in the verb, and French does the exact opposite, every time, with no exceptions to learn.

wrong.en: My back makes pain, which is understood and is not what anybody says

right.en: I have pain at the back

beats.coach: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. That is the next twenty-five minutes.

beats.speaker: Le pharmacien
beats.fr: Depuis quand ? Je vais vous donner quelque chose pour ça.
beats.en: Since when? I am going to give you something for that.
beats.stage: He stays in French, and the conversation continues.

beats.text: One sentence changed shape and the whole exchange stayed in French. The word was never the problem.

closing.text: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. Both halves of this lesson are that one sentence.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the middle two are the same move twice.

goals.t: Name fourteen parts of the body
goals.s: Head to foot, each with the little word that belongs to it, because that word is what the rest of the lesson runs on.
One frame, four shapes, and you already own three of them from the prepositions lesson.
The same frame again, with the eyes and the hair, and the colours you already learned.

goals.t: Know where mon and ma stop
goals.s: You met them three lessons ago and this is the one place French takes them back off you.

sections.title: The Head, Six Words
sections.hint: Swipe through the six.
sections.say: Six words, and the little word in front of each one matters more than usual here.

cards.label: the la kind
cards.body: the head

cards.label: always plural
cards.body: the hair

cards.label: the le kind
cards.body: the nose

cards.label: the la kind
cards.body: the mouth

cards.label: the la kind
cards.body: the tooth

cards.label: the l' kind
cards.body: the ear

sections.title: Arms, Hands, Back
sections.hint: Five more.
sections.say: Five more, and one of them is the word from the pharmacy.

cards.label: the le kind
cards.body: the arm

cards.label: the la kind
cards.body: the hand

cards.label: the le kind
cards.body: the back

cards.label: the le kind
cards.body: the stomach

cards.label: the le kind
cards.body: the neck

sections.title: Down To The Floor
sections.hint: The last three.
sections.say: Three, and then you have the whole body.

cards.label: the la kind
cards.body: the leg

cards.label: the le kind
cards.body: the knee

cards.label: the le kind
cards.body: the foot

sections.title: Which Little Word?
sections.say: Sort them. The little word is the part you have to store, and it decides everything later.

check.q: Which of these is NOT the le kind?
check.why: la jambe. Nothing about a leg explains why it is the la kind, which is exactly why the little word has to be stored with the word rather than worked out.

sections.title: One Eye, Two Eyes
sections.hint: Two cards.
sections.say: These two look unrelated and they are the same word. You will almost always want the second.

cards.label: One of them
cards.body: The eye. You will hardly ever need this on its own, and it is here so the plural does not look like a different word entirely.

cards.label: The pair, and what you will actually say
cards.body: The eyes. Always plural, like les cheveux, and anything you say about them takes a plural ending too.

sections.title: The Sentence That Changed Shape
sections.hint: Three cards, and the first one is the whole lesson.
sections.say: One card with both languages on it, because the whole teaching is which slot the person sits in.

cards.label: The same idea, built two ways
cards.head: Where does the person go?
cards.body: English puts the person on the noun, in my, and the hurting in the verb. French puts the person in the verb, in j'ai, and leaves the head with its ordinary la. Same meaning, opposite build.

cards.label: So the frame is fixed
cards.head: avoir + mal + à + the body part
cards.body: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. Change the person and only the verb moves.

cards.label: And mal takes nothing
cards.head: Never un mal, never le mal
cards.body: Mal sits bare in this frame. Le mal exists and means something else entirely, so adding a little word in front of it changes the sentence into philosophy.

sections.title: The Four Shapes
sections.frSub: À la, au, aux, à l'
sections.say: You already have all four of these. Tap any row to hear it.

detail.title: The la kind changes nothing
detail.body: À la stays exactly as it is. This is the easy one and it is half the body.

detail.title: À plus le becomes au
detail.body: You met this in the prepositions lesson and it has not changed. À le is never written.

rows.say: J’ai mal aux dents depuis hier soir.

detail.title: À plus les becomes aux
detail.body: Same rule, plural. Teeth almost always hurt in the plural, so this is the shape you will want.
detail.say: J’ai mal aux dents depuis hier soir.

detail.title: À l' changes nothing either
detail.body: The one people expect to contract and it does not. À l' behaves like à la, not like au.

sections.title: Does It Change?
sections.say: Two buckets. Only two of the four little words ever change.

check.q: Your knee hurts. What do you say?
check.why: au genou. Le genou is the le kind, and à plus le is written au every single time. À le genou is not something you will ever see written down.

sections.title: Where Mon And Ma Stop
sections.say: You learned these three lessons ago and they were right. Here is the one place they are not.

errors.wrong: Mon dos fait mal.
errors.why: The person is already in j'ai, so putting it on the noun as well says it twice. This is the sentence from the pharmacy and it is the most common one there is.

errors.wrong: Ma tête fait mal.
errors.why: Same shape, same repair. The head keeps its ordinary la and you never reach for ma at all.

errors.wrong: Mes yeux sont bleus.
errors.why: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. Describing works exactly like hurting, which is why this lesson is one idea and not two.

sections.title: Au, À La, Or Aux?
sections.say: These three really are different sounds, unlike most of what this lesson asks of your ear.

lines.en: My back hurts.
My head hurts.

lines.fr: J’ai mal aux dents depuis hier soir.
lines.en: I have had a toothache since last night.

questions.q: In the first line, which shape did you hear?
questions.why: au, one syllable, because le dos is the le kind. This is one of the few things in this lesson your ear can genuinely settle.

questions.q: Which of the three lines had two syllables between mal and the body part?
questions.why: The second. À la is two, au and aux are one each, so the la kind is audibly longer.

sections.title: The Frame, In Real Sentences
sections.say: Five sentences from the corpus. The frame does not change in any of them.

examples.note: à la, first person.
au, third person. Only the verb moved.

examples.fr: Mon frère a mal au dos.
examples.note: The person can be a whole noun and the frame holds.

examples.fr: J’ai mal aux dents depuis hier soir.
examples.en: I have had a toothache since last night.
examples.note: aux, and you can add when.
à l', which does not contract.

sections.title: The Same Move Again
sections.hint: Three cards.
sections.say: If you have the hurting frame, you already have this one. It is the same sentence.

cards.label: The same idea, built two ways
cards.head: Where does the person go?
cards.body: English hangs the person on the noun and puts the colour in the verb. French puts the person in j'ai and leaves the eyes with les. You have seen this exact swap already.

cards.label: Any person, any feature
cards.head: avoir + les + the feature + the word for it
cards.body: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. Nothing here is new except the words on the end.

cards.label: And hair is plural
cards.head: les cheveux, always
cards.body: Hair is one thing in English and many in French, so the word after it takes a plural ending you will never hear.

sections.title: Colours On The Eyes And The Hair
sections.say: You did the colours already. Both of these words are plural, so every colour takes the s.

detail.title: The s you cannot hear
detail.body: Bleu becomes bleus because les yeux is plural. It sounds exactly the same, which is why this is a writing decision rather than a listening one.

detail.title: Same again
detail.body: Vert becomes verts. The t was already silent and the s changes nothing about the sound.

detail.title: And on the hair
detail.body: Blond becomes blonds for the same reason. Les cheveux is plural whether you think of hair as one thing or not.

sections.title: The Two That Refuse
sections.hint: Three cards, and this is the one people get wrong for years.
sections.say: You met this rule with clothes. Here is where it actually costs you something.

cards.label: Brown eyes, and the ending that must not be there
cards.head: marron never changes
cards.body: Les yeux is plural and marron takes nothing anyway, because marron is a chestnut being borrowed as a colour and the chestnut keeps its own shape.

cards.label: Two words, so neither half moves
cards.head: châtain clair never changes
cards.fr: Elle a les cheveux châtain clair.
cards.body: Once a colour is built from two words it has stopped being a plain colour, so the endings never reach it. Same idea, not a second rule.

cards.label: Why this is one idea and not three
cards.head: Borrowed things keep their shape
cards.fr: les yeux marron · les cheveux châtain clair
cards.body: A nut and a two word description. Neither is a plain colour word, so nothing attaches to either.

sections.title: Hair, And What Is On A Face
sections.hint: Four cards.
sections.say: Four words that finish the description, and two of them did not exist in this corpus until now.

cards.label: Newly written for this lesson
cards.body: Blond, fair. Takes a plural s after les cheveux, like any ordinary colour.

cards.label: Newly written for this lesson
cards.body: Curly. Also takes the plural s, and also silent.

cards.label: Already in the corpus
cards.body: The beard. Il a une barbe, with the un kind, because a beard is a thing you have rather than a feature everyone has.

cards.label: Already in the corpus
cards.body: The moustache. Same shape as the beard.

sections.title: Three Ways This Goes Wrong
sections.say: All three are things a careful learner does, which is what makes them stick.

errors.wrong: Il a les yeux marrons.
errors.why: The s looks like being careful and it is the single most noticeable written error in this lesson. Marron is a nut and nothing attaches to it.

errors.wrong: Elle a les cheveux long.
errors.why: Les cheveux is plural, so long takes the s. You cannot hear it, which is exactly why it has to be worked out rather than listened for.

errors.wrong: Ses yeux sont bleus.
errors.why: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. It is understood, and it is the phrasebook sentence rather than the one anybody says.

sections.title: Everything In One Place
sections.say: Every word from this lesson, grouped the way you met them.

sections.title: The Waiting Room
sections.say: One short passage. Every sentence in it uses the frame you have just learned.
sections.text: Il est neuf heures et la salle d'attente est pleine. Un homme attend près de la porte. Il a les cheveux blonds et il a les yeux marron. Il a mal au dos depuis trois jours. À côté de lui, une femme lit son téléphone. Elle a les cheveux longs et châtain clair, et elle porte des lunettes. Son fils a mal aux dents et il ne veut pas parler. Le médecin ouvre la porte et regarde sa liste. « Monsieur Barré ? » L'homme se lève lentement, parce que son dos ne va toujours pas bien.

glossary.note: The feminine of plein, agreeing with la salle.
From attendre. It does not mean to attend.
A1.25 owns this shape. Here it is context, not something you have to produce.

questions.q: What is wrong with the man by the door?
questions.a: His back hurts, and it has for three days.

questions.q: How is the woman described?
questions.a: Long light brown hair, and she wears glasses.

questions.q: Why will the boy not talk?
questions.a: He has toothache.

sections.title: Flip And Recall
sections.say: The fourteen parts, front to back.

sections.title: Write What You Hear
sections.say: Seven sentences. The silent endings are the whole point of this one.

sections.title: Say Where It Hurts
sections.say: Say each one out loud. The frame is what is being listened for, not your accent.

sections.title: Describing Someone At The Station
sections.setting: A friend is meeting your brother off a train and has never seen him.

turns.ai: Il ressemble à quoi, ton frère ?
turns.en: What does your brother look like?
turns.user: Il a les cheveux frisés et les yeux marron.
turns.userEn: He has curly hair and brown eyes.

alts.fr: Il a les yeux marron et les cheveux frisés.
alts.en: He has brown eyes and curly hair.

turns.ai: Et ses cheveux, ils sont longs ?
turns.en: And his hair, is it long?
turns.user: Non, il a les cheveux courts.
turns.userEn: No, he has short hair.

turns.ai: Il a une barbe ?
turns.en: Does he have a beard?
turns.user: Oui, il a une barbe.
turns.userEn: Yes, he has a beard.

alts.fr: Oui, une barbe et une moustache.
alts.en: Yes, a beard and a moustache.

turns.ai: Parfait. Et il va bien en ce moment ?
turns.en: Perfect. And is he well at the moment?
turns.user: Il a mal au dos depuis trois jours.
turns.userEn: His back has hurt for three days.

turns.ai: Ah, le pauvre. Il marche lentement alors ?
turns.en: Oh, poor thing. So he walks slowly?
turns.user: Oui, parce qu'il a mal au dos.
turns.userEn: Yes, because his back hurts.

turns.ai: Compris. Je le trouverai sans problème.
turns.en: Understood. I will find him without any trouble.
turns.user: Merci beaucoup.
turns.userEn: Thank you very much.

sections.title: Before The Exam
sections.say: Six cards. Again, hard or easy on each.

cards.back: My head hurts. The person is in the verb.
Her back hurts. À plus le is au.
My ear hurts. À l' does not contract.
I have blue eyes. Never mes yeux sont.
He has brown eyes. Marron takes nothing.

cards.front: Elle a les cheveux châtain clair.
cards.back: She has light brown hair. Neither half changes.
cards.say: Elle a les cheveux châtain clair.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One number matters here and it is the last one.
sections.body: You have the fourteen parts and both halves of the frame. What is left is the exam, and the only thing in it that is genuinely new is the pair of colours that refuse to change.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. A round you fail gives you its drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The parts
rounds.say: The words, quickly.

questions.q: Listen. Which part of the body is it?
questions.why: la jambe, the leg. It is one of the la kind, which is worth storing now because it decides whether you say à la or au later.

questions.q: Which of these is the word for the back?
questions.why: le dos, with a silent s. It is the word from the pharmacy scene and the one this lesson opened on.

questions.q: Write the French for the tooth, with its little word.
questions.why: la dent. It is the la kind, and in practice you will nearly always want it plural, as les dents.

questions.q: Which one of these is always plural in French?
questions.why: les cheveux. Hair is one thing in English and many in French, and les yeux behaves the same way.

rounds.label: Where it hurts
rounds.say: The body part decides the shape.

questions.q: Your back hurts. Complete: J'ai mal ___ dos.
questions.why: au. Le dos is the le kind, and à plus le is written au every time. À le dos is never written down.

questions.q: Your ear hurts. Write the whole sentence.
questions.why: à l'oreille, unchanged. This is the one people expect to contract, and it behaves like à la rather than like au.

questions.q: Fix this. « J'ai mal à les dents. »
questions.why: aux dents. À plus les is aux, the same contraction you already use for going places. À les is never written.

questions.q: Which of these body parts does NOT change the little word after à?
questions.why: la tête. À la is left alone, and so is à l'. Only le and les ever contract.

rounds.label: Where mon and ma stop
rounds.say: The half of this lesson that contradicts the last one.

questions.q: Fix this. « Mon dos fait mal. »
questions.why: Every word in the original is correct and the shape is English. The person belongs in the verb, and the back keeps its ordinary little word.

questions.q: Why is « Ma tête fait mal » not what people say?
opts: The person is already in the verb, so saying it twice marks the sentence
Because tête is feminine and ma is wrong for it
Because fait is the wrong verb for a head
Because the sentence is too short to be polite
questions.why: The person goes in the verb. Ma tête is perfectly good French in other sentences; it is this frame that will not take it.

questions.q: Which verb does this frame always use?
questions.why: avoir. J'ai mal, il a mal, elle a mal. Être is what English makes you expect and it is not used here at all.

questions.q: Your head hurts. Write the whole sentence.
questions.why: J'ai mal à la tête. The la kind, so nothing contracts, and the person never appears on the noun.

rounds.label: Describing someone
rounds.say: The same move, on a face.

questions.q: You want to say she has green eyes. What do you write?
questions.why: Elle a les yeux verts. The person is in a, and the eyes keep les. The first option is understood and is the phrasebook sentence rather than the one anybody says.

questions.q: He has blond hair. Write the whole sentence.
questions.why: Il a les cheveux blonds, with the s on blonds because les cheveux is plural. You will never hear that s.

questions.q: Fix this. « Mes yeux sont bleus. »
questions.why: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. Describing and hurting are the same sentence with different words on the end.

questions.q: Listen. What colour are the eyes?
questions.why: marron, brown. Nothing in the sound tells you whether an s was written, which is what makes the next round a writing problem rather than a listening one.

rounds.label: The s you cannot hear
rounds.say: Both of these words are plural, always.

questions.q: Les cheveux and the word long. Write the colour word as it should appear.
questions.why: longs, with an s, because les cheveux is plural. It sounds exactly like long and the only reason to write it is the noun in front.

questions.q: How many of these are spelled correctly? « les yeux bleus », « les cheveux blonds », « les yeux vert »
questions.why: Two. The third needs verts, because les yeux is plural like everything else here. Nothing about the sound would have told you.

questions.q: Why does the colour take an s after les yeux?
opts: Because eye colours are always plural in French
Because les yeux is plural, so the word describing it matches
Because the colour comes after the noun
Because you can hear the s in careful speech
questions.why: The noun is plural, so the word describing it matches. It is the rule you already met with colours, applied to a word that happens to always be plural.

questions.q: She has curly hair. Write the word for curly as it should appear.
questions.why: frisés. Same silent s as blonds and longs, for the same reason, on a word that did not exist in this corpus until this lesson.

rounds.label: The two that refuse
rounds.say: The last round, and you already know why.

questions.q: Fix this. « Il a les yeux marrons. »
questions.why: marron, with nothing added. The s is the most noticeable written error in this lesson and it looks exactly like being careful.

questions.q: Why does marron refuse the s when bleu takes it?
opts: Because marron is longer than bleu
Because marron is irregular and has to be memorised on its own
Because brown is not a real colour in French
Because marron is a nut being borrowed as a colour, and it keeps its own shape
questions.why: It is a chestnut being used as a colour. You met this with clothes already, and it is one idea rather than a list of exceptions.

questions.q: Say this out loud: he has brown eyes.
questions.why: Nothing in the sound tells anybody whether you wrote the s, which is exactly why that error survives. Saying it and writing it are two separate skills here.

questions.q: What do marron and châtain clair have in common?
opts: Both are shades of brown, so both are irregular
Neither is a plain colour word, so neither ever changes
Both are only used for hair
Both take an s only after les cheveux
questions.why: Neither is a plain colour word. A nut and a two word description, so the endings never reach either of them. One idea, not two things to memorise.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: One sentence, two jobs.
sections.body: You can name fourteen parts of the body, say which one hurts, and describe what somebody looks like. All three run on the same sentence. The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les.
points: J'ai mal au dos, and the person never appears on the noun
Au and aux contract, à la and à l' do not
Les yeux and les cheveux are plural, so the colour takes a silent s
Marron and châtain clair take nothing at all

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that the little word in front follows it, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, introduced in a1.04
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07
Adjective agreement, the silent plural -s, and the invariable colours marron and orange, introduced in a1.13
The possessive adjectives mon, ma, mes and their determiner slot, introduced in a1.17
The contraction of à with the definite article: à + le = au, à + les = aux, and that à la and à l' do not contract, introduced in a1.21
grammarIntroduced: The avoir mal à frame: an inalienable body part taking a definite article where English takes a possessive
The same frame for physical description: avoir + definite article + feature + adjective
That the possessive is excluded from both frames, which bounds the rule a1.17 introduced
Plural agreement on les yeux and les cheveux, both of which are plural-only nouns
Invariable colour adjectives applied to a person: marron and the compound châtain clair

overview.introFr: Vous connaissez déjà les mots du corps. Ce qui bloque la phrase, c'est la forme autour d'eux, et c'est une seule forme pour dire où vous avez mal et pour décrire quelqu'un.

acts.title: The Word Was Not The Problem
acts.milestone: You have seen the sentence this lesson exists to fix.

acts.title: Head To Toe
acts.milestone: Fourteen parts, each with the little word that belongs to it.

acts.title: Where It Hurts
acts.milestone: You can say which part of you hurts, in any of the four shapes.

acts.title: What They Look Like
acts.milestone: The same frame, on a face, including the two colours that refuse it.

acts.title: Say It About Someone
acts.milestone: You have produced the frame yourself, in writing and out loud.

acts.title: The Exam
acts.milestone: Done. Both halves of the body lesson are one sentence.

lessons.reframe: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les.

errorTriggers.description: Names the wrong body part, or the right one with the wrong little word.
Writes à le or à les instead of au or aux.
Uses mon, ma, mes or ses on the body part instead of the definite article.
Builds the frame with être or faire instead of avoir.
Leaves the colour singular after les yeux or les cheveux.
Adds an ending to marron or to châtain clair.

drills.title: The little word, again
drills.coach: Sort them once more. The little word is the part that decides everything downstream.

drills.title: One check
drills.q: Which one is the la kind?
drills.why: la main. There is nothing about a hand that explains it, which is why it is stored rather than worked out.

drills.title: Only two of the four move
drills.coach: À plus le is au and à plus les is aux. À la and à l' are left alone.

drills.title: One check
drills.q: Complete: J'ai mal ___ pied.
drills.why: au pied. Le pied is the le kind, so à le is written au.

drills.title: The person is in the verb
drills.coach: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. Read each one and find the sentence that put the person in the wrong place.

drills.title: One check
drills.q: Which one is what people actually say?
opts: Je suis mal à la tête.
drills.why: J'ai mal à la tête. The person is in j'ai and the head keeps la.

drills.title: Always avoir
drills.coach: Every sentence in this lesson is an avoir sentence. Être is what English makes you expect.

drills.title: One check
drills.q: She has blue eyes. Which verb do you need?
drills.why: avoir. Elle a les yeux bleus, not elle est.

drills.title: The s you cannot hear
drills.coach: Les yeux and les cheveux are plural, so whatever follows takes an s you will never hear.

drills.title: One check
drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: les cheveux longs. Both words are plural and neither plural is audible.

drills.title: The two that refuse
drills.coach: A nut and a two word description. Neither is a plain colour word, so nothing attaches to either.

drills.title: One check
drills.q: Brown eyes. Which one?
drills.why: les yeux marron, with nothing added, whatever the noun in front of it is doing.

sections.title: The frame
sections.body: The person goes in the verb. The body part takes le, la or les. avoir + mal + à + the body part, and the body part keeps whichever little word it always had. Change the person and only the verb moves: j'ai mal, tu as mal, il a mal, elle a mal, nous avons mal.

sections.title: The same frame
sections.body: avoir + les + the feature + the word for it. Les yeux and les cheveux are both plural, so anything after them takes an s you cannot hear. Never mes yeux sont, never ses cheveux sont.

sections.title: What changes and what does not
Words you will meet next door
sections.body: La fièvre and la douleur sit in this same theme and belong to the doctor lesson rather than this one. Grand, petit, jeune and vieux belong to the adjectives lessons. None of them is taught here and all of them are waiting.

theFrame.title: How French says something hurts
theFrame.body: French puts the person in the verb and leaves the body part with its ordinary little word. You say the equivalent of "I have pain at the head" rather than "my head hurts". Nothing about it is optional: this is simply how the sentence is built.

examples.note: The person is in j'ai. The head keeps la.
Same shape, different person, and le dos becomes au dos.

theFourShapes.term: à la, au, aux, à l'
theFourShapes.title: The four shapes of the little word
theFourShapes.body: You already have these from the prepositions lesson. À plus le becomes au and à plus les becomes aux, while à la and à l' are left alone. The body part decides which one you get, and you never choose it freely.

examples.note: le dos, so au dos.
les dents, so aux dents.
l'oreille, so à l'oreille, with no change at all.

notYours.title: Where the possessive stops
notYours.body: You learned mon, ma and mes recently and they are right almost everywhere. This is the place they stop. A body part inside these sentences takes le, la or les, because the person is already carried by the verb and saying it twice is what marks the sentence as foreign.

examples.note: Not « ma tête fait mal ». The person is in j'ai.
Not « mes yeux sont bleus ». The person is in j'ai.

describing.title: Describing someone, the French way
describing.body: The same move again. Where English says his eyes are blue, French says he has the blue eyes. The person is in the verb, and the eyes and the hair keep les.

examples.note: J'ai, then les yeux. Never « mes yeux sont ».
Elle a, then les cheveux.

bothPlural.title: Two words that are always plural
bothPlural.body: Hair is one thing in English and many in French, and so is the pair of eyes. Both take les, and any colour or shape word after them takes an s to match. You cannot hear that s, which is exactly what a1.13 warned you about.

examples.note: bleus, with an s you never pronounce.
longs, same silent s.

leftAlone.title: The colours that refuse the s
leftAlone.body: You met this in the colours lesson: a colour that started life as something else keeps its own shape. Marron is a chestnut. Châtain clair is two words. Neither ever takes an ending, and the eyes and the hair are where you will meet both.

examples.note: marron, with nothing added, after a plural les yeux.
Two words, and neither half changes.

recorded.desc: The frame, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE: "Mon dos fait mal." immediately followed by "J'ai mal au dos." The learner must hear these AS A CONTRAST. Recorded apart they become two performances and the learner compares delivery instead of grammar, which loses the whole scene.

The four shapes, ONE TAKE, in this order and adjacent: "à la tête", "au dos", "aux dents", "à l'oreille". This is the only genuinely audible distinction in the lesson and the whole listening mission rests on the four being separable by ear in a single voice.

The fourteen parts, each with its article, read at an even pace. NEVER record a part without its article: the article is what the rest of the lesson runs on and a bare noun teaches the wrong storage. "les yeux" is [lay ZYUH], WITH the liaison, which is the decision this lesson took against fr.a1.mots-essentiels.002 and must not be silently normalised back.
The describing frame: "J'ai les yeux bleus." and "Elle a les cheveux longs." Adjacent in one take so the shared shape is audible across two different people.

ADJACENT IN THE SAME TAKE, and this constraint cannot be recovered later: "les yeux bleus" then "les yeux marron". The teaching is that the second adds nothing where the first added an s, and the learner needs both side by side to trust that the sound is identical.

lessons.title: La routine quotidienne
lessons.intro: One little word decides whether you are describing your evenings or tonight, and two times of day refuse it completely. This is how to name the parts of a day, walk through one in order from waking up to dropping off, and say most of it about yourself.

sections.title: The Evening That Never Got Arranged

say.text: Every word correct, understood completely, and nothing gets booked. Watch the little word.

setting.place: A language exchange in a room above a café, chairs being stacked

beats.text: Three weeks into a language exchange in Nantes. You have been getting on well with Claire, and neither of you has suggested doing anything outside the class yet.
Today she does. You have understood every word of the conversation so far, which is new, and you are enjoying it.

beats.speaker: Claire
beats.stage: She is packing her bag. It is a real invitation and she is waiting for a real answer.

beats.prompt: You are free tonight, and you would like to say so. Which line comes out?

options.en: the words for evening you already know
a different little word, and one this lesson does not teach

followUp.works: Yes, and hold onto that for a moment, because the word that makes it work is not one this lesson is going to teach you. Watch the other one first.
followUp.breaks: Every word correct. She understands you completely. Watch what gets arranged.

beats.speaker: You
beats.en: (Understood. Every word real. Not the evening you meant)

beats.speaker: Claire
beats.fr: Ah, super. On trouvera un soir, alors !
beats.en: Ah, great. We will find an evening sometime, then!
beats.stage: She is pleased. She has just learned that you are generally free in the evenings, which is useful and is not a plan.

beats.heading: Nothing went wrong, and nothing got arranged
beats.body: She understood you and she was pleased. You told her something true about your life and she heard it as exactly that: a fact about your evenings in general, rather than an answer about tonight.

wrong.en: In the evenings, as a rule. Understood, and not an answer to when

right.en: The evening takes a little word. Midday takes none

beats.coach: The parts of the day take le. Midi and minuit take nothing. That little word is not decoration: it is the difference between your evenings and this evening.

beats.text: The word that would have fixed it belongs to a later lesson. What this half hour gives you is the half you can act on now: what the little word means when it is there, and the two times of day that refuse it.

closing.text: The parts of the day take le. Midi and minuit take nothing. That is the next half hour.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things, and the first one is smaller than it looks.

goals.t: Name the parts of a day
goals.s: With the little word that comes with them, because that word is carrying the meaning rather than decorating it.

goals.t: Know the two that refuse it
goals.s: Midi and minuit take nothing at all, and one of them is where most people put a le that does not exist.

goals.t: Walk through a day in order
goals.s: From getting up to going to bed, using verbs the app has already published and you have never been shown.

goals.t: Say what you do, about yourself
goals.s: Whole phrases in the first person, learned whole, with the small word at the front that half of them carry.

sections.title: A Day, In Order
sections.say: Six moves, start to finish. Nothing to learn yet. This is the shape the rest of the lesson fills in.
steps: se réveiller and then se lever. Waking up and getting out of bed are two different verbs in French and they happen in that order, which is worth knowing before either of them is a card.
se doucher, s'habiller, se brosser les dents. The washing part of a morning, and all three of them start with the same small word. That word is coming back in act three.
prendre le petit déjeuner, then aller au travail. Breakfast and then out of the door. This is the only step of the six with no small word in it at all.
travailler until midi, then déjeuner. Here is the first place the little word goes missing, and it is not an accident: midday is one of the two times of day that refuses it.
rentrer, préparer le dîner, dîner. Home, cooking, eating. le soir takes its little word back, and it will keep it for the rest of the day.
se reposer, se coucher, dormir. Resting, going to bed, sleeping. Three verbs and only two of them carry the small word, which is the thing to notice rather than to learn right now.

sections.title: Four Parts, Four Little Words
sections.hint: Four cards, and none of them is a word list.
sections.say: The four stretches of a day, each with the word that comes attached to it.

cards.label: what you already do
cards.head: You have been given this rule once already
cards.body: The days lesson taught that le lundi means every Monday and not this one. That is the same little word doing the same job here, on a different set of nouns. Nothing new is being asked of you except to notice how far it reaches.

cards.label: the four
cards.head: Morning, afternoon, evening, night
cards.fr: le matin · l'après-midi · le soir · la nuit
cards.sub: luh mah-TAⁿ · lah-preh-mee-DEE · luh SWAHR · lah NWEE
cards.body: Four stretches of time and four little words. The one in front of the afternoon has been shortened because the word behind it starts on a vowel, which is a repair you have watched the language make since the definite articles lesson.

cards.label: what it is doing
cards.head: It means the ones that keep happening
cards.fr: Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange.
cards.sub: In the morning, I drink an orange juice.
cards.body: This sentence is not about one particular morning. The little word in front is what makes it about mornings as a habit, and that sentence was written by nobody trying to teach you anything. It is just how the thing is said.

cards.label: and at the end of the sentence too
cards.head: The same word, wherever it sits
cards.sub: We have dinner together in the evening.
cards.body: The time can go at the front with a comma or at the end with nothing, and the little word travels with it either way. The parts of the day take le. Midi and minuit take nothing.

sections.title: The Ones That Take It, And The Ones That Do Not
sections.frSub: Avec ou sans le petit mot
sections.say: Two columns. The left-hand side takes a little word and the right-hand side takes nothing at all. Tap any cell to hear it.

detail.title: The morning, and midday
detail.body: le matin [luh mah-TAⁿ] is a stretch of hours. midi [mee-DEE] is a point on the clock. That is the whole reason one of them is marked as a habit and the other is not: a point does not repeat, it just arrives.

detail.title: The afternoon, and midnight
detail.body: l'après-midi [lah-preh-mee-DEE] has had its little word shortened in front of the vowel, which is the same repair as l'école and l'ami. minuit [mee-NWEE] refuses one entirely, exactly like midday.

detail.title: In the evenings, and at midday
detail.body: le soir on its own already means in the evenings. For lunch you say à midi, with no little word in it at all. These are not two ways of saying one thing. They are what each of these words does.

detail.title: At night, and at midnight
detail.body: la nuit [lah NWEE] takes the feminine little word, because the night is one of the two here that does. à minuit takes none, and that is the pattern of this whole table: the stretches take one and the points do not.

sections.title: What The Little Word Is Actually Saying
sections.hint: Three cards on a word you have already been taught once.
sections.say: It is not the. It is every.

cards.label: the rule you have
cards.head: Le lundi was every Monday
cards.fr: le matin · le soir · la nuit
cards.sub: the same little word, on a bigger set of nouns
cards.body: The days lesson made this exact point and then stopped at days. It does not stop at days. Every stretch of a day behaves the same way, which means you already had this rule and were only ever shown a seventh of it.

cards.label: the habit, in the wild
cards.head: A morning that keeps happening
cards.fr: Il boit un café noir chaque matin.
cards.sub: He drinks a black coffee every morning.
cards.body: Here the habit is said with a different word entirely and means the same thing. French has more than one way to mark something as regular, and they can sit in the same sentence without arguing.

cards.label: both at once
cards.head: When the little word feels too quiet
cards.fr: Je me lève à sept heures tous les jours.
cards.sub: I get up at seven every day.
cards.body: The little word says it and tous les jours says it again out loud. Both in one sentence, and it is ordinary French rather than a mistake. Reach for the second one when you want to be certain rather than subtle.

cards.label: it reaches further than the day
cards.head: The weekend takes one too
cards.body: le week-end is a stretch of time like the parts of a day, so it behaves like one. Nothing here taught you that, and you can work it out from the rule rather than recall it, which is what having a rule is for.

sections.title: The Two That Take Nothing
sections.hint: Three cards, and the middle one is a number.
sections.say: Two words in the middle of the set refuse the little word completely.

cards.label: the two
cards.head: Midi and minuit go bare
cards.body: No little word in front, and no little word waiting to be added. These are the names of two exact moments rather than stretches of time, and a moment does not need marking as one that repeats.

cards.label: how sure we are
cards.head: Le midi appears 0 times
cards.body: Across the 27,353 French sentences published in this app, à midi turns up fifty-one times and le midi turns up not once. That is not a preference somebody has about style. It is a shape the language does not make.

cards.label: in a sentence
cards.head: Lunch, at the hour with no little word
cards.fr: Je déjeune à midi avec mes collègues.
cards.sub: I have lunch at noon with my colleagues.
cards.body: Nothing in front of midi, and nothing missing either. The parts of the day take le. Midi and minuit take nothing.

sections.title: Which Ones Take It?
sections.say: Two groups of times and a question about each. Nothing here is about what you do.

groups.label: the ones that take a little word

check.q: All four of those carry a little word. What is that word telling you?
opts: That the speaker is being formal
That there is only one of them
That this happens regularly rather than once
check.why: That it happens regularly. The days lesson taught you this with le lundi and it works the same way here: le matin is mornings as a rule, not one particular morning. The little word is carrying the meaning rather than pointing at anything.

check.q: Why do midi and minuit refuse the little word when the other four take it?
opts: They name a single moment rather than a stretch of time
They are both about the middle of something
check.why: They name a moment. Le matin covers four or five hours and can sensibly be marked as something that repeats. Midday is a point on the clock: it arrives, and there is nothing to mark.

check.q: You have already said le matin. What does adding tous les jours change?
opts: It makes the sentence past tense
It is required whenever the little word appears
It says the same thing again, louder
check.why: Nothing changes about the meaning. tous les jours states the habit out loud instead of leaving it to the little word, and French is happy to do both in one sentence. Use it when the little word alone feels too quiet.

check.q: Somebody asks what time you eat lunch. Which of these is not a thing anybody says?
check.why: le midi. It appears zero times in 27,353 published sentences, which is as close to a flat no as a corpus gets. The parts of the day take le. Midi and minuit take nothing.

sections.title: The Day, Banked
sections.say: Ten words, in two groups, and the groups are the rule.

themes.title: stretches of time, which take one
points on the clock, which take none

sections.title: The Morning, In Order
sections.hint: Four cards, and the order is part of the content.
sections.say: Waking, getting up, washing, out of the door.

cards.label: two verbs, not one
cards.head: Waking up and getting up are separate
cards.body: English blurs these and French does not. One is your eyes opening and the other is your feet hitting the floor, and there can be a long time between them. Both carry the same small word at the front.

cards.label: the washing three
cards.head: All three take the same small word
cards.fr: se doucher · s'habiller · se brosser les dents
cards.body: The small word has been shortened in front of the vowel on the middle one, which by now should be the least surprising thing here. The last of the three ends on a nasal vowel with no consonant behind it, despite four letters trying.

cards.label: breakfast and out
cards.head: The one step with no small word in it
cards.fr: prendre le petit déjeuner · aller au travail
cards.body: Neither of these carries the small word, and that is worth seeing early so the small word does not start to look like something every verb has. Roughly half of a French day carries it and the other half does not.

cards.label: the object it starts with
cards.head: What wakes you up
cards.body: An alarm and a shower, both carrying the little word that tells you which kind of noun they are. Il se lève tout de suite après le réveil. puts the first of them in an ordinary sentence.

sections.title: The Small Word At The Front
sections.hint: Three cards on a word that is not optional.
sections.say: About half the verbs in a day carry it. Learn it as part of the verb.

cards.label: store it with the verb
cards.head: It is part of the word, not in front of it
cards.body: The noun gender lesson asked you to store the little word with the noun rather than beside it. This is that habit again, on verbs. If you store the verb without it you have stored half of one.

cards.label: about yourself
cards.head: When it is you, it changes shape
cards.fr: Je me lève à sept heures.
cards.sub: I get up at seven o'clock.
cards.body: Talking about yourself turns that small word into a different one. This is a whole phrase to learn whole rather than a rule to apply: three of them will carry you through a morning.

cards.label: twice in one line
cards.head: And it happens as often as the verbs do
cards.fr: Je me douche avant de m'habiller.
cards.body: Two verbs in this sentence and both of them carry it. What the small word does across every other person is a lesson of its own and it is a whole band from here. Nothing you need today depends on it.

sections.title: Three People, Three Small Words
sections.frSub: Je me, tu te, il se
sections.say: Three people, and these three are the ones the app has real sentences for. Tap a row to hear it.

cells: Je me réveille à sept heures tous les matins.
rows.say: je me réveille. Je me réveille à sept heures tous les matins.

detail.title: About yourself
detail.body: je me réveille [zhuh muh ray-VEY]. The small word has become me because the sentence is about you, and that is the one you will use most.
detail.say: Je me réveille à sept heures tous les matins.

cells: Tu te douches rapidement avant l'école.
rows.say: tu te douches. Tu te douches rapidement avant l'école.

detail.title: About the person you are talking to
detail.body: It becomes te. Tu te douches rapidement avant l'école. is the corpus's own sentence and it is the shape you will hear turned back on you when somebody asks about your morning.
detail.say: Tu te douches rapidement avant l'école.

cells: Il se lève tout de suite après le réveil.
rows.say: il se lève. Il se lève tout de suite après le réveil.

detail.title: About somebody else
detail.body: It stays as se. Compare il dort [eel DOR], which is the same person with a verb that carries no small word at all, so the two sit side by side.

cells: Nous nous levons tard le dimanche.
rows.say: nous prenons. Nous nous levons tard le dimanche.

detail.title: About a group you are in
detail.body: nous prenons [noo pruh-NOHⁿ] has no small word, because prendre is one of the verbs that never carries one. Nous nous levons tard le dimanche. shows a verb that does, in the same person, so the two can be compared without leaving the row.
detail.say: Nous nous levons tard le dimanche.

sections.title: The Middle And The End Of A Day
sections.hint: Four cards, and one of them is the word this lesson added.
sections.say: Working, eating, going home, going to bed.

cards.label: the middle
cards.head: Work, a break, and lunch
cards.body: Il arrive au bureau à huit heures. is where most of it starts. The middle of a day is the shortest part of this lesson on purpose: the interesting thing about it is midi refusing the little word, and act two handled that.

cards.label: the general word for it
cards.head: And the verb for eating anything at all
cards.body: The first is eating in general and the other two are the two meals with their own verbs. French gives lunch and dinner a verb each and then keeps a general one as well, which English does not do.

cards.label: home
cards.head: Back, cooking, eating
cards.body: Elle rentre à la maison vers dix-huit heures. puts the first of these in a sentence with a time on the end of it, which is the shape most of a day is described in.

cards.label: the end
cards.head: Resting, bed, sleep
cards.fr: se reposer · se coucher · s'endormir · dormir
cards.body: Three of those four carry the small word from act three and the last one does not. dormir is the word everybody expects to meet first and it arrives last, because it is the one thing in a day you do not decide to do.

cards.label: the last one, in a sentence
cards.head: Dropping off, and what happens just before it
cards.fr: Elle éteint la lumière avant de s'endormir.
cards.sub: She turns off the light before falling asleep.
cards.body: s'endormir is not a thing you do, it is a thing that happens to you, and this sentence puts it where it belongs: after the last decision of the day rather than instead of one.

sections.title: The Verbs, Banked
sections.say: Nineteen verbs in three groups, and the groups are the times of day.

themes.title: the morning, waking to out of the door

cards.sub: suh doo-SHAY · to take a shower
suh bro-SAY lay DAHⁿ · to brush one's teeth
PRAHⁿDR luh puh-tee day-zhuh-NAY · to have breakfast
ah-LAY oh trah-VAHY · to go to work

themes.title: the middle: work, a break, lunch

cards.sub: la POHZ day-zhuh-NAY · the lunch break

themes.title: the evening and the night, home to asleep

cards.sub: pray-pah-RAY luh dee-NAY · to make dinner
suh koo-SHAY · to go to bed

themes.title: three things a day is built around

sections.title: When Does It Happen?
sections.say: Three groups of verbs and one question about each. The groups are the day.

check.q: Two of those verbs are about being awake. Which comes first?
check.why: se réveiller first. Your eyes open, and at some later point your feet reach the floor. French keeps those as two separate verbs where English blurs them into one, and the gap between them is often the longest part of a morning.

check.q: You want to say you have lunch at midday. Which is right?
check.why: à midi, with nothing in front of midi at all. The first option is the one people reach for after learning le matin and le soir, and it appears zero times in the whole corpus.

check.q: Which of those four carries no small word at the front?
check.why: dîner. Eating dinner is something you do rather than something you do to yourself, and French marks that difference with the small word. Resting, going to bed and dropping off all carry one.

check.q: You are describing your day and you want to say the evening part is a habit. What carries that?
opts: Putting the time at the end of the sentence
The little word in front of le soir
check.why: The little word. The parts of the day take le. Midi and minuit take nothing. Putting the time at the front or the end changes nothing about the meaning, which is worth knowing separately, and saying the verb twice is not a thing.

sections.title: What Goes Wrong
sections.say: Four, one per screen, and the first one is the one this whole lesson exists for.

errors.wrong: Je déjeuner le midi.
errors.right: Je déjeune à midi avec mes collègues.
errors.why: This is the error the rule creates rather than one it fixes: you learn le matin, you generalise, and you reach the two words that refuse it. le midi appears zero times in 27,353 published sentences.

errors.wrong: Je lever à sept heures.
errors.right: Je me lève à sept heures.
errors.why: The small word at the front is not optional and it is not decoration. Dropping it leaves a verb that means doing the thing to something else, and a listener will wait for you to say what.

errors.wrong: Le soir, je suis libre.
errors.why: Both are correct French and they mean different things. The first says you are generally free in the evenings and the second says tonight. This lesson teaches the first; the word behind the second belongs to a later unit.

errors.wrong: le matin je bois un café.
errors.right: Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange.
errors.why: Nothing is wrong with the words. When the time goes at the front, French puts a comma after it. Leaving that comma out is the one thing in this lesson nobody could ever hear.

sections.title: Listen For The Little Word
sections.say: Five lines. The word you are listening for is unstressed and very short, which is exactly why it goes missing.

lines.fr: Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange.
lines.en: In the morning, I drink an orange juice.

lines.fr: Je déjeune à midi avec mes collègues.
lines.en: I have lunch at noon with my colleagues.
We have dinner together in the evening.

lines.fr: Il se couche tôt pendant la semaine.
lines.en: He goes to bed early during the week.

lines.fr: Elle rentre à la maison vers dix-huit heures.
lines.en: She comes home around six in the evening.

questions.q: In the first line, where does the time sit in the sentence?
opts: At the front, with a comma after it
questions.why: At the front, with a comma. French does this comfortably and the rest of the sentence does not change to accommodate it. You never have to do it yourself, and you do have to be able to hear it.

questions.q: In the second line, what comes immediately before midi?
questions.why: à and nothing else. There is no little word in there and there is no gap where one should be. That is what this word does.

questions.q: In the third line, is the speaker describing one evening or a habit?
opts: It cannot be told from the sentence
questions.why: A habit. The little word in front of the evening is the only thing in that sentence saying so, and it is one syllable long and completely unstressed.

questions.q: The fourth line has a word meaning early. Which is it?
questions.why: tôt is early and tard is late. They are short, they sound nothing alike, and they are the two most useful words in this lesson that are not times of day.

questions.q: In the last line, roughly when does she get home?
questions.why: Around six. The sentence uses the twenty-four hour clock, which is ordinary in French for anything scheduled, and the clock lesson already gave you the numbers for it.

sections.title: The Time Can Go Either End
sections.say: The same sentence twice. Only the position of the time changes, and nothing else moves.

cells: Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange.
Je bois un jus d'orange le matin.
rows.say: Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange.

detail.title: Both are ordinary French
detail.body: The little word travels with the time wherever the time goes, and no other word in the sentence changes. If you never front anything, every sentence you say is still correct.
detail.say: Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange.

detail.title: The comma is the only extra
detail.body: Fronting costs one comma in writing and nothing at all in speech. This is the single thing in the lesson that exists only on paper.

cells: À midi, je déjeune avec mes collègues.
Je déjeune à midi avec mes collègues.
rows.say: Je déjeune à midi avec mes collègues.

detail.title: And the bare one behaves the same
detail.body: Moving midi to the front does not give it a little word. Nothing about the position changes which of these two groups a time belongs to.
detail.say: Je déjeune à midi avec mes collègues.

sections.title: A Day, Written Down
sections.say: One passage. Tap any underlined word for what it is doing.
sections.text: Sophie works in a bookshop in Rennes and her days are more regular than she would like. « Je me réveille à sept heures tous les matins. » she says, and then admits that getting out of bed takes another twenty minutes. « Je me douche avant de m'habiller. » Breakfast is coffee standing up. « Il boit un café noir chaque matin. » is how her flatmate describes it, which Sophie says is unfair but accurate. She opens the shop at ten and « Je déjeune à midi avec mes collègues. » in the small park behind it when the weather allows. The afternoon is the long part. « Elle rentre à la maison vers dix-huit heures. » and the evening starts properly from there. « Nous dînons ensemble le soir. » with her flatmate most days, and afterwards there is usually a film that neither of them finishes. « Il se couche vers vingt-deux heures. » on a working night, which she is aware is early, and « Nous nous levons tard le dimanche. » at the weekend to make up for it. Asked whether she would change any of it, she says only the mornings. Asked whether she is free this evening, she says « Ce soir, oui », and the two words do a job that none of the rest of this passage can do.

questions.q: What time does Sophie wake up, and how long does it take her to actually get up?
questions.a: Seven, and about another twenty minutes.

questions.q: Where does she have lunch, and what is notable about how the time is said?
questions.a: In the park behind the shop, at midday, and midday takes no little word in front of it.

questions.q: What is different about the last two words of the passage compared with every other time in it?
questions.a: They mean this particular evening rather than evenings in general, and they use a different little word which this lesson does not teach.

glossary.note: A second way of saying the habit, doing the job the little word does elsewhere.
No little word, ever. A point on the clock rather than a stretch of the day.
With its little word, meaning evenings as a rule rather than one evening.
The small word at the front, in the shape it takes for somebody else.
Late. Its opposite is three letters long and sounds nothing like it.

sections.title: The Day, Both Ways
sections.say: Ten cards. The times first, then the verbs that matter most.

sections.title: Write What You Hear
sections.say: Three sentences. Every one of them hands you a tile you must not use.

sections.title: Say Your Day
sections.say: The times of day and six verbs, out loud. The little word is short and unstressed, and it still has to be there.

sections.title: When Are You Free?
sections.say: The conversation from mission one, and this time you have the words.
sections.setting: The same room above the café, three weeks later. Claire is packing her bag again.

turns.ai: Tu es libre quand, en général ?
turns.en: When are you generally free?
turns.user: le soir
turns.userEn: In the evenings.

alts.en: I am free in the evenings.

turns.ai: Et midi ? Tu déjeunes où ?
turns.en: And at midday? Where do you have lunch?
turns.user: Je déjeune à midi avec mes collègues.

turns.ai: Tu te couches tard, toi ?
turns.en: Do you go to bed late?

turns.userEn: I go to bed early during the week.
