sections.title: Where You Are
sections.say: One card, and then the exam.
sections.body: You have the shape of a day, the little word that marks a habit, and the two times that refuse it. What is left is proving that the second of those is a rule you hold rather than a card you remember.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The little word
rounds.say: What it is, and what it is doing there.

questions.q: You want to say that you read in the evenings, as a habit. Which words do you use for the evening part?
questions.why: le soir, with its little word and nothing else. The little word is what makes it evenings in general rather than one particular evening, and it is the same word the days lesson used on le lundi.

questions.q: Write the two words for the morning, with the little word in front.
questions.why: le matin. Written whole rather than as a bare article, because a two-letter answer typed on its own is a coin toss rather than a test.

questions.q: le week-end was never taught as a part of the day in this lesson. Does it take a little word?
opts: Only when it is at the front of a sentence
Yes, and it means weekends in general
questions.why: Yes. It is a stretch of time rather than a point on the clock, so it behaves like le matin and le soir rather than like midi. You could answer that without having been told, which is the point.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Matin, je bois un café. » What is missing?
accept: Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange.
Le matin, je bois un café.
le matin je bois un cafe
questions.answer: Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange.
questions.why: The little word in front of the morning. Without it the sentence has no way of saying this is a habit, and a bare part of the day at the front of a sentence is not a shape French makes.

rounds.label: Midday and midnight
rounds.say: The two words the rule does not reach.

questions.q: You have lunch at midday. Write the two words for at midday.
questions.why: à midi. Two words and no little word between them. If a le crept in, that is the rule from round one over-applying itself, which is exactly what it does.

questions.q: How many times does le midi appear in the 27,353 French sentences published in this app?
opts: About the same as à midi
questions.why: Zero. à midi appears fifty-one times. That gap is not a matter of taste, and it is the strongest single piece of evidence in this lesson.

questions.q: Which of these is a shape French does not make?
questions.why: le minuit. Midnight behaves exactly like midday: it is a point on the clock, so there is nothing to mark as habitual and no little word goes in front of it.

questions.q: Why do midi and minuit behave differently from the other four?
opts: They are the only two that are masculine
They name a moment rather than a stretch of time
They are always used with numbers
questions.why: They name a moment. le matin covers several hours and can sensibly be marked as something that repeats. Midday arrives, and there is nothing there to mark.

rounds.label: Saying it is a habit
rounds.say: The little word, and the loud version of it.

questions.q: What is the difference between le soir and Ce soir?
opts: The first is evenings in general and the second is this evening
The first is formal and the second is not
questions.why: The first is your evenings as a rule and the second is tonight. This lesson teaches the first. The word that makes the second work is a later unit's, and it is what the opening scene was about.

questions.q: Listen. Is this sentence about a habit or about one particular day?
questions.why: A habit. The only thing in that sentence saying so is the little word in front of the evening, which is one syllable long, completely unstressed, and the easiest thing in the sentence to miss.

questions.q: Write the three words that say a habit out loud, the ones meaning every day.
questions.why: tous les jours. It does not replace the little word and it does not compete with it. French will use both in one sentence, which is what Je me lève à sept heures tous les jours. does.

questions.q: Say that you get up at seven.
questions.target: Je me lève à sept heures.
accept: Je me lève à sept heures.
je me lève à sept heures
questions.answer: Je me lève à sept heures.
questions.why: The small word has become me because the sentence is about you, and the hour comes from the clock lesson unchanged. This is a whole phrase rather than a rule you are applying.

rounds.label: The small word at the front
rounds.say: About half the verbs in a day carry it.

questions.q: Which of these verbs does not carry the small word at the front?
questions.why: dîner. Eating dinner is something you do rather than something you do to yourself, and French marks that difference. Going to bed, showering and getting up all carry the small word.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Je lève à sept heures. » Fix it.
accept: Je me lève à sept heures.
je me lève à sept heures
Je me lève à sept heures
questions.answer: Je me lève à sept heures.
questions.why: The small word is missing. Without it the verb means lifting something else, and a listener will wait for you to say what you lifted.

questions.q: In Tu te douches rapidement avant l'école., what has the small word become?
questions.why: te, because the sentence is about the person being spoken to. Three persons, three shapes, and those three are the only ones this lesson shows you. What it does across every other person is a lesson of its own.

questions.q: Write the two words meaning you get up, about yourself, with no time on the end.
questions.why: The small word becomes me and sits between you and the verb. Learned whole rather than assembled, which is all an A1 learner needs from it.

rounds.label: The day in order
rounds.say: From getting up to going to bed.

questions.q: Which comes first in a French morning?
questions.why: se réveiller. Waking up and getting up are two different verbs in French and there is often a considerable gap between them. English tends to use one word for both.

questions.q: Which of these happens last?
questions.why: s'endormir, dropping off, which comes after resting, after getting home and after dinner. It is also the one thing in a day you do not decide to do.

questions.q: Say what you do in the evening, using the verb for having dinner.
questions.why: The little word on the evening is doing the habit, and the verb carries no small word at the front. Both halves of this lesson in one short sentence.

questions.q: Write the word meaning early.
questions.why: tôt is early and tard is late. Neither takes a little word, because neither is a time of day: they describe when something happened relative to what you expected.

rounds.label: All of it at once
rounds.say: Both halves in the same sentence, which is where it actually goes wrong.

questions.q: Which sentence is right?
opts: Je déjeune le midi et je dîne le soir.
Je déjeune à midi et je dîne le soir.
Je déjeune à midi et je dîne à le soir.
Je déjeune midi et je dîne le le soir.
questions.why: Midday takes à and nothing else; the evening takes its little word. The other three each get one half right and the other half wrong, which is exactly what happens when the rule is remembered as one thing instead of two.

questions.q: Listen. Which part of the day is this?
questions.say: Elle rentre à la maison vers dix-huit heures.
questions.why: The evening. The sentence gives the hour on the twenty-four hour clock rather than naming the part of the day, so the answer comes from the number and not from a word you were listening for.

questions.q: Somebody writes « Je me couche à minuit tous les jours le nuit. » One part of that is wrong. Fix the whole sentence.
accept: Je me couche à minuit tous les jours.
je me couche à minuit tous les jours
Je me couche à minuit tous les jours
questions.answer: Je me couche à minuit tous les jours.
questions.why: The last two words have to go. The hour is already given by à minuit and the habit by tous les jours, so la nuit on the end is a second time of day in a sentence that already had one.

questions.q: Write the verb meaning to eat, in general, rather than the one for lunch or the one for dinner.
questions.why: manger. French gives lunch and dinner a verb each and keeps a general one as well, which English does not do. It opens on a nasal vowel with no n sound behind it: [mahⁿ-ZHAY].

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can name the parts of a day with the little word that marks them as habits, handle the two times of day that refuse that word entirely, walk a day through in order from waking up to dropping off, and say a good deal of it about yourself with the small word at the front that about half the verbs carry. The habit underneath all of that is one you have now been asked for three times: French stores a small word with the thing it belongs to, because the small word is doing work the word itself cannot do. The article did it for nouns, and now it does it for times of day. What that small word at the front of a verb does across every other person is a whole lesson, and it is a band from here. Nothing in this one needed it.
points: The parts of the day take le. Midi and minuit take nothing. Four take it and two refuse it, and that is the lesson.
The little word means every one of them, not this one. It is the same word the days lesson used on le lundi.
Tous les jours says the same thing out loud when the little word feels too quiet, and both can sit in one sentence.
About half the verbs in a day carry a small word at the front. Store it with the verb, and use three whole phrases about yourself.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that the article in front of a noun is the choice that gender makes, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, and the elision of le and la in front of a vowel, introduced in a1.04
The habitual definite article on a day name, as in le lundi meaning every Monday, introduced in a1.08
Subject pronouns je, tu, il, elle and nous, introduced in a1.05
Clock times, including the twenty-four hour forms used for anything scheduled, introduced in a1.12
The present of être and avoir, introduced in a1.06 and a1.07
Elision as a repair for two vowels meeting, introduced in sons.07
grammarIntroduced: The habitual definite article extended from day names to the parts of the day
That midi and minuit take no article at all, and combine with à rather than with le
Reflexive verbs as whole lexical items in three attested persons only, with the paradigm reserved for a2.22
Fronting a time adjunct with a comma, as a reading skill rather than a production requirement
tous les jours as an explicit habitual marker alongside the article

errorTriggers.description: Says a part of the day bare, as English does: « Matin, je bois un café. » Understood, and it loses the only thing in the sentence that said this was a habit rather than one morning.
Has the rule and over-applies it: « Je déjeune le midi. » The error the lesson's own rule creates, and the phrase appears zero times in 27,353 published sentences.
Reads or says a part of the day with its little word and hears it as one particular one, or reaches for the little word to mean this evening. The scene is built on it.
Drops the small word at the front of the verb: « Je lève à sept heures. » Leaves a verb that means doing the thing to something else, and a listener waits to be told what.
Treats waking up and getting up as one verb, or reaches for dormir when the sentence needs se coucher. Costs nothing in comprehension and makes a described day sound assembled rather than lived.
Gets one half of the rule right and the other half wrong inside one sentence: « Je déjeune à midi et je dîne à le soir. » The error that survives everything except practising both halves together.

drills.title: Which ones take it?
drills.coach: Sort by whether the word names a stretch of time or a point on the clock. Four of these are stretches and two are points, and the two points are the ones that refuse the little word.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: What does the little word in front of a part of the day tell you?
opts: That there is one of them
That the speaker is being formal
drills.why: That it happens regularly. The same word the days lesson taught on le lundi, doing the same job on a bigger set of nouns.

drills.title: Midday and midnight
drills.coach: Two of these six take à and nothing else. The other four take a little word and no à at all. If you find yourself putting both in front of one word, that is the two halves of the rule colliding.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You have lunch at midday. Which is right?
drills.why: à midi. No little word in front of midday, ever, and the first option appears zero times in the whole published corpus.

drills.title: A habit, or one particular one?
pairs: in the evenings, as a rule
I get up at seven, every day
Je me lève à sept heures tous les jours.
he drinks a black coffee every morning
Il boit un café noir chaque matin.
we have dinner together in the evenings
drills.coach: Every one of these is about something that repeats, and in every one the thing carrying that meaning is either the little word or a phrase saying it out loud. Nothing here is about one particular day.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: le soir. Is that this evening, or evenings in general?
drills.why: Evenings in general. The word for this evening uses a different little word, and it belongs to a later lesson.

drills.title: The small word at the front
drills.coach: Every one of these carries the small word and it is part of the verb rather than something in front of it. When the sentence is about you, that word becomes me.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Somebody says « Je lève à sept heures. » What is missing?
opts: The small word before the verb
The little word before the hour
drills.why: The small word. Without it the verb means lifting something else, and the sentence is left waiting for an object.

drills.title: What happens when?
drills.coach: Three of these six belong to a morning and three to the end of a day. The one that catches people is dormir, which is not going to bed: it is what happens afterwards.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which comes first?
drills.why: se réveiller. Your eyes open first and your feet reach the floor later, and French keeps those as two separate verbs.

drills.title: Both halves, one sentence
pairs: I have dinner in the evenings
I get up early in the mornings
Je me lève tôt le matin
I go to bed at midnight
drills.coach: Each of these has one time that takes a little word or one that takes none, and half of them have a verb carrying the small word as well. Getting one half right and the other wrong in the same sentence is the most common thing that happens next.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which sentence is right?
opts: Je déjeune le midi et je dîne le soir.
Je déjeune à midi et je dîne le soir.
Je déjeune à midi et je dîne à le soir.
drills.why: Midday takes à and nothing else. The evening takes its little word and no à. The other two each get one half right.

the same, with the little word shortened before the vowel

sections.title: What the little word is doing
sections.body: It is not the. It is every. Le matin means mornings as a rule rather than one particular morning, which is exactly what le lundi meant in the days lesson and exactly as far as that lesson took it. It reaches every stretch of a day, and the weekend as well. When you want to be certain rather than subtle, tous les jours says the same thing out loud and the two can sit in one sentence without arguing. Midi and minuit are the two words in this set that refuse it: they name single moments rather than stretches of time, and a moment does not repeat, it just arrives. Across the published French in this app, à midi appears fifty-one times and le midi appears none. If you find yourself putting a little word in front of midday, that is this rule over-applying itself, which is a good sign that you have it.

sections.title: A day, in order
rows: se réveiller · se lever · se doucher · s'habiller · prendre le petit déjeuner
rentrer · préparer le dîner · dîner · se reposer

sections.title: The small word at the front of the verb
sections.body: About half the verbs in a French day carry a small word stuck to the front: se lever, se doucher, s'habiller, se coucher. It is not optional and it is not decoration. Store it as part of the verb, the way the noun gender lesson asked you to store the article as part of the noun. When you talk about yourself it becomes me: je me lève, je me douche, je me couche. Three whole phrases, learned whole, which is all you need to describe your own morning. What that word does across every other person is a lesson of its own and it is a band from here. The verbs that do not carry it are just as common: dormir, travailler, déjeuner, dîner, rentrer and manger all go bare, so the small word is a fact about particular verbs rather than a thing French does to verbs in general.

partsTakeLe.title: Le matin, and it means every morning
partsTakeLe.body: The morning, the afternoon, the evening and the night all carry a little word in front of them in French, and it is not there for emphasis. It is doing the job English does with a plural: le matin is mornings in general, the ones that keep happening, rather than one particular morning. You have already been given this exact rule once. The days lesson taught that le lundi means every Monday and not this one, and this is the same word doing the same work on a different set of nouns. Nothing new is being asked of you here except to notice that it reaches further than days.

examples.note: Le matin at the front of a sentence, meaning every morning, in a line nobody wrote to teach it.
And le soir doing the same job at the other end of the day.

midiTakesNothing.title: Midi and minuit go bare
midiTakesNothing.body: Two words in the middle of this set refuse the little word entirely. Midi and minuit take nothing at all: you say à midi, never le midi, and the corpus is unusually clear about it. Across 27,353 published French sentences in this app, à midi appears 51 times and le midi appears zero times. That is not a style preference, it is a shape the language does not make. The reason is that midi and minuit are already the names of exact moments rather than stretches of the day, and a moment does not need marking as habitual. Le matin covers four or five hours. Midi is a point.

examples.note: à midi, with nothing in front of midi, in the corpus's own sentence.
And the word as it is stored: bare, with no article attached to it.

seIsPartOfTheVerb.term: the se belongs to the verb
seIsPartOfTheVerb.title: Store se lever, never lever
seIsPartOfTheVerb.body: About half the verbs in a French day arrive with a small word stuck to the front of them: se lever, se doucher, s'habiller, se coucher. That word is not optional and it is not decoration, and the useful thing to do with it at this stage is to store it as part of the verb, exactly the way the noun gender lesson asked you to store the article as part of the noun. When you use one of these about yourself, the se becomes me: je me lève, je me douche, je me couche. Three whole phrases, learned whole. The full set of what that little word does to every person is a lesson of its own, and it is a band away.

examples.note: The se has become me because the sentence is about you.
The same change twice in one sentence, which is what the whole phrase buys you.

everyDayOutLoud.title: Tous les jours, when the article is not enough
everyDayOutLoud.body: The little word in front already says that something is habitual, and there are moments when you want to be certain rather than subtle. Tous les jours says it in three words and cannot be missed. It is not a replacement for the article and it does not compete with it: French will happily use both in one sentence, which is worth seeing once so it does not look like a mistake. Reach for it when the article alone feels too quiet, and let the article do the work the rest of the time.

examples.note: The habit stated twice in one line, and both halves are ordinary French.
The phrase on its own, as it is stored.

fronting.title: Le matin, and then everything else
fronting.body: French is comfortable putting the time at the front of a sentence with a comma after it, and it is worth recognising because it looks like a different sentence when it is not. Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange says exactly what je bois un jus d'orange le matin says. Nothing moves except the time phrase, and nothing else in the sentence changes to accommodate it. This is a thing to be able to read rather than a thing you have to do. If you never front anything, every sentence you say is still correct.

examples.note: The time at the front, with its comma, and the rest of the sentence untouched.
The same meaning with the time at the end instead, and chaque matin in place of the article.

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. « le matin » AND « à midi » ARE ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, read straight through with no gap and no reset. Then, in the SAME take, « le soir » and « à minuit ». The claim the whole lesson rests on is that these are two behaviours of one set of words, and two separate recordings are two performances: a reader who records the bare pair in its own session will lean on the à, and the learner will hear that lean as a difference in emphasis rather than as the absence of a word. THE LITTLE WORD MUST NOT BE STRESSED. le in « le matin » is unstressed, short and almost swallowed, and that is exactly why learners lose it. A reader who gives it weight to be helpful is teaching a sound the learner will never hear again and hiding the actual difficulty. KEEP THE NASAL CLOSED ON matin. It is /matɛ̃/ with a nasal vowel and NO n sound behind it: the app respells it mah-TAⁿ deliberately, and this build repaired that row from mah-TAN precisely because a reader following the old transcription would let an n out of it.
clipIds: Je déjeune à midi avec mes collègues.

recorded.desc: THE FOUR PARTS OF THE DAY, EACH READ WITH ITS LITTLE WORD ATTACHED AND NEVER WITHOUT IT. le matin, l'après-midi, le soir, la nuit. Read as ONE LIST in one take at an even pace, because the learner is being asked to store the little word as part of the phrase and a pause between the two teaches the opposite. NO PART OF THE DAY IS EVER RECORDED BARE in this lesson, and there is no clip anywhere of le, la or l' on its own. They are unstressed function words that only exist attached to something, and a clip of one alone is a sound the learner will never meet again. If a request for one arrives, the request is the mistake. Then the two published sentences in the same take: « Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange. » and « Il boit un café noir chaque matin. » The first FRONTS the time and must carry a real comma pause; the second does not and must not.
clipIds: Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange.
Il boit un café noir chaque matin.
Je me lève à sept heures tous les jours.

recorded.desc: THE SMALL WORD AT THE FRONT OF THE VERB, AND THE THREE PERSONS, ADJACENT IN ONE TAKE. « se lever » then « je me lève » then « tu te douches » then « il se lève », straight through. The whole point is that only the small word changes, so any difference in pace, pitch or weight between them teaches something that is not there. DO NOT RECORD A FOURTH AND FIFTH PERSON. « vous vous levez » and « ils se lèvent » are deliberately absent from this lesson: they have zero sentences behind them in the corpus and the full set belongs to a later unit. If a clip list arrives containing either, it has been padded and the padding should be removed rather than recorded. Then the three published sentences, same take: « Je me lève à sept heures. », « Je me douche avant de m'habiller. », « Il se lève tout de suite après le réveil. »
clipIds: Je me lève à sept heures.
Je me douche avant de m'habiller.
Il se lève tout de suite après le réveil.

recorded.desc: THE MORNING VERBS IN THE ORDER THEY HAPPEN, one take: se réveiller, se lever, se doucher, s'habiller, se brosser les dents, prendre le petit déjeuner, aller au travail. The order is content here rather than convenience, so read them as a sequence rather than as a list of unrelated words. TWO PRONUNCIATION DECISIONS THAT MUST NOT BE QUIETLY CHANGED. « les dents » is /dɑ̃/: one nasal vowel, and NONE of the n, the t or the s is sounded. « prendre » opens on a nasal that the app's shared transcription checker cannot see, and this build wrote it PRAHⁿDR on purpose; the corpus elsewhere carries PRAHNDR, which is wrong and passes the checker anyway. Also in this take: le réveil, la douche, le café, each whole and each with its little word.

THE MIDDAY AND EVENING VERBS, one take: travailler, déjeuner, manger, rentrer, préparer le dîner, dîner, se reposer, se coucher, s'endormir, dormir. « manger » IS /mɑ̃ʒe/ WITH A NASAL VOWEL AND NO n SOUND. This is the one row this lesson authored and it was written mahⁿ-ZHAY specifically because the same word is published elsewhere in the corpus as mahn-ZHAY, which lets an n out of it. Read the nasal, not the n. « s'endormir » was repaired by this build for the same reason and carries the same constraint. Then the published sentences: « Nous dînons ensemble le soir. », « Il se couche tôt pendant la semaine. », « Il se couche vers vingt-deux heures. », « Elle rentre à la maison vers dix-huit heures. »
clipIds: Il se couche tôt pendant la semaine.
Il se couche vers vingt-deux heures.
Elle rentre à la maison vers dix-huit heures.

recorded.desc: THE FIVE LISTENING LINES, READ AT ORDINARY CONVERSATIONAL PACE AND NOT SLOWED DOWN. The thing the learner is listening for is a single unstressed syllable, and slowing the line down gives that syllable a prominence it does not have in speech, which turns a hard exercise into a trivial one and teaches nothing. The 0.65 speed is available in the player if they need it. « Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange. » CARRIES A REAL COMMA PAUSE and the others do not. That contrast is the content of the fronting mission, so it has to survive into the recording. NEVER RECORD A TIME PHRASE IN ISOLATION for this section. The whole difficulty is that the little word disappears inside a sentence at speed, and a clip of the phrase alone removes the difficulty being tested.
clipIds: Le matin, je bois un jus d'orange.
Je déjeune à midi avec mes collègues.
Il se couche tôt pendant la semaine.
Elle rentre à la maison vers dix-huit heures.

recorded.desc: The opening scene, French bubbles only. Claire is a language-exchange partner in her twenties packing up at the end of a session, warm and unhurried. HER REPLY MUST SOUND GENUINELY PLEASED AND COMPLETELY UNSUSPICIOUS. She has not noticed an error, because there is no error: she has been told something true and useful and has responded to it. Any hint that she is humouring the learner turns the scene into a correction and loses the entire point, which is that nothing visibly went wrong and nothing got arranged either. « On trouvera un soir, alors ! » IS THE LINE THAT CARRIES THE COST and it must be read as warmly as it reads on the page. It is a friendly non-answer, and the learner should not hear it as one until the break card tells them.
clipIds: Ah, super. On trouvera un soir, alors !

lessons.title: La nourriture
lessons.intro: Sixty words you will use every day, each one stored with the little word it arrives with. Then the choice nobody teaches: what you like is all of it, and what you are eating is some of it, and the verb in front decides which one you need.

sections.title: The Dinner That Happened In English

say.text: Every word correct, one word wrong, and the evening switches language. Watch which word.

setting.place: A flat with something already in the oven

beats.text: Salomé has been invited to dinner at a colleague's flat. She has been learning French for four months and she has been looking forward to this all week.
Her host is cooking and wants to get it right, so he asks the ordinary question a host asks.
She knows this one. She finished the partitive lesson two days ago and she knows exactly which word goes in front of food you have not counted.

beats.stage: Every word is a real word.

beats.prompt: One word is wrong. Which sentence should it have been?

options.en: I like some chicken.
I like chicken.

followUp.works: Chicken as a whole idea rather than a portion of it. After aimer it is always le, la or les, and that is the whole lesson.
followUp.breaks: That is the sentence the evening turned on. Du is right for what you are eating and wrong for what you like, and the rule behind it was taught to you two lessons ago.

beats.heading: He understood her perfectly
beats.body: Nothing was misheard and nothing was corrected. He heard somebody still assembling sentences, switched to English to make it easier for her, and the evening she had been looking forward to happened in English.

wrong.en: I like some chicken.

beats.coach: She had a rule, the rule was correct, and it does not reach this far. That is the only thing between these two lines.

beats.text: Sixty food words is the easy half of this lesson. Choosing between those two little words is the half that decides which language the evening happens in.

closing.text: Aimer takes the whole thing. Manger takes a part of it. That is the next half hour, and sixty words to use it on.

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do
sections.say: Four things. The first is a word list and the other three are one decision.

goals.s: Each one stored with its article, because the article is the half you cannot work out later.
J'aime le pain. The whole category, and the ordinary little word in front of it.
Je mange du pain. Some of it, using the word the last lesson gave you.

goals.t: Keep them apart in a negative
goals.s: One of the two changes when you say no and the other does not, which is where this gets tested.

sections.title: Half A Word Is Not A Word
sections.hint: Four cards before any food list.
sections.say: Four cards before the shelves, because this habit is what the shelves are for.

cards.label: what you already do
cards.head: You have been asked for this twice already
cards.body: The noun gender lesson asked you to store the article rather than the noun. The countries lesson asked again. Food is where you will use it most often, because these are the words that come up every single day.

cards.label: nothing in the word tells you
cards.head: Two things from the same fridge
cards.body: Milk is the le kind and cream is the la kind. Same shelf, both white, both poured into coffee, and nothing about either predicts its article. This is not a rule with exceptions. There is no rule underneath it.

cards.label: the guess feels safe here
cards.head: You know what a tomato is
cards.body: Familiar objects are exactly where people stop storing the article, because the word feels like something they already own in English. La tomate and le citron. Knowing what the thing is has never once helped.

cards.label: why it matters this much
cards.head: One fact, and everything after it
cards.fr: J'aime le café. · Je bois du café.
cards.sub: I like coffee. · I drink coffee.
cards.body: The same noun twice, with two different words in front. Which one you need depends on the verb, and you can only choose at all if the noun arrived with its article. Aimer takes the whole thing. Manger takes a part of it.

sections.title: The Ones That Hide It
sections.say: Six words where the little word has shrunk to l' and taken the answer with it. Commit before you tap.

check.q: l'eau and l'huile are both the la kind. What on the card told you that?
check.why: Nothing did. Both start with a vowel, so the article shrank to l' before you ever saw it, and the sound gives you nothing either. These are stored or they are guessed.

check.q: Three of the six l' words are the le kind. Which of these is one of them?
opts: all three are the la kind
check.why: l'oignon is the le kind, and so are l'ail and l'œuf. L'eau and l'huile are the la kind. Six words, split three and three, and the card looks identical either way.

check.q: You meet a new food word beginning with a vowel. What do you write down?
opts: The word and what it means
The word and how to say it
The word and which kind it is
check.why: Which kind it is, because the card will never tell you again. For every other noun the article is sitting there in front of it. For these six it has vanished into an apostrophe.

sections.title: Which Kind?
sections.say: Three questions across the whole set. None of them is about what the food is.

groups.label: the ones that only come in plural

check.q: Which of these would a French speaker never say?
check.why: Une pâte is not a thing anybody orders, the way a spaghetti is not a thing in English. These words live in the plural and take les, or des when you are having some of them.

check.q: le lait, la crème, le beurre, la farine. What decides which is which?
opts: Whether it comes from an animal
Nothing you can see or hear
The last letter of the word
check.why: Nothing you can see or hear. Two of those four end in an e and one of them is the le kind. Four things from one shelf and the only way to get them right is to have stored them.

check.q: You have sixty food words now. What is the one thing worth checking about each of them?
opts: Whether you can hear the ending
Whether English has the same word
Which little word it arrived with
check.why: Which little word it arrived with. Everything the rest of this lesson asks you to do needs that one fact, and none of it can be worked out from the food.

sections.title: What You Like Is All Of It
sections.hint: The half nobody teaches.
sections.say: Five cards. This is the half of the lesson that the last lesson set you up to get wrong.

cards.label: the ordinary case
cards.head: Coffee, as an idea
cards.body: You are not talking about the cup in front of you. You are talking about coffee, everywhere, as a category, and French marks that with the same little word you learned for the bread on the table.

cards.label: and in the plural
cards.head: It works the same way for a plural food
cards.fr: Les enfants aiment les pâtes au fromage.
cards.sub: The children like pasta with cheese.
cards.body: Les pâtes, because pasta as a category is plural in French. The rule does not change when the food does.

cards.label: not just aimer
cards.head: Four verbs, one behaviour
cards.fr: Je préfère les légumes frais aux légumes surgelés.
cards.sub: I prefer fresh vegetables to frozen vegetables.
cards.body: Préférer does exactly what aimer does, and so do adorer and détester. This is a small family of verbs that all point at the whole category, and they all take the ordinary article.

cards.label: the trap, named
cards.head: The last lesson taught you the other word
cards.body: The partitive lesson spent its whole length teaching you that uncounted food takes du, and it was right. It does not reach aimer. This is the single most common thing to get wrong in this lesson and it is made by the lesson before it.

cards.label: the line to keep
cards.head: One sentence to carry out of here
cards.fr: J'aime le café. · Je bois du café.
cards.sub: I like coffee. · I drink coffee.
cards.body: Aimer takes the whole thing. Manger takes a part of it.

sections.say: Nine sentences nobody wrote to teach this. Tap any row to hear it.

sections.title: Whole Or Part?
sections.say: Two questions, and the second is the one that catches people.

items.fr: Les enfants aiment les pâtes au fromage.

check.q: You want to say you like fish, in general. Which one?

groups.label: and when you have just been taught otherwise

check.q: The partitive lesson said uncounted food takes du. Why is that not the answer here?
opts: Because liking is about the whole thing, not an amount
check.why: Because you are not talking about an amount at all. Du answers the question how much, and liking something has no how much in it. The partitive rule is correct and this is simply not a place it applies.

sections.title: What You Are Eating Is Some Of It
sections.hint: Nothing new to learn here.
sections.say: Four cards, and you already know all of this. The only new thing is that it is now a choice.

cards.label: the word you already have
cards.head: Some bread, not bread as an idea
cards.body: This is the partitive lesson, unchanged. You are having an amount of bread, so the word in front says an amount of. Nothing here is new and nothing here has been revised.

cards.label: all three shapes
cards.head: du, de la, des, chosen the way they always were
cards.fr: Je bois du café. · Ils mangent des légumes verts chaque soir.
cards.sub: I drink coffee. · They eat green vegetables every evening.
cards.body: Which of the three you use is decided by the noun, exactly as before. What is new in this lesson is that you had to decide to be in this column at all.

cards.label: two in one sentence
cards.head: An ordinary meal has several of these
cards.fr: Nous mangeons du pain avec du beurre.
cards.body: Bread and butter, each with its own little word. Real sentences about food stack these up, which is why the choice has to be automatic rather than worked out.

cards.label: the verb decides
cards.head: The same noun, the other column
cards.fr: Je bois du café. · J'aime le café.
cards.sub: Two verbs. One noun. Two different words.
cards.body: Nothing about coffee changed between these two sentences. Aimer takes the whole thing. Manger takes a part of it.

sections.say: One of the two columns changes when you say no. The other does not, and that is the test.

items.fr: Je ne mange pas de pain.

check.q: One of those two kept its little word and one changed it. Which changed?
check.why: The eating one. Du collapses to de after a negative, which the partitive lesson taught. Le does not collapse at all, so « Je n'aime pas le café » keeps its le exactly as it was.

check.q: You do not like fish. Which is right?
check.why: Je n'aime pas le poisson. The collapse to de belongs to the amount words, and aimer never used one. Its little word is untouched by the negative.

sections.title: The Same Food, Twice
sections.frSub: J'aime le café · Je bois du café
sections.say: Left is what you like. Right is what you are having. Same food on every row.

rows.say: J'aime le café. Je bois du café.

detail.title: The same coffee, twice

detail.say: J'aime le café. Je bois du café.

rows.say: J'aime le pain. Je mange du pain.

detail.title: And the same bread

detail.say: J'aime le pain. Je mange du pain.

detail.title: And in the negative, only one moves
detail.body: The left keeps its le untouched. On the right du has collapsed to de. That asymmetry is the last thing this lesson tests.
detail.say: Je n'aime pas le café. Je ne mange pas de pain.

sections.title: Which Column Was That?
sections.say: Six words where the article has disappeared into the sound. Listen to all six, then answer.

lines.en: egg
orange
onion
garlic
water
oil

questions.q: Three of those six are the la kind. Which of these is one of them?
questions.why: l'huile is the la kind, along with l'eau and l'orange. The other three are the le kind, and not one of the six tells you which it is.

questions.q: What did the sound tell you about which kind each word was?
questions.why: Nothing at all. The elided article is the same sound either way, which is exactly why these six have to be stored rather than worked out.

sections.title: A Note On The Fridge
sections.say: Four lines off a note, and both columns are in it.
sections.text: Somebody has left a note on the fridge for the person cooking tonight, and between four short lines it uses both halves of this lesson. « J'aime le café. » That is the first line, and it is about coffee in general rather than any particular cup. Underneath, a note about what is actually in the kitchen right now. « Nous mangeons du pain avec du beurre. » Two foods, two small words, and both of them are amounts rather than categories. The third line is the one worth reading twice, because it is a negative and only one of its two halves behaves the way you would expect. « Je ne mange pas de pain. » And the last line answers a question the cook had asked earlier about what to buy. « Est-ce que tu préfères le thé ou le café ? »

glossary.note: Coffee as a whole category, so the ordinary little word. This is the half the scene got wrong.
An amount of bread rather than bread as an idea, which is the partitive lesson unchanged.
The amount word collapses to de after a negative. Aimer never had one, so it has nothing to collapse.
Both categories, both with the ordinary word, inside a question.

questions.q: The first line says le and the second says du. What decided between them?
questions.a: The verb in front. Liking something points at the whole category and takes le, la or les. Eating or drinking something points at an amount and takes du, de la or des. Nothing about the coffee or the bread came into it.

questions.q: The third line is a negative. Why is it worth reading twice?
questions.a: Because the amount word collapses to de after a negative, so du pain becomes de pain. That is the partitive rule and it is correct. What it does not do is reach the other column: a negative sentence about liking something keeps its le untouched.

questions.q: The last line is a question rather than a statement. Does that change anything?
questions.a: No. It is still about tea and coffee as categories, so it still takes the ordinary little word. The choice is made by the verb, not by whether the sentence is a question, a statement or a negative.

sections.title: The Four Ways This Goes Wrong
sections.say: Four, and the first one is made by the lesson you did before this one.

errors.wrong: J'aime du pain.
errors.why: The commonest error in this lesson by a distance, and it comes from applying the partitive rule correctly in a place it does not reach. Liking has no amount in it.

errors.wrong: Je mange le pain.
errors.why: This is a real sentence and it means something else: the bread, a specific one you have both already talked about. If you mean some bread, it is du.

errors.wrong: Je n'aime pas de café.
errors.why: The collapse to de belongs to the amount words. Aimer never had one, so there is nothing there to collapse and the le stays exactly where it was.

errors.wrong: Je voudrais une pâte.
errors.why: Pâtes lives in the plural in French and has no everyday singular, the way a spaghetti is not a thing in English. Frites and céréales behave the same way.

sections.title: Flip and Recall
sections.say: English on the front. Every front asks for the article too, because a food word without one is half a card.

cards.back: Je ne mange pas de pain.
cards.say: Je ne mange pas de pain.

sections.title: Spell What You Hear
sections.say: Five lines. On every one of them the word you have to work out is two letters long.

sections.title: Say It Out Loud
sections.say: Ten lines, and not one of them is a small word on its own. These words only exist attached to something.

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck
sections.say: Rate each card as again, hard or easy. The ones you mark again come back.

cards.front: You like coffee, as a thing in the world.
cards.back: J'aime le café. The whole category, so le.

cards.front: You are drinking coffee right now.
cards.back: Je bois du café. An amount of it, so du.
Je n'aime pas le café. The le is untouched by the negative.
Je ne mange pas de pain. Du collapses to de. This column does that and the other does not.
cards.say: Je ne mange pas de pain.

cards.back: l'eau [LOH] The la kind, and the card will never show you that.
l'oignon [loh-NYOHⁿ] The le kind, hidden the same way.

cards.front: Milk and cream, from the same shelf.
cards.back: le lait · la crème One of each kind, and nothing predicts which.
les pâtes [lay PAHT] Plural in French, with no singular anybody uses.

cards.front: Which verbs point at the whole category?
cards.back: aimer, adorer, détester, préférer. All four take le, la or les.
cards.say: Je préfère les légumes frais aux légumes surgelés.

cards.front: Which verbs point at an amount?
cards.back: manger, boire, prendre. All three take du, de la or des.

cards.front: What is the one line to carry out of this lesson?
cards.back: Aimer takes the whole thing. Manger takes a part of it.
cards.say: J'aime le café. Je bois du café.

sections.title: Where You Stand
sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have watched an evening move quietly into English over one small word, and nothing that was said in it was hard. Since then you have stored a set of everyday foods the way they are actually used, met the six whose article vanishes into an apostrophe, and learned to choose between two columns you already owned separately. What is left tells you whether the choice is automatic yet. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and missing too many in a round gets you that round's drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the penalty.

sections.title: The Exam
sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get that round's drill before the next one starts.

rounds.label: The article
rounds.say: The fact everything else needs.

questions.q: Which of these is the way to store a food word?
questions.why: le pain. The article is part of the word and it is the half you cannot recover later. Aimer takes the whole thing. Manger takes a part of it.

questions.q: Write the word for cheese, with its article.
questions.why: le fromage. Written whole rather than as a bare article, because a two-letter answer typed on its own is a coin toss rather than a test.

questions.q: le lait and la crème sit on the same shelf. What decides which article each takes?
opts: Nothing you can see or hear
questions.why: Nothing you can see or hear. There is no rule underneath this and no pattern to find. The two words are stored with their articles or they are guessed at.

questions.q: Write the word for grapes, with its article.
questions.why: le raisin. Grapes are singular in French for the fruit as a whole, and it is the le kind while la banane and la cerise beside it on the same shelf are not.

rounds.label: The ones that hide it
rounds.say: Six words, and the card tells you nothing.

questions.q: l'eau. Which kind is it?
questions.why: The la kind. You cannot see it and you cannot hear it, which is exactly why these six are worth learning as a short list rather than one at a time.

questions.q: l'oignon. Which kind is it?
questions.why: The le kind, and it looks identical to l'eau on the card. Three of the six are the le kind and three are the la kind.

questions.q: Listen. Which kind is this one?
questions.why: l'huile is the la kind. The sound gives you nothing at all here, which is the point of the whole group.

questions.q: Why do these six words need learning differently from the other fifty-four?
opts: Their article is not visible on the card
questions.why: The article has shrunk to an apostrophe, so the one fact you need is not on the card and is not in the sound either. Every other food word shows you its article every time you look at it.

rounds.label: What you like
rounds.say: The half the lesson before this one set you up to get wrong.

questions.q: You are telling somebody that you like bread, in general.
questions.why: J'aime le pain. Bread as a whole category, so the ordinary little word. The first option is the sentence the opening scene turned on.

questions.q: Correct this sentence: J'adore du chocolat.
questions.why: Adorer behaves exactly like aimer: it points at the whole category, so le. Du answers how much, and loving something has no how much in it.

questions.q: Which of these four verbs does NOT take le, la or les with a food?
questions.why: boire. It points at an amount you are drinking, so it takes du, de la or des. The other three all point at the whole category.

questions.q: Write: I like fish.
questions.why: J'aime le poisson. Fish as a category. Note that the spelling check ignores the apostrophe, so what is being tested here is the le.

questions.q: The last lesson taught you that uncounted food takes du. Why does that not apply after aimer?
opts: Because liking has no amount in it
Because aimer is an irregular verb
Because du is only for drinks
questions.why: Because there is no amount involved. Du answers the question how much, and liking something is not a quantity of it. The partitive rule is correct and this is simply not a place it reaches.

rounds.label: What you are having
rounds.say: The column you already owned, now that it is a choice.

questions.q: You are at a table and you are eating some bread.
questions.why: Je mange du pain. An amount of bread. The first option is a real sentence meaning the bread, a specific one you have both already mentioned.

questions.q: Write: I am drinking some water.
questions.why: Je bois de l'eau. Eau is the la kind and starts with a vowel, so de la shortens to de l'. That shortening is the partitive lesson's and has not changed.

questions.q: Correct this sentence: Je mange le fromage tous les jours.
accept: Je mange du fromage tous les jours.
je mange du fromage tous les jours
questions.answer: Je mange du fromage tous les jours.
questions.why: Du, because you are eating an amount of cheese rather than one specific cheese you have both been discussing. With le it is grammatical and means something else.

questions.q: Which sentence means you are having some chicken right now?
questions.why: Je mange du poulet. The first is about liking chicken in general, the second is about one specific chicken you have both already mentioned, and the third is not a sentence.

questions.q: Say it out loud: you are drinking some coffee.
questions.why: Je bois du café. Du is unstressed and runs straight into the noun. It is never a word you stop on.

rounds.label: Choosing between them
rounds.say: Both columns in one round, including the negative.

questions.q: Same food, two sentences. Which pair is right?
opts: J'aime du café. / Je bois le café.
J'aime le café. / Je bois du café.
J'aime le café. / Je bois le café.
J'aime du café. / Je bois du café.
questions.why: Liking points at the whole category and drinking points at an amount, so le on the left and du on the right. Nothing about the coffee changed between the two.

questions.q: You do not like cheese. Write it.
questions.why: The le survives the negative untouched. There is no amount word in the sentence, so there is nothing to collapse to de.

questions.q: Correct this sentence: Je ne mange pas du poisson.
accept: Je ne mange pas de poisson.
je ne mange pas de poisson
questions.answer: Je ne mange pas de poisson.
questions.why: Du collapses to de after a negative, which the partitive lesson taught. This is the column where that happens.

questions.q: Write: I do not eat cheese.
accept: Je ne mange pas de fromage.
je ne mange pas de fromage
questions.answer: Je ne mange pas de fromage.
questions.why: Je ne mange pas de fromage. Du collapses to de after the negative. Compare the sentence two questions ago, where the liking column kept its le untouched.

questions.q: Listen, and say which column this sentence is in.
questions.why: It is a liking sentence, and you can tell from the le surviving the negative. An eating sentence would have collapsed to de.

rounds.label: The sixty
rounds.say: The word list, and the three that behave differently.

questions.q: Which of these would a French speaker never say?
questions.why: Une pâte. Pâtes lives in the plural with no everyday singular, the way a spaghetti is not a thing in English. Frites and céréales are the same.

questions.q: Correct this: Je voudrais une frite.
questions.why: Frites is plural, and you are asking for an amount of them, so des. One chip is not what anybody is ordering.

questions.q: Write the word for water, with its article.
questions.why: l'eau. The article shrank to l', which is why this word has to be learned along with the fact that it is the la kind.

questions.q: Say it out loud: you like bread.
questions.why: The pattern is J'aime le, and the little word runs straight into the noun without a stop. Say the whole thing as one run rather than three words.

sections.title: What You Can Do Now
sections.say: Four things, and then what carries into the next unit.
sections.body: You can name sixty everyday foods with the article each one is stored with, say what you like and what you are having and keep the two apart, handle the six words whose article has vanished into an apostrophe, and get the negative right in both columns when only one of them changes. The thing worth keeping underneath all of it is that the choice is made by the verb rather than by the food. Nothing about bread decides whether it is le pain or du pain, and once that is automatic you stop translating the sentence and start saying it.
points: Aimer takes the whole thing. Manger takes a part of it. The verb decides, and the food never does.
aimer, adorer, détester and préférer take le, la or les. manger, boire and prendre take du, de la or des.
In a negative the amount word collapses to de, and the other column does not move at all.
Six food words hide their article in an apostrophe, and pâtes, frites and céréales have no singular.

grammarAssumed: Noun gender, and that the article in front of a noun is the choice that gender makes, introduced in a1.03
le, la, l' and les, and the elision of le and la in front of a vowel, introduced in a1.04
un, une and des, and the difference between first mention and second, introduced in a1.11
du, de la and des for an uncounted amount, and their collapse to de after a negative, introduced in a1.29
ne ... pas around the verb, introduced in a1.18
The full present of avoir, which j'ai faim and j'ai soif are built on, introduced in a1.07
est-ce que as the safe question frame, introduced in a1.19
grammarIntroduced: That aimer, adorer, détester and préférer take the definite article with a food, because they name a category rather than a quantity
That manger, boire and prendre take the partitive with a food, which is a1.29's rule applied rather than a new one
That the negative collapse to de reaches the partitive column and not the definite one
Sixty food nouns as a set, each stored with its article
That an elided l' conceals gender, and which six food nouns it conceals it on
Plural-only food nouns, and that they have no singular in ordinary use

overview.introFr: Soixante mots du quotidien, et un choix que le verbe fait à votre place.

acts.title: The article is part of the word
acts.milestone: You have watched an evening switch language over one small word.

acts.title: The shelves
acts.milestone: Sixty foods, each stored the way it is used, in seven groups you can see the end of.

acts.title: What you like
acts.milestone: The whole category, and the rule from the last lesson that does not reach it.

acts.title: What you are having
acts.milestone: The column you already owned, and the negative that only moves one of them.

acts.title: At the table
acts.milestone: Both columns on one screen, with the same food on every row.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: Lesson complete. Everything here carries straight into any conversation that happens near food.

lessons.reframe: Aimer takes the whole thing. Manger takes a part of it.

errorTriggers.description: Stored the food without its article, so the fact every later choice needs is simply not available. The error that happens weeks before any of the others, and the one familiar objects invite most.
Cannot recover the gender of l'eau, l'huile, l'oignon, l'ail, l'œuf or l'orange, because the article vanished into an apostrophe and the sound carries nothing either.

Says « j'aime du pain », applying a1.29's partitive rule to a verb it does not reach. THE CENTRAL ERROR OF THIS LESSON, and it is created by the lesson immediately upstream rather than by carelessness.
Over-corrects after learning the rule above and says « je mange le pain » when meaning some bread. Grammatical, and a different sentence: it names a specific loaf both speakers already know about.
Collapses the wrong column in a negative: « je n'aime pas de café » (there was no amount word to collapse) or « je ne mange pas du pain » (there was one and it did not collapse).
Invents a singular for pâtes, frites or céréales, or treats the les on them as a definite article and reaches for a singular partitive.

drills.title: Which little word came with it?
drills.coach: None of these can be worked out. Two things from the same fridge take different articles, and two red things from the same shelf do too. The article is a fact about the word rather than about the food.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You meet a new food word. What goes into your head with it?
drills.why: Its article, because every choice this lesson asks you to make needs it and none of them can be made without it.

drills.title: The article is hiding
drills.coach: Six words, three of each, and the card looks identical for all six. This is a short list and it is worth learning as a list, because you will not be able to reason your way to any of them.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: l'huile and l'ail. Which is the la kind?
drills.why: l'huile is the la kind and l'ail is the le kind. Nothing in the spelling or the sound separates them, which is why the six are learned together.

drills.title: Liking is about all of it
buckets: takes du, de la or des
drills.coach: Sort by the verb rather than by the food. Aimer, adorer, détester and préférer point at the whole category. Manger, boire and prendre point at an amount. Nothing about the food itself decides.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want to say you love cheese.
drills.why: J'adore le fromage. Cheese as a whole category. Du answers how much, and loving something has no how much in it.

drills.title: Eating is about some of it
drills.coach: The same test in the other direction. If you could put a quantity on it, you are in the amount column. If you are naming the thing as an idea, you are not.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are eating some chicken right now.
drills.why: Je mange du poulet. The first is grammatical and means the chicken, a specific one you have both already talked about.

drills.title: Which one moves?
drills.coach: Only the amount column collapses. The category column never had an amount word in it, so a negative has nothing to act on and the le, la or les stays exactly where it was.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You do not like coffee.
drills.why: Je n'aime pas le café. There is no amount word in the sentence, so the negative has nothing to collapse and the le is untouched.

drills.title: No singular anybody uses
drills.coach: Three of these live in the plural and have no everyday singular, the way a spaghetti is not a thing in English. The rest behave normally.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You want some chips.
drills.why: Je voudrais des frites. Plural, and an amount of them, so des. One chip is not what anybody is asking for.

sheets.title: Both columns, and all sixty words
contains: The six that hide their article

sections.title: The verb chooses, not the food
What each column is doing, and the negative
sections.body: The choice is made by the verb and never by the food. Aimer, adorer, détester and préférer all point at a thing as a category, so they take the ordinary little word: j'aime le pain, je déteste le poisson, je préfère les légumes. Manger, boire and prendre point at an amount of something, so they take the words the partitive lesson gave you: je mange du pain, je bois de l'eau, je prends de la soupe. The same food appears in both columns with a different word in front of it, and nothing about the food has changed. The negative is where this gets tested, because only one of the two columns moves. After a negative, du, de la and des all collapse to a bare de: je ne mange pas de pain. The other column has no amount word in it at all, so there is nothing for the negative to act on and it stays exactly as it was: je n'aime pas le pain, with the le untouched. Getting that asymmetry the wrong way round is the commonest mistake once the two columns themselves are secure.

sections.title: The six that hide which kind they are
sections.body: In front of a vowel the little word shrinks to l', and once it has shrunk the card cannot tell you which kind the word is and neither can the sound. There are six of them in this lesson and they split three and three. The la kind: l'eau, l'huile, l'orange. The le kind: l'oignon, l'ail, l'œuf. There is no pattern connecting the members of either group and there is nothing to work out, so these six are worth learning as a short list rather than one at a time as they turn up. The moment it matters is the moment something has to follow: de l'eau against du poisson, or an adjective that has to agree behind them.

articleIsPartOfIt.term: the article is part of the word
articleIsPartOfIt.title: Store le pain, never pain
articleIsPartOfIt.body: Food words in French are almost never said bare. It is le pain, la pomme, l'eau, and the little word in front is not decoration. You met this habit with noun gender and again with countries, and it arrives here on the words you will use most often. Nothing about a tomato tells you it is the la kind and nothing about bread tells you it is the le kind. The corpus stores every one of these sixty words with its article for exactly this reason, and the card you are shown is the whole word.

examples.note: le pain, stored the way it is used.
la pomme, and the article is the only difference between them.

theApostropheHides.term: l' hides which kind it is
theApostropheHides.title: l'eau and l'oignon look identical and are not
theApostropheHides.body: In front of a vowel the little word shrinks to l', and once it has shrunk you cannot see which kind the word is. L'eau is the la kind. L'oignon is the le kind. L'huile is the la kind and l'ail is the le kind, and nothing on the card or in the sound tells you which is which. These are the words you will still be getting wrong in a month, so they are worth learning as a small list rather than meeting one at a time. When you learn one, learn what it turns into when something follows it.

examples.note: l'eau is the la kind, and you cannot hear it.
l'oignon is the le kind, and you cannot hear that either.

wholeThing.title: What you like is all of it, always
wholeThing.body: When you say you like something, you are not talking about the piece in front of you. You are talking about bread, everywhere, as an idea. French marks that with the ordinary little word: j'aime le pain, j'adore le fromage, je déteste le poisson. This catches almost everybody, because the lesson just before this one spent its whole length teaching you that uncounted food takes du, and that rule is right and does not reach this far. After aimer, adorer, détester and préférer, it is le, la or les, every time, with no exceptions to remember.

examples.note: Coffee as a whole idea, not a cup of it.
And it survives a negative: still le, not de.

aPartOfIt.title: What you are eating is some of it
aPartOfIt.body: Eating and drinking are different. You are not consuming bread as an idea, you are having some, so the word in front changes to the one you already know: je mange du pain, je bois de l'eau, je prends de la soupe. This is not a new rule and there is nothing to learn here that you have not already been taught. The only new thing is that it is a CHOICE, and that the verb in front is what makes it. Same noun, different verb, different little word.

examples.note: The same coffee, now a quantity of it.
And in a negative it collapses to de, which aimer never does.

noSingular.term: words that only come in plural
noSingular.title: les pâtes, les frites, les céréales
noSingular.body: A few foods are plural in French and have no everyday singular. You would not order une pâte or une frite any more than you would ask for a spaghetti in English. They take les, they take des when you are having some, and the words behind them agree. There are only a handful and you have met most of them already, so this is a thing to recognise rather than a thing to study.

examples.note: les pâtes, plural in French and singular in English.
les frites, the same shape.

recorded.desc: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT NOTE IN THIS LESSON. « J'aime le café. » AND « Je bois du café. » ARE ONE TAKE, one voice, one pace, read straight through with no gap and no reset. Then, in the SAME take, « Je n'aime pas le café. » and « Je ne mange pas de pain. » The claim the whole lesson rests on is that these are one decision made two ways, and two separate recordings are two performances: a reader who records the liking column in its own session will lean on the le, and the learner will hear that lean as a difference in emphasis rather than as a difference in meaning. NEITHER LITTLE WORD IS STRESSED. Both le and du are unstressed and run straight into the noun. A reader who separates them is teaching the learner to stop on the word this lesson needs them to say without thinking.
clipIds: Je ne mange pas de pain.

recorded.desc: THE SIX ELIDED WORDS IN ONE TAKE, ADJACENT, ONE VOICE: l'eau, l'huile, l'orange, l'oignon, l'ail, l'œuf. The teaching point is that the elided article sounds IDENTICAL regardless of which kind the word is, and that only holds if one voice says all six in one pass. Recorded apart, the learner compares six performances and may hear a difference that is not in the language.

EVERY NASAL CLOSED, NO N SOUND BEHIND IT. le pain is /pɛ̃/ and the app respells it luh PAⁿ deliberately; a reader who lets an n out of it is teaching the error the transcription repairs. The same applies to le croissant, le jambon (TWO nasals), le poisson, le citron, le raisin, le melon, l'oignon, le champignon (TWO), le vin, la confiture, la viande, l'orange and un sandwich. AND THE OPPOSITE, WHICH MATTERS AS MUCH: la crème, la banane, la farine and la pomme have REAL m and n sounds and must NOT be nasalised. Their transcriptions carry no superscript on purpose.

The sixty food cards, read one per clip, at an even pace with no list intonation. A reader who performs these as a shopping list will drop the pitch on every word after the first, and each card is heard on its own rather than in sequence. le bœuf is ONE syllable in the noun, /bœf/, and must not be stretched into two.

lessons.title: Bilan A1 : leçon par leçon
lessons.intro: One round for each of the twenty-nine A1 lessons, five questions each. Nothing new is taught. A round that goes badly names the lesson to sit again, and drills it before the next round starts.
grammarAssumed: The whole A1 band, a1.01 to a1.29. Every question quotes a lesson that has already been taught and none of them is taught again here

overview.introFr: Vingt-neuf séries de cinq questions, une par leçon.

acts.title: What this is
acts.milestone: You know what the next hour asks of you.

acts.title: Twenty-nine rounds
acts.milestone: Every lesson in the band, asked about by name.

lessons.reframe: A wrong answer names the half hour to sit again.

errorTriggers.description: Opens with the wrong register, or answers a formula with the wrong formula.
Loses a number to its shape: the et, the s on quatre-vingts, the comma in a price.
Reaches for the wrong little word. Le for du, un after être, des where de was wanted.
Uses être where French uses avoir, or picks the wrong form for on, ils and vous.
Drops the article that makes a day or a part of the day habitual, or mixes two clocks.
Puts the weather in the wrong frame: il est for il fait, or a person where the sky goes.
Fails to agree an adjective, or agrees one that never moves.
Puts the describing word on the English side of the noun.
Agrees the possessive with the owner rather than with the thing owned.
Collapses an article that does not collapse, or leaves one that does.
Stacks two question methods, or drops the hyphen, the t or the elision.
Omits the de a multi-word preposition needs, or picks the wrong contraction.

drills.title: Which one, and when
drills.coach: Arriving and leaving take different words, and bonsoir and bonne soirée are the pair that get swapped. One is hello, the other is goodbye.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are leaving a dinner at eleven at night. Which?
drills.why: Bonne soirée. Bonsoir is for arriving and bonne nuit says you are going to bed.

drills.title: The shapes that trip
drills.coach: Two rules and both are about what follows. et on the six that end in one, and the s only when nothing comes after.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is 81?
drills.why: quatre-vingt-un. The s goes the moment anything follows, and 81 never takes et.

drills.title: One of them, some of it, all of it
pairs: coffee as a thing you like
pas le café, in J'aime pas le café
drills.coach: Three articles and they are not interchangeable. Ask what the verb points at: one of them, an amount, or the whole category.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which means: I eat bread
drills.why: du pain, an amount. le pain would be the whole loaf on the table.

drills.title: Has, not is
drills.coach: English is it, French has it, and the list of states is short enough to learn whole. The one exception is a job, which takes être and no article.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which means: I am thirty
drills.why: J'ai trente ans. French has its age, and ans is never dropped.

drills.title: Once, or every week
pairs: in the morning, as a habit
drills.coach: The little word is the whole meaning. le makes it a habit, en names a month, and a point on the clock takes nothing at all.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: You are free every Saturday. Which?
drills.why: le samedi. Without the le you have offered exactly one Saturday.

drills.title: Makes, has, is
drills.coach: Three frames and one adjective. The weather makes, a person has, a thing is. pleut and neige are already whole and take no il fait.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: It is cold outside. Which?
drills.why: Il fait froid. Il a froid is a person, and il est froid is an object.

drills.title: What moves, and what never does
drills.coach: Most adjectives agree and you can usually hear it. marron and orange never move, because both were things before they were colours.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is right for brown shoes?
drills.why: marron never agrees. Des marrons would be a bag of chestnuts.

drills.title: In front, or behind
drills.coach: Ten words go in front and everything else goes behind. When in doubt, put it after: the group behind is the whole rest of the language.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: A colour goes behind the noun. English puts it first and French does not.

drills.title: What is owned, not who owns it
drills.coach: The possessive agrees with the thing owned. Whether the owner is a man or a woman never enters into it, which is the opposite of English.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Her father. Which?
drills.why: son père. père is masculine, so son, whoever the owner is.

drills.title: What collapses, and what does not
drills.coach: Wrap the verb, then ask what the verb was. After avoir, un and du become de. After être, nothing moves, and le never moves at all.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Turn « J'ai une voiture » negative.
drills.why: After avoir, une collapses to de.

drills.title: Pick one method
pairs: a has no t of its own
drills.coach: Three methods and you use one at a time. Est-ce que is the one that is never wrong, spoken or written.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is wrong?
drills.why: The last one stacks two methods and asks the question twice.

drills.title: One word, or a phrase
drills.coach: A one-word preposition goes straight onto the noun. A phrase needs de first, and then de and à contract with le and les.

drills.title: One more time
drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: à côté DE. A multi-word preposition always needs its de.

say.text: You have done the band. This asks whether it stayed.

setting.place: A kitchen table, the phone propped against a cup
setting.time: Whenever you got to the end

beats.text: Twenty-nine lessons. The first one was bonjour and the last one was a kitchen. Somewhere in the middle a few of them quietly stopped being yours.
This is not a lesson. Nothing new is taught here and nothing is explained twice. It asks, lesson by lesson, which ones held.
